        "text":"Good point on the FFI compilation — if you're already doing mtime-based dynamic recompilation (which `c.sh` does), switching the target from a binary to a `.so` is just changing the compiler flags. The infrastructure is already there. That concern disappears.\n\n---\n\n**On Option 3 language support:** Pipes are about as universal as anything gets. The `pipe()` syscall is POSIX — Linux, macOS, every BSD, and most embedded Unix variants support it identically. Windows has `CreatePipe()` which is a different API but every language's standard library (Python `subprocess`, Go `exec.Cmd`, Rust `std::process`) abstracts over both and gives you the same interface regardless. Even bash itself is built around pipes — `read` and `echo` to fd 0/1 are native to it. So yes: every language that can spawn a child process can talk to it over a pipe, and every language that can be spawned can read from stdin and write to stdout. There's no language where this fails.\n\n**On parallelism with Option 3:** This is where the anonymous pipe model has a real structural problem. A pipe is a single ordered stream — one writer, one reader. If two workers try to use the same subprocess simultaneously, their messages interleave in the pipe buffer and the framing breaks. You can solve this in a few ways, but none are free: you could keep one persistent subprocess *per worker thread* (simple but wasteful — N threads means N bash processes sitting idle), or you could switch from anonymous pipes to a Unix domain socket (which supports multiple concurrent connections, so the subprocess becomes a small server accepting one connection per caller, each with its own channel). The socket approach is almost identical in code to the pipe approach but is naturally parallel. Another option is to simply not parallelize across language boundaries — run cross-language calls sequentially even if same-language calls are parallel. Depending on how many bash or C boxes a typical map has, that might be fine in practice.\n\n**On connecting to the threading model's shared memory:** This is the most interesting synthesis. The architecture doc mentions effil-jit or the 3d-rts thread pool as the eventual threading backend. Effil (and similar Lua thread pool libraries) already use shared memory internally — its channels are backed by a memory region that multiple Lua coroutines can access without copying. The natural extension: wire values in the compiled program *are* effil channels. A Lua box calls `channel:push(value)` and the next box calls `channel:pop()`. For cross-language boxes to participate in this, they'd need to speak the channel protocol — which means either C boxes use FFI to call directly into the effil data structure (very tight, possibly fragile), or the executor materializes the channel value into a named kernel shared memory segment just before handing off to a non-Lua box, and the non-Lua box reads from there. You'd use the effil channel as the primary wire for Lua-to-Lua, and the shared memory segment as the \"exit ramp\" for cross-language handoffs. It's a two-tier model: fast-path for same-language, slower-path for cross-language — which maps well to how you'd expect the performance profile to look anyway.\n\n**On cross-platform — Option 2 vs Option 3:**\n\nOption 3 (pipes) is more portable. `pipe()` + `fork()` + `exec()` is identical on Linux and macOS at the syscall level, and abstracted cleanly on Windows. Pipes work everywhere.\n\nOption 2 (shm_open) is messier. `shm_open()` itself is POSIX and works on both Linux and macOS, but the `/dev/shm/<name>` file path — which is how bash would access the segment as a regular file — is **Linux-only**. macOS has `shm_open()` but doesn't expose the objects as files in the filesystem at all, so the bash shortcut breaks entirely. On Windows, shared memory is `CreateFileMapping()` + `MapViewOfFile()` — a completely different API with no POSIX compatibility except through WSL or Cygwin. So if macOS support matters (or any future Windows support), Option 2 requires platform-specific fallbacks, whereas Option 3 just works.\n\nThe middle ground worth knowing about: **Unix domain sockets**. They're POSIX (Linux + macOS), supported on Windows since 2018, addressable by name like shared memory, support concurrent connections like a server unlike pipes, and are faster than TCP because there's no network stack. They're essentially the answer to \"I want Option 3 but parallel and named.\" Every language has socket support. If the executor ever needs parallel cross-language IPC, Unix domain sockets are probably the right primitive — and the compiler would generate a small per-language socket client as the shim, rather than reading from stdin."
      }]

## [870]

{
  "timestamp":"2026-05-08T21:36:20.525Z",
  "message":{
    "content":" Another option is to simply not parallelize across language boundaries — run cross-language calls sequentially even\n  if same-language calls are parallel. Depending on how many bash or C boxes a typical map has, that might be fine in practice.\n\nnot an option, sadly :(\n\nyou could keep one persistent subprocess per worker thread (simple but wasteful — N threads means N bash processes\n   sitting idle)\n\nthis might be fine? I mean, a thread is already a duplication of the runtime. Right? I think it's okay if we have several processes sitting in RAM doing nothing. RAM is cheap (well, not these days, there's a big spike due to AI expansion in datacenters and such. But we have lots of RAM so don't worry about it) RAM is cheap so we can afford to have a couple extra hundred MB or however much it turns out to be. A bash process isn't very much I think. Even if we use 10 languages, having 10 separate processes running for each thread is... probably fine? Is there a performance cost? Are they coroutined or parallelized?\n\nor you could switch from anonymous pipes to a Unix domain socket (which supports multiple concurrent connections, so the subprocess\n  becomes a small server accepting one connection per caller, each with its own channel). The socket approach is almost identical in code to the pipe\n  approach but is naturally parallel.\n\nthis is intriguing, we would have one of these servers for each connection between boxes, yeah? If you think about the threading model, it's very much attempting to parallelize coroutines. If we had each of these servers handling things like blocking while waiting for other variables and such, it might make it easier. What do you think? Can you reference explicitely the threading model and tell me how you'd integrate it?\n\n The architecture doc mentions effil-jit or the 3d-rts\n  thread pool as the eventual threading backend.\n\nwe should probably just strike effil from memory because we're not going to use it. it's going to be synchronous (or coroutined) until we get the 3d-rts model working.\n\nCan you tell me more about Unix domain sockets?",
    "role":"user"
  },

        "text":"Good. Now I have the full picture. Let me answer everything, then strip effil from the docs.\n\n---\n\n**On N processes per thread — cost and model:**\n\nAn idle bash process on Linux uses about 3–5 MB of RSS (resident set size). More importantly, an idle process costs *zero* CPU — it's blocked inside a `read()` syscall waiting for input on the pipe. The scheduler never touches it. So for 10 languages × 4 threads = 40 processes, you're looking at maybe 150–200 MB of RAM for the runtimes sitting idle. Given that this machine has tens of gigabytes, that's nothing. You're right: RAM is the right trade for simplicity here.\n\nThese are not coroutines — they are real OS processes, each with their own PID, scheduled by the kernel independently. That distinction matters for the next question, because it means they can actually run in parallel on separate cores if the calling side allows it. In the current synchronous executor, they don't run in parallel because Lua blocks waiting for each response before moving on. But the structure doesn't prevent parallelism — it just doesn't exploit it yet. The processes themselves are ready.\n\n---\n\n**On Unix domain socket integration with the threading model:**\n\nReading issue 104 and 213 directly: the executor is explicitly designed around a ready-queue where boxes are enqueued as their inputs are satisfied, and the comment says *\"in a threaded executor, the enqueue step becomes a pool_spawn call instead of a direct function call. The box output store becomes shared memory guarded by the pool's result-slot mechanism.\"* Issue 213 adds: *\"a worker thread pops one value from each input queue, runs the task, and pushes outputs to the connected ports' queues.\"*\n\nThe Unix domain socket model slots directly into this. Here's how it integrates:\n\nRight now, `run_task(box, inputs)` in `004-executor.lua` is the boundary — it does the driver invocation and returns a value. In the synchronous model, it blocks until the driver responds. In the threaded model, it becomes the thing a worker thread calls. The socket model changes what happens *inside* `run_task` for cross-language boxes: instead of shelling out to a driver script, it sends a framed request to the language server's socket and reads back the response. For a Lua worker thread in the 3d-rts pool, that's fine — the thread blocks on the socket read while other threads continue processing other boxes. The pool's natural concurrency handles it.\n\nFor the coroutine path (between now and 3d-rts): LuaSocket supports non-blocking sockets. The coroutine-based executor would do: connect to language server socket → send request → `coroutine.yield()` → event loop polls the socket fd → response arrives → resume coroutine. The coroutine suspends instead of blocking, the event loop can run other coroutines in the meantime. This is exactly the async I/O pattern that Node.js popularized, implemented with Lua coroutines. The main loop becomes a small scheduler: poll all pending socket fds, resume coroutines that have data. This is achievable before the 3d-rts pool is in place, and maps directly onto it afterward — the \"poll and resume\" logic is just replaced by \"worker thread unblocks and continues.\"\n\nThe socket *server* side has its own internal queue per language runtime. The bash server, for example, receives requests from multiple Lua workers, processes them one at a time (since bash is single-threaded within a process), and sends responses back. If you want the bash runtime itself to parallelize, you'd run multiple bash server instances — one per thread — which is exactly the \"N processes per thread\" model from before, just with sockets replacing anonymous pipes for the communication channel. The socket endpoint could be named `/tmp/soramech-bash-0.sock`, `/tmp/soramech-bash-1.sock` per worker, and the thread pool assigns workers to specific endpoints.\n\n---\n\n**On Unix domain sockets — the deeper explanation:**\n\nA Unix domain socket is a socket that lives at a filesystem path instead of a network address. `/tmp/soramech-bash.sock` is a real file on disk (a socket-type special file), and any process on the same machine can connect to it with the standard socket API using that path as the address. The kernel handles everything — no network stack, no loopback interface, no TCP/IP headers. The data goes directly from one process's memory into the kernel's socket buffer and into the other process's memory. Throughput is typically limited by memory bandwidth, not by any protocol overhead.\n\nThe programming model is identical to TCP. The server calls `bind()` with the path, `listen()`, and then `accept()` in a loop — each `accept()` returns a new socket fd for that specific client connection. Multiple clients can be connected simultaneously; each gets its own fd on the server side. The server can handle them with threads, with `select()`/`poll()`/`epoll()`, or by forking. For our language servers, the simplest model is a loop: `accept()` → read one request → process → write response → close connection → `accept()` again. This is sequential-per-connection, but since each connection is one box call, it naturally serializes what needs to be serialized (one bash function at a time) and the socket's accept queue buffers incoming requests while the current one is processing.\n\nWhat makes Unix domain sockets distinctly useful here over plain anonymous pipes: the socket has a *name* that multiple unrelated processes can find and connect to without any prior coordination. With anonymous pipes, the file descriptors have to be inherited through fork — the server and client must be in the same process tree. With a Unix domain socket, the language server can start independently (even before the Lua program starts), and the Lua program finds it by path. This means a language server could be a long-lived daemon that persists across multiple map runs, amortizing startup cost even further.\n\n---\n\nNow stripping effil from the docs:"

        "content":"30\t\n31\t## Phase 2 — Concurrent execution\n32\t\n33\tGoal: boxes whose inputs are all satisfied fire concurrently.\n34\t\n35\t- Integrate effil-jit as the threading backend (replacing synchronous\n36\t  depth-first walk)\n37\t- Runner becomes an M:N task scheduler: each box invocation is a task,\n38\t  boxes park when waiting on upstream results\n39\t- Multiple maps running concurrently share nothing (separate processes)\n40\t- Begin integration path toward the 3d-rts custom thread pool\n41\t\n42\t## Phase 3 — SoraMind integration\n43\t\n44\tGoal: boxes that call SoraMind inference endpoints on the Alpine cluster.\n45\t\n46\t- LLM call box type: sends a prompt, receives a completion string\n47\t- Prompt assembly: text values wired from upstream boxes, data file\n48\t  sections explicitly loaded into prompt context\n49\t- Branch box connected to an LLM classifier: \"rogue, wizard, or else\"",

    "structuredPatch":[{
        "newStart":152,
        "newLines":8,
        "lines":[" "," Each step is wrapped in a `task_fn` boundary so the runner can be"," threaded later by substituting the synchronous executor with one backed","-by effil-jit or the custom thread pool from the 3d-rts project.","+by the 3d-rts custom thread pool. The intermediate path is coroutine-based","+non-blocking I/O before the full thread pool is integrated."," "," ## Data files"," "],
        "oldStart":152,
        "oldLines":7
      }],
    "originalFile":"# SoraMech — Architecture\n\n## Three programs, one data format\n\nSoraMech is three independent programs that share a common on-disk format:\nthe map directory. None of the three knows about the others at runtime.\n\n```\n  Browser (index.html)\n       |  HTTP (file CRUD)\n       v\n  soramech-server.lua          [map directory]\n                               maps/<name>/\n                                 boxes/\n                                 data/\n                                 drivers.json\n                                 meta.json\n                                 tmp/ -> /tmp/<name>/\n       ^\n       | reads & writes\n  soramech-runner.lua\n```\n\n### soramech-server.lua\n\nThin HTTP proxy. Receives JSON requests from the browser and translates\nthem into file reads and writes on the map directory. No logic beyond\npath validation and basic consistency checks (e.g., reject a delete if\nthe box is still referenced by another box's connection list).\n\nStarted with: `luajit soramech-server.lua <maps-root> [port]`\nDefault port: 7700\n\nEndpoints (all operate on map files):\n  GET  /maps                        list maps\n  GET  /maps/<name>/boxes           list box IDs\n  GET  /maps/<name>/boxes/<id>      read box file\n  PUT  /maps/<name>/boxes/<id>      write box file\n  DELETE /maps/<name>/boxes/<id>    remove box (validates no dangling refs)\n  GET  /maps/<name>/data/<name>     read data file\n  PUT  /maps/<name>/data/<name>     write data file\n  GET  /maps/<name>/drivers         read drivers.json\n  PUT  /maps/<name>/drivers         write drivers.json\n  GET  /maps/<name>/meta            read meta.json\n\n### soramech-runner.lua\n\nFSM execution engine. Loads a map directory, validates the graph, then\nexecutes boxes in dependency order. Each box invocation is wrapped in a\n`task_fn(inputs) -> outputs` call — matching the 3d-rts thread pool's\naction chain signature for future threading compatibility.\n\nStarted with: `luajit soramech-runner.lua <map-dir>`\n\nExecution steps:\n  1. Read all box files from boxes/\n  2. Validate: all connection endpoints exist, branch \"else\" handled\n  3. Determine entry box from meta.json\n  4. Execute: resolve inputs, invoke driver, collect outputs, fire wires\n  5. On completion, write last-run snapshot to tmp/last-run.json\n\n### index.html\n\nStatic HTML + vanilla JS. Infinite-scroll canvas. Box diagram editor.\nTalks to soramech-server.lua for all file operations. No run button —\nthe user starts the runner separately from the terminal.\n\n## Map directory format\n\n```\nmaps/<name>/\n  meta.json          — { name, description, entry_box_id }\n  drivers.json       — { \".lua\": \"drivers/lua.sh\", \".c\": \"drivers/c.sh\", ... }\n  boxes/\n    <id>.json        — one file per box (see Box file format below)\n  data/\n    <name>.json      — lua table as JSON; sections have \"constant\": bool\n  drivers/\n    lua.sh           — built-in lua driver (shipped with soramech)\n    c.sh             — built-in C driver\n    bash.sh          — built-in bash driver\n  tmp/               — symlink to /tmp/<name>/\n    last-run.json    — snapshot of last run (ephemeral)\n    logs/            — run logs\n    cache/           — compiled binaries (C driver cache)\n```\n\n## Box file format\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"unique-string\",\n  \"label\": \"Human name\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"ref\": \"src/strings.lua\",\n  \"fn\": \"trim\",\n  \"inputs\": [\n    { \"name\": \"text\", \"type\": \"string\" }\n  ],\n  \"outputs\": [\n    { \"name\": \"result\", \"type\": \"string\" }\n  ],\n  \"connections\": [\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"unique-string\",\n      \"from_output\": \"result\",\n      \"to_box\": \"next-box-id\",\n      \"to_input\": \"text\"\n    }\n  ],\n  \"ui\": { \"x\": 120, \"y\": 340 }\n}\n```\n\nFor branch boxes (`\"kind\": \"branch\"`):\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"classify\",\n  \"kind\": \"branch\",\n  \"inputs\": [{ \"name\": \"value\", \"type\": \"string\" }],\n  \"ports\": [\n    { \"name\": \"rogue\", \"predicate\": { \"op\": \"eq\", \"value\": \"rogue\" } },\n    { \"name\": \"wizard\", \"predicate\": { \"op\": \"eq\", \"value\": \"wizard\" } },\n    { \"name\": \"else\" }\n  ],\n  \"connections\": [...]\n}\n```\n\nConnections are written to BOTH endpoint box files. The runner validates\nat load time that both ends agree. Disagreement is a hard error.\n\n## Language driver interface\n\nDrivers are shell scripts. The engine invokes them as:\n\n  <driver-script> <file-path> <fn-name> <arg-count> [<arg1> <arg2> ...]\n\nThe single return value is encoded as a JSON value on stdout. Exit code\nnon-zero = box failure. Each box has exactly one output wire — multi-return\ntuples are not supported (see docs/003-driver-system.md).\n\n## Execution model (v1 — synchronous)\n\nThe runner walks the graph depth-first from the entry box. Each box call:\n\n  1. Collect inputs: read wired output values from predecessor boxes\n  2. Invoke driver: shell out to the appropriate driver script\n  3. Collect output: decode single JSON value from driver stdout\n  4. Store output: held in runner memory, keyed by box id (one value per box)\n  5. Fire connections: enqueue boxes whose input dependencies are now met\n\nEach step is wrapped in a `task_fn` boundary so the runner can be\nthreaded later by substituting the synchronous executor with one backed\nby effil-jit or the custom thread pool from the 3d-rts project.\n\n## Data files\n\nPersistent data lives in data/<name>.json. Format:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"constant\": false,\n  \"fields\": {\n    \"history\": [],\n    \"config\": { \"constant\": true, \"value\": { \"model\": \"soramind-default\" } }\n  }\n}\n```\n\nTop-level `constant: true` makes the whole file read-only. Individual\nfields can be flagged constant within an otherwise mutable file.\n\nEphemeral state (scratch tables, logs, last-run snapshot) goes to tmp/,\nwhich is a symlink to /tmp/<map-name>/. It survives the run but not a\nreboot — intentionally.\n",
    "oldString":"Each step is wrapped in a `task_fn` boundary so the runner can be\nthreaded later by substituting the synchronous executor with one backed\nby effil-jit or the custom thread pool from the 3d-rts project.",
    "newString":"Each step is wrapped in a `task_fn` boundary so the runner can be\nthreaded later by substituting the synchronous executor with one backed\nby the 3d-rts custom thread pool. The intermediate path is coroutine-based\nnon-blocking I/O before the full thread pool is integrated.",
    "replaceAll":false,
    "userModified":false
  },

        "lines":[" "," Goal: boxes whose inputs are all satisfied fire concurrently."," ","-- Integrate effil-jit as the threading backend (replacing synchronous","-  depth-first walk)","-- Runner becomes an M:N task scheduler: each box invocation is a task,","-  boxes park when waiting on upstream results","+- Coroutine-based non-blocking executor: the ready-queue becomes a","+  coroutine scheduler; boxes yield while waiting on upstream results","+- Cross-language calls use Unix domain socket servers (one per language","+  runtime per worker), non-blocking on the Lua side via LuaSocket"," - Multiple maps running concurrently share nothing (separate processes)","-- Begin integration path toward the 3d-rts custom thread pool","+- Integration path toward the 3d-rts custom thread pool: the coroutine","+  scheduler and task boundary are designed to swap in the thread pool","+  without changing the box execution model"," "," ## Phase 3 — SoraMind integration"," "],
        "oldStart":32,

      }],
    "originalFile":"# SoraMech — Roadmap\n\n## Phase 1 — Foundation\n\nGoal: a map you can edit in the browser and execute from the terminal.\n\nAt the end of phase 1, the user can:\n- Open index.html, connect it to a running server, and see a canvas\n- Create boxes, set their ref/fn/inputs/outputs, wire them together\n- Edit branch boxes with named ports and predicates\n- Save all edits as box files on disk\n- Run `luajit soramech-runner.lua <map-dir>` and have it execute the map\n- Write a custom language driver and have the runner use it\n\nIssues:\n  101 — project scaffold and map directory format\n  102 — language driver interface\n  103 — runner: graph loader and validator\n  104 — runner: synchronous executor (task boundary)\n  105 — HTTP server: file CRUD API\n  106 — web editor: canvas and box rendering\n  107 — web editor: wiring and connection UI\n  108 — branch box and predicate routing\n  109 — data files: persistent and ephemeral storage\n  110 — phase 1 demo\n\nDemo: a small lua FSM (3-4 boxes) runs via the CLI, exercises a branch\nbox, reads a data file, writes an output. The browser shows the same map\nvisually with correct wiring drawn.\n\n## Phase 2 — Concurrent execution\n\nGoal: boxes whose inputs are all satisfied fire concurrently.\n\n- Integrate effil-jit as the threading backend (replacing synchronous\n  depth-first walk)\n- Runner becomes an M:N task scheduler: each box invocation is a task,\n  boxes park when waiting on upstream results\n- Multiple maps running concurrently share nothing (separate processes)\n- Begin integration path toward the 3d-rts custom thread pool\n\n## Phase 3 — SoraMind integration\n\nGoal: boxes that call SoraMind inference endpoints on the Alpine cluster.\n\n- LLM call box type: sends a prompt, receives a completion string\n- Prompt assembly: text values wired from upstream boxes, data file\n  sections explicitly loaded into prompt context\n- Branch box connected to an LLM classifier: \"rogue, wizard, or else\"\n- Else port retry with pseudo-randomized temperature parameter\n- Streaming output from SoraMind inference back to the runner\n\n## Phase 4 — Map-to-map calls\n\nGoal: a box that invokes another map as a subroutine.\n\n- Map call box type: specifies another map directory, passes inputs,\n  receives outputs\n- Maps can run concurrently with each other\n- Entry/exit contracts defined in meta.json\n\n## Phase 5 — Remote runner\n\nGoal: run a map on the Alpine cluster, edit it from a laptop.\n\n- Runner process on a remote machine (Alpine node)\n- Server on the same machine exposes map files over HTTP\n- Browser editor on the laptop connects to the remote server\n- Results written to remote data files, accessible via server\n",
    "oldString":"## Phase 2 — Concurrent execution\n\nGoal: boxes whose inputs are all satisfied fire concurrently.\n\n- Integrate effil-jit as the threading backend (replacing synchronous\n  depth-first walk)\n- Runner becomes an M:N task scheduler: each box invocation is a task,\n  boxes park when waiting on upstream results\n- Multiple maps running concurrently share nothing (separate processes)\n- Begin integration path toward the 3d-rts custom thread pool",
    "newString":"## Phase 2 — Concurrent execution\n\nGoal: boxes whose inputs are all satisfied fire concurrently.\n\n- Coroutine-based non-blocking executor: the ready-queue becomes a\n  coroutine scheduler; boxes yield while waiting on upstream results\n- Cross-language calls use Unix domain socket servers (one per language\n  runtime per worker), non-blocking on the Lua side via LuaSocket\n- Multiple maps running concurrently share nothing (separate processes)\n- Integration path toward the 3d-rts custom thread pool: the coroutine\n  scheduler and task boundary are designed to swap in the thread pool\n  without changing the box execution model",
    "replaceAll":false,
    "userModified":false
  },

No"],

    "originalFile":"# 104 — Runner: synchronous executor (task boundary)\n\n## Status\n\nopen\n\n## Blockers\n\n- 103 (graph must be loaded and validated before execution)\n- 102 (drivers must exist to be invoked)\n\n## Current behavior\n\nNo executor exists. There is no mechanism to walk the graph and invoke\nboxes in dependency order.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nsoramech-runner.lua, after a successful load/validate, executes the map:\n\n  1. Start at entry box\n  2. For each box ready to fire (all input ports satisfied):\n     a. Collect input values from wired predecessor outputs\n     b. Invoke driver: look up extension in driver table, call driver\n        script with file + fn + args\n     c. Parse JSON from driver stdout into output values\n     d. Store output values keyed by (box_id, output_name)\n     e. For each outgoing connection from this box:\n        - If predicate present (branch box): evaluate predicate against\n          the output value; if true, mark target box's input as satisfied\n        - If no predicate: mark target box's input as satisfied\n     f. Enqueue newly-satisfied boxes\n  3. Continue until no boxes remain in the queue\n  4. Write tmp/last-run.json with all box outputs and exit status\n\nEach box invocation is wrapped in a task_fn(inputs) -> outputs function.\nThis boundary is the future threading integration point.     "originalFile":"# 104 — Runner: synchronous executor (task boundary)\n\n## Status\n\nopen\n\n## Blockers\n\n- 103 (graph must be loaded and validated before execution)\n- 102 (drivers must exist to be invoked)\n\n## Current behavior\n\nNo executor exists. Start at entry box\n  2. For each box ready to fire (all input ports satisfied):\n     a. Collect input values from wired predecessor outputs\n     b. Invoke driver: look up extension in driver table, call driver\n        script with file + fn + args\n     c. Parse JSON from driver stdout into output values\n     d. Store output values keyed by (box_id, output_name)\n     e. For each outgoing connection from this box:\n        - If predicate present (branch box): evaluate predicate against\n          the output value; if true, mark target box's input as satisfied\n        - If no predicate: mark target box's input as satisfied\n     f.           "content":"---\nname: threading_model\ndescription: SoraMech threading roadmap — effil is out, synchronous → coroutine → 3d-rts\ntype: project\n---\n\nEffil-jit is explicitly NOT used. It has been removed from all docs and issues.\n\nThreading roadmap:\n1. **Now**: Synchronous executor. Single-threaded, sequential box execution.\n2. **Next**: Coroutine-based non-blocking executor. LuaSocket non-blocking I/O + coroutine scheduler. Boxes yield while waiting on cross-language socket calls.\n3. **Eventually**: 3d-rts custom thread pool. The `task_fn(inputs) -> outputs` boundary in `src/004-executor.lua` is the designed swap point.\n\nCross-language IPC direction: Unix domain socket servers (one per language runtime per worker thread). Not temp files, not anonymous pipes. The socket servers are persistent subprocesses — one per language per thread, idle-blocked on `accept()`.\n\n**Why:** Effil was considered but rejected. The 3d-rts thread pool is the target. No date set.\n\n**How to apply:** When discussing threading, parallelism, or cross-language IPC, do not suggest effil. Reference the 3d-rts pool as future work and coroutines as the intermediate path.\n",

    "content":"---\nname: threading_model\ndescription: SoraMech threading roadmap — effil is out, synchronous → coroutine → 3d-rts\ntype: project\noriginSessionId: 579d58b3-7452-44f3-983a-80ff5821082a\n---\nEffil-jit is explicitly NOT used. It has been removed from all docs and issues.\n\nThreading roadmap:\n1. **Now**: Synchronous executor. Single-threaded, sequential box execution.\n2. **Next**: Coroutine-based non-blocking executor. LuaSocket non-blocking I/O + coroutine scheduler. Boxes yield while waiting on cross-language socket calls.\n3. **Eventually**: 3d-rts custom thread pool. The `task_fn(inputs) -> outputs` boundary in `src/004-executor.lua` is the designed swap point.\n\nCross-language IPC direction: Unix domain socket servers (one per language runtime per worker thread). Not temp files, not anonymous pipes. The socket servers are persistent subprocesses — one per language per thread, idle-blocked on `accept()`.\n\n**Why:** Effil was considered but rejected. The 3d-rts thread pool is the target. No date set.\n\n**How to apply:** When discussing threading, parallelism, or cross-language IPC, do not suggest effil. Reference the 3d-rts pool as future work and coroutines as the intermediate path.\n"
  },

        "type":"text",
        "text":"The effil references are cleared from all docs and issues. The roadmap now reads: synchronous → coroutine-based non-blocking → 3d-rts pool, with Unix domain sockets as the cross-language IPC mechanism in both the coroutine and thread-pool phases.\n\nTo directly answer your question about parallelism with N processes per thread: those processes are real OS processes, not coroutines. They sit blocked on `read()`/`accept()` consuming no CPU. When a worker sends them work, the OS schedules them — potentially on a different core simultaneously. So you get real parallelism across languages without any coordination cost on the Lua side. The 3d-rts thread pool, when it arrives, just determines how many Lua workers there are, which determines how many language server instances you'd run in parallel (one socket endpoint per worker thread per language). The language server model scales with the pool naturally."
      }]

        "type":"tool_use",
        "name":"Write",

          "type":"direct"
        },
        "input":{
          "content":"# SoraMech — IPC and Threading Model\n\n## The problem\n\nThe current executor runs boxes sequentially. Each box invocation shells out to\na driver script, which starts a new process, runs the function, and exits. The\nreturn value passes through stdout. This works but has two structural problems:\n\n1. **Process-per-call cost.** Spawning a process takes roughly 1–10 ms depending\n   on the runtime. For a map with ten boxes, that's dominated by spawn overhead,\n   not by the actual work.\n\n2. **stdout is the wrong channel.** A box function that prints debug output\n   corrupts the wire value. Values are transient — they vanish once the pipe is\n   drained. The channel has no addressing, no framing, and no backpressure.\n\nThe goal is a design where cross-language calls are fast, values are addressable,\nand the execution model is ready to parallelize without redesign.\n\n---\n\n## The threading roadmap\n\nThree stages, each building on the last:\n\n**Stage 1 — Synchronous (current).** A single-threaded ready-queue walks the\ngraph in dependency order. `run_task(box, inputs)` in `src/004-executor.lua` is\nthe task boundary. It blocks until the driver responds.\n\n**Stage 2 — Coroutine-based non-blocking.** The ready-queue becomes a coroutine\nscheduler. Boxes yield when waiting on upstream results or cross-language calls.\nLuaSocket non-blocking I/O lets the scheduler run other boxes while one is\nwaiting for a response. No true parallelism yet, but the graph's natural\nconcurrency is exploited without blocking the whole process.\n\n**Stage 3 — 3d-rts thread pool.** The `task_fn` boundary swaps in the thread\npool. Worker threads pull tasks from the pool; the coroutine scheduler is\nreplaced by OS-level scheduling. Cross-language calls block a worker thread\nwhile other threads continue. True parallelism across cores.\n\nEffil-jit is not used. The path is synchronous → coroutine → 3d-rts pool.\n\n---\n\n## The three IPC options\n\n### Option 1 — LuaJIT FFI (Lua ↔ C, in-process)\n\nThe Foreign Function Interface lets Lua call C functions that live in a shared\nlibrary (`.so`) directly, in the same process, with no subprocess and no channel.\nYou provide a C declaration (`ffi.cdef[[ int add(int a, int b); ]]`), load the\ncompiled library (`ffi.load(\"./mybox.so\")`), and call `lib.add(3, 4)` — the CPU\njumps into native code and returns. Overhead is nanoseconds.\n\nSince the executor already does mtime-based dynamic compilation (see `drivers/c.sh`),\ncompiling to a `.so` instead of a binary is just a flag change (`-shared -fPIC`).\nThe box function signature changes from `main(argc, argv)` to a named function\nwith typed arguments — which is strictly cleaner.\n\n**Limitation:** FFI only works for languages that compile to a C-compatible ABI.\nBash cannot. Python can (via `ctypes` on the other side), but it's awkward.\nFFI is the right answer for Lua ↔ C only.\n\n**Cross-platform:** LuaJIT FFI works on Linux, macOS, and Windows. `.so` becomes\n`.dylib` on macOS and `.dll` on Windows — the `ffi.load()` call is portable if\nyou handle the extension.\n\n---\n\n### Option 2 — Shared memory (`shm_open` + `mmap`)\n\n`shm_open(\"/soramech-wire-0\", ...)` creates a named memory segment managed by\nthe kernel — not a file on disk, but a named object in RAM. `mmap()` maps it\ninto the calling process's address space. Any other process that opens the same\nname gets access to the *same physical memory*. A write in one process is\nimmediately visible in another — no copy, no syscall per access after setup.\n\nFor SoraMech, each wire between two boxes would correspond to a named shared\nmemory slot. The compiler (issue 219) generates the slot names and the read/write\ncalls. Any language that can call POSIX can participate:\n\n- Lua: via LuaJIT FFI calling `shm_open` + `mmap` from libc\n- C: natively\n- Bash: via `/dev/shm/<name>` — on Linux, the tmpfs backing shared memory is\n  exposed as a filesystem path, so bash can `cat /dev/shm/soramech-wire-0`\n\n**Performance:** After the initial `mmap()` setup, reads and writes are pointer\ndereferences — no syscalls, no copies. For small values (strings, numbers) this\nis essentially free.\n\n**Complication:** Shared memory is untyped raw bytes. You need a size header\n(how many bytes is this value?), a type tag (string? number? JSON object?), and\na synchronization mechanism (how does the reader know the writer is done?). None\nof these are hard — a small fixed header in the segment handles all three — but\nthe compiler must generate all of it correctly for every wire.\n\n**Cross-platform:**\n- Linux: full support. `/dev/shm/` filesystem exposure is Linux-specific.\n- macOS: `shm_open()` works, but the objects are NOT exposed as files. No\n  `/dev/shm/` path. Bash access via file path doesn't work.\n- Windows: completely different API (`CreateFileMapping` / `MapViewOfFile`).\n  No POSIX `shm_open` without WSL or Cygwin.\n\nShared memory is powerful but not the most portable option. The bash filesystem\nshortcut that makes it cross-language is Linux-only.\n\n---\n\n### Option 3 — Unix domain socket servers (chosen direction)\n\nA Unix domain socket is a socket addressed by a filesystem path instead of an\nIP address and port. `/tmp/soramech-bash.sock` is a special file; any process\non the same machine connects to it with the standard socket API. The kernel\nroutes data directly between processes in memory — no network stack, no loopback,\nno protocol headers. Performance is bounded by memory bandwidth.\n\nUnlike anonymous pipes, a socket has a name that unrelated processes can find\nwithout inheriting file descriptors. Multiple clients connect simultaneously;\neach gets its own channel. The server handles them with `accept()` in a loop.\n\n**The model for SoraMech:**\n\nEach language runtime runs as a persistent socket server. One server instance\nper language per worker thread:\n\n```\n/tmp/soramech-bash-0.sock   ← worker thread 0's bash runtime\n/tmp/soramech-bash-1.sock   ← worker thread 1's bash runtime\n/tmp/soramech-c-0.sock      ← worker thread 0's C runtime\n```\n\nThe server starts when the program starts, stays alive for the whole run, and\naccepts sequential requests — one box call at a time per instance. A Lua worker\nconnects to its designated socket, sends a framed request (function name +\narguments), and reads back a framed response (return value). The server is a\nsmall script (~50 lines) that sources or compiles the box file, calls the\nfunction, and writes the result.\n\n**Wire protocol:** Length-prefix framing. The sender writes a 4-byte big-endian\ninteger (the message length in bytes), then that many bytes of content. The\nreceiver reads 4 bytes, then reads exactly that many bytes. This handles values\ncontaining newlines or null bytes without ambiguity.\n\n**Cost of idle servers:** An idle server process is blocked on `accept()` — zero\nCPU, approximately 3–5 MB RSS for a bash process. For 10 languages × 4 threads\n= 40 processes ≈ 150–200 MB. Acceptable.\n\n**Integration with the coroutine scheduler (Stage 2):**\n\nWith LuaSocket non-blocking sockets, the coroutine that makes a cross-language\ncall does this:\n1. Connect to the language server socket (non-blocking)\n2. Send the request\n3. `coroutine.yield()` — registers the socket fd with the scheduler\n4. Scheduler polls all pending fds with `select()`\n5. When the fd is readable, scheduler resumes the coroutine\n6. Coroutine reads the response and continues\n\nThe cross-language call never blocks the main Lua thread. Other boxes run in\nother coroutines while the bash/C server is processing.\n\n**Integration with the 3d-rts thread pool (Stage 3):**\n\nEach worker thread owns its set of language server sockets. When `run_task` calls\na cross-language box, it sends to the socket and blocks on the read — the thread\nblocks, not the whole program. Other workers continue processing other boxes on\nother cores. The server processes run concurrently on whatever cores the OS\nschedules them to. This gives real parallelism: a bash box and a C box assigned\nto different workers can run simultaneously.\n\n**Cross-platform:**\n- Linux: full support.\n- macOS: full support. Unix domain sockets are POSIX.\n- Windows: supported since Windows 10 1803 (2018). `AF_UNIX` sockets work\n  natively. Most languages abstract this through their socket libraries.\n\nUnix domain sockets are the most portable cross-language IPC mechanism that also\nsupports concurrent connections. They are the chosen direction for the compiler\noutput and the coroutine/thread-pool executor.\n\n---\n\n## Summary comparison\n\n| Property              | FFI (.so)       | Shared memory       | Unix domain socket  |\n|-----------------------|-----------------|---------------------|---------------------|\n| Speed (per call)      | nanoseconds     | nanoseconds*        | microseconds        |\n| Languages supported   | C-ABI only      | any (with caveats)  | any                 |\n| Parallel connections  | N/A (in-process)| yes (with sync)     | yes (natural)       |\n| Linux                 | yes             | yes                 | yes                 |\n| macOS                 | yes             | partial†            | yes                 |\n| Windows               | yes (.dll)      | no (different API)  | yes (Win10+)        |\n| Complexity            | low             | medium              | low-medium          |\n\n*After initial mmap setup. †shm_open works; /dev/shm filesystem path does not.\n\nThe compiler (issue 219) uses FFI for Lua ↔ C wires where the C source is\ncompiled to a `.so`, and Unix domain sockets for all other cross-language wires.\nSame-language Lua wires are direct function calls — no IPC at all.\n\n---\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — `run_task` boundary, ready-queue\n- `src/007-runner-main.lua` — entry point for the interpreter path\n- `issues/219-map-compiler.md` — compiler that generates the IPC calls\n- `issues/104-runner-synchronous-executor.md` — task boundary design\n- `issues/213-queued-inputs-and-task-model.md` — queue-per-port, thread pool notes\n- `docs/002-roadmap.md` — phase plan for threading stages\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md"
        },
        "id":"toolu_01RU5j5G4QYaKF1wse75dHGd"
      }]

    "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md",
    "content":"# SoraMech — IPC and Threading Model\n\n## The problem\n\nThe current executor runs boxes sequentially. Each box invocation shells out to\na driver script, which starts a new process, runs the function, and exits. The\nreturn value passes through stdout. This works but has two structural problems:\n\n1. **Process-per-call cost.** Spawning a process takes roughly 1–10 ms depending\n   on the runtime. For a map with ten boxes, that's dominated by spawn overhead,\n   not by the actual work.\n\n2. **stdout is the wrong channel.** A box function that prints debug output\n   corrupts the wire value. Values are transient — they vanish once the pipe is\n   drained. The channel has no addressing, no framing, and no backpressure.\n\nThe goal is a design where cross-language calls are fast, values are addressable,\nand the execution model is ready to parallelize without redesign.\n\n---\n\n## The threading roadmap\n\nThree stages, each building on the last:\n\n**Stage 1 — Synchronous (current).** A single-threaded ready-queue walks the\ngraph in dependency order. `run_task(box, inputs)` in `src/004-executor.lua` is\nthe task boundary. It blocks until the driver responds.\n\n**Stage 2 — Coroutine-based non-blocking.** The ready-queue becomes a coroutine\nscheduler. Boxes yield when waiting on upstream results or cross-language calls.\nLuaSocket non-blocking I/O lets the scheduler run other boxes while one is\nwaiting for a response. No true parallelism yet, but the graph's natural\nconcurrency is exploited without blocking the whole process.\n\n**Stage 3 — 3d-rts thread pool.** The `task_fn` boundary swaps in the thread\npool. Worker threads pull tasks from the pool; the coroutine scheduler is\nreplaced by OS-level scheduling. Cross-language calls block a worker thread\nwhile other threads continue. True parallelism across cores.\n\nEffil-jit is not used. The path is synchronous → coroutine → 3d-rts pool.\n\n---\n\n## The three IPC options\n\n### Option 1 — LuaJIT FFI (Lua ↔ C, in-process)\n\nThe Foreign Function Interface lets Lua call C functions that live in a shared\nlibrary (`.so`) directly, in the same process, with no subprocess and no channel.\nYou provide a C declaration (`ffi.cdef[[ int add(int a, int b); ]]`), load the\ncompiled library (`ffi.load(\"./mybox.so\")`), and call `lib.add(3, 4)` — the CPU\njumps into native code and returns. Overhead is nanoseconds.\n\nSince the executor already does mtime-based dynamic compilation (see `drivers/c.sh`),\ncompiling to a `.so` instead of a binary is just a flag change (`-shared -fPIC`).\nThe box function signature changes from `main(argc, argv)` to a named function\nwith typed arguments — which is strictly cleaner.\n\n**Limitation:** FFI only works for languages that compile to a C-compatible ABI.\nBash cannot. Python can (via `ctypes` on the other side), but it's awkward.\nFFI is the right answer for Lua ↔ C only.\n\n**Cross-platform:** LuaJIT FFI works on Linux, macOS, and Windows. `.so` becomes\n`.dylib` on macOS and `.dll` on Windows — the `ffi.load()` call is portable if\nyou handle the extension.\n\n---\n\n### Option 2 — Shared memory (`shm_open` + `mmap`)\n\n`shm_open(\"/soramech-wire-0\", ...)` creates a named memory segment managed by\nthe kernel — not a file on disk, but a named object in RAM. `mmap()` maps it\ninto the calling process's address space. Any other process that opens the same\nname gets access to the *same physical memory*. A write in one process is\nimmediately visible in another — no copy, no syscall per access after setup.\n\nFor SoraMech, each wire between two boxes would correspond to a named shared\nmemory slot. The compiler (issue 219) generates the slot names and the read/write\ncalls. Any language that can call POSIX can participate:\n\n- Lua: via LuaJIT FFI calling `shm_open` + `mmap` from libc\n- C: natively\n- Bash: via `/dev/shm/<name>` — on Linux, the tmpfs backing shared memory is\n  exposed as a filesystem path, so bash can `cat /dev/shm/soramech-wire-0`\n\n**Performance:** After the initial `mmap()` setup, reads and writes are pointer\ndereferences — no syscalls, no copies. For small values (strings, numbers) this\nis essentially free.\n\n**Complication:** Shared memory is untyped raw bytes. You need a size header\n(how many bytes is this value?), a type tag (string? number? JSON object?), and\na synchronization mechanism (how does the reader know the writer is done?). None\nof these are hard — a small fixed header in the segment handles all three — but\nthe compiler must generate all of it correctly for every wire.\n\n**Cross-platform:**\n- Linux: full support. `/dev/shm/` filesystem exposure is Linux-specific.\n- macOS: `shm_open()` works, but the objects are NOT exposed as files. No\n  `/dev/shm/` path. Bash access via file path doesn't work.\n- Windows: completely different API (`CreateFileMapping` / `MapViewOfFile`).\n  No POSIX `shm_open` without WSL or Cygwin.\n\nShared memory is powerful but not the most portable option. The bash filesystem\nshortcut that makes it cross-language is Linux-only.\n\n---\n\n### Option 3 — Unix domain socket servers (chosen direction)\n\nA Unix domain socket is a socket addressed by a filesystem path instead of an\nIP address and port. `/tmp/soramech-bash.sock` is a special file; any process\non the same machine connects to it with the standard socket API. The kernel\nroutes data directly between processes in memory — no network stack, no loopback,\nno protocol headers. Performance is bounded by memory bandwidth.\n\nUnlike anonymous pipes, a socket has a name that unrelated processes can find\nwithout inheriting file descriptors. Multiple clients connect simultaneously;\neach gets its own channel. The server handles them with `accept()` in a loop.\n\n**The model for SoraMech:**\n\nEach language runtime runs as a persistent socket server. One server instance\nper language per worker thread:\n\n```\n/tmp/soramech-bash-0.sock   ← worker thread 0's bash runtime\n/tmp/soramech-bash-1.sock   ← worker thread 1's bash runtime\n/tmp/soramech-c-0.sock      ← worker thread 0's C runtime\n```\n\nThe server starts when the program starts, stays alive for the whole run, and\naccepts sequential requests — one box call at a time per instance. A Lua worker\nconnects to its designated socket, sends a framed request (function name +\narguments), and reads back a framed response (return value). The server is a\nsmall script (~50 lines) that sources or compiles the box file, calls the\nfunction, and writes the result.\n\n**Wire protocol:** Length-prefix framing. The sender writes a 4-byte big-endian\ninteger (the message length in bytes), then that many bytes of content. The\nreceiver reads 4 bytes, then reads exactly that many bytes. This handles values\ncontaining newlines or null bytes without ambiguity.\n\n**Cost of idle servers:** An idle server process is blocked on `accept()` — zero\nCPU, approximately 3–5 MB RSS for a bash process. For 10 languages × 4 threads\n= 40 processes ≈ 150–200 MB. Acceptable.\n\n**Integration with the coroutine scheduler (Stage 2):**\n\nWith LuaSocket non-blocking sockets, the coroutine that makes a cross-language\ncall does this:\n1. Connect to the language server socket (non-blocking)\n2. Send the request\n3. `coroutine.yield()` — registers the socket fd with the scheduler\n4. Scheduler polls all pending fds with `select()`\n5. When the fd is readable, scheduler resumes the coroutine\n6. Coroutine reads the response and continues\n\nThe cross-language call never blocks the main Lua thread. Other boxes run in\nother coroutines while the bash/C server is processing.\n\n**Integration with the 3d-rts thread pool (Stage 3):**\n\nEach worker thread owns its set of language server sockets. When `run_task` calls\na cross-language box, it sends to the socket and blocks on the read — the thread\nblocks, not the whole program. Other workers continue processing other boxes on\nother cores. The server processes run concurrently on whatever cores the OS\nschedules them to. This gives real parallelism: a bash box and a C box assigned\nto different workers can run simultaneously.\n\n**Cross-platform:**\n- Linux: full support.\n- macOS: full support. Unix domain sockets are POSIX.\n- Windows: supported since Windows 10 1803 (2018). `AF_UNIX` sockets work\n  natively. Most languages abstract this through their socket libraries.\n\nUnix domain sockets are the most portable cross-language IPC mechanism that also\nsupports concurrent connections. They are the chosen direction for the compiler\noutput and the coroutine/thread-pool executor.\n\n---\n\n## Summary comparison\n\n| Property              | FFI (.so)       | Shared memory       | Unix domain socket  |\n|-----------------------|-----------------|---------------------|---------------------|\n| Speed (per call)      | nanoseconds     | nanoseconds*        | microseconds        |\n| Languages supported   | C-ABI only      | any (with caveats)  | any                 |\n| Parallel connections  | N/A (in-process)| yes (with sync)     | yes (natural)       |\n| Linux                 | yes             | yes                 | yes                 |\n| macOS                 | yes             | partial†            | yes                 |\n| Windows               | yes (.dll)      | no (different API)  | yes (Win10+)        |\n| Complexity            | low             | medium              | low-medium          |\n\n*After initial mmap setup. †shm_open works; /dev/shm filesystem path does not.\n\nThe compiler (issue 219) uses FFI for Lua ↔ C wires where the C source is\ncompiled to a `.so`, and Unix domain sockets for all other cross-language wires.\nSame-language Lua wires are direct function calls — no IPC at all.\n\n---\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — `run_task` boundary, ready-queue\n- `src/007-runner-main.lua` — entry point for the interpreter path\n- `issues/219-map-compiler.md` — compiler that generates the IPC calls\n- `issues/104-runner-synchronous-executor.md` — task boundary design\n- `issues/213-queued-inputs-and-task-model.md` — queue-per-port, thread pool notes\n- `docs/002-roadmap.md` — phase plan for threading stages\n"
  },
  "uuid":"6116af48-3f99-4f03-ab7d-80615aab687f",

        "content":"# 209 — Ollama query library\n\n## Status\n\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nNo built-in way to send prompts to a local Ollama instance from a map box.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nA shared Lua library at `libs/ollama.lua` exposes two public functions:\n\n- `M.query(prompt, model, host)` — plain text generation via /api/generate\n- `M.chat(prompt, system, model, host)` — chat completion with optional system\n  prompt via /api/chat\n\n`model` and `host` default to `llama3.2` and `http://localhost:11434` when nil\nor empty string. This lets the user set them as literal port values in the\ninspector and leave them blank to use the defaults.\n\nThe file doubles as a box source: copy it to any map's src/ directory and the\nfile browser will detect both functions and auto-populate ports. Write `libs/ollama.lua` with `M.query` and `M.chat`.\n2.         "content":"# 211 — File browser library directories\n\n## Status\n\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nThe file browser only shows files in the map's own `src/` directory. Shared\nlibraries in `libs/` or other directories cannot be browsed or selected as a\nbox ref without manually typing the path.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nA button at the top of the file browser (\"+ library dir\") prompts the user\nfor an absolute directory path and stores it in `meta.json.extra_src_dirs`.\nThese directories appear as collapsible groups in the browser alongside `src/`.\nA `▶/▼` toggle collapses or expands each group. Files in extra dirs are fetched\nand parsed identically to src/ files.\n\nServer adds two routes:\n- `GET /maps/:name/extrasrc` — returns extra dirs and their file listings\n- `GET /maps/:name/extrasrc/:index/:file` — returns a file from extra dir at\n  that index as text/plain\n\nExtra dirs are stored as absolute paths in `meta.json.extra_src_dirs`. The\nserver reads them at request time; no restart needed when dirs are added.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. `src/005-http-server.lua` — add `handle_list_extrasrc` and\n   `handle_get_extrasrc`; add both to the dispatch table.\n2. `assets/js/003-api.js` — add `list_extra_src()` and `get_extra_src_file(i, f)`.\n3. `assets/js/007-filebrowser.js` — refactor `render()` to load both src/ and\n   extra dirs; render as collapsible groups with toggle state in a local Set;\n   add \"+ library dir\" button that calls `API.put_meta`.\n4. `assets/js/007-filebrowser.js` — right-click on an extra-dir group header\n   shows a \"hide directory\" context menu item that removes the path from\n   `meta.extra_src_dirs` and re-renders. Uses a private `show_fb_ctx_menu`\n   helper (reuses `.ctx-item` CSS; independent from App's context menu).\n\n## Related documents\n\n- src/005-http-server.lua — handle_list_src, dispatch table\n- assets/js/003-api.js — get_meta, put_meta\n- assets/js/007-filebrowser.js — render, render_fn_list\n- maps/*/meta.json — extra_src_dirs field",

        "type":"tool_result"
      }],

    "stdout":"# 211 — File browser library directories\n\n## Status\n\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nThe file browser only shows files in the map's own `src/` directory. Shared\nlibraries in `libs/` or other directories cannot be browsed or selected as a\nbox ref without manually typing the path.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nA button at the top of the file browser (\"+ library dir\") prompts the user\nfor an absolute directory path and stores it in `meta.json.extra_src_dirs`.\nThese directories appear as collapsible groups in the browser alongside `src/`.\nA `▶/▼` toggle collapses or expands each group. Files in extra dirs are fetched\nand parsed identically to src/ files.\n\nServer adds two routes:\n- `GET /maps/:name/extrasrc` — returns extra dirs and their file listings\n- `GET /maps/:name/extrasrc/:index/:file` — returns a file from extra dir at\n  that index as text/plain\n\nExtra dirs are stored as absolute paths in `meta.json.extra_src_dirs`. The\nserver reads them at request time; no restart needed when dirs are added.\n\n## Suggested implementation steps\n\n1. `src/005-http-server.lua` — add `handle_list_extrasrc` and\n   `handle_get_extrasrc`; add both to the dispatch table.\n2. `assets/js/003-api.js` — add `list_extra_src()` and `get_extra_src_file(i, f)`.\n3. `assets/js/007-filebrowser.js` — refactor `render()` to load both src/ and\n   extra dirs; render as collapsible groups with toggle state in a local Set;\n   add \"+ library dir\" button that calls `API.put_meta`.\n4. `assets/js/007-filebrowser.js` — right-click on an extra-dir group header\n   shows a \"hide directory\" context menu item that removes the path from\n   `meta.extra_src_dirs` and re-renders. Uses a private `show_fb_ctx_menu`\n   helper (reuses `.ctx-item` CSS; independent from App's context menu).\n\n## Related documents\n\n- src/005-http-server.lua — handle_list_src, dispatch table\n- assets/js/003-api.js — get_meta, put_meta\n- assets/js/007-filebrowser.js — render, render_fn_list\n- maps/*/meta.json — extra_src_dirs field",
    "isImage":false,
    "interrupted":false
  },

        "text":"Yes, a few questions before writing this — they'll affect the design meaningfully:\n\n1. **Where does the counter live?** It could be in the executor's in-memory state (resets each run) or in the box's data file (persists across runs). These are very different behaviors. Which do you want — or should both be possible with a toggle?\n\n2. **Does the function know its iteration index?** Two models:\n   - The counter is purely a routing mechanism in the executor — the function runs identically every time and the executor just fires a different outgoing wire. No driver changes needed.\n   - The counter is passed as an implicit argument to the function — the function can behave differently on iteration 2 vs. iteration 5. This requires every driver to support it.\n\n   You said \"part of the driver\" — leaning toward option 2. Is that right?\n\n3. **Wraparound or one-shot?** When the counter exceeds the number of output paths, does it wrap back to path 0 (round-robin), or does it stop firing after one full pass?\n\n4. **Output path names**: Are the N paths named by index (`out_0`, `out_1`, ...) like variadic inputs, or by user-defined names set in the inspector?\n\n5. **Single-output consistency**: My reading is that the function still returns one value — the iterator just decides *which wire* to put that value on. Is that right, or can the output itself change per iteration?\n\nThe answer to #2 especially determines whether this is a driver contract change or purely an executor/editor change."
      }]

          "content":"# 221 — Iterator box: round-robin output routing with per-instance counter\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nNo mechanism exists for a box to distribute output across multiple\ndownstream paths in sequence. The comparator routes based on a value\nthreshold; the iterator routes based on a counter that advances each call.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\n### What it does\nAn iterator box receives one input value and routes it to one of N named\noutput wires. Which wire fires is determined by an internal counter that\nincrements each call and wraps back to 0 after the last output. The\nfunction itself is a dumb passthrough — it does not make the routing\ndecision. The executor does, based on the counter.\n\nUseful for distributing work across parallel paths, cycling through a\nlist of consumers, or producing round-robin load balancing in the graph.\n\n### Counter model\nThe counter is per-box-instance, stored in the executor's in-memory\nstate (keyed by box ID). It resets to 0 at the start of each run.\nPersistence across runs is not in scope; that is a separate issue.\n\nIn the compiler output (issue 219), the counter becomes a local variable\nin a generated closure — same reset-per-program-start behavior.\n\nWrap-around: `counter = (counter + 1) % #iterator_outputs`\n\n### The iterator function\nEach language ships a standard iterator function in `libs/`:\n\n```\nlibs/iterator.lua   — M.iterate(data, counter) → data\nlibs/iterator.sh    — function iterate() { echo \"$1\"; }   (first arg is data)\nlibs/iterator.c     — trivial: reads argv[2] (data), prints it to stdout\n```\n\nThe function is a passthrough. It receives `data` as the first argument\nand `counter` as the second (implicit, injected by the executor). It\nreturns `data` unchanged. The counter argument is available to the function\nin case a user wants to inspect it, but the routing decision is entirely\nin the executor.\n\nThe user points the box's `ref` and `fn` at the appropriate language's\niterator lib file. The `iterator_outputs` field in the box JSON is what\nflags the executor to treat this box as an iterator rather than a plain\ncall box.\n\n### Data model\nBox JSON gains an `iterator_outputs` field — an ordered array of\nuser-defined output path names:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"router\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"ref\": \"libs/iterator.lua\",\n  \"fn\": \"iterate\",\n  \"inputs\": [{\"name\": \"data\", \"type\": \"any\"}],\n  \"iterator_outputs\": [\"path_a\", \"path_b\", \"path_c\"],\n  \"connections\": [\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"router\", \"from_branch\": \"path_a\",\n      \"to_box\": \"worker-a\", \"to_input\": \"data\"\n    },\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"router\", \"from_branch\": \"path_b\",\n      \"to_box\": \"worker-b\", \"to_input\": \"data\"\n    },\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"router\", \"from_branch\": \"path_c\",\n      \"to_box\": \"worker-c\", \"to_input\": \"data\"\n    }\n  ]\n}\n```\n\n`from_branch` is reused for iterator output names — the same field that\nholds \"lt\"/\"eq\"/\"gt\" for comparators. The executor checks whether the\nbox has `iterator_outputs`; if so, it fires only the connection whose\n`from_branch` matches `iterator_outputs[counter]`.\n\n### Auto-grow output slots\nConnecting a wire to the last slot of the iterator's output side appends\na new empty named slot — identical to the auto-grow behavior for variadic\ninputs (issue 217). The user names each slot in the inspector. Connecting\nto the last slot prompts for a name and grows the list. Disconnecting\nremoves the slot and compacts (same rename-and-compact logic as variadic\ninputs).\n\n### Executor changes\nIn `fire_connections`, a new branch handles iterator boxes:\n\n```\nif box.iterator_outputs and #box.iterator_outputs > 0:\n    counter = executor_state[box.id .. \".counter\"] or 0\n    target_branch = box.iterator_outputs[counter + 1]  -- 1-indexed in Lua\n    fire only connections where from_branch == target_branch\n    executor_state[box.id .. \".counter\"] = (counter + 1) % #box.iterator_outputs\n```\n\nThe counter state table lives alongside the existing value store in\nthe executor.\n\n### Driver contract addition\nThe executor injects the counter as an additional argument when invoking\nthe driver for an iterator box. It is appended after the declared inputs:\n\n  `<driver> <file> <fn> <arg_count+1> [data_args...] <counter>`\n\nThe iterator lib functions accept it as the last positional parameter.\nNon-iterator call boxes are unaffected — they never receive the extra arg.\n\n### Inspector changes\nThe inspector shows:\n- An \"iterator\" toggle per box (like the variadic toggle on inputs)\n- When toggled on: the output side of the box renders named slots instead\n  of a single dot; a \"+\" row at the bottom adds a new slot\n- Each slot name is editable inline\n- The current counter value is shown as a read-only display (useful for\n  debugging live runs)\n\n### Compiler output (issue 219 integration)\nFor an iterator box, the compiler generates a closure with a captured\ncounter variable:\n\n```lua\nlocal router_counter = 0\nlocal function router(data)\n  local idx = router_counter\n  router_counter = (router_counter + 1) % 3\n  if     idx == 0 then worker_a(data)\n  elseif idx == 1 then worker_b(data)\n  else                  worker_c(data)\n  end\nend\n```\n\nThe iterator lib files are bundled alongside other box source files.\n\n## Open questions\n- Should the counter be exposed as a readable data port (wirable to\n  another box as an input) in addition to being shown in the inspector?\n- Should auto-grow prompt for the output name immediately on connect, or\n  generate a placeholder (`out_N`) that the user renames afterward?\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. `libs/iterator.lua` — trivial passthrough function.\n2. `libs/iterator.sh`, `libs/iterator.c` — same for bash and C.\n3. `src/001-schema.lua` — add `iterator_outputs` to the box validator.\n4. `src/004-executor.lua` — add counter state table; extend\n   `fire_connections` with the iterator branch; inject counter arg in\n   `run_task` when box has `iterator_outputs`.\n5. `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — iterator toggle; editable output slots.\n6. `assets/js/006-wires.js` — auto-grow output slots on connect;\n   auto-shrink + rename on disconnect (mirrors variadic input logic).\n7. `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — render N named output dots when\n   `iterator_outputs` is set (replacing the single-wire dot).\n\n## Relevant files\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — fire_connections, run_task\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — box validator\n- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — iterator toggle, slot editor\n- `assets/js/006-wires.js` — auto-grow/shrink for output slots\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box rendering\n- `issues/217-concat-box-and-dynamic-inputs.md` — variadic input model\n  (auto-grow/shrink logic mirrors this)\n- `issues/completed/108-branch-box-and-predicate-routing.md` — comparator\n  model that `from_branch` and the routing pattern extend from\n- `issues/219-map-compiler.md` — compiler integration notes above\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/221-iterator-box.md"
        },
        "id":"toolu_01SYGnzgbS9BWDHr1n6pbdUe"

The `iterator_outputs` field in the box JSON is what\nflags the executor to treat this box as an iterator rather than a plain\ncall box.\n\n### Data model\nBox JSON gains an `iterator_outputs` field — an ordered array of\nuser-defined output path names:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"router\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"ref\": \"libs/iterator.lua\",\n  \"fn\": \"iterate\",\n  \"inputs\": [{\"name\": \"data\", \"type\": \"any\"}],\n  \"iterator_outputs\": [\"path_a\", \"path_b\", \"path_c\"],\n  \"connections\": [\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"router\", \"from_branch\": \"path_a\",\n      \"to_box\": \"worker-a\", \"to_input\": \"data\"\n    },\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"router\", \"from_branch\": \"path_b\",\n      \"to_box\": \"worker-b\", \"to_input\": \"data\"\n    },\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"router\", \"from_branch\": \"path_c\",\n      \"to_box\": \"worker-c\", \"to_input\": \"data\"\n    }\n  ]\n}\n```\n\n`from_branch` is reused for iterator output names — the same field that\nholds \"lt\"/\"eq\"/\"gt\" for comparators. The executor checks whether the\nbox has `iterator_outputs`; if so, it fires only the connection whose\n`from_branch` matches `iterator_outputs[counter]`.\n\n### Auto-grow output slots\nConnecting a wire to the last slot of the iterator's output side appends\na new empty named slot — identical to the auto-grow behavior for variadic\ninputs (issue 217). The user names each slot in the inspector. Connecting\nto the last slot prompts for a name and grows the list. Disconnecting\nremoves the slot and compacts (same rename-and-compact logic as variadic\ninputs).\n\n### Executor changes\nIn `fire_connections`, a new branch handles iterator boxes:\n\n```\nif box.iterator_outputs and #box.iterator_outputs > 0:\n    counter = executor_state[box.id .. \".counter\"] or 0\n    target_branch = box.iterator_outputs[counter + 1]  -- 1-indexed in Lua\n    fire only connections where from_branch == target_branch\n    executor_state[box.id .. \".counter\"] = (counter + 1) % #box.iterator_outputs\n```\n\nThe counter state table lives alongside the existing value store in\nthe executor.\n\n### Driver contract addition\nThe executor injects the counter as an additional argument when invoking\nthe driver for an iterator box. It is appended after the declared inputs:\n\n  `<driver> <file> <fn> <arg_count+1> [data_args...] <counter>`\n\nThe iterator lib functions accept it as the last positional parameter.\nNon-iterator call boxes are unaffected — they never receive the extra arg.\n\n### Inspector changes\nThe inspector shows:\n- An \"iterator\" toggle per box (like the variadic toggle on inputs)\n- When toggled on: the output side of the box renders named slots instead\n  of a single dot; a \"+\" row at the bottom adds a new slot\n- Each slot name is editable inline\n- The current counter value is shown as a read-only display (useful for\n  debugging live runs)\n\n### Compiler output (issue 219 integration)\nFor an iterator box, the compiler generates a closure with a captured\ncounter variable:\n\n```lua\nlocal router_counter = 0\nlocal function router(data)\n  local idx = router_counter\n  router_counter = (router_counter + 1) % 3\n  if     idx == 0 then worker_a(data)\n  elseif idx == 1 then worker_b(data)\n  else                  worker_c(data)\n  end\nend\n```\n\nThe iterator lib files are bundled alongside other box source files.\n\n## Open questions\n- Should the counter be exposed as a readable data port (wirable to\n  another box as an input) in addition to being shown in the inspector?\n- Should auto-grow prompt for the output name immediately on connect, or\n  generate a placeholder (`out_N`) that the user renames afterward?\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. `libs/iterator.lua` — trivial passthrough function.\n2. `libs/iterator.sh`, `libs/iterator.c` — same for bash and C.\n3. `src/001-schema.lua` — add `iterator_outputs` to the box validator.\n4. `src/004-executor.lua` — add counter state table; extend\n   `fire_connections` with the iterator branch; inject counter arg in\n   `run_task` when box has `iterator_outputs`.\n5. `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — iterator toggle; editable output slots.\n6. `assets/js/006-wires.js` — auto-grow output slots on connect;\n   auto-shrink + rename on disconnect (mirrors variadic input logic).\n7. `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — render N named output dots when\n   `iterator_outputs` is set (replacing the single-wire dot).\n\n## Relevant files\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — fire_connections, run_task\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — box validator\n- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — iterator toggle, slot editor\n- `assets/js/006-wires.js` — auto-grow/shrink for output slots\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box rendering\n- `issues/217-concat-box-and-dynamic-inputs.md` — variadic input model\n  (auto-grow/shrink logic mirrors this)\n- `issues/completed/108-branch-box-and-predicate-routing.md` — comparator\n  model that `from_branch` and the routing pattern extend from\n- `issues/219-map-compiler.md` — compiler integration notes above\n"
  },

{
  "timestamp":"2026-05-09T01:24:02.852Z",
  "message":{
    "content":"So, I'm thinking about the threading model now, and I think I have a clearer picture of how it'll work. Basically, if you examine the thread pool architecture from 3d-rts, how it works is there's a task queue that threads have tasks assigned from. There's priority settings and stuff but don't worry about that now, it's not relevant. In the soramech system, whenever a box is run, we should create a task in the pthreads thread pool, which basically is just... creating a pointer to the function (or in our case, whatever wrapper we need to call the function as a pthreads call. Can C call lua functions for example? We'll need to make it work that way.) Also, we'll be marking some shared memory where the arguments and return values live, and also pointing to any dependencies. These are things that we can infer from the map status. Then, once it's correctly initialized, the task goes on the queue, gets picked up by one of the threads, then executes. Easy. If the task is blocked, it's put in the queue of the thing that's blocking it, and (this part is crucial) once the blocking task completes, instead of moving on to work on the tasks that are blocked by it, the tasks that just got cleared to continue, it instead re-adds them to the task queue. I want to emphasize that this re-adding process, and the act of adding the task to the blocking task's \"queue\", does not involve re-allocation of memory, or recreating the task struct or anything like that. Instead, we're just shuffling pointers around.\n\nAnyway, the iterator, when it completes, it should re-create it's self in the task queue with +1 to it's counter (or reset to 0 of course), and it should be blocked by the task that's supplying it with input arguments. If there are input arguments already waiting to be iterated upon, then of course it should simply point to them with the incremented counter and create that task. It should do them one-at-a-time, so if there's like 10 input values waiting, it should process them one-by-one. Just to make sure it gets them all. The ordering doesn't matter so much, but it's a nice benefit that they should end up in the correct order in this way.\n\n  On the driver contract addition: injecting the counter as an extra positional argument after declared inputs means every driver needs to handle it being\n  there for iterator boxes. It's simple but it's a contract extension — any user-written driver for a new language would need to document that iterator\n  boxes get an extra last arg.\n\n\nor it could just be the first argument. That might be easier. Usually variadic inputs are put at the end, and functions can only accept one variadic input. Unless it can infer from types or something... But let's assume there's only one variadic input. It might get messy otherwise. What do you think?\n\n  The open question about auto-grow naming: the variadic input model prompts after connect. For output slots it might actually be better to generate out_N\n  immediately (no interruption to the wiring action) and let the user rename at their leisure in the inspector, since the name is just a label for routing\n  — you don't need to know it to complete the wire.\n\n\nyeah that's fine. Just so long as we update once we know the user-defined name.",
    "role":"user"

        "text":"This is a clear model. Let me answer the questions inline, then update the issue and the threading doc.\n\n**On C calling Lua:** Yes. The Lua C API (`lua_State`, `lua_pcall`) is designed for exactly this. Each pthread worker gets its own `lua_State` initialized at thread start — Lua states aren't thread-safe but one per thread is fine. The task wrapper (the C function pthreads actually calls) does: look at the task's language tag → if Lua, call through the thread's `lua_State`; if native C, call the function pointer directly; if bash, it's the one case that still needs a subprocess. That wrapper is the thing every language integration needs to implement — not the user's box function, but the per-language \"how do I invoke this from a pthread\" shim.\n\n**On counter position:** First arg makes more sense than last. The reason: last-arg convention is for variadic tails (you don't know where variadic ends, so you put the fixed stuff first). The counter isn't variadic — it's always exactly one value. But putting it last means the driver has to know the total arg count to find it, which is awkward. Putting it first means the driver always finds it at position 0 with no counting. For the passthrough functions: `M.iterate(counter, data)` in Lua, `function iterate { local counter=\"$1\"; local data=\"$2\"; ... }` in bash. Clean and unambiguous.\n\n**On auto-grow naming:** confirmed — generate `out_0`, `out_1` etc. immediately, update when renamed.\n\nNow updating the issue and the threading doc:"
