    "originalFile":"# 221 — Iterator box: round-robin output routing with per-instance counter\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nNo mechanism exists for a box to distribute output across multiple\ndownstream paths in sequence. The comparator routes based on a value\nthreshold; the iterator routes based on a counter that advances each call.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\n### What it does\nAn iterator box receives one input value and routes it to one of N named\noutput wires. Which wire fires is determined by an internal counter that\nincrements each call and wraps back to 0 after the last output. The\nfunction itself is a dumb passthrough — it does not make the routing\ndecision. The executor does, based on the counter.\n\nUseful for distributing work across parallel paths, cycling through a\nlist of consumers, or producing round-robin load balancing in the graph.\n\n### Counter model\nThe counter is per-box-instance, stored in the executor's in-memory\nstate (keyed by box ID). It resets to 0 at the start of each run.\nPersistence across runs is not in scope; that is a separate issue.\n\nIn the compiler output (issue 219), the counter becomes a local variable\nin a generated closure — same reset-per-program-start behavior.\n\nWrap-around: `counter = (counter + 1) % #iterator_outputs`\n\n### The iterator function\nEach language ships a standard iterator function in `libs/`:\n\n```\nlibs/iterator.lua   — M.iterate(data, counter) → data\nlibs/iterator.sh    — function iterate() { echo \"$1\"; }   (first arg is data)\nlibs/iterator.c     — trivial: reads argv[2] (data), prints it to stdout\n```\n\nThe function is a passthrough. It receives `data` as the first argument\nand `counter` as the second (implicit, injected by the executor). It\nreturns `data` unchanged. The counter argument is available to the function\nin case a user wants to inspect it, but the routing decision is entirely\nin the executor.\n\nThe user points the box's `ref` and `fn` at the appropriate language's\niterator lib file. The `iterator_outputs` field in the box JSON is what\nflags the executor to treat this box as an iterator rather than a plain\ncall box.\n\n### Data model\nBox JSON gains an `iterator_outputs` field — an ordered array of\nuser-defined output path names:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"router\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"ref\": \"libs/iterator.lua\",\n  \"fn\": \"iterate\",\n  \"inputs\": [{\"name\": \"data\", \"type\": \"any\"}],\n  \"iterator_outputs\": [\"path_a\", \"path_b\", \"path_c\"],\n  \"connections\": [\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"router\", \"from_branch\": \"path_a\",\n      \"to_box\": \"worker-a\", \"to_input\": \"data\"\n    },\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"router\", \"from_branch\": \"path_b\",\n      \"to_box\": \"worker-b\", \"to_input\": \"data\"\n    },\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"router\", \"from_branch\": \"path_c\",\n      \"to_box\": \"worker-c\", \"to_input\": \"data\"\n    }\n  ]\n}\n```\n\n`from_branch` is reused for iterator output names — the same field that\nholds \"lt\"/\"eq\"/\"gt\" for comparators. The executor checks whether the\nbox has `iterator_outputs`; if so, it fires only the connection whose\n`from_branch` matches `iterator_outputs[counter]`.\n\n### Auto-grow output slots\nConnecting a wire to the last slot of the iterator's output side appends\na new empty named slot — identical to the auto-grow behavior for variadic\ninputs (issue 217). The user names each slot in the inspector. Connecting\nto the last slot prompts for a name and grows the list. Disconnecting\nremoves the slot and compacts (same rename-and-compact logic as variadic\ninputs).\n\n### Executor changes\nIn `fire_connections`, a new branch handles iterator boxes:\n\n```\nif box.iterator_outputs and #box.iterator_outputs > 0:\n    counter = executor_state[box.id .. \".counter\"] or 0\n    target_branch = box.iterator_outputs[counter + 1]  -- 1-indexed in Lua\n    fire only connections where from_branch == target_branch\n    executor_state[box.id .. \".counter\"] = (counter + 1) % #box.iterator_outputs\n```\n\nThe counter state table lives alongside the existing value store in\nthe executor.\n\n### Driver contract addition\nThe executor injects the counter as an additional argument when invoking\nthe driver for an iterator box. a \"+\" row at the bottom adds a new slot\n- Each slot name is editable inline\n- The current counter value is shown as a read-only display (useful for\n  debugging live runs)\n\n### Compiler output (issue 219 integration)\nFor an iterator box, the compiler generates a closure with a captured\ncounter variable:\n\n```lua\nlocal router_counter = 0\nlocal function router(data)\n  local idx = router_counter\n  router_counter = (router_counter + 1) % 3\n  if     idx == 0 then worker_a(data)\n  elseif idx == 1 then worker_b(data)\n  else                  worker_c(data)\n  end\nend\n```\n\nThe iterator lib files are bundled alongside other box source files.\n\n## Open questions\n- Should the counter be exposed as a readable data port (wirable to\n  another box as an input) in addition to being shown in the inspector?\n- Should auto-grow prompt for the output name immediately on connect, or\n  generate a placeholder (`out_N`) that the user renames afterward?\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. `libs/iterator.lua` — trivial passthrough function.\n2. `libs/iterator.sh`, `libs/iterator.c` — same for bash and C.\n3. `src/001-schema.lua` — add `iterator_outputs` to the box validator.\n4. `src/004-executor.lua` — add counter state table;     "originalFile":"# 221 — Iterator box: round-robin output routing with per-instance counter\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nNo mechanism exists for a box to distribute output across multiple\ndownstream paths in sequence. The comparator routes based on a value\nthreshold; the iterator routes based on a counter that advances each call.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\n### What it does\nAn iterator box receives one input value and routes it to one of N named\noutput wires. Which wire fires is determined by an internal counter that\nincrements each call and wraps back to 0 after the last output. The\nfunction itself is a dumb passthrough — it does not make the routing\ndecision. The executor does, based on the counter.\n\nUseful for distributing work across parallel paths, cycling through a\nlist of consumers, or producing round-robin load balancing in the graph.\n\n### Counter model\nThe counter is per-box-instance, stored in the executor's in-memory\nstate (keyed by box ID). It resets to 0 at the start of each run.\nPersistence across runs is not in scope; that is a separate issue.\n\nIn the compiler output (issue 219), the counter becomes a local variable\nin a generated closure — same reset-per-program-start behavior.\n\nWrap-around: `counter = (counter + 1) % #iterator_outputs`\n\n### The iterator function\nEach language ships a standard iterator function in `libs/`:\n\n```\nlibs/iterator.lua  — M.iterate(counter, data) → data\nlibs/iterator.sh   — function iterate() { local counter=\"$1\"; echo \"$2\"; }\nlibs/iterator.c    — reads argv[2] (counter), argv[3] (data); prints data\n```\n\nThe counter is the FIRST argument (position 0 in the driver's arg list,\nbefore the declared inputs). This is intentional: last-arg convention is\nfor variadic tails where the count is unknown; the counter is always\nexactly one value and is always findable at position 0 without counting.\nThe function returns `data` unchanged. The routing decision is entirely\nin the executor.\n\nThe user points the box's `ref` and `fn` at the appropriate language's\niterator lib file. The `iterator_outputs` field in the box JSON is what\nflags the executor to treat this box as an iterator rather than a plain\ncall box.\n\n### Data model\nBox JSON gains an `iterator_outputs` field — an ordered array of\nuser-defined output path names:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"router\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"ref\": \"libs/iterator.lua\",\n  \"fn\": \"iterate\",\n  \"inputs\": [{\"name\": \"data\", \"type\": \"any\"}],\n  \"iterator_outputs\": [\"path_a\", \"path_b\", \"path_c\"],\n  \"connections\": [\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"router\", \"from_branch\": \"path_a\",\n      \"to_box\": \"worker-a\", \"to_input\": \"data\"\n    },\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"router\", \"from_branch\": \"path_b\",\n      \"to_box\": \"worker-b\", \"to_input\": \"data\"\n    },\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"router\", \"from_branch\": \"path_c\",\n      \"to_box\": \"worker-c\", \"to_input\": \"data\"\n    }\n  ]\n}\n```\n\n`from_branch` is reused for iterator output names — the same field that\nholds \"lt\"/\"eq\"/\"gt\" for comparators. The executor checks whether the\nbox has `iterator_outputs`; if so, it fires only the connection whose\n`from_branch` matches `iterator_outputs[counter]`.\n\n### Auto-grow output slots\nConnecting a wire to the last slot of the iterator's output side appends\na new empty named slot — identical to the auto-grow behavior for variadic\ninputs (issue 217). The user names each slot in the inspector. Connecting\nto the last slot prompts for a name and grows the list. Disconnecting\nremoves the slot and compacts (same rename-and-compact logic as variadic\ninputs).\n\n### Executor changes\nIn `fire_connections`, a new branch handles iterator boxes:\n\n```\nif box.iterator_outputs and #box.iterator_outputs > 0:\n    counter = executor_state[box.id .. \".counter\"] or 0\n    target_branch = box.iterator_outputs[counter + 1]  -- 1-indexed in Lua\n    fire only connections where from_branch == target_branch\n    executor_state[box.id .. \".counter\"] = (counter + 1) % #box.iterator_outputs\n```\n\nThe counter state table lives alongside the existing value store in\nthe executor.\n\n### Driver contract addition\nThe executor injects the counter as an additional argument when invoking\nthe driver for an iterator box. It is appended after the declared inputs:\n\n  `<driver> <file> <fn> <arg_count+1> [data_args...] <counter>`\n\nThe iterator lib functions accept it as the last positional parameter.\nNon-iterator call boxes are unaffected — they never receive the extra arg.\n\n### Inspector changes\nThe inspector shows:\n- An \"iterator\" toggle per box (like the variadic toggle on inputs)\n- When toggled on: the output side of the box renders named slots instead\n  of a single dot; a \"+\" row at the bottom adds a new slot\n- Each slot name is editable inline\n- The current counter value is shown as a read-only display (useful for\n  debugging live runs)\n\n### Compiler output (issue 219 integration)\nFor an iterator box, the compiler generates a closure with a captured\ncounter variable:\n\n```lua\nlocal router_counter = 0\nlocal function router(data)\n  local idx = router_counter\n  router_counter = (router_counter + 1) % 3\n  if     idx == 0 then worker_a(data)\n  elseif idx == 1 then worker_b(data)\n  else                  worker_c(data)\n  end\nend\n```\n\nThe iterator lib files are bundled alongside other box source files.\n\n## Open questions\n- Should the counter be exposed as a readable data port (wirable to\n  another box as an input) in addition to being shown in the inspector?\n- Should auto-grow prompt for the output name immediately on connect, or\n  generate a placeholder (`out_N`) that the user renames afterward?\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. `libs/iterator.lua` — trivial passthrough function.\n2. `libs/iterator.sh`, `libs/iterator.c` — same for bash and C.\n3. `src/001-schema.lua` — add `iterator_outputs` to the box validator.\n4. `src/004-executor.lua` — add counter state table; extend\n   `fire_connections` with the iterator branch; inject counter arg in\n   `run_task` when box has `iterator_outputs`.\n5. `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — iterator toggle; editable output slots.\n6. `assets/js/006-wires.js` — auto-grow output slots on connect;\n   auto-shrink + rename on disconnect (mirrors variadic input logic).\n7. `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — render N named output dots when\n   `iterator_outputs` is set (replacing the single-wire dot).\n\n## Relevant files\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — fire_connections, run_task\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — box validator\n- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — iterator toggle, slot editor\n- `assets/js/006-wires.js` — auto-grow/shrink for output slots\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box rendering\n- `issues/217-concat-box-and-dynamic-inputs.md` — variadic input model\n  (auto-grow/shrink logic mirrors this)\n- `issues/completed/108-branch-box-and-predicate-routing.md` — comparator\n  model that `from_branch` and the routing pattern extend from\n- `issues/219-map-compiler.md` — compiler integration notes above\n",

        "input":{
          "new_string":"### Threading model integration (3d-rts thread pool)\n\nIn the pthreads task pool, each box execution is a task struct containing:\n- A function pointer to the language-specific invocation wrapper\n- A pointer to shared memory holding the input arguments and return value\n- A pointer list of dependency tasks (upstream boxes whose output this box\n  needs before it can run)\n- For iterator boxes: a `counter` field (integer, part of the task struct)\n\n**Blocking:** when a task cannot run because its dependencies haven't\ncompleted, it is placed in the blocking task's waiting list. No memory is\nallocated — the task struct stays alive, only a pointer to it is moved.\nWhen the blocking task completes and writes its return value to shared\nmemory, it walks its waiting list and re-adds each waiting task to the\nmain queue (again, pointer move only — no reallocation or struct copying).\n\n**Iterator self-re-add:** when an iterator task completes, it does not\nterminate. Instead:\n1. It increments its own `counter` field (or wraps to 0).\n2. It checks if there is another pending input value in its input queue.\n3. If yes: it updates its input pointer to the next pending value, then\n   re-adds itself to the main task queue. No new allocation.\n4. If no: it adds itself to the waiting list of its upstream dependency,\n   to be re-added when the next input value arrives.\n\nThis means the iterator task struct is allocated once and lives for the\nduration of the run, cycling through the queue as many times as there are\ninput values to process. Input values are processed one-at-a-time in\narrival order — if 10 values are queued, the iterator visits the queue 10\ntimes, each time firing a different output path and advancing the counter.\n\n**C calling Lua:** the per-thread invocation wrapper is a C function\n(pthreads requires a C entry point). Each worker thread initializes its\nown `lua_State` at startup — Lua states are not thread-safe but one per\nthread is fine. The wrapper dispatches on language tag: if Lua, calls\nthrough the thread's `lua_State` via `lua_pcall`; if native C, calls the\nfunction pointer directly (no interpreter overhead); if bash, spawns a\nsubprocess (the one case that doesn't map cleanly to pthreads — see\ndocs/004-ipc-and-threading.md for options).\n\n## Open questions",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/221-iterator-box.md",
          "replace_all":false,
          "old_string":"## Open questions"
        },
        "id":"toolu_01Ub4H1WgLChoYF1Sn2p8TGW"
      }]

    "originalFile":"# 221 — Iterator box: round-robin output routing with per-instance counter\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nNo mechanism exists for a box to distribute output across multiple\ndownstream paths in sequence. The comparator routes based on a value\nthreshold; the iterator routes based on a counter that advances each call.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\n### What it does\nAn iterator box receives one input value and routes it to one of N named\noutput wires. Which wire fires is determined by an internal counter that\nincrements each call and wraps back to 0 after the last output. The\nfunction itself is a dumb passthrough — it does not make the routing\ndecision. The executor does, based on the counter.\n\nUseful for distributing work across parallel paths, cycling through a\nlist of consumers, or producing round-robin load balancing in the graph.\n\n### Counter model\nThe counter is per-box-instance, stored in the executor's in-memory\nstate (keyed by box ID). It resets to 0 at the start of each run.\nPersistence across runs is not in scope; that is a separate issue.\n\nIn the compiler output (issue 219), the counter becomes a local variable\nin a generated closure — same reset-per-program-start behavior.\n\nWrap-around: `counter = (counter + 1) % #iterator_outputs`\n\n### The iterator function\nEach language ships a standard iterator function in `libs/`:\n\n```\nlibs/iterator.lua  — M.iterate(counter, data) → data\nlibs/iterator.sh   — function iterate() { local counter=\"$1\"; echo \"$2\"; }\nlibs/iterator.c    — reads argv[2] (counter), argv[3] (data); prints data\n```\n\nThe counter is the FIRST argument (position 0 in the driver's arg list,\nbefore the declared inputs). This is intentional: last-arg convention is\nfor variadic tails where the count is unknown; the counter is always\nexactly one value and is always findable at position 0 without counting.\nThe function returns `data` unchanged. The routing decision is entirely\nin the executor.\n\nThe user points the box's `ref` and `fn` at the appropriate language's\niterator lib file. The `iterator_outputs` field in the box JSON is what\nflags the executor to treat this box as an iterator rather than a plain\ncall box.\n\n### Data model\nBox JSON gains an `iterator_outputs` field — an ordered array of\nuser-defined output path names:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"router\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"ref\": \"libs/iterator.lua\",\n  \"fn\": \"iterate\",\n  \"inputs\": [{\"name\": \"data\", \"type\": \"any\"}],\n  \"iterator_outputs\": [\"path_a\", \"path_b\", \"path_c\"],\n  \"connections\": [\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"router\", \"from_branch\": \"path_a\",\n      \"to_box\": \"worker-a\", \"to_input\": \"data\"\n    },\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"router\", \"from_branch\": \"path_b\",\n      \"to_box\": \"worker-b\", \"to_input\": \"data\"\n    },\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"router\", \"from_branch\": \"path_c\",\n      \"to_box\": \"worker-c\", \"to_input\": \"data\"\n    }\n  ]\n}\n```\n\n`from_branch` is reused for iterator output names — the same field that\nholds \"lt\"/\"eq\"/\"gt\" for comparators. The executor checks whether the\nbox has `iterator_outputs`; if so, it fires only the connection whose\n`from_branch` matches `iterator_outputs[counter]`.\n\n### Auto-grow output slots\nConnecting a wire to the last slot of the iterator's output side appends\na new empty named slot — identical to the auto-grow behavior for variadic\ninputs (issue 217). The user names each slot in the inspector. Connecting\nto the last slot prompts for a name and grows the list. Disconnecting\nremoves the slot and compacts (same rename-and-compact logic as variadic\ninputs).\n\n### Executor changes\nIn `fire_connections`, a new branch handles iterator boxes:\n\n```\nif box.iterator_outputs and #box.iterator_outputs > 0:\n    counter = executor_state[box.id .. \".counter\"] or 0\n    target_branch = box.iterator_outputs[counter + 1]  -- 1-indexed in Lua\n    fire only connections where from_branch == target_branch\n    executor_state[box.id .. \".counter\"] = (counter + 1) % #box.iterator_outputs\n```\n\nThe counter state table lives alongside the existing value store in\nthe executor.\n\n### Driver contract addition\nThe executor injects the counter as the first argument when invoking the\ndriver for an iterator box, before any declared input values:\n\n  `<driver> <file> <fn> <arg_count+1> <counter> [data_args...]`\n\nThe counter is always at position 0 in the arg list — no counting required\nto find it. Non-iterator call boxes are unaffected.\n\n### Inspector changes\nThe inspector shows:\n- An \"iterator\" toggle per box (like the variadic toggle on inputs)\n- When toggled on: the output side of the box renders named slots instead\n  of a single dot; a \"+\" row at the bottom adds a new slot\n- Each slot name is editable inline\n- The current counter value is shown as a read-only display (useful for\n  debugging live runs)\n\n### Compiler output (issue 219 integration)\nFor an iterator box, the compiler generates a closure with a captured\ncounter variable:\n\n```lua\nlocal router_counter = 0\nlocal function router(data)\n  local idx = router_counter\n  router_counter = (router_counter + 1) % 3\n  if     idx == 0 then worker_a(data)\n  elseif idx == 1 then worker_b(data)\n  else                  worker_c(data)\n  end\nend\n```\n\nThe iterator lib files are bundled alongside other box source files.\n\n## Open questions\n- Should the counter be exposed as a readable data port (wirable to\n  another box as an input) in addition to being shown in the inspector?\n- Should auto-grow prompt for the output name immediately on connect, or\n  generate a placeholder (`out_N`) that the user renames afterward?\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. `libs/iterator.lua` — trivial passthrough function.\n2. `libs/iterator.sh`, `libs/iterator.c` — same for bash and C.\n3. `src/001-schema.lua` — add `iterator_outputs` to the box validator.\n4. `src/004-executor.lua` — add counter state table; extend\n   `fire_connections` with the iterator branch; inject counter arg in\n   `run_task` when box has `iterator_outputs`.\n5. `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — iterator toggle; editable output slots.\n6. `assets/js/006-wires.js` — auto-grow output slots on connect;\n   auto-shrink + rename on disconnect (mirrors variadic input logic).\n7. `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — render N named output dots when\n   `iterator_outputs` is set (replacing the single-wire dot).\n\n## Relevant files\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — fire_connections, run_task\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — box validator\n- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — iterator toggle, slot editor\n- `assets/js/006-wires.js` — auto-grow/shrink for output slots\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box rendering\n- `issues/217-concat-box-and-dynamic-inputs.md` — variadic input model\n  (auto-grow/shrink logic mirrors this)\n- `issues/completed/108-branch-box-and-predicate-routing.md` — comparator\n  model that `from_branch` and the routing pattern extend from\n- `issues/219-map-compiler.md` — compiler integration notes above\n",
    "oldString":"## Open questions",
    "newString":"### Threading model integration (3d-rts thread pool)\n\nIn the pthreads task pool, each box execution is a task struct containing:\n- A function pointer to the language-specific invocation wrapper\n- A pointer to shared memory holding the input arguments and return value\n- A pointer list of dependency tasks (upstream boxes whose output this box\n  needs before it can run)\n- For iterator boxes: a `counter` field (integer, part of the task struct)\n\n**Blocking:** when a task cannot run because its dependencies haven't\ncompleted, it is placed in the blocking task's waiting list. No memory is\nallocated — the task struct stays alive, only a pointer to it is moved.\nWhen the blocking task completes and writes its return value to shared\nmemory, it walks its waiting list and re-adds each waiting task to the\nmain queue (again, pointer move only — no reallocation or struct copying).\n\n**Iterator self-re-add:** when an iterator task completes, it does not\nterminate. Instead:\n1. It increments its own `counter` field (or wraps to 0).\n2. It checks if there is another pending input value in its input queue.\n3. If yes: it updates its input pointer to the next pending value, then\n   re-adds itself to the main task queue. No new allocation.\n4. If no: it adds itself to the waiting list of its upstream dependency,\n   to be re-added when the next input value arrives.\n\nThis means the iterator task struct is allocated once and lives for the\nduration of the run, cycling through the queue as many times as there are\ninput values to process. Input values are processed one-at-a-time in\narrival order — if 10 values are queued, the iterator visits the queue 10\ntimes, each time firing a different output path and advancing the counter.\n\n**C calling Lua:** the per-thread invocation wrapper is a C function\n(pthreads requires a C entry point). Each worker thread initializes its\nown `lua_State` at startup — Lua states are not thread-safe but one per\nthread is fine. The wrapper dispatches on language tag: if Lua, calls\nthrough the thread's `lua_State` via `lua_pcall`; if native C, calls the\nfunction pointer directly (no interpreter overhead); if bash, spawns a\nsubprocess (the one case that doesn't map cleanly to pthreads — see\ndocs/004-ipc-and-threading.md for options).\n\n## Open questions",
    "replaceAll":false,
    "userModified":false
  },

Each box invocation shells out to\n6\ta driver script, which starts a new process, runs the function, and exits. The\n7\treturn value passes through stdout. This works but has two structural problems:\n8\t\n9\t1. **Process-per-call cost.** Spawning a process takes roughly 1–10 ms depending\n10\t   on the runtime. For a map with ten boxes, that's dominated by spawn overhead,\n11\t   not by the actual work.\n12\t\n13\t2. **stdout is the wrong channel.** A box function that prints debug output\n14\t   corrupts the wire value. Values are transient — they vanish once the pipe is\n15\t   drained. The channel has no addressing, no framing, and no backpressure.\n16\t\n17\tThe goal is a design where cross-language calls are fast, values are addressable,\n18\tand the execution model is ready to parallelize without redesign.\n19\t\n20\t---\n21\t\n22\t## The threading roadmap\n23\t\n24\tThree stages, each building on the last:\n25\t\n26\t**Stage 1 — Synchronous (current).** A single-threaded ready-queue walks the\n27\tgraph in dependency order. `run_task(box, inputs)` in `src/004-executor.lua` is\n28\tthe task boundary. No true parallelism yet, but the graph's natural\n34\tconcurrency is exploited without blocking the whole process.\n35\t\n36\t**Stage 3 — 3d-rts thread pool.** The `task_fn` boundary swaps in the thread\n37\tpool. Worker threads pull tasks from the pool; the coroutine scheduler is\n38\treplaced by OS-level scheduling. Cross-language calls block a worker thread\n39\twhile other threads continue. True parallelism across cores.\n40\t\n41\tEffil-jit is not used. The path is synchronous → coroutine → 3d-rts pool.\n42\t\n43\t---\n44\t\n45\t## The three IPC options",

      "content":"# SoraMech — IPC and Threading Model\n\n## The problem\n\nThe current executor runs boxes sequentially. Each box invocation shells out to\na driver script, which starts a new process, runs the function, and exits. The\nreturn value passes through stdout. This works but has two structural problems:\n\n1. **Process-per-call cost.** Spawning a process takes roughly 1–10 ms depending\n   on the runtime. For a map with ten boxes, that's dominated by spawn overhead,\n   not by the actual work.\n\n2. **stdout is the wrong channel.** A box function that prints debug output\n   corrupts the wire value. Values are transient — they vanish once the pipe is\n   drained. The channel has no addressing, no framing, and no backpressure.\n\nThe goal is a design where cross-language calls are fast, values are addressable,\nand the execution model is ready to parallelize without redesign.\n\n---\n\n## The threading roadmap\n\nThree stages, each building on the last:\n\n**Stage 1 — Synchronous (current).** A single-threaded ready-queue walks the\ngraph in dependency order. `run_task(box, inputs)` in `src/004-executor.lua` is\nthe task boundary. It blocks until the driver responds.\n\n**Stage 2 — Coroutine-based non-blocking.** The ready-queue becomes a coroutine\nscheduler. Boxes yield when waiting on upstream results or cross-language calls.\nLuaSocket non-blocking I/O lets the scheduler run other boxes while one is\nwaiting for a response. No true parallelism yet, but the graph's natural\nconcurrency is exploited without blocking the whole process.\n\n**Stage 3 — 3d-rts thread pool.** The `task_fn` boundary swaps in the thread\npool. Worker threads pull tasks from the pool; the coroutine scheduler is\nreplaced by OS-level scheduling. Cross-language calls block a worker thread\nwhile other threads continue. True parallelism across cores.\n\nEffil-jit is not used. The path is synchronous → coroutine → 3d-rts pool.\n\n---\n\n## The three IPC options"
    }
  },

          "new_string":"**Stage 3 — 3d-rts thread pool.** The `task_fn` boundary swaps in the thread\npool. Worker threads pull tasks from the pool; the coroutine scheduler is\nreplaced by OS-level scheduling. Cross-language calls block a worker thread\nwhile other threads continue. True parallelism across cores.\n\nEffil-jit is not used. The path is synchronous → coroutine → 3d-rts pool.\n\n---\n\n## Stage 3 detail: pthreads task model\n\nEach box execution in the thread pool is a **task struct** containing:\n\n- **Function pointer** — the language-specific invocation wrapper (a C\n  function, since pthreads requires a C entry point)\n- **Shared memory pointer** — the region holding the input arguments and\n  return value for this invocation\n- **Dependency list** — pointers to the tasks this task is waiting on\n- **Waiting list** — pointers to tasks that are waiting on this task\n- **Counter** (iterator boxes only) — current iteration index, updated\n  in-place when the iterator re-queues itself\n\nTask structs are allocated once at run start, one per box (not one per\ninvocation). They live for the entire run.\n\n### Blocking and unblocking — pointer-only transitions\n\nWhen a task cannot run (upstream output not yet available), it is placed\nin its upstream task's waiting list. This is a pointer move — no\nallocation, no struct copy. The task struct stays exactly where it is.\n\nWhen an upstream task completes and writes its return value to shared\nmemory, it walks its waiting list and re-adds each entry to the main task\nqueue. Again, a pointer move only. The unblocked task's struct is\nunchanged; only its position in the queue changes.\n\nThis means \"blocked\", \"queued\", and \"running\" are states defined by which\nlist a task's pointer currently lives in — not by any field in the struct.\n\n### Per-thread language runtimes\n\nEach worker thread initializes its own language runtimes at startup:\n- **Lua:** one `lua_State` per thread. Lua states are not thread-safe, but\n  one per thread requires no locking. The task wrapper calls the box\n  function via `lua_pcall`.\n- **C:** the compiled box function is called directly through the function\n  pointer. No interpreter, no overhead beyond the call itself.\n- **Bash/other:** a persistent subprocess per thread (Unix domain socket\n  server model — see Option 3 above). The task wrapper sends a request and\n  blocks the thread waiting for the response.\n\n### Iterator self-re-queue\n\nAn iterator task does not terminate after one invocation. When it\ncompletes:\n1. It increments its `counter` field in-place (or wraps to 0).\n2. It checks its input queue for the next pending value.\n3. If a value is waiting: it updates its input pointer and re-adds itself\n   to the main task queue. No allocation — the same task struct re-enters\n   the queue with updated state.\n4. If no value is waiting: it adds itself to the upstream task's waiting\n   list, to be re-added when the next input arrives.\n\nInput values are processed one-at-a-time in arrival order. Ten queued\ninputs means the iterator task visits the queue ten times, advancing the\ncounter and firing a different output path each time.",

    "originalFile":"# SoraMech — IPC and Threading Model\n\n## The problem\n\nThe current executor runs boxes sequentially. Each box invocation shells out to\na driver script, which starts a new process, runs the function, and exits. The\nreturn value passes through stdout. This works but has two structural problems:\n\n1. **Process-per-call cost.** Spawning a process takes roughly 1–10 ms depending\n   on the runtime. For a map with ten boxes, that's dominated by spawn overhead,\n   not by the actual work.\n\n2. **stdout is the wrong channel.** A box function that prints debug output\n   corrupts the wire value. Values are transient — they vanish once the pipe is\n   drained. The channel has no addressing, no framing, and no backpressure.\n\nThe goal is a design where cross-language calls are fast, values are addressable,\nand the execution model is ready to parallelize without redesign.\n\n---\n\n## The threading roadmap\n\nThree stages, each building on the last:\n\n**Stage 1 — Synchronous (current).** A single-threaded ready-queue walks the\ngraph in dependency order. `run_task(box, inputs)` in `src/004-executor.lua` is\nthe task boundary. It blocks until the driver responds.\n\n**Stage 2 — Coroutine-based non-blocking.** The ready-queue becomes a coroutine\nscheduler. Boxes yield when waiting on upstream results or cross-language calls.\nLuaSocket non-blocking I/O lets the scheduler run other boxes while one is\nwaiting for a response. No true parallelism yet, but the graph's natural\nconcurrency is exploited without blocking the whole process.\n\n**Stage 3 — 3d-rts thread pool.** The `task_fn` boundary swaps in the thread\npool. Worker threads pull tasks from the pool; the coroutine scheduler is\nreplaced by OS-level scheduling. Cross-language calls block a worker thread\nwhile other threads continue. True parallelism across cores.\n\nEffil-jit is not used. The path is synchronous → coroutine → 3d-rts pool.\n\n---\n\n## The three IPC options\n\n### Option 1 — LuaJIT FFI (Lua ↔ C, in-process)\n\nThe Foreign Function Interface lets Lua call C functions that live in a shared\nlibrary (`.so`) directly, in the same process, with no subprocess and no channel.\nYou provide a C declaration (`ffi.cdef[[ int add(int a, int b); ]]`), load the\ncompiled library (`ffi.load(\"./mybox.so\")`), and call `lib.add(3, 4)` — the CPU\njumps into native code and returns. Overhead is nanoseconds.\n\nSince the executor already does mtime-based dynamic compilation (see `drivers/c.sh`),\ncompiling to a `.so` instead of a binary is just a flag change (`-shared -fPIC`).\nThe box function signature changes from `main(argc, argv)` to a named function\nwith typed arguments — which is strictly cleaner.\n\n**Limitation:** FFI only works for languages that compile to a C-compatible ABI.\nBash cannot. Python can (via `ctypes` on the other side), but it's awkward.\nFFI is the right answer for Lua ↔ C only.\n\n**Cross-platform:** LuaJIT FFI works on Linux, macOS, and Windows. `.so` becomes\n`.dylib` on macOS and `.dll` on Windows — the `ffi.load()` call is portable if\nyou handle the extension.\n\n---\n\n### Option 2 — Shared memory (`shm_open` + `mmap`)\n\n`shm_open(\"/soramech-wire-0\", ...)` creates a named memory segment managed by\nthe kernel — not a file on disk, but a named object in RAM. `mmap()` maps it\ninto the calling process's address space. Any other process that opens the same\nname gets access to the *same physical memory*. A write in one process is\nimmediately visible in another — no copy, no syscall per access after setup.\n\nFor SoraMech, each wire between two boxes would correspond to a named shared\nmemory slot. The compiler (issue 219) generates the slot names and the read/write\ncalls. Any language that can call POSIX can participate:\n\n- Lua: via LuaJIT FFI calling `shm_open` + `mmap` from libc\n- C: natively\n- Bash: via `/dev/shm/<name>` — on Linux, the tmpfs backing shared memory is\n  exposed as a filesystem path, so bash can `cat /dev/shm/soramech-wire-0`\n\n**Performance:** After the initial `mmap()` setup, reads and writes are pointer\ndereferences — no syscalls, no copies. For small values (strings, numbers) this\nis essentially free.\n\n**Complication:** Shared memory is untyped raw bytes. You need a size header\n(how many bytes is this value?), a type tag (string? number? JSON object?), and\na synchronization mechanism (how does the reader know the writer is done?). None\nof these are hard — a small fixed header in the segment handles all three — but\nthe compiler must generate all of it correctly for every wire.\n\n**Cross-platform:**\n- Linux: full support. `/dev/shm/` filesystem exposure is Linux-specific.\n- macOS: `shm_open()` works, but the objects are NOT exposed as files. No\n  `/dev/shm/` path. Bash access via file path doesn't work.\n- Windows: completely different API (`CreateFileMapping` / `MapViewOfFile`).\n  No POSIX `shm_open` without WSL or Cygwin.\n\nShared memory is powerful but not the most portable option. The bash filesystem\nshortcut that makes it cross-language is Linux-only.\n\n---\n\n### Option 3 — Unix domain socket servers (chosen direction)\n\nA Unix domain socket is a socket addressed by a filesystem path instead of an\nIP address and port. `/tmp/soramech-bash.sock` is a special file; any process\non the same machine connects to it with the standard socket API. The kernel\nroutes data directly between processes in memory — no network stack, no loopback,\nno protocol headers. Performance is bounded by memory bandwidth.\n\nUnlike anonymous pipes, a socket has a name that unrelated processes can find\nwithout inheriting file descriptors. Multiple clients connect simultaneously;\neach gets its own channel. The server handles them with `accept()` in a loop.\n\n**The model for SoraMech:**\n\nEach language runtime runs as a persistent socket server. One server instance\nper language per worker thread:\n\n```\n/tmp/soramech-bash-0.sock   ← worker thread 0's bash runtime\n/tmp/soramech-bash-1.sock   ← worker thread 1's bash runtime\n/tmp/soramech-c-0.sock      ← worker thread 0's C runtime\n```\n\nThe server starts when the program starts, stays alive for the whole run, and\naccepts sequential requests — one box call at a time per instance. A Lua worker\nconnects to its designated socket, sends a framed request (function name +\narguments), and reads back a framed response (return value). The server is a\nsmall script (~50 lines) that sources or compiles the box file, calls the\nfunction, and writes the result.\n\n**Wire protocol:** Length-prefix framing. The sender writes a 4-byte big-endian\ninteger (the message length in bytes), then that many bytes of content. The\nreceiver reads 4 bytes, then reads exactly that many bytes. This handles values\ncontaining newlines or null bytes without ambiguity.\n\n**Cost of idle servers:** An idle server process is blocked on `accept()` — zero\nCPU, approximately 3–5 MB RSS for a bash process. For 10 languages × 4 threads\n= 40 processes ≈ 150–200 MB. Acceptable.\n\n**Integration with the coroutine scheduler (Stage 2):**\n\nWith LuaSocket non-blocking sockets, the coroutine that makes a cross-language\ncall does this:\n1. Connect to the language server socket (non-blocking)\n2. Send the request\n3. `coroutine.yield()` — registers the socket fd with the scheduler\n4. Scheduler polls all pending fds with `select()`\n5. When the fd is readable, scheduler resumes the coroutine\n6. Coroutine reads the response and continues\n\nThe cross-language call never blocks the main Lua thread. Other boxes run in\nother coroutines while the bash/C server is processing.\n\n**Integration with the 3d-rts thread pool (Stage 3):**\n\nEach worker thread owns its set of language server sockets. When `run_task` calls\na cross-language box, it sends to the socket and blocks on the read — the thread\nblocks, not the whole program. Other workers continue processing other boxes on\nother cores. The server processes run concurrently on whatever cores the OS\nschedules them to. This gives real parallelism: a bash box and a C box assigned\nto different workers can run simultaneously.\n\n**Cross-platform:**\n- Linux: full support.\n- macOS: full support. Unix domain sockets are POSIX.\n- Windows: supported since Windows 10 1803 (2018). `AF_UNIX` sockets work\n  natively. Most languages abstract this through their socket libraries.\n\nUnix domain sockets are the most portable cross-language IPC mechanism that also\nsupports concurrent connections. They are the chosen direction for the compiler\noutput and the coroutine/thread-pool executor.\n\n---\n\n## Summary comparison\n\n| Property              | FFI (.so)       | Shared memory       | Unix domain socket  |\n|-----------------------|-----------------|---------------------|---------------------|\n| Speed (per call)      | nanoseconds     | nanoseconds*        | microseconds        |\n| Languages supported   | C-ABI only      | any (with caveats)  | any                 |\n| Parallel connections  | N/A (in-process)| yes (with sync)     | yes (natural)       |\n| Linux                 | yes             | yes                 | yes                 |\n| macOS                 | yes             | partial†            | yes                 |\n| Windows               | yes (.dll)      | no (different API)  | yes (Win10+)        |\n| Complexity            | low             | medium              | low-medium          |\n\n*After initial mmap setup. †shm_open works; /dev/shm filesystem path does not.\n\nThe compiler (issue 219) uses FFI for Lua ↔ C wires where the C source is\ncompiled to a `.so`, and Unix domain sockets for all other cross-language wires.\nSame-language Lua wires are direct function calls — no IPC at all.\n\n---\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — `run_task` boundary, ready-queue\n- `src/007-runner-main.lua` — entry point for the interpreter path\n- `issues/219-map-compiler.md` — compiler that generates the IPC calls\n- `issues/104-runner-synchronous-executor.md` — task boundary design\n- `issues/213-queued-inputs-and-task-model.md` — queue-per-port, thread pool notes\n- `docs/002-roadmap.md` — phase plan for threading stages\n",
    "oldString":"**Stage 3 — 3d-rts thread pool.** The `task_fn` boundary swaps in the thread\npool. Worker threads pull tasks from the pool; the coroutine scheduler is\nreplaced by OS-level scheduling. Cross-language calls block a worker thread\nwhile other threads continue. True parallelism across cores.\n\nEffil-jit is not used. The path is synchronous → coroutine → 3d-rts pool.",
    "newString":"**Stage 3 — 3d-rts thread pool.** The `task_fn` boundary swaps in the thread\npool. Worker threads pull tasks from the pool; the coroutine scheduler is\nreplaced by OS-level scheduling. Cross-language calls block a worker thread\nwhile other threads continue. True parallelism across cores.\n\nEffil-jit is not used. The path is synchronous → coroutine → 3d-rts pool.\n\n---\n\n## Stage 3 detail: pthreads task model\n\nEach box execution in the thread pool is a **task struct** containing:\n\n- **Function pointer** — the language-specific invocation wrapper (a C\n  function, since pthreads requires a C entry point)\n- **Shared memory pointer** — the region holding the input arguments and\n  return value for this invocation\n- **Dependency list** — pointers to the tasks this task is waiting on\n- **Waiting list** — pointers to tasks that are waiting on this task\n- **Counter** (iterator boxes only) — current iteration index, updated\n  in-place when the iterator re-queues itself\n\nTask structs are allocated once at run start, one per box (not one per\ninvocation). They live for the entire run.\n\n### Blocking and unblocking — pointer-only transitions\n\nWhen a task cannot run (upstream output not yet available), it is placed\nin its upstream task's waiting list. This is a pointer move — no\nallocation, no struct copy. The task struct stays exactly where it is.\n\nWhen an upstream task completes and writes its return value to shared\nmemory, it walks its waiting list and re-adds each entry to the main task\nqueue. Again, a pointer move only. The unblocked task's struct is\nunchanged; only its position in the queue changes.\n\nThis means \"blocked\", \"queued\", and \"running\" are states defined by which\nlist a task's pointer currently lives in — not by any field in the struct.\n\n### Per-thread language runtimes\n\nEach worker thread initializes its own language runtimes at startup:\n- **Lua:** one `lua_State` per thread. Lua states are not thread-safe, but\n  one per thread requires no locking. The task wrapper calls the box\n  function via `lua_pcall`.\n- **C:** the compiled box function is called directly through the function\n  pointer. No interpreter, no overhead beyond the call itself.\n- **Bash/other:** a persistent subprocess per thread (Unix domain socket\n  server model — see Option 3 above). The task wrapper sends a request and\n  blocks the thread waiting for the response.\n\n### Iterator self-re-queue\n\nAn iterator task does not terminate after one invocation. When it\ncompletes:\n1. It increments its `counter` field in-place (or wraps to 0).\n2. It checks its input queue for the next pending value.\n3. If a value is waiting: it updates its input pointer and re-adds itself\n   to the main task queue. No allocation — the same task struct re-enters\n   the queue with updated state.\n4. If no value is waiting: it adds itself to the upstream task's waiting\n   list, to be re-added when the next input arrives.\n\nInput values are processed one-at-a-time in arrival order. Ten queued\ninputs means the iterator task visits the queue ten times, advancing the\ncounter and firing a different output path each time.",

    "stdout":"# 006 — Threading Architecture Walkthrough\n\nA six-part guided tour of the threading model. `004-architecture.md`\nis the spec; this document is the narrative companion that threads\nthrough the spec, the issue files, and the implementation library\nin the order a new reader needs to build mental model.\n\nEach part begins with a **status line** distinguishing what's\n*designed but not built*, what's *built and adopted*, and what's\n*being redesigned to fix a bug*. The threading model is not a\nsingle deliverable — it's a stack of decisions, some of which are\nreal on disk today and some of which are still on paper. Readers\nwho skip the status lines will conflate the plan with the reality.\n\nThe six parts:\n\n1. The two-thread split and the boundary — *designed (102), not built*\n2. The snapshot handoff — *designed (102), not built*\n3. The input queue — *designed (102), not built*\n4. The task pool reality — *built (114, 122) and adopted (107); redesign in flight (127)*\n5. Modifier-ring batching — *design pattern, not yet built; aligns with 127*\n6. Implications and implementation — *running notes*\n\n---\n\n## Part 1/6 — Two threads, one boundary\n\n**Status:** Designed in `issues/102-threading-model.md`. **Not yet\nbuilt.** The current binary runs everything on the main thread;\nissue 102's two-pthread split is what *will* exist. Movement\nnevertheless already runs on the task pool today — see Part 4.\n\nThe whole design starts from a single decision: **the renderer and the simulation must not share game state directly.** Everything else is consequence.\n\n### The two threads\n\nThere are *three threads of attention but two real OS threads*:\n\n- **Main thread** — owns the raylib window. Each frame it does three things, in this order:\n  1. polls raylib input and translates it into *semantic* events (not \"key W is down\" but `MOVE_ORDER(x,y,chain_id)`),\n  2. pushes those events onto the input queue,\n  3. reads the latest published snapshot and renders it.\n  It never reads or writes simulation state. It doesn't even know what a unit *is* internally — only what's in the snapshot struct.\n\n- **Simulation thread** — owns *all* game state. Runs a fixed-rate tick loop (`SIM_TICK_HZ` in `010-config.h`, e.g. 60Hz). Each tick:\n  1. drains the input queue,\n  2. applies events to state,\n  3. runs systems (movement, combat, projectiles, factories) — possibly delegating per-unit work to the task pool from Part 4,\n  4. builds a fresh snapshot in a back buffer,\n  5. swaps front/back snapshot pointers under a lock,\n  6. sleeps until the next tick boundary.\n\nThe \"third thread of attention\" is the input pipeline — it's logically its own flow, but it lives inside the main thread's frame loop; it doesn't need its own OS thread.\n\n### The boundary: exactly two locks (at this layer)\n\nThis is the part worth memorizing, because it's the entire concurrency surface of the *main↔sim* boundary:\n\n- **Mutex 1 — input queue** (`040-input.c`). Main thread holds it briefly to push; sim thread holds it briefly to drain. Fixed-capacity ring; producer never blocks meaningfully.\n- **Mutex 2 — snapshot pointer swap** (`110-snapshot.c`). Sim thread holds it for the duration of a *pointer swap* (front ↔ back). Main thread holds it just long enough to grab the front pointer. The actual snapshot bytes are never copied across threads — only ownership of which buffer is \"current\" flips.\n\nThe task pool (Part 4) introduces additional locks *inside the sim\nside* of the boundary — `reg_lk` (registry) and `qlk` (ready queue),\nplus per-task atomics. Those don't cross the main↔sim boundary;\nthey're internal to the sim's own execution model.\n\nBeyond those, nothing is shared. The terrain heightmap is built once at startup and treated as read-only thereafter; raylib's GL state lives entirely on the main thread; simulation arrays live entirely on the sim thread (with the pool's worker threads being part of \"the sim side\" of the boundary).\n\n### Why this shape\n\nThe properties that fall out of two threads + two locks:\n\n- **Render decouples from sim load.** If a tick stalls (the issue suggests deliberately `usleep`-ing 100ms inside one tick as a sanity test), the main thread still has a valid front snapshot to render — the marker pauses for a tick, but camera/zoom stay smooth. That test is the litmus that the decoupling actually holds.\n- **No dropped inputs.** The queue absorbs bursts; the sim drains whatever accumulated since last tick.\n- **Every tick is a pure function of `(prior state, drained input events)`.** This is what makes future replay/test harnesses possible without redesign — and it's also what makes the parallel work inside the sim (Part 4) safe.\n\n### What's *not* in this part\n\n- The shape of the snapshot struct itself — Part 2.\n- Why input events carry `shift_chain_id` — Part 3.\n- *How* the sim tick internally executes work — Part 4 (and it's not the slice-by-tenths shape `004-architecture.md` originally documented; the project chose a different shape, see Part 4).\n\n---\n\n## Part 2/6 — The snapshot handoff\n\n**Status:** Designed in `issues/102-threading-model.md`. **Not yet\nbuilt.** As of 107's completion log, the renderer reads unit state\ndirectly from the unit pool with inline extrapolation between task\nupdates (`render_pos = u->position + heading * speed * cos²(err) * (render_now - last_update_t)`).\nThis is acknowledged-temporary; the snapshot indirection from this\npart replaces it when 102 lands.\n\nThe snapshot is the **only** mechanism by which simulation state crosses to the renderer. If you understand this one struct and its swap, you understand half the program.\n\n### What a snapshot is\n\nA snapshot is a **flat, copyable struct** — no pointers into sim-owned memory, no live references, nothing the renderer could follow back into simulation territory. Conceptually it holds:\n\n- arrays of unit positions, orientations, health, unit identifiers,\n- the projectile array (positions, velocities, lifetimes),\n- current orders / order chains (so the renderer can draw waypoint lines),\n- the current selection,\n- factories and their rally chains.\n\nIt is **sized for the maximum unit count** (`MAX_UNITS` in `010-config.h`) — fixed capacity, no allocation per tick. The sim writes into pre-allocated arrays and the renderer reads from pre-allocated arrays. No malloc on the hot path, ever.\n\n### Double buffering\n\nTwo snapshot buffers exist at all times — call them A and B. At any instant:\n\n- one is the **front** (what the renderer is allowed to read),\n- the other is the **back** (what the sim is currently writing into).\n\nA tick looks like:\n\n1. Sim writes a fresh snapshot into the back buffer (no lock — nobody else touches back).\n2. Sim takes the snapshot mutex, swaps the two pointers (`front ↔ back`), releases.\n3. What was the back buffer is now the front; what was the front is now the back, and the *next* tick will overwrite it.\n\nThe renderer side:\n\n1. Take the snapshot mutex, copy the *front pointer* into a local variable, release.\n2. Render from that pointer for the rest of the frame.\n\n### Why this is fast\n\nThe lock is held for **a pointer swap** on the sim side and **a pointer read** on the render side. That's nanoseconds. The actual snapshot bytes — kilobytes of unit/projectile arrays — are never copied across the boundary and never contended. The renderer reads a buffer that the sim has promised not to touch until *after* the next swap.\n\nCrucially: the renderer can hold onto its front pointer for an entire frame without blocking the sim, because the sim only writes to back. The two threads operate on disjoint memory between swaps.\n\n### \"Possibly one tick old, which is fine\"\n\nThe architecture doc calls this out explicitly: the front snapshot the renderer sees might be from the tick that just ended, or from one tick ago if the sim is mid-write. Either way, the renderer never blocks waiting for fresh data, and never sees a torn half-written snapshot. At 60Hz sim and 144Hz render, several frames will redraw the same snapshot — that's the expected, correct behavior. Interpolation between snapshots is a *future* optimization; the inline extrapolation 107 ships today is the placeholder until the snapshot itself lands.\n\n### What it protects against\n\n- **No torn reads.** The swap is atomic at the pointer level — the renderer either sees the old snapshot in full or the new snapshot in full, never a mix.\n- **No stalls.** The renderer always has *something* valid to draw. Even if the sim does a 100ms tick, the renderer keeps redrawing the most recent front.\n- **No simulation→render coupling.** The renderer literally cannot reach into sim state; the type system makes it inexpressible. Conversely, nothing the renderer does (camera moves, frame drops) can perturb simulation determinism.\n\n### What's *not* in the snapshot\n\n- Camera state — that lives entirely on the main thread; it isn't sim state.\n- Input state (key-down, mouse-down) — the main thread translates those into events before they cross the boundary.\n- Anything raylib-specific (textures, models, GL handles) — those are render-thread-only resources, looked up *by id* from the snapshot's unit type identifiers.\n\nThis is what `src/110-snapshot.c` / `.h` will own per issue 102, step 2: the buffer pair, the mutex, and the two primitives `snapshot_publish()` (sim-side, swap) and `snapshot_acquire()` (render-side, grab front pointer).\n\n---\n\n## Part 3/6 — The input queue and shift-chain IDs\n\n**Status:** Designed in `issues/102-threading-model.md`. **Not yet\nbuilt.** The current binary's main loop reads input and acts on\nstate inline. Phase 1 gameplay issues 108–119 will demand semantic\nevents as they land; that's the trigger that pulls 102 forward.\n\nIf part 2 is \"how state flows sim→render,\" part 3 is the mirror: **how intent flows main→sim**. Same shape (one mutex, fixed-capacity buffer, no shared pointers), different content.\n\n### Why a queue at all\n\nThe naïve alternative would be: main thread sets some \"pending order\" globals, sim thread reads them. That falls apart immediately — the sim ticks at a fixed rate (60Hz), the main thread polls input at frame rate (often 144Hz+), and a single tick boundary might span *multiple* user actions. A click followed 3ms later by a shift-click must both reach the sim, in order, even if they happened between two ticks.\n\nSo: a **fixed-capacity ring queue** of events, protected by one mutex. Main thread pushes; sim thread drains the entire queue at the start of each tick. Bursts are absorbed by the ring; nothing is dropped under normal load. This capacity is larger than you'd expect, because memory is cheap and we want to ensure there's no overwrites.\n\n### Semantic, not raw\n\nThis is the part of the design that does the most work. The queue does **not** carry \"key W went down\" or \"mouse moved to (x,y)\". It carries **already-interpreted game intentions**:\n\n-- this isn't true. We should recieve the input from the user in the raylib thread, then write it to a mailbox for each type of input in use. the E key. The mouse position. Etc. Each render tick, we write whatever is in the raylib input queue straight to the array of ring-buffers, each for each key, each input item thing. We may end up writing more than one. Well, depends on how raylib's input buffer is implemented... \n\n-- anyway we should have the inputs just passed straight to the thread-pool ready-task-list. The function they should run is essentially: \"mouse_update_position()\" or \"E_key_pressed()\" all defined in the same file with the same semantics. Each one corresponds to various game activities, which are stored as a pointer to a \"key_activity\" datastructure. This datastructure is pulled from a config file, and can be edited while in-game - simply update what happens when you press what keys in what context. Ideally, with a keyboard command (like ctrl+shift+spacebar+right-shift+enter) that says \"whatever I press next is the new keybind for the most recent input action I did\" then if there's modifiers held down, even keys like abcde's, it'll record them as chord keys that trigger particular events. These are created and managed dynamically - programmatically generated and managed in the raylib thread. They won't change very often, but they will trigger constantly as the user is inputting all of their commands.\n\n- `SELECT_RECT(x0,y0,x1,y1)` — completed drag rectangle on mouse release.\n- `SELECT_CLICK(x,y)` — single click without drag.\n- `MOVE_ORDER(world_x, world_y, shift_chain_id)` — right-click, already raycast through the camera into world coordinates.\n- `FACTORY_PLACE(world_x, world_y)` — placement-mode confirmation.\n- `RALLY_DRAG_START(factory_id)` / `RALLY_DRAG_MOVE(x,y)` / `RALLY_DRAG_COMMIT(shift_chain_id)`.\n\nTwo important consequences:\n\n1. **The sim has no concept of a mouse, a key, or a screen.** It receives world coordinates and entity ids. This is what lets the simulation be deterministic and replay-friendly — you could feed it a recorded event log and get bit-identical results.\n2. **The camera lives entirely on the main thread.** The screen→world raycast is done on the main thread *before* the event is enqueued, using the heightmap (which is read-only-shared, built once at startup). The sim never sees the camera.\n\nThis is what the doc means by \"the main thread is *stateless about the game* — it only knows about windowing, input mapping, and chain-id bookkeeping.\"\n\n### Shift-chain IDs — the one piece of cross-thread bookkeeping\n\nThis is the subtle bit. When you shift-click to chain waypoints, the sim needs to know \"this `MOVE_ORDER` extends the previous chain\" vs. \"this is a fresh chain.\" But the sim doesn't see your shift key — it only sees the events you enqueue. So:\n\n- Each time the user **presses-and-holds shift**, the main thread allocates a fresh `shift_chain_id` (a monotonically increasing integer).\n\n... huh? that doesn't seem right. What the hey.\n\n- Every order event emitted *while shift remains held* carries that same id.\n- When shift is **released**, the id is closed; the next press allocates a new one.\n\nWhen the sim drains events:\n\n- Two `MOVE_ORDER`s with the same `shift_chain_id` → same chain, append in arrival order.\n- A `MOVE_ORDER` with a `shift_chain_id` it hasn't seen before → start a new chain (and replace any existing one for the affected units).\n- A `MOVE_ORDER` with `shift_chain_id == 0` (or whatever sentinel \"no shift\") → a singleton chain that replaces.\n\nThe beauty: the main thread holds **no game state** to do this. It tracks one integer counter and one \"currently-open id, or none.\" That's it. The sim thread holds **no input/keyboard state** to interpret it — it just compares ids it receives to ids it has already seen for that selection. Each side's bookkeeping is local to itself.\n\nThe same scheme generalizes to rally-chain dragging on factories (`RALLY_DRAG_*` events share a `shift_chain_id` for shift-extending an existing rally chain).\n\nthe integer counter should intentionally stack overflow when it wants to wrap around. It should be unsigned. Nobody's going to queue up 60 bazillion movement orders. It's fine.\n\n### What the boundary looks like end-to-end (once 102 lands)\n\nPutting parts 1–3 together, one full round trip:\n\n1. User right-clicks at screen `(450, 320)` while holding shift.\n2. Main thread, in its frame loop:\n   - notes shift is held → uses current `shift_chain_id`,\n   - raycasts `(450, 320)` through the camera against the heightmap → world `(x, y)`,\n   - takes the input-queue mutex, pushes `MOVE_ORDER(x, y, chain_id)`, releases.\n3. Some milliseconds later, the sim thread starts a tick:\n   - takes the input-queue mutex, drains all pending events into a local list, releases,\n   - sees the `MOVE_ORDER`, recognizes the chain id, appends a waypoint to the chain for the currently-selected units,\n   - dispatches per-unit work to the task pool (Part 4),\n   - writes a new snapshot to back, swaps front/back under the snapshot mutex.\n4. The next render frame:\n   - takes the snapshot mutex, grabs the front pointer, releases,\n   - draws units at their new positions and the order chain as a polyline.\n\nTwo locks at the boundary, both held for trivial durations, and a clean data boundary. That's the concurrency story for the *main↔sim split*. The story *inside* the sim is Part 4.\n\n---\n\n## Part 4/6 — The task pool reality\n\n**Status:** Library shipped (`libs/900-task-pool.{h,c}`, issue 114\niter4.5). Wired into the game build as a process-wide singleton\n(issue 122, `src/040-game-pool`, 4 workers). Adopted by movement\nin Shape B (issue 107 re-open, completion 2026-04-29). **Bug-driven\nredesign in flight (issue 127):** Shape B exposed a \"snap\"\nproblem when the OS preempts a worker mid-action; the fix is to\nmake the pool *frame-locked* rather than free-running.\n\nThis is the part where the original walkthrough (commit\n`b2207e86`, drafted from issue 102 alone) got most things wrong.\nThe pool isn't coroutines, the sim isn't fully serial, and the\nadopted parallel pattern isn't slice-by-tenths.\n\n### What the pool actually is\n\nFive iterations of design (recorded in issue 114's \"Design\nevolution\" section) landed at: **action-array tasks with parking\non a per-blocker waiters list.** Concretely:\n\n- **A task is a flat array of small atomic functions.** Each\n  function (\"action\") returns one of `ACT_ADVANCE` (next\n  index), `ACT_JUMP` (to a named index), `ACT_BLOCK` (suspend\n  on another task's GUID; resume at the same index when woken),\n  `ACT_DONE` (skip remaining actions). The \"resume point\" is a\n  single `unsigned int current_index` — trivially serializable,\n  naturally re-enterable. No `swapcontext`, no per-task stacks,\n  no trampoline. Standard C function calls only.\n- **Per-action arguments and per-action results** live in\n  parallel arrays alongside the actions array. Each result slot\n  is write-once by convention; reading uses\n  `pool_result_slot(pool, id, slot, &out)` which returns a\n  `slot_status_t` enum (`SLOT_PENDING`, `SLOT_FILLED`,\n  `SLOT_OUT_OF_RANGE`, `SLOT_UNKNOWN_ID`) so callers can\n  distinguish \"action k hasn't run yet\" from \"action k ran and\n  legitimately wrote NULL.\"\n- **A GUID registry** (open-addressed hashmap, capacity 4096)\n  maps `task_id_t` (uint64) to `task_t *` with refcounts. Every\n  external handle is a GUID; the pool never hands out raw\n  pointers.\n- **Ten priority queues**, indexed 1 (highest) to 10 (lowest).\n  A *cycler* picks which queue to consult next, following the\n  pattern `1; 1,2; 1,2,3; …; 1..10` and repeating. Period is\n  54 steps. High priorities dominate without starving low ones.\n  Empty queues at the current step are skipped; the cycler\n  still advances.\n- **Parking on waiters[].** When an action returns `ACT_BLOCK`\n  with a target GUID, the worker appends the blocked task's id\n  to the *target's* waiters[] array and sets the blocked\n  task's state to `TASK_PARKED`. The parked task is in no\n  queue and consumes zero CPU. When the target eventually\n  reaches DONE, the worker walks the waiters[] and pushes\n  each waiter back onto its priority queue. Iter4.5 tests\n  reduced parking-related polling from ~113k retries to\n  exactly 1.\n- **Promote-on-blocked-target.** When task A parks on B, if B\n  is in the ready queue at priority p > 1, the worker promotes\n  B to p−1 (toward higher priority). A unparks sooner because\n  B runs sooner. Demote-on-block was tried (iter4) and deleted\n  (iter4.5) — parking made it pointless.\n- **Self-rescheduling pattern.** A task's last action enqueues\n  a fresh copy of itself via `pool_spawn`. One-line idiom for\n  per-frame update loops without holding a worker hostage.\n\nThe library has no dependency on raylib or game state. It's\nexercised by 9 tests in `tests/` covering sequential actions,\ncross-task result-slot waits, mid-task park/wake, self-\nrescheduling, priority cycling, result slots, parking promote\nsemantics, slot-status disambiguation, and many-waiter bursts.\n\nactions get GUID's of other tasks which may block them when the tasks are\ncreated. You will always know when a blockable task is being made exactly\nwhich task it is that might block it - so multiple tasks can interleave.\nwhen there are no reference counts remaining, a task can be cleaned.\n\n### How the pool is integrated\n\nIssue 122 (completed 2026-04-28) wired the library into the game\nbuild. `Makefile` now compiles `libs/900-task-pool.c` alongside\n`src/*.c` and adds `-I.../libs -D_XOPEN_SOURCE=600`. A thin\nwrapper `src/040-game-pool.{h,c}` exposes a process-wide\nsingleton:\n\n- `game_pool_init(N)` — called once after `units_init`. Creates\n  the pool with N workers. Default N=4 (typical desktop has\n  4–16 cores; profiling will dictate any change).\n- `game_pool()` — returns the singleton handle.\n- `game_pool_shutdown()` — destroys it before\n  `terrain_shutdown` / `CloseWindow`.\n\nThis issue deliberately did *not* migrate any game system to use\nthe pool. The first migration (issue 107 re-open) followed\nimmediately; subsequent adoptions land with the issues that\nintroduce their systems (113 combat / HP regen, 112 projectile\narc, 116 factory production).\n\n### Shape A vs Shape B — and why Shape B won for movement\n\n`docs/004-architecture.md` describes a slice-by-tenths\nparallel-for pattern: split a per-unit pass into ~10 contiguous\nslices, dispatch each slice as a task, run the merge step after\njoin. That's Shape A — the originally-planned shape, still the\nright choice for a per-tick batched system.\n\nIssue 107 (Shape B) shipped a different shape for movement:\n**per-unit self-rescheduling tasks.** Each unit with an active\ntarget owns a movement task that re-enqueues itself each tick:\n\n```\nmovement_task_actions = [\n    [0] move_advance       // read target, slew yaw, step forward, resnap Z, arrival check\n    [1] move_reschedule    // if still moving: spawn next iteration; else clear movement_task_id\n]\n```\n\nthese types of actions can't add new actions to their own task, but they can\ncreate new tasks with whatever types of motions they're programmed to remote.\n\nWhy Shape B was chosen for movement:\n\n- The user's stated preference for \"self-rescheduling for things\n  like walking toward a location\" is direct guidance.\n- **Stationary units consume zero scheduler time.** A\n  slice-by-tenths pass iterates every unit every tick whether\n  it's moving or not; per-unit tasks only exist for units with\n  active orders.\n- The per-tick task-struct overhead (one `task_t` per moving\n  unit per tick) is bounded and acceptable at Phase 1 unit\n  counts (six initially; hundreds after factory production).\n- Switching to Shape A later is mechanical — the action\n  body is already a function of (unit, dt) — if profiling\n  ever shows per-unit task overhead dominating.\n\nShape A remains the right fit for systems where every entity\n*does* need updating every tick (HP regen on all units; LoS\nscans). Shape B is the right fit for systems where only a\nfraction of entities are active in any given tick. Adoption is\nper-system; future migrations will pick a shape per their\nprofile.\n\n### Timestamp-based motion\n\nShape B's movement task uses `last_update_t` (double, seconds,\nvia raylib's `GetTime()`):\n\n```\nmove_advance:\n    now = GetTime()\n    dt = now - u->last_update_t\n    apply turn (UNIT_TURN_RATE * dt, capped by remaining error)\n    apply forward step (UNIT_SPEED * dt * cos²(angular_error))\n    resnap Z to terrain\n    arrival check (clears has_target within UNIT_REACH_RADIUS)\n    u->last_update_t = now\n    return ACT_ADVANCE\n```\n\nThe point of timestamp-based motion: a task that runs every\ntick at priority 2 produces the same total displacement as a\ntask that runs every fifth tick at priority 10 — it just steps\nin larger chunks. Scheduler-induced cadence variation is\nabsorbed by the math.\n\n### The snap — and why timestamp-based motion alone isn't enough\n\nShape B shipped with a known issue: with 6 units and `T` to\nscatter, 5 move smoothly while 1 stays visually stationary for\n1–3 seconds, then teleports. Fans run at full speed during\nmovement.\n\nRoot cause: `move_advance` captures `now = GetTime()` at the\n*start* of the action, runs its arithmetic, and writes\n`u->last_update_t = now` at the *end*. If the OS preempts the\nworker thread between the capture and the write, real time\nadvances during the preemption but the captured `now` does not.\nThe next iteration sees `dt = GetTime() - last_update_t` of\n1–3 seconds and computes a correct-but-large step.\n\nThis isn't a movement bug — it's the *architecture* announcing\nthat \"poll as fast as possible, math will fix it\" doesn't work\nwhen the underlying scheduling is non-uniform. Two band-aids\nconsidered and rejected:\n\n- \"Read `GetTime()` at end of action\" → drops the preempted\n  time; unit covers less than physically correct distance.\n- \"Cap dt at 100ms\" → same, more aggressively. Bad for combat\n  hit-detection correctness.\n\nThe accurate fix is to bound how often the action runs. That's\nissue 127.\n\n### Frame-ring scheduling (issue 127, in flight)\n\nReplace the single set of priority queues with a **ring of\nframe slots**, each containing its own ten priority queues.\nWorkers only pop from `frames[current_frame]`. Spawns default\nto `frames[(current_frame + 1) % SIZE]`. Three spawn variants:\n\n- `pool_spawn(...)` — implicit \"schedule for next frame.\"\n  Cannot land in the current frame.\n- `pool_spawn_in(N, ...)` — schedule N frames out (relative).\n  N=1 is the default. N=0 is rejected.\n- `pool_spawn_in_current(...)` — escape hatch for input\n  handlers that legitimately need to react this frame.\n\nMain thread calls `pool_advance_frame(pool)` after\n`EndDrawing()`. The call **stalls** until the current slot is\nfully drained (empty across all priorities AND no parked\ntasks waiting on tasks in this slot). Only then does\n`current_frame` advance.\n\nWhat this fixes:\n\n- Movement runs exactly once per frame. With `SetTargetFPS(60)`,\n  `dt ≈ 16.67ms ± small jitter`. No 1–3 second snaps; lost\n  preemption time becomes part of the next normally-sized\n  frame's `dt`, capped by the frame budget itself.\n- The cycler still runs *within* a single frame's queues —\n  same logic, scoped per-slot.\n- Periodics (\"run every N frames\") become a one-line idiom:\n  the reschedule action calls `pool_spawn_in(N, ...)`. Issue\n  123's dedicated periodics design is **superseded** by this.\n- The same stall semantics make lockstep multiplayer\n  determinism a natural fit later: every client agrees on\n  end-of-frame-N state before exchanging inputs for N+1.\n\nWhat stays the same:\n\n- Action-array tasks, GUIDs, refcounts.\n- Parking on waiters[], promote-on-blocked-target.\n- Result slots and `slot_status_t`.\n- Self-rescheduling pattern (just calls `pool_spawn_in(1, ...)`\n  instead of `pool_spawn(...)`).\n\n### The other open task-pool issues\n\n- **123 — periodics.** Superseded by 127.\n- **124 — stable-index task storage.** Exploratory iter5;\n  user explicitly pushed back on pre-planning it. May land if\n  cheap live-task iteration becomes a real need.\n- **125 — API hardening.** Future pass: abort-on-unknown-id\n  for `pool_is_done`/`pool_ref`/`pool_unref`/`pool_result_slot`,\n  wrapper-struct `task_id_t` to enforce move-vs-clone, hide\n  `park`/`wake` behind named internal helpers. None of these\n  change mechanics; they sharpen edges.\n\n### What's *not* in this part\n\n- The merge step from `004-architecture.md` (intent records,\n  deterministic sort, single-threaded apply). Movement under\n  Shape B doesn't use it — the action is slice-disjoint to\n  begin with (each task touches one unit). Combat and damage\n  in 113/112 will need it because cross-unit effects are\n  unavoidable. The intent-records pattern is the right shape\n  for those passes; it just hasn't been exercised yet.\n- The modifier-domain extension of intent records — Part 5.\n\n---\n\n## Part 5/6 — Modifier-ring batching\n\n**Status:** Design pattern, captured here. **Not yet built.**\nAligns naturally with the frame-ring delivery from Part 4 (issue\n127). The pattern generalizes the merge-step from\n`004-architecture.md` to the *modifier* domain (e.g. \"+20%\nspeed,\" \"1.3× damage,\" \"regen rate +0.05/s\").\n\n### The pattern\n\nEach tick, the totals of modifiers being applied to each unit are\n*accumulated* during the frame's parallel pass and *applied* at\nthe start of the next frame. Modifier intents are written to a\n**separate memory location**, one slot per frame index in the\nframe ring, so accumulation in frame N doesn't perturb the\nmodifiers being applied to units mid-frame N.\n\nConceptually, alongside the frame ring's task queues:\n\n```\nstruct frame_slot {\n    /* (existing) ten priority queues for tasks scheduled this frame */\n    /* ... */\n\n    /* (new) modifier intents accumulated by tasks running in this frame */\n    modifier_intent_t *intents;\n    int                n_intents;\n    int                cap_intents;\n};\n```\n\nThe flow:\n\n1. During frame N execution, any task that wants to apply a\n   modifier (e.g., a \"speed boost\" buff task, a \"damage taken\n   modifier\" effect) appends an intent into `frames[N].intents`.\n   Each intent is small: `{ target_unit_id, modifier_kind,\n   value }`.\n2. At the start of frame N+1 (just after `pool_advance_frame`\n   has stalled-and-flipped), a single-threaded sweep folds\n   `frames[N].intents` into per-unit modifier sums. Multiple\n   `+X%` intents into the same target sum naturally; conflicts\n   between modifier kinds resolve via a fixed application\n   order.\n3. Frame N+1's tasks read the freshly-applied modifiers when\n   they run. They emit their *own* intents into\n   `frames[N+1].intents` for frame N+2 to consume.\n\nThis is the merge-step pattern from `004-architecture.md`\n(produce intents in a parallel pass, apply single-threaded)\ndelivered through the frame ring instead of through a\nwithin-tick collect-and-merge.\n\n### Why a *ring* (not just \"next tick\")\n\nThe frame ring is already a circular structure (Part 4).         "tool_use_id":"toolu_013DD2oCrmrnwMjgvy9YqMK5",
        "content":"# 127 — Task pool: frame-ring scheduling\n\n## Status\n\nTODO. Next concrete piece of work after 107 lands. Direct successor\nto issue 123 (which is now superseded — periodics are subsumed by\nthis design as \"schedule into frame N+k\").\n\n## Why this exists\n\nIssue 107's Shape B movement (per-unit self-rescheduling tasks at\npriority 2) exposed a fundamental architectural problem with\nself-rescheduling-at-max-rate: **timestamp-based motion is\nmathematically correct under variable cadence, but cadence\nvariability is unbounded.** A worker thread can be off-CPU for\n1-3 seconds when the system is contended; when it resumes, the\nunit's next step has to cover that real-time delta in one frame.\nThe result is a visual snap from old position to new position,\nwith no smooth interpolation.\n\nThis is not a small bug. It's the architecture announcing that\n\"poll as fast as possible, math will fix it\" doesn't work when\nthe underlying scheduling is non-uniform. The fix is to bound\ncadence variability — make `dt` approximately constant by\nlocking task execution to frame boundaries.\n\n## Snap reproduction (motivating example, captured 2026-04-29)\n\n- 6 units, press T, all get random targets via\n  `units_set_target` → `pool_spawn` per unit.\n- 5 units move smoothly toward their new targets.\n- 1 unit stays visually stationary for 1-3 seconds, then snaps\n  (instantly translates and rotates) to a new position.\n- Fans run at full speed while units are moving.\n\nRoot cause: in `move_advance`, `now = GetTime()` is captured at\nthe start of the action; the action does its arithmetic; at the\nend, `u->last_update_t = now` writes that *start-of-action* `now`\nvalue. If the OS preempts the worker between the capture and the\nwrite (as happens occasionally on a contended system), real-time\nadvances during the preemption but the captured `now` does not.\nThe next iteration sees `dt = GetTime() - last_update_t` of 1-3\nseconds, computes a correct-but-large step, and the unit teleports.\n\nNo band-aid in this layer fixes the issue without losing physical\ncorrectness:\n- \"Read GetTime() at end of action\" → drops the preempted time;\n  unit covers less total distance.\n- \"Cap dt at 100ms\" → same thing, more aggressively.\n\nThe only correct fix: bound how often the action runs. If\nmovement runs exactly once per frame and frame rate is bounded\n(`SetTargetFPS(60)`), `dt ≈ 16.67ms ± small jitter`. No\naccumulation, no snap, no lost distance.\n\n## Intended design\n\nA **ring of frame slots**, each slot itself containing the same\nten priority queues we have today. Concretely on `task_pool_t`:\n\n```c\n#define FRAME_RING_SIZE 8        // tunable — how many frames of lookahead\nstruct task_pool {\n    // ... existing fields except the queue arrays ...\n    struct {\n        struct task **queues[N_PRIORITIES + 1];\n        int queue_lens[N_PRIORITIES + 1];\n        int queue_caps[N_PRIORITIES + 1];\n        int n_ready_total;\n    } frames[FRAME_RING_SIZE];\n    int current_frame;             // index into frames[]; the slot workers drain.\n    int next_frame_offset;         // == 1 typically — \"next frame\" is current+1 mod size.\n};\n```\n\nWorkers only pop from `frames[current_frame]`. New spawns always\nland in `frames[(current_frame + offset) % FRAME_RING_SIZE]`,\nwhere `offset >= 1` (the rule below).\n\n### Spawning rules",
        "is_error":false,
        "type":"tool_result"
      }],
    "role":"user"
  },
