```json
    "stdout":"# 127 — Task pool: frame-ring scheduling\n\n## Status\n\nTODO. Next concrete piece of work after 107 lands. Direct successor\nto issue 123 (which is now superseded — periodics are subsumed by\nthis design as \"schedule into frame N+k\").\n\n## Why this exists\n\nIssue 107's Shape B movement (per-unit self-rescheduling tasks at\npriority 2) exposed a fundamental architectural problem with\nself-rescheduling-at-max-rate: **timestamp-based motion is\nmathematically correct under variable cadence, but cadence\nvariability is unbounded.** A worker thread can be off-CPU for\n1-3 seconds when the system is contended; when it resumes, the\nunit's next step has to cover that real-time delta in one frame.\nThe result is a visual snap from old position to new position,\nwith no smooth interpolation.\n\nThis is not a small bug. It's the architecture announcing that\n\"poll as fast as possible, math will fix it\" doesn't work when\nthe underlying scheduling is non-uniform. The fix is to bound\ncadence variability — make `dt` approximately constant by\nlocking task execution to frame boundaries.\n\n## Snap reproduction (motivating example, captured 2026-04-29)\n\n- 6 units, press T, all get random targets via\n  `units_set_target` → `pool_spawn` per unit.\n- 5 units move smoothly toward their new targets.\n- 1 unit stays visually stationary for 1-3 seconds, then snaps\n  (instantly translates and rotates) to a new position.\n- Fans run at full speed while units are moving.\n\nRoot cause: in `move_advance`, `now = GetTime()` is captured at\nthe start of the action; the action does its arithmetic; at the\nend, `u->last_update_t = now` writes that *start-of-action* `now`\nvalue. If the OS preempts the worker between the capture and the\nwrite (as happens occasionally on a contended system), real-time\nadvances during the preemption but the captured `now` does not.\nThe next iteration sees `dt = GetTime() - last_update_t` of 1-3\nseconds, computes a correct-but-large step, and the unit teleports.\n\nNo band-aid in this layer fixes the issue without losing physical\ncorrectness:\n- \"Read GetTime() at end of action\" → drops the preempted time;\n  unit covers less total distance.\n- \"Cap dt at 100ms\" → same thing, more aggressively.\n\nThe only correct fix: bound how often the action runs. If\nmovement runs exactly once per frame and frame rate is bounded\n(`SetTargetFPS(60)`), `dt ≈ 16.67ms ± small jitter`. No\naccumulation, no snap, no lost distance.\n\n## Intended design\n\nA **ring of frame slots**, each slot itself containing the same\nten priority queues we have today. Concretely on `task_pool_t`:\n\n```c\n#define FRAME_RING_SIZE 8        // tunable — how many frames of lookahead\nstruct task_pool {\n    // ... existing fields except the queue arrays ...\n    struct {\n        struct task **queues[N_PRIORITIES + 1];\n        int queue_lens[N_PRIORITIES + 1];\n        int queue_caps[N_PRIORITIES + 1];\n        int n_ready_total;\n    } frames[FRAME_RING_SIZE];\n    int current_frame;             // index into frames[]; the slot workers drain.\n    int next_frame_offset;         // == 1 typically — \"next frame\" is current+1 mod size.\n};\n```\n\nWorkers only pop from `frames[current_frame]`. New spawns always\nland in `frames[(current_frame + offset) % FRAME_RING_SIZE]`,\nwhere `offset >= 1` (the rule below).\n\n### Spawning rules",

Workers run \"tasks\", where each task is a\n4\t// flat array of small atomic action functions executed in sequence.\n5\t// Actions can advance, jump, block, or finish the task. Each task\n6\t// has a parallel `result_slots[]` array (write-once per slot by the\n7\t// owning action) plus a parallel `result_filled[]` bool array that\n8\t// distinguishes \"action k hasn't run yet\" from \"action k ran and\n9\t// chose to write NULL.\" Tasks have priorities (1 = highest, 10 =\n10\t// lowest) scheduled via the cycler pattern (1; 1,2; 1,2,3; ...;\n11\t// 1..10; 1,2; ...) so high priority dominates without starving low.\n12\t//\n13\t// See issues/114-coroutine-pool-library.md for the full design\n14\t// rationale, including the four-iteration history (coroutines →\n15\t// continuation-passing → action-array → demote-on-block) that led\n16\t// to the current shape.\n17\t//\n18\t// Quick mental model:\n19\t//\n20\t//     pool          — N worker pthreads sharing a registry, ten\n21\t//                     priority queues (arrays-of-pointers), and a\n22\t//                     refcounted task table.\n23\t//     task          — a row in the registry, identified by a 64-bit\n24\t//                     GUID, containing actions[], action_args[],\n25\t//                     result_slots[], result_filled[], and a\n26\t//                     mutable priority field.\n27\t//     action        — a function `action_result_t f(task_ctx_t *)`.\n28\t//                     Reads ctx->args, may write to its own result\n29\t//                     slot, returns one of ACT_ADVANCE, ACT_JUMP,\n30\t//                     ACT_BLOCK, ACT_DONE.\n31\t//     ACT_BLOCK     — \"I can't progress right now.\" The library\n32\t//                     parks the task on the blocker's waiters[]\n33\t//                     list (zero CPU until woken), and promotes\n34\t//                     the blocker by one level if it's in the\n35\t//                     ready queue. When the blocker reaches DONE,\n36\t//                     it walks its waiters[] and pushes each onto\n37\t//                     the ready queue, where workers pick them up\n38\t//                     and re-run the blocking action. ctx->block_on\n39\t//                     MUST be a valid id of a non-self task; the\n40\t//                     library aborts otherwise.\n41\t//\n42\t// Cross-task waits are expressed by reading another task's result\n43\t// slot via pool_result_slot inside an action. If the slot is\n44\t// SLOT_PENDING, the action sets ctx->block_on to the producer's id\n45\t// and returns ACT_BLOCK.\n46\t//\n47\t// Wait cycles (A parks on B, B parks on A) are not detected. Both\n48\t// park forever. Callers must avoid them.\n49\t\n50\t#ifndef TASK_POOL_H\n51\t#define TASK_POOL_H\n52\t\n53\t#include <stddef.h>\n54\t#include <stdint.h>\n55\t\n56\t// Opaque pool handle.\n57\ttypedef struct task_pool task_pool_t;\n58\t\n59\t// Task identifier. 0 is the \"no task\" sentinel; real GUIDs start at 1.\n60\ttypedef uint64_t task_id_t;\n61\t#define TASK_ID_NONE ((task_id_t)0)\n62\t\n63\t// What an action wants to happen next. Returned from every action;\n64\t// the worker dispatches on this value to decide whether to run the\n65\t// next action, jump, suspend, or end the task.\n66\ttypedef enum {\n67\t    ACT_ADVANCE,  // run actions[current_index + 1] next.\n68\t    ACT_JUMP,     // run actions[ctx->jump_to] next. Must set jump_to.\n69\t    ACT_BLOCK,    // park self on block_on's waiters[]; promote block_on\n70\t                  // if in ready queue. When block_on reaches DONE, this\n71\t                  // task is pushed back onto the ready queue and the same\n72\t                  // action runs again. ctx->block_on must be valid.\n73\t    ACT_DONE,     // task is finished. Skip remaining actions.\n74\t} action_result_t;\n75\t\n76\t// Result of a pool_result_slot read. Distinguishes \"not yet\n77\t// written\" from \"written, and the value happens to be NULL\" — both\n78\t// would collapse to NULL under a pointer-only return.\n79\ttypedef enum {\n80\t    SLOT_FILLED,         // action k completed; *out is its (possibly NULL) value.\n81\t    SLOT_PENDING,        // action k has not yet completed.\n82\t    SLOT_OUT_OF_RANGE,   // slot < 0 or slot >= n_actions.\n83\t    SLOT_UNKNOWN_ID,     // id not in the registry.\n84\t} slot_status_t;\n85\t\n86\t// Forward declaration so task_ctx_t can hold a pool pointer.\n87\tstruct task_pool;\n88\t\n89\t// Per-call context passed to every action. The library parks self on\n114\t                                        //   that task's waiters list. An\n115\t                                        //   invalid block_on (NONE, self, or\n116\t                                        //   missing-from-registry) is a\n117\t                                        //   programming bug — the library\n118\t                                        //   aborts with a diagnostic.\n119\t} task_ctx_t;\n120\t\n121\ttypedef action_result_t (*action_fn_t)(task_ctx_t *ctx);\n122\t\n123\t// ─── pool lifecycle ──────────────────────────────────────────────\n124\t\n125\t// Create a pool of n_workers pthreads. n_workers must be >= 1.\n126\t// Returns NULL on bad arg / allocation failure.\n127\ttask_pool_t *pool_create(int n_workers);\n128\t\n129\t// Signal shutdown, join all workers, free the pool. Tasks remaining\n130\t// at destroy time are leaked — caller is expected to have spun the\n131\t// pool down to quiescence first.\n132\tvoid pool_destroy(task_pool_t *pool);\n133\t\n134\t// ─── spawning ────────────────────────────────────────────────────\n135\t\n136\t// Spawn a task with the given actions array and parallel per-action\n137\t// args array (both of length n_actions, both copied internally).\n138\t//\n139\t// `priority` is clamped to [1, 10]. 1 is highest, 10 is lowest.\n140\t//\n141\t// As of iter4: there is no `deps` parameter. Cross-task waits are\n142\t// expressed by reading another task's result slot via\n143\t// `pool_result_slot` inside an action and returning ACT_BLOCK\n144\t// (with `block_on` set to the producer's id) if the slot is pending.\n145\t//\n146\t// Returns the task's GUID, or TASK_ID_NONE on error.\n147\ttask_id_t pool_spawn(task_pool_t *pool,\n148\t                     const action_fn_t *actions,\n149\t                     void *const      *action_args,\n150\t                     int               n_actions,\n151\t                     int               priority);\n152\t\n153\t// ─── refcount ────────────────────────────────────────────────────\n154\t\n155\t// Bump the refcount on a task.       "content":"// 900-task-pool.h\n//\n// Action-array task pool. Each task\n// has a parallel `result_slots[]` array (write-once per slot by the\n// owning action) plus a parallel `result_filled[]` bool array that\n// distinguishes \"action k hasn't run yet\" from \"action k ran and\n// chose to write NULL.\" Tasks have priorities (1 = highest, 10 =\n// lowest) scheduled via the cycler pattern (1; 1,2; 1,2,3; ...;\n// 1..10; 1,2; ...) so high priority dominates without starving low.\n//\n// See issues/114-coroutine-pool-library.md for the full design\n// rationale, including the four-iteration history (coroutines →\n// continuation-passing → action-array → demote-on-block) that led\n// to the current shape.\n//\n// Quick mental model:\n//\n//     pool          — N worker pthreads sharing a registry, ten\n//                     priority queues (arrays-of-pointers), and a\n//                     refcounted task table.\n//     task          — a row in the registry, identified by a 64-bit\n//                     GUID, containing actions[], action_args[],\n//                     result_slots[], result_filled[], and a\n//                     mutable priority field.\n//     action        — a function `action_result_t f(task_ctx_t *)`.\n//                     Reads ctx->args, may write to its own result\n//                     slot, returns one of ACT_ADVANCE, ACT_JUMP,\n//                     ACT_BLOCK, ACT_DONE.\n//     ACT_BLOCK     — \"I can't progress right now.\" The library\n//                     parks the task on the blocker's waiters[]\n//                     list (zero CPU until woken), and promotes\n//                     the blocker by one level if it's in the\n//                     ready queue. When the blocker reaches DONE,\n//                     it walks its waiters[] and pushes each onto\n//                     the ready queue, where workers pick them up\n//                     and re-run the blocking action. ctx->block_on\n//                     MUST be a valid id of a non-self task; the\n//                     library aborts otherwise.\n//\n// Cross-task waits are expressed by reading another task's result\n// slot via pool_result_slot inside an action. If the slot is\n// SLOT_PENDING, the action sets ctx->block_on to the producer's id\n// and returns ACT_BLOCK.\n//\n// Wait cycles (A parks on B, B parks on A) are not detected. Both\n// park forever. Callers must avoid them.\n\n#ifndef TASK_POOL_H\n#define TASK_POOL_H\n\n#include <stddef.h>\n#include <stdint.h>\n\n// Opaque pool handle.\ntypedef struct task_pool task_pool_t;\n\n// Task identifier. 0 is the \"no task\" sentinel; real GUIDs start at 1.\ntypedef uint64_t task_id_t;\n#define TASK_ID_NONE ((task_id_t)0)\n\n// What an action wants to happen next. Returned from every action;\n// the worker dispatches on this value to decide whether to run the\n// next action, jump, suspend, or end the task.\ntypedef enum {\n    ACT_ADVANCE,  // run actions[current_index + 1] next.\n    ACT_JUMP,     // run actions[ctx->jump_to] next. Must set jump_to.\n    ACT_BLOCK,    // park self on block_on's waiters[]; promote block_on\n                  // if in ready queue. When block_on reaches DONE, this\n                  // task is pushed back onto the ready queue and the same\n                  // action runs again. ctx->block_on must be valid.\n    ACT_DONE,     // task is finished. Skip remaining actions.\n} action_result_t;\n\n// Result of a pool_result_slot read. Distinguishes \"not yet\n// written\" from \"written, and the value happens to be NULL\" — both\n// would collapse to NULL under a pointer-only return.\ntypedef enum {\n    SLOT_FILLED,         // action k completed; *out is its (possibly NULL) value.\n    SLOT_PENDING,        // action k has not yet completed.\n    SLOT_OUT_OF_RANGE,   // slot < 0 or slot >= n_actions.\n    SLOT_UNKNOWN_ID,     // id not in the registry.\n} slot_status_t;\n\n// Forward declaration so task_ctx_t can hold a pool pointer.\nstruct task_pool;\n\n// Per-call context passed to every action. Fields are grouped:\n// identity, inputs, outputs, and a back-pointer to the pool so\n// actions can call pool_result_slot without args plumbing.\ntypedef struct task_ctx {\n    // ─── identity ────────────────────────────────────────\n    task_id_t           self_id;\n    int                 current_index;\n\n    // ─── inputs ──────────────────────────────────────────\n    void               *args;           // = action_args[current_index].\n    void              **result_slots;   // = task->result_slots; result_slots[k]\n                                        // is action k's output (NULL or value).\n    int                 n_slots;        // = task's n_actions; bound for result_slots.\n    struct task_pool   *pool;           // for pool_result_slot etc.\n    int                 priority;       // task's current priority (1=high, 10=low).\n                                        // May differ from spawn-time priority due\n                                        // to demote-on-block accumulation. Action\n                                        // can use this to know whether it's running\n                                        // degraded.\n\n    // ─── outputs ─────────────────────────────────────────\n    int                 jump_to;        // valid ONLY when returning ACT_JUMP.\n    task_id_t           block_on;       // REQUIRED when returning ACT_BLOCK.\n                                        //   Must be a valid id of a non-self\n                                        //   task. The library parks self on\n                                        //   that task's waiters list. An\n                                        //   invalid block_on (NONE, self, or\n                                        //   missing-from-registry) is a\n                                        //   programming bug — the library\n                                        //   aborts with a diagnostic.\n} task_ctx_t;\n\ntypedef action_result_t (*action_fn_t)(task_ctx_t *ctx);\n\n// ─── pool lifecycle ──────────────────────────────────────────────\n\n// Create a pool of n_workers pthreads. n_workers must be >= 1.\n// Returns NULL on bad arg / allocation failure.\ntask_pool_t *pool_create(int n_workers);\n\n// Signal shutdown, join all workers, free the pool.         "content":"// 002-task-pool-cross-task-result-wait.c\n//\n// Tests: libs/900-task-pool — the iter4 pattern for waiting on\n// another task's output. Replaces the iter3 spawn-time-deps test:\n// iter4 has no `deps` parameter on pool_spawn; cross-task waits\n// happen at runtime via pool_result_slot reads inside actions\n// paired with ACT_BLOCK.\n//\n// What this verifies:\n//   - Task A reads task B's result slot via pool_result_slot. While\n//     B's slot is SLOT_PENDING, A returns ACT_BLOCK with\n//     block_on = B's id.\n//   - The same action runs again later (after demote-and-requeue)\n//     and eventually sees SLOT_FILLED, then advances.\n//   - A's downstream action observes B's value (i.e. the BLOCK\n//     actually waited; A did not advance past the slot read while\n//     B was still pending).\n//\n// What this does NOT verify (covered elsewhere):\n//   - That ACT_BLOCK demoted A's priority — see 003.\n//   - That ACT_BLOCK promoted B's priority — see 007.\n\n#include \"../libs/900-task-pool.h\"\n\n#include <pthread.h>\n#include <stdatomic.h>\n#include <stdio.h>\n#include <stdlib.h>\n#include <time.h>\n\n// What A's wait action observed: -2 = never ran, -1 = unexpected\n// status, otherwise the value A read from B's slot (expect 42).\nstatic atomic_int a_observed_b_value = -2;\nstatic atomic_int a_block_attempts   = 0;\n\n// B writes 42 to its slot 0 after a deliberate sleep so A\n// definitely sees SLOT_PENDING on its first attempt.\nstatic action_result_t b_step(task_ctx_t *ctx) {\n    struct timespec ts = { .tv_sec = 0, .tv_nsec = 50 * 1000 * 1000 };\n    nanosleep(&ts, NULL);\n    int *v = malloc(sizeof *v);\n    *v = 42;\n    ctx->result_slots[ctx->current_index] = v;\n    return ACT_ADVANCE;\n}\n\n// A's \"wait for B's slot 0\" action. *(int *)raw : -1);\n        return ACT_ADVANCE;\n    }\n    atomic_store(&a_observed_b_value, -99);\n    return ACT_ADVANCE;\n}\n\nstatic action_result_t a_done(task_ctx_t *ctx) {\n    (void)ctx;\n    return ACT_DONE;\n}\n\nint main(void) {\n    task_pool_t *pool = pool_create(2);\n    if (!pool) { fprintf(stderr, \"pool_create failed\\n\"); return 1; }\n\n    action_fn_t b_acts[1] = { b_step };\n    task_id_t   b_id = pool_spawn(pool, b_acts, NULL, 1, /*priority=*/3);\n    pool_ref(pool, b_id);\n\n    static task_id_t b_holder;\n    b_holder = b_id;\n    action_fn_t a_acts[2] = { a_wait_on_b, a_done };\n    void       *a_argv[2] = { &b_holder,    NULL };\n    pool_spawn(pool, a_acts, a_argv, 2, /*priority=*/3);\n\n    struct timespec ts = { .tv_sec = 0, .tv_nsec = 300 * 1000 * 1000 };\n    nanosleep(&ts, NULL);\n\n    int observed = atomic_load(&a_observed_b_value);\n    int blocks   = atomic_load(&a_block_attempts);\n    printf(\"A observed B's slot value = %d (expected 42)\\n\", observed);\n    // With iter4.5 parking, A's block-action should run exactly twice\n    // total (the count tracked here is the number of BLOCK returns,\n    // not invocations): once to park, once to advance after wake.\n    // Since we count only the BLOCK returns, expect exactly 1.\n    printf(\"A returned ACT_BLOCK %d time(s) (expected 1 with parking; iter4 spinning saw ~100k)\\n\", blocks);\n\n    void *raw = NULL;\n    if (pool_result_slot(pool, b_id, 0, &raw) == SLOT_FILLED) free(raw);\n    pool_unref(pool, b_id);\n\n    pool_destroy(pool);\n\n    int ok = (observed == 42) && (blocks == 1);\n    printf(\"%s\\n\", ok ? While\n//     B's slot is SLOT_PENDING, A returns ACT_BLOCK with\n//     block_on = B's id.\n//   - The same action runs again later (after demote-and-requeue)\n//     and eventually sees SLOT_FILLED, then advances.\n//   - A's downstream action observes B's value (i.e. the BLOCK\n//     actually waited; A did not advance past the slot read while\n//     B was still pending).\n//\n// What this does NOT verify (covered elsewhere):\n//   - That ACT_BLOCK demoted A's priority — see 003.\n//   - That ACT_BLOCK promoted B's priority — see 007.\n\n#include \"../libs/900-task-pool.h\"\n\n#include <pthread.h>\n#include <stdatomic.h>\n#include <stdio.h>\n#include <stdlib.h>\n#include <time.h>\n\n// What A's wait action observed: -2 = never ran, -1 = unexpected\n// status, otherwise the value A read from B's slot (expect 42).\nstatic atomic_int a_observed_b_value = -2;\nstatic atomic_int a_block_attempts   = 0;\n\n// B writes 42 to its slot 0 after a deliberate sleep so A\n// definitely sees SLOT_PENDING on its first attempt.\nstatic action_result_t b_step(task_ctx_t *ctx) {\n    struct timespec ts = { .tv_sec = 0, .tv_nsec = 50 * 1000 * 1000 };\n    nanosleep(&ts, NULL);\n    int *v = malloc(sizeof *v);\n    *v = 42;\n    ctx->result_slots[ctx->current_index] = v;\n    return ACT_ADVANCE;\n}\n\n// A's \"wait for B's slot 0\" action. Polls via pool_result_slot;\n// blocks while pending, advances once filled.\nstatic action_result_t a_wait_on_b(task_ctx_t *ctx) {\n    task_id_t b_id = *(task_id_t *)ctx->args;\n    void *raw = NULL;\n    slot_status_t s = pool_result_slot(ctx->pool, b_id, 0, &raw);\n\n    if (s == SLOT_PENDING) {\n        atomic_fetch_add(&a_block_attempts, 1);\n        ctx->block_on = b_id;\n        return ACT_BLOCK;\n    }\n    if (s == SLOT_FILLED) {\n        atomic_store(&a_observed_b_value, raw ? *(int *)raw : -1);\n        return ACT_ADVANCE;\n    }\n    atomic_store(&a_observed_b_value, -99);\n    return ACT_ADVANCE;\n}\n\nstatic action_result_t a_done(task_ctx_t *ctx) {\n    (void)ctx;\n    return ACT_DONE;\n}\n\nint main(void) {\n    task_pool_t *pool = pool_create(2);\n    if (!pool) { fprintf(stderr, \"pool_create failed\\n\"); return 1; }\n\n    action_fn_t b_acts[1] = { b_step };\n    task_id_t   b_id = pool_spawn(pool, b_acts, NULL, 1, /*priority=*/3);\n    pool_ref(pool, b_id);\n\n    static task_id_t b_holder;\n    b_holder = b_id;\n    action_fn_t a_acts[2] = { a_wait_on_b, a_done };\n    void       *a_argv[2] = { &b_holder,    NULL };\n    pool_spawn(pool, a_acts, a_argv, 2, /*priority=*/3);\n\n    struct timespec ts = { .tv_sec = 0, .tv_nsec = 300 * 1000 * 1000 };\n    nanosleep(&ts, NULL);\n\n    int observed = atomic_load(&a_observed_b_value);\n    int blocks   = atomic_load(&a_block_attempts);\n    printf(\"A observed B's slot value = %d (expected 42)\\n\", observed);\n    // With iter4.5 parking, A's block-action should run exactly twice\n    // total (the count tracked here is the number of BLOCK returns,\n    // not invocations): once to park, once to advance after wake.\n    // Since we count only the BLOCK returns, expect exactly 1.\n    printf(\"A returned ACT_BLOCK %d time(s) (expected 1 with parking; iter4 spinning saw ~100k)\\n\", blocks);\n\n    void *raw = NULL;\n    if (pool_result_slot(pool, b_id, 0, &raw) == SLOT_FILLED) free(raw);\n    pool_unref(pool, b_id);\n\n    pool_destroy(pool);\n\n    int ok = (observed == 42) && (blocks == 1);\n    printf(\"%s\\n\", ok ? \"PASS\" : \"FAIL\");\n    return ok ? 0 : 1;\n}",
    "isImage":false,
    "interrupted":false
  },
```

```json
        "content":"// 004-task-pool-self-rescheduling.c\n//\n// Tests: libs/900-task-pool — the self-rescheduling pattern.\n//\n// What this verifies:\n//   - A task whose final action calls pool_spawn to enqueue a fresh\n//     copy of itself (with incremented state) can iterate N times\n//     and then stop on a condition.\n//   - Each iteration runs exactly once per spawn — no duplication\n//     or skipping under the action-array / re-entry mechanics.\n//\n// Pattern under test (the \"per-frame update loop without holding a\n// worker hostage\" idiom from the design discussion):\n//   actions[0] = \"do this iteration's work\"\n//   actions[1] = \"if (current < target) spawn next iteration\"\n//\n// What this does NOT verify (covered elsewhere):\n//   - Self-rescheduling that BLOCKs partway — out of scope.\n\n#include \"../libs/900-task-pool.h\"\n\n#include <pthread.h>\n#include <stdatomic.h>\n#include <stdio.h>\n#include <stdlib.h>\n#include <time.h>\n\n#define TARGET 7\n\nstatic atomic_int iterations_observed = 0;\n\nstatic task_pool_t *g_pool = NULL;\n\ntypedef struct {\n    int current;\n    int target;\n} iter_state_t;\n\nstatic action_result_t do_work(task_ctx_t *ctx) {\n    (void)ctx;\n    atomic_fetch_add(&iterations_observed, 1);\n    return ACT_ADVANCE;\n}\n\nstatic action_result_t maybe_reschedule(task_ctx_t *ctx) {\n    iter_state_t *s = (iter_state_t *)ctx->args;\n    if (s->current >= s->target) {\n        free(s);\n        return ACT_DONE;\n    }\n    iter_state_t *next = malloc(sizeof *next);\n    next->current = s->current + 1;\n    next->target  = s->target;\n    free(s);\n\n    action_fn_t  acts[2] = { do_work, maybe_reschedule };\n    void        *args[2] = { next,    next };\n    pool_spawn(g_pool, acts, args, 2, /*priority=*/5);\n    return ACT_DONE;\n}\n\nint main(void) {\n    g_pool = pool_create(2);\n    if (!g_pool) { fprintf(stderr, \"pool_create failed\\n\");     "content":"# 301 — Thread pool lifecycle and per-worker initialization\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nThe executor (`src/004-executor.lua`) runs boxes synchronously in a\nsingle Lua coroutine. There is no thread pool, no pthreads, and no\nper-thread language runtime state.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\n### Pool source\nThe thread pool is the 3d-rts pool library at\n`/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h`\n(and its `.c` companion). It is vendored into SoraMech — copied, not\nsymlinked — so SoraMech's compilation does not depend on the 3d-rts\nworking tree. Vendored copy lives at `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.h`\nand `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.c`.\n\n### Where the pool lives in the process\nThe pool is owned by the map runner's C entry point. One pool per map\nrun. It is created after the graph is loaded and validated, and\ndestroyed after all tasks reach `ACT_DONE` and the result has been\nwritten.\n\nBecause SoraMech's runner is currently a Lua program\n(`src/007-runner-main.lua`), the pool-based executor requires a thin C\nwrapper around it. The C wrapper (`src/008-pool-runner.c`) is the new\nentry point for threaded execution:\n\n```c\nint main(int argc, char **argv) {\n    // 1. parse map path from argv\n    // 2. load and validate graph (calls into Lua via lua_State or C loader)\n    // 3. pool = pool_create(n_workers)   // n_workers from env or config\n    // 4. init per-worker state (see below)\n    // 5. submit tasks for all entry-point boxes\n    // 6. wait for pool to drain (all tasks ACT_DONE)\n    // 7. pool_destroy(pool)\n    // 8. write last-run.json\n}\n```\n\nThe existing `src/007-runner-main.lua` remains for the synchronous\npath. The pool runner is an additional entry point, not a replacement\nof the Lua runner during development.\n\n### Per-worker state\nEach worker thread needs its own language runtime state. This is\ninitialized once per thread at pool startup, before any tasks run,\nand torn down at shutdown.\n\nThe pool does not currently expose a \"worker init\" hook — workers are\nplain pthreads. The per-worker state is allocated by the C entry point\nand passed to tasks via a global array indexed by thread ID:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    lua_State   *L;        // one per worker; initialized before tasks start\n    int          thread_idx;\n} worker_ctx_t;\n\nstatic worker_ctx_t worker_ctxs[MAX_WORKERS];\n```\n\nTasks retrieve their worker context by mapping `pthread_self()` to the\ncorrect index. This mapping is built during pool startup before tasks\nare submitted.\n\nAlternatively: store `worker_ctx_t *` in thread-local storage (`__thread`\npointer), set by each worker immediately after pool_create returns\ncontrol. This is simpler and avoids the `pthread_self()` lookup per task.\nDecision deferred to implementation.\n\n### Lua state per worker\nEach worker's `lua_State` is initialized with:\n- The standard libraries (`luaL_openlibs`)\n- The SoraMech libs directory on `package.path`\n- The map's `src/` directory on `package.path`\n- Any extra src dirs from `meta.json src_dirs`\n\nWorker Lua states are independent. They do not share globals. Box\nfunctions loaded in worker 0's state are not visible in worker 1's\nstate. This is intentional — Lua states are not thread-safe, and\nsharing them would require locking on every call.\n\n### Pool size\nNumber of worker threads defaults to the number of logical CPUs\n(`sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_ONLN)`), capped at a compile-time maximum\n(`MAX_WORKERS`, initially 16). Can be overridden by an environment\nvariable `SORAMECH_WORKERS=N`.\n\n### Shutdown and quiescence\nAfter all entry-point tasks are submitted, the runner waits for the\npool to drain. The pool does not expose a \"wait for all tasks\"\nfunction directly — the runner monitors task completion by tracking\nhow many tasks have been spawned and counting `ACT_DONE` transitions,\nor by using a terminal \"sink task\" that only runs after all upstream\ntasks complete and signals a condition variable.\n\nDesign note: the 3d-rts pool's `pool_destroy` joins all workers but\ndoes not guarantee tasks have completed — it destroys whatever remains.\nThe runner must quiesce the task graph before calling `pool_destroy`.\n\n## Open questions\n- Worker init hook: thread-local storage vs. global array + pthread_self\n  lookup. TLS is simpler; global array avoids TLS portability concerns.\n- How does the C entry point load the box graph? Options: embed a\n  minimal Lua state for graph loading only (separate from worker states),\n  or port the loader to C. Embedding a loader-only Lua state is simpler\n  and reuses the existing `003-loader.lua`.\n- Quiescence mechanism: condition variable on a counter, or a sentinel\n  task. The sentinel task pattern is cleaner (no shared counter).\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. Vendor `900-task-pool.h` + `.c` into `libs/task-pool/`.\n2. Write `src/008-pool-runner.c` — C entry point that loads the graph\n   via an embedded lua_State (loader-only), creates the pool, and\n   initializes per-worker lua_States.\n3. Add `Makefile` target `soramech-pool` that compiles the C runner\n   and links against the vendored pool.\n4. Smoke test: single-box map, pool with 2 workers, box runs, result\n   written. No task graph complexity yet.\n\n## Relevant files\n- `/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h` — pool API\n- `src/003-loader.lua` — graph loader to embed in the C runner\n- `src/007-runner-main.lua` — synchronous runner (remains unchanged)\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — synchronous executor (the thing being replaced)\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — threading roadmap and stage model\n"
  },
```

```json
        "totalLines":132,
        "content":"# 301 — Thread pool lifecycle and per-worker initialization\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nThe executor (`src/004-executor.lua`) runs boxes synchronously in a\nsingle Lua coroutine. There is no thread pool, no pthreads, and no\nper-thread language runtime state.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\n### Pool source\nThe thread pool is the 3d-rts pool library at\n`/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h`\n(and its `.c` companion). It is vendored into SoraMech — copied, not\nsymlinked — so SoraMech's compilation does not depend on the 3d-rts\nworking tree. Vendored copy lives at `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.h`\nand `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.c`.\n\n### Where the pool lives in the process\nThe pool is owned by the map runner's C entry point. One pool per map\nrun. It is created after the graph is loaded and validated, and\ndestroyed after all tasks reach `ACT_DONE` and the result has been\nwritten.\n\nBecause SoraMech's runner is currently a Lua program\n(`src/007-runner-main.lua`), the pool-based executor requires a thin C\nwrapper around it. The C wrapper (`src/008-pool-runner.c`) is the new\nentry point for threaded execution:\n\n```c\nint main(int argc, char **argv) {\n    // 1. parse map path from argv\n    // 2. load and validate graph (calls into Lua via lua_State or C loader)\n    // 3. pool = pool_create(n_workers)   // n_workers from env or config\n    // 4. init per-worker state (see below)\n    // 5. submit tasks for all entry-point boxes\n    // 6. wait for pool to drain (all tasks ACT_DONE)\n    // 7. pool_destroy(pool)\n    // 8. write last-run.json\n}\n```\n\nThe existing `src/007-runner-main.lua` remains for the synchronous\npath. The pool runner is an additional entry point, not a replacement\nof the Lua runner during development.\n\n### Per-worker state\nEach worker thread needs its own language runtime state. This is\ninitialized once per thread at pool startup, before any tasks run,\nand torn down at shutdown.\n\nThe pool does not currently expose a \"worker init\" hook — workers are\nplain pthreads. The per-worker state is allocated by the C entry point\nand passed to tasks via a global array indexed by thread ID:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    lua_State   *L;        // one per worker; initialized before tasks start\n    int          thread_idx;\n} worker_ctx_t;\n\nstatic worker_ctx_t worker_ctxs[MAX_WORKERS];\n```\n\nTasks retrieve their worker context by mapping `pthread_self()` to the\ncorrect index. This mapping is built during pool startup before tasks\nare submitted.\n\nAlternatively: store `worker_ctx_t *` in thread-local storage (`__thread`\npointer), set by each worker immediately after pool_create returns\ncontrol. This is simpler and avoids the `pthread_self()` lookup per task.\nDecision deferred to implementation.\n\n### Lua state per worker\nEach worker's `lua_State` is initialized with:\n- The standard libraries (`luaL_openlibs`)\n- The SoraMech libs directory on `package.path`\n- The map's `src/` directory on `package.path`\n- Any extra src dirs from `meta.json src_dirs`\n\nWorker Lua states are independent. They do not share globals. Box\nfunctions loaded in worker 0's state are not visible in worker 1's\nstate. This is intentional — Lua states are not thread-safe, and\nsharing them would require locking on every call.\n\n### Pool size\nNumber of worker threads defaults to the number of logical CPUs\n(`sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_ONLN)`), capped at a compile-time maximum\n(`MAX_WORKERS`, initially 16). Can be overridden by an environment\nvariable `SORAMECH_WORKERS=N`.\n\n### Shutdown and quiescence\nAfter all entry-point tasks are submitted, the runner waits for the\npool to drain. The pool does not expose a \"wait for all tasks\"\nfunction directly — the runner monitors task completion by tracking\nhow many tasks have been spawned and counting `ACT_DONE` transitions,\nor by using a terminal \"sink task\" that only runs after all upstream\ntasks complete and signals a condition variable.\n\nDesign note: the 3d-rts pool's `pool_destroy` joins all workers but\ndoes not guarantee tasks have completed — it destroys whatever remains.\nThe runner must quiesce the task graph before calling `pool_destroy`.\n\n## Open questions\n- Worker init hook: thread-local storage vs. global array + pthread_self\n  lookup. TLS is simpler; global array avoids TLS portability concerns.\n- How does the C entry point load the box graph? Options: embed a\n  minimal Lua state for graph loading only (separate from worker states),\n  or port the loader to C. Embedding a loader-only Lua state is simpler\n  and reuses the existing `003-loader.lua`.\n- Quiescence mechanism: condition variable on a counter, or a sentinel\n  task. The sentinel task pattern is cleaner (no shared counter).\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. Vendor `900-task-pool.h` + `.c` into `libs/task-pool/`.\n2. Write `src/008-pool-runner.c` — C entry point that loads the graph\n   via an embedded lua_State (loader-only), creates the pool, and\n   initializes per-worker lua_States.\n3. Add `Makefile` target `soramech-pool` that compiles the C runner\n   and links against the vendored pool.\n4. Smoke test: single-box map, pool with 2 workers, box runs, result\n   written. No task graph complexity yet.\n\n## Relevant files\n- `/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h` — pool API\n- `src/003-loader.lua` — graph loader to embed in the C runner\n- `src/007-runner-main.lua` — synchronous runner (remains unchanged)\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — synchronous executor (the thing being replaced)\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — threading roadmap and stage model\n"
      }
```

```json
{

  "type":"attachment",
  "isSidechain":false,
  "attachment":{
    "type":"file",
    "content":{
      "type":"text",
      "file":{
        "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md",
        "numLines":271,
        "startLine":1,
        "totalLines":271,
        "content":"# SoraMech — IPC and Threading Model\n\n## The problem\n\nThe current executor runs boxes sequentially. Each box invocation shells out to\na driver script, which starts a new process, runs the function, and exits. The\nreturn value passes through stdout. This works but has two structural problems:\n\n1. **Process-per-call cost.** Spawning a process takes roughly 1–10 ms depending\n   on the runtime. For a map with ten boxes, that's dominated by spawn overhead,\n   not by the actual work.\n\n2. **stdout is the wrong channel.** A box function that prints debug output\n   corrupts the wire value. Values are transient — they vanish once the pipe is\n   drained. The channel has no addressing, no framing, and no backpressure.\n\nThe goal is a design where cross-language calls are fast, values are addressable,\nand the execution model is ready to parallelize without redesign.\n\n---\n\n## The threading roadmap\n\nThree stages, each building on the last:\n\n**Stage 1 — Synchronous (current).** A single-threaded ready-queue walks the\ngraph in dependency order. `run_task(box, inputs)` in `src/004-executor.lua` is\nthe task boundary. It blocks until the driver responds.\n\n**Stage 2 — Coroutine-based non-blocking.** The ready-queue becomes a coroutine\nscheduler. Boxes yield when waiting on upstream results or cross-language calls.\nLuaSocket non-blocking I/O lets the scheduler run other boxes while one is\nwaiting for a response. No true parallelism yet, but the graph's natural\nconcurrency is exploited without blocking the whole process.\n\n**Stage 3 — 3d-rts thread pool.** The `task_fn` boundary swaps in the thread\npool. Worker threads pull tasks from the pool; the coroutine scheduler is\nreplaced by OS-level scheduling. Cross-language calls block a worker thread\nwhile other threads continue. True parallelism across cores.\n\nEffil-jit is not used. The path is synchronous → coroutine → 3d-rts pool.\n\n---\n\n## Stage 3 detail: pthreads task model\n\nEach box execution in the thread pool is a **task struct** containing:\n\n- **Function pointer** — the language-specific invocation wrapper (a C\n  function, since pthreads requires a C entry point)\n- **Shared memory pointer** — the region holding the input arguments and\n  return value for this invocation\n- **Dependency list** — pointers to the tasks this task is waiting on\n- **Waiting list** — pointers to tasks that are waiting on this task\n- **Counter** (iterator boxes only) — current iteration index, updated\n  in-place when the iterator re-queues itself\n\nTask structs are allocated once at run start, one per box (not one per\ninvocation). They live for the entire run.\n\n### Blocking and unblocking — pointer-only transitions\n\nWhen a task cannot run (upstream output not yet available), it is placed\nin its upstream task's waiting list. This is a pointer move — no\nallocation, no struct copy. The task struct stays exactly where it is.\n\nWhen an upstream task completes and writes its return value to shared\nmemory, it walks its waiting list and re-adds each entry to the main task\nqueue. Again, a pointer move only. The unblocked task's struct is\nunchanged; only its position in the queue changes.\n\nThis means \"blocked\", \"queued\", and \"running\" are states defined by which\nlist a task's pointer currently lives in — not by any field in the struct.\n\n### Per-thread language runtimes\n\nEach worker thread initializes its own language runtimes at startup:\n- **Lua:** one `lua_State` per thread. Lua states are not thread-safe, but\n  one per thread requires no locking. The task wrapper calls the box\n  function via `lua_pcall`.\n- **C:** the compiled box function is called directly through the function\n  pointer. No interpreter, no overhead beyond the call itself.\n- **Bash/other:** a persistent subprocess per thread (Unix domain socket\n  server model — see Option 3 above). The task wrapper sends a request and\n  blocks the thread waiting for the response.\n\n### Iterator self-re-queue\n\nAn iterator task does not terminate after one invocation. When it\ncompletes:\n1. It increments its `counter` field in-place (or wraps to 0).\n2. It checks its input queue for the next pending value.\n3. If a value is waiting: it updates its input pointer and re-adds itself\n   to the main task queue. No allocation — the same task struct re-enters\n   the queue with updated state.\n4. If no value is waiting: it adds itself to the upstream task's waiting\n   list, to be re-added when the next input arrives.\n\nInput values are processed one-at-a-time in arrival order. Ten queued\ninputs means the iterator task visits the queue ten times, advancing the\ncounter and firing a different output path each time.\n\n---\n\n## The three IPC options\n\n### Option 1 — LuaJIT FFI (Lua ↔ C, in-process)\n\nThe Foreign Function Interface lets Lua call C functions that live in a shared\nlibrary (`.so`) directly, in the same process, with no subprocess and no channel.\nYou provide a C declaration (`ffi.cdef[[ int add(int a, int b); ]]`), load the\ncompiled library (`ffi.load(\"./mybox.so\")`), and call `lib.add(3, 4)` — the CPU\njumps into native code and returns. Overhead is nanoseconds.\n\nSince the executor already does mtime-based dynamic compilation (see `drivers/c.sh`),\ncompiling to a `.so` instead of a binary is just a flag change (`-shared -fPIC`).\nThe box function signature changes from `main(argc, argv)` to a named function\nwith typed arguments — which is strictly cleaner.\n\n**Limitation:** FFI only works for languages that compile to a C-compatible ABI.\nBash cannot. Python can (via `ctypes` on the other side), but it's awkward.\nFFI is the right answer for Lua ↔ C only.\n\n**Cross-platform:** LuaJIT FFI works on Linux, macOS, and Windows. `.so` becomes\n`.dylib` on macOS and `.dll` on Windows — the `ffi.load()` call is portable if\nyou handle the extension.\n\n---\n\n### Option 2 — Shared memory (`shm_open` + `mmap`)\n\n`shm_open(\"/soramech-wire-0\", ...)` creates a named memory segment managed by\nthe kernel — not a file on disk, but a named object in RAM. `mmap()` maps it\ninto the calling process's address space. Any other process that opens the same\nname gets access to the *same physical memory*. A write in one process is\nimmediately visible in another — no copy, no syscall per access after setup.\n\nFor SoraMech, each wire between two boxes would correspond to a named shared\nmemory slot. The compiler (issue 219) generates the slot names and the read/write\ncalls. Any language that can call POSIX can participate:\n\n- Lua: via LuaJIT FFI calling `shm_open` + `mmap` from libc\n- C: natively\n- Bash: via `/dev/shm/<name>` — on Linux, the tmpfs backing shared memory is\n  exposed as a filesystem path, so bash can `cat /dev/shm/soramech-wire-0`\n\n**Performance:** After the initial `mmap()` setup, reads and writes are pointer\ndereferences — no syscalls, no copies. For small values (strings, numbers) this\nis essentially free.\n\n**Complication:** Shared memory is untyped raw bytes. You need a size header\n(how many bytes is this value?), a type tag (string? number? JSON object?), and\na synchronization mechanism (how does the reader know the writer is done?). None\nof these are hard — a small fixed header in the segment handles all three — but\nthe compiler must generate all of it correctly for every wire.\n\n**Cross-platform:**\n- Linux: full support. `/dev/shm/` filesystem exposure is Linux-specific.\n- macOS: `shm_open()` works, but the objects are NOT exposed as files. No\n  `/dev/shm/` path. Bash access via file path doesn't work.\n- Windows: completely different API (`CreateFileMapping` / `MapViewOfFile`).\n  No POSIX `shm_open` without WSL or Cygwin.\n\nShared memory is powerful but not the most portable option. The bash filesystem\nshortcut that makes it cross-language is Linux-only.\n\n---\n\n### Option 3 — Unix domain socket servers (chosen direction)\n\nA Unix domain socket is a socket addressed by a filesystem path instead of an\nIP address and port. `/tmp/soramech-bash.sock` is a special file; any process\non the same machine connects to it with the standard socket API. The kernel\nroutes data directly between processes in memory — no network stack, no loopback,\nno protocol headers. Performance is bounded by memory bandwidth.\n\nUnlike anonymous pipes, a socket has a name that unrelated processes can find\nwithout inheriting file descriptors. Multiple clients connect simultaneously;\neach gets its own channel. The server handles them with `accept()` in a loop.\n\n**The model for SoraMech:**\n\nEach language runtime runs as a persistent socket server. One server instance\nper language per worker thread:\n\n```\n/tmp/soramech-bash-0.sock   ← worker thread 0's bash runtime\n/tmp/soramech-bash-1.sock   ← worker thread 1's bash runtime\n/tmp/soramech-c-0.sock      ← worker thread 0's C runtime\n```\n\nThe server starts when the program starts, stays alive for the whole run, and\naccepts sequential requests — one box call at a time per instance. A Lua worker\nconnects to its designated socket, sends a framed request (function name +\narguments), and reads back a framed response (return value). The server is a\nsmall script (~50 lines) that sources or compiles the box file, calls the\nfunction, and writes the result.\n\n**Wire protocol:** Length-prefix framing. The sender writes a 4-byte big-endian\ninteger (the message length in bytes), then that many bytes of content. The\nreceiver reads 4 bytes, then reads exactly that many bytes. This handles values\ncontaining newlines or null bytes without ambiguity.\n\n**Cost of idle servers:** An idle server process is blocked on `accept()` — zero\nCPU, approximately 3–5 MB RSS for a bash process. For 10 languages × 4 threads\n= 40 processes ≈ 150–200 MB. Acceptable.\n\n**Integration with the coroutine scheduler (Stage 2):**\n\nWith LuaSocket non-blocking sockets, the coroutine that makes a cross-language\ncall does this:\n1. Connect to the language server socket (non-blocking)\n2. Send the request\n3. `coroutine.yield()` — registers the socket fd with the scheduler\n4. Scheduler polls all pending fds with `select()`\n5. When the fd is readable, scheduler resumes the coroutine\n6. Coroutine reads the response and continues\n\nThe cross-language call never blocks the main Lua thread. Other boxes run in\nother coroutines while the bash/C server is processing.\n\n**Integration with the 3d-rts thread pool (Stage 3):**\n\nEach worker thread owns its set of language server sockets. When `run_task` calls\na cross-language box, it sends to the socket and blocks on the read — the thread\nblocks, not the whole program. Other workers continue processing other boxes on\nother cores. The server processes run concurrently on whatever cores the OS\nschedules them to. This gives real parallelism: a bash box and a C box assigned\nto different workers can run simultaneously.\n\n**Cross-platform:**\n- Linux: full support.\n- macOS: full support. Unix domain sockets are POSIX.\n- Windows: supported since Windows 10 1803 (2018). `AF_UNIX` sockets work\n  natively. Most languages abstract this through their socket libraries.\n\nUnix domain sockets are the most portable cross-language IPC mechanism that also\nsupports concurrent connections. They are the chosen direction for the compiler\noutput and the coroutine/thread-pool executor.\n\n---\n\n## Summary comparison\n\n| Property              | FFI (.so)       | Shared memory       | Unix domain socket  |\n|-----------------------|-----------------|---------------------|---------------------|\n| Speed (per call)      | nanoseconds     | nanoseconds*        | microseconds        |\n| Languages supported   | C-ABI only      | any (with caveats)  | any                 |\n| Parallel connections  | N/A (in-process)| yes (with sync)     | yes (natural)       |\n| Linux                 | yes             | yes                 | yes                 |\n| macOS                 | yes             | partial†            | yes                 |\n| Windows               | yes (.dll)      | no (different API)  | yes (Win10+)        |\n| Complexity            | low             | medium              | low-medium          |\n\n*After initial mmap setup. †shm_open works; /dev/shm filesystem path does not.\n\nThe compiler (issue 219) uses FFI for Lua ↔ C wires where the C source is\ncompiled to a `.so`, and Unix domain sockets for all other cross-language wires.\nSame-language Lua wires are direct function calls — no IPC at all.\n\n---\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — `run_task` boundary, ready-queue\n- `src/007-runner-main.lua` — entry point for the interpreter path\n- `issues/219-map-compiler.md` — compiler that generates the IPC calls\n- `issues/104-runner-synchronous-executor.md` — task boundary design\n- `issues/213-queued-inputs-and-task-model.md` — queue-per-port, thread pool notes\n- `docs/002-roadmap.md` — phase plan for threading stages\n"
      }
    },
    "displayPath":"docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md",
    "filename":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md"
  },

}
```

```json
{

  "parentUuid":"e16ce1f0-c2e1-448e-8611-6a9c8d2a9714",
  "version":"2.1.121",

      "file":{
        "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/221-iterator-box.md",
        "numLines":216,
        "startLine":1,
        "totalLines":216,
        "content":"# 221 — Iterator box: round-robin output routing with per-instance counter\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nNo mechanism exists for a box to distribute output across multiple\ndownstream paths in sequence. The comparator routes based on a value\nthreshold; the iterator routes based on a counter that advances each call.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\n### What it does\nAn iterator box receives one input value and routes it to one of N named\noutput wires. Which wire fires is determined by an internal counter that\nincrements each call and wraps back to 0 after the last output. The\nfunction itself is a dumb passthrough — it does not make the routing\ndecision. The executor does, based on the counter.\n\nUseful for distributing work across parallel paths, cycling through a\nlist of consumers, or producing round-robin load balancing in the graph.\n\n### Counter model\nThe counter is per-box-instance, stored in the executor's in-memory\nstate (keyed by box ID). It resets to 0 at the start of each run.\nPersistence across runs is not in scope; that is a separate issue.\n\nIn the compiler output (issue 219), the counter becomes a local variable\nin a generated closure — same reset-per-program-start behavior.\n\nWrap-around: `counter = (counter + 1) % #iterator_outputs`\n\n### The iterator function\nEach language ships a standard iterator function in `libs/`:\n\n```\nlibs/iterator.lua  — M.iterate(counter, data) → data\nlibs/iterator.sh   — function iterate() { local counter=\"$1\"; echo \"$2\"; }\nlibs/iterator.c    — reads argv[2] (counter), argv[3] (data); prints data\n```\n\nThe counter is the FIRST argument (position 0 in the driver's arg list,\nbefore the declared inputs). This is intentional: last-arg convention is\nfor variadic tails where the count is unknown; the counter is always\nexactly one value and is always findable at position 0 without counting.\nThe function returns `data` unchanged. The routing decision is entirely\nin the executor.\n\nThe user points the box's `ref` and `fn` at the appropriate language's\niterator lib file. The `iterator_outputs` field in the box JSON is what\nflags the executor to treat this box as an iterator rather than a plain\ncall box.\n\n### Data model\nBox JSON gains an `iterator_outputs` field — an ordered array of\nuser-defined output path names:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"router\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"ref\": \"libs/iterator.lua\",\n  \"fn\": \"iterate\",\n  \"inputs\": [{\"name\": \"data\", \"type\": \"any\"}],\n  \"iterator_outputs\": [\"path_a\", \"path_b\", \"path_c\"],\n  \"connections\": [\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"router\", \"from_branch\": \"path_a\",\n      \"to_box\": \"worker-a\", \"to_input\": \"data\"\n    },\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"router\", \"from_branch\": \"path_b\",\n      \"to_box\": \"worker-b\", \"to_input\": \"data\"\n    },\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"router\", \"from_branch\": \"path_c\",\n      \"to_box\": \"worker-c\", \"to_input\": \"data\"\n    }\n  ]\n}\n```\n\n`from_branch` is reused for iterator output names — the same field that\nholds \"lt\"/\"eq\"/\"gt\" for comparators. The executor checks whether the\nbox has `iterator_outputs`; if so, it fires only the connection whose\n`from_branch` matches `iterator_outputs[counter]`.\n\n### Auto-grow output slots\nConnecting a wire to the last slot of the iterator's output side appends\na new empty named slot — identical to the auto-grow behavior for variadic\ninputs (issue 217). The user names each slot in the inspector. Connecting\nto the last slot prompts for a name and grows the list. Disconnecting\nremoves the slot and compacts (same rename-and-compact logic as variadic\ninputs).\n\n### Executor changes\nIn `fire_connections`, a new branch handles iterator boxes:\n\n```\nif box.iterator_outputs and #box.iterator_outputs > 0:\n    counter = executor_state[box.id .. \".counter\"] or 0\n    target_branch = box.iterator_outputs[counter + 1]  -- 1-indexed in Lua\n    fire only connections where from_branch == target_branch\n    executor_state[box.id .. \".counter\"] = (counter + 1) % #box.iterator_outputs\n```\n\nThe counter state table lives alongside the existing value store in\nthe executor.\n\n### Driver contract addition\nThe executor injects the counter as the first argument when invoking the\ndriver for an iterator box, before any declared input values:\n\n  `<driver> <file> <fn> <arg_count+1> <counter> [data_args...]`\n\nThe counter is always at position 0 in the arg list — no counting required\nto find it. Non-iterator call boxes are unaffected.\n\n### Inspector changes\nThe inspector shows:\n- An \"iterator\" toggle per box (like the variadic toggle on inputs)\n- When toggled on: the output side of the box renders named slots instead\n  of a single dot; a \"+\" row at the bottom adds a new slot\n- Each slot name is editable inline\n- The current counter value is shown as a read-only display (useful for\n  debugging live runs)\n\n### Compiler output (issue 219 integration)\nFor an iterator box, the compiler generates a closure with a captured\ncounter variable:\n\n```lua\nlocal router_counter = 0\nlocal function router(data)\n  local idx = router_counter\n  router_counter = (router_counter + 1) % 3\n  if     idx == 0 then worker_a(data)\n  elseif idx == 1 then worker_b(data)\n  else                  worker_c(data)\n  end\nend\n```\n\nThe iterator lib files are bundled alongside other box source files.\n\n### Threading model integration (3d-rts thread pool)\n\nIn the pthreads task pool, each box execution is a task struct containing:\n- A function pointer to the language-specific invocation wrapper\n- A pointer to shared memory holding the input arguments and return value\n- A pointer list of dependency tasks (upstream boxes whose output this box\n  needs before it can run)\n- For iterator boxes: a `counter` field (integer, part of the task struct)\n\n**Blocking:** when a task cannot run because its dependencies haven't\ncompleted, it is placed in the blocking task's waiting list. No memory is\nallocated — the task struct stays alive, only a pointer to it is moved.\nWhen the blocking task completes and writes its return value to shared\nmemory, it walks its waiting list and re-adds each waiting task to the\nmain queue (again, pointer move only — no reallocation or struct copying).\n\n**Iterator self-re-add:** when an iterator task completes, it does not\nterminate. Instead:\n1. It increments its own `counter` field (or wraps to 0).\n2. It checks if there is another pending input value in its input queue.\n3. If yes: it updates its input pointer to the next pending value, then\n   re-adds itself to the main task queue. No new allocation.\n4. If no: it adds itself to the waiting list of its upstream dependency,\n   to be re-added when the next input value arrives.\n\nThis means the iterator task struct is allocated once and lives for the\nduration of the run, cycling through the queue as many times as there are\ninput values to process. Input values are processed one-at-a-time in\narrival order — if 10 values are queued, the iterator visits the queue 10\ntimes, each time firing a different output path and advancing the counter.\n\n**C calling Lua:** the per-thread invocation wrapper is a C function\n(pthreads requires a C entry point). Each worker thread initializes its\nown `lua_State` at startup — Lua states are not thread-safe but one per\nthread is fine. The wrapper dispatches on language tag: if Lua, calls\nthrough the thread's `lua_State` via `lua_pcall`; if native C, calls the\nfunction pointer directly (no interpreter overhead); if bash, spawns a\nsubprocess (the one case that doesn't map cleanly to pthreads — see\ndocs/004-ipc-and-threading.md for options).\n\n## Open questions\n- Should the counter be exposed as a readable data port (wirable to\n  another box as an input) in addition to being shown in the inspector?\n- Should auto-grow prompt for the output name immediately on connect, or\n  generate a placeholder (`out_N`) that the user renames afterward?\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. `libs/iterator.lua` — trivial passthrough function.\n2. `libs/iterator.sh`, `libs/iterator.c` — same for bash and C.\n3. `src/001-schema.lua` — add `iterator_outputs` to the box validator.\n4. `src/004-executor.lua` — add counter state table; extend\n   `fire_connections` with the iterator branch; inject counter arg in\n   `run_task` when box has `iterator_outputs`.\n5. `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — iterator toggle; editable output slots.\n6. `assets/js/006-wires.js` — auto-grow output slots on connect;\n   auto-shrink + rename on disconnect (mirrors variadic input logic).\n7. `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — render N named output dots when\n   `iterator_outputs` is set (replacing the single-wire dot).\n\n## Relevant files\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — fire_connections, run_task\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — box validator\n- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — iterator toggle, slot editor\n- `assets/js/006-wires.js` — auto-grow/shrink for output slots\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box rendering\n- `issues/217-concat-box-and-dynamic-inputs.md` — variadic input model\n  (auto-grow/shrink logic mirrors this)\n- `issues/completed/108-branch-box-and-predicate-routing.md` — comparator\n  model that `from_branch` and the routing pattern extend from\n- `issues/219-map-compiler.md` — compiler integration notes above\n"
      }
    },
    "displayPath":"issues/221-iterator-box.md",
    "filename":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/221-iterator-box.md"
```

## [1179]

```json
{
  "timestamp":"2026-05-09T01:56:07.312Z",
  "message":{
    "content":"Okay so the first thing I see is that we're relying on there being a lua runner. This is currently true, but we're going to want to have a different runner for each user-defined language. In-fact, can you make an issue file in phase 2 for a drop-down menu (that doesn't do anything yet) that lets the user select what the \"main\" language of the map is, with the idea being that other languages will incur a performance penalty? Or is that even true, because everything's being passed into a C pthreads call anyway? ... now that I think of it, the only truly \"native\" language would be C, wouldn't it? Oh also we'd need a button (that doesn't currently do anything) which \"compiles\" the map into an executable binary and assets directory (which includes all the src files and it's where we'd store the binaries that we compile on-the-fly). Now that I think of it, I think even C shouldn't be a special case, which might allow the users to swap to a different thread language (maybe) eventually if they want that. I can't imagine they would want to, but if we make even the C language calls go through the same system as the other language calls, then it should help unify them.\n\nSo, to clarify, what we want is... for each box that is run, create a task in the pthread library's task queue. In the task, include auto-generated wrappers that converts it into something that C can run, whether that means spinning up an interpreter (and keeping it running, for future tasks) or whatever should be defined in the language spec that users can define. Then, when the task is picked up by a thread, execute it in whatever way the language the function-box is written in demands. These things, the generic abstracted application methodology for each language, should be functional and usable for any type of function written in that language. Once the language spec is written, it should be able to run any kind of functionality that that language provides. I don't think we should be converting code to another language dynamically, or transpiling to another language or anything like that - instead, we should just require the user to define wrappers, runners, drivers, or whatever else might be necessary to run the functions they want to run.\n\nAlso. Questions about where the workers should store their variables. Everything, or at least most things, should be in shared memory. Anything related to a task should be in shared memory. This ideally would be memory that is accessible to any language - in-fact it must be. Arguments should have assigned slots, and return values should have slots assigned for them as well. That way, if something blocks something else, all it has to do is wait until the assigned return value slot is filled before it knows it should run. Similarly, if something is waiting for input, it can just wait until it's input slot is filled before it runs. Keep in mind, we can assign the input of one task to be the output of another task, and it's just... fine. There is reference counting included as well, so keep track of that. Meaning, we only clear memory and re-use the slot when nobody has a reference to it - that way, if a function returns, it's return value slot is kept open because some other function is waiting for it as it's input - there's a reference still for it so it won't get cleared. The rest of the function, the stuff that the other task isn't waiting on, that stuff can be cleared. Once the stuff that has no references is cleared, the task that DOES have a reference to it takes responsibility for clearing it.",
    "role":"user"
  },
```

```json
        "input":{
          "content":"# 222 — Compile button and assets directory\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nThe editor has no mechanism to trigger compilation of a map. Maps are only\nrunnable via the synchronous interpreter path (`src/007-runner-main.lua`).\nThere is no compiled artifact, no assets directory, and no binary output.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\n### UI: compile button\nA \"Compile\" button appears in the editor toolbar. Clicking it does nothing\nyet — it is a placeholder for the compilation pipeline (issue 219). The\nbutton is present so the UI layout is established before the backend is wired\nin.\n\nThe button label is \"Compile\". It has no loading state, no progress\nindicator, and no output for now. It simply exists in the toolbar next to\nthe existing controls.\n\n### Compiled artifacts: assets directory\nWhen compilation is eventually wired in, pressing the button triggers a\nbuild that produces a self-contained output directory alongside the map:\n\n```\nmaps/<map-name>/compiled/\n    pool-runner          ← the compiled C entry point (008-pool-runner.c)\n    src/                 ← copy of all source files used by the map\n    bin/                 ← compiled per-box binaries (C boxes → .so or binary)\n    manifest.json        ← list of every box, its language, and its binary path\n```\n\nThe compiled directory is the map's deployment artifact. Running\n`maps/<map-name>/compiled/pool-runner` executes the map using the thread\npool executor, with no dependency on the editor or the Lua interpreter path.\n\nThe `src/` copy inside `compiled/` is what the pool runner references at\nruntime — box files are not read from the map's live src/ during execution.\nThis isolates deployed maps from edits in progress.\n\n### Language-agnostic design note\nThe compile step does not treat any language as special. Each box's language\ndetermines which invocation wrapper is selected at compile time. The same\nbuild path handles a Lua box, a C box, and a Bash box without branching on\nthe language at the top level. The per-language wrapper spec (issue 303) is\nwhat parameterizes the build for each box.\n\n## Open questions\n- Should the compile button be disabled until the map has at least one entry\n  box designated? Or always enabled (and let the backend reject invalid maps)?\n- Where in the toolbar does it live — left side with map controls, or right\n  side with a \"run\" / \"export\" group?\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. Add a \"Compile\" button element to the editor toolbar in `assets/index.html`.\n2. Wire a click handler in `assets/js/005-app.js` that logs \"compile clicked\"\n   (placeholder). No server call yet.\n3. Leave the `compiled/` directory layout as a comment in the handler — the\n   structure is established here for when issue 219 fills it in.\n\n## Relevant files\n- `assets/index.html` — editor toolbar\n- `assets/js/005-app.js` — click handler\n- `issues/219-map-compiler.md` — compilation pipeline that this button triggers\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — per-language invocation wrapper spec\n  (to be written; parameterizes what goes into `compiled/bin/`)\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/222-compile-button-and-assets-directory.md"
        },
        "id":"toolu_013Ejb9Hae84z9NVUREWMKNA"
      }]
  },
```

```json
          "content":"# 301 — Thread pool lifecycle and per-worker initialization\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nThe executor (`src/004-executor.lua`) runs boxes synchronously in a\nsingle Lua coroutine. There is no thread pool, no pthreads, and no\nper-thread language runtime state.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\n### Pool source\nThe thread pool is the 3d-rts pool library at\n`/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h`\n(and its `.c` companion). It is vendored into SoraMech — copied, not\nsymlinked — so SoraMech's compilation does not depend on the 3d-rts\nworking tree. Vendored copy lives at `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.h`\nand `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.c`.\n\n### Where the pool lives in the process\nThe pool is owned by the map runner's C entry point. One pool per map\nrun. It is created after the graph is loaded and validated, and\ndestroyed after all tasks reach `ACT_DONE` and the result has been\nwritten.\n\nThe C wrapper (`src/008-pool-runner.c`) is the entry point for threaded\nexecution:\n\n```c\nint main(int argc, char **argv) {\n    // 1. parse map path from argv\n    // 2. load and validate graph (calls into a loader-only lua_State)\n    // 3. pool = pool_create(n_workers)\n    // 4. init per-worker language runtime handles (see below)\n    // 5. submit tasks for all entry-point boxes\n    // 6. wait for pool to drain (all tasks ACT_DONE)\n    // 7. pool_destroy(pool)\n    // 8. write last-run.json\n}\n```\n\nThe existing `src/007-runner-main.lua` remains for the synchronous\ninterpreter path. The pool runner is an additional entry point, not a\nreplacement during development.\n\n### Per-worker language runtimes\nNo language is treated as the \"native\" or preferred language at the\nthread level. Every box — regardless of language — goes through the\nsame task dispatch path. The per-box cost is determined by that box's\ninvocation wrapper, not by any map-level language setting.\n\nEach worker thread holds a set of language runtime handles, one per\nlanguage it may be asked to run. These are initialized once at pool\nstartup, before any tasks are submitted, and torn down at shutdown:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    void   *lua;          // lua_State*, or NULL if Lua not used in this map\n    void   *bash_sock;    // fd to persistent bash socket server, or -1\n    // additional language handles added here as language specs are written\n    int     thread_idx;\n} worker_ctx_t;\n\nstatic worker_ctx_t worker_ctxs[MAX_WORKERS];\n```\n\nOnly the language handles actually needed by the map are initialized.\nIf the map contains no Bash boxes, no Bash socket server is started for\nany worker. The graph loader determines which languages are present and\npasses that set to the pool runner at startup.\n\nThe per-language initialization protocol is defined by the language\nruntime spec (issue 303). The pool runner calls each spec's `init`\nfunction at startup and its `teardown` function at shutdown.\n\n### Worker context access\nWorker context is stored in thread-local storage (`__thread\nworker_ctx_t *current_worker`), set by each worker immediately after\nthe thread is started. This is simpler than a global array +\n`pthread_self()` lookup and avoids per-task overhead.\n\n### Pool size\nNumber of worker threads defaults to the number of logical CPUs\n(`sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_ONLN)`), capped at a compile-time maximum\n(`MAX_WORKERS`, initially 16). Can be overridden by an environment\nvariable `SORAMECH_WORKERS=N`.\n\n### Wire value slots (issue 302)\nAll inter-task values live in shared memory, not in worker-local\nstorage. Each wire in the graph has an assigned slot in a shared\nmemory region. Workers read from their input slots and write to their\noutput slots. The pool runner allocates the slot region at startup,\nbefore tasks are submitted. See issue 302 for the slot layout and\nreference counting protocol.\n\n### Shutdown and quiescence\nAfter all entry-point tasks are submitted, the runner waits for the\npool to drain using a sentinel task: a task that has no function of its\nown and depends on every terminal box. When the sentinel reaches\n`ACT_DONE`, all upstream work is guaranteed complete. The runner then\ncalls `pool_destroy`.\n\n`pool_destroy` joins all workers but does not guarantee tasks have\ncompleted on its own — the sentinel ensures quiescence before it is\ncalled.\n\n## Open questions\n- Graph loading: embed a loader-only `lua_State` in the C runner (reuses\n  `003-loader.lua`) vs port the loader to C. Loader-only lua_State is\n  simpler and reuses existing code.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. Vendor `900-task-pool.h` + `.c` into `libs/task-pool/`.\n2. Write `src/008-pool-runner.c` — C entry point that loads the graph\n   via an embedded loader-only `lua_State`, creates the pool, and\n   initializes per-worker language runtime handles using the language\n   spec registry (issue 303).\n3. Add `Makefile` target `soramech-pool` that compiles the C runner and\n   links against the vendored pool.\n4. Smoke test: single-box Lua map, pool with 2 workers, box runs, result\n   written. No task graph complexity yet.\n\n## Relevant files\n- `/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h` — pool API\n- `src/003-loader.lua` — graph loader to embed in the C runner\n- `src/007-runner-main.lua` — synchronous runner (remains unchanged)\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — synchronous executor (the thing being replaced)\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — shared memory slot layout and refcounting\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — per-language init/call/teardown protocol\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — threading roadmap and IPC options\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md"
        },

One pool per map\nrun. The pool runner is an additional entry point, not a replacement\nof the Lua runner during development.\n\n### Per-worker state\nEach worker thread needs its own language runtime state. This is\ninitialized once per thread at pool startup, before any tasks run,\nand torn down at shutdown.\n\nThe pool does not currently expose a \"worker init\" hook — workers are\nplain pthreads. The per-worker state is allocated by the C entry point\nand passed to tasks via a global array indexed by thread ID:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    lua_State   *L;        // one per worker; initialized before tasks start\n    int          thread_idx;\n} worker_ctx_t;\n\nstatic worker_ctx_t worker_ctxs[MAX_WORKERS];\n```\n\nTasks retrieve their worker context by mapping `pthread_self()` to the\ncorrect index. This mapping is built during pool startup before tasks\nare submitted.\n\nAlternatively: store `worker_ctx_t *` in thread-local storage (`__thread`\npointer), set by each worker immediately after pool_create returns\ncontrol. This is simpler and avoids the `pthread_self()` lookup per task.\nDecision deferred to implementation.\n\n### Lua state per worker\nEach worker's `lua_State` is initialized with:\n- The standard libraries (`luaL_openlibs`)\n- The SoraMech libs directory on `package.path`\n- The map's `src/` directory on `package.path`\n- Any extra src dirs from `meta.json src_dirs`\n\nWorker Lua states are independent. They do not share globals. Box\nfunctions loaded in worker 0's state are not visible in worker 1's\nstate. This is intentional — Lua states are not thread-safe, and\nsharing them would require locking on every call.\n\n### Pool size\nNumber of worker threads defaults to the number of logical CPUs\n(`sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_ONLN)`), capped at a compile-time maximum\n(`MAX_WORKERS`, initially 16). Can be overridden by an environment\nvariable `SORAMECH_WORKERS=N`.\n\n### Shutdown and quiescence\nAfter all entry-point tasks are submitted, the runner waits for the\npool to drain. The pool does not expose a \"wait for all tasks\"\nfunction directly — the runner monitors task completion by tracking\nhow many tasks have been spawned and counting `ACT_DONE` transitions,\nor by using a terminal \"sink task\" that only runs after all upstream\ntasks complete and signals a condition variable.\n\nDesign note: the 3d-rts pool's `pool_destroy` joins all workers but\ndoes not guarantee tasks have completed — it destroys whatever remains.\nThe runner must quiesce the task graph before calling `pool_destroy`.\n\n## Open questions\n- Worker init hook: thread-local storage vs. global array + pthread_self\n  lookup. Options: embed a\n  minimal Lua state for graph loading only (separate from worker states),\n  or port the loader to C. The sentinel task pattern is cleaner (no shared counter).\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. Vendor `900-task-pool.h` + `.c` into `libs/task-pool/`.\n2. Write `src/008-pool-runner.c` — C entry point that loads the graph\n   via an embedded lua_State (loader-only), creates the pool, and\n   initializes per-worker lua_States.\n3. This is simpler than a global array +\n`pthread_self()` lookup and avoids per-task overhead.\n\n### Pool size\nNumber of worker threads defaults to the number of logical CPUs\n(`sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_ONLN)`), capped at a compile-time maximum\n(`MAX_WORKERS`, initially 16). Can be overridden by an environment\nvariable `SORAMECH_WORKERS=N`.\n\n### Wire value slots (issue 302)\nAll inter-task values live in shared memory, not in worker-local\nstorage. Each wire in the graph has an assigned slot in a shared\nmemory region. Workers read from their input slots and write to their\noutput slots. The pool runner allocates the slot region at startup,\nbefore tasks are submitted. See issue 302 for the slot layout and\nreference counting protocol.\n\n### Shutdown and quiescence\nAfter all entry-point tasks are submitted, the runner waits for the\npool to drain using a sentinel task: a task that has no function of its\nown and depends on every terminal box. When the sentinel reaches\n`ACT_DONE`, all upstream work is guaranteed complete. The runner then\ncalls `pool_destroy`.\n\n`pool_destroy` joins all workers but does not guarantee tasks have\ncompleted on its own — the sentinel ensures quiescence before it is\ncalled.\n\n## Open questions\n- Graph loading: embed a loader-only `lua_State` in the C runner (reuses\n  `003-loader.lua`) vs port the loader to C. Loader-only lua_State is\n  simpler and reuses existing code.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. Vendor `900-task-pool.h` + `.c` into `libs/task-pool/`.\n2. Write `src/008-pool-runner.c` — C entry point that loads the graph\n   via an embedded loader-only `lua_State`, creates the pool, and\n   initializes per-worker language runtime handles using the language\n   spec registry (issue 303).\n3. Add `Makefile` target `soramech-pool` that compiles the C runner and\n   links against the vendored pool.\n4. Smoke test: single-box Lua map, pool with 2 workers, box runs, result\n   written. No task graph complexity yet.\n\n## Relevant files\n- `/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h` — pool API\n- `src/003-loader.lua` — graph loader to embed in the C runner\n- `src/007-runner-main.lua` — synchronous runner (remains unchanged)\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — synchronous executor (the thing being replaced)\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — shared memory slot layout and refcounting\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — per-language init/call/teardown protocol\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — threading roadmap and IPC options\n"
  },
```
