          "content":"# 302 — Wire value slot store: shared memory with reference counting\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nWire values are passed through stdout pipes and transient strings. Values\nhave no addressable location, no reference count, and no cross-language\naccessibility. Each value vanishes once the pipe is drained.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\n### Purpose\nEvery wire in the map graph corresponds to a slot in a shared memory region.\nSlots are the universal value exchange point for all tasks. Any language\nruntime can read from or write to a slot using the same protocol. No language\nhas a privileged access path — a Lua worker and a Bash worker read the same\nbytes from the same region.\n\nA task's input slots are the outputs of its upstream tasks. When a task is\nsubmitted to the pool, its inputs are identified by slot IDs. The task\nblocks until all its input slots are marked filled. When the task completes,\nit writes its return value to its output slot and decrements its references\nto the input slots it consumed.\n\n### Slot layout\nEach slot is a fixed-size header followed by a variable-size value region:\n\n```\nOffset  Size  Field\n------  ----  -----\n0       4     refcount       (atomic int32, starts at number of downstream tasks)\n4       4     value_size     (bytes of value data, 0 if not yet filled)\n8       1     type_tag       (0=none, 1=string, 2=number, 3=json, 4=bytes)\n9       1     filled         (0=empty, 1=ready; set last after value_size written)\n10      2     _pad           (alignment)\n12      N     value_data     (up to MAX_SLOT_VALUE_SIZE bytes)\n```\n\n`filled` is set with a memory barrier after `value_size` and `value_data`\nare written, so a reader that sees `filled == 1` is guaranteed to see the\ncomplete value.\n\n### Reference counting protocol\nAt map startup, the pool runner computes each slot's initial refcount: the\nnumber of downstream tasks that will read from it. This is derived from the\ngraph's connection list and does not change at runtime.\n\nWhen a task finishes reading a slot (it has extracted the value it needed),\nit calls `slot_unref(slot_id)`. When the refcount drops to zero, the task\nthat performed the final unref is responsible for clearing the slot (zeroing\nthe header, marking filled=0, resetting value_size=0). The slot is then\navailable for reuse by a future run or iteration.\n\nNo centralized garbage collector is needed. Clearing is deterministic:\nwhoever drops the last reference does the work.\n\n### Slot region layout\nThe full region is a single contiguous block allocated at map startup:\n\n```\n[slot_region_header_t]       — total slot count, slot stride, magic\n[slot_t * n_slots]           — one slot per wire in the graph\n```\n\nThe stride is fixed at compile time (`SLOT_STRIDE = 12 + MAX_SLOT_VALUE_SIZE`).\nSlot `i` starts at `base + sizeof(slot_region_header_t) + i * SLOT_STRIDE`.\n\n### Backing store\nThe region is created with `shm_open` + `mmap`. The shared memory object\nis named `/soramech-<map-id>-wires`. Any language runtime that opens the\nsame name and maps it gets access to the same physical memory — no copies,\nno syscalls per access after initial setup.\n\nSynchronization for blocked tasks (waiting on an empty slot) uses a mutex\nand condition variable per slot, stored in the slot header. When a producer\ncalls `slot_write`, it signals the slot's condition variable, waking any\ntask blocked on it.\n\nFor languages that cannot call POSIX directly (e.g. Bash), the Unix domain\nsocket server wrapper (docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md, Option 3) reads and\nwrites slot values on behalf of the calling script. The script passes the\nslot ID; the wrapper does the mmap access.\n\n### Pool runner integration\nAt startup, the pool runner:\n1. Calls `slot_region_create(n_wires)` — creates and maps the shared memory.\n2. Walks the graph's connection list to assign a slot ID to each wire.\n3. Computes and sets each slot's initial refcount.\n4. Stores the `(wire → slot_id)` mapping in a table accessible to the task\n   dispatch layer.\n\nAt shutdown, `slot_region_destroy()` unmaps and unlinks the shared memory\nobject.\n\n### Task dispatch layer integration\nWhen the task dispatch layer (issue 304) invokes a box, it:\n1. Waits until all input slot IDs report `filled == 1`.\n2. Extracts the input values from the slots.\n3. Calls the language runtime's `invoke` function with the extracted values.\n4. Writes the returned value to the box's output slot.\n5. Calls `slot_unref` on each consumed input slot.\n\nThe dispatch layer is the only code that reads and writes slots. Language\nruntimes receive and return plain values (strings, numbers, blobs) — they\ndo not interact with slot IDs directly.\n\n### C API surface\n\n```c\nslot_region_t *slot_region_create(int n_slots);\nvoid           slot_region_destroy(slot_region_t *region);\n\nvoid  slot_write(slot_region_t *r, int id, const void *data, int size, uint8_t type_tag);\nint   slot_read (slot_region_t *r, int id, void *buf, int buf_size); // returns bytes read\nvoid  slot_ref  (slot_region_t *r, int id);\nvoid  slot_unref(slot_region_t *r, int id);\nvoid  slot_wait (slot_region_t *r, int id); // blocks until filled == 1\n```\n\n## Open questions\n- `MAX_SLOT_VALUE_SIZE`: large values (image bytes, long strings) may not fit\n  in the fixed stride. Two options: (a) cap at a generous fixed limit (e.g.\n  64 KB) and error on overflow; (b) store large values in a separate tmpfs\n  file and put the path in the slot. Option (a) is simpler; option (b) is\n  needed only if large-value boxes are ever required.\n- Per-slot mutex vs a central poll: condition variables per slot are clean\n  but add ~40 bytes per slot (pthread_mutex_t + pthread_cond_t). Alternative:\n  a single semaphore that any writer posts to, combined with a filled-check\n  loop. Per-slot is less contention and cleaner to reason about; start there.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. Write `src/slot-store.h` and `src/slot-store.c` — the C API above.\n2. Unit test: two threads; thread A writes a slot, thread B blocks on it,\n   receives the value, unrefs. Verify slot is cleared after unref.\n3. Integrate into `src/008-pool-runner.c`: call `slot_region_create` at\n   startup, pass region pointer into the task dispatch layer.\n4. Add slot ID assignment to the graph loader output (a new field in the\n   in-memory graph representation alongside the existing connection list).\n\n## Relevant files\n- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — pool entry point that owns the slot region\n- `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.h` — pool API (refcounting is complementary)\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle; slot region\n  created and destroyed alongside the pool\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — the layer that reads/writes slots\n  around each box invocation (to be written)\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — IPC options; shm_open + mmap is Option 2\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md"

When a task is\nsubmitted to the pool, its inputs are identified by slot IDs. The task\nblocks until all its input slots are marked filled. When the task completes,\nit writes its return value to its output slot and decrements its references\nto the input slots it consumed.\n\n### Slot layout\nEach slot is a fixed-size header followed by a variable-size value region:\n\n```\nOffset  Size  Field\n------  ----  -----\n0       4     refcount       (atomic int32, starts at number of downstream tasks)\n4       4     value_size     (bytes of value data, 0 if not yet filled)\n8       1     type_tag       (0=none, 1=string, 2=number, 3=json, 4=bytes)\n9       1     filled         (0=empty, 1=ready; set last after value_size written)\n10      2     _pad           (alignment)\n12      N     value_data     (up to MAX_SLOT_VALUE_SIZE bytes)\n```\n\n`filled` is set with a memory barrier after `value_size` and `value_data`\nare written, so a reader that sees `filled == 1` is guaranteed to see the\ncomplete value.\n\n### Reference counting protocol\nAt map startup, the pool runner computes each slot's initial refcount: the\nnumber of downstream tasks that will read from it. This is derived from the\ngraph's connection list and does not change at runtime.\n\nWhen a task finishes reading a slot (it has extracted the value it needed),\nit calls `slot_unref(slot_id)`. When the refcount drops to zero, the task\nthat performed the final unref is responsible for clearing the slot (zeroing\nthe header, marking filled=0, resetting value_size=0). The slot is then\navailable for reuse by a future run or iteration.\n\nNo centralized garbage collector is needed. Clearing is deterministic:\nwhoever drops the last reference does the work.\n\n### Slot region layout\nThe full region is a single contiguous block allocated at map startup:\n\n```\n[slot_region_header_t]       — total slot count, slot stride, magic\n[slot_t * n_slots]           — one slot per wire in the graph\n```\n\nThe stride is fixed at compile time (`SLOT_STRIDE = 12 + MAX_SLOT_VALUE_SIZE`).\nSlot `i` starts at `base + sizeof(slot_region_header_t) + i * SLOT_STRIDE`.\n\n### Backing store\nThe region is created with `shm_open` + `mmap`. The shared memory object\nis named `/soramech-<map-id>-wires`. Any language runtime that opens the\nsame name and maps it gets access to the same physical memory — no copies,\nno syscalls per access after initial setup.\n\nSynchronization for blocked tasks (waiting on an empty slot) uses a mutex\nand condition variable per slot, stored in the slot header. When a producer\ncalls `slot_write`, it signals the slot's condition variable, waking any\ntask blocked on it.\n\nFor languages that cannot call POSIX directly (e.g. Bash), the Unix domain\nsocket server wrapper (docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md, Option 3) reads and\nwrites slot values on behalf of the calling script. The script passes the\nslot ID; the wrapper does the mmap access.\n\n### Pool runner integration\nAt startup, the pool runner:\n1. Calls `slot_region_create(n_wires)` — creates and maps the shared memory.\n2. Walks the graph's connection list to assign a slot ID to each wire.\n3. Computes and sets each slot's initial refcount.\n4. Stores the `(wire → slot_id)` mapping in a table accessible to the task\n   dispatch layer.\n\nAt shutdown, `slot_region_destroy()` unmaps and unlinks the shared memory\nobject.\n\n### Task dispatch layer integration\nWhen the task dispatch layer (issue 304) invokes a box, it:\n1. Waits until all input slot IDs report `filled == 1`.\n2. Extracts the input values from the slots.\n3. Calls the language runtime's `invoke` function with the extracted values.\n4. Writes the returned value to the box's output slot.\n5. Calls `slot_unref` on each consumed input slot.\n\nThe dispatch layer is the only code that reads and writes slots. Language\nruntimes receive and return plain values (strings, numbers, blobs) — they\ndo not interact with slot IDs directly.\n\n### C API surface\n\n```c\nslot_region_t *slot_region_create(int n_slots);\nvoid           slot_region_destroy(slot_region_t *region);\n\nvoid  slot_write(slot_region_t *r, int id, const void *data, int size, uint8_t type_tag);\nint   slot_read (slot_region_t *r, int id, void *buf, int buf_size); // returns bytes read\nvoid  slot_ref  (slot_region_t *r, int id);\nvoid  slot_unref(slot_region_t *r, int id);\nvoid  slot_wait (slot_region_t *r, int id); // blocks until filled == 1\n```\n\n## Open questions\n- `MAX_SLOT_VALUE_SIZE`: large values (image bytes, long strings) may not fit\n  in the fixed stride. Two options: (a) cap at a generous fixed limit (e.g.\n  64 KB) and error on overflow; (b) store large values in a separate tmpfs\n  file and put the path in the slot. Option (a) is simpler; option (b) is\n  needed only if large-value boxes are ever required.\n- Per-slot mutex vs a central poll: condition variables per slot are clean\n  but add ~40 bytes per slot (pthread_mutex_t + pthread_cond_t). Alternative:\n  a single semaphore that any writer posts to, combined with a filled-check\n  loop. Per-slot is less contention and cleaner to reason about; start there.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. Write `src/slot-store.h` and `src/slot-store.c` — the C API above.\n2. Unit test: two threads; thread A writes a slot, thread B blocks on it,\n   receives the value, unrefs. Verify slot is cleared after unref.\n3. Integrate into `src/008-pool-runner.c`: call `slot_region_create` at\n   startup, pass region pointer into the task dispatch layer.\n4. Add slot ID assignment to the graph loader output (a new field in the\n   in-memory graph representation alongside the existing connection list).\n\n## Relevant files\n- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — pool entry point that owns the slot region\n- `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.h` — pool API (refcounting is complementary)\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle; slot region\n  created and destroyed alongside the pool\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — the layer that reads/writes slots\n  around each box invocation (to be written)\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — IPC options; shm_open + mmap is Option 2\n"
  },

```json
{
  "timestamp":"2026-05-09T02:21:38.798Z",
  "message":{
    "content":"In 301 it says the synchronous path remains as an alternative entry point, but we want to only be parallelized. We'll need to mark all the places that will be refactored according to that specification. Phase 2, it's fine if it's synchronous. But from phase-3 and onward we are only using the thread pool.\n\nAlso, it says the pool runner allocates slots at startup. But, that doesn't really make sense. We'll need to allocate new slots everytime a task is created.\n\nNot sure what that sentinel task in 301 is all about. Can you clarify? why do we need that, what functions does it serve?\n\nAlso, let's port the loader to C. We should have all the functionality for the system built into the part of the program that's handling and managing the thread pool.\n\nOkay 302 already is off because it says \"every wire in the map graph corresponds to a slot in a shared memory region\" that's not quite right. This has to be fully asynchronous. We should always expect that there be multiple people writing to the same memory location. So, lots of little ring buffers, and all the mechanics required to maintain them. In addition, it's not one slot per wire - rather, one slot per *task*, and each wire corresponds to a connection between tasks. The box is the slot, not the wire. And, we can have multiple slots for the same box, one for each time it's called. New slots being created dynamically when required. The wire is the reference that keeps things alive and is counted, the wire is the relationship, the mapping of outputs to inputs, it is the timing mechanism that defines when we can operate. It blocks things, it clears things, it is the guidance counselor and arbiter.\n\nsomething I noticed on the \"task dispatch layer integration\" - we can build the task ahead of time, marking out slots and filling in what information we know, but we shouldn't add it to the ready queue until all the inputs are available. I think. Actually, I'm not sure. Lemme think about it.\n\nMAX_SLOT_VALUE_SIZE should be provided when we're creating the task. I think? Anyway it should be provided each time, and it should exactly refer to the exact amount of memory needed. For the same reason that you ask C arrays to include the number of arguments (or be null terminated, which is... not ideal).\n\nAlso, we should have a per-slot mutex. It can just be a single bit flag flipped that corresponds to the n'th slot being touched by another thread. Or if that's too complex, premature optimization and all that, then we can just do a boolean or something.",
    "role":"user"
  },

          "content":"# 301 — Thread pool lifecycle and per-worker initialization\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nThe executor (`src/004-executor.lua`) runs boxes synchronously in a\nsingle Lua coroutine. There is no thread pool, no pthreads, and no\nper-thread language runtime state.\n\n## Phase model\n\nPhase 2 is the synchronous interpreter path. It is the development\ntarget while editor work is in progress.\n\nPhase 3 is the thread pool path. It is the only execution path going\nforward. The synchronous interpreter does not stay around as an\nalternative entry point — once phase 3 lands, the pool runner\nreplaces it. There is no \"fallback to synchronous\" mode.\n\n### Phase 2 → 3 refactor surface\n\nThe following components are replaced (not extended) in phase 3:\n\n| Phase 2 file                  | Phase 3 replacement                  |\n|-------------------------------|--------------------------------------|\n| `src/003-loader.lua`          | C loader inside `src/008-pool-runner.c` |\n| `src/004-executor.lua`        | C task dispatch layer (issue 304)    |\n| `src/007-runner-main.lua`     | `src/008-pool-runner.c`              |\n| `drivers/*.sh`                | Language runtime spec (issue 303)    |\n\nAll threading-pool-adjacent functionality is C code that lives next to\nthe pool. There is no embedded Lua runtime for graph loading or\ndispatch — Lua appears only as a language runtime that boxes can use,\non equal footing with C, Bash, and any future language.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\n### Pool source\nThe thread pool is the 3d-rts pool library at\n`/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h`\n(and its `.c` companion). It is vendored into SoraMech — copied, not\nsymlinked — so SoraMech's compilation does not depend on the 3d-rts\nworking tree. Vendored copy lives at `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.h`\nand `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.c`.\n\n### Where the pool lives in the process\nThe pool is owned by the map runner's C entry point. One pool per map\nrun. It is created after the graph is loaded and validated, and\ndestroyed after the run completes.\n\nThe C entry point (`src/008-pool-runner.c`):\n\n```c\nint main(int argc, char **argv) {\n    // 1. parse map path from argv\n    // 2. load and validate graph (C loader, no Lua involved)\n    // 3. determine which language runtimes the map uses\n    // 4. pool = pool_create(n_workers)\n    // 5. init per-worker language runtime handles for each language present\n    // 6. submit tasks for all entry-point boxes\n    // 7. wait for active task count to reach zero\n    // 8. pool_destroy(pool)\n    // 9. write last-run.json\n}\n```\n\n### Graph loading: ported to C\nThe graph loader is ported from `src/003-loader.lua` to C and lives\ninside (or alongside) `008-pool-runner.c`. The pool runner has no\nembedded Lua state for loader purposes. JSON parsing uses a small\nvendored C JSON library (cJSON or similar; decision deferred to\nimplementation).\n\nLua appears in the runner only when a box's language is Lua — and even\nthen, only inside that worker's language runtime handle. The pool\nrunner itself does not link to liblua at the top level.\n\n### Per-worker language runtimes\nNo language is treated as the \"native\" or preferred language at the\nthread level. Every box — regardless of language — goes through the\nsame task dispatch path. The per-box cost is determined by that box's\ninvocation wrapper, not by any map-level language setting.\n\nEach worker thread holds a set of language runtime handles, one per\nlanguage it may be asked to run. These are initialized once at pool\nstartup, before any tasks are submitted, and torn down at shutdown:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    void   *handles[N_LANGS];   // opaque per-language runtime state\n    int     thread_idx;\n} worker_ctx_t;\n```\n\nOnly the language handles actually needed by the map are initialized.\nIf the map contains no Bash boxes, no Bash handle is started for any\nworker. The graph loader determines which languages are present and\npasses that set to the pool runner at startup.\n\nThe per-language initialization protocol is defined by the language\nruntime spec (issue 303). The pool runner calls each spec's `init`\nfunction at startup and its `teardown` function at shutdown.\n\n### Worker context access\nWorker context is stored in thread-local storage (`__thread\nworker_ctx_t *current_worker`), set by each worker immediately after\nthe thread is started. This avoids per-task `pthread_self()` lookups.\n\n### Pool size\nNumber of worker threads defaults to the number of logical CPUs\n(`sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_ONLN)`), capped at a compile-time maximum\n(`MAX_WORKERS`, initially 16). Can be overridden by an environment\nvariable `SORAMECH_WORKERS=N`.\n\n### Slots are owned by tasks (issue 302)\nSlots are allocated when a task is created, not pre-allocated at\nstartup. A task allocates its output slot(s) at submission time, with\nsize specified by the task's language and function. The pool runner\ndoes not own a slot region — slots are per-task allocations that\noutlive the task only as long as wires hold references to them. See\nissue 302 for the slot lifecycle.\n\n### Quiescence\nThe runner tracks an active-task counter, incremented on `pool_spawn`\nand decremented when a task reaches `ACT_DONE`. The main thread waits\non a condition variable that signals when the counter reaches zero.\n\nThis naturally handles iterators that re-queue themselves: each\nre-queue increments the counter, each completion decrements. The run\nends when no task is in flight and no waiter is blocked on an unfilled\nslot. (A run that deadlocks — a task waiting on a slot that no producer\nwill ever fill — is detected separately and reported as an error.)\n\n## Open questions\n- Vendored JSON library: cJSON, jsmn, or hand-rolled. cJSON is heavier\n  but easiest. Decision deferred.\n- Deadlock detection: how aggressively to detect tasks blocked on\n  slots that will never be filled. A periodic scan, or instrumented\n  through the slot store's wait-list.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. Vendor `900-task-pool.h` + `.c` into `libs/task-pool/`.\n2. Vendor a JSON parser into `libs/json/`.\n3. Port `003-loader.lua` to C inside `src/008-pool-runner.c`.\n4. Write the pool lifecycle skeleton: pool_create, worker context TLS,\n   active-task counter, quiescence wait.\n5. Add `Makefile` target `soramech-pool` that compiles the C runner and\n   links against the vendored pool and JSON parser.\n6. Smoke test: single-box Lua map, pool with 2 workers, box runs, result\n   written. No task graph complexity yet.\n\n## Relevant files\n- `/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h` — pool API\n- `src/003-loader.lua` — current Lua loader, to be ported to C\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — current synchronous executor, to be replaced\n- `src/007-runner-main.lua` — current Lua runner, to be replaced\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — per-task slot lifecycle\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — per-language init/call/teardown\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — replaces 004-executor.lua\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — threading roadmap and IPC options\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md"
        },

    "originalFile":"# 301 — Thread pool lifecycle and per-worker initialization\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nThe executor (`src/004-executor.lua`) runs boxes synchronously in a\nsingle Lua coroutine. There is no thread pool, no pthreads, and no\nper-thread language runtime state.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\n### Pool source\nThe thread pool is the 3d-rts pool library at\n`/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h`\n(and its `.c` companion). It is vendored into SoraMech — copied, not\nsymlinked — so SoraMech's compilation does not depend on the 3d-rts\nworking tree. Vendored copy lives at `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.h`\nand `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.c`.\n\n### Where the pool lives in the process\nThe pool is owned by the map runner's C entry point. One pool per map\nrun. It is created after the graph is loaded and validated, and\ndestroyed after all tasks reach `ACT_DONE` and the result has been\nwritten.\n\nThe C wrapper (`src/008-pool-runner.c`) is the entry point for threaded\nexecution:\n\n```c\nint main(int argc, char **argv) {\n    // 1. parse map path from argv\n    // 2. load and validate graph (calls into a loader-only lua_State)\n    // 3. pool = pool_create(n_workers)\n    // 4. init per-worker language runtime handles (see below)\n    // 5. submit tasks for all entry-point boxes\n    // 6. wait for pool to drain (all tasks ACT_DONE)\n    // 7. pool_destroy(pool)\n    // 8. write last-run.json\n}\n```\n\nThe existing `src/007-runner-main.lua` remains for the synchronous\ninterpreter path. The pool runner is an additional entry point, not a\nreplacement during development.\n\n### Per-worker language runtimes\nNo language is treated as the \"native\" or preferred language at the\nthread level. Every box — regardless of language — goes through the\nsame task dispatch path. The per-box cost is determined by that box's\ninvocation wrapper, not by any map-level language setting.\n\nEach worker thread holds a set of language runtime handles, one per\nlanguage it may be asked to run. These are initialized once at pool\nstartup, before any tasks are submitted, and torn down at shutdown:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    void   *lua;          // lua_State*, or NULL if Lua not used in this map\n    void   *bash_sock;    // fd to persistent bash socket server, or -1\n    // additional language handles added here as language specs are written\n    int     thread_idx;\n} worker_ctx_t;\n\nstatic worker_ctx_t worker_ctxs[MAX_WORKERS];\n```\n\nOnly the language handles actually needed by the map are initialized.\nIf the map contains no Bash boxes, no Bash socket server is started for\nany worker. The graph loader determines which languages are present and\npasses that set to the pool runner at startup.\n\nThe per-language initialization protocol is defined by the language\nruntime spec (issue 303). The pool runner calls each spec's `init`\nfunction at startup and its `teardown` function at shutdown.\n\n### Worker context access\nWorker context is stored in thread-local storage (`__thread\nworker_ctx_t *current_worker`), set by each worker immediately after\nthe thread is started. This is simpler than a global array +\n`pthread_self()` lookup and avoids per-task overhead.\n\n### Pool size\nNumber of worker threads defaults to the number of logical CPUs\n(`sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_ONLN)`), capped at a compile-time maximum\n(`MAX_WORKERS`, initially 16). Can be overridden by an environment\nvariable `SORAMECH_WORKERS=N`.\n\n### Wire value slots (issue 302)\nAll inter-task values live in shared memory, not in worker-local\nstorage. Each wire in the graph has an assigned slot in a shared\nmemory region. Workers read from their input slots and write to their\noutput slots. The pool runner allocates the slot region at startup,\nbefore tasks are submitted. See issue 302 for the slot layout and\nreference counting protocol.\n\n### Shutdown and quiescence\nAfter all entry-point tasks are submitted, the runner waits for the\npool to drain using a sentinel task: a task that has no function of its\nown and depends on every terminal box. When the sentinel reaches\n`ACT_DONE`, all upstream work is guaranteed complete. The runner then\ncalls `pool_destroy`.\n\n`pool_destroy` joins all workers but does not guarantee tasks have\ncompleted on its own — the sentinel ensures quiescence before it is\ncalled.\n\n## Open questions\n- Graph loading: embed a loader-only `lua_State` in the C runner (reuses\n  `003-loader.lua`) vs port the loader to C. Loader-only lua_State is\n  simpler and reuses existing code.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. Vendor `900-task-pool.h` + `.c` into `libs/task-pool/`.\n2. Write `src/008-pool-runner.c` — C entry point that loads the graph\n   via an embedded loader-only `lua_State`, creates the pool, and\n   initializes per-worker language runtime handles using the language\n   spec registry (issue 303).\n3. Add `Makefile` target `soramech-pool` that compiles the C runner and\n   links against the vendored pool.\n4. Smoke test: single-box Lua map, pool with 2 workers, box runs, result\n   written. No task graph complexity yet.\n\n## Relevant files\n- `/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h` — pool API\n- `src/003-loader.lua` — graph loader to embed in the C runner\n- `src/007-runner-main.lua` — synchronous runner (remains unchanged)\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — synchronous executor (the thing being replaced)\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — shared memory slot layout and refcounting\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — per-language init/call/teardown protocol\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — threading roadmap and IPC options\n",

    "content":"# 301 — Thread pool lifecycle and per-worker initialization\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nThe executor (`src/004-executor.lua`) runs boxes synchronously in a\nsingle Lua coroutine. There is no thread pool, no pthreads, and no\nper-thread language runtime state.\n\n## Phase model\n\nPhase 2 is the synchronous interpreter path. It is the development\ntarget while editor work is in progress.\n\nPhase 3 is the thread pool path. It is the only execution path going\nforward. The synchronous interpreter does not stay around as an\nalternative entry point — once phase 3 lands, the pool runner\nreplaces it. There is no \"fallback to synchronous\" mode.\n\n### Phase 2 → 3 refactor surface\n\nThe following components are replaced (not extended) in phase 3:\n\n| Phase 2 file                  | Phase 3 replacement                  |\n|-------------------------------|--------------------------------------|\n| `src/003-loader.lua`          | C loader inside `src/008-pool-runner.c` |\n| `src/004-executor.lua`        | C task dispatch layer (issue 304)    |\n| `src/007-runner-main.lua`     | `src/008-pool-runner.c`              |\n| `drivers/*.sh`                | Language runtime spec (issue 303)    |\n\nAll threading-pool-adjacent functionality is C code that lives next to\nthe pool. There is no embedded Lua runtime for graph loading or\ndispatch — Lua appears only as a language runtime that boxes can use,\non equal footing with C, Bash, and any future language.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\n### Pool source\nThe thread pool is the 3d-rts pool library at\n`/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h`\n(and its `.c` companion). It is vendored into SoraMech — copied, not\nsymlinked — so SoraMech's compilation does not depend on the 3d-rts\nworking tree. Vendored copy lives at `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.h`\nand `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.c`.\n\n### Where the pool lives in the process\nThe pool is owned by the map runner's C entry point. One pool per map\nrun. It is created after the graph is loaded and validated, and\ndestroyed after the run completes.\n\nThe C entry point (`src/008-pool-runner.c`):\n\n```c\nint main(int argc, char **argv) {\n    // 1. parse map path from argv\n    // 2. load and validate graph (C loader, no Lua involved)\n    // 3. determine which language runtimes the map uses\n    // 4. pool = pool_create(n_workers)\n    // 5. init per-worker language runtime handles for each language present\n    // 6. submit tasks for all entry-point boxes\n    // 7. wait for active task count to reach zero\n    // 8. pool_destroy(pool)\n    // 9. write last-run.json\n}\n```\n\n### Graph loading: ported to C\nThe graph loader is ported from `src/003-loader.lua` to C and lives\ninside (or alongside) `008-pool-runner.c`. The pool runner has no\nembedded Lua state for loader purposes. JSON parsing uses a small\nvendored C JSON library (cJSON or similar; decision deferred to\nimplementation).\n\nLua appears in the runner only when a box's language is Lua — and even\nthen, only inside that worker's language runtime handle. The pool\nrunner itself does not link to liblua at the top level.\n\n### Per-worker language runtimes\nNo language is treated as the \"native\" or preferred language at the\nthread level. Every box — regardless of language — goes through the\nsame task dispatch path. The per-box cost is determined by that box's\ninvocation wrapper, not by any map-level language setting.\n\nEach worker thread holds a set of language runtime handles, one per\nlanguage it may be asked to run. These are initialized once at pool\nstartup, before any tasks are submitted, and torn down at shutdown:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    void   *handles[N_LANGS];   // opaque per-language runtime state\n    int     thread_idx;\n} worker_ctx_t;\n```\n\nOnly the language handles actually needed by the map are initialized.\nIf the map contains no Bash boxes, no Bash handle is started for any\nworker. The graph loader determines which languages are present and\npasses that set to the pool runner at startup.\n\nThe per-language initialization protocol is defined by the language\nruntime spec (issue 303). The pool runner calls each spec's `init`\nfunction at startup and its `teardown` function at shutdown.\n\n### Worker context access\nWorker context is stored in thread-local storage (`__thread\nworker_ctx_t *current_worker`), set by each worker immediately after\nthe thread is started. This avoids per-task `pthread_self()` lookups.\n\n### Pool size\nNumber of worker threads defaults to the number of logical CPUs\n(`sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_ONLN)`), capped at a compile-time maximum\n(`MAX_WORKERS`, initially 16). Can be overridden by an environment\nvariable `SORAMECH_WORKERS=N`.\n\n### Slots are owned by tasks (issue 302)\nSlots are allocated when a task is created, not pre-allocated at\nstartup. A task allocates its output slot(s) at submission time, with\nsize specified by the task's language and function. The pool runner\ndoes not own a slot region — slots are per-task allocations that\noutlive the task only as long as wires hold references to them. See\nissue 302 for the slot lifecycle.\n\n### Quiescence\nThe runner tracks an active-task counter, incremented on `pool_spawn`\nand decremented when a task reaches `ACT_DONE`. The main thread waits\non a condition variable that signals when the counter reaches zero.\n\nThis naturally handles iterators that re-queue themselves: each\nre-queue increments the counter, each completion decrements. The run\nends when no task is in flight and no waiter is blocked on an unfilled\nslot. (A run that deadlocks — a task waiting on a slot that no producer\nwill ever fill — is detected separately and reported as an error.)\n\n## Open questions\n- Vendored JSON library: cJSON, jsmn, or hand-rolled. cJSON is heavier\n  but easiest. Decision deferred.\n- Deadlock detection: how aggressively to detect tasks blocked on\n  slots that will never be filled. A periodic scan, or instrumented\n  through the slot store's wait-list.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. Vendor `900-task-pool.h` + `.c` into `libs/task-pool/`.\n2. Vendor a JSON parser into `libs/json/`.\n3. Port `003-loader.lua` to C inside `src/008-pool-runner.c`.\n4. Write the pool lifecycle skeleton: pool_create, worker context TLS,\n   active-task counter, quiescence wait.\n5. Add `Makefile` target `soramech-pool` that compiles the C runner and\n   links against the vendored pool and JSON parser.\n6. Smoke test: single-box Lua map, pool with 2 workers, box runs, result\n   written. No task graph complexity yet.\n\n## Relevant files\n- `/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h` — pool API\n- `src/003-loader.lua` — current Lua loader, to be ported to C\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — current synchronous executor, to be replaced\n- `src/007-runner-main.lua` — current Lua runner, to be replaced\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — per-task slot lifecycle\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — per-language init/call/teardown\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — replaces 004-executor.lua\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — threading roadmap and IPC options\n"

        "input":{
          "content":"# 302 — Per-task slot store with wire-held references\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nWire values are passed through stdout pipes and transient strings. Values\nhave no addressable location, no reference count, and no cross-language\naccessibility. Each value vanishes once the pipe is drained.\n\n## Concept\n\n### Slots belong to tasks, not wires\nA **slot** is the memory region that holds a task's output. Slots are\ncreated when tasks are created. A box that runs once produces one slot;\na box that runs ten times (an iterator) produces ten slots, one per\ninvocation. Slots live in shared memory so any language runtime can read\nor write them without copying.\n\nA **wire** is the relationship between two tasks: it says \"task B's input\nN reads from task A's output M.\" Wires hold references to slots. They\nare the timing mechanism — a task does not become ready until every\ninput wire reports its source slot is filled. They are also the lifetime\nmechanism — a slot is freed only after every wire that referenced it has\nreleased it.\n\nThe wire is the arbiter. The slot is just memory.\n\n### Multiple writers, ring buffers\nSome slots have multiple producers writing concurrently. The clearest\ncase is a queued input on a downstream task: many upstream tasks all push\ntheir outputs into the same input queue (issue 213). That queue is a\nring buffer, with the appropriate atomics so producers don't clobber each\nother and the consumer always sees a coherent value.\n\nMost output slots have a single producer (the task itself) and one or\nmore consumers (the wires that read from it). Single-producer slots\ndon't need ring buffer machinery — just the per-slot lock for safe read\nduring the brief window between write and unref.\n\n### Asynchrony\nThe store is fully asynchronous. Slots are allocated, filled, read, and\nfreed at any time, on any thread, with no global lock. Synchronization\nis per-slot. There is no central allocator-wide mutex.\n\n## Slot layout\n\nEach slot is a small header followed by a value region whose size is\nspecified by the task at allocation time:\n\n```\nOffset  Size  Field\n------  ----  -----\n0       4     refcount        (atomic int32)\n4       4     value_size      (bytes of value data, 0 if not yet filled)\n8       4     value_capacity  (allocated bytes, set at slot creation)\n12      1     type_tag        (0=none, 1=string, 2=number, 3=json, 4=bytes)\n13      1     filled          (0=empty, 1=ready)\n14      1     touched         (0=free, 1=another thread is mutating)\n15      1     _pad\n16      N     value_data      (N == value_capacity)\n```\n\n`value_capacity` is exactly the size requested by the task — no global\nmaximum. This mirrors the C convention of passing array sizes alongside\narrays. Slots may have wildly different sizes within the same run.\n\n`touched` is a single-byte flag toggled around any mutation of the\nheader (refcount changes, filled flip, etc.). A reader that finds\n`touched == 1` retries. This is the simplest possible per-slot lock; if\ncontention becomes a problem, replace with a proper mutex without\nchanging the API.\n\n`filled` is set last, with a memory barrier, so a reader that observes\n`filled == 1` is guaranteed to see the complete value.\n\n## Reference counting protocol\n\nWhen a task is submitted, the dispatch layer:\n1. Allocates the task's output slot(s) with the requested capacity.\n2. For each wire reading from the slot, calls `slot_ref` on the slot.\n   The wire holds that reference for as long as it might still need to\n   read.\n3. When the consumer task finishes reading, it calls `slot_unref` on\n   the wire's slot. The wire is then dead.\n4. When the refcount drops to zero, the task that performed the final\n   unref clears the slot (frees the backing memory or marks it\n   reusable).\n\nNo central garbage collector. Clearing is deterministic — last unref\ndoes the work.\n\n## Backing store\n\nSlots live in shared memory created with `shm_open` + `mmap`. The\nshared memory object is named `/soramech-<run-id>`. Allocation inside\nthe region is handled by a per-run allocator (a simple bump allocator\nor a small free-list allocator — start with bump, add free-list when\nslot reuse becomes worth it).\n\nAny language runtime that opens the same shared memory name and maps it\ngets access to the same physical memory. For languages that cannot call\nPOSIX directly (e.g. Bash), the language runtime spec (issue 303) is\nresponsible for proxying slot reads and writes through the language's\nruntime server.\n\nSynchronization for blocked tasks (waiting on an empty slot) is handled\nby the dispatch layer (issue 304) — typically a wait list per slot.\nProducers signal waiters when they flip `filled`.\n\n## Slot creation\n\nSlot creation happens inside the dispatch layer at task submission. The\ncaller specifies the value capacity:\n\n```c\nslot_id_t slot_alloc(slot_store_t *store, int capacity, uint8_t type_tag);\n```\n\nThe slot is created with `refcount = 0`, `filled = 0`. The dispatch\nlayer then increments the refcount once per wire reading from it before\nthe task is exposed to consumers.\n\n## Ring-buffer slots (queued inputs)\n\nA downstream task with a queued input has a single slot that acts as a\nring buffer for incoming values. Producers push values, the consumer\ndrains them in arrival order. The buffer's capacity and value-stride\nare set at creation time. The implementation is a fixed-size ring with\natomic head/tail pointers — standard MPSC ring buffer.\n\nThis is a separate slot kind from the single-value output slot.\nDistinguished by a flag in the slot header (or a separate slot type\ntag — decision deferred).\n\n## C API surface\n\n```c\n// Single-value slot\nslot_id_t slot_alloc        (slot_store_t *s, int capacity, uint8_t type_tag);\nvoid      slot_write        (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, const void *data, int size);\nint       slot_read         (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size);\nvoid      slot_ref          (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id);\nvoid      slot_unref        (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id);  // frees if refcount → 0\n\n// Ring-buffer slot\nslot_id_t slot_ring_alloc   (slot_store_t *s, int slot_capacity, int n_slots);\nvoid      slot_ring_push    (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, const void *data, int size);\nint       slot_ring_pop     (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size);\n```\n\n## Open question — submission timing\n\nWhen the dispatch layer builds a task, it knows the task's input wires\nand output slots before any input is filled. The unresolved question:\n\n- **Option A**: build the task struct early, hold it in a \"blocked\" set,\n  add to the ready queue only when all inputs are filled.\n- **Option B**: build and submit immediately, let the task itself block\n  on its input slots via `ACT_BLOCK` on the first input.\n\nOption A is cleaner — the ready queue contains only runnable tasks.\nOption B uses the pool's existing block-and-wake machinery, fewer\nmoving parts.\n\nDecision deferred. Likely Option B, but want to think about it once\nthe dispatch layer (issue 304) is being written.\n\n## Open questions\n- Allocation strategy: bump allocator vs free-list. Bump is simpler;\n  free-list reuses memory across tasks. Start with bump.\n- Type tag granularity: do we need a \"json\" tag distinct from \"string\",\n  or is everything string + size at this layer? Probably size + opaque\n  bytes; the type tag becomes advisory only.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. Write `src/slot-store.h` and `src/slot-store.c` — the C API above.\n2. Unit test single-value slots: thread A writes, thread B reads,\n   refcount decrements, slot freed when last ref dropped.\n3. Unit test ring-buffer slots: multiple producers push, single consumer\n   drains in order, no values lost or duplicated.\n4. Integrate into `src/008-pool-runner.c`: shared memory created at\n   startup, store handle passed to the dispatch layer.\n\n## Relevant files\n- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — pool entry point, owns the shared memory region\n- `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.h` — pool API (refcounting is complementary)\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — task dispatch reads/writes slots\n- `issues/213-queued-inputs-and-task-model.md` — queued input model that\n  ring-buffer slots implement\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — IPC options; shm_open + mmap is Option 2\n",

    "originalFile":"# 302 — Wire value slot store: shared memory with reference counting\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nWire values are passed through stdout pipes and transient strings. Values\nhave no addressable location, no reference count, and no cross-language\naccessibility. Each value vanishes once the pipe is drained.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\n### Purpose\nEvery wire in the map graph corresponds to a slot in a shared memory region.\nSlots are the universal value exchange point for all tasks. Any language\nruntime can read from or write to a slot using the same protocol. No language\nhas a privileged access path — a Lua worker and a Bash worker read the same\nbytes from the same region.\n\nA task's input slots are the outputs of its upstream tasks. When a task is\nsubmitted to the pool, its inputs are identified by slot IDs. The task\nblocks until all its input slots are marked filled. When the task completes,\nit writes its return value to its output slot and decrements its references\nto the input slots it consumed.\n\n### Slot layout\nEach slot is a fixed-size header followed by a variable-size value region:\n\n```\nOffset  Size  Field\n------  ----  -----\n0       4     refcount       (atomic int32, starts at number of downstream tasks)\n4       4     value_size     (bytes of value data, 0 if not yet filled)\n8       1     type_tag       (0=none, 1=string, 2=number, 3=json, 4=bytes)\n9       1     filled         (0=empty, 1=ready; set last after value_size written)\n10      2     _pad           (alignment)\n12      N     value_data     (up to MAX_SLOT_VALUE_SIZE bytes)\n```\n\n`filled` is set with a memory barrier after `value_size` and `value_data`\nare written, so a reader that sees `filled == 1` is guaranteed to see the\ncomplete value.\n\n### Reference counting protocol\nAt map startup, the pool runner computes each slot's initial refcount: the\nnumber of downstream tasks that will read from it. This is derived from the\ngraph's connection list and does not change at runtime.\n\nWhen a task finishes reading a slot (it has extracted the value it needed),\nit calls `slot_unref(slot_id)`. When the refcount drops to zero, the task\nthat performed the final unref is responsible for clearing the slot (zeroing\nthe header, marking filled=0, resetting value_size=0). The slot is then\navailable for reuse by a future run or iteration.\n\nNo centralized garbage collector is needed. Clearing is deterministic:\nwhoever drops the last reference does the work.\n\n### Slot region layout\nThe full region is a single contiguous block allocated at map startup:\n\n```\n[slot_region_header_t]       — total slot count, slot stride, magic\n[slot_t * n_slots]           — one slot per wire in the graph\n```\n\nThe stride is fixed at compile time (`SLOT_STRIDE = 12 + MAX_SLOT_VALUE_SIZE`).\nSlot `i` starts at `base + sizeof(slot_region_header_t) + i * SLOT_STRIDE`.\n\n### Backing store\nThe region is created with `shm_open` + `mmap`. The shared memory object\nis named `/soramech-<map-id>-wires`. Any language runtime that opens the\nsame name and maps it gets access to the same physical memory — no copies,\nno syscalls per access after initial setup.\n\nSynchronization for blocked tasks (waiting on an empty slot) uses a mutex\nand condition variable per slot, stored in the slot header. When a producer\ncalls `slot_write`, it signals the slot's condition variable, waking any\ntask blocked on it.\n\nFor languages that cannot call POSIX directly (e.g. Bash), the Unix domain\nsocket server wrapper (docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md, Option 3) reads and\nwrites slot values on behalf of the calling script. The script passes the\nslot ID; the wrapper does the mmap access.\n\n### Pool runner integration\nAt startup, the pool runner:\n1. Calls `slot_region_create(n_wires)` — creates and maps the shared memory.\n2. Walks the graph's connection list to assign a slot ID to each wire.\n3. Computes and sets each slot's initial refcount.\n4. Stores the `(wire → slot_id)` mapping in a table accessible to the task\n   dispatch layer.\n\nAt shutdown, `slot_region_destroy()` unmaps and unlinks the shared memory\nobject.\n\n### Task dispatch layer integration\nWhen the task dispatch layer (issue 304) invokes a box, it:\n1. Waits until all input slot IDs report `filled == 1`.\n2. Extracts the input values from the slots.\n3. Calls the language runtime's `invoke` function with the extracted values.\n4. Writes the returned value to the box's output slot.\n5. Calls `slot_unref` on each consumed input slot.\n\nThe dispatch layer is the only code that reads and writes slots. Language\nruntimes receive and return plain values (strings, numbers, blobs) — they\ndo not interact with slot IDs directly.\n\n### C API surface\n\n```c\nslot_region_t *slot_region_create(int n_slots);\nvoid           slot_region_destroy(slot_region_t *region);\n\nvoid  slot_write(slot_region_t *r, int id, const void *data, int size, uint8_t type_tag);\nint   slot_read (slot_region_t *r, int id, void *buf, int buf_size); // returns bytes read\nvoid  slot_ref  (slot_region_t *r, int id);\nvoid  slot_unref(slot_region_t *r, int id);\nvoid  slot_wait (slot_region_t *r, int id); // blocks until filled == 1\n```\n\n## Open questions\n- `MAX_SLOT_VALUE_SIZE`: large values (image bytes, long strings) may not fit\n  in the fixed stride. Two options: (a) cap at a generous fixed limit (e.g.\n  64 KB) and error on overflow; (b) store large values in a separate tmpfs\n  file and put the path in the slot. Option (a) is simpler; option (b) is\n  needed only if large-value boxes are ever required.\n- Per-slot mutex vs a central poll: condition variables per slot are clean\n  but add ~40 bytes per slot (pthread_mutex_t + pthread_cond_t). Alternative:\n  a single semaphore that any writer posts to, combined with a filled-check\n  loop. Per-slot is less contention and cleaner to reason about; start there.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. Write `src/slot-store.h` and `src/slot-store.c` — the C API above.\n2. Unit test: two threads; thread A writes a slot, thread B blocks on it,\n   receives the value, unrefs. Verify slot is cleared after unref.\n3. Integrate into `src/008-pool-runner.c`: call `slot_region_create` at\n   startup, pass region pointer into the task dispatch layer.\n4. Add slot ID assignment to the graph loader output (a new field in the\n   in-memory graph representation alongside the existing connection list).\n\n## Relevant files\n- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — pool entry point that owns the slot region\n- `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.h` — pool API (refcounting is complementary)\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle; slot region\n  created and destroyed alongside the pool\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — the layer that reads/writes slots\n  around each box invocation (to be written)\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — IPC options; shm_open + mmap is Option 2\n",
    "userModified":false,
    "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md",
    "content":"# 302 — Per-task slot store with wire-held references\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nWire values are passed through stdout pipes and transient strings. Values\nhave no addressable location, no reference count, and no cross-language\naccessibility. Each value vanishes once the pipe is drained.\n\n## Concept\n\n### Slots belong to tasks, not wires\nA **slot** is the memory region that holds a task's output. Slots are\ncreated when tasks are created. A box that runs once produces one slot;\na box that runs ten times (an iterator) produces ten slots, one per\ninvocation. Slots live in shared memory so any language runtime can read\nor write them without copying.\n\nA **wire** is the relationship between two tasks: it says \"task B's input\nN reads from task A's output M.\" Wires hold references to slots. They\nare the timing mechanism — a task does not become ready until every\ninput wire reports its source slot is filled. They are also the lifetime\nmechanism — a slot is freed only after every wire that referenced it has\nreleased it.\n\nThe wire is the arbiter. The slot is just memory.\n\n### Multiple writers, ring buffers\nSome slots have multiple producers writing concurrently. The clearest\ncase is a queued input on a downstream task: many upstream tasks all push\ntheir outputs into the same input queue (issue 213). That queue is a\nring buffer, with the appropriate atomics so producers don't clobber each\nother and the consumer always sees a coherent value.\n\nMost output slots have a single producer (the task itself) and one or\nmore consumers (the wires that read from it). Single-producer slots\ndon't need ring buffer machinery — just the per-slot lock for safe read\nduring the brief window between write and unref.\n\n### Asynchrony\nThe store is fully asynchronous. Slots are allocated, filled, read, and\nfreed at any time, on any thread, with no global lock. Synchronization\nis per-slot. There is no central allocator-wide mutex.\n\n## Slot layout\n\nEach slot is a small header followed by a value region whose size is\nspecified by the task at allocation time:\n\n```\nOffset  Size  Field\n------  ----  -----\n0       4     refcount        (atomic int32)\n4       4     value_size      (bytes of value data, 0 if not yet filled)\n8       4     value_capacity  (allocated bytes, set at slot creation)\n12      1     type_tag        (0=none, 1=string, 2=number, 3=json, 4=bytes)\n13      1     filled          (0=empty, 1=ready)\n14      1     touched         (0=free, 1=another thread is mutating)\n15      1     _pad\n16      N     value_data      (N == value_capacity)\n```\n\n`value_capacity` is exactly the size requested by the task — no global\nmaximum. This mirrors the C convention of passing array sizes alongside\narrays. Slots may have wildly different sizes within the same run.\n\n`touched` is a single-byte flag toggled around any mutation of the\nheader (refcount changes, filled flip, etc.). A reader that finds\n`touched == 1` retries. This is the simplest possible per-slot lock; if\ncontention becomes a problem, replace with a proper mutex without\nchanging the API.\n\n`filled` is set last, with a memory barrier, so a reader that observes\n`filled == 1` is guaranteed to see the complete value.\n\n## Reference counting protocol\n\nWhen a task is submitted, the dispatch layer:\n1. Allocates the task's output slot(s) with the requested capacity.\n2. For each wire reading from the slot, calls `slot_ref` on the slot.\n   The wire holds that reference for as long as it might still need to\n   read.\n3. When the consumer task finishes reading, it calls `slot_unref` on\n   the wire's slot. The wire is then dead.\n4. When the refcount drops to zero, the task that performed the final\n   unref clears the slot (frees the backing memory or marks it\n   reusable).\n\nNo central garbage collector. Clearing is deterministic — last unref\ndoes the work.\n\n## Backing store\n\nSlots live in shared memory created with `shm_open` + `mmap`. The\nshared memory object is named `/soramech-<run-id>`. Allocation inside\nthe region is handled by a per-run allocator (a simple bump allocator\nor a small free-list allocator — start with bump, add free-list when\nslot reuse becomes worth it).\n\nAny language runtime that opens the same shared memory name and maps it\ngets access to the same physical memory. For languages that cannot call\nPOSIX directly (e.g. Bash), the language runtime spec (issue 303) is\nresponsible for proxying slot reads and writes through the language's\nruntime server.\n\nSynchronization for blocked tasks (waiting on an empty slot) is handled\nby the dispatch layer (issue 304) — typically a wait list per slot.\nProducers signal waiters when they flip `filled`.\n\n## Slot creation\n\nSlot creation happens inside the dispatch layer at task submission. The\ncaller specifies the value capacity:\n\n```c\nslot_id_t slot_alloc(slot_store_t *store, int capacity, uint8_t type_tag);\n```\n\nThe slot is created with `refcount = 0`, `filled = 0`. The dispatch\nlayer then increments the refcount once per wire reading from it before\nthe task is exposed to consumers.\n\n## Ring-buffer slots (queued inputs)\n\nA downstream task with a queued input has a single slot that acts as a\nring buffer for incoming values. Producers push values, the consumer\ndrains them in arrival order. The buffer's capacity and value-stride\nare set at creation time. The implementation is a fixed-size ring with\natomic head/tail pointers — standard MPSC ring buffer.\n\nThis is a separate slot kind from the single-value output slot.\nDistinguished by a flag in the slot header (or a separate slot type\ntag — decision deferred).\n\n## C API surface\n\n```c\n// Single-value slot\nslot_id_t slot_alloc        (slot_store_t *s, int capacity, uint8_t type_tag);\nvoid      slot_write        (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, const void *data, int size);\nint       slot_read         (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size);\nvoid      slot_ref          (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id);\nvoid      slot_unref        (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id);  // frees if refcount → 0\n\n// Ring-buffer slot\nslot_id_t slot_ring_alloc   (slot_store_t *s, int slot_capacity, int n_slots);\nvoid      slot_ring_push    (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, const void *data, int size);\nint       slot_ring_pop     (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size);\n```\n\n## Open question — submission timing\n\nWhen the dispatch layer builds a task, it knows the task's input wires\nand output slots before any input is filled. The unresolved question:\n\n- **Option A**: build the task struct early, hold it in a \"blocked\" set,\n  add to the ready queue only when all inputs are filled.\n- **Option B**: build and submit immediately, let the task itself block\n  on its input slots via `ACT_BLOCK` on the first input.\n\nOption A is cleaner — the ready queue contains only runnable tasks.\nOption B uses the pool's existing block-and-wake machinery, fewer\nmoving parts.\n\nDecision deferred. Likely Option B, but want to think about it once\nthe dispatch layer (issue 304) is being written.\n\n## Open questions\n- Allocation strategy: bump allocator vs free-list. Bump is simpler;\n  free-list reuses memory across tasks. Start with bump.\n- Type tag granularity: do we need a \"json\" tag distinct from \"string\",\n  or is everything string + size at this layer? Probably size + opaque\n  bytes; the type tag becomes advisory only.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. Write `src/slot-store.h` and `src/slot-store.c` — the C API above.\n2. Unit test single-value slots: thread A writes, thread B reads,\n   refcount decrements, slot freed when last ref dropped.\n3. Unit test ring-buffer slots: multiple producers push, single consumer\n   drains in order, no values lost or duplicated.\n4. Integrate into `src/008-pool-runner.c`: shared memory created at\n   startup, store handle passed to the dispatch layer.\n\n## Relevant files\n- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — pool entry point, owns the shared memory region\n- `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.h` — pool API (refcounting is complementary)\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — task dispatch reads/writes slots\n- `issues/213-queued-inputs-and-task-model.md` — queued input model that\n  ring-buffer slots implement\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — IPC options; shm_open + mmap is Option 2\n"
  },

  "message":{

      }],

  "slug":"snug-booping-dove",

  "userType":"external",
  "toolUseResult":{
    "type":"create",
    "structuredPatch":[],
    "userModified":false,
    "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md",
    "content":"# 303 — Language runtime spec: pluggable per-language invocation\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nEach language has an ad-hoc driver script (`drivers/lua.sh`, `drivers/bash.sh`,\n`drivers/c.sh`). The driver is invoked per box call: spawn a process, run\nthe function, read stdout, exit. Adding a new language means writing a new\ndriver script and modifying the executor to know about it.\n\nThere is no shared interface, no persistent runtime, and no way for a user\nto add a language without touching SoraMech internals.\n\n## Concept\n\nThe language runtime spec is the user-extensible interface that defines how\na language's functions are invoked from inside the thread pool. Every\nlanguage goes through this interface — there is no special path for any\nlanguage. Lua is a spec. C is a spec. Bash is a spec. A user adding Python\nwrites another spec.\n\nThe pool runner does not know how to \"run a Lua function.\" It knows how to\ncall `lang->invoke(...)`. The Lua spec is the thing that knows how to run a\nLua function.\n\nThe user provides the bridging code. SoraMech does not transpile, rewrite,\nor convert box source between languages. If the user wants Rust, the user\nwrites a Rust spec.\n\n## The interface\n\nEach language spec is a C library that exports a single symbol:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    const char *name;       // \"lua\", \"bash\", \"c\", \"python\", ...\n    const char *file_ext;   // \".lua\", \".sh\", \".c\", \".py\" — for box file resolution\n\n    // Once-per-worker. Returns an opaque handle stored in worker_ctx.\n    // Called at pool startup, before any tasks run.\n    void *(*init)(int worker_idx);\n\n    // Once-per-worker. Called at pool shutdown.\n    void  (*teardown)(void *handle);\n\n    // Optional: called once per box source file at map load.\n    // For languages that compile (C → .so), this is where compilation\n    // happens. For languages that don't (Lua, Bash), this is NULL.\n    int   (*compile)(const char *src_path, const char *out_path);\n\n    // The invocation. Inputs are arrays of (bytes, size) pairs,\n    // already read from slots by the dispatch layer. The spec writes\n    // its return value into out_buf and sets *out_size.\n    //\n    // Returns 0 on success, nonzero on error.\n    int   (*invoke)(void *handle,\n                    const char *file_path,\n                    const char *fn_name,\n                    const void **input_data, const int *input_sizes, int n_inputs,\n                    void *out_buf, int out_buf_capacity, int *out_size);\n} lang_spec_t;\n\nextern lang_spec_t soramech_lang_spec;\n```\n\nThe spec library is built as a `.so` and loaded by the pool runner at\nstartup via `dlopen` / `dlsym`. The runner iterates `langs/*/spec.so`,\nloads each, and registers it under its `name`.\n\n## Slot access boundary\n\nSpecs do not see slot IDs. The dispatch layer (issue 304) reads input\nvalues from slots into raw byte buffers, hands them to `invoke`, receives\nthe output bytes, and writes them to the output slot. This decouples\nspecs from slot internals — a spec only deals with values.\n\nIf a future language wants zero-copy access (e.g. memory-mapping a slot\ndirectly into a Python bytearray), the interface can be extended. Do not\nadd it preemptively.\n\n## Per-language layout\n\nSpecs live under `langs/<name>/`:\n\n```\nlangs/lua/\n    spec.c              ← implements lang_spec_t (handles → lua_State)\n    Makefile            ← builds spec.so\n    spec.so             ← built artifact\n\nlangs/bash/\n    spec.c              ← bridges to bash-server.sh via Unix domain socket\n    bash-server.sh      ← persistent subprocess started by spec.init\n    Makefile\n\nlangs/c/\n    spec.c              ← uses dlopen/dlsym; compile = gcc -shared -fPIC\n    Makefile\n\nlangs/python/           ← user-added; not shipped\n    spec.c\n    Makefile\n```\n\nThe pool runner has no compiled-in knowledge of any specific language.\nEven Lua is loaded as a `.so` at startup. This keeps the boundary honest\n— there is no temptation to special-case the \"shipped\" languages.\n\n## Built-in specs (shipped, not privileged)\n\nSoraMech ships specs for:\n- **Lua** — handle is a `lua_State`. `invoke` calls `luaL_loadfile` (cached)\n  + `lua_pcall`. Args pushed as Lua strings; return read as Lua string.\n- **C** — handle is a small `dlopen` handle cache. `compile` runs\n  `gcc -shared -fPIC -o <out_path> <src_path>`. `invoke` does\n  `dlsym` + direct call.\n- **Bash** — handle is a Unix domain socket connected to a persistent\n  bash subprocess (`bash-server.sh`). `invoke` sends a framed request,\n  reads a framed response.\n\nThese are the reference implementations. They demonstrate the spec\ninterface for in-process FFI (Lua, C) and for out-of-process socket\nservers (Bash, and any future language whose runtime cannot be embedded).\n\n## Compilation\n\nThe optional `compile` hook runs at map load (or at editor compile-button\ntime, issue 219). For C, it produces a `.so` next to the source. For\nLua and Bash, no compilation step is needed; `compile` is `NULL`.\n\nCompilation outputs go in the map's `compiled/bin/` directory (issue\n222). The dispatch layer passes the compiled artifact path to `invoke`,\nnot the original source path, when a compiled artifact exists.\n\n## Iterator counter prepending\n\nThe iterator counter (issue 221) is prepended to the input array by the\ndispatch layer, not by the spec. From the spec's perspective, an\niterator box just has one extra input. The spec doesn't know which\ninput is the counter — that's a graph-level concept.\n\n## Error propagation\n\nA nonzero return from `invoke` marks the task as failed. The dispatch\nlayer leaves the output slot unfilled and records the failure in the\ntask's status. Downstream consumers blocked on the unfilled slot will\neither time out or be cancelled — the failure propagation policy is\nthe dispatch layer's concern (issue 304), not the spec's.\n\nThe spec is responsible for catching language-level errors (Lua\n`error()`, C segfault via signal handler, Bash nonzero exit) and\ntranslating them into a nonzero return.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Per-spec configuration: should specs read a `langs/<name>/config.json`\n  for things like compiler flags, server startup args, etc.? Or is\n  hard-coding inside `spec.c` fine for the user-extensible model?\n- Hot reload: if a user edits a box file, do we re-run `compile` and\n  invalidate the `dlopen` cache? Probably yes for C, no-op for Lua and\n  Bash. The dispatch layer should ping the spec with a `reload` callback\n  — but that adds another interface function. Defer until needed.\n- How does a user discover the spec interface? A header file\n  `langs/lang-spec.h` that defines `lang_spec_t` and is included by\n  every spec implementation. Yes, do that.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Write `langs/lang-spec.h` — the public interface header.\n2. Write `langs/lua/spec.c` first. Lua is the easiest because it's already\n   our default language and the existing driver gives a reference behavior.\n3. Write `langs/c/spec.c` — adds `compile` callback, exercises the dlopen\n   path.\n4. Write `langs/bash/spec.c` + `langs/bash/bash-server.sh` — exercises\n   the out-of-process socket model. This is the proof that languages\n   without an embeddable runtime fit the same interface.\n5. Pool runner registry: `dlopen` every `langs/*/spec.so` at startup,\n   register by `name`. Box files are routed to specs by `file_ext`.\n6. Smoke test: a map with one Lua box, one C box, one Bash box, all\n   running in the pool, all going through the spec interface. No\n   special-cased code paths.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `drivers/lua.sh`, `drivers/bash.sh`, `drivers/c.sh` — current ad-hoc\n  drivers, replaced by `langs/<name>/spec.c`\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool startup invokes\n  spec `init` per worker per language\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — dispatch layer reads slots and\n  passes raw bytes to specs (specs do not touch slots)\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — calls `invoke` per task\n- `issues/222-compile-button-and-assets-directory.md` — compile button\n  runs spec `compile` for every box\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — Option 1 (FFI) and Option 3 (Unix\n  socket) describe the two execution models specs implement\n"
  },
  "uuid":"b1ac0407-9996-4e14-92ff-5ae537ab8a57",

}

Do not\nadd it preemptively.\n\n## Per-language layout\n\nSpecs live under `langs/<name>/`:\n\n```\nlangs/lua/\n    spec.c              ← implements lang_spec_t (handles → lua_State)\n    Makefile            ← builds spec.so\n    spec.so             ← built artifact\n\nlangs/bash/\n    spec.c              ← bridges to bash-server.sh via Unix domain socket\n    bash-server.sh      ← persistent subprocess started by spec.init\n    Makefile\n\nlangs/c/\n    spec.c              ← uses dlopen/dlsym; compile = gcc -shared -fPIC\n    Makefile\n\nlangs/python/           ← user-added; not shipped\n    spec.c\n    Makefile\n```\n\nThe pool runner has no compiled-in knowledge of any specific language.\nEven Lua is loaded as a `.so` at startup. This keeps the boundary honest\n— there is no temptation to special-case the \"shipped\" languages.\n\n## Built-in specs (shipped, not privileged)\n\nSoraMech ships specs for:\n- **Lua** — handle is a `lua_State`. `invoke` calls `luaL_loadfile` (cached)\n  + `lua_pcall`. Args pushed as Lua strings; return read as Lua string.\n- **C** — handle is a small `dlopen` handle cache. `compile` runs\n  `gcc -shared -fPIC -o <out_path> <src_path>`. `invoke` does\n  `dlsym` + direct call.\n- **Bash** — handle is a Unix domain socket connected to a persistent\n  bash subprocess (`bash-server.sh`). `invoke` sends a framed request,\n  reads a framed response.\n\nThese are the reference implementations. They demonstrate the spec\ninterface for in-process FFI (Lua, C) and for out-of-process socket\nservers (Bash, and any future language whose runtime cannot be embedded).\n\n## Compilation\n\nThe optional `compile` hook runs at map load (or at editor compile-button\ntime, issue 219). For C, it produces a `.so` next to the source. For\nLua and Bash, no compilation step is needed; `compile` is `NULL`.\n\nCompilation outputs go in the map's `compiled/bin/` directory (issue\n222). The dispatch layer passes the compiled artifact path to `invoke`,\nnot the original source path, when a compiled artifact exists.\n\n## Iterator counter prepending\n\nThe iterator counter (issue 221) is prepended to the input array by the\ndispatch layer, not by the spec. From the spec's perspective, an\niterator box just has one extra input. The spec doesn't know which\ninput is the counter — that's a graph-level concept.\n\n## Error propagation\n\nA nonzero return from `invoke` marks the task as failed. The dispatch\nlayer leaves the output slot unfilled and records the failure in the\ntask's status. Downstream consumers blocked on the unfilled slot will\neither time out or be cancelled — the failure propagation policy is\nthe dispatch layer's concern (issue 304), not the spec's.\n\nThe spec is responsible for catching language-level errors (Lua\n`error()`, C segfault via signal handler, Bash nonzero exit) and\ntranslating them into a nonzero return.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Per-spec configuration: should specs read a `langs/<name>/config.json`\n  for things like compiler flags, server startup args, etc.? Or is\n  hard-coding inside `spec.c` fine for the user-extensible model?\n- Hot reload: if a user edits a box file, do we re-run `compile` and\n  invalidate the `dlopen` cache? Probably yes for C, no-op for Lua and\n  Bash. The dispatch layer should ping the spec with a `reload` callback\n  — but that adds another interface function. Defer until needed.\n- How does a user discover the spec interface? A header file\n  `langs/lang-spec.h` that defines `lang_spec_t` and is included by\n  every spec implementation. Yes, do that.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Write `langs/lang-spec.h` — the public interface header.\n2. Write `langs/lua/spec.c` first. Lua is the easiest because it's already\n   our default language and the existing driver gives a reference behavior.\n3. Write `langs/c/spec.c` — adds `compile` callback, exercises the dlopen\n   path.\n4. Write `langs/bash/spec.c` + `langs/bash/bash-server.sh` — exercises\n   the out-of-process socket model. This is the proof that languages\n   without an embeddable runtime fit the same interface.\n5. Pool runner registry: `dlopen` every `langs/*/spec.so` at startup,\n   register by `name`. Box files are routed to specs by `file_ext`.\n6. Smoke test: a map with one Lua box, one C box, one Bash box, all\n   running in the pool, all going through the spec interface. No\n   special-cased code paths.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `drivers/lua.sh`, `drivers/bash.sh`, `drivers/c.sh` — current ad-hoc\n  drivers, replaced by `langs/<name>/spec.c`\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool startup invokes\n  spec `init` per worker per language\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — dispatch layer reads slots and\n  passes raw bytes to specs (specs do not touch slots)\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — calls `invoke` per task\n- `issues/222-compile-button-and-assets-directory.md` — compile button\n  runs spec `compile` for every box\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — Option 1 (FFI) and Option 3 (Unix\n  socket) describe the two execution models specs implement\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md"
        },
        "id":"toolu_01VTBT2j6ic1FNW5PbrR4rDo"
      }]
