    "snippet":"1\t# 301 — Thread pool lifecycle and per-worker initialization\n2\t\n3\t## Status\n4\topen\n5\t\n6\t## Current behavior\n7\tThe executor (`src/004-executor.lua`) runs boxes synchronously in a\n8\tsingle Lua coroutine. There is no thread pool, no pthreads, and no\n9\tper-thread language runtime state.\n10\t\n11\t## Phase model\n12\t\n13\tPhase 2 is the synchronous interpreter path. It is the development\n14\ttarget while editor work is in progress.\n15\t\n16\tPhase 3 is the thread pool path. It is the only execution path going\n17\tforward. The synchronous interpreter does not stay around as an\n18\talternative entry point — once phase 3 lands, the pool runner\n19\treplaces it. There is no \"fallback to synchronous\" mode.\n20\t\n21\t### Phase 2 → 3 refactor surface\n22\t\n23\tThe following components are replaced (not extended) in phase 3:\n24\t\n25\t| Phase 2 file                  | Phase 3 replacement                  |\n26\t|-------------------------------|--------------------------------------|\n27\t| `src/003-loader.lua`          | C loader inside `src/008-pool-runner.c` |\n28\t| `src/004-executor.lua`        | C task dispatch layer (issue 304)    |\n29\t| `src/007-runner-main.lua`     | `src/008-pool-runner.c`              |\n30\t| `drivers/*.sh`                | Language runtime spec (issue 303)    |\n31\t\n32\tAll threading-pool-adjacent functionality is C code that lives next to\n33\tthe pool. There is no embedded Lua runtime for graph loading or\n34\tdispatch — Lua appears only as a language runtime that boxes can use,\n35\ton equal footing with C, Bash, and any future language.\n36\t\n37\t## Intended behavior\n38\t\n39\t### Pool source\n40\tThe thread pool is the 3d-rts pool library at\n41\t`/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h`\n42\t(and its `.c` companion). It is vendored into SoraMech — copied, not\n43\tsymlinked — so SoraMech's compilation does not depend on the 3d-rts\n44\tworking tree. Vendored copy lives at `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.h`\n45\tand `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.c`.\n46\t\n47\t### Where the pool lives in the process\n48\tThe pool is owned by the map runner's C entry point. One pool per map\n49\trun. It is created after the graph is loaded and validated, and\n50\tdestroyed after the run completes.\n51\t\n52\tThe C entry point (`src/008-pool-runner.c`):\n53\t\n54\t```c\n55\tint main(int argc, char **argv) {\n56\t    // 1. parse map path from argv\n57\t    // 2. load and validate graph (C loader, no Lua involved)\n58\t    // 3. determine which language runtimes the map uses\n59\t    // 4. pool = pool_create(n_workers)\n60\t    // 5. init per-worker language runtime handles for each language present\n61\t    // 6. submit tasks for all entry-point boxes\n62\t    // 7. wait for active task count to reach zero\n63\t    // 8. pool_destroy(pool)\n64\t    // 9. write last-run.json\n65\t}\n66\t```\n67\t\n68\t### Graph loading: ported to C\n69\tThe graph loader is ported from `src/003-loader.lua` to C and lives\n70\tinside (or alongside) `008-pool-runner.c`. The pool runner has no\n71\tembedded Lua state for loader purposes. JSON parsing uses a small\n72\tvendored C JSON library (cJSON or similar; decision deferred to\n73\timplementation).\n74\t\n75\tLua appears in the runner only when a box's language is Lua — and even\n76\tthen, only inside that worker's language runtime handle. The pool\n77\trunner itself does not link to liblua at the top level.\n78\t\n79\t### Per-worker language runtimes\n80\tNo language is treated as the \"native\" or preferred language at the\n81\tthread level. Every box — regardless of language — goes through the\n82\tsame task dispatch path. The per-box cost is determined by that box's\n83\tinvocation wrapper, not by any map-level language setting.\n84\t\n85\tEach worker thread holds a set of language runtime handles, one per\n86\tlanguage it may be asked to run. These are initialized once at pool\n87\tstartup, before any tasks are submitted, and torn down at shutdown:\n88\t\n89\t```c\n90\ttypedef struct {\n91\t    void   *handles[N_LANGS];   // opaque per-language runtime state\n92\t    int     thread_idx;\n93\t} worker_ctx_t;\n94\t```\n95\t\n96\tOnly the language handles actually needed by the map are initialized.\n97\tIf the map contains no Bash boxes, no Bash handle is started for any\n98\tworker. The graph loader determines which languages are present and\n99\tpasses that set to the pool runner at startup.\n100\t\n101\tThe per-language initialization protocol is defined by the language\n102\truntime spec (issue 303). The pool runner calls each spec's `init`\n103\tfunction at startup and its `teardown` function at shutdown.\n104\t\n105\t### Worker context access\n106\tWorker context is stored in thread-local storage (`__thread\n107\tworker_ctx_t *current_worker`), set by each worker immediately after\n108\tthe thread is started. This avoids per-task `pthread_self()` lookups.\n109\t\n110\t### Pool size\n111\tNumber of worker threads defaults to the number of logical CPUs\n112\t(`sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_ONLN)`), capped at a compile-time maximum\n113\t(`MAX_WORKERS`, initially 16). Can be overridden by an environment\n114\tvariable `SORAMECH_WORKERS=N`.\n115\t\n116\t### Slots are owned by tasks (issue 302)\n117\tSlots are allocated when a task is created, not pre-allocated at\n118\tstartup. A task allocates its output slot(s) at submission time, with\n119\tsize specified by the task's language and function. The pool runner\n120\tdoes not own a slot region — slots are per-task allocations that\n121\toutlive the task only as long as wires hold references to them. See\n122\tissue 302 for the slot lifecycle.\n123\t\n124\t### Quiescence\n125\tThe runner tracks an active-task counter, incremented on `pool_spawn`\n126\tand decremented when a task reaches `ACT_DONE`. The main thread waits\n127\ton a condition variable that signals when the counter reaches zero.\n128\t\n129\tThis naturally handles iterators that re-queue themselves: each\n130\tre-queue increments the counter, each completion decrements. The run\n131\tends when no task is in flight and no waiter is blocked on an unfilled\n132\tslot. (A run that deadlocks — a task waiting on a slot that no producer\n133\twill ever fill — is detected separately and reported as an error.)\n134\t\n135\t## Open questions\n136\t- Vendored JSON library: cJSON, jsmn, or hand-rolled. cJSON is heavier\n137\t  but easiest. Decision deferred.\n138\t- Deadlock detection: how aggressively to detect tasks blocked on\n139\t  slots that will never be filled. A periodic scan, or instrumented\n140\t  through the slot store's wait-list.\n141\t\n142\t  -- I don't see how this could ever happen. Can you provide some examples?\n143\t\n144\t## Suggested implementation sequence\n145\t1. Vendor `900-task-pool.h` + `.c` into `libs/task-pool/`.\n146\t2. Vendor a JSON parser into `libs/json/`.\n147\t3. Port `003-loader.lua` to C inside `src/008-pool-runner.c`.\n148\t4. Write the pool lifecycle skeleton: pool_create, worker context TLS,\n149\t   active-task counter, quiescence wait.\n150\t5. Add `Makefile` target `soramech-pool` that compiles the C runner and\n151\t   links against the vendored pool and JSON parser.\n152\t6. Smoke test: single-box Lua map, pool with 2 workers, box runs, result\n153\t   written. No task graph complexity yet.\n154\t\n155\t## Relevant files\n156\t- `/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h` — pool API\n157\t- `src/003-loader.lua` — current Lua loader, to be ported to C\n158\t- `src/004-executor.lua` — current synchronous executor, to be replaced\n159\t- `src/007-runner-main.lua` — current Lua runner, to be replaced\n160\t- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — per-task slot lifecycle\n161\t- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — per-language init/call/teardown\n162\t- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — replaces 004-executor.lua\n163\t- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — threading roadmap and IPC options",

    "snippet":"1\t# 302 — Per-task slot store with wire-held references\n2\t\n3\t## Status\n4\topen\n5\t\n6\t## Current behavior\n7\tWire values are passed through stdout pipes and transient strings. Values\n8\thave no addressable location, no reference count, and no cross-language\n9\taccessibility. Each value vanishes once the pipe is drained.\n10\t\n11\t## Concept\n12\t\n13\t### Slots belong to tasks, not wires\n14\tA **slot** is the memory region that holds a task's output. Slots are\n15\tcreated when tasks are created. A box that runs once produces one slot;\n16\ta box that runs ten times (an iterator) produces ten slots, one per\n17\tinvocation. Slots live in shared memory so any language runtime can read\n18\tor write them without copying.\n19\t\n20\tA **wire** is the relationship between two tasks: it says \"task B's input\n21\tN reads from task A's output M.\" Wires hold references to slots. They\n22\tare the timing mechanism — a task does not become ready until every\n23\tinput wire reports its source slot is filled. They are also the lifetime\n24\tmechanism — a slot is freed only after every wire that referenced it has\n25\treleased it.\n26\t\n27\tThe wire is the arbiter. The slot is just memory.\n28\t\n29\t### Multiple writers, ring buffers\n30\tSome slots have multiple producers writing concurrently. The clearest\n31\tcase is a queued input on a downstream task: many upstream tasks all push\n32\ttheir outputs into the same input queue (issue 213). That queue is a\n33\tring buffer, with the appropriate atomics so producers don't clobber each\n34\tother and the consumer always sees a coherent value.\n35\t\n36\tMost output slots have a single producer (the task itself) and one or\n37\tmore consumers (the wires that read from it). Single-producer slots\n38\tdon't need ring buffer machinery — just the per-slot lock for safe read\n39\tduring the brief window between write and unref.\n40\t\n41\t### Asynchrony\n42\tThe store is fully asynchronous. Slots are allocated, filled, read, and\n43\tfreed at any time, on any thread, with no global lock. Synchronization\n44\tis per-slot. There is no central allocator-wide mutex.\n45\t\n46\t## Slot layout\n47\t\n48\tEach slot is a small header followed by a value region whose size is\n49\tspecified by the task at allocation time:\n50\t\n51\t```\n52\tOffset  Size  Field\n53\t------  ----  -----\n54\t0       4     refcount        (atomic int32)\n55\t4       4     value_size      (bytes of value data, 0 if not yet filled)\n56\t8       4     value_capacity  (allocated bytes, set at slot creation)\n57\t12      1     type_tag        (0=none, 1=string, 2=number, 3=json, 4=bytes)\n58\t13      1     filled          (0=empty, 1=ready)\n59\t14      1     touched         (0=free, 1=another thread is mutating)\n60\t15      1     _pad\n61\t16      N     value_data      (N == value_capacity)\n62\t```\n63\t\n64\t`value_capacity` is exactly the size requested by the task — no global\n65\tmaximum. This mirrors the C convention of passing array sizes alongside\n66\tarrays. Slots may have wildly different sizes within the same run.\n67\t\n68\t`touched` is a single-byte flag toggled around any mutation of the\n69\theader (refcount changes, filled flip, etc.). A reader that finds\n70\t`touched == 1` retries. This is the simplest possible per-slot lock; if\n71\tcontention becomes a problem, replace with a proper mutex without\n72\tchanging the API.\n73\t\n74\t`filled` is set last, with a memory barrier, so a reader that observes\n75\t`filled == 1` is guaranteed to see the complete value.\n76\t\n77\t## Reference counting protocol\n78\t\n79\tWhen a task is submitted, the dispatch layer:\n80\t1. Allocates the task's output slot(s) with the requested capacity.\n81\t2. For each wire reading from the slot, calls `slot_ref` on the slot.\n82\t   The wire holds that reference for as long as it might still need to\n83\t   read.\n84\t3. When the consumer task finishes reading, it calls `slot_unref` on\n85\t   the wire's slot. The wire is then dead.\n86\t4. When the refcount drops to zero, the task that performed the final\n87\t   unref clears the slot (frees the backing memory or marks it\n88\t   reusable).\n89\t\n90\tNo central garbage collector. Clearing is deterministic — last unref\n91\tdoes the work.\n92\t\n93\t## Backing store\n94\t\n95\tSlots live in shared memory created with `shm_open` + `mmap`. The\n96\tshared memory object is named `/soramech-<run-id>`. Allocation inside\n97\tthe region is handled by a per-run allocator (a simple bump allocator\n98\tor a small free-list allocator — start with bump, add free-list when\n99\tslot reuse becomes worth it).\n100\t\n101\tAny language runtime that opens the same shared memory name and maps it\n102\tgets access to the same physical memory. For languages that cannot call\n103\tPOSIX directly (e.g. Bash), the language runtime spec (issue 303) is\n104\tresponsible for proxying slot reads and writes through the language's\n105\truntime server.\n106\t\n107\tSynchronization for blocked tasks (waiting on an empty slot) is handled\n108\tby the dispatch layer (issue 304) — typically a wait list per slot.\n109\tProducers signal waiters when they flip `filled`.\n110\t\n111\t## Slot creation\n112\t\n113\tSlot creation happens inside the dispatch layer at task submission. The\n114\tcaller specifies the value capacity:\n115\t\n116\t```c\n117\tslot_id_t slot_alloc(slot_store_t *store, int capacity, uint8_t type_tag);\n118\t```\n119\t\n120\tThe slot is created with `refcount = 0`, `filled = 0`. The dispatch\n121\tlayer then increments the refcount once per wire reading from it before\n122\tthe task is exposed to consumers.\n123\t\n124\t## Ring-buffer slots (queued inputs)\n125\t\n126\tA downstream task with a queued input has a single slot that acts as a\n127\tring buffer for incoming values. Producers push values, the consumer\n128\tdrains them in arrival order. The buffer's capacity and value-stride\n129\tare set at creation time. The implementation is a fixed-size ring with\n130\tatomic head/tail pointers — standard MPSC ring buffer.\n131\t\n132\tThis is a separate slot kind from the single-value output slot.\n133\tDistinguished by a flag in the slot header (or a separate slot type\n134\ttag — decision deferred).\n135\t\n136\t-- actually, they should all be designed with ring-buffers. We don't want to\n137\t   overcomplicate it from the user's point of view, and my understanding is that\n138\t   it doesn't add too much complexity or memory or CPU requirements. If we\n139\t   define one type of structure that handles all of the ring buffers for tasks,\n140\t   then that's not too complex is it?\n141\t\n142\t## C API surface\n143\t\n144\t```c\n145\t// Single-value slot\n146\tslot_id_t slot_alloc        (slot_store_t *s, int capacity, uint8_t type_tag);\n147\tvoid      slot_write        (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, const void *data, int size);\n148\tint       slot_read         (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size);\n149\tvoid      slot_ref          (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id);\n150\tvoid      slot_unref        (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id);  // frees if refcount → 0\n151\t\n152\t// Ring-buffer slot\n153\tslot_id_t slot_ring_alloc   (slot_store_t *s, int slot_capacity, int n_slots);\n154\tvoid      slot_ring_push    (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, const void *data, int size);\n155\tint       slot_ring_pop     (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size);\n156\t```\n157\t\n158\t## Open question — submission timing\n159\t\n160\tWhen the dispatch layer builds a task, it knows the task's input wires\n161\tand output slots before any input is filled. The unresolved question:\n162\t\n163\t- **Option A**: build the task struct early, hold it in a \"blocked\" set,\n164\t  add to the ready queue only when all inputs are filled.\n165\t- **Option B**: build and submit immediately, let the task itself block\n166\t  on its input slots via `ACT_BLOCK` on the first input.\n167\t\n168\tOption A is cleaner — the ready queue contains only runnable tasks.\n169\tOption B uses the pool's existing block-and-wake machinery, fewer\n170\tmoving parts.\n171\t\n172\tDecision deferred.     "snippet":"1\t# 303 — Language runtime spec: pluggable per-language invocation\n2\t\n3\t## Status\n4\topen\n5\t\n6\t## Current behavior\n7\tEach language has an ad-hoc driver script (`drivers/lua.sh`, `drivers/bash.sh`,\n8\t`drivers/c.sh`). The driver is invoked per box call: spawn a process, run\n9\tthe function, read stdout, exit. Adding a new language means writing a new\n10\tdriver script and modifying the executor to know about it.\n11\t\n12\tThere is no shared interface, no persistent runtime, and no way for a user\n13\tto add a language without touching SoraMech internals.\n14\t\n15\t## Concept\n16\t\n17\tThe language runtime spec is the user-extensible interface that defines how\n18\ta language's functions are invoked from inside the thread pool. Every\n19\tlanguage goes through this interface — there is no special path for any\n20\tlanguage. Lua is a spec. C is a spec. Bash is a spec. A user adding Python\n21\twrites another spec.\n22\t\n23\tThe pool runner does not know how to \"run a Lua function.\" It knows how to\n24\tcall `lang->invoke(...)`. The Lua spec is the thing that knows how to run a\n25\tLua function.\n26\t\n27\tThe user provides the bridging code. SoraMech does not transpile, rewrite,\n28\tor convert box source between languages. If the user wants Rust, the user\n29\twrites a Rust spec.\n30\t\n31\t## The interface\n32\t\n33\tEach language spec is a C library that exports a single symbol:\n34\t\n35\t```c\n36\ttypedef struct {\n37\t    const char *name;       // \"lua\", \"bash\", \"c\", \"python\", ...\n38\t    const char *file_ext;   // \".lua\", \".sh\", \".c\", \".py\" — for box file resolution\n39\t\n40\t    // Once-per-worker. Returns an opaque handle stored in worker_ctx.\n41\t    // Called at pool startup, before any tasks run.\n42\t    void *(*init)(int worker_idx);\n43\t\n44\t    // Once-per-worker. Called at pool shutdown.\n45\t    void  (*teardown)(void *handle);\n46\t\n47\t    // Optional: called once per box source file at map load.\n48\t    // For languages that compile (C → .so), this is where compilation\n49\t    // happens. For languages that don't (Lua, Bash), this is NULL.\n50\t    int   (*compile)(const char *src_path, const char *out_path);\n51\t\n52\t    // The invocation. Inputs are arrays of (bytes, size) pairs,\n53\t    // already read from slots by the dispatch layer. The spec writes\n54\t    // its return value into out_buf and sets *out_size.\n55\t    //\n56\t    // Returns 0 on success, nonzero on error.\n57\t    int   (*invoke)(void *handle,\n58\t                    const char *file_path,\n59\t                    const char *fn_name,\n60\t                    const void **input_data, const int *input_sizes, int n_inputs,\n61\t                    void *out_buf, int out_buf_capacity, int *out_size);\n62\t} lang_spec_t;\n63\t\n64\textern lang_spec_t soramech_lang_spec;\n65\t```\n66\t\n67\tThe spec library is built as a `.so` and loaded by the pool runner at\n68\tstartup via `dlopen` / `dlsym`. The runner iterates `langs/*/spec.so`,\n69\tloads each, and registers it under its `name`.\n70\t\n71\t## Slot access boundary\n72\t\n73\tSpecs do not see slot IDs. The dispatch layer (issue 304) reads input\n74\tvalues from slots into raw byte buffers, hands them to `invoke`, receives\n75\tthe output bytes, and writes them to the output slot. This decouples\n76\tspecs from slot internals — a spec only deals with values.\n77\t\n78\tIf a future language wants zero-copy access (e.g. memory-mapping a slot\n79\tdirectly into a Python bytearray), the interface can be extended. Do not\n80\tadd it preemptively.\n81\t\n82\t## Per-language layout\n83\t\n84\tSpecs live under `langs/<name>/`:\n85\t\n86\t```\n87\tlangs/lua/\n88\t    spec.c              ← implements lang_spec_t (handles → lua_State)\n89\t    Makefile            ← builds spec.so\n90\t    spec.so             ← built artifact\n91\t\n92\tlangs/bash/\n93\t    spec.c              ← bridges to bash-server.sh via Unix domain socket\n94\t    bash-server.sh      ← persistent subprocess started by spec.init\n95\t    Makefile\n96\t\n97\tlangs/c/\n98\t    spec.c              ← uses dlopen/dlsym; compile = gcc -shared -fPIC\n99\t    Makefile\n100\t\n101\tlangs/python/           ← user-added; not shipped\n102\t    spec.c\n103\t    Makefile\n104\t```\n105\t\n106\tThe pool runner has no compiled-in knowledge of any specific language.\n107\tEven Lua is loaded as a `.so` at startup. This keeps the boundary honest\n108\t— there is no temptation to special-case the \"shipped\" languages.\n109\t\n110\t## Built-in specs (shipped, not privileged)\n111\t\n112\tSoraMech ships specs for:\n113\t- **Lua** — handle is a `lua_State`. `invoke` calls `luaL_loadfile` (cached)\n114\t  + `lua_pcall`. Args pushed as Lua strings; return read as Lua string.\n115\t- **C** — handle is a small `dlopen` handle cache. `compile` runs\n116\t  `gcc -shared -fPIC -o <out_path> <src_path>`. `invoke` does\n117\t  `dlsym` + direct call.\n118\t- **Bash** — handle is a Unix domain socket connected to a persistent\n119\t  bash subprocess (`bash-server.sh`). `invoke` sends a framed request,\n120\t  reads a framed response.\n121\t\n122\tThese are the reference implementations. They demonstrate the spec\n123\tinterface for in-process FFI (Lua, C) and for out-of-process socket\n124\tservers (Bash, and any future language whose runtime cannot be embedded).\n125\t\n126\t## Compilation\n127\t\n128\tThe optional `compile` hook runs at map load (or at editor compile-button\n129\ttime, issue 219). For C, it produces a `.so` next to the source. For\n130\tLua and Bash, no compilation step is needed; `compile` is `NULL`.\n131\t\n132\tCompilation outputs go in the map's `compiled/bin/` directory (issue\n133\t222). The dispatch layer passes the compiled artifact path to `invoke`,\n134\tnot the original source path, when a compiled artifact exists.\n135\t\n136\t## Iterator counter prepending\n137\t\n138\tThe iterator counter (issue 221) is prepended to the input array by the\n139\tdispatch layer, not by the spec. From the spec's perspective, an\n140\titerator box just has one extra input. The spec doesn't know which\n141\tinput is the counter — that's a graph-level concept.\n142\t\n143\t## Error propagation\n144\t\n145\tA nonzero return from `invoke` marks the task as failed. The dispatch\n146\tlayer leaves the output slot unfilled and records the failure in the\n147\ttask's status. Downstream consumers blocked on the unfilled slot will\n148\teither time out or be cancelled — the failure propagation policy is\n149\tthe dispatch layer's concern (issue 304), not the spec's.\n150\t\n151\t-- any errors should crash the program. If the invoke returns a non-zero value\n152\t   it should crash hard. It shouldn't return invalid values! Also, we shouldn't\n153\t   have situations where tasks can fail to return correct values - if we do,\n154\t   then we are opening ourselves up to a lot of problems. Also, we don't want\n155\t   to build in systems that check for failures and stalled tasks. That's\n156\t   extra complexity and has a runtime cost. Not ideal! If the code has a bug,\n157\t   then it should not be used in production until the bug is fixed. If a bug\n158\t   crashes something in production because you didn't notice it, well, you\n159\t   better fix it quickly...\n160\t\n161\tThe spec is responsible for catching language-level errors (Lua\n162\t`error()`, C segfault via signal handler, Bash nonzero exit) and\n163\ttranslating them into a nonzero return.\n164\t\n165\t## Open questions\n166\t\n167\t- Per-spec configuration: should specs read a `langs/<name>/config.json`\n168\t  for things like compiler flags, server startup args, etc.? Or is\n169\t  hard-coding inside `spec.c` fine for the user-extensible model?\n170\t\n171\t-- we can just hard-code them. Doesn't make sense to have a different file.\n172\t\n173\t- Hot reload: if a user edits a box file, do we re-run `compile` and\n174\t  invalidate the `dlopen` cache? Probably yes for C, no-op for Lua and\n175\t  Bash. The dispatch layer should ping the spec with a `reload` callback\n176\t  — but that adds another interface function. Defer until needed.\n177\t\n178\t-- eh, let's just ignore this. The user will hit compile, it will re-compile\n179\t   all the files that have changed, or like you said just no-op for interpreted\n180\t   languages, and it'll just... work itself out. We don't have to worry about it\n181\t\n182\t- How does a user discover the spec interface? A header file\n\n... [36 lines truncated] ...",
    "filename":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md"

    "originalFile":"# 301 — Thread pool lifecycle and per-worker initialization\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nThe executor (`src/004-executor.lua`) runs boxes synchronously in a\nsingle Lua coroutine. There is no thread pool, no pthreads, and no\nper-thread language runtime state.\n\n## Phase model\n\nPhase 2 is the synchronous interpreter path. It is the development\ntarget while editor work is in progress.\n\nPhase 3 is the thread pool path. It is the only execution path going\nforward. The synchronous interpreter does not stay around as an\nalternative entry point — once phase 3 lands, the pool runner\nreplaces it. There is no \"fallback to synchronous\" mode.\n\n### Phase 2 → 3 refactor surface\n\nThe following components are replaced (not extended) in phase 3:\n\n| Phase 2 file                  | Phase 3 replacement                  |\n|-------------------------------|--------------------------------------|\n| `src/003-loader.lua`          | C loader inside `src/008-pool-runner.c` |\n| `src/004-executor.lua`        | C task dispatch layer (issue 304)    |\n| `src/007-runner-main.lua`     | `src/008-pool-runner.c`              |\n| `drivers/*.sh`                | Language runtime spec (issue 303)    |\n\nAll threading-pool-adjacent functionality is C code that lives next to\nthe pool. There is no embedded Lua runtime for graph loading or\ndispatch — Lua appears only as a language runtime that boxes can use,\non equal footing with C, Bash, and any future language.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\n### Pool source\nThe thread pool is the 3d-rts pool library at\n`/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h`\n(and its `.c` companion). It is vendored into SoraMech — copied, not\nsymlinked — so SoraMech's compilation does not depend on the 3d-rts\nworking tree. Vendored copy lives at `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.h`\nand `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.c`.\n\n### Where the pool lives in the process\nThe pool is owned by the map runner's C entry point. One pool per map\nrun. It is created after the graph is loaded and validated, and\ndestroyed after the run completes.\n\nThe C entry point (`src/008-pool-runner.c`):\n\n```c\nint main(int argc, char **argv) {\n    // 1. parse map path from argv\n    // 2. load and validate graph (C loader, no Lua involved)\n    // 3. determine which language runtimes the map uses\n    // 4. pool = pool_create(n_workers)\n    // 5. init per-worker language runtime handles for each language present\n    // 6. submit tasks for all entry-point boxes\n    // 7. wait for active task count to reach zero\n    // 8. pool_destroy(pool)\n    // 9. write last-run.json\n}\n```\n\n### Graph loading: ported to C\nThe graph loader is ported from `src/003-loader.lua` to C and lives\ninside (or alongside) `008-pool-runner.c`. The pool runner has no\nembedded Lua state for loader purposes. JSON parsing uses a small\nvendored C JSON library (cJSON or similar; decision deferred to\nimplementation).\n\nLua appears in the runner only when a box's language is Lua — and even\nthen, only inside that worker's language runtime handle. The pool\nrunner itself does not link to liblua at the top level.\n\n### Per-worker language runtimes\nNo language is treated as the \"native\" or preferred language at the\nthread level. Every box — regardless of language — goes through the\nsame task dispatch path. The per-box cost is determined by that box's\ninvocation wrapper, not by any map-level language setting.\n\nEach worker thread holds a set of language runtime handles, one per\nlanguage it may be asked to run. These are initialized once at pool\nstartup, before any tasks are submitted, and torn down at shutdown:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    void   *handles[N_LANGS];   // opaque per-language runtime state\n    int     thread_idx;\n} worker_ctx_t;\n```\n\nOnly the language handles actually needed by the map are initialized.\nIf the map contains no Bash boxes, no Bash handle is started for any\nworker. The graph loader determines which languages are present and\npasses that set to the pool runner at startup.\n\nThe per-language initialization protocol is defined by the language\nruntime spec (issue 303). The pool runner calls each spec's `init`\nfunction at startup and its `teardown` function at shutdown.\n\n### Worker context access\nWorker context is stored in thread-local storage (`__thread\nworker_ctx_t *current_worker`), set by each worker immediately after\nthe thread is started. This avoids per-task `pthread_self()` lookups.\n\n### Pool size\nNumber of worker threads defaults to the number of logical CPUs\n(`sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_ONLN)`), capped at a compile-time maximum\n(`MAX_WORKERS`, initially 16). Can be overridden by an environment\nvariable `SORAMECH_WORKERS=N`.\n\n### Slots are owned by tasks (issue 302)\nSlots are allocated when a task is created, not pre-allocated at\nstartup. A task allocates its output slot(s) at submission time, with\nsize specified by the task's language and function. The pool runner\ndoes not own a slot region — slots are per-task allocations that\noutlive the task only as long as wires hold references to them. See\nissue 302 for the slot lifecycle.\n\n### Quiescence\nThe runner tracks an active-task counter, incremented on `pool_spawn`\nand decremented when a task reaches `ACT_DONE`. The main thread waits\non a condition variable that signals when the counter reaches zero.\n\nThis naturally handles iterators that re-queue themselves: each\nre-queue increments the counter, each completion decrements. The run\nends when no task is in flight and no waiter is blocked on an unfilled\nslot. (A run that deadlocks — a task waiting on a slot that no producer\nwill ever fill — is detected separately and reported as an error.)\n\n## Open questions\n- Vendored JSON library: cJSON, jsmn, or hand-rolled. cJSON is heavier\n  but easiest. Decision deferred.\n- Deadlock detection: how aggressively to detect tasks blocked on\n  slots that will never be filled. A periodic scan, or instrumented\n  through the slot store's wait-list.\n\n  -- I don't see how this could ever happen. Can you provide some examples?\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. Vendor `900-task-pool.h` + `.c` into `libs/task-pool/`.\n2. Vendor a JSON parser into `libs/json/`.\n3. Port `003-loader.lua` to C inside `src/008-pool-runner.c`.\n4. Write the pool lifecycle skeleton: pool_create, worker context TLS,\n   active-task counter, quiescence wait.\n5. Add `Makefile` target `soramech-pool` that compiles the C runner and\n   links against the vendored pool and JSON parser.\n6. Smoke test: single-box Lua map, pool with 2 workers, box runs, result\n   written. No task graph complexity yet.\n\n## Relevant files\n- `/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h` — pool API\n- `src/003-loader.lua` — current Lua loader, to be ported to C\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — current synchronous executor, to be replaced\n- `src/007-runner-main.lua` — current Lua runner, to be replaced\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — per-task slot lifecycle\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — per-language init/call/teardown\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — replaces 004-executor.lua\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — threading roadmap and IPC options\n",
    "oldString":"## Open questions\n- Vendored JSON library: cJSON, jsmn, or hand-rolled. cJSON is heavier\n  but easiest. Decision deferred.\n- Deadlock detection: how aggressively to detect tasks blocked on\n  slots that will never be filled. A periodic scan, or instrumented\n  through the slot store's wait-list.\n\n  -- I don't see how this could ever happen. Can you provide some examples?",
    "newString":"## Open questions\n- Vendored JSON library: cJSON, jsmn, or hand-rolled. cJSON is heavier\n  but easiest. Decision deferred.",

Vendored copy lives at `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.h`\nand `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.c`.\n\n### Where the pool lives in the process\nThe pool is owned by the map runner's C entry point. One pool per map\nrun. It is created after the graph is loaded and validated, and\ndestroyed after the run completes.\n\nThe C entry point (`src/008-pool-runner.c`):\n\n```c\nint main(int argc, char **argv) {\n    // 1. parse map path from argv\n    // 2. load and validate graph (C loader, no Lua involved)\n    // 3. determine which language runtimes the map uses\n    // 4. pool = pool_create(n_workers)\n    // 5. init per-worker language runtime handles for each language present\n    // 6. submit tasks for all entry-point boxes\n    // 7. wait for active task count to reach zero\n    // 8. pool_destroy(pool)\n    // 9. write last-run.json\n}\n```\n\n### Graph loading: ported to C\nThe graph loader is ported from `src/003-loader.lua` to C and lives\ninside (or alongside) `008-pool-runner.c`. The pool runner has no\nembedded Lua state for loader purposes. JSON parsing uses a small\nvendored C JSON library (cJSON or similar; decision deferred to\nimplementation).\n\nLua appears in the runner only when a box's language is Lua — and even\nthen, only inside that worker's language runtime handle. The pool\nrunner itself does not link to liblua at the top level.\n\n### Per-worker language runtimes\nNo language is treated as the \"native\" or preferred language at the\nthread level. Every box — regardless of language — goes through the\nsame task dispatch path. The per-box cost is determined by that box's\ninvocation wrapper, not by any map-level language setting.\n\nEach worker thread holds a set of language runtime handles, one per\nlanguage it may be asked to run. These are initialized once at pool\nstartup, before any tasks are submitted, and torn down at shutdown:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    void   *handles[N_LANGS];   // opaque per-language runtime state\n    int     thread_idx;\n} worker_ctx_t;\n```\n\nOnly the language handles actually needed by the map are initialized.\nIf the map contains no Bash boxes, no Bash handle is started for any\nworker. The graph loader determines which languages are present and\npasses that set to the pool runner at startup.\n\nThe per-language initialization protocol is defined by the language\nruntime spec (issue 303). The pool runner calls each spec's `init`\nfunction at startup and its `teardown` function at shutdown.\n\n### Worker context access\nWorker context is stored in thread-local storage (`__thread\nworker_ctx_t *current_worker`), set by each worker immediately after\nthe thread is started. This avoids per-task `pthread_self()` lookups.\n\n### Pool size\nNumber of worker threads defaults to the number of logical CPUs\n(`sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_ONLN)`), capped at a compile-time maximum\n(`MAX_WORKERS`, initially 16). Can be overridden by an environment\nvariable `SORAMECH_WORKERS=N`.\n\n### Slots are owned by tasks (issue 302)\nSlots are allocated when a task is created, not pre-allocated at\nstartup. A task allocates its output slot(s) at submission time, with\nsize specified by the task's language and function. The pool runner\ndoes not own a slot region — slots are per-task allocations that\noutlive the task only as long as wires hold references to them. See\nissue 302 for the slot lifecycle.\n\n### Quiescence\nThe runner tracks an active-task counter, incremented on `pool_spawn`\nand decremented when a task reaches `ACT_DONE`. The main thread waits\non a condition variable that signals when the counter reaches zero.\n\nThis naturally handles iterators that re-queue themselves: each\nre-queue increments the counter, each completion decrements. The run\nends when no task is in flight and no waiter is blocked on an unfilled\nslot. (A run that deadlocks — a task waiting on a slot that no producer\nwill ever fill — is detected separately and reported as an error.)\n\n## Open questions\n- Vendored JSON library: cJSON, jsmn, or hand-rolled. cJSON is heavier\n  but easiest. Decision deferred.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. Vendor `900-task-pool.h` + `.c` into `libs/task-pool/`.\n2. Vendor a JSON parser into `libs/json/`.\n3. Port `003-loader.lua` to C inside `src/008-pool-runner.c`.\n4. Write the pool lifecycle skeleton: pool_create, worker context TLS,\n   active-task counter, quiescence wait.\n5. Add `Makefile` target `soramech-pool` that compiles the C runner and\n   links against the vendored pool and JSON parser.\n6. Smoke test: single-box Lua map, pool with 2 workers, box runs, result\n   written. No task graph complexity yet.\n\n## Relevant files\n- `/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h` — pool API\n- `src/003-loader.lua` — current Lua loader, to be ported to C\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — current synchronous executor, to be replaced\n- `src/007-runner-main.lua` — current Lua runner, to be replaced\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — per-task slot lifecycle\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — per-language init/call/teardown\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — replaces 004-executor.lua\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — threading roadmap and IPC options\n",

(A run that deadlocks — a task waiting on a slot that no producer\nwill ever fill — is detected separately and reported as an error.)",

Errors\ninside a task crash the program (issue 303), so there is no\nhalf-completed-producer case to worry about. An iterator parking\nbecause its upstream queue is empty is not deadlock — it is the\nnatural end-of-stream condition; once the active-task counter reaches\nzero with the iterator parked, the run ends cleanly.",

    "originalFile":"# 302 — Per-task slot store with wire-held references\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nWire values are passed through stdout pipes and transient strings. Values\nhave no addressable location, no reference count, and no cross-language\naccessibility. Each value vanishes once the pipe is drained.\n\n## Concept\n\n### Slots belong to tasks, not wires\nA **slot** is the memory region that holds a task's output. Slots are\ncreated when tasks are created. A box that runs once produces one slot;\na box that runs ten times (an iterator) produces ten slots, one per\ninvocation. Slots live in shared memory so any language runtime can read\nor write them without copying.\n\nA **wire** is the relationship between two tasks: it says \"task B's input\nN reads from task A's output M.\" Wires hold references to slots. They\nare the timing mechanism — a task does not become ready until every\ninput wire reports its source slot is filled. They are also the lifetime\nmechanism — a slot is freed only after every wire that referenced it has\nreleased it.\n\nThe wire is the arbiter. The slot is just memory.\n\n### Multiple writers, ring buffers\nSome slots have multiple producers writing concurrently. The clearest\ncase is a queued input on a downstream task: many upstream tasks all push\ntheir outputs into the same input queue (issue 213). That queue is a\nring buffer, with the appropriate atomics so producers don't clobber each\nother and the consumer always sees a coherent value.\n\nMost output slots have a single producer (the task itself) and one or\nmore consumers (the wires that read from it). Single-producer slots\ndon't need ring buffer machinery — just the per-slot lock for safe read\nduring the brief window between write and unref.\n\n### Asynchrony\nThe store is fully asynchronous. Slots are allocated, filled, read, and\nfreed at any time, on any thread, with no global lock. Synchronization\nis per-slot. There is no central allocator-wide mutex.\n\n## Slot layout\n\nEach slot is a small header followed by a value region whose size is\nspecified by the task at allocation time:\n\n```\nOffset  Size  Field\n------  ----  -----\n0       4     refcount        (atomic int32)\n4       4     value_size      (bytes of value data, 0 if not yet filled)\n8       4     value_capacity  (allocated bytes, set at slot creation)\n12      1     type_tag        (0=none, 1=string, 2=number, 3=json, 4=bytes)\n13      1     filled          (0=empty, 1=ready)\n14      1     touched         (0=free, 1=another thread is mutating)\n15      1     _pad\n16      N     value_data      (N == value_capacity)\n```\n\n`value_capacity` is exactly the size requested by the task — no global\nmaximum. This mirrors the C convention of passing array sizes alongside\narrays. Slots may have wildly different sizes within the same run.\n\n`touched` is a single-byte flag toggled around any mutation of the\nheader (refcount changes, filled flip, etc.). A reader that finds\n`touched == 1` retries. This is the simplest possible per-slot lock; if\ncontention becomes a problem, replace with a proper mutex without\nchanging the API.\n\n`filled` is set last, with a memory barrier, so a reader that observes\n`filled == 1` is guaranteed to see the complete value.\n\n## Reference counting protocol\n\nWhen a task is submitted, the dispatch layer:\n1. Allocates the task's output slot(s) with the requested capacity.\n2. For each wire reading from the slot, calls `slot_ref` on the slot.\n   The wire holds that reference for as long as it might still need to\n   read.\n3. When the consumer task finishes reading, it calls `slot_unref` on\n   the wire's slot. The wire is then dead.\n4. When the refcount drops to zero, the task that performed the final\n   unref clears the slot (frees the backing memory or marks it\n   reusable).\n\nNo central garbage collector. Clearing is deterministic — last unref\ndoes the work.\n\n## Backing store\n\nSlots live in shared memory created with `shm_open` + `mmap`. The\nshared memory object is named `/soramech-<run-id>`. Allocation inside\nthe region is handled by a per-run allocator (a simple bump allocator\nor a small free-list allocator — start with bump, add free-list when\nslot reuse becomes worth it).\n\nAny language runtime that opens the same shared memory name and maps it\ngets access to the same physical memory. For languages that cannot call\nPOSIX directly (e.g. Bash), the language runtime spec (issue 303) is\nresponsible for proxying slot reads and writes through the language's\nruntime server.\n\nSynchronization for blocked tasks (waiting on an empty slot) is handled\nby the dispatch layer (issue 304) — typically a wait list per slot.\nProducers signal waiters when they flip `filled`.\n\n## Slot creation\n\nSlot creation happens inside the dispatch layer at task submission. The\ncaller specifies the value capacity:\n\n```c\nslot_id_t slot_alloc(slot_store_t *store, int capacity, uint8_t type_tag);\n```\n\nThe slot is created with `refcount = 0`, `filled = 0`. The dispatch\nlayer then increments the refcount once per wire reading from it before\nthe task is exposed to consumers.\n\n## Ring-buffer slots (queued inputs)\n\nA downstream task with a queued input has a single slot that acts as a\nring buffer for incoming values. Producers push values, the consumer\ndrains them in arrival order. The buffer's capacity and value-stride\nare set at creation time. The implementation is a fixed-size ring with\natomic head/tail pointers — standard MPSC ring buffer.\n\nThis is a separate slot kind from the single-value output slot.\nDistinguished by a flag in the slot header (or a separate slot type\ntag — decision deferred).\n\n-- actually, they should all be designed with ring-buffers. We don't want to\n   overcomplicate it from the user's point of view, and my understanding is that\n   it doesn't add too much complexity or memory or CPU requirements. If we\n   define one type of structure that handles all of the ring buffers for tasks,\n   then that's not too complex is it?\n\n## C API surface\n\n```c\n// Single-value slot\nslot_id_t slot_alloc        (slot_store_t *s, int capacity, uint8_t type_tag);\nvoid      slot_write        (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, const void *data, int size);\nint       slot_read         (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size);\nvoid      slot_ref          (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id);\nvoid      slot_unref        (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id);  // frees if refcount → 0\n\n// Ring-buffer slot\nslot_id_t slot_ring_alloc   (slot_store_t *s, int slot_capacity, int n_slots);\nvoid      slot_ring_push    (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, const void *data, int size);\nint       slot_ring_pop     (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size);\n```\n\n## Open question — submission timing\n\nWhen the dispatch layer builds a task, it knows the task's input wires\nand output slots before any input is filled. The unresolved question:\n\n- **Option A**: build the task struct early, hold it in a \"blocked\" set,\n  add to the ready queue only when all inputs are filled.\n- **Option B**: build and submit immediately, let the task itself block\n  on its input slots via `ACT_BLOCK` on the first input.\n\nOption A is cleaner — the ready queue contains only runnable tasks.\nOption B uses the pool's existing block-and-wake machinery, fewer\nmoving parts.\n\nDecision deferred. Likely Option B, but want to think about it once\nthe dispatch layer (issue 304) is being written.\n\n-- build the task struct early, fill in all the data we can, and submit it to\n   the queue. The first time it's picked up it'll be validated and it will be\n   known that it's not ready yet - at that point, it'll be added to the queue of\n   the blocking task, to fill in the required inputs (therefore unblocking it)\n   and to re-add it to the ready task pool. Actually, skip the first step, and\n   just if there's any blocked inputs then just add it to the first one\n   immediately.\n\n## Open questions\n- Allocation strategy: bump allocator vs free-list. Bump is simpler;\n  free-list reuses memory across tasks. Start with bump.\n\n  -- please describe both of those in more detail.\n\n- Type tag granularity: do we need a \"json\" tag distinct from \"string\",\n  or is everything string + size at this layer? Probably size + opaque\n  bytes; the type tag becomes advisory only.\n  \n  -- huh? where is this tag type used? we are passing more than just strings as\n     inputs. Json? who-son? type tag? huh? where? who's son? whose on? jake?\n     huh? json? what does that mean?\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. Write `src/slot-store.h` and `src/slot-store.c` — the C API above.\n2. Unit test single-value slots: thread A writes, thread B reads,\n   refcount decrements, slot freed when last ref dropped.\n3. Unit test ring-buffer slots: multiple producers push, single consumer\n   drains in order, no values lost or duplicated.\n4. Integrate into `src/008-pool-runner.c`: shared memory created at\n   startup, store handle passed to the dispatch layer.\n\n## Relevant files\n- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — pool entry point, owns the shared memory region\n- `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.h` — pool API (refcounting is complementary)\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — task dispatch reads/writes slots\n- `issues/213-queued-inputs-and-task-model.md` — queued input model that\n  ring-buffer slots implement\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — IPC options; shm_open + mmap is Option 2\n",

    "originalFile":"# 302 — Per-task slot store with wire-held references\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nWire values are passed through stdout pipes and transient strings. Values\nhave no addressable location, no reference count, and no cross-language\naccessibility. Each value vanishes once the pipe is drained.\n\n## Concept\n\n### Slots belong to tasks, not wires\nA **slot** is the memory region that holds a task's output. Slots are\ncreated when tasks are created. A box that runs once produces one slot;\na box that runs ten times (an iterator) produces ten slots, one per\ninvocation. Slots live in shared memory so any language runtime can read\nor write them without copying.\n\nA **wire** is the relationship between two tasks: it says \"task B's input\nN reads from task A's output M.\" Wires hold references to slots. They\nare the timing mechanism — a task does not become ready until every\ninput wire reports its source slot is filled. They are also the lifetime\nmechanism — a slot is freed only after every wire that referenced it has\nreleased it.\n\nThe wire is the arbiter. The slot is just memory.\n\n### All slots are ring buffers\nThere is one slot type. It is a ring buffer of `n_cells` cells, each\nof `cell_capacity` bytes. The `n_cells = 1` case is the trivial ring\nholding a single value; the `n_cells = N` case is a queue.\n\nA single-output box allocates a 1-cell ring. The producer pushes once,\nconsumers read the head. An iterator that produces 10 outputs over its\nlifetime allocates 10 separate 1-cell rings (one per invocation, per\nthe box-not-wire-is-the-slot model below).\n\nA box with a queued input allocates a multi-cell ring as the input's\nholding pen — many upstream wires push into it, the consumer drains it\nin arrival order.\n\nSame data structure, same API, same per-slot lock. The dispatch layer\nparameterizes `n_cells` based on whether the slot is being used for\nfan-out or fan-in.\n\n### Asynchrony\nThe store is fully asynchronous. Slots are allocated, filled, read, and\nfreed at any time, on any thread, with no global lock. Synchronization\nis per-slot. There is no central allocator-wide mutex.\n\n## Slot layout\n\nEach slot is a small header followed by a value region whose size is\nspecified by the task at allocation time:\n\n```\nOffset  Size  Field\n------  ----  -----\n0       4     refcount        (atomic int32)\n4       4     value_size      (bytes of value data, 0 if not yet filled)\n8       4     value_capacity  (allocated bytes, set at slot creation)\n12      1     type_tag        (0=none, 1=string, 2=number, 3=json, 4=bytes)\n13      1     filled          (0=empty, 1=ready)\n14      1     touched         (0=free, 1=another thread is mutating)\n15      1     _pad\n16      N     value_data      (N == value_capacity)\n```\n\n`value_capacity` is exactly the size requested by the task — no global\nmaximum. This mirrors the C convention of passing array sizes alongside\narrays. Slots may have wildly different sizes within the same run.\n\n`touched` is a single-byte flag toggled around any mutation of the\nheader (refcount changes, filled flip, etc.). A reader that finds\n`touched == 1` retries. This is the simplest possible per-slot lock; if\ncontention becomes a problem, replace with a proper mutex without\nchanging the API.\n\n`filled` is set last, with a memory barrier, so a reader that observes\n`filled == 1` is guaranteed to see the complete value.\n\n## Reference counting protocol\n\nWhen a task is submitted, the dispatch layer:\n1. Allocates the task's output slot(s) with the requested capacity.\n2. For each wire reading from the slot, calls `slot_ref` on the slot.\n   The wire holds that reference for as long as it might still need to\n   read.\n3. When the consumer task finishes reading, it calls `slot_unref` on\n   the wire's slot. The wire is then dead.\n4. When the refcount drops to zero, the task that performed the final\n   unref clears the slot (frees the backing memory or marks it\n   reusable).\n\nNo central garbage collector. Clearing is deterministic — last unref\ndoes the work.\n\n## Backing store\n\nSlots live in shared memory created with `shm_open` + `mmap`. The\nshared memory object is named `/soramech-<run-id>`. Allocation inside\nthe region is handled by a per-run allocator (a simple bump allocator\nor a small free-list allocator — start with bump, add free-list when\nslot reuse becomes worth it).\n\nAny language runtime that opens the same shared memory name and maps it\ngets access to the same physical memory. For languages that cannot call\nPOSIX directly (e.g. Bash), the language runtime spec (issue 303) is\nresponsible for proxying slot reads and writes through the language's\nruntime server.\n\nSynchronization for blocked tasks (waiting on an empty slot) is handled\nby the dispatch layer (issue 304) — typically a wait list per slot.\nProducers signal waiters when they flip `filled`.\n\n## Slot creation\n\nSlot creation happens inside the dispatch layer at task submission. The\ncaller specifies the value capacity:\n\n```c\nslot_id_t slot_alloc(slot_store_t *store, int capacity, uint8_t type_tag);\n```\n\nThe slot is created with `refcount = 0`, `filled = 0`. The dispatch\nlayer then increments the refcount once per wire reading from it before\nthe task is exposed to consumers.\n\n## Ring-buffer slots (queued inputs)\n\nA downstream task with a queued input has a single slot that acts as a\nring buffer for incoming values. Producers push values, the consumer\ndrains them in arrival order. The buffer's capacity and value-stride\nare set at creation time. The implementation is a fixed-size ring with\natomic head/tail pointers — standard MPSC ring buffer.\n\nThis is a separate slot kind from the single-value output slot.\nDistinguished by a flag in the slot header (or a separate slot type\ntag — decision deferred).\n\n-- actually, they should all be designed with ring-buffers. We don't want to\n   overcomplicate it from the user's point of view, and my understanding is that\n   it doesn't add too much complexity or memory or CPU requirements. If we\n   define one type of structure that handles all of the ring buffers for tasks,\n   then that's not too complex is it?\n\n## C API surface\n\n```c\n// Single-value slot\nslot_id_t slot_alloc        (slot_store_t *s, int capacity, uint8_t type_tag);\nvoid      slot_write        (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, const void *data, int size);\nint       slot_read         (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size);\nvoid      slot_ref          (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id);\nvoid      slot_unref        (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id);  // frees if refcount → 0\n\n// Ring-buffer slot\nslot_id_t slot_ring_alloc   (slot_store_t *s, int slot_capacity, int n_slots);\nvoid      slot_ring_push    (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, const void *data, int size);\nint       slot_ring_pop     (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size);\n```\n\n## Open question — submission timing\n\nWhen the dispatch layer builds a task, it knows the task's input wires\nand output slots before any input is filled. The unresolved question:\n\n- **Option A**: build the task struct early, hold it in a \"blocked\" set,\n  add to the ready queue only when all inputs are filled.\n- **Option B**: build and submit immediately, let the task itself block\n  on its input slots via `ACT_BLOCK` on the first input.\n\nOption A is cleaner — the ready queue contains only runnable tasks.\nOption B uses the pool's existing block-and-wake machinery, fewer\nmoving parts.\n\nDecision deferred. Likely Option B, but want to think about it once\nthe dispatch layer (issue 304) is being written.\n\n-- build the task struct early, fill in all the data we can, and submit it to\n   the queue. The first time it's picked up it'll be validated and it will be\n   known that it's not ready yet - at that point, it'll be added to the queue of\n   the blocking task, to fill in the required inputs (therefore unblocking it)\n   and to re-add it to the ready task pool. Actually, skip the first step, and\n   just if there's any blocked inputs then just add it to the first one\n   immediately.\n\n## Open questions\n- Allocation strategy: bump allocator vs free-list. Bump is simpler;\n  free-list reuses memory across tasks. Start with bump.\n\n  -- please describe both of those in more detail.\n\n- Type tag granularity: do we need a \"json\" tag distinct from \"string\",\n  or is everything string + size at this layer? Probably size + opaque\n  bytes; the type tag becomes advisory only.\n  \n  -- huh? where is this tag type used? we are passing more than just strings as\n     inputs. Json? who-son? type tag? huh? where? who's son? whose on? jake?\n     huh? json? what does that mean?\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. Write `src/slot-store.h` and `src/slot-store.c` — the C API above.\n2. Unit test single-value slots: thread A writes, thread B reads,\n   refcount decrements, slot freed when last ref dropped.\n3. Unit test ring-buffer slots: multiple producers push, single consumer\n   drains in order, no values lost or duplicated.\n4. Integrate into `src/008-pool-runner.c`: shared memory created at\n   startup, store handle passed to the dispatch layer.\n\n## Relevant files\n- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — pool entry point, owns the shared memory region\n- `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.h` — pool API (refcounting is complementary)\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — task dispatch reads/writes slots\n- `issues/213-queued-inputs-and-task-model.md` — queued input model that\n  ring-buffer slots implement\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — IPC options; shm_open + mmap is Option 2\n",
    "oldString":"## Slot layout\n\nEach slot is a small header followed by a value region whose size is\nspecified by the task at allocation time:\n\n```\nOffset  Size  Field\n------  ----  -----\n0       4     refcount        (atomic int32)\n4       4     value_size      (bytes of value data, 0 if not yet filled)\n8       4     value_capacity  (allocated bytes, set at slot creation)\n12      1     type_tag        (0=none, 1=string, 2=number, 3=json, 4=bytes)\n13      1     filled          (0=empty, 1=ready)\n14      1     touched         (0=free, 1=another thread is mutating)\n15      1     _pad\n16      N     value_data      (N == value_capacity)\n```\n\n`value_capacity` is exactly the size requested by the task — no global\nmaximum. The implementation is a fixed-size ring with\natomic head/tail pointers — standard MPSC ring buffer.\n\nThis is a separate slot kind from the single-value output slot.\nDistinguished by a flag in the slot header (or a separate slot type\ntag — decision deferred).\n\n-- actually, they should all be designed with ring-buffers. We don't want to\n   overcomplicate it from the user's point of view, and my understanding is that\n   it doesn't add too much complexity or memory or CPU requirements. If we\n   define one type of structure that handles all of the ring buffers for tasks,\n   then that's not too complex is it?\n\n## C API surface\n\n```c\n// Single-value slot\nslot_id_t slot_alloc        (slot_store_t *s, int capacity, uint8_t type_tag);\nvoid      slot_write        (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, const void *data, int size);\nint       slot_read         (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size);\nvoid      slot_ref          (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id);\nvoid      slot_unref        (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id);  // frees if refcount → 0\n\n// Ring-buffer slot\nslot_id_t slot_ring_alloc   (slot_store_t *s, int slot_capacity, int n_slots);\nvoid      slot_ring_push    (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, const void *data, int size);\nint       slot_ring_pop     (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size);\n```"

    "originalFile":"# 302 — Per-task slot store with wire-held references\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nWire values are passed through stdout pipes and transient strings. Values\nhave no addressable location, no reference count, and no cross-language\naccessibility. Each value vanishes once the pipe is drained.\n\n## Concept\n\n### Slots belong to tasks, not wires\nA **slot** is the memory region that holds a task's output. Slots are\ncreated when tasks are created. A box that runs once produces one slot;\na box that runs ten times (an iterator) produces ten slots, one per\ninvocation. Slots live in shared memory so any language runtime can read\nor write them without copying.\n\nA **wire** is the relationship between two tasks: it says \"task B's input\nN reads from task A's output M.\" Wires hold references to slots. They\nare the timing mechanism — a task does not become ready until every\ninput wire reports its source slot is filled. They are also the lifetime\nmechanism — a slot is freed only after every wire that referenced it has\nreleased it.\n\nThe wire is the arbiter. The slot is just memory.\n\n### All slots are ring buffers\nThere is one slot type. It is a ring buffer of `n_cells` cells, each\nof `cell_capacity` bytes. The `n_cells = 1` case is the trivial ring\nholding a single value; the `n_cells = N` case is a queue.\n\nA single-output box allocates a 1-cell ring. The producer pushes once,\nconsumers read the head. An iterator that produces 10 outputs over its\nlifetime allocates 10 separate 1-cell rings (one per invocation, per\nthe box-not-wire-is-the-slot model below).\n\nA box with a queued input allocates a multi-cell ring as the input's\nholding pen — many upstream wires push into it, the consumer drains it\nin arrival order.\n\nSame data structure, same API, same per-slot lock. The dispatch layer\nparameterizes `n_cells` based on whether the slot is being used for\nfan-out or fan-in.\n\n### Asynchrony\nThe store is fully asynchronous. Slots are allocated, filled, read, and\nfreed at any time, on any thread, with no global lock. Synchronization\nis per-slot. There is no central allocator-wide mutex.\n\n## Slot layout\n\nEach slot is a header followed by `n_cells` cells, each `cell_capacity`\nbytes. The header tracks ring-buffer state and lifetime:\n\n```\nSlot header\nOffset  Size  Field\n------  ----  -----\n0       4     refcount        (atomic int32; lifetime counter)\n4       4     cell_capacity   (bytes per cell, set at allocation)\n8       4     n_cells         (ring size, set at allocation; 1 for single-value)\n12      4     head            (read index, mod n_cells)\n16      4     tail            (write index, mod n_cells; cells_filled = tail - head)\n20      1     touched         (per-slot lock: 0=free, 1=another thread mutating)\n21      3     _pad\n24      …     cells           (n_cells * (4-byte size + cell_capacity bytes))\n```\n\nEach cell stores a 4-byte filled-size followed by `cell_capacity`\nbytes of value data. Cells have wildly different capacities across\nslots — capacity is per-slot, not global. The C convention of passing\nsizes alongside arrays applies: the task that allocates a slot knows\nhow big it needs the cells.\n\n`touched` is a single-byte flag toggled around any header mutation\n(push, pop, refcount changes). A reader that finds `touched == 1`\nspins until it clears. This is the simplest possible per-slot lock —\nif contention proves to matter, replace with a proper mutex without\nchanging the API.\n\nWrites to a cell complete with a memory barrier before `tail` is\nadvanced, so a reader that observes `head < tail` is guaranteed to\nsee the complete value at the head cell.\n\n## Reference counting protocol\n\nWhen a task is submitted, the dispatch layer:\n1. Allocates the task's output slot(s) with the requested capacity.\n2. For each wire reading from the slot, calls `slot_ref` on the slot.\n   The wire holds that reference for as long as it might still need to\n   read.\n3. When the consumer task finishes reading, it calls `slot_unref` on\n   the wire's slot. The wire is then dead.\n4. When the refcount drops to zero, the task that performed the final\n   unref clears the slot (frees the backing memory or marks it\n   reusable).\n\nNo central garbage collector. Clearing is deterministic — last unref\ndoes the work.\n\n## Backing store\n\nSlots live in shared memory created with `shm_open` + `mmap`. The\nshared memory object is named `/soramech-<run-id>`. Allocation inside\nthe region is handled by a per-run allocator (a simple bump allocator\nor a small free-list allocator — start with bump, add free-list when\nslot reuse becomes worth it).\n\nAny language runtime that opens the same shared memory name and maps it\ngets access to the same physical memory. For languages that cannot call\nPOSIX directly (e.g. Bash), the language runtime spec (issue 303) is\nresponsible for proxying slot reads and writes through the language's\nruntime server.\n\nSynchronization for blocked tasks (waiting on an empty slot) is handled\nby the dispatch layer (issue 304) — typically a wait list per slot.\nProducers signal waiters when they flip `filled`.\n\n## Slot creation\n\nSlot creation happens inside the dispatch layer at task submission. The\ncaller specifies the value capacity:\n\n```c\nslot_id_t slot_alloc(slot_store_t *store, int capacity, uint8_t type_tag);\n```\n\nThe slot is created with `refcount = 0`, `filled = 0`. The dispatch\nlayer then increments the refcount once per wire reading from it before\nthe task is exposed to consumers.\n\n## Ring-buffer slots (queued inputs)\n\nA downstream task with a queued input has a single slot that acts as a\nring buffer for incoming values. Producers push values, the consumer\ndrains them in arrival order. The buffer's capacity and value-stride\nare set at creation time. The implementation is a fixed-size ring with\natomic head/tail pointers — standard MPSC ring buffer.\n\nThis is a separate slot kind from the single-value output slot.\nDistinguished by a flag in the slot header (or a separate slot type\ntag — decision deferred).\n\n-- actually, they should all be designed with ring-buffers. We don't want to\n   overcomplicate it from the user's point of view, and my understanding is that\n   it doesn't add too much complexity or memory or CPU requirements. If we\n   define one type of structure that handles all of the ring buffers for tasks,\n   then that's not too complex is it?\n\n## C API surface\n\n```c\n// Single-value slot\nslot_id_t slot_alloc        (slot_store_t *s, int capacity, uint8_t type_tag);\nvoid      slot_write        (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, const void *data, int size);\nint       slot_read         (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size);\nvoid      slot_ref          (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id);\nvoid      slot_unref        (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id);  // frees if refcount → 0\n\n// Ring-buffer slot\nslot_id_t slot_ring_alloc   (slot_store_t *s, int slot_capacity, int n_slots);\nvoid      slot_ring_push    (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, const void *data, int size);\nint       slot_ring_pop     (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size);\n```\n\n## Open question — submission timing\n\nWhen the dispatch layer builds a task, it knows the task's input wires\nand output slots before any input is filled. The unresolved question:\n\n- **Option A**: build the task struct early, hold it in a \"blocked\" set,\n  add to the ready queue only when all inputs are filled.\n- **Option B**: build and submit immediately, let the task itself block\n  on its input slots via `ACT_BLOCK` on the first input.\n\nOption A is cleaner — the ready queue contains only runnable tasks.\nOption B uses the pool's existing block-and-wake machinery, fewer\nmoving parts.\n\nDecision deferred. Likely Option B, but want to think about it once\nthe dispatch layer (issue 304) is being written.\n\n-- build the task struct early, fill in all the data we can, and submit it to\n   the queue. The first time it's picked up it'll be validated and it will be\n   known that it's not ready yet - at that point, it'll be added to the queue of\n   the blocking task, to fill in the required inputs (therefore unblocking it)\n   and to re-add it to the ready task pool. Actually, skip the first step, and\n   just if there's any blocked inputs then just add it to the first one\n   immediately.\n\n## Open questions\n- Allocation strategy: bump allocator vs free-list. Bump is simpler;\n  free-list reuses memory across tasks. Start with bump.\n\n  -- please describe both of those in more detail.\n\n- Type tag granularity: do we need a \"json\" tag distinct from \"string\",\n  or is everything string + size at this layer? Probably size + opaque\n  bytes; the type tag becomes advisory only.\n  \n  -- huh? where is this tag type used? we are passing more than just strings as\n     inputs. Json? who-son? type tag? huh? where? who's son? whose on? jake?\n     huh? json? what does that mean?\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. Write `src/slot-store.h` and `src/slot-store.c` — the C API above.\n2. Unit test single-value slots: thread A writes, thread B reads,\n   refcount decrements, slot freed when last ref dropped.\n3. Unit test ring-buffer slots: multiple producers push, single consumer\n   drains in order, no values lost or duplicated.\n4. Integrate into `src/008-pool-runner.c`: shared memory created at\n   startup, store handle passed to the dispatch layer.\n\n## Relevant files\n- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — pool entry point, owns the shared memory region\n- `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.h` — pool API (refcounting is complementary)\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — task dispatch reads/writes slots\n- `issues/213-queued-inputs-and-task-model.md` — queued input model that\n  ring-buffer slots implement\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — IPC options; shm_open + mmap is Option 2\n",

The\ncaller specifies the value capacity:\n\n```c\nslot_id_t slot_alloc(slot_store_t *store, int capacity, uint8_t type_tag);\n```\n\nThe slot is created with `refcount = 0`, `filled = 0`. The dispatch\nlayer then increments the refcount once per wire reading from it before\nthe task is exposed to consumers.\n\n## Ring-buffer slots (queued inputs)\n\nA downstream task with a queued input has a single slot that acts as a\nring buffer for incoming values.
