    "originalFile":"# 302 — Per-task slot store with wire-held references\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nWire values are passed through stdout pipes and transient strings. Values\nhave no addressable location, no reference count, and no cross-language\naccessibility. Each value vanishes once the pipe is drained.\n\n## Concept\n\n### Slots belong to tasks, not wires\nA **slot** is the memory region that holds a task's output. Slots are\ncreated when tasks are created. A box that runs once produces one slot;\na box that runs ten times (an iterator) produces ten slots, one per\ninvocation. Slots live in shared memory so any language runtime can read\nor write them without copying.\n\nA **wire** is the relationship between two tasks: it says \"task B's input\nN reads from task A's output M.\" Wires hold references to slots. They\nare the timing mechanism — a task does not become ready until every\ninput wire reports its source slot is filled. They are also the lifetime\nmechanism — a slot is freed only after every wire that referenced it has\nreleased it.\n\nThe wire is the arbiter. The slot is just memory.\n\n### All slots are ring buffers\nThere is one slot type. It is a ring buffer of `n_cells` cells, each\nof `cell_capacity` bytes. The `n_cells = 1` case is the trivial ring\nholding a single value; the `n_cells = N` case is a queue.\n\nA single-output box allocates a 1-cell ring. The producer pushes once,\nconsumers read the head. An iterator that produces 10 outputs over its\nlifetime allocates 10 separate 1-cell rings (one per invocation, per\nthe box-not-wire-is-the-slot model below).\n\nA box with a queued input allocates a multi-cell ring as the input's\nholding pen — many upstream wires push into it, the consumer drains it\nin arrival order.\n\nSame data structure, same API, same per-slot lock. The dispatch layer\nparameterizes `n_cells` based on whether the slot is being used for\nfan-out or fan-in.\n\n### Asynchrony\nThe store is fully asynchronous. Slots are allocated, filled, read, and\nfreed at any time, on any thread, with no global lock. Synchronization\nis per-slot. There is no central allocator-wide mutex.\n\n## Slot layout\n\nEach slot is a header followed by `n_cells` cells, each `cell_capacity`\nbytes. The header tracks ring-buffer state and lifetime:\n\n```\nSlot header\nOffset  Size  Field\n------  ----  -----\n0       4     refcount        (atomic int32; lifetime counter)\n4       4     cell_capacity   (bytes per cell, set at allocation)\n8       4     n_cells         (ring size, set at allocation; 1 for single-value)\n12      4     head            (read index, mod n_cells)\n16      4     tail            (write index, mod n_cells; cells_filled = tail - head)\n20      1     touched         (per-slot lock: 0=free, 1=another thread mutating)\n21      3     _pad\n24      …     cells           (n_cells * (4-byte size + cell_capacity bytes))\n```\n\nEach cell stores a 4-byte filled-size followed by `cell_capacity`\nbytes of value data. Cells have wildly different capacities across\nslots — capacity is per-slot, not global. The C convention of passing\nsizes alongside arrays applies: the task that allocates a slot knows\nhow big it needs the cells.\n\n`touched` is a single-byte flag toggled around any header mutation\n(push, pop, refcount changes). A reader that finds `touched == 1`\nspins until it clears. This is the simplest possible per-slot lock —\nif contention proves to matter, replace with a proper mutex without\nchanging the API.\n\nWrites to a cell complete with a memory barrier before `tail` is\nadvanced, so a reader that observes `head < tail` is guaranteed to\nsee the complete value at the head cell.\n\n## Reference counting protocol\n\nWhen a task is submitted, the dispatch layer:\n1. Allocates the task's output slot(s) with the requested capacity.\n2. For each wire reading from the slot, calls `slot_ref` on the slot.\n   The wire holds that reference for as long as it might still need to\n   read.\n3. When the consumer task finishes reading, it calls `slot_unref` on\n   the wire's slot. The wire is then dead.\n4. When the refcount drops to zero, the task that performed the final\n   unref clears the slot (frees the backing memory or marks it\n   reusable).\n\nNo central garbage collector. Clearing is deterministic — last unref\ndoes the work.\n\n## Backing store\n\nSlots live in shared memory created with `shm_open` + `mmap`. The\nshared memory object is named `/soramech-<run-id>`. Allocation inside\nthe region is handled by a per-run allocator (a simple bump allocator\nor a small free-list allocator — start with bump, add free-list when\nslot reuse becomes worth it).\n\nAny language runtime that opens the same shared memory name and maps it\ngets access to the same physical memory. For languages that cannot call\nPOSIX directly (e.g. Bash), the language runtime spec (issue 303) is\nresponsible for proxying slot reads and writes through the language's\nruntime server.\n\nSynchronization for blocked tasks (waiting on an empty slot) is handled\nby the dispatch layer (issue 304) — typically a wait list per slot.\nProducers signal waiters when they flip `filled`.\n\n## Slot creation\n\nSlot creation happens inside the dispatch layer at task submission. The\ncaller specifies the cell capacity (bytes per value) and the ring size\n(number of cells, 1 for single-value):\n\n```c\nslot_id_t slot_alloc(slot_store_t *store, int cell_capacity, int n_cells);\n```\n\nThe slot is created with `refcount = 0`, `head = tail = 0`. The\ndispatch layer then increments the refcount once per consumer (one ref\nper fan-out wire for a 1-cell slot; one ref for the consumer task on a\nqueued-input slot) before the task is exposed.\n\n## C API surface\n\n```c\nslot_id_t slot_alloc (slot_store_t *s, int cell_capacity, int n_cells);\nvoid      slot_push  (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, const void *data, int size);\nint       slot_peek  (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size); // non-destructive: read head, leave it\nint       slot_pop   (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size); // destructive: read head, advance head\nvoid      slot_wait  (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id); // blocks until tail > head\nvoid      slot_ref   (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id);\nvoid      slot_unref (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id); // frees backing memory when refcount → 0\n```\n\nSingle-value (1-cell) slot use: producer `push` once, each consumer\n`peek` once, then `unref`. Cells are not popped — fan-out consumers\nall read the same value, and the slot is freed when the last consumer\nunrefs.\n\nQueued-input (N-cell) slot use: producers `push` repeatedly, the\nconsumer `pop`s in arrival order. The consumer holds the only ref.\nWhen the consumer task is done with its queue, it `unref`s and the\nslot is freed.\n\n## Open question — submission timing\n\nWhen the dispatch layer builds a task, it knows the task's input wires\nand output slots before any input is filled. The unresolved question:\n\n- **Option A**: build the task struct early, hold it in a \"blocked\" set,\n  add to the ready queue only when all inputs are filled.\n- **Option B**: build and submit immediately, let the task itself block\n  on its input slots via `ACT_BLOCK` on the first input.\n\nOption A is cleaner — the ready queue contains only runnable tasks.\nOption B uses the pool's existing block-and-wake machinery, fewer\nmoving parts.\n\nDecision deferred. Likely Option B, but want to think about it once\nthe dispatch layer (issue 304) is being written.\n\n-- build the task struct early, fill in all the data we can, and submit it to\n   the queue. The first time it's picked up it'll be validated and it will be\n   known that it's not ready yet - at that point, it'll be added to the queue of\n   the blocking task, to fill in the required inputs (therefore unblocking it)\n   and to re-add it to the ready task pool. Actually, skip the first step, and\n   just if there's any blocked inputs then just add it to the first one\n   immediately.\n\n## Open questions\n- Allocation strategy: bump allocator vs free-list. Bump is simpler;\n  free-list reuses memory across tasks. Start with bump.\n\n  -- please describe both of those in more detail.\n\n- Type tag granularity: do we need a \"json\" tag distinct from \"string\",\n  or is everything string + size at this layer? Probably size + opaque\n  bytes; the type tag becomes advisory only.\n  \n  -- huh? where is this tag type used? we are passing more than just strings as\n     inputs. Json? who-son? type tag? huh? where? who's son? whose on? jake?\n     huh? json? what does that mean?\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. Write `src/slot-store.h` and `src/slot-store.c` — the C API above.\n2. Unit test single-value slots: thread A writes, thread B reads,\n   refcount decrements, slot freed when last ref dropped.\n3. Unit test ring-buffer slots: multiple producers push, single consumer\n   drains in order, no values lost or duplicated.\n4. Integrate into `src/008-pool-runner.c`: shared memory created at\n   startup, store handle passed to the dispatch layer.\n\n## Relevant files\n- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — pool entry point, owns the shared memory region\n- `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.h` — pool API (refcounting is complementary)\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — task dispatch reads/writes slots\n- `issues/213-queued-inputs-and-task-model.md` — queued input model that\n  ring-buffer slots implement\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — IPC options; shm_open + mmap is Option 2\n",

    "newString":"## Submission timing\n\nThe dispatch layer builds the task struct as soon as the graph asks\nfor it — output slots allocated, all known data filled in, input wire\nreferences attached. It is then submitted directly to the pool. The\npool's existing block-and-wake machinery handles the rest:\n\n- If any input slots are unfilled at the moment of submission, the\n  dispatch action immediately `ACT_BLOCK`s on the first unfilled\n  input. The pool parks the task on that slot's wait list.\n- When the upstream producer pushes, it walks the wait list and wakes\n  the parked tasks. The action re-runs from the top, checks the next\n  input, blocks again if needed.\n- When all inputs are present, the action proceeds to invoke the box.\n\nThere is no separate \"blocked tasks\" set held by the dispatch layer.\nThe pool is the only thing that tracks blocked tasks. This avoids\nduplicating the wait-list machinery the pool already has.",

          "new_string":"## Allocation strategy\n\nThe slot store allocates cells out of the shared memory region. Two\ncandidate allocators, both viable:\n\n### Bump allocator\nA single pointer (the \"bump pointer\") tracks the next free byte in the\nregion. Every allocation reads the current pointer, advances it by the\nrequested size, and returns the old value. There is no per-allocation\ndeallocation — the bump pointer only moves forward. The whole region\nis reset (or unmapped and recreated) at the end of the run.\n\n- Pros: allocation is a single atomic add. No fragmentation. Trivial\n  to implement (about 20 lines of C).\n- Cons: freed slots cannot be reused within a run. A long-running map\n  with iterators that allocate per-iteration slots will exhaust the\n  region in proportion to total iterations, not concurrent slot count.\n\n### Free-list allocator\nThe region is divided into chunks. A linked list of free chunks is\nmaintained. Allocation walks the list looking for a chunk large enough\n(first-fit or best-fit), splits it if much larger than needed, and\nreturns it. Deallocation prepends the freed chunk back onto the list,\noptionally coalescing with adjacent free chunks to reduce\nfragmentation.\n\n- Pros: freed memory is reused. A long-running iterator allocates and\n  frees per iteration without growing the region.\n- Cons: more code (a few hundred lines). Allocation is O(N) walking\n  the list, though that can be improved with size-class buckets or a\n  buddy allocator if it ever matters. Susceptible to fragmentation\n  when allocations are many sizes.\n\nRecommendation: start with the bump allocator. Switch to free-list if\nthe bump pointer hits the region size in a real workload.\n\n## No type tags\n\nSlots store opaque bytes. The producer wrote N bytes; the consumer\nreads N bytes. What those bytes mean is the language spec's business\non each side, and the wire's metadata in the graph (issue 219's\ncompiler can check producer-output type vs consumer-input type at\nbuild time). The C convention of passing\nsizes alongside arrays applies: the task that allocates a slot knows\nhow big it needs the cells.\n\n`touched` is a single-byte flag toggled around any header mutation\n(push, pop, refcount changes). A reader that finds `touched == 1`\nspins until it clears. This is the simplest possible per-slot lock —\nif contention proves to matter, replace with a proper mutex without\nchanging the API.\n\nWrites to a cell complete with a memory barrier before `tail` is\nadvanced, so a reader that observes `head < tail` is guaranteed to\nsee the complete value at the head cell.\n\n## Reference counting protocol\n\nWhen a task is submitted, the dispatch layer:\n1. Allocates the task's output slot(s) with the requested capacity.\n2. For each wire reading from the slot, calls `slot_ref` on the slot.\n   The wire holds that reference for as long as it might still need to\n   read.\n3. When the consumer task finishes reading, it calls `slot_unref` on\n   the wire's slot. The wire is then dead.\n4. When the refcount drops to zero, the task that performed the final\n   unref clears the slot (frees the backing memory or marks it\n   reusable).\n\nNo central garbage collector. Clearing is deterministic — last unref\ndoes the work.\n\n## Backing store\n\nSlots live in shared memory created with `shm_open` + `mmap`. The\nshared memory object is named `/soramech-<run-id>`. Allocation inside\nthe region is handled by a per-run allocator (a simple bump allocator\nor a small free-list allocator — start with bump, add free-list when\nslot reuse becomes worth it).\n\nAny language runtime that opens the same shared memory name and maps it\ngets access to the same physical memory. For languages that cannot call\nPOSIX directly (e.g. Bash), the language runtime spec (issue 303) is\nresponsible for proxying slot reads and writes through the language's\nruntime server.\n\nSynchronization for blocked tasks (waiting on an empty slot) is handled\nby the dispatch layer (issue 304) — typically a wait list per slot.\nProducers signal waiters when they flip `filled`.\n\n## Slot creation\n\nSlot creation happens inside the dispatch layer at task submission. The\ncaller specifies the cell capacity (bytes per value) and the ring size\n(number of cells, 1 for single-value):\n\n```c\nslot_id_t slot_alloc(slot_store_t *store, int cell_capacity, int n_cells);\n```\n\nThe slot is created with `refcount = 0`, `head = tail = 0`. The\ndispatch layer then increments the refcount once per consumer (one ref\nper fan-out wire for a 1-cell slot; one ref for the consumer task on a\nqueued-input slot) before the task is exposed.\n\n## C API surface\n\n```c\nslot_id_t slot_alloc (slot_store_t *s, int cell_capacity, int n_cells);\nvoid      slot_push  (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, const void *data, int size);\nint       slot_peek  (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size); // non-destructive: read head, leave it\nint       slot_pop   (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size); // destructive: read head, advance head\nvoid      slot_wait  (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id); // blocks until tail > head\nvoid      slot_ref   (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id);\nvoid      slot_unref (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id); // frees backing memory when refcount → 0\n```\n\nSingle-value (1-cell) slot use: producer `push` once, each consumer\n`peek` once, then `unref`. Cells are not popped — fan-out consumers\nall read the same value, and the slot is freed when the last consumer\nunrefs.\n\nQueued-input (N-cell) slot use: producers `push` repeatedly, the\nconsumer `pop`s in arrival order. The consumer holds the only ref.\nWhen the consumer task is done with its queue, it `unref`s and the\nslot is freed.\n\n## Submission timing\n\nThe dispatch layer builds the task struct as soon as the graph asks\nfor it — output slots allocated, all known data filled in, input wire\nreferences attached. It is then submitted directly to the pool. The\npool's existing block-and-wake machinery handles the rest:\n\n- If any input slots are unfilled at the moment of submission, the\n  dispatch action immediately `ACT_BLOCK`s on the first unfilled\n  input. The pool parks the task on that slot's wait list.\n- When the upstream producer pushes, it walks the wait list and wakes\n  the parked tasks. The action re-runs from the top, checks the next\n  input, blocks again if needed.\n- When all inputs are present, the action proceeds to invoke the box.\n\nThere is no separate \"blocked tasks\" set held by the dispatch layer.\nThe pool is the only thing that tracks blocked tasks. This avoids\nduplicating the wait-list machinery the pool already has.\n\n## Open questions\n- Allocation strategy: bump allocator vs free-list. Bump is simpler;\n  free-list reuses memory across tasks. Start with bump.\n\n  -- please describe both of those in more detail.\n\n- Type tag granularity: do we need a \"json\" tag distinct from \"string\",\n  or is everything string + size at this layer? Probably size + opaque\n  bytes; the type tag becomes advisory only.\n  \n  -- huh? where is this tag type used? we are passing more than just strings as\n     inputs. Json? who-son? type tag? huh? where? who's son? whose on? jake?\n     huh? json? what does that mean?\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. Write `src/slot-store.h` and `src/slot-store.c` — the C API above.\n2. Unit test single-value slots: thread A writes, thread B reads,\n   refcount decrements, slot freed when last ref dropped.\n3. Unit test ring-buffer slots: multiple producers push, single consumer\n   drains in order, no values lost or duplicated.\n4. Integrate into `src/008-pool-runner.c`: shared memory created at\n   startup, store handle passed to the dispatch layer.\n\n## Relevant files\n- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — pool entry point, owns the shared memory region\n- `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.h` — pool API (refcounting is complementary)\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — task dispatch reads/writes slots\n- `issues/213-queued-inputs-and-task-model.md` — queued input model that\n  ring-buffer slots implement\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — IPC options; shm_open + mmap is Option 2\n",

Start with bump.\n\n  -- please describe both of those in more detail.\n\n- Type tag granularity: do we need a \"json\" tag distinct from \"string\",\n  or is everything string + size at this layer? Probably size + opaque\n  bytes; the type tag becomes advisory only.\n  \n  -- huh? where is this tag type used? we are passing more than just strings as\n     inputs. Json? who-son? type tag? huh? where? who's son? whose on? jake?\n     huh? json? what does that mean?",
    "newString":"## Allocation strategy\n\nThe slot store allocates cells out of the shared memory region. Two\ncandidate allocators, both viable:\n\n### Bump allocator\nA single pointer (the \"bump pointer\") tracks the next free byte in the\nregion. Every allocation reads the current pointer, advances it by the\nrequested size, and returns the old value. There is no per-allocation\ndeallocation — the bump pointer only moves forward. The whole region\nis reset (or unmapped and recreated) at the end of the run.\n\n- Pros: allocation is a single atomic add. No fragmentation. Trivial\n  to implement (about 20 lines of C).\n- Cons: freed slots cannot be reused within a run. A long-running map\n  with iterators that allocate per-iteration slots will exhaust the\n  region in proportion to total iterations, not concurrent slot count.\n\n### Free-list allocator\nThe region is divided into chunks. A linked list of free chunks is\nmaintained. Allocation walks the list looking for a chunk large enough\n(first-fit or best-fit), splits it if much larger than needed, and\nreturns it. Deallocation prepends the freed chunk back onto the list,\noptionally coalescing with adjacent free chunks to reduce\nfragmentation.\n\n- Pros: freed memory is reused. A long-running iterator allocates and\n  frees per iteration without growing the region.\n- Cons: more code (a few hundred lines). Allocation is O(N) walking\n  the list, though that can be improved with size-class buckets or a\n  buddy allocator if it ever matters. Susceptible to fragmentation\n  when allocations are many sizes.\n\nRecommendation: start with the bump allocator. Switch to free-list if\nthe bump pointer hits the region size in a real workload.\n\n## No type tags\n\nSlots store opaque bytes. The producer wrote N bytes; the consumer\nreads N bytes. What those bytes mean is the language spec's business\non each side, and the wire's metadata in the graph (issue 219's\ncompiler can check producer-output type vs consumer-input type at\nbuild time). The slot store does not interpret values — it does not\nneed to know if they are strings, numbers, JSON, images, or anything\nelse. Removed the type-tag field from the header for that reason.",
    "replaceAll":false,
    "userModified":false
  },

    "originalFile":"# 303 — Language runtime spec: pluggable per-language invocation\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nEach language has an ad-hoc driver script (`drivers/lua.sh`, `drivers/bash.sh`,\n`drivers/c.sh`). The driver is invoked per box call: spawn a process, run\nthe function, read stdout, exit. Adding a new language means writing a new\ndriver script and modifying the executor to know about it.\n\nThere is no shared interface, no persistent runtime, and no way for a user\nto add a language without touching SoraMech internals.\n\n## Concept\n\nThe language runtime spec is the user-extensible interface that defines how\na language's functions are invoked from inside the thread pool. Every\nlanguage goes through this interface — there is no special path for any\nlanguage. Lua is a spec. C is a spec. Bash is a spec. A user adding Python\nwrites another spec.\n\nThe pool runner does not know how to \"run a Lua function.\" It knows how to\ncall `lang->invoke(...)`. The Lua spec is the thing that knows how to run a\nLua function.\n\nThe user provides the bridging code. SoraMech does not transpile, rewrite,\nor convert box source between languages. If the user wants Rust, the user\nwrites a Rust spec.\n\n## The interface\n\nEach language spec is a C library that exports a single symbol:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    const char *name;       // \"lua\", \"bash\", \"c\", \"python\", ...\n    const char *file_ext;   // \".lua\", \".sh\", \".c\", \".py\" — for box file resolution\n\n    // Once-per-worker. Returns an opaque handle stored in worker_ctx.\n    // Called at pool startup, before any tasks run.\n    void *(*init)(int worker_idx);\n\n    // Once-per-worker. Called at pool shutdown.\n    void  (*teardown)(void *handle);\n\n    // Optional: called once per box source file at map load.\n    // For languages that compile (C → .so), this is where compilation\n    // happens. For languages that don't (Lua, Bash), this is NULL.\n    int   (*compile)(const char *src_path, const char *out_path);\n\n    // The invocation. Inputs are arrays of (bytes, size) pairs,\n    // already read from slots by the dispatch layer. The spec writes\n    // its return value into out_buf and sets *out_size.\n    //\n    // Returns 0 on success, nonzero on error.\n    int   (*invoke)(void *handle,\n                    const char *file_path,\n                    const char *fn_name,\n                    const void **input_data, const int *input_sizes, int n_inputs,\n                    void *out_buf, int out_buf_capacity, int *out_size);\n} lang_spec_t;\n\nextern lang_spec_t soramech_lang_spec;\n```\n\nThe spec library is built as a `.so` and loaded by the pool runner at\nstartup via `dlopen` / `dlsym`. The runner iterates `langs/*/spec.so`,\nloads each, and registers it under its `name`.\n\n## Slot access boundary\n\nSpecs do not see slot IDs. The dispatch layer (issue 304) reads input\nvalues from slots into raw byte buffers, hands them to `invoke`, receives\nthe output bytes, and writes them to the output slot. This decouples\nspecs from slot internals — a spec only deals with values.\n\nIf a future language wants zero-copy access (e.g. memory-mapping a slot\ndirectly into a Python bytearray), the interface can be extended. Do not\nadd it preemptively.\n\n## Per-language layout\n\nSpecs live under `langs/<name>/`:\n\n```\nlangs/lua/\n    spec.c              ← implements lang_spec_t (handles → lua_State)\n    Makefile            ← builds spec.so\n    spec.so             ← built artifact\n\nlangs/bash/\n    spec.c              ← bridges to bash-server.sh via Unix domain socket\n    bash-server.sh      ← persistent subprocess started by spec.init\n    Makefile\n\nlangs/c/\n    spec.c              ← uses dlopen/dlsym; compile = gcc -shared -fPIC\n    Makefile\n\nlangs/python/           ← user-added; not shipped\n    spec.c\n    Makefile\n```\n\nThe pool runner has no compiled-in knowledge of any specific language.\nEven Lua is loaded as a `.so` at startup. This keeps the boundary honest\n— there is no temptation to special-case the \"shipped\" languages.\n\n## Built-in specs (shipped, not privileged)\n\nSoraMech ships specs for:\n- **Lua** — handle is a `lua_State`. `invoke` calls `luaL_loadfile` (cached)\n  + `lua_pcall`. Args pushed as Lua strings; return read as Lua string.\n- **C** — handle is a small `dlopen` handle cache. `compile` runs\n  `gcc -shared -fPIC -o <out_path> <src_path>`. `invoke` does\n  `dlsym` + direct call.\n- **Bash** — handle is a Unix domain socket connected to a persistent\n  bash subprocess (`bash-server.sh`). `invoke` sends a framed request,\n  reads a framed response.\n\nThese are the reference implementations. They demonstrate the spec\ninterface for in-process FFI (Lua, C) and for out-of-process socket\nservers (Bash, and any future language whose runtime cannot be embedded).\n\n## Compilation\n\nThe optional `compile` hook runs at map load (or at editor compile-button\ntime, issue 219). For C, it produces a `.so` next to the source. For\nLua and Bash, no compilation step is needed; `compile` is `NULL`.\n\nCompilation outputs go in the map's `compiled/bin/` directory (issue\n222). The dispatch layer passes the compiled artifact path to `invoke`,\nnot the original source path, when a compiled artifact exists.\n\n## Iterator counter prepending\n\nThe iterator counter (issue 221) is prepended to the input array by the\ndispatch layer, not by the spec. From the spec's perspective, an\niterator box just has one extra input. The spec doesn't know which\ninput is the counter — that's a graph-level concept.\n\n## Error propagation\n\nA nonzero return from `invoke` marks the task as failed. The dispatch\nlayer leaves the output slot unfilled and records the failure in the\ntask's status. Downstream consumers blocked on the unfilled slot will\neither time out or be cancelled — the failure propagation policy is\nthe dispatch layer's concern (issue 304), not the spec's.\n\n-- any errors should crash the program. If the invoke returns a non-zero value\n   it should crash hard. It shouldn't return invalid values! Also, we shouldn't\n   have situations where tasks can fail to return correct values - if we do,\n   then we are opening ourselves up to a lot of problems. Also, we don't want\n   to build in systems that check for failures and stalled tasks. That's\n   extra complexity and has a runtime cost. Not ideal! If the code has a bug,\n   then it should not be used in production until the bug is fixed. If a bug\n   crashes something in production because you didn't notice it, well, you\n   better fix it quickly...\n\nThe spec is responsible for catching language-level errors (Lua\n`error()`, C segfault via signal handler, Bash nonzero exit) and\ntranslating them into a nonzero return.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Per-spec configuration: should specs read a `langs/<name>/config.json`\n  for things like compiler flags, server startup args, etc.? Or is\n  hard-coding inside `spec.c` fine for the user-extensible model?\n\n-- we can just hard-code them. Doesn't make sense to have a different file.\n\n- Hot reload: if a user edits a box file, do we re-run `compile` and\n  invalidate the `dlopen` cache? Probably yes for C, no-op for Lua and\n  Bash. The dispatch layer should ping the spec with a `reload` callback\n  — but that adds another interface function. Defer until needed.\n\n-- eh, let's just ignore this. The user will hit compile, it will re-compile\n   all the files that have changed, or like you said just no-op for interpreted\n   languages, and it'll just... work itself out. We don't have to worry about it\n\n- How does a user discover the spec interface? A header file\n  `langs/lang-spec.h` that defines `lang_spec_t` and is included by\n  every spec implementation. Yes, do that.\n\n  -- Um. We should write into the readme about it so they know it's an option.\n     and there should be docs related to it so they know how to modify specs.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Write `langs/lang-spec.h` — the public interface header.\n2. Write `langs/lua/spec.c` first. Lua is the easiest because it's already\n   our default language and the existing driver gives a reference behavior.\n3. Write `langs/c/spec.c` — adds `compile` callback, exercises the dlopen\n   path.\n4. Write `langs/bash/spec.c` + `langs/bash/bash-server.sh` — exercises\n   the out-of-process socket model. This is the proof that languages\n   without an embeddable runtime fit the same interface.\n5. Pool runner registry: `dlopen` every `langs/*/spec.so` at startup,\n   register by `name`. Box files are routed to specs by `file_ext`.\n6. Smoke test: a map with one Lua box, one C box, one Bash box, all\n   running in the pool, all going through the spec interface. No\n   special-cased code paths.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `drivers/lua.sh`, `drivers/bash.sh`, `drivers/c.sh` — current ad-hoc\n  drivers, replaced by `langs/<name>/spec.c`\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool startup invokes\n  spec `init` per worker per language\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — dispatch layer reads slots and\n  passes raw bytes to specs (specs do not touch slots)\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — calls `invoke` per task\n- `issues/222-compile-button-and-assets-directory.md` — compile button\n  runs spec `compile` for every box\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — Option 1 (FFI) and Option 3 (Unix\n  socket) describe the two execution models specs implement\n",

    "originalFile":"# 303 — Language runtime spec: pluggable per-language invocation\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nEach language has an ad-hoc driver script (`drivers/lua.sh`, `drivers/bash.sh`,\n`drivers/c.sh`). The driver is invoked per box call: spawn a process, run\nthe function, read stdout, exit. Adding a new language means writing a new\ndriver script and modifying the executor to know about it.\n\nThere is no shared interface, no persistent runtime, and no way for a user\nto add a language without touching SoraMech internals.\n\n## Concept\n\nThe language runtime spec is the user-extensible interface that defines how\na language's functions are invoked from inside the thread pool. Every\nlanguage goes through this interface — there is no special path for any\nlanguage. Lua is a spec. C is a spec. Bash is a spec. A user adding Python\nwrites another spec.\n\nThe pool runner does not know how to \"run a Lua function.\" It knows how to\ncall `lang->invoke(...)`. The Lua spec is the thing that knows how to run a\nLua function.\n\nThe user provides the bridging code. SoraMech does not transpile, rewrite,\nor convert box source between languages. If the user wants Rust, the user\nwrites a Rust spec.\n\n## The interface\n\nEach language spec is a C library that exports a single symbol:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    const char *name;       // \"lua\", \"bash\", \"c\", \"python\", ...\n    const char *file_ext;   // \".lua\", \".sh\", \".c\", \".py\" — for box file resolution\n\n    // Once-per-worker. Returns an opaque handle stored in worker_ctx.\n    // Called at pool startup, before any tasks run.\n    void *(*init)(int worker_idx);\n\n    // Once-per-worker. Called at pool shutdown.\n    void  (*teardown)(void *handle);\n\n    // Optional: called once per box source file at map load.\n    // For languages that compile (C → .so), this is where compilation\n    // happens. For languages that don't (Lua, Bash), this is NULL.\n    int   (*compile)(const char *src_path, const char *out_path);\n\n    // The invocation. Inputs are arrays of (bytes, size) pairs,\n    // already read from slots by the dispatch layer. The spec writes\n    // its return value into out_buf and sets *out_size.\n    //\n    // Returns 0 on success, nonzero on error.\n    int   (*invoke)(void *handle,\n                    const char *file_path,\n                    const char *fn_name,\n                    const void **input_data, const int *input_sizes, int n_inputs,\n                    void *out_buf, int out_buf_capacity, int *out_size);\n} lang_spec_t;\n\nextern lang_spec_t soramech_lang_spec;\n```\n\nThe spec library is built as a `.so` and loaded by the pool runner at\nstartup via `dlopen` / `dlsym`. The runner iterates `langs/*/spec.so`,\nloads each, and registers it under its `name`.\n\n## Slot access boundary\n\nSpecs do not see slot IDs. The dispatch layer (issue 304) reads input\nvalues from slots into raw byte buffers, hands them to `invoke`, receives\nthe output bytes, and writes them to the output slot. This decouples\nspecs from slot internals — a spec only deals with values.\n\nIf a future language wants zero-copy access (e.g. memory-mapping a slot\ndirectly into a Python bytearray), the interface can be extended. Do not\nadd it preemptively.\n\n## Per-language layout\n\nSpecs live under `langs/<name>/`:\n\n```\nlangs/lua/\n    spec.c              ← implements lang_spec_t (handles → lua_State)\n    Makefile            ← builds spec.so\n    spec.so             ← built artifact\n\nlangs/bash/\n    spec.c              ← bridges to bash-server.sh via Unix domain socket\n    bash-server.sh      ← persistent subprocess started by spec.init\n    Makefile\n\nlangs/c/\n    spec.c              ← uses dlopen/dlsym; compile = gcc -shared -fPIC\n    Makefile\n\nlangs/python/           ← user-added; not shipped\n    spec.c\n    Makefile\n```\n\nThe pool runner has no compiled-in knowledge of any specific language.\nEven Lua is loaded as a `.so` at startup. This keeps the boundary honest\n— there is no temptation to special-case the \"shipped\" languages.\n\n## Built-in specs (shipped, not privileged)\n\nSoraMech ships specs for:\n- **Lua** — handle is a `lua_State`. `invoke` calls `luaL_loadfile` (cached)\n  + `lua_pcall`. Args pushed as Lua strings; return read as Lua string.\n- **C** — handle is a small `dlopen` handle cache. `compile` runs\n  `gcc -shared -fPIC -o <out_path> <src_path>`. `invoke` does\n  `dlsym` + direct call.\n- **Bash** — handle is a Unix domain socket connected to a persistent\n  bash subprocess (`bash-server.sh`). `invoke` sends a framed request,\n  reads a framed response.\n\nThese are the reference implementations. They demonstrate the spec\ninterface for in-process FFI (Lua, C) and for out-of-process socket\nservers (Bash, and any future language whose runtime cannot be embedded).\n\n## Compilation\n\nThe optional `compile` hook runs at map load (or at editor compile-button\ntime, issue 219). For C, it produces a `.so` next to the source. For\nLua and Bash, no compilation step is needed; `compile` is `NULL`.\n\nCompilation outputs go in the map's `compiled/bin/` directory (issue\n222). The dispatch layer passes the compiled artifact path to `invoke`,\nnot the original source path, when a compiled artifact exists.\n\n## Iterator counter prepending\n\nThe iterator counter (issue 221) is prepended to the input array by the\ndispatch layer, not by the spec. From the spec's perspective, an\niterator box just has one extra input. The spec doesn't know which\ninput is the counter — that's a graph-level concept.\n\n## Errors crash the program\n\nA nonzero return from `invoke` is a fatal error. The dispatch layer\nprints the error context (box id, function name, language) to stderr\nand aborts the process. There is no recovery, no retry, no per-task\n\"failed\" state, no fallback. There are no timeouts on stalled tasks,\nno wait-list garbage collection, no failure propagation through the\ngraph.\n\nThe reasoning: a task that cannot produce a correct return value is a\nbug. Bugs do not belong in production. Building in detection and\nrecovery for bug states adds runtime cost and complexity to handle a\ncase that should not exist. If a bug surfaces in production, the\nprogram crashes loudly; the developer fixes the bug and redeploys.\n\nThe spec is still responsible for catching language-level errors (Lua\n`error()`, C signals it can intercept, Bash nonzero exit) and\ntranslating them into a nonzero return — so that the dispatch layer\nsees a clean signal instead of an undefined post-error state. Once\nreturned, the program ends.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Per-spec configuration: should specs read a `langs/<name>/config.json`\n  for things like compiler flags, server startup args, etc.? Or is\n  hard-coding inside `spec.c` fine for the user-extensible model?\n\n-- we can just hard-code them. Doesn't make sense to have a different file.\n\n- Hot reload: if a user edits a box file, do we re-run `compile` and\n  invalidate the `dlopen` cache? Probably yes for C, no-op for Lua and\n  Bash. The dispatch layer should ping the spec with a `reload` callback\n  — but that adds another interface function. Defer until needed.\n\n-- eh, let's just ignore this. The user will hit compile, it will re-compile\n   all the files that have changed, or like you said just no-op for interpreted\n   languages, and it'll just... work itself out. We don't have to worry about it\n\n- How does a user discover the spec interface? A header file\n  `langs/lang-spec.h` that defines `lang_spec_t` and is included by\n  every spec implementation. Yes, do that.\n\n  -- Um. We should write into the readme about it so they know it's an option.\n     and there should be docs related to it so they know how to modify specs.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Write `langs/lang-spec.h` — the public interface header.\n2. Write `langs/lua/spec.c` first. Lua is the easiest because it's already\n   our default language and the existing driver gives a reference behavior.\n3. Write `langs/c/spec.c` — adds `compile` callback, exercises the dlopen\n   path.\n4. Write `langs/bash/spec.c` + `langs/bash/bash-server.sh` — exercises\n   the out-of-process socket model. This is the proof that languages\n   without an embeddable runtime fit the same interface.\n5. Pool runner registry: `dlopen` every `langs/*/spec.so` at startup,\n   register by `name`. Box files are routed to specs by `file_ext`.\n6. Smoke test: a map with one Lua box, one C box, one Bash box, all\n   running in the pool, all going through the spec interface. No\n   special-cased code paths.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `drivers/lua.sh`, `drivers/bash.sh`, `drivers/c.sh` — current ad-hoc\n  drivers, replaced by `langs/<name>/spec.c`\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool startup invokes\n  spec `init` per worker per language\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — dispatch layer reads slots and\n  passes raw bytes to specs (specs do not touch slots)\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — calls `invoke` per task\n- `issues/222-compile-button-and-assets-directory.md` — compile button\n  runs spec `compile` for every box\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — Option 1 (FFI) and Option 3 (Unix\n  socket) describe the two execution models specs implement\n",

    "newString":"## User-facing documentation\n\nThe interface is published in `langs/lang-spec.h`, which every spec\nimplementation includes. That header is the source of truth for the\ncontract.\n\nUser-facing docs that mention the language spec system:\n- `README.md` — short paragraph in the features list pointing out that\n  any language can be added by writing a spec, with a one-line example\n  of what that means\n- `docs/005-language-specs.md` (to be written) — the long-form guide\n  on writing a spec: walk through the Lua spec as a small reference,\n  show what `init` / `invoke` / `teardown` do, point at the C spec for\n  the `compile`-using case and the Bash spec for the\n  socket-server case\n- `docs/000-table-of-contents.md` — index entry for the new doc\n\nWithout these the spec system is invisible — users would never know it\nexists or how to extend it.\n\n## Open questions\n\n(none currently)",

    "snippet":"1\t# 302 — Per-task slot store with wire-held references\n2\t\n3\t## Status\n4\topen\n5\t\n6\t## Current behavior\n7\tWire values are passed through stdout pipes and transient strings. Values\n8\thave no addressable location, no reference count, and no cross-language\n9\taccessibility. Each value vanishes once the pipe is drained.\n10\t\n11\t## Concept\n12\t\n13\t### Slots belong to tasks, not wires\n14\tA **slot** is the memory region that holds a task's output. Slots are\n15\tcreated when tasks are created. A box that runs once produces one slot;\n16\ta box that runs ten times (an iterator) produces ten slots, one per\n17\tinvocation. Slots live in shared memory so any language runtime can read\n18\tor write them without copying.\n19\t\n20\tA **wire** is the relationship between two tasks: it says \"task B's input\n21\tN reads from task A's output M.\" Wires hold references to slots. They\n22\tare the timing mechanism — a task does not become ready until every\n23\tinput wire reports its source slot is filled. They are also the lifetime\n24\tmechanism — a slot is freed only after every wire that referenced it has\n25\treleased it.\n26\t\n27\tThe wire is the arbiter. The slot is just memory.\n28\t\n29\t### All slots are ring buffers\n30\tThere is one slot type. It is a ring buffer of `n_cells` cells, each\n31\tof `cell_capacity` bytes. The `n_cells = 1` case is the trivial ring\n32\tholding a single value; the `n_cells = N` case is a queue.\n33\t\n34\tA single-output box allocates a 1-cell ring. The producer pushes once,\n35\tconsumers read the head. An iterator that produces 10 outputs over its\n36\tlifetime allocates 10 separate 1-cell rings (one per invocation, per\n37\tthe box-not-wire-is-the-slot model below).\n38\t\n39\tA box with a queued input allocates a multi-cell ring as the input's\n40\tholding pen — many upstream wires push into it, the consumer drains it\n41\tin arrival order.\n42\t\n43\tSame data structure, same API, same per-slot lock. The dispatch layer\n44\tparameterizes `n_cells` based on whether the slot is being used for\n45\tfan-out or fan-in.\n46\t\n47\t### Asynchrony\n48\tThe store is fully asynchronous. Slots are allocated, filled, read, and\n49\tfreed at any time, on any thread, with no global lock. Synchronization\n50\tis per-slot. There is no central allocator-wide mutex.\n51\t\n52\t## Slot layout\n53\t\n54\tEach slot is a header followed by `n_cells` cells, each `cell_capacity`\n55\tbytes. The header tracks ring-buffer state and lifetime:\n56\t\n57\t```\n58\tSlot header\n59\tOffset  Size  Field\n60\t------  ----  -----\n61\t0       4     refcount        (atomic int32; lifetime counter)\n62\t4       4     cell_capacity   (bytes per cell, set at allocation)\n63\t8       4     n_cells         (ring size, set at allocation; 1 for single-value)\n64\t12      4     head            (read index, mod n_cells)\n65\t16      4     tail            (write index, mod n_cells; cells_filled = tail - head)\n66\t20      1     touched         (per-slot lock: 0=free, 1=another thread mutating)\n67\t21      3     _pad\n68\t24      …     cells           (n_cells * (4-byte size + cell_capacity bytes))\n69\t```\n70\t\n71\tEach cell stores a 4-byte filled-size followed by `cell_capacity`\n72\tbytes of value data. Cells have wildly different capacities across\n73\tslots — capacity is per-slot, not global. The C convention of passing\n74\tsizes alongside arrays applies: the task that allocates a slot knows\n75\thow big it needs the cells.\n76\t\n77\t`touched` is a single-byte flag toggled around any header mutation\n78\t(push, pop, refcount changes). A reader that finds `touched == 1`\n79\tspins until it clears. This is the simplest possible per-slot lock —\n80\tif contention proves to matter, replace with a proper mutex without\n81\tchanging the API.\n82\t\n83\tWrites to a cell complete with a memory barrier before `tail` is\n84\tadvanced, so a reader that observes `head < tail` is guaranteed to\n85\tsee the complete value at the head cell.\n86\t\n87\t## Reference counting protocol\n88\t\n89\tWhen a task is submitted, the dispatch layer:\n90\t1. Allocates the task's output slot(s) with the requested capacity.\n91\t2. For each wire reading from the slot, calls `slot_ref` on the slot.\n92\t   The wire holds that reference for as long as it might still need to\n93\t   read.\n94\t3. When the consumer task finishes reading, it calls `slot_unref` on\n95\t   the wire's slot. The wire is then dead.\n96\t4. When the refcount drops to zero, the task that performed the final\n97\t   unref clears the slot (frees the backing memory or marks it\n98\t   reusable).\n99\t\n100\tNo central garbage collector. Clearing is deterministic — last unref\n101\tdoes the work.\n102\t\n103\t## Backing store\n104\t\n105\tSlots live in shared memory created with `shm_open` + `mmap`. The\n106\tshared memory object is named `/soramech-<run-id>`. Allocation inside\n107\tthe region is handled by a per-run allocator (a simple bump allocator\n108\tor a small free-list allocator — start with bump, add free-list when\n109\tslot reuse becomes worth it).\n110\t\n111\tAny language runtime that opens the same shared memory name and maps it\n112\tgets access to the same physical memory. For languages that cannot call\n113\tPOSIX directly (e.g. Bash), the language runtime spec (issue 303) is\n114\tresponsible for proxying slot reads and writes through the language's\n115\truntime server.\n116\t\n117\tSynchronization for blocked tasks (waiting on an empty slot) is handled\n118\tby the dispatch layer (issue 304) — typically a wait list per slot.\n119\tProducers signal waiters when they flip `filled`.\n120\t\n121\t## Slot creation\n122\t\n123\tSlot creation happens inside the dispatch layer at task submission. The\n124\tcaller specifies the cell capacity (bytes per value) and the ring size\n125\t(number of cells, 1 for single-value):\n126\t\n127\t```c\n128\tslot_id_t slot_alloc(slot_store_t *store, int cell_capacity, int n_cells);\n129\t```\n130\t\n131\tThe slot is created with `refcount = 0`, `head = tail = 0`. The\n132\tdispatch layer then increments the refcount once per consumer (one ref\n133\tper fan-out wire for a 1-cell slot; one ref for the consumer task on a\n134\tqueued-input slot) before the task is exposed.\n135\t\n136\t## C API surface\n137\t\n138\t```c\n139\tslot_id_t slot_alloc (slot_store_t *s, int cell_capacity, int n_cells);\n140\tvoid      slot_push  (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, const void *data, int size);\n141\tint       slot_peek  (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size); // non-destructive: read head, leave it\n142\tint       slot_pop   (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size); // destructive: read head, advance head\n143\tvoid      slot_wait  (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id); // blocks until tail > head\n144\tvoid      slot_ref   (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id);\n145\tvoid      slot_unref (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id); // frees backing memory when refcount → 0\n146\t```\n147\t\n148\tSingle-value (1-cell) slot use: producer `push` once, each consumer\n149\t`peek` once, then `unref`. Cells are not popped — fan-out consumers\n150\tall read the same value, and the slot is freed when the last consumer\n151\tunrefs.\n152\t\n153\tQueued-input (N-cell) slot use: producers `push` repeatedly, the\n154\tconsumer `pop`s in arrival order. The consumer holds the only ref.\n155\tWhen the consumer task is done with its queue, it `unref`s and the\n156\tslot is freed.\n157\t\n158\t## Submission timing\n159\t\n160\tThe dispatch layer builds the task struct as soon as the graph asks\n161\tfor it — output slots allocated, all known data filled in, input wire\n162\treferences attached. It is then submitted directly to the pool. The\n163\tpool's existing block-and-wake machinery handles the rest:\n164\t\n165\t- If any input slots are unfilled at the moment of submission, the\n166\t  dispatch action immediately `ACT_BLOCK`s on the first unfilled\n167\t  input. The pool parks the task on that slot's wait list.\n168\t- When the upstream producer pushes, it walks the wait list and wakes\n169\t  the parked tasks. The action re-runs from the top, checks the next\n170\t  input, blocks again if needed.\n171\t- When all inputs are present, the action proceeds to invoke the box.\n172\t\n173\tThere is no separate \"blocked tasks\" set held by the dispatch layer.\n174\tThe pool is the only thing that tracks blocked tasks. This avoids\n175\tduplicating the wait-list machinery the pool already has.\n176\t\n\n... [87 lines truncated] ...",

    "oldString":"## Allocation strategy\n\nThe slot store allocates cells out of the shared memory region. Two\ncandidate allocators, both viable:\n\n### Bump allocator\nA single pointer (the \"bump pointer\") tracks the next free byte in the\nregion. Every allocation reads the current pointer, advances it by the\nrequested size, and returns the old value. There is no per-allocation\ndeallocation — the bump pointer only moves forward. The whole region\nis reset (or unmapped and recreated) at the end of the run.\n\n- Pros: allocation is a single atomic add. No fragmentation. Trivial\n  to implement (about 20 lines of C).\n- Cons: freed slots cannot be reused within a run. A long-running map\n  with iterators that allocate per-iteration slots will exhaust the\n  region in proportion to total iterations, not concurrent slot count.\n\n### Free-list allocator\nThe region is divided into chunks. A linked list of free chunks is\nmaintained. Allocation walks the list looking for a chunk large enough\n(first-fit or best-fit), splits it if much larger than needed, and\nreturns it. Deallocation prepends the freed chunk back onto the list,\noptionally coalescing with adjacent free chunks to reduce\nfragmentation.\n\n- Pros: freed memory is reused. A long-running iterator allocates and\n  frees per iteration without growing the region.\n- Cons: more code (a few hundred lines). Allocation is O(N) walking\n  the list, though that can be improved with size-class buckets or a\n  buddy allocator if it ever matters. Susceptible to fragmentation\n  when allocations are many sizes.\n\nRecommendation: start with the bump allocator. Switch to free-list if\nthe bump pointer hits the region size in a real workload.\n\n-- I think we can just stick with a bump allocator all the time. Keep in mind,\n   we won't know what users are going to use this for. We have no idea what a\n   real workload will look like. Assume there's no such thing as a real workload.\n\n-- okay I know I said a bump allocator, but what we really should do is have a\n   list of all the available slots, just, in an array or something. There should\n   be a different list for each size that slots might be - we can tell by looking\n   at the map at compile time. Each box will require a certain size, so we can\n   build out a list for each of the sizes required. Then, at runtime, when we\n   need to allocate a slot, just look at the smallest sized list. If there's any\n   available slots, assign that one. If not, then check the next larger of the\n   slot types. Keep going until you find a valid slot. When de-allocating, add\n   the slot to the relevant list. If you're allocating a slot that's larger than\n   needed, test and see if you can slice off a slot at the end and add that to\n   a small slot list. If not, that's fine, just bundle it with the task. oh well\n\n-- if you need to allocate something large but there's no available slots for it\n   then try and coalesce contiguous slots if you can. If you can't, then allocate\n   more memory and append the newly created (malloc'd or whatever) slots to the\n   required lists.\n\n-- do you see any edge cases I didn't consider? Does this design make sense?",
    "newString":"## Allocation strategy: size-class free lists with coalescing fallback\n\nThe slot store uses a segregated free-list allocator. The map is\nanalyzed at compile time to enumerate every distinct slot size the\ngraph will need (each call box declares its output slot size; each\nqueued-input ring declares its total size from cell capacity × queue\ndepth). The allocator builds one free list per distinct size class.\n\n### The lists\nEach size class is an array (or linked list) of free slots of exactly\nthat size. At startup, each list is pre-populated with enough slots\nto cover the static box count for that size. Lists grow during the\nrun if demand exceeds the pre-allocation.\n\nEach list has its own mutex — allocation and deallocation in different\nsize classes never contend with each other.\n\n### Allocation\nGiven a request for size N bytes:\n1. Find the smallest size class with `class_size ≥ N`.\n2. If that class has a free slot, pop it. Done.\n3. Otherwise, try the next larger size class. Repeat.\n4. If a larger class hits, the slot is oversized for the request.\n   Try to slice the unused tail into a residual slot. If the residual\n   is at least as large as the smallest size class, push it onto that\n   class's list. Otherwise skip the slice — oversize the allocation\n   and live with the waste until the slot is freed.\n5. If no size class has a free slot, attempt to coalesce: walk the\n   address-ordered chunk list looking for adjacent free chunks that\n   together meet the requested size. If found, merge them and return\n   the combined chunk.\n6. If coalescing fails, grow the region (see \"Growth\" below) and\n   append the new slots to the appropriate lists. Then try again.\n\n### Deallocation\nWhen refcount drops to zero, the slot is pushed onto its size class's\nfree list. Coalescing is not eager — it happens only when allocation\nfails to find a fit.\n\n### Coalescing requires a physical-order chunk list\nCoalescing needs to know which chunks are physically adjacent in the\nregion. The size-class free lists don't carry that information. The\nallocator therefore maintains an address-ordered doubly-linked list of\nall chunks (free and allocated), separate from the per-size-class\nlists. When coalescing runs, it walks this physical-order list looking\nfor runs of free chunks.\n\n### Growth\nWhen all lists are exhausted and coalescing cannot satisfy a request,\nthe allocator grows. For now, growth uses `malloc` to allocate a new\nchunk in the process heap, divides it into slots, and appends them to\nthe relevant size-class lists. This is fine as long as no spec needs\ndirect child-process access to slot memory — currently Bash goes\nthrough a socket, so cross-process visibility is not a hard\nrequirement.\n\nIf a future spec needs cross-process slot access, swap `malloc` for\n`ftruncate(shm_fd, new_size)` + `mremap`, which extends the original\nshm-backed region while preserving its visibility from anyone who has\nopened the same shm name.\n\n### Variable-size box outputs\nEach box declares its maximum output size at compile time. The\nallocator uses that as the slot's class. If the actual output exceeds\nthe declared maximum, that is an error — the program aborts (per the\nhard-crash policy in issue 303).\n\n### Why this design\n- Compile-time enumeration makes every common allocation a single\n  pop from a list. No size-comparison loops, no walks of free space.\n- Slicing residuals cannot fragment beyond the granularity of the\n  smallest declared size class, since smaller residuals are simply\n  not split.\n- Coalescing is the safety valve for unusual allocation patterns,\n  and it costs nothing on the common path.\n- Growth is rare — if pre-allocation matches static demand, it never\n  fires.",

        "text":"**On the design**: yes, the size-class free-list with growth is sound — it's the same family as jemalloc / tcmalloc. A few edge cases worth recording:\n\n- **Cross-process growth**: if any spec ever needs to access slots directly from a child process (today only Bash does, and it goes through a socket so it doesn't), heap `malloc` won't be visible there. The shm-safe equivalent is `ftruncate(fd, new_size)` + `mremap`. For now Bash uses sockets, so plain `malloc` is fine — but flag the assumption.\n- **Coalescing needs a physical-order chunk list** (a doubly-linked list of all chunks, free or used, in address order). Per-size-class lists don't tell you which chunks are physically adjacent. Adds bookkeeping but is standard.\n- **Residual slicing** is only worth it if the residual ≥ the smallest size class. Otherwise you make a sub-minimum dead chunk that can never be used. Easy guard: if `residual < smallest_class`, skip the split and oversize the allocation (your \"bundle it with the task\" path).\n- **Variable-size outputs**: boxes must declare a max output size at compile time so we know which class the slot belongs to. Outputs that exceed that are an error (or trigger growth into a larger class).\n- **Per-class mutex**: each size-class free list needs its own lock, since allocations and frees can happen on any thread concurrently.\n- **Size-class granularity**: do we use exact-size classes (one per distinct size in the map) or power-of-2 buckets? Exact gives perfect fit but possibly many classes; power-of-2 caps the count but wastes some bytes per slot. With the compile-time analysis you described, exact classes are tractable since the set is known.\n\nUpdating 302 now and then writing 304:"

        "input":{
          "content":"# 304 — Task dispatch layer (C, replaces synchronous executor)\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nThe synchronous executor at `src/004-executor.lua` walks the graph in\ndependency order, calling each box's driver, capturing stdout, decoding\nJSON, and propagating values to downstream boxes. Single-threaded,\nblocking, runs in Lua coroutines.\n\n## Concept\n\nThe task dispatch layer is the C component that runs inside each pool\nworker. The pool calls a single C action — `dispatch_action` — per\ntask. That action is the one place in the runtime that:\n\n- Reads from and writes to slots\n- Calls `lang_spec->invoke`\n- Manages slot refcounts on consumed inputs\n- Implements iterator routing and self-rescheduling\n- Implements comparator branch routing\n- Spawns successor tasks when its box's outputs feed downstream boxes\n\nThere is no Lua-level executor in the phase 3 path. `004-executor.lua`\nis replaced wholesale.\n\n## Task struct\n\nThe dispatch layer's per-task state lives in a `dispatch_task_t`\nallocated when the task is submitted to the pool:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    int           box_id;          // index into the graph's box array\n    int           n_inputs;\n    slot_id_t    *input_slots;     // array of n_inputs slot IDs\n    slot_id_t     output_slot;     // single output slot\n    int           counter;         // iterator only; ignored otherwise\n} dispatch_task_t;\n```\n\nThe pool passes this pointer to the action via `task_ctx_t.args`.\nMultiple successor invocations of an iterator produce multiple\n`dispatch_task_t`s (with new counter values), each with its own output\nslot.\n\n## The dispatch action\n\n```c\naction_result_t dispatch_action(task_ctx_t *ctx, void *arg);\n```\n\nPhases, in order:\n\n### 1. Check inputs\nWalk `input_slots`. For each, ask the slot store whether a value is\navailable (1-cell: `tail > head` and the cell is filled; queued: same\ncondition).\n\nIf any input is unavailable: set `ctx->block_on` to a wait handle for\nthat slot and return `ACT_BLOCK`. The pool parks the task on that\nslot's wait list. When a producer pushes, the slot store wakes the\nparked tasks; the pool re-runs the action from the top.\n\n### 2. Read inputs into byte buffers\nFor each input:\n- 1-cell slot: `slot_peek` into the input buffer. The slot is not\n  drained — fan-out consumers all peek.\n- Queued slot: `slot_pop` into the input buffer. The cell is drained.\n\nBuffer ownership: the action allocates a small array of `(void*,\nint)` pairs on the stack, with each pointer aimed at a stack-allocated\nor heap-allocated buffer sized to the slot's cell capacity. Heap is\nused only when capacity exceeds a stack limit (e.g. 4 KB).\n\n### 3. Iterator counter prepending\nIf the box is an iterator (has `iterator_outputs` in the graph), the\ncounter is prepended to the input array as input position 0 before\ncalling `invoke`. The language spec sees one extra argument; it does\nnot know it is the counter. (This matches the contract in issue 221.)\n\n### 4. Invoke\nLook up the box's language spec by its `lang` field. Find the worker's\nlanguage handle in `current_worker->handles[lang_idx]`. Call\n`lang->invoke` with the input buffers, an output buffer, and an\noutput-size pointer. Nonzero return → abort the program (issue 303).\n\n### 5. Write output\n`slot_push(output_slot, output_buf, output_size)`. The slot store\nperforms the memory barrier and walks the slot's wait list to wake\nany consumers parked on this slot.\n\n### 6. Unref consumed inputs\nFor each 1-cell input slot, call `slot_unref`. The slot is freed when\nits refcount drops to zero (which happens when the last fan-out\nconsumer reads it). Queued-input slots are not unref'd here — those\nslots are held for the life of the consumer task across many\ninvocations.\n\n### 7. Post-action: routing\nTwo cases:\n\n- **Comparator** (issue 108): the output is a `(value, branch)` pair\n  where `branch` is one of `lt` / `eq` / `gt`. The dispatch layer\n  fires only the connection whose `from_branch` matches.\n- **Iterator** (issue 221): fire only the connection whose\n  `from_branch` matches `iterator_outputs[counter]`. Then increment\n  `counter` mod `n_iter_outputs` and spawn a successor\n  `dispatch_task_t` with the same `input_slots` and the new counter.\n  The successor immediately blocks on the input queue if it is\n  empty; otherwise it picks up the next queued value.\n\nPlain call boxes fire all outgoing connections unconditionally.\n\n\"Firing\" a connection means submitting a `dispatch_task_t` for the\ndownstream box, with `input_slots[i]` set to the upstream's\n`output_slot` for the wired position. Refcount on the upstream slot\nis incremented per fan-out wire at firing time.\n\n### 8. Return ACT_DONE\nThe action completes. The pool decrements the active-task counter\n(issue 301). If the counter reaches zero and the runner is waiting,\nthe run ends.\n\n## Initial submission\n\nThe pool runner walks the graph at startup to find entry-point boxes\n— boxes with no inputs, or with inputs that come only from `data`\nboxes (literal values). It builds and submits a `dispatch_task_t` per\nentry box. From that point, all further submissions come from\npost-action firing.\n\n## Comparator vs iterator vs plain call\n\nThree box modes drive routing differently:\n\n| Mode        | Output kind        | Routing behavior                              |\n|-------------|--------------------|-----------------------------------------------|\n| Plain call  | single value       | fire all outgoing connections                 |\n| Comparator  | (value, lt/eq/gt)  | fire connections matching the branch tag      |\n| Iterator    | single value + counter | fire connection matching counter slot, then re-spawn |\n\nThe dispatch action checks the box's mode after invoke and dispatches\ninto the appropriate routing helper. Three small functions, not a\nsingle switch, to keep each mode's logic isolated.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Output buffer sizing: stack-allocated up to a fixed cap, then heap\n  for larger. What is the cap? 4 KB is generous for typical strings.\n- Queued-input slot lifetime: the consumer holds the only ref. When\n  does the consumer drop the ref? When its iterator parks for the\n  last time? When the run ends? Probably \"when no upstream producers\n  remain alive\" — but detecting that requires tracking producer\n  liveness. Defer until the iterator implementation is being written.\n- Comparator output encoding: the comparator returns a value plus a\n  branch tag. How is the tag encoded in the slot's bytes? Options:\n  (a) prepend a 1-byte tag, (b) encode in a struct the dispatch layer\n  unpacks, (c) the comparator's spec writes both into the slot in a\n  defined format. Decision deferred — depends on whether the\n  language spec or the dispatch layer is responsible for the\n  comparator semantics.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Define `dispatch_task_t` and the `dispatch_action` skeleton.\n2. Implement phase 1 (input check + ACT_BLOCK).\n3. Implement phase 2 (input read into buffers).\n4. Implement phase 4 (invoke); skip iterator counter for now.\n5. Implement phase 5 (output write).\n6. Implement phase 6 (unref consumed 1-cell inputs).\n7. Test an iterator map.\n11. Wire up entry-box initial submission in the pool runner.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — synchronous executor that this layer replaces\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool that runs this action\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — slot API used here\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — `invoke` interface called here\n- `issues/221-iterator-box.md` — iterator routing and self-rescheduling\n- `issues/completed/108-branch-box-and-predicate-routing.md` — comparator routing\n- `issues/213-queued-inputs-and-task-model.md` — queued-input slot semantics\n",

    "content":"# 304 — Task dispatch layer (C, replaces synchronous executor)\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nThe synchronous executor at `src/004-executor.lua` walks the graph in\ndependency order, calling each box's driver, capturing stdout, decoding\nJSON, and propagating values to downstream boxes. Single-threaded,\nblocking, runs in Lua coroutines.\n\n## Concept\n\nThe task dispatch layer is the C component that runs inside each pool\nworker. The pool calls a single C action — `dispatch_action` — per\ntask. That action is the one place in the runtime that:\n\n- Reads from and writes to slots\n- Calls `lang_spec->invoke`\n- Manages slot refcounts on consumed inputs\n- Implements iterator routing and self-rescheduling\n- Implements comparator branch routing\n- Spawns successor tasks when its box's outputs feed downstream boxes\n\nThere is no Lua-level executor in the phase 3 path. `004-executor.lua`\nis replaced wholesale.\n\n## Task struct\n\nThe dispatch layer's per-task state lives in a `dispatch_task_t`\nallocated when the task is submitted to the pool:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    int           box_id;          // index into the graph's box array\n    int           n_inputs;\n    slot_id_t    *input_slots;     // array of n_inputs slot IDs\n    slot_id_t     output_slot;     // single output slot\n    int           counter;         // iterator only; ignored otherwise\n} dispatch_task_t;\n```\n\nThe pool passes this pointer to the action via `task_ctx_t.args`.\nMultiple successor invocations of an iterator produce multiple\n`dispatch_task_t`s (with new counter values), each with its own output\nslot.\n\n## The dispatch action\n\n```c\naction_result_t dispatch_action(task_ctx_t *ctx, void *arg);\n```\n\nPhases, in order:\n\n### 1. Check inputs\nWalk `input_slots`. For each, ask the slot store whether a value is\navailable (1-cell: `tail > head` and the cell is filled; queued: same\ncondition).\n\nIf any input is unavailable: set `ctx->block_on` to a wait handle for\nthat slot and return `ACT_BLOCK`. The pool parks the task on that\nslot's wait list. When a producer pushes, the slot store wakes the\nparked tasks; the pool re-runs the action from the top.\n\n### 2. Read inputs into byte buffers\nFor each input:\n- 1-cell slot: `slot_peek` into the input buffer. The slot is not\n  drained — fan-out consumers all peek.\n- Queued slot: `slot_pop` into the input buffer. The cell is drained.\n\nBuffer ownership: the action allocates a small array of `(void*,\nint)` pairs on the stack, with each pointer aimed at a stack-allocated\nor heap-allocated buffer sized to the slot's cell capacity. Heap is\nused only when capacity exceeds a stack limit (e.g. 4 KB).\n\n### 3. Iterator counter prepending\nIf the box is an iterator (has `iterator_outputs` in the graph), the\ncounter is prepended to the input array as input position 0 before\ncalling `invoke`. The language spec sees one extra argument; it does\nnot know it is the counter. (This matches the contract in issue 221.)\n\n### 4. Invoke\nLook up the box's language spec by its `lang` field. Find the worker's\nlanguage handle in `current_worker->handles[lang_idx]`. Call\n`lang->invoke` with the input buffers, an output buffer, and an\noutput-size pointer. Nonzero return → abort the program (issue 303).\n\n### 5. Write output\n`slot_push(output_slot, output_buf, output_size)`. The slot store\nperforms the memory barrier and walks the slot's wait list to wake\nany consumers parked on this slot.\n\n### 6. Unref consumed inputs\nFor each 1-cell input slot, call `slot_unref`. The slot is freed when\nits refcount drops to zero (which happens when the last fan-out\nconsumer reads it). Queued-input slots are not unref'd here — those\nslots are held for the life of the consumer task across many\ninvocations.\n\n### 7. Post-action: routing\nTwo cases:\n\n- **Comparator** (issue 108): the output is a `(value, branch)` pair\n  where `branch` is one of `lt` / `eq` / `gt`. The dispatch layer\n  fires only the connection whose `from_branch` matches.\n- **Iterator** (issue 221): fire only the connection whose\n  `from_branch` matches `iterator_outputs[counter]`. Then increment\n  `counter` mod `n_iter_outputs` and spawn a successor\n  `dispatch_task_t` with the same `input_slots` and the new counter.\n  The successor immediately blocks on the input queue if it is\n  empty; otherwise it picks up the next queued value.\n\nPlain call boxes fire all outgoing connections unconditionally.\n\n\"Firing\" a connection means submitting a `dispatch_task_t` for the\ndownstream box, with `input_slots[i]` set to the upstream's\n`output_slot` for the wired position. Refcount on the upstream slot\nis incremented per fan-out wire at firing time.\n\n### 8. Return ACT_DONE\nThe action completes. The pool decrements the active-task counter\n(issue 301). If the counter reaches zero and the runner is waiting,\nthe run ends.\n\n## Initial submission\n\nThe pool runner walks the graph at startup to find entry-point boxes\n— boxes with no inputs, or with inputs that come only from `data`\nboxes (literal values). It builds and submits a `dispatch_task_t` per\nentry box. From that point, all further submissions come from\npost-action firing.\n\n## Comparator vs iterator vs plain call\n\nThree box modes drive routing differently:\n\n| Mode        | Output kind        | Routing behavior                              |\n|-------------|--------------------|-----------------------------------------------|\n| Plain call  | single value       | fire all outgoing connections                 |\n| Comparator  | (value, lt/eq/gt)  | fire connections matching the branch tag      |\n| Iterator    | single value + counter | fire connection matching counter slot, then re-spawn |\n\nThe dispatch action checks the box's mode after invoke and dispatches\ninto the appropriate routing helper. Three small functions, not a\nsingle switch, to keep each mode's logic isolated.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Output buffer sizing: stack-allocated up to a fixed cap, then heap\n  for larger. What is the cap? 4 KB is generous for typical strings.\n- Queued-input slot lifetime: the consumer holds the only ref. When\n  does the consumer drop the ref? When its iterator parks for the\n  last time? When the run ends? Probably \"when no upstream producers\n  remain alive\" — but detecting that requires tracking producer\n  liveness. Defer until the iterator implementation is being written.\n- Comparator output encoding: the comparator returns a value plus a\n  branch tag. How is the tag encoded in the slot's bytes? Options:\n  (a) prepend a 1-byte tag, (b) encode in a struct the dispatch layer\n  unpacks, (c) the comparator's spec writes both into the slot in a\n  defined format. Decision deferred — depends on whether the\n  language spec or the dispatch layer is responsible for the\n  comparator semantics.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Define `dispatch_task_t` and the `dispatch_action` skeleton.\n2. Implement phase 1 (input check + ACT_BLOCK).\n3. Implement phase 2 (input read into buffers).\n4. Implement phase 4 (invoke); skip iterator counter for now.\n5. Implement phase 5 (output write).\n6. Implement phase 6 (unref consumed 1-cell inputs).\n7. Smoke test: `hello` map (one box, no routing) end-to-end through\n   the pool. Assert the output slot contains the expected value.\n8. Implement plain-call fan-out firing (phase 7 path 1).\n9. Implement comparator branch routing (phase 7 path 2). Test\n   `branch-test` map.\n10. Implement iterator counter prepending (phase 3) and self-respawn\n    (phase 7 path 3). Test an iterator map.\n11. Wire up entry-box initial submission in the pool runner.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — synchronous executor that this layer replaces\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool that runs this action\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — slot API used here\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — `invoke` interface called here\n- `issues/221-iterator-box.md` — iterator routing and self-rescheduling\n- `issues/completed/108-branch-box-and-predicate-routing.md` — comparator routing\n- `issues/213-queued-inputs-and-task-model.md` — queued-input slot semantics\n"

Added the edge-case notes inline:\n- compile-time enumeration of distinct sizes drives the lists\n- per-class mutex\n- residual slicing only if residual ≥ smallest class\n- coalescing requires a separate address-ordered chunk list\n- growth via `malloc` for now, with the `ftruncate` + `mremap` swap-in noted for if cross-process slot access ever becomes a requirement\n- variable-output-size boxes must declare a max at compile time; overflow aborts\n\n**304 — task dispatch layer** is the C action that runs in each pool worker. Eight phases per task: check inputs → read inputs → prepend iterator counter → invoke → write output → unref → route → done. Three routing modes (plain call, comparator, iterator) handled by separate helpers, not a switch. Initial submission is by the pool runner walking entry-point boxes at startup; everything after that is firing from post-action.\n\nThree open questions called out:\n- output buffer stack/heap cap (4 KB suggested)\n- when the consumer drops its ref on a queued-input slot\n- how the comparator's `(value, branch)` pair is encoded into a slot's bytes (1-byte tag prefix? struct? language-spec responsibility?)\n\nReady for the next pass of corrections."
      }]
