    "snippet":"1\t# 302 — Per-task slot store with wire-held references\n2\t\n3\t## Status\n4\topen\n5\t\n6\t## Current behavior\n7\tWire values are passed through stdout pipes and transient strings. Values\n8\thave no addressable location, no reference count, and no cross-language\n9\taccessibility. Each value vanishes once the pipe is drained.\n10\t\n11\t## Concept\n12\t\n13\t### Slots belong to tasks, not wires\n14\tA **slot** is the memory region that holds a task's output. Slots are\n15\tcreated when tasks are created. A box that runs once produces one slot;\n16\ta box that runs ten times (an iterator) produces ten slots, one per\n17\tinvocation. Slots live in shared memory so any language runtime can read\n18\tor write them without copying.\n19\t\n20\tA **wire** is the relationship between two tasks: it says \"task B's input\n21\tN reads from task A's output M.\" Wires hold references to slots. They\n22\tare the timing mechanism — a task does not become ready until every\n23\tinput wire reports its source slot is filled. They are also the lifetime\n24\tmechanism — a slot is freed only after every wire that referenced it has\n25\treleased it.\n26\t\n27\tThe wire is the arbiter. The slot is just memory.\n28\t\n29\t### All slots are ring buffers\n30\tThere is one slot type. It is a ring buffer of `n_cells` cells, each\n31\tof `cell_capacity` bytes. The `n_cells = 1` case is the trivial ring\n32\tholding a single value; the `n_cells = N` case is a queue.\n33\t\n34\tA single-output box allocates a 1-cell ring. The producer pushes once,\n35\tconsumers read the head. An iterator that produces 10 outputs over its\n36\tlifetime allocates 10 separate 1-cell rings (one per invocation, per\n37\tthe box-not-wire-is-the-slot model below).\n38\t\n39\tA box with a queued input allocates a multi-cell ring as the input's\n40\tholding pen — many upstream wires push into it, the consumer drains it\n41\tin arrival order.\n42\t\n43\tSame data structure, same API, same per-slot lock. The dispatch layer\n44\tparameterizes `n_cells` based on whether the slot is being used for\n45\tfan-out or fan-in.\n46\t\n47\t### Asynchrony\n48\tThe store is fully asynchronous. Slots are allocated, filled, read, and\n49\tfreed at any time, on any thread, with no global lock. Synchronization\n50\tis per-slot. There is no central allocator-wide mutex.\n51\t\n52\t## Slot layout\n53\t\n54\tEach slot is a header followed by `n_cells` cells, each `cell_capacity`\n55\tbytes. The header tracks ring-buffer state and lifetime:\n56\t\n57\t```\n58\tSlot header\n59\tOffset  Size  Field\n60\t------  ----  -----\n61\t0       4     refcount        (atomic int32; lifetime counter)\n62\t4       4     cell_capacity   (bytes per cell, set at allocation)\n63\t8       4     n_cells         (ring size, set at allocation; 1 for single-value)\n64\t12      4     head            (read index, mod n_cells)\n65\t16      4     tail            (write index, mod n_cells; cells_filled = tail - head)\n66\t20      1     touched         (per-slot lock: 0=free, 1=another thread mutating)\n67\t21      3     _pad\n68\t24      …     cells           (n_cells * (4-byte size + cell_capacity bytes))\n69\t```\n70\t\n71\tEach cell stores a 4-byte filled-size followed by `cell_capacity`\n72\tbytes of value data. Cells have wildly different capacities across\n73\tslots — capacity is per-slot, not global. The C convention of passing\n74\tsizes alongside arrays applies: the task that allocates a slot knows\n75\thow big it needs the cells.\n76\t\n77\t`touched` is a single-byte flag toggled around any header mutation\n78\t(push, pop, refcount changes). A reader that finds `touched == 1`\n79\tspins until it clears. This is the simplest possible per-slot lock —\n80\tif contention proves to matter, replace with a proper mutex without\n81\tchanging the API.\n82\t\n83\tWrites to a cell complete with a memory barrier before `tail` is\n84\tadvanced, so a reader that observes `head < tail` is guaranteed to\n85\tsee the complete value at the head cell.\n86\t\n87\t## Reference counting protocol\n88\t\n89\tWhen a task is submitted, the dispatch layer:\n90\t1. Allocates the task's output slot(s) with the requested capacity.\n91\t2. For each wire reading from the slot, calls `slot_ref` on the slot.\n92\t   The wire holds that reference for as long as it might still need to\n93\t   read.\n94\t3. When the consumer task finishes reading, it calls `slot_unref` on\n95\t   the wire's slot. The wire is then dead.\n96\t4. When the refcount drops to zero, the task that performed the final\n97\t   unref clears the slot (frees the backing memory or marks it\n98\t   reusable).\n99\t\n100\tNo central garbage collector. Clearing is deterministic — last unref\n101\tdoes the work.\n102\t\n103\t## Backing store\n104\t\n105\tSlots live in shared memory created with `shm_open` + `mmap`. The\n106\tshared memory object is named `/soramech-<run-id>`. Allocation inside\n107\tthe region is handled by a per-run allocator (a simple bump allocator\n108\tor a small free-list allocator — start with bump, add free-list when\n109\tslot reuse becomes worth it).\n110\t\n111\tAny language runtime that opens the same shared memory name and maps it\n112\tgets access to the same physical memory. For languages that cannot call\n113\tPOSIX directly (e.g. Bash), the language runtime spec (issue 303) is\n114\tresponsible for proxying slot reads and writes through the language's\n115\truntime server.\n116\t\n117\tSynchronization for blocked tasks (waiting on an empty slot) is handled\n118\tby the dispatch layer (issue 304) — typically a wait list per slot.\n119\tProducers signal waiters when they flip `filled`.\n120\t\n121\t## Slot creation\n122\t\n123\tSlot creation happens inside the dispatch layer at task submission. The\n124\tcaller specifies the cell capacity (bytes per value) and the ring size\n125\t(number of cells, 1 for single-value):\n126\t\n127\t```c\n128\tslot_id_t slot_alloc(slot_store_t *store, int cell_capacity, int n_cells);\n129\t```\n130\t\n131\tThe slot is created with `refcount = 0`, `head = tail = 0`. The\n132\tdispatch layer then increments the refcount once per consumer (one ref\n133\tper fan-out wire for a 1-cell slot; one ref for the consumer task on a\n134\tqueued-input slot) before the task is exposed.\n135\t\n136\t## C API surface\n137\t\n138\t```c\n139\tslot_id_t slot_alloc (slot_store_t *s, int cell_capacity, int n_cells);\n140\tvoid      slot_push  (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, const void *data, int size);\n141\tint       slot_peek  (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size); // non-destructive: read head, leave it\n142\tint       slot_pop   (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size); // destructive: read head, advance head\n143\tvoid      slot_wait  (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id); // blocks until tail > head\n144\tvoid      slot_ref   (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id);\n145\tvoid      slot_unref (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id); // frees backing memory when refcount → 0\n146\t```\n147\t\n148\tSingle-value (1-cell) slot use: producer `push` once, each consumer\n149\t`peek` once, then `unref`. Cells are not popped — fan-out consumers\n150\tall read the same value, and the slot is freed when the last consumer\n151\tunrefs.\n152\t\n153\tQueued-input (N-cell) slot use: producers `push` repeatedly, the\n154\tconsumer `pop`s in arrival order. The consumer holds the only ref.\n155\tWhen the consumer task is done with its queue, it `unref`s and the\n156\tslot is freed.\n157\t\n158\t## Submission timing\n159\t\n160\tThe dispatch layer builds the task struct as soon as the graph asks\n161\tfor it — output slots allocated, all known data filled in, input wire\n162\treferences attached. It is then submitted directly to the pool. The\n163\tpool's existing block-and-wake machinery handles the rest:\n164\t\n165\t- If any input slots are unfilled at the moment of submission, the\n166\t  dispatch action immediately `ACT_BLOCK`s on the first unfilled\n167\t  input. The pool parks the task on that slot's wait list.\n168\t- When the upstream producer pushes, it walks the wait list and wakes\n169\t  the parked tasks. The action re-runs from the top, checks the next\n170\t  input, blocks again if needed.\n171\t- When all inputs are present, the action proceeds to invoke the box.\n172\t\n173\tThere is no separate \"blocked tasks\" set held by the dispatch layer.\n174\tThe pool is the only thing that tracks blocked tasks. This avoids\n175\tduplicating the wait-list machinery the pool already has.\n176\t\n\n... [147 lines truncated] ...",

    "snippet":"1\t# 304 — Task dispatch layer (C, replaces synchronous executor)\n2\t\n3\t## Status\n4\topen\n5\t\n6\t## Current behavior\n7\tThe synchronous executor at `src/004-executor.lua` walks the graph in\n8\tdependency order, calling each box's driver, capturing stdout, decoding\n9\tJSON, and propagating values to downstream boxes. Single-threaded,\n10\tblocking, runs in Lua coroutines.\n11\t\n12\t## Concept\n13\t\n14\tThe task dispatch layer is the C component that runs inside each pool\n15\tworker. The pool calls a single C action — `dispatch_action` — per\n16\ttask. That action is the one place in the runtime that:\n17\t\n18\t- Reads from and writes to slots\n19\t- Calls `lang_spec->invoke`\n20\t- Manages slot refcounts on consumed inputs\n21\t- Implements iterator routing and self-rescheduling\n22\t- Implements comparator branch routing\n23\t- Spawns successor tasks when its box's outputs feed downstream boxes\n24\t\n25\tThere is no Lua-level executor in the phase 3 path. `004-executor.lua`\n26\tis replaced wholesale.\n27\t\n28\t## Task struct\n29\t\n30\tThe dispatch layer's per-task state lives in a `dispatch_task_t`\n31\tallocated when the task is submitted to the pool:\n32\t\n33\t```c\n34\ttypedef struct {\n35\t    int           box_id;          // index into the graph's box array\n36\t    int           n_inputs;\n37\t    slot_id_t    *input_slots;     // array of n_inputs slot IDs\n38\t    slot_id_t     output_slot;     // single output slot\n39\t    int           counter;         // iterator only; ignored otherwise\n40\t} dispatch_task_t;\n41\t```\n42\t\n43\tThe pool passes this pointer to the action via `task_ctx_t.args`.\n44\tMultiple successor invocations of an iterator produce multiple\n45\t`dispatch_task_t`s (with new counter values), each with its own output\n46\tslot.\n47\t\n48\t## The dispatch action\n49\t\n50\t```c\n51\taction_result_t dispatch_action(task_ctx_t *ctx, void *arg);\n52\t```\n53\t\n54\tPhases, in order:\n55\t\n56\t### 1. Check inputs\n57\tWalk `input_slots`. For each, ask the slot store whether a value is\n58\tavailable (1-cell: `tail > head` and the cell is filled; queued: same\n59\tcondition).\n60\t\n61\tIf any input is unavailable: set `ctx->block_on` to a wait handle for\n62\tthat slot and return `ACT_BLOCK`. The pool parks the task on that\n63\tslot's wait list. When a producer pushes, the slot store wakes the\n64\tparked tasks; the pool re-runs the action from the top.\n65\t\n66\t-- question... is the waiting list attached to the wire, the blocking box, or\n67\t   the blocked box? I know the blocking box is the one that wakes it up, but,\n68\t   where is the task parked?\n69\t\n70\t### 2. Read inputs into byte buffers\n71\tFor each input:\n72\t- 1-cell slot: `slot_peek` into the input buffer. The slot is not\n73\t  drained — fan-out consumers all peek.\n74\t- Queued slot: `slot_pop` into the input buffer. The cell is drained.\n75\t\n76\tBuffer ownership: the action allocates a small array of `(void*,\n77\tint)` pairs on the stack, with each pointer aimed at a stack-allocated\n78\tor heap-allocated buffer sized to the slot's cell capacity. Heap is\n79\tused only when capacity exceeds a stack limit (e.g. 4 KB).\n80\t\n81\t### 3. Iterator counter prepending\n82\tIf the box is an iterator (has `iterator_outputs` in the graph), the\n83\tcounter is prepended to the input array as input position 0 before\n84\tcalling `invoke`. The language spec sees one extra argument; it does\n85\tnot know it is the counter. (This matches the contract in issue 221.)\n86\t\n87\t-- hold on, does the language spec even need to see the counter at all? the\n88\t   iteration I think can be entirely confined to the task dispatch layer. Same\n89\t   for the comparison functionality.\n90\t\n91\t### 4. Invoke\n92\tLook up the box's language spec by its `lang` field. Find the worker's\n93\tlanguage handle in `current_worker->handles[lang_idx]`. Call\n94\t`lang->invoke` with the input buffers, an output buffer, and an\n95\toutput-size pointer. Nonzero return → abort the program (issue 303).\n96\t\n97\t-- question... wouldn't it return the values that the box function returns? if\n98\t   the language spec is running a function... how would it get the values\n99\t   produced by that function back to the shared memory if not by returning them?\n100\t\n101\t### 5. Write output\n102\t`slot_push(output_slot, output_buf, output_size)`. The slot store\n103\tperforms the memory barrier and walks the slot's wait list to wake\n104\tany consumers parked on this slot.\n105\t\n106\t### 6. Unref consumed inputs\n107\tFor each 1-cell input slot, call `slot_unref`. The slot is freed when\n108\tits refcount drops to zero (which happens when the last fan-out\n109\tconsumer reads it). Queued-input slots are not unref'd here — those\n110\tslots are held for the life of the consumer task across many\n111\tinvocations.\n112\t\n113\t-- can you explain this part a bit more? What's a 1-cell input? I get the refcounting\n114\t   part, and the de-allocating when there's no references remaining. But, what\n115\t   does it mean to be held across many invocations?\n116\t\n117\t### 7. Post-action: routing\n118\tTwo cases:\n119\t\n120\t- **Comparator** (issue 108): the output is a `(value, branch)` pair\n121\t  where `branch` is one of `lt` / `eq` / `gt`. The dispatch layer\n122\t  fires only the connection whose `from_branch` matches.\n123\t- **Iterator** (issue 221): fire only the connection whose\n124\t  `from_branch` matches `iterator_outputs[counter]`. Then increment\n125\t  `counter` mod `n_iter_outputs` and spawn a successor\n126\t  `dispatch_task_t` with the same `input_slots` and the new counter.\n127\t  The successor immediately blocks on the input queue if it is\n128\t  empty; otherwise it picks up the next queued value.\n129\t\n130\tPlain call boxes fire all outgoing connections unconditionally.\n131\t\n132\t\"Firing\" a connection means submitting a `dispatch_task_t` for the\n133\tdownstream box, with `input_slots[i]` set to the upstream's\n134\t`output_slot` for the wired position. Refcount on the upstream slot\n135\tis incremented per fan-out wire at firing time.\n136\t\n137\t### 8. Return ACT_DONE\n138\tThe action completes. The pool decrements the active-task counter\n139\t(issue 301). If the counter reaches zero and the runner is waiting,\n140\tthe run ends.\n141\t\n142\t## Initial submission\n143\t\n144\tThe pool runner walks the graph at startup to find entry-point boxes\n145\t— boxes with no inputs, or with inputs that come only from `data`\n146\tboxes (literal values). It builds and submits a `dispatch_task_t` per\n147\tentry box. From that point, all further submissions come from\n148\tpost-action firing.\n149\t\n150\t## Comparator vs iterator vs plain call\n151\t\n152\tThree box modes drive routing differently:\n153\t\n154\t| Mode        | Output kind        | Routing behavior                              |\n155\t|-------------|--------------------|-----------------------------------------------|\n156\t| Plain call  | single value       | fire all outgoing connections                 |\n157\t| Comparator  | (value, lt/eq/gt)  | fire connections matching the branch tag      |\n158\t| Iterator    | single value + counter | fire connection matching counter slot, then re-spawn |\n159\t\n160\tThe dispatch action checks the box's mode after invoke and dispatches\n161\tinto the appropriate routing helper. Three small functions, not a\n162\tsingle switch, to keep each mode's logic isolated.\n163\t\n164\t## Open questions\n165\t\n166\t- Output buffer sizing: stack-allocated up to a fixed cap, then heap\n167\t  for larger. What is the cap? 4 KB is generous for typical strings.\n168\t\n169\t-- 4kb seems like a lot to me, on the stack? but sure. I don't know what a\n170\t   typical workload could be because there's no typical use-case defined.\n171\t   I think we should think of a way to handle large and small buffers both.\n172\t   we should be able to define them at runtime, programmatically and dynamically\n173\t\n174\t- Queued-input slot lifetime: the consumer holds the only ref. When\n175\t  does the consumer drop the ref? When its iterator parks for the\n176\t  last time? When the run ends? Probably \"when no upstream producers\n177\t  remain alive\" — but detecting that requires tracking producer\n178\t  liveness. Defer until the iterator implementation is being written.\n179\t\n180\t-- It drops the ref (and de-allocates if it's the only ref remaining) when the\n\n... [41 lines truncated] ...",

Coalescing is not eager — it happens only when allocation\nfails to find a fit.\n\n-- as part of the cleanup operation, we could have it coalesce with the nearby\n   contiguous slots. That might reduce the number of stalled allocations. I\n   think the part that blocks runtime execution will be the allocation process,\n   the cleanup is just something that a particular thread has to handle. The\n   thread has already done it's job during the cleanup step, so theoretically\n   nothing can be waiting on it. However, allocations might slow or block other\n   operations from proceeding. It's better to try and coalesce in the cleanup\n   step if we can, but only for contiguous slots.\n\n### Coalescing requires a physical-order chunk list\nCoalescing needs to know which chunks are physically adjacent in the\nregion. The size-class free lists don't carry that information. The\nallocator therefore maintains an address-ordered doubly-linked list of\nall chunks (free and allocated), separate from the per-size-class\nlists. When coalescing runs, it walks this physical-order list looking\nfor runs of free chunks.\n\n-- what if we just had an array (that grows in size if needed) that stores\n   the starting point of each chunk, and another array that stores the ending\n   point of each chunk, with the index shared between them? So index 1 in both\n   arrays would point to the start, and the end, of a particular chunk. That\n   way we don't have to walk through the doubly linked list, we can just go\n   directly to the correct index. Right? Am I missing anything? I think I might.\n\n### Growth\nWhen all lists are exhausted and coalescing cannot satisfy a request,\nthe allocator grows. For now, growth uses `malloc` to allocate a new\nchunk in the process heap, divides it into slots, and appends them to\nthe relevant size-class lists. This is fine as long as no spec needs\ndirect child-process access to slot memory — currently Bash goes\nthrough a socket, so cross-process visibility is not a hard\nrequirement.\n\nIf a future spec needs cross-process slot access, swap `malloc` for\n`ftruncate(shm_fd, new_size)` + `mremap`, which extends the original\nshm-backed region while preserving its visibility from anyone who has\nopened the same shm name.\n\n-- I think we should do the shared memory allocation actually, instead of the\n   c version. This memory we're talking about is necessarily shared across\n   threads, though, now that I think about it, do we need that shared memory at\n   all? If the C thread runner is passing to each language runner the values\n   instead of the memory locations, then... Do we really need that type of\n   memory? what do you think? We might be able to get away with just having the\n   C system manage the memory...\n\n### Variable-size box outputs\nEach box declares its maximum output size at compile time. The\nallocator uses that as the slot's class. If the actual output exceeds\nthe declared maximum, that is an error — the program aborts (per the\nhard-crash policy in issue 303).\n\n-- what if we instead just, accepted larger output sizes (like if we don't know\n   the size at compile time) and store them somewhere and keep a pointer to it.\n   then, we can split them into the shared memory somehow. Ideas about how to do\n   that? I don't think we should error because this is a pretty common case.\n\n### Why this design\n- Compile-time enumeration makes every common allocation a single\n  pop from a list. No size-comparison loops, no walks of free space.\n- Slicing residuals cannot fragment beyond the granularity of the\n  smallest declared size class, since smaller residuals are simply\n  not split.\n- Coalescing is the safety valve for unusual allocation patterns,\n  and it costs nothing on the common path.\n- Growth is rare — if pre-allocation matches static demand, it never\n  fires.\n\n## No type tags\n\nSlots store opaque bytes. The producer wrote N bytes; the consumer\nreads N bytes. What those bytes mean is the language spec's business\non each side, and the wire's metadata in the graph (issue 219's\ncompiler can check producer-output type vs consumer-input type at\nbuild time). The slot store does not interpret values — it does not\nneed to know if they are strings, numbers, JSON, images, or anything\nelse. Removed the type-tag field from the header for that reason.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. Write `src/slot-store.h` and `src/slot-store.c` — the C API above.\n2. Unit test single-value slots: thread A writes, thread B reads,\n   refcount decrements, slot freed when last ref dropped.\n3. Unit test ring-buffer slots: multiple producers push, single consumer\n   drains in order, no values lost or duplicated.\n4. Integrate into `src/008-pool-runner.c`: shared memory created at\n   startup, store handle passed to the dispatch layer.\n\n## Relevant files\n- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — pool entry point, owns the shared memory region\n- `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.h` — pool API (refcounting is complementary)\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — task dispatch reads/writes slots\n- `issues/213-queued-inputs-and-task-model.md` — queued input model that\n  ring-buffer slots implement\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — IPC options; shm_open + mmap is Option 2\n"
    }

        "text":"Let me address each comment, then update both files.\n\n**Answers to your questions:**\n\n**(302) Shared memory across processes — do we need it?** No, you're right. Plain heap memory, thread-shared, is sufficient. This drops `shm_open` / `mmap` / `mremap` entirely. Big simplification.\n\n**(302) Unknown / variable / variadic sizes (LLM context, arrays):** Two-tier model. Slots in size-class lists are fixed; variable-size payloads go in a separate large-value heap allocated on demand. The slot stores `(size, pointer)` pointing into the large-value heap. A box that emits a 4-MB LLM response: dispatch layer allocates 4 MB in the large-value heap, writes the bytes there, stores the handle in the slot. Consumer reads the handle, follows it to the bytes. Heap is reference-counted alongside the slot.\n\n**(302) Two-array chunk tracking vs doubly-linked list:** Your idea works but the arrays must stay sorted by start-address for O(1) neighbor lookup, which makes inserts/deletes O(N) without an index. The doubly-linked list gives O(1) splits/merges/neighbors at the cost of pointer chasing. For our scale (probably thousands of chunks, not millions), the linked list is simpler and fast enough. Arrays become the right answer if profiling shows linear chunk-walks dominate.\n\n**(302) Cleanup task post-grow/coalesce + eager coalesce on dealloc:** Both. Cheap on the dealloc path: check the chunk's two physical neighbors; if either is free, merge. The deferred cleanup task does broader sweeps after a grow event.\n\n**(304) Wait list location:** Attached to the slot. Producer pushes → slot's wake-waiters routine notifies the pool → pool re-runs the parked tasks.\n\n**(304) Counter / comparator in dispatch only:** Yes, agreed. Iterator routing and comparator routing live entirely in the dispatch layer. No spec involvement. Iterator boxes are pure-passthrough at the data level — copy input → output, route by counter, increment, re-spawn. Comparator boxes don't even need a function — read input, compare to threshold, route. This means iterators/comparators don't have a `ref`/`fn` (an update to issue 221).\n\n**(304) \"1-cell input\" terminology:** A slot with `n_cells = 1` (single value). \"Held across invocations\" was about queued-input slots persisting through iterator re-spawns — same slot, many pops over the iterator's lifetime. Will rephrase.\n\n**(304) Output buffer dynamic sizing:** Right call — heap-allocated to the slot's cell capacity, no fixed cap. For variable-size outputs, the spec writes into a buffer the dispatch layer reallocates if needed.\n\n**(304) Queued slot ref drop:** Got it — producers hold refs while alive; consumer holds a ref while consuming; slot freed when all drop. The refs themselves are how we track producer liveness.\n\nApplying edits now:"

        "input":{
          "new_string":"## Reference counting protocol\n\nEvery party that may still touch a slot holds a reference. The slot is\nfreed when the count reaches zero. The references themselves are how\nwe track liveness — there is no separate \"is this producer / consumer\nstill alive\" mechanism.\n\n### Single-output (1-cell) slot\n1. Task allocates its output slot with `refcount = 0`.\n2. For each fan-out wire reading from the slot, `slot_ref` is called.\n   The wire holds that reference until its consumer is done reading.\n3. After the consumer reads (peek), it calls `slot_unref`.\n4. When refcount reaches zero, the unrefing task frees the slot.\n\n### Queued (N-cell) slot\nThe consumer's input queue. Producers and the consumer all hold refs:\n1. The consumer task allocates the queue slot with one ref for itself.\n2. Each producer that may push into the queue increments the refcount\n   when it is constructed; the ref is dropped when that producer's\n   box function ends.\n3. The consumer drops its ref when its own box function ends (i.e.\n   when the iterator stops re-spawning because no more inputs are\n   coming).\n4. When the last ref drops, the queue is freed.\n\nThe producer-side ref is what makes \"no more inputs are coming\"\ndetectable: when the queue's refcount equals 1 (only the consumer\nholds it) and the queue is empty, no upstream task can push again,\nso the iterator's natural end-of-stream condition fires.\n\n### Wait list\nEach slot also owns a wait list — pointers to tasks parked on the\nslot waiting for a value. When a producer pushes, the slot walks the\nwait list and tells the pool to re-run those tasks. The wait list is\nattached to the slot, not to the producer or the consumer.\n\n## Backing store\n\nSlots are allocated from process heap memory. The slot store owns a\nper-run allocator (described under \"Allocation strategy\" below) that\nhands out memory chunks to slots. Plain `malloc`-class memory is\nsufficient — every worker thread in the process can read and write\nit, and no spec ever needs to access it from a child process.\n\nSynchronization within a slot uses the per-slot `touched` flag for\nheader mutations and a per-slot wait list (above) for blocked tasks.\nThere is no allocator-wide mutex on the read/write path; only the\nper-size-class free lists in the allocator have their own locks.",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md",
          "replace_all":false,
          "old_string":"## Reference counting protocol\n\nWhen a task is submitted, the dispatch layer:\n1. Allocates the task's output slot(s) with the requested capacity.\n2. For each wire reading from the slot, calls `slot_ref` on the slot.\n   The wire holds that reference for as long as it might still need to\n   read.\n3. When the consumer task finishes reading, it calls `slot_unref` on\n   the wire's slot. The wire is then dead.\n4. When the refcount drops to zero, the task that performed the final\n   unref clears the slot (frees the backing memory or marks it\n   reusable).\n\nNo central garbage collector. Clearing is deterministic — last unref\ndoes the work.\n\n## Backing store\n\nSlots live in shared memory created with `shm_open` + `mmap`. The\nshared memory object is named `/soramech-<run-id>`. Allocation inside\nthe region is handled by a per-run allocator (a simple bump allocator\nor a small free-list allocator — start with bump, add free-list when\nslot reuse becomes worth it).\n\nAny language runtime that opens the same shared memory name and maps it\ngets access to the same physical memory. For languages that cannot call\nPOSIX directly (e.g. Bash), the language runtime spec (issue 303) is\nresponsible for proxying slot reads and writes through the language's\nruntime server.\n\nSynchronization for blocked tasks (waiting on an empty slot) is handled\nby the dispatch layer (issue 304) — typically a wait list per slot.\nProducers signal waiters when they flip `filled`."
        },
        "id":"toolu_01HknHDViggMczydew6BLTtM"
      }]
  },

          "type":"direct"
        },
        "input":{
          "new_string":"6. If coalescing fails, grow the region (see \"Growth\" below) and\n   append the new slots to the appropriate lists. Then try again.\n7. After steps 5 or 6 complete, queue a deferred cleanup task on the\n   pool. Cleanup runs on a worker thread later and walks the\n   chunk list to opportunistically coalesce contiguous free chunks\n   into the largest possible chunks. Cleanup is best-effort — it\n   does not block any other thread. If memory fragments faster than\n   cleanup can keep up, the next allocation grows the heap; that's\n   fine.\n\n### Deallocation\nWhen refcount drops to zero, the slot is pushed onto its size class's\nfree list. The deallocator also performs a cheap eager-coalesce step:\ncheck the slot's two physical neighbors; if either is free, merge\nthem and push the combined chunk onto the appropriate size class.\nThis is O(1) given the doubly-linked chunk list (see below) and keeps\nsmall-scale fragmentation in check without needing the deferred\ncleanup task to run.",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md",
          "replace_all":false,
          "old_string":"6. If coalescing fails, grow the region (see \"Growth\" below) and\n   append the new slots to the appropriate lists. Then try again.\n\n   -- also, after allocation completes, in case 5 and 6 both, add a task to the\n      task list to try and clean up the allocated memory slots. Merge and\n      coalesce and all that, but instead of just looking for a valid slot, try\n      and coalesce them to the largest available slot if possible. It's okay if\n      it's a little fragmented. Over time, as tasks clear themselves, this\n      should resolve. If it doesn't, we'll just allocate more memory. It's okay.\n\n### Deallocation\nWhen refcount drops to zero, the slot is pushed onto its size class's\nfree list. Coalescing is not eager — it happens only when allocation\nfails to find a fit.\n\n-- as part of the cleanup operation, we could have it coalesce with the nearby\n   contiguous slots. That might reduce the number of stalled allocations. I\n   think the part that blocks runtime execution will be the allocation process,\n   the cleanup is just something that a particular thread has to handle. The\n   thread has already done it's job during the cleanup step, so theoretically\n   nothing can be waiting on it. However, allocations might slow or block other\n   operations from proceeding. It's better to try and coalesce in the cleanup\n   step if we can, but only for contiguous slots."
        },
        "id":"toolu_019rKWUBMu3CxoTphrZijFLf"
      }]

    "content":[{

          "type":"direct"
        },
        "input":{
          "new_string":"### Physical-order chunk list (for coalescing)\nCoalescing needs to know which chunks are physically adjacent in\nmemory. The size-class free lists don't carry that information.\n\nTwo viable representations:\n\n- **Doubly-linked list** of all chunks (free and allocated) in\n  address order. Splits and merges are O(1) given the chunk pointer.\n  Neighbor lookup is O(1). Pointer chasing is the cost.\n- **Two parallel arrays** (`start[i]`, `end[i]`) sorted by start\n  address. Lookup by binary search is O(log N), but inserts and\n  deletes are O(N) without an additional index. Cache-friendly to\n  scan.\n\nThe linked list is simpler and has the right asymptotic behavior for\nsplits/merges, which dominate. Start there. If profiling later shows\nlist traversal is hot, switch to the array form with an auxiliary\nindex — the API doesn't change.\n\n### Large-value heap (variable-size payloads)\n\nFor values whose size is not known at compile time — long LLM\nresponses, dynamically-sized arrays, anything where the upper bound\nis not a useful number to allocate — the slot does not hold the value\ndirectly. Instead, the slot holds a small fixed-size handle:\n\n```\n{ uint32_t size; uint32_t lvh_offset; }\n```\n\n`lvh_offset` points into a separate **large-value heap**, a\nplain `malloc`-backed region used only for variable-size payloads.\nWhen a box produces a 4 MB LLM response, the dispatch layer:\n1. Allocates 4 MB in the large-value heap.\n2. Writes the bytes there.\n3. Stores the handle (size = 4 MB, offset = …) in the slot.\n\nThe consumer reads the handle from the slot, follows the offset,\ncopies the bytes (or works with them in place). When the slot's\nrefcount hits zero, the slot's deallocator also frees the\nlarge-value-heap region.\n\nThe slot allocator is unchanged — it always sees fixed-size slots.\nThe two-tier approach keeps the hot path simple while still\nsupporting unbounded outputs.\n\nA box opts into large-value output by declaring its output as\n\"variable-size\" in the graph. Compile-time-known outputs use the\nfixed-size path with no indirection.\n\n### Growth\nWhen all size-class lists are exhausted and coalescing cannot satisfy\na request, the allocator grows by calling `malloc` for a new region,\ndividing it into slots, and appending them to the relevant size-class\nlists. Plain heap memory is fine — no spec needs cross-process access\nto slot memory.",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md",
          "replace_all":false,
          "old_string":"### Coalescing requires a physical-order chunk list\nCoalescing needs to know which chunks are physically adjacent in the\nregion. The size-class free lists don't carry that information. The\nallocator therefore maintains an address-ordered doubly-linked list of\nall chunks (free and allocated), separate from the per-size-class\nlists. When coalescing runs, it walks this physical-order list looking\nfor runs of free chunks.\n\n-- what if we just had an array (that grows in size if needed) that stores\n   the starting point of each chunk, and another array that stores the ending\n   point of each chunk, with the index shared between them? So index 1 in both\n   arrays would point to the start, and the end, of a particular chunk. That\n   way we don't have to walk through the doubly linked list, we can just go\n   directly to the correct index. Right? Am I missing anything? I think I might.\n\n### Growth\nWhen all lists are exhausted and coalescing cannot satisfy a request,\nthe allocator grows. For now, growth uses `malloc` to allocate a new\nchunk in the process heap, divides it into slots, and appends them to\nthe relevant size-class lists. This is fine as long as no spec needs\ndirect child-process access to slot memory — currently Bash goes\nthrough a socket, so cross-process visibility is not a hard\nrequirement.\n\nIf a future spec needs cross-process slot access, swap `malloc` for\n`ftruncate(shm_fd, new_size)` + `mremap`, which extends the original\nshm-backed region while preserving its visibility from anyone who has\nopened the same shm name.\n\n-- I think we should do the shared memory allocation actually, instead of the\n   c version. This memory we're talking about is necessarily shared across\n   threads, though, now that I think about it, do we need that shared memory at\n   all? If the C thread runner is passing to each language runner the values\n   instead of the memory locations, then... Do we really need that type of\n   memory? what do you think? We might be able to get away with just having the\n   C system manage the memory...\n\n### Variable-size box outputs\nEach box declares its maximum output size at compile time. The\nallocator uses that as the slot's class. If the actual output exceeds\nthe declared maximum, that is an error — the program aborts (per the\nhard-crash policy in issue 303).\n\n-- what if we instead just, accepted larger output sizes (like if we don't know\n   the size at compile time) and store them somewhere and keep a pointer to it.\n   then, we can split them into the shared memory somehow. Ideas about how to do\n   that? I don't think we should error because this is a pretty common case."
        },
        "id":"toolu_0143ax37iRgXrrxcHiPwLP52"
      }]
  },

    "originalFile":"# 304 — Task dispatch layer (C, replaces synchronous executor)\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nThe synchronous executor at `src/004-executor.lua` walks the graph in\ndependency order, calling each box's driver, capturing stdout, decoding\nJSON, and propagating values to downstream boxes. Single-threaded,\nblocking, runs in Lua coroutines.\n\n## Concept\n\nThe task dispatch layer is the C component that runs inside each pool\nworker. The pool calls a single C action — `dispatch_action` — per\ntask. That action is the one place in the runtime that:\n\n- Reads from and writes to slots\n- Calls `lang_spec->invoke`\n- Manages slot refcounts on consumed inputs\n- Implements iterator routing and self-rescheduling\n- Implements comparator branch routing\n- Spawns successor tasks when its box's outputs feed downstream boxes\n\nThere is no Lua-level executor in the phase 3 path. `004-executor.lua`\nis replaced wholesale.\n\n## Task struct\n\nThe dispatch layer's per-task state lives in a `dispatch_task_t`\nallocated when the task is submitted to the pool:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    int           box_id;          // index into the graph's box array\n    int           n_inputs;\n    slot_id_t    *input_slots;     // array of n_inputs slot IDs\n    slot_id_t     output_slot;     // single output slot\n    int           counter;         // iterator only; ignored otherwise\n} dispatch_task_t;\n```\n\nThe pool passes this pointer to the action via `task_ctx_t.args`.\nMultiple successor invocations of an iterator produce multiple\n`dispatch_task_t`s (with new counter values), each with its own output\nslot.\n\n## The dispatch action\n\n```c\naction_result_t dispatch_action(task_ctx_t *ctx, void *arg);\n```\n\nPhases, in order:\n\n### 1. Check inputs\nWalk `input_slots`. For each, ask the slot store whether a value is\navailable (1-cell: `tail > head` and the cell is filled; queued: same\ncondition).\n\nIf any input is unavailable: set `ctx->block_on` to a wait handle for\nthat slot and return `ACT_BLOCK`. The pool parks the task on that\nslot's wait list. When a producer pushes, the slot store wakes the\nparked tasks; the pool re-runs the action from the top.\n\n-- question... is the waiting list attached to the wire, the blocking box, or\n   the blocked box? I know the blocking box is the one that wakes it up, but,\n   where is the task parked?\n\n### 2. Read inputs into byte buffers\nFor each input:\n- 1-cell slot: `slot_peek` into the input buffer. The slot is not\n  drained — fan-out consumers all peek.\n- Queued slot: `slot_pop` into the input buffer. The cell is drained.\n\nBuffer ownership: the action allocates a small array of `(void*,\nint)` pairs on the stack, with each pointer aimed at a stack-allocated\nor heap-allocated buffer sized to the slot's cell capacity. Heap is\nused only when capacity exceeds a stack limit (e.g. 4 KB).\n\n### 3. Iterator counter prepending\nIf the box is an iterator (has `iterator_outputs` in the graph), the\ncounter is prepended to the input array as input position 0 before\ncalling `invoke`. The language spec sees one extra argument; it does\nnot know it is the counter. (This matches the contract in issue 221.)\n\n-- hold on, does the language spec even need to see the counter at all? the\n   iteration I think can be entirely confined to the task dispatch layer. Same\n   for the comparison functionality.\n\n### 4. Invoke\nLook up the box's language spec by its `lang` field. Find the worker's\nlanguage handle in `current_worker->handles[lang_idx]`. Call\n`lang->invoke` with the input buffers, an output buffer, and an\noutput-size pointer. Nonzero return → abort the program (issue 303).\n\n-- question... wouldn't it return the values that the box function returns? if\n   the language spec is running a function... how would it get the values\n   produced by that function back to the shared memory if not by returning them?\n\n### 5. Write output\n`slot_push(output_slot, output_buf, output_size)`. The slot store\nperforms the memory barrier and walks the slot's wait list to wake\nany consumers parked on this slot.\n\n### 6. Unref consumed inputs\nFor each 1-cell input slot, call `slot_unref`. The slot is freed when\nits refcount drops to zero (which happens when the last fan-out\nconsumer reads it). Queued-input slots are not unref'd here — those\nslots are held for the life of the consumer task across many\ninvocations.\n\n-- can you explain this part a bit more? What's a 1-cell input? I get the refcounting\n   part, and the de-allocating when there's no references remaining. But, what\n   does it mean to be held across many invocations?\n\n### 7. Post-action: routing\nTwo cases:\n\n- **Comparator** (issue 108): the output is a `(value, branch)` pair\n  where `branch` is one of `lt` / `eq` / `gt`. The dispatch layer\n  fires only the connection whose `from_branch` matches.\n- **Iterator** (issue 221): fire only the connection whose\n  `from_branch` matches `iterator_outputs[counter]`. Then increment\n  `counter` mod `n_iter_outputs` and spawn a successor\n  `dispatch_task_t` with the same `input_slots` and the new counter.\n  The successor immediately blocks on the input queue if it is\n  empty; otherwise it picks up the next queued value.\n\nPlain call boxes fire all outgoing connections unconditionally.\n\n\"Firing\" a connection means submitting a `dispatch_task_t` for the\ndownstream box, with `input_slots[i]` set to the upstream's\n`output_slot` for the wired position. Refcount on the upstream slot\nis incremented per fan-out wire at firing time.\n\n### 8. Return ACT_DONE\nThe action completes. The pool decrements the active-task counter\n(issue 301). If the counter reaches zero and the runner is waiting,\nthe run ends.\n\n## Initial submission\n\nThe pool runner walks the graph at startup to find entry-point boxes\n— boxes with no inputs, or with inputs that come only from `data`\nboxes (literal values). It builds and submits a `dispatch_task_t` per\nentry box. From that point, all further submissions come from\npost-action firing.\n\n## Comparator vs iterator vs plain call\n\nThree box modes drive routing differently:\n\n| Mode        | Output kind        | Routing behavior                              |\n|-------------|--------------------|-----------------------------------------------|\n| Plain call  | single value       | fire all outgoing connections                 |\n| Comparator  | (value, lt/eq/gt)  | fire connections matching the branch tag      |\n| Iterator    | single value + counter | fire connection matching counter slot, then re-spawn |\n\nThe dispatch action checks the box's mode after invoke and dispatches\ninto the appropriate routing helper. Three small functions, not a\nsingle switch, to keep each mode's logic isolated.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Output buffer sizing: stack-allocated up to a fixed cap, then heap\n  for larger. What is the cap? 4 KB is generous for typical strings.\n\n-- 4kb seems like a lot to me, on the stack? but sure. I don't know what a\n   typical workload could be because there's no typical use-case defined.\n   I think we should think of a way to handle large and small buffers both.\n   we should be able to define them at runtime, programmatically and dynamically\n\n- Queued-input slot lifetime: the consumer holds the only ref. When\n  does the consumer drop the ref? When its iterator parks for the\n  last time? When the run ends? Probably \"when no upstream producers\n  remain alive\" — but detecting that requires tracking producer\n  liveness. Defer until the iterator implementation is being written.\n\n-- It drops the ref (and de-allocates if it's the only ref remaining) when the\n   box function ends, as part of it's cleanup phase. The references are the\n   mechanism that tracks producer liveness.\n\n- Comparator output encoding: the comparator returns a value plus a\n  branch tag. How is the tag encoded in the slot's bytes? Options:\n  (a) prepend a 1-byte tag, (b) encode in a struct the dispatch layer\n  unpacks, (c) the comparator's spec writes both into the slot in a\n  defined format. Decision deferred — depends on whether the\n  language spec or the dispatch layer is responsible for the\n  comparator semantics.\n\n-- what's a branch tag? The dispatch layer is responsible for comparison\n   semantics.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Define `dispatch_task_t` and the `dispatch_action` skeleton.\n2. Implement phase 1 (input check + ACT_BLOCK).\n3. Implement phase 2 (input read into buffers).\n4. Implement phase 4 (invoke); skip iterator counter for now.\n5. Implement phase 5 (output write).\n6. Implement phase 6 (unref consumed 1-cell inputs).\n7. Smoke test: `hello` map (one box, no routing) end-to-end through\n   the pool. Assert the output slot contains the expected value.\n8. Implement plain-call fan-out firing (phase 7 path 1).\n9. Implement comparator branch routing (phase 7 path 2). Test\n   `branch-test` map.\n10. Implement iterator counter prepending (phase 3) and self-respawn\n    (phase 7 path 3). Test an iterator map.\n11. Wire up entry-box initial submission in the pool runner.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — synchronous executor that this layer replaces\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool that runs this action\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — slot API used here\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — `invoke` interface called here\n- `issues/221-iterator-box.md` — iterator routing and self-rescheduling\n- `issues/completed/108-branch-box-and-predicate-routing.md` — comparator routing\n- `issues/213-queued-inputs-and-task-model.md` — queued-input slot semantics\n",
    "oldString":"### 1. Check inputs\nWalk `input_slots`. For each, ask the slot store whether a value is\navailable (1-cell: `tail > head` and the cell is filled; queued: same\ncondition).\n\nIf any input is unavailable: set `ctx->block_on` to a wait handle for\nthat slot and return `ACT_BLOCK`. The pool parks the task on that\nslot's wait list. When a producer pushes, the slot store wakes the\nparked tasks; the pool re-runs the action from the top.\n\n-- question... is the waiting list attached to the wire, the blocking box, or\n   the blocked box?     "originalFile":"# 304 — Task dispatch layer (C, replaces synchronous executor)\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nThe synchronous executor at `src/004-executor.lua` walks the graph in\ndependency order, calling each box's driver, capturing stdout, decoding\nJSON, and propagating values to downstream boxes. Single-threaded,\nblocking, runs in Lua coroutines.\n\n## Concept\n\nThe task dispatch layer is the C component that runs inside each pool\nworker. The pool calls a single C action — `dispatch_action` — per\ntask. That action is the one place in the runtime that:\n\n- Reads from and writes to slots\n- Calls `lang_spec->invoke`\n- Manages slot refcounts on consumed inputs\n- Implements iterator routing and self-rescheduling\n- Implements comparator branch routing\n- Spawns successor tasks when its box's outputs feed downstream boxes\n\nThere is no Lua-level executor in the phase 3 path. `004-executor.lua`\nis replaced wholesale.\n\n## Task struct\n\nThe dispatch layer's per-task state lives in a `dispatch_task_t`\nallocated when the task is submitted to the pool:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    int           box_id;          // index into the graph's box array\n    int           n_inputs;\n    slot_id_t    *input_slots;     // array of n_inputs slot IDs\n    slot_id_t     output_slot;     // single output slot\n    int           counter;         // iterator only; ignored otherwise\n} dispatch_task_t;\n```\n\nThe pool passes this pointer to the action via `task_ctx_t.args`.\nMultiple successor invocations of an iterator produce multiple\n`dispatch_task_t`s (with new counter values), each with its own output\nslot.\n\n## The dispatch action\n\n```c\naction_result_t dispatch_action(task_ctx_t *ctx, void *arg);\n```\n\nPhases, in order:\n\n### 1. Check inputs\nWalk `input_slots`. For each, ask the slot store whether a value is\navailable (`tail > head`, cell filled).\n\nIf any input is unavailable, the dispatch action returns `ACT_BLOCK`\nwith `ctx->block_on` set to a wait handle for that slot. The pool\nparks the task on **the slot's** wait list — not on a wire's list and\nnot on the upstream box's list. The slot owns the wait list because\nthe slot is the thing that gets filled; whoever pushes into the slot\nwalks its wait list and wakes everyone parked there. When the action\nis re-run, it starts again at phase 1, checks the next input, blocks\nagain if needed.\n\n### 2. Read inputs into byte buffers\nFor each input:\n- 1-cell slot: `slot_peek` into the input buffer. The slot is not\n  drained — fan-out consumers all peek.\n- Queued slot: `slot_pop` into the input buffer. The cell is drained.\n\nBuffer ownership: the action allocates a small array of `(void*,\nint)` pairs on the stack, with each pointer aimed at a stack-allocated\nor heap-allocated buffer sized to the slot's cell capacity. Heap is\nused only when capacity exceeds a stack limit (e.g. 4 KB).\n\n### 3. Iterator counter prepending\nIf the box is an iterator (has `iterator_outputs` in the graph), the\ncounter is prepended to the input array as input position 0 before\ncalling `invoke`. The language spec sees one extra argument; it does\nnot know it is the counter. (This matches the contract in issue 221.)\n\n-- hold on, does the language spec even need to see the counter at all? the\n   iteration I think can be entirely confined to the task dispatch layer. Same\n   for the comparison functionality.\n\n### 4. Invoke\nLook up the box's language spec by its `lang` field. Find the worker's\nlanguage handle in `current_worker->handles[lang_idx]`. Call\n`lang->invoke` with the input buffers, an output buffer, and an\noutput-size pointer. Nonzero return → abort the program (issue 303).\n\n-- question... wouldn't it return the values that the box function returns? if\n   the language spec is running a function... how would it get the values\n   produced by that function back to the shared memory if not by returning them?\n\n### 5. Write output\n`slot_push(output_slot, output_buf, output_size)`. The slot store\nperforms the memory barrier and walks the slot's wait list to wake\nany consumers parked on this slot.\n\n### 6. Unref consumed inputs\nFor each 1-cell input slot, call `slot_unref`. The slot is freed when\nits refcount drops to zero (which happens when the last fan-out\nconsumer reads it). Queued-input slots are not unref'd here — those\nslots are held for the life of the consumer task across many\ninvocations.\n\n-- can you explain this part a bit more? What's a 1-cell input? I get the refcounting\n   part, and the de-allocating when there's no references remaining. But, what\n   does it mean to be held across many invocations?\n\n### 7. Post-action: routing\nTwo cases:\n\n- **Comparator** (issue 108): the output is a `(value, branch)` pair\n  where `branch` is one of `lt` / `eq` / `gt`. The dispatch layer\n  fires only the connection whose `from_branch` matches.\n- **Iterator** (issue 221): fire only the connection whose\n  `from_branch` matches `iterator_outputs[counter]`. Then increment\n  `counter` mod `n_iter_outputs` and spawn a successor\n  `dispatch_task_t` with the same `input_slots` and the new counter.\n  The successor immediately blocks on the input queue if it is\n  empty; otherwise it picks up the next queued value.\n\nPlain call boxes fire all outgoing connections unconditionally.\n\n\"Firing\" a connection means submitting a `dispatch_task_t` for the\ndownstream box, with `input_slots[i]` set to the upstream's\n`output_slot` for the wired position. Refcount on the upstream slot\nis incremented per fan-out wire at firing time.\n\n### 8. Return ACT_DONE\nThe action completes. The pool decrements the active-task counter\n(issue 301). If the counter reaches zero and the runner is waiting,\nthe run ends.\n\n## Initial submission\n\nThe pool runner walks the graph at startup to find entry-point boxes\n— boxes with no inputs, or with inputs that come only from `data`\nboxes (literal values). It builds and submits a `dispatch_task_t` per\nentry box. From that point, all further submissions come from\npost-action firing.\n\n## Comparator vs iterator vs plain call\n\nThree box modes drive routing differently:\n\n| Mode        | Output kind        | Routing behavior                              |\n|-------------|--------------------|-----------------------------------------------|\n| Plain call  | single value       | fire all outgoing connections                 |\n| Comparator  | (value, lt/eq/gt)  | fire connections matching the branch tag      |\n| Iterator    | single value + counter | fire connection matching counter slot, then re-spawn |\n\nThe dispatch action checks the box's mode after invoke and dispatches\ninto the appropriate routing helper. Three small functions, not a\nsingle switch, to keep each mode's logic isolated.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Output buffer sizing: stack-allocated up to a fixed cap, then heap\n  for larger. What is the cap? 4 KB is generous for typical strings.\n\n-- 4kb seems like a lot to me, on the stack? but sure. I don't know what a\n   typical workload could be because there's no typical use-case defined.\n   I think we should think of a way to handle large and small buffers both.\n   we should be able to define them at runtime, programmatically and dynamically\n\n- Queued-input slot lifetime: the consumer holds the only ref. When\n  does the consumer drop the ref? When its iterator parks for the\n  last time? When the run ends? Probably \"when no upstream producers\n  remain alive\" — but detecting that requires tracking producer\n  liveness. Defer until the iterator implementation is being written.\n\n-- It drops the ref (and de-allocates if it's the only ref remaining) when the\n   box function ends, as part of it's cleanup phase. The references are the\n   mechanism that tracks producer liveness.\n\n- Comparator output encoding: the comparator returns a value plus a\n  branch tag. How is the tag encoded in the slot's bytes? Options:\n  (a) prepend a 1-byte tag, (b) encode in a struct the dispatch layer\n  unpacks, (c) the comparator's spec writes both into the slot in a\n  defined format. Decision deferred — depends on whether the\n  language spec or the dispatch layer is responsible for the\n  comparator semantics.\n\n-- what's a branch tag? The dispatch layer is responsible for comparison\n   semantics.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Define `dispatch_task_t` and the `dispatch_action` skeleton.\n2. Implement phase 1 (input check + ACT_BLOCK).\n3. Implement phase 2 (input read into buffers).\n4. Implement phase 4 (invoke); skip iterator counter for now.\n5. Implement phase 5 (output write).\n6. Implement phase 6 (unref consumed 1-cell inputs).\n7. Smoke test: `hello` map (one box, no routing) end-to-end through\n   the pool. Assert the output slot contains the expected value.\n8. Implement plain-call fan-out firing (phase 7 path 1).\n9. Implement comparator branch routing (phase 7 path 2). Test\n   `branch-test` map.\n10. Implement iterator counter prepending (phase 3) and self-respawn\n    (phase 7 path 3). Test an iterator map.\n11. Wire up entry-box initial submission in the pool runner.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — synchronous executor that this layer replaces\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool that runs this action\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — slot API used here\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — `invoke` interface called here\n- `issues/221-iterator-box.md` — iterator routing and self-rescheduling\n- `issues/completed/108-branch-box-and-predicate-routing.md` — comparator routing\n- `issues/213-queued-inputs-and-task-model.md` — queued-input slot semantics\n",

Dispatch by box mode\nThe action now branches on the box's mode:\n\n- **Plain call box**: proceed to phase 4 (invoke) and phase 5 (write\n  output) as below.\n- **Comparator box**: skip invoke entirely. Read the input value,\n  compare to the box's stored threshold, and proceed to phase 7 with\n  the result of the comparison.     "newString":"### 6. Unref consumed inputs\nFor each single-value input slot (`n_cells = 1`), the dispatch action\ncalls `slot_unref` after peeking. Each fan-out wire holds one ref; as\neach consumer reads and unrefs, the count decrements. When the last\nconsumer unrefs, the slot is freed.\n\nQueued input slots are different. They are not unref'd at the end of\neach invocation. The same queue persists across multiple invocations\nof the same iterator: an iterator pops one value, runs, re-spawns\nitself with a new dispatch_task_t, and the new task uses the **same**\nqueued-input slot to pop the next value. The slot stays alive\nbecause:\n- Each upstream producer holds a ref while the producer is alive.\n- The consumer (iterator) holds a ref while it is still consuming.\n- The slot is freed when all upstream producers have ended (their\n  refs dropped) and the iterator has ended (its ref dropped).\n\nSo the slot's lifetime ≠ one invocation; it equals the duration of\nthe iterator's whole consumption cycle.",

Fire only the connection whose `from_branch`\n  matches. The output slot carries the input value through unchanged\n  — comparators do not transform data.\n- **Iterator**: fire only the connection whose `from_branch` matches\n  `iterator_outputs[counter]`.       "content":"| Iterator    | single value + counter | fire connection matching counter slot, then re-spawn |\n\nThe dispatch action checks the box's mode after invoke and dispatches\ninto the appropriate routing helper. Three small functions, not a\nsingle switch, to keep each mode's logic isolated.\n\n## Open questions\n\n(none currently — earlier questions resolved as follows:)\n\n- Output buffer sizing: heap-allocated to the box's declared output\n  size at runtime. No fixed cap. Variable-size outputs go through the\n  large-value heap (issue 302).\n- Queued-input slot lifetime: producers hold refs while alive,\n  consumer holds a ref while consuming, slot freed when all drop.\n  References are the producer-liveness tracking mechanism.\n- Comparator output encoding: dispatch layer handles comparison\n  semantics directly. No spec involvement, no encoded \"branch tag\" in\n  the slot — the branch is a routing-time value computed by the\n  dispatch layer from the input.\n   box function ends, as part of it's cleanup phase. The references are the\n   mechanism that tracks producer liveness.\n\n- Comparator output encoding: the comparator returns a value plus a\n  branch tag. How is the tag encoded in the slot's bytes? Options:\n  (a) prepend a 1-byte tag, (b) encode in a struct the dispatch layer\n  unpacks, (c) the comparator's spec writes both into the slot in a\n  defined format. Decision deferred — depends on whether the\n  language spec or the dispatch layer is responsible for the\n  comparator semantics.\n\n-- what's a branch tag? The dispatch layer is responsible for comparison\n   semantics.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Define `dispatch_task_t` and the `dispatch_action` skeleton.\n2. Implement phase 1 (input check + ACT_BLOCK).\n3. Implement phase 2 (input read into buffers).\n4. Implement phase 4 (invoke); skip iterator counter for now.\n5. Implement phase 5 (output write).\n6. Implement phase 6 (unref consumed 1-cell inputs).\n7. Smoke test: `hello` map (one box, no routing) end-to-end through\n   the pool. Assert the output slot contains the expected value.\n8. Implement plain-call fan-out firing (phase 7 path 1).\n9. Implement comparator branch routing (phase 7 path 2). Test\n   `branch-test` map.\n10. Implement iterator counter prepending (phase 3) and self-respawn\n    (phase 7 path 3). Test an iterator map.\n11. Wire up entry-box initial submission in the pool runner.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — synchronous executor that this layer replaces\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool that runs this action\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — slot API used here\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — `invoke` interface called here\n- `issues/221-iterator-box.md` — iterator routing and self-rescheduling\n- `issues/completed/108-branch-box-and-predicate-routing.md` — comparator routing\n- `issues/213-queued-inputs-and-task-model.md` — queued-input slot semantics\n"

        "text":"Both files updated. Summary of significant changes:\n\n**302**:\n- Slots now in process heap, not shared memory. `shm_open` / `mmap` / `mremap` removed entirely. Reasoning captured: specs only see byte pointers, never raw slot addresses, so cross-process visibility is unnecessary.\n- Refcount section reframed: producers also hold refs on queued slots; the refs themselves are the producer-liveness tracking mechanism. Slot freed when all producers and consumer have dropped their refs.\n- New \"Wait list\" subsection clarifying the wait list is attached to the slot.\n- Allocator: added deferred cleanup-task post-grow; added eager-coalesce on dealloc (check both physical neighbors, merge if free).\n- Physical-order chunk list section now compares doubly-linked list vs two-array representation, with linked list as the recommended starting point and the API-stable swap to arrays as a fallback.\n- New \"Large-value heap\" subsection: variable-size payloads (LLM responses, dynamic arrays) live in a separate `malloc`-backed heap; the slot stores a `(size, offset)` handle pointing into it. Slot allocator stays simple, unbounded outputs supported.\n- Growth section simplified — plain `malloc`, no `ftruncate` swap-in needed.\n\n**304**:\n- Phase 1 clarified: wait list is on the slot.\n- Phase 2 buffer sizing: heap-allocated to slot's `cell_capacity`, no fixed cap. Variable-size goes through the large-value heap.\n- New phase 3: dispatch by box mode. Comparator and iterator boxes skip invoke entirely — the dispatch layer owns those semantics. Iterator boxes are pure passthrough at the data level. Note added that this means issue 221's iterator-as-passthrough-function disappears (will need to update 221).\n- Phase 4 (invoke) rewritten for plain call boxes only, with the spec contract spelled out: load → marshal inputs to native types → call → marshal return to bytes → write to `out_buf`, set `*out_size`, return 0.\n- Phase 6 rewritten with full clarification of \"1-cell\" (`n_cells = 1`) vs queued, and how queued slots persist across iterator re-spawns.\n- Phase 7 routing table updated: comparator and iterator marked \"no invoke,\" routing logic clearer.\n- Open questions resolved into the body; section now empty.\n\nIssue 221 needs a follow-up edit to drop the iterator-passthrough function. Want me to do that now, write 305, or wait for review?"
      }]

        "lines":[" ### What it does"," An iterator box receives one input value and routes it to one of N named"," output wires.     "originalFile":"# 221 — Iterator box: round-robin output routing with per-instance counter\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nNo mechanism exists for a box to distribute output across multiple\ndownstream paths in sequence. The comparator routes based on a value\nthreshold; the iterator routes based on a counter that advances each call.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\n### What it does\nAn iterator box receives one input value and routes it to one of N named\noutput wires. Which wire fires is determined by an internal counter that\nincrements each call and wraps back to 0 after the last output. The\nfunction itself is a dumb passthrough — it does not make the routing\ndecision. The executor does, based on the counter.\n\nUseful for distributing work across parallel paths, cycling through a\nlist of consumers, or producing round-robin load balancing in the graph.\n\n### Counter model\nThe counter is per-box-instance, stored in the executor's in-memory\nstate (keyed by box ID). It resets to 0 at the start of each run.\nPersistence across runs is not in scope; that is a separate issue.\n\nIn the compiler output (issue 219), the counter becomes a local variable\nin a generated closure — same reset-per-program-start behavior.\n\nWrap-around: `counter = (counter + 1) % #iterator_outputs`\n\n### The iterator function\nEach language ships a standard iterator function in `libs/`:\n\n```\nlibs/iterator.lua  — M.iterate(counter, data) → data\nlibs/iterator.sh   — function iterate() { local counter=\"$1\"; echo \"$2\"; }\nlibs/iterator.c    — reads argv[2] (counter), argv[3] (data); prints data\n```\n\nThe counter is the FIRST argument (position 0 in the driver's arg list,\nbefore the declared inputs). This is intentional: last-arg convention is\nfor variadic tails where the count is unknown; the counter is always\nexactly one value and is always findable at position 0 without counting.\nThe function returns `data` unchanged. The routing decision is entirely\nin the executor.\n\nThe user points the box's `ref` and `fn` at the appropriate language's\niterator lib file. The `iterator_outputs` field in the box JSON is what\nflags the executor to treat this box as an iterator rather than a plain\ncall box.\n\n### Data model\nBox JSON gains an `iterator_outputs` field — an ordered array of\nuser-defined output path names:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"router\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"ref\": \"libs/iterator.lua\",\n  \"fn\": \"iterate\",\n  \"inputs\": [{\"name\": \"data\", \"type\": \"any\"}],\n  \"iterator_outputs\": [\"path_a\", \"path_b\", \"path_c\"],\n  \"connections\": [\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"router\", \"from_branch\": \"path_a\",\n      \"to_box\": \"worker-a\", \"to_input\": \"data\"\n    },\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"router\", \"from_branch\": \"path_b\",\n      \"to_box\": \"worker-b\", \"to_input\": \"data\"\n    },\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"router\", \"from_branch\": \"path_c\",\n      \"to_box\": \"worker-c\", \"to_input\": \"data\"\n    }\n  ]\n}\n```\n\n`from_branch` is reused for iterator output names — the same field that\nholds \"lt\"/\"eq\"/\"gt\" for comparators. The executor checks whether the\nbox has `iterator_outputs`; if so, it fires only the connection whose\n`from_branch` matches `iterator_outputs[counter]`.\n\n### Auto-grow output slots\nConnecting a wire to the last slot of the iterator's output side appends\na new empty named slot — identical to the auto-grow behavior for variadic\ninputs (issue 217). The user names each slot in the inspector. Connecting\nto the last slot prompts for a name and grows the list. Disconnecting\nremoves the slot and compacts (same rename-and-compact logic as variadic\ninputs).\n\n### Executor changes\nIn `fire_connections`, a new branch handles iterator boxes:\n\n```\nif box.iterator_outputs and #box.iterator_outputs > 0:\n    counter = executor_state[box.id .. \".counter\"] or 0\n    target_branch = box.iterator_outputs[counter + 1]  -- 1-indexed in Lua\n    fire only connections where from_branch == target_branch\n    executor_state[box.id .. \".counter\"] = (counter + 1) % #box.iterator_outputs\n```\n\nThe counter state table lives alongside the existing value store in\nthe executor.\n\n### Driver contract addition\nThe executor injects the counter as the first argument when invoking the\ndriver for an iterator box, before any declared input values:\n\n  `<driver> <file> <fn> <arg_count+1> <counter> [data_args...]`\n\nThe counter is always at position 0 in the arg list — no counting required\nto find it. Non-iterator call boxes are unaffected.\n\n### Inspector changes\nThe inspector shows:\n- An \"iterator\" toggle per box (like the variadic toggle on inputs)\n- When toggled on: the output side of the box renders named slots instead\n  of a single dot; a \"+\" row at the bottom adds a new slot\n- Each slot name is editable inline\n- The current counter value is shown as a read-only display (useful for\n  debugging live runs)\n\n### Compiler output (issue 219 integration)\nFor an iterator box, the compiler generates a closure with a captured\ncounter variable:\n\n```lua\nlocal router_counter = 0\nlocal function router(data)\n  local idx = router_counter\n  router_counter = (router_counter + 1) % 3\n  if     idx == 0 then worker_a(data)\n  elseif idx == 1 then worker_b(data)\n  else                  worker_c(data)\n  end\nend\n```\n\nThe iterator lib files are bundled alongside other box source files.\n\n### Threading model integration (3d-rts thread pool)\n\nIn the pthreads task pool, each box execution is a task struct containing:\n- A function pointer to the language-specific invocation wrapper\n- A pointer to shared memory holding the input arguments and return value\n- A pointer list of dependency tasks (upstream boxes whose output this box\n  needs before it can run)\n- For iterator boxes: a `counter` field (integer, part of the task struct)\n\n**Blocking:** when a task cannot run because its dependencies haven't\ncompleted, it is placed in the blocking task's waiting list. No memory is\nallocated — the task struct stays alive, only a pointer to it is moved.\nWhen the blocking task completes and writes its return value to shared\nmemory, it walks its waiting list and re-adds each waiting task to the\nmain queue (again, pointer move only — no reallocation or struct copying).\n\n**Iterator self-re-add:** when an iterator task completes, it does not\nterminate. Instead:\n1. It increments its own `counter` field (or wraps to 0).\n2. It checks if there is another pending input value in its input queue.\n3. If yes: it updates its input pointer to the next pending value, then\n   re-adds itself to the main task queue. No new allocation.\n4. If no: it adds itself to the waiting list of its upstream dependency,\n   to be re-added when the next input value arrives.\n\nThis means the iterator task struct is allocated once and lives for the\nduration of the run, cycling through the queue as many times as there are\ninput values to process. Input values are processed one-at-a-time in\narrival order — if 10 values are queued, the iterator visits the queue 10\ntimes, each time firing a different output path and advancing the counter.\n\n**C calling Lua:** the per-thread invocation wrapper is a C function\n(pthreads requires a C entry point). Each worker thread initializes its\nown `lua_State` at startup — Lua states are not thread-safe but one per\nthread is fine. The wrapper dispatches on language tag: if Lua, calls\nthrough the thread's `lua_State` via `lua_pcall`; if native C, calls the\nfunction pointer directly (no interpreter overhead); if bash, spawns a\nsubprocess (the one case that doesn't map cleanly to pthreads — see\ndocs/004-ipc-and-threading.md for options).\n\n## Open questions\n- Should the counter be exposed as a readable data port (wirable to\n  another box as an input) in addition to being shown in the inspector?\n- Should auto-grow prompt for the output name immediately on connect, or\n  generate a placeholder (`out_N`) that the user renames afterward?\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. `libs/iterator.lua` — trivial passthrough function.\n2. `libs/iterator.sh`, `libs/iterator.c` — same for bash and C.\n3. `src/001-schema.lua` — add `iterator_outputs` to the box validator.\n4. `src/004-executor.lua` — add counter state table; extend\n   `fire_connections` with the iterator branch; inject counter arg in\n   `run_task` when box has `iterator_outputs`.\n5. `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — iterator toggle; editable output slots.\n6. `assets/js/006-wires.js` — auto-grow output slots on connect;\n   auto-shrink + rename on disconnect (mirrors variadic input logic).\n7. `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — render N named output dots when\n   `iterator_outputs` is set (replacing the single-wire dot).\n\n## Relevant files\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — fire_connections, run_task\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — box validator\n- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — iterator toggle, slot editor\n- `assets/js/006-wires.js` — auto-grow/shrink for output slots\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box rendering\n- `issues/217-concat-box-and-dynamic-inputs.md` — variadic input model\n  (auto-grow/shrink logic mirrors this)\n- `issues/completed/108-branch-box-and-predicate-routing.md` — comparator\n  model that `from_branch` and the routing pattern extend from\n- `issues/219-map-compiler.md` — compiler integration notes above\n",
    "oldString":"### What it does\nAn iterator box receives one input value and routes it to one of N named\noutput wires. Which wire fires is determined by an internal counter that\nincrements each call and wraps back to 0 after the last output. The\nfunction itself is a dumb passthrough — it does not make the routing\ndecision. The executor does, based on the counter.\n\nUseful for distributing work across parallel paths, cycling through a\nlist of consumers, or producing round-robin load balancing in the graph.",
