    "originalFile":"# 221 — Iterator box: round-robin output routing with per-instance counter\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nNo mechanism exists for a box to distribute output across multiple\ndownstream paths in sequence. The comparator routes based on a value\nthreshold; the iterator routes based on a counter that advances each call.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\n### What it does\nAn iterator box receives one input value and routes it to one of N named\noutput wires. Which wire fires is determined by an internal counter that\nincrements each call and wraps back to 0 after the last output. There is\nno function — the dispatch layer copies input directly to output, no\nlanguage spec is invoked. The iterator is a pure routing primitive.\n\nUseful for distributing work across parallel paths, cycling through a\nlist of consumers, or producing round-robin load balancing in the graph.\n\n### Counter model\nThe counter is per-box-instance, stored in the executor's in-memory\nstate (keyed by box ID). It resets to 0 at the start of each run.\nPersistence across runs is not in scope; that is a separate issue.\n\nIn the compiler output (issue 219), the counter becomes a local variable\nin a generated closure — same reset-per-program-start behavior.\n\nWrap-around: `counter = (counter + 1) % #iterator_outputs`\n\n### The iterator function\nEach language ships a standard iterator function in `libs/`:\n\n```\nlibs/iterator.lua  — M.iterate(counter, data) → data\nlibs/iterator.sh   — function iterate() { local counter=\"$1\"; echo \"$2\"; }\nlibs/iterator.c    — reads argv[2] (counter), argv[3] (data); prints data\n```\n\nThe counter is the FIRST argument (position 0 in the driver's arg list,\nbefore the declared inputs). This is intentional: last-arg convention is\nfor variadic tails where the count is unknown; the counter is always\nexactly one value and is always findable at position 0 without counting.\nThe function returns `data` unchanged. The routing decision is entirely\nin the executor.\n\nThe user points the box's `ref` and `fn` at the appropriate language's\niterator lib file. The `iterator_outputs` field in the box JSON is what\nflags the executor to treat this box as an iterator rather than a plain\ncall box.\n\n### Data model\nBox JSON gains an `iterator_outputs` field — an ordered array of\nuser-defined output path names:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"router\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"ref\": \"libs/iterator.lua\",\n  \"fn\": \"iterate\",\n  \"inputs\": [{\"name\": \"data\", \"type\": \"any\"}],\n  \"iterator_outputs\": [\"path_a\", \"path_b\", \"path_c\"],\n  \"connections\": [\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"router\", \"from_branch\": \"path_a\",\n      \"to_box\": \"worker-a\", \"to_input\": \"data\"\n    },\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"router\", \"from_branch\": \"path_b\",\n      \"to_box\": \"worker-b\", \"to_input\": \"data\"\n    },\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"router\", \"from_branch\": \"path_c\",\n      \"to_box\": \"worker-c\", \"to_input\": \"data\"\n    }\n  ]\n}\n```\n\n`from_branch` is reused for iterator output names — the same field that\nholds \"lt\"/\"eq\"/\"gt\" for comparators. The executor checks whether the\nbox has `iterator_outputs`; if so, it fires only the connection whose\n`from_branch` matches `iterator_outputs[counter]`.\n\n### Auto-grow output slots\nConnecting a wire to the last slot of the iterator's output side appends\na new empty named slot — identical to the auto-grow behavior for variadic\ninputs (issue 217). The user names each slot in the inspector. Connecting\nto the last slot prompts for a name and grows the list. Disconnecting\nremoves the slot and compacts (same rename-and-compact logic as variadic\ninputs).\n\n### Executor changes\nIn `fire_connections`, a new branch handles iterator boxes:\n\n```\nif box.iterator_outputs and #box.iterator_outputs > 0:\n    counter = executor_state[box.id .. \".counter\"] or 0\n    target_branch = box.iterator_outputs[counter + 1]  -- 1-indexed in Lua\n    fire only connections where from_branch == target_branch\n    executor_state[box.id .. \".counter\"] = (counter + 1) % #box.iterator_outputs\n```\n\nThe counter state table lives alongside the existing value store in\nthe executor.\n\n### Driver contract addition\nThe executor injects the counter as the first argument when invoking the\ndriver for an iterator box, before any declared input values:\n\n  `<driver> <file> <fn> <arg_count+1> <counter> [data_args...]`\n\nThe counter is always at position 0 in the arg list — no counting required\nto find it. Non-iterator call boxes are unaffected.\n\n### Inspector changes\nThe inspector shows:\n- An \"iterator\" toggle per box (like the variadic toggle on inputs)\n- When toggled on: the output side of the box renders named slots instead\n  of a single dot; a \"+\" row at the bottom adds a new slot\n- Each slot name is editable inline\n- The current counter value is shown as a read-only display (useful for\n  debugging live runs)\n\n### Compiler output (issue 219 integration)\nFor an iterator box, the compiler generates a closure with a captured\ncounter variable:\n\n```lua\nlocal router_counter = 0\nlocal function router(data)\n  local idx = router_counter\n  router_counter = (router_counter + 1) % 3\n  if     idx == 0 then worker_a(data)\n  elseif idx == 1 then worker_b(data)\n  else                  worker_c(data)\n  end\nend\n```\n\nThe iterator lib files are bundled alongside other box source files.\n\n### Threading model integration (3d-rts thread pool)\n\nIn the pthreads task pool, each box execution is a task struct containing:\n- A function pointer to the language-specific invocation wrapper\n- A pointer to shared memory holding the input arguments and return value\n- A pointer list of dependency tasks (upstream boxes whose output this box\n  needs before it can run)\n- For iterator boxes: a `counter` field (integer, part of the task struct)\n\n**Blocking:** when a task cannot run because its dependencies haven't\ncompleted, it is placed in the blocking task's waiting list. No memory is\nallocated — the task struct stays alive, only a pointer to it is moved.\nWhen the blocking task completes and writes its return value to shared\nmemory, it walks its waiting list and re-adds each waiting task to the\nmain queue (again, pointer move only — no reallocation or struct copying).\n\n**Iterator self-re-add:** when an iterator task completes, it does not\nterminate. Instead:\n1. It increments its own `counter` field (or wraps to 0).\n2. It checks if there is another pending input value in its input queue.\n3. If yes: it updates its input pointer to the next pending value, then\n   re-adds itself to the main task queue. No new allocation.\n4. If no: it adds itself to the waiting list of its upstream dependency,\n   to be re-added when the next input value arrives.\n\nThis means the iterator task struct is allocated once and lives for the\nduration of the run, cycling through the queue as many times as there are\ninput values to process. Input values are processed one-at-a-time in\narrival order — if 10 values are queued, the iterator visits the queue 10\ntimes, each time firing a different output path and advancing the counter.\n\n**C calling Lua:** the per-thread invocation wrapper is a C function\n(pthreads requires a C entry point). Each worker thread initializes its\nown `lua_State` at startup — Lua states are not thread-safe but one per\nthread is fine. The wrapper dispatches on language tag: if Lua, calls\nthrough the thread's `lua_State` via `lua_pcall`; if native C, calls the\nfunction pointer directly (no interpreter overhead); if bash, spawns a\nsubprocess (the one case that doesn't map cleanly to pthreads — see\ndocs/004-ipc-and-threading.md for options).\n\n## Open questions\n- Should the counter be exposed as a readable data port (wirable to\n  another box as an input) in addition to being shown in the inspector?\n- Should auto-grow prompt for the output name immediately on connect, or\n  generate a placeholder (`out_N`) that the user renames afterward?\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. `libs/iterator.lua` — trivial passthrough function.\n2. `libs/iterator.sh`, `libs/iterator.c` — same for bash and C.\n3. `src/001-schema.lua` — add `iterator_outputs` to the box validator.\n4. `src/004-executor.lua` — add counter state table; extend\n   `fire_connections` with the iterator branch; inject counter arg in\n   `run_task` when box has `iterator_outputs`.\n5. `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — iterator toggle; editable output slots.\n6. `assets/js/006-wires.js` — auto-grow output slots on connect;\n   auto-shrink + rename on disconnect (mirrors variadic input logic).\n7. `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — render N named output dots when\n   `iterator_outputs` is set (replacing the single-wire dot).\n\n## Relevant files\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — fire_connections, run_task\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — box validator\n- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — iterator toggle, slot editor\n- `assets/js/006-wires.js` — auto-grow/shrink for output slots\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box rendering\n- `issues/217-concat-box-and-dynamic-inputs.md` — variadic input model\n  (auto-grow/shrink logic mirrors this)\n- `issues/completed/108-branch-box-and-predicate-routing.md` — comparator\n  model that `from_branch` and the routing pattern extend from\n- `issues/219-map-compiler.md` — compiler integration notes above\n",

The dispatch layer\nchecks whether the box has `iterator_outputs`; if so, it routes by\ncounter as described above.\n\n### Auto-grow output slots\nConnecting a wire to the last slot of the iterator's output side appends\na new empty named slot — identical to the auto-grow behavior for variadic\ninputs (issue 217). The user names each slot in the inspector. Connecting\nto the last slot prompts for a name and grows the list. Disconnecting\nremoves the slot and compacts (same rename-and-compact logic as variadic\ninputs).\n\n### Executor changes\nIn `fire_connections`, a new branch handles iterator boxes:\n\n```\nif box.iterator_outputs and #box.iterator_outputs > 0:\n    counter = executor_state[box.id .. \".counter\"] or 0\n    target_branch = box.iterator_outputs[counter + 1]  -- 1-indexed in Lua\n    fire only connections where from_branch == target_branch\n    executor_state[box.id .. \".counter\"] = (counter + 1) % #box.iterator_outputs\n```\n\nThe counter state table lives alongside the existing value store in\nthe executor.\n\n### Driver contract addition\nThe executor injects the counter as the first argument when invoking the\ndriver for an iterator box, before any declared input values:\n\n  `<driver> <file> <fn> <arg_count+1> <counter> [data_args...]`\n\nThe counter is always at position 0 in the arg list — no counting required\nto find it. Non-iterator call boxes are unaffected.\n\n### Inspector changes\nThe inspector shows:\n- An \"iterator\" toggle per box (like the variadic toggle on inputs)\n- When toggled on: the output side of the box renders named slots instead\n  of a single dot; a \"+\" row at the bottom adds a new slot\n- Each slot name is editable inline\n- The current counter value is shown as a read-only display (useful for\n  debugging live runs)\n\n### Compiler output (issue 219 integration)\nFor an iterator box, the compiler generates a closure with a captured\ncounter variable:\n\n```lua\nlocal router_counter = 0\nlocal function router(data)\n  local idx = router_counter\n  router_counter = (router_counter + 1) % 3\n  if     idx == 0 then worker_a(data)\n  elseif idx == 1 then worker_b(data)\n  else                  worker_c(data)\n  end\nend\n```\n\nThe iterator lib files are bundled alongside other box source files.\n\n### Threading model integration (3d-rts thread pool)\n\nIn the pthreads task pool, each box execution is a task struct containing:\n- A function pointer to the language-specific invocation wrapper\n- A pointer to shared memory holding the input arguments and return value\n- A pointer list of dependency tasks (upstream boxes whose output this box\n  needs before it can run)\n- For iterator boxes: a `counter` field (integer, part of the task struct)\n\n**Blocking:** when a task cannot run because its dependencies haven't\ncompleted, it is placed in the blocking task's waiting list. No memory is\nallocated — the task struct stays alive, only a pointer to it is moved.\nWhen the blocking task completes and writes its return value to shared\nmemory, it walks its waiting list and re-adds each waiting task to the\nmain queue (again, pointer move only — no reallocation or struct copying).\n\n**Iterator self-re-add:** when an iterator task completes, it does not\nterminate. Instead:\n1. It increments its own `counter` field (or wraps to 0).\n2. It checks if there is another pending input value in its input queue.\n3. If yes: it updates its input pointer to the next pending value, then\n   re-adds itself to the main task queue. No new allocation.\n4. If no: it adds itself to the waiting list of its upstream dependency,\n   to be re-added when the next input value arrives.\n\nThis means the iterator task struct is allocated once and lives for the\nduration of the run, cycling through the queue as many times as there are\ninput values to process. Input values are processed one-at-a-time in\narrival order — if 10 values are queued, the iterator visits the queue 10\ntimes, each time firing a different output path and advancing the counter.\n\n**C calling Lua:** the per-thread invocation wrapper is a C function\n(pthreads requires a C entry point). Each worker thread initializes its\nown `lua_State` at startup — Lua states are not thread-safe but one per\nthread is fine. The wrapper dispatches on language tag: if Lua, calls\nthrough the thread's `lua_State` via `lua_pcall`; if native C, calls the\nfunction pointer directly (no interpreter overhead); if bash, spawns a\nsubprocess (the one case that doesn't map cleanly to pthreads — see\ndocs/004-ipc-and-threading.md for options).\n\n## Open questions\n- Should the counter be exposed as a readable data port (wirable to\n  another box as an input) in addition to being shown in the inspector?\n- Should auto-grow prompt for the output name immediately on connect, or\n  generate a placeholder (`out_N`) that the user renames afterward?\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. `libs/iterator.lua` — trivial passthrough function.\n2. `libs/iterator.sh`, `libs/iterator.c` — same for bash and C.\n3. `src/001-schema.lua` — add `iterator_outputs` to the box validator.\n4. `src/004-executor.lua` — add counter state table; extend\n   `fire_connections` with the iterator branch; inject counter arg in\n   `run_task` when box has `iterator_outputs`.\n5. `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — iterator toggle; editable output slots.\n6. `assets/js/006-wires.js` — auto-grow output slots on connect;\n   auto-shrink + rename on disconnect (mirrors variadic input logic).\n7. `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — render N named output dots when\n   `iterator_outputs` is set (replacing the single-wire dot).\n\n## Relevant files\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — fire_connections, run_task\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — box validator\n- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — iterator toggle, slot editor\n- `assets/js/006-wires.js` — auto-grow/shrink for output slots\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box rendering\n- `issues/217-concat-box-and-dynamic-inputs.md` — variadic input model\n  (auto-grow/shrink logic mirrors this)\n- `issues/completed/108-branch-box-and-predicate-routing.md` — comparator\n  model that `from_branch` and the routing pattern extend from\n- `issues/219-map-compiler.md` — compiler integration notes above\n",

    "originalFile":"# 221 — Iterator box: round-robin output routing with per-instance counter\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nNo mechanism exists for a box to distribute output across multiple\ndownstream paths in sequence. The wrapper dispatches on language tag: if Lua, calls\nthrough the thread's `lua_State` via `lua_pcall`; if native C, calls the\nfunction pointer directly (no interpreter overhead); if bash, spawns a\nsubprocess (the one case that doesn't map cleanly to pthreads — see\ndocs/004-ipc-and-threading.md for options).\n\n## Open questions\n- Should the counter be exposed as a readable data port (wirable to\n  another box as an input) in addition to being shown in the inspector?\n- Should auto-grow prompt for the output name immediately on connect, or\n  generate a placeholder (`out_N`) that the user renames afterward?\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. `libs/iterator.lua` — trivial passthrough function.\n2. `libs/iterator.sh`, `libs/iterator.c` — same for bash and C.\n3. `src/001-schema.lua` — add `iterator_outputs` to the box validator.\n4. `src/004-executor.lua` — add counter state table; extend\n   `fire_connections` with the iterator branch; inject counter arg in\n   `run_task` when box has `iterator_outputs`.\n5. `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — iterator toggle; editable output slots.\n6. `assets/js/006-wires.js` — auto-grow output slots on connect;\n   auto-shrink + rename on disconnect (mirrors variadic input logic).\n7. `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — render N named output dots when\n   `iterator_outputs` is set (replacing the single-wire dot).\n\n## Relevant files\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — fire_connections, run_task\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — box validator\n- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — iterator toggle, slot editor\n- `assets/js/006-wires.js` — auto-grow/shrink for output slots\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box rendering\n- `issues/217-concat-box-and-dynamic-inputs.md` — variadic input model\n  (auto-grow/shrink logic mirrors this)\n- `issues/completed/108-branch-box-and-predicate-routing.md` — comparator\n  model that `from_branch` and the routing pattern extend from\n- `issues/219-map-compiler.md` — compiler integration notes above\n",
    "oldString":"### Compiler output (issue 219 integration)\nFor an iterator box, the compiler generates a closure with a captured\ncounter variable:\n\n```lua\nlocal router_counter = 0\nlocal function router(data)\n  local idx = router_counter\n  router_counter = (router_counter + 1) % 3\n  if     idx == 0 then worker_a(data)\n  elseif idx == 1 then worker_b(data)\n  else                  worker_c(data)\n  end\nend\n```\n\nThe iterator lib files are bundled alongside other box source files.\n\n### Threading model integration (3d-rts thread pool)\n\nIn the pthreads task pool, each box execution is a task struct containing:\n- A function pointer to the language-specific invocation wrapper\n- A pointer to shared memory holding the input arguments and return value\n- A pointer list of dependency tasks (upstream boxes whose output this box\n  needs before it can run)\n- For iterator boxes: a `counter` field (integer, part of the task struct)\n\n**Blocking:** when a task cannot run because its dependencies haven't\ncompleted, it is placed in the blocking task's waiting list. No memory is\nallocated — the task struct stays alive, only a pointer to it is moved.\nWhen the blocking task completes and writes its return value to shared\nmemory, it walks its waiting list and re-adds each waiting task to the\nmain queue (again, pointer move only — no reallocation or struct copying).\n\n**Iterator self-re-add:** when an iterator task completes, it does not\nterminate. Instead:\n1. It increments its own `counter` field (or wraps to 0).\n2. It checks if there is another pending input value in its input queue.\n3. If yes: it updates its input pointer to the next pending value, then\n   re-adds itself to the main task queue. No new allocation.\n4. If no: it adds itself to the waiting list of its upstream dependency,\n   to be re-added when the next input value arrives.\n\nThis means the iterator task struct is allocated once and lives for the\nduration of the run, cycling through the queue as many times as there are\ninput values to process. Input values are processed one-at-a-time in\narrival order — if 10 values are queued, the iterator visits the queue 10\ntimes, each time firing a different output path and advancing the counter.\n\n**C calling Lua:** the per-thread invocation wrapper is a C function\n(pthreads requires a C entry point). Each worker thread initializes its\nown `lua_State` at startup — Lua states are not thread-safe but one per\nthread is fine. The wrapper dispatches on language tag: if Lua, calls\nthrough the thread's `lua_State` via `lua_pcall`; if native C, calls the\nfunction pointer directly (no interpreter overhead); if bash, spawns a\nsubprocess (the one case that doesn't map cleanly to pthreads — see\ndocs/004-ipc-and-threading.md for options).",
    "newString":"### Compiler output (issue 219 integration)\nFor an iterator box, the compiler emits a counter variable and a\nrouting function — no inner function call, since the iterator does\nnot invoke anything:\n\n```lua\nlocal router_counter = 0\nlocal function router(data)\n  local idx = router_counter\n  router_counter = (router_counter + 1) % 3\n  if     idx == 0 then worker_a(data)\n  elseif idx == 1 then worker_b(data)\n  else                  worker_c(data)\n  end\nend\n```\n\nNo iterator lib file is bundled — there is none.\n\n### Threading model\nIterator routing in the thread pool runner is fully described in issue\n304. Briefly: each invocation is a `dispatch_task_t` with the current\ncounter value; on completion the dispatch action fires the routing\nconnection, increments the counter, and submits a successor task.     "originalFile":"# 221 — Iterator box: round-robin output routing with per-instance counter\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nNo mechanism exists for a box to distribute output across multiple\ndownstream paths in sequence. The comparator routes based on a value\nthreshold; the iterator routes based on a counter that advances each call.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\n### What it does\nAn iterator box receives one input value and routes it to one of N named\noutput wires. Which wire fires is determined by an internal counter that\nincrements each call and wraps back to 0 after the last output. There is\nno function — the dispatch layer copies input directly to output, no\nlanguage spec is invoked. The iterator is a pure routing primitive.\n\nUseful for distributing work across parallel paths, cycling through a\nlist of consumers, or producing round-robin load balancing in the graph.\n\n### Counter model\nThe counter is per-box-instance, stored in the executor's in-memory\nstate (keyed by box ID). It resets to 0 at the start of each run.\nPersistence across runs is not in scope; that is a separate issue.\n\nIn the compiler output (issue 219), the counter becomes a local variable\nin a generated closure — same reset-per-program-start behavior.\n\nWrap-around: `counter = (counter + 1) % #iterator_outputs`\n\n### No function — pure dispatch primitive\nThere is no iterator function in any language. There are no\n`libs/iterator.lua` / `iterator.sh` / `iterator.c` files. The dispatch\nlayer (issue 304) recognizes iterator boxes by the presence of\n`iterator_outputs` in the box JSON and handles routing itself:\n\n1. Read the input value from the input slot.\n2. Copy it directly into the output slot.\n3. Fire the connection whose `from_branch` matches\n   `iterator_outputs[counter]`.\n4. Increment counter mod `n_iter_outputs`.\n5. Re-spawn a successor dispatch task with the new counter value.\n\nThis replaces the earlier \"passthrough function\" design. The function\nwas always identity, so there was nothing to invoke — the dispatch\nlayer does the copy directly and skips the language spec entirely.\n\n### Data model\nBox JSON has an `iterator_outputs` field — an ordered array of\nuser-defined output path names. Iterator boxes do not carry `ref` or\n`fn`; those fields are absent (or, if present, ignored):\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"router\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"inputs\": [{\"name\": \"data\", \"type\": \"any\"}],\n  \"iterator_outputs\": [\"path_a\", \"path_b\", \"path_c\"],\n  \"connections\": [\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"router\", \"from_branch\": \"path_a\",\n      \"to_box\": \"worker-a\", \"to_input\": \"data\"\n    },\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"router\", \"from_branch\": \"path_b\",\n      \"to_box\": \"worker-b\", \"to_input\": \"data\"\n    },\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"router\", \"from_branch\": \"path_c\",\n      \"to_box\": \"worker-c\", \"to_input\": \"data\"\n    }\n  ]\n}\n```\n\n`from_branch` is reused for iterator output names — the same field\nthat holds \"lt\" / \"eq\" / \"gt\" for comparators. The dispatch layer\nchecks whether the box has `iterator_outputs`; if so, it routes by\ncounter as described above.\n\n### Auto-grow output slots\nConnecting a wire to the last slot of the iterator's output side appends\na new empty named slot — identical to the auto-grow behavior for variadic\ninputs (issue 217). The user names each slot in the inspector. Connecting\nto the last slot prompts for a name and grows the list. Disconnecting\nremoves the slot and compacts (same rename-and-compact logic as variadic\ninputs).\n\n### Dispatch layer integration\nThe dispatch layer (issue 304) is where iterator semantics live. The\ncounter is stored on the `dispatch_task_t` for each iterator\ninvocation; successor tasks carry the next counter value. There is no\nlanguage driver, no function call, no executor-state table — just the\ncounter on the task struct.\n\nSee issue 304 for the full dispatch flow. The iterator-specific path\nis short: read input slot, copy to output slot, fire the routing\nconnection, increment counter, re-spawn.\n\n### Inspector changes\nThe inspector shows:\n- An \"iterator\" toggle per box (like the variadic toggle on inputs)\n- When toggled on: the output side of the box renders named slots instead\n  of a single dot; a \"+\" row at the bottom adds a new slot\n- Each slot name is editable inline\n- The current counter value is shown as a read-only display (useful for\n  debugging live runs)\n\n### Compiler output (issue 219 integration)\nFor an iterator box, the compiler emits a counter variable and a\nrouting function — no inner function call, since the iterator does\nnot invoke anything:\n\n```lua\nlocal router_counter = 0\nlocal function router(data)\n  local idx = router_counter\n  router_counter = (router_counter + 1) % 3\n  if     idx == 0 then worker_a(data)\n  elseif idx == 1 then worker_b(data)\n  else                  worker_c(data)\n  end\nend\n```\n\nNo iterator lib file is bundled — there is none.\n\n### Threading model\nIterator routing in the thread pool runner is fully described in issue\n304. The\ninput slot is a queued (multi-cell) ring buffer that persists across\nre-spawns. See issues 302 (slot store) and 304 (dispatch layer) for\nthe full picture.\n\n## Open questions\n- Should the counter be exposed as a readable data port (wirable to\n  another box as an input) in addition to being shown in the inspector?\n- Should auto-grow prompt for the output name immediately on connect, or\n  generate a placeholder (`out_N`) that the user renames afterward?\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. `libs/iterator.lua` — trivial passthrough function.\n2. `libs/iterator.sh`, `libs/iterator.c` — same for bash and C.\n3. `src/001-schema.lua` — add `iterator_outputs` to the box validator.\n4. `src/004-executor.lua` — add counter state table; extend\n   `fire_connections` with the iterator branch; inject counter arg in\n   `run_task` when box has `iterator_outputs`.\n5. `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — iterator toggle; editable output slots.\n6. `assets/js/006-wires.js` — auto-grow output slots on connect;\n   auto-shrink + rename on disconnect (mirrors variadic input logic).\n7. `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — render N named output dots when\n   `iterator_outputs` is set (replacing the single-wire dot).\n\n## Relevant files\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — fire_connections, run_task\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — box validator\n- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — iterator toggle, slot editor\n- `assets/js/006-wires.js` — auto-grow/shrink for output slots\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box rendering\n- `issues/217-concat-box-and-dynamic-inputs.md` — variadic input model\n  (auto-grow/shrink logic mirrors this)\n- `issues/completed/108-branch-box-and-predicate-routing.md` — comparator\n  model that `from_branch` and the routing pattern extend from\n- `issues/219-map-compiler.md` — compiler integration notes above\n",

    "originalFile":"# 221 — Iterator box: round-robin output routing with per-instance counter\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nNo mechanism exists for a box to distribute output across multiple\ndownstream paths in sequence. The comparator routes based on a value\nthreshold; the iterator routes based on a counter that advances each call.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\n### What it does\nAn iterator box receives one input value and routes it to one of N named\noutput wires. Which wire fires is determined by an internal counter that\nincrements each call and wraps back to 0 after the last output. There is\nno function — the dispatch layer copies input directly to output, no\nlanguage spec is invoked. The iterator is a pure routing primitive.\n\nUseful for distributing work across parallel paths, cycling through a\nlist of consumers, or producing round-robin load balancing in the graph.\n\n### Counter model\nThe counter is per-box-instance, stored in the executor's in-memory\nstate (keyed by box ID). It resets to 0 at the start of each run.\nPersistence across runs is not in scope; that is a separate issue.\n\nIn the compiler output (issue 219), the counter becomes a local variable\nin a generated closure — same reset-per-program-start behavior.\n\nWrap-around: `counter = (counter + 1) % #iterator_outputs`\n\n### No function — pure dispatch primitive\nThere is no iterator function in any language. There are no\n`libs/iterator.lua` / `iterator.sh` / `iterator.c` files. The dispatch\nlayer (issue 304) recognizes iterator boxes by the presence of\n`iterator_outputs` in the box JSON and handles routing itself:\n\n1. Read the input value from the input slot.\n2. Copy it directly into the output slot.\n3. Fire the connection whose `from_branch` matches\n   `iterator_outputs[counter]`.\n4. Increment counter mod `n_iter_outputs`.\n5. Re-spawn a successor dispatch task with the new counter value.\n\nThis replaces the earlier \"passthrough function\" design. The function\nwas always identity, so there was nothing to invoke — the dispatch\nlayer does the copy directly and skips the language spec entirely.\n\n### Data model\nBox JSON has an `iterator_outputs` field — an ordered array of\nuser-defined output path names. Iterator boxes do not carry `ref` or\n`fn`; those fields are absent (or, if present, ignored):\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"router\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"inputs\": [{\"name\": \"data\", \"type\": \"any\"}],\n  \"iterator_outputs\": [\"path_a\", \"path_b\", \"path_c\"],\n  \"connections\": [\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"router\", \"from_branch\": \"path_a\",\n      \"to_box\": \"worker-a\", \"to_input\": \"data\"\n    },\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"router\", \"from_branch\": \"path_b\",\n      \"to_box\": \"worker-b\", \"to_input\": \"data\"\n    },\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"router\", \"from_branch\": \"path_c\",\n      \"to_box\": \"worker-c\", \"to_input\": \"data\"\n    }\n  ]\n}\n```\n\n`from_branch` is reused for iterator output names — the same field\nthat holds \"lt\" / \"eq\" / \"gt\" for comparators. The dispatch layer\nchecks whether the box has `iterator_outputs`; if so, it routes by\ncounter as described above.\n\n### Auto-grow output slots\nConnecting a wire to the last slot of the iterator's output side appends\na new empty named slot — identical to the auto-grow behavior for variadic\ninputs (issue 217). The user names each slot in the inspector. Connecting\nto the last slot prompts for a name and grows the list. Disconnecting\nremoves the slot and compacts (same rename-and-compact logic as variadic\ninputs).\n\n### Dispatch layer integration\nThe dispatch layer (issue 304) is where iterator semantics live. The\ncounter is stored on the `dispatch_task_t` for each iterator\ninvocation; successor tasks carry the next counter value. There is no\nlanguage driver, no function call, no executor-state table — just the\ncounter on the task struct.\n\nSee issue 304 for the full dispatch flow. The iterator-specific path\nis short: read input slot, copy to output slot, fire the routing\nconnection, increment counter, re-spawn.\n\n### Inspector changes\nThe inspector shows:\n- An \"iterator\" toggle per box (like the variadic toggle on inputs)\n- When toggled on: the output side of the box renders named slots instead\n  of a single dot; a \"+\" row at the bottom adds a new slot\n- Each slot name is editable inline\n- The current counter value is shown as a read-only display (useful for\n  debugging live runs)\n\n### Compiler output (issue 219 integration)\nFor an iterator box, the compiler emits a counter variable and a\nrouting function — no inner function call, since the iterator does\nnot invoke anything:\n\n```lua\nlocal router_counter = 0\nlocal function router(data)\n  local idx = router_counter\n  router_counter = (router_counter + 1) % 3\n  if     idx == 0 then worker_a(data)\n  elseif idx == 1 then worker_b(data)\n  else                  worker_c(data)\n  end\nend\n```\n\nNo iterator lib file is bundled — there is none.\n\n### Threading model\nIterator routing in the thread pool runner is fully described in issue\n304. Briefly: each invocation is a `dispatch_task_t` with the current\ncounter value; on completion the dispatch action fires the routing\nconnection, increments the counter, and submits a successor task. The\ninput slot is a queued (multi-cell) ring buffer that persists across\nre-spawns. See issues 302 (slot store) and 304 (dispatch layer) for\nthe full picture.\n\n## Open questions\n- Should the counter be exposed as a readable data port (wirable to\n  another box as an input) in addition to being shown in the inspector?\n- Should auto-grow prompt for the output name immediately on connect, or\n  generate a placeholder (`out_N`) that the user renames afterward?\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. `src/001-schema.lua` — add `iterator_outputs` to the box validator;\n   when present, `ref` and `fn` are not required.\n2. `src/004-executor.lua` (phase 2 path) — add per-box counter state;\n   extend `fire_connections` to route by `iterator_outputs[counter]`\n   and copy input → output without invoking a driver.\n3. `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — iterator toggle; editable output slots.\n4. `assets/js/006-wires.js` — auto-grow output slots on connect;\n   auto-shrink + rename on disconnect (mirrors variadic input logic).\n5. `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — render N named output dots when\n   `iterator_outputs` is set (replacing the single-wire dot).\n6. (Phase 3) Implement iterator dispatch in `src/008-pool-runner.c` per\n   issue 304 — counter on `dispatch_task_t`, successor re-spawn.\n\n## Relevant files\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — fire_connections, run_task\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — box validator\n- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — iterator toggle, slot editor\n- `assets/js/006-wires.js` — auto-grow/shrink for output slots\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box rendering\n- `issues/217-concat-box-and-dynamic-inputs.md` — variadic input model\n  (auto-grow/shrink logic mirrors this)\n- `issues/completed/108-branch-box-and-predicate-routing.md` — comparator\n  model that `from_branch` and the routing pattern extend from\n- `issues/219-map-compiler.md` — compiler integration notes above\n",
    "oldString":"## Relevant files\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — fire_connections, run_task\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — box validator\n- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — iterator toggle, slot editor\n- `assets/js/006-wires.js` — auto-grow/shrink for output slots\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box rendering\n- `issues/217-concat-box-and-dynamic-inputs.md` — variadic input model\n  (auto-grow/shrink logic mirrors this)\n- `issues/completed/108-branch-box-and-predicate-routing.md` — comparator\n  model that `from_branch` and the routing pattern extend from\n- `issues/219-map-compiler.md` — compiler integration notes above",
    "newString":"## Relevant files\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — phase 2 fire_connections / route-by-counter\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — box validator (`iterator_outputs` field)\n- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — iterator toggle, slot editor\n- `assets/js/006-wires.js` — auto-grow/shrink for output slots\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box rendering\n- `issues/217-concat-box-and-dynamic-inputs.md` — variadic input model\n  (auto-grow/shrink logic mirrors this)\n- `issues/completed/108-branch-box-and-predicate-routing.md` — comparator\n  model that `from_branch` and the routing pattern extend from\n- `issues/219-map-compiler.md` — compiler integration\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — phase 3 iterator dispatch (no\n  function invocation; routing only)",

          "content":"# 305 — C graph loader (replaces 003-loader.lua)\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nThe phase 2 loader at `src/003-loader.lua` reads a map directory's\n`boxes/*.json`, `data/*.json`, and metadata, decodes JSON via dkjson,\nruns schema validation, builds the in-memory graph table, and detects\nentry boxes. It is Lua. The synchronous executor consumes its output.\n\nThe phase 3 pool runner (issue 301) cannot embed a Lua state for\nloading — Lua appears in the runner only as a per-box language runtime,\nnever as the runner's own scripting layer. The loader is therefore\nported to C and lives inside (or alongside) `src/008-pool-runner.c`.\n\n## Concept\n\nThe C graph loader is the first phase of the pool runner's startup. It:\n1. Walks the map directory.\n2. Parses every JSON file.\n3. Validates schema and connection topology.\n4. Builds a single `graph_t` struct that the pool runner and dispatch\n   layer consume.\n\nThe loader is a one-shot at startup. It crashes the program on any\nvalidation failure (per the hard-crash policy in issue 303). There is\nno recovery, no skip-bad-boxes mode.\n\n## Inputs\n\nThe map directory layout (unchanged from phase 2):\n\n```\nmaps/<name>/\n    meta.json          ← entry box, src_dirs, run-level metadata\n    boxes/*.json       ← one file per box\n    data/*.json        ← static data values (literal inputs)\n    src/*              ← box function source files (resolved via meta.src_dirs)\n```\n\nThe loader is given the map directory path as a C string.\n\n## Output: `graph_t`\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    int           n_boxes;\n    box_t        *boxes;            // array of box descriptors\n    int           n_connections;\n    connection_t *connections;\n    int           n_size_classes;\n    int          *size_classes;     // distinct slot sizes the graph uses\n    int           n_entry_boxes;\n    int          *entry_box_ids;    // indices into boxes[]\n    int           n_languages;\n    const char  **languages;        // distinct language names used\n} graph_t;\n\ntypedef struct {\n    char         *id;               // user-defined box id (\"classifier\", \"stamp\", …)\n    char         *kind;             // \"call\" | \"data\"\n    char         *lang;             // \"lua\" | \"c\" | \"bash\" | ...; NULL for data and iterator/comparator\n    char         *ref;               // file path; NULL for data/iterator/comparator\n    char         *fn;                // function name; NULL for data/iterator/comparator\n    int           n_inputs;\n    input_decl_t *inputs;\n    int           output_capacity;  // bytes; 0 if variable-size (uses large-value heap)\n    int           is_comparator;\n    int           is_iterator;\n    int           n_iter_outputs;\n    char        **iter_output_names;\n    // …\n} box_t;\n\ntypedef struct {\n    int   from_box_id;\n    char *from_branch;              // NULL for plain call; \"lt\"/\"eq\"/\"gt\" for comparator;\n                                    // iterator output name otherwise\n    int   to_box_id;\n    char *to_input_name;\n    int   to_input_index;\n} connection_t;\n```\n\nStrings are owned by the graph (allocated from a single arena attached\nto the graph; freed when the graph is destroyed at the end of the run).\n\n## Loading phases\n\n### 1. Directory walk\nOpen the map directory, enumerate `boxes/`, `data/`, and the optional\n`meta.json`. Each entry is queued for parsing.\n\n### 2. JSON parse\nUse the vendored JSON parser (issue 301 lists cJSON / jsmn / hand-rolled\nas candidates). Each file becomes a parsed JSON tree. Parse errors are\nfatal — print the file path and the parser's error message, abort.\n\n### 3. Schema validation\nCheck each box's required fields:\n- `id`, `kind` always required.\n- For `kind == \"call\"`: either (a) `lang`, `ref`, `fn` (plain call\n  box), or (b) `iterator_outputs` (iterator box, no `ref`/`fn`), or\n  (c) `comparator` field set (comparator box, no `ref`/`fn`).\n- For `kind == \"data\"`: a `value` field; no `inputs` or `connections`.\n\nBox ids must be unique across the map. Connection endpoints must\nreference valid box ids and valid input names.\n\nSchema rules mirror `src/001-schema.lua`. The C validator is a port of\nthat file's logic, simplified by the absence of port-named branching\n(removed in issue 108 cleanup).\n\n### 4. Topology validation\n- Every connection's `from_box` and `to_box` exist.\n- Every connection's `to_input_name` matches a declared input on the\n  destination box.\n- No non-iterator cycles. The validator runs DFS; any cycle that does\n  not pass through an iterator box is rejected.\n- Every required input has at least one connection feeding it (or is\n  fed by a `data` box).\n\nValidation failure aborts the program with a precise error message —\nwhich box, which connection, what was wrong.\n\n### 5. Slot size class enumeration\nWalk every box and queued-input declaration to enumerate the distinct\nslot sizes the graph will need. Each unique size becomes a size class\nin the slot allocator (issue 302). Output:\n\n```c\ngraph->size_classes      = { 64, 256, 1024, 65536 };  // example\ngraph->n_size_classes    = 4;\n```\n\nThe slot allocator pre-populates each class's free list with enough\nslots to cover the static box count for that size, before any tasks\nare submitted.\n\n### 6. Entry-box detection\nA box is an entry box if either:\n- It has zero inputs, or\n- All of its inputs are connected only to `data` boxes (literal values\n  with no upstream computation).\n\nEntry boxes are submitted to the pool first; everything else fires from\npost-action routing in the dispatch layer.\n\n### 7. Language enumeration\nCollect the distinct `lang` values across all plain call boxes. The\npool runner uses this set to decide which language specs (issue 303)\nto load and which per-worker handles to initialize.\n\nIterator and comparator boxes have no `lang` and contribute nothing\nhere.\n\n## Error policy\n\nAny failure in any phase aborts the program. The loader prints:\n- The map path\n- The phase that failed (parse / schema / topology / etc.)\n- The specific file or box that caused the failure\n- The parser's or validator's diagnostic message\n\nThen `exit(1)`. There is no partial-load mode.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- JSON library choice: cJSON (heaviest, easiest, well-maintained),\n  jsmn (tiny, no allocations, manual tree walking), or hand-rolled\n  (smallest dependency footprint, more code). Decision deferred to\n  implementation time.\n- Arena size: the graph's string arena needs an initial size. A few\n  KB is fine for small maps; large maps with many boxes might need\n  more. Grow on demand vs pre-size from the file count.\n- Whether to keep `src/003-loader.lua` around for the phase 2\n  synchronous path. Since phase 2 is going away when phase 3 lands\n  (issue 301), the Lua loader retires with it. No long-term parity.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Vendor the chosen JSON parser into `libs/json/`.\n2. Define `graph_t`, `box_t`, `connection_t`, `input_decl_t` in\n   `src/008-pool-runner.c` (or a sibling header).\n3. Implement phase 1 (directory walk) and phase 2 (parse). Smoke test:\n   load `maps/hello`, print the parsed tree.\n4. Implement phase 3 (schema validation) one rule at a time. Each\n   rule has a unit test against a malformed map fixture.\n5. Implement phase 4 (topology validation), including the cycle\n   detector. Test against `maps/branch-test` (valid) and a fixture\n   with a non-iterator cycle (invalid).\n6. Implement phase 5 (size class enumeration). Output should match\n   the box outputs declared in `maps/hello` and `maps/classify-demo`.\n7. Implement phases 6 (entry boxes) and 7 (languages). Verify against\n   known maps.\n8. Wire the loader into `src/008-pool-runner.c`'s `main` so the pool\n   runner starts by loading and validating before doing anything\n   else.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/003-loader.lua` — phase 2 loader, ported by this issue\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — phase 2 schema validator, also ported\n- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — pool runner that owns and uses the loader\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle that\n  consumes the graph\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — slot allocator that consumes\n  the size class list\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — spec registry that consumes\n  the language list\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — dispatch layer that consumes\n  the box and connection arrays\n- `issues/219-map-compiler.md` — the compiler is the other consumer of\n  the same validation logic; the C loader and the compiler should\n  share validation code if possible\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/305-c-graph-loader.md"
        },

The C validator is a port of\nthat file's logic, simplified by the absence of port-named branching\n(removed in issue 108 cleanup).\n\n### 4. Topology validation\n- Every connection's `from_box` and `to_box` exist.\n- Every connection's `to_input_name` matches a declared input on the\n  destination box.\n- No non-iterator cycles. The validator runs DFS; any cycle that does\n  not pass through an iterator box is rejected.\n- Every required input has at least one connection feeding it (or is\n  fed by a `data` box).\n\nValidation failure aborts the program with a precise error message —\nwhich box, which connection, what was wrong.\n\n### 5. Slot size class enumeration\nWalk every box and queued-input declaration to enumerate the distinct\nslot sizes the graph will need. Each unique size becomes a size class\nin the slot allocator (issue 302). Output:\n\n```c\ngraph->size_classes      = { 64, 256, 1024, 65536 };  // example\ngraph->n_size_classes    = 4;\n```\n\nThe slot allocator pre-populates each class's free list with enough\nslots to cover the static box count for that size, before any tasks\nare submitted.\n\n### 6. Entry-box detection\nA box is an entry box if either:\n- It has zero inputs, or\n- All of its inputs are connected only to `data` boxes (literal values\n  with no upstream computation).\n\nEntry boxes are submitted to the pool first; everything else fires from\npost-action routing in the dispatch layer.\n\n### 7. Language enumeration\nCollect the distinct `lang` values across all plain call boxes. The\npool runner uses this set to decide which language specs (issue 303)\nto load and which per-worker handles to initialize.\n\nIterator and comparator boxes have no `lang` and contribute nothing\nhere.\n\n## Error policy\n\nAny failure in any phase aborts the program. The loader prints:\n- The map path\n- The phase that failed (parse / schema / topology / etc.)\n- The specific file or box that caused the failure\n- The parser's or validator's diagnostic message\n\nThen `exit(1)`. There is no partial-load mode.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- JSON library choice: cJSON (heaviest, easiest, well-maintained),\n  jsmn (tiny, no allocations, manual tree walking), or hand-rolled\n  (smallest dependency footprint, more code). Decision deferred to\n  implementation time.\n- Arena size: the graph's string arena needs an initial size. A few\n  KB is fine for small maps; large maps with many boxes might need\n  more. Grow on demand vs pre-size from the file count.\n- Whether to keep `src/003-loader.lua` around for the phase 2\n  synchronous path. Since phase 2 is going away when phase 3 lands\n  (issue 301), the Lua loader retires with it. No long-term parity.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Vendor the chosen JSON parser into `libs/json/`.\n2. Define `graph_t`, `box_t`, `connection_t`, `input_decl_t` in\n   `src/008-pool-runner.c` (or a sibling header).\n3. Implement phase 1 (directory walk) and phase 2 (parse). Smoke test:\n   load `maps/hello`, print the parsed tree.\n4. Implement phase 3 (schema validation) one rule at a time. Each\n   rule has a unit test against a malformed map fixture.\n5. Implement phase 4 (topology validation), including the cycle\n   detector. Test against `maps/branch-test` (valid) and a fixture\n   with a non-iterator cycle (invalid).\n6. Implement phase 5 (size class enumeration). Output should match\n   the box outputs declared in `maps/hello` and `maps/classify-demo`.\n7. Implement phases 6 (entry boxes) and 7 (languages). Verify against\n   known maps.\n8. Wire the loader into `src/008-pool-runner.c`'s `main` so the pool\n   runner starts by loading and validating before doing anything\n   else.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/003-loader.lua` — phase 2 loader, ported by this issue\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — phase 2 schema validator, also ported\n- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — pool runner that owns and uses the loader\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle that\n  consumes the graph\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — slot allocator that consumes\n  the size class list\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — spec registry that consumes\n  the language list\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — dispatch layer that consumes\n  the box and connection arrays\n- `issues/219-map-compiler.md` — the compiler is the other consumer of\n  the same validation logic; the C loader and the compiler should\n  share validation code if possible\n"
  },

    "snippet":"1\t# 305 — C graph loader (replaces 003-loader.lua)\n2\t\n3\t## Status\n4\topen\n5\t\n6\t## Current behavior\n7\tThe phase 2 loader at `src/003-loader.lua` reads a map directory's\n8\t`boxes/*.json`, `data/*.json`, and metadata, decodes JSON via dkjson,\n9\truns schema validation, builds the in-memory graph table, and detects\n10\tentry boxes. It is Lua. The synchronous executor consumes its output.\n11\t\n12\tThe phase 3 pool runner (issue 301) cannot embed a Lua state for\n13\tloading — Lua appears in the runner only as a per-box language runtime,\n14\tnever as the runner's own scripting layer. The loader is therefore\n15\tported to C and lives inside (or alongside) `src/008-pool-runner.c`.\n16\t\n17\t## Concept\n18\t\n19\tThe C graph loader is the first phase of the pool runner's startup. It:\n20\t1. Walks the map directory.\n21\t2. Parses every JSON file.\n22\t3. Validates schema and connection topology.\n23\t4. Builds a single `graph_t` struct that the pool runner and dispatch\n24\t   layer consume.\n25\t\n26\tThe loader is a one-shot at startup. It crashes the program on any\n27\tvalidation failure (per the hard-crash policy in issue 303). There is\n28\tno recovery, no skip-bad-boxes mode.\n29\t\n30\t## Inputs\n31\t\n32\tThe map directory layout (unchanged from phase 2):\n33\t\n34\t```\n35\tmaps/<name>/\n36\t    meta.json          ← entry box, src_dirs, run-level metadata\n37\t    boxes/*.json       ← one file per box\n38\t    data/*.json        ← static data values (literal inputs)\n39\t    src/*              ← box function source files (resolved via meta.src_dirs)\n40\t```\n41\t\n42\tThe loader is given the map directory path as a C string.\n43\t\n44\t## Output: `graph_t`\n45\t\n46\t```c\n47\ttypedef struct {\n48\t    int           n_boxes;\n49\t    box_t        *boxes;            // array of box descriptors\n50\t    int           n_connections;\n51\t    connection_t *connections;\n52\t    int           n_size_classes;\n53\t    int          *size_classes;     // distinct slot sizes the graph uses\n54\t    int           n_entry_boxes;\n55\t    int          *entry_box_ids;    // indices into boxes[]\n56\t    int           n_languages;\n57\t    const char  **languages;        // distinct language names used\n58\t} graph_t;\n59\t\n60\ttypedef struct {\n61\t    char         *id;               // user-defined box id (\"classifier\", \"stamp\", …)\n62\t    char         *kind;             // \"call\" | \"data\"\n63\t    char         *lang;             // \"lua\" | \"c\" | \"bash\" | ...;         "text":"**Answering your questions on 305:**\n\n**(1) call vs data kinds:** Yes, exactly. A `call` box runs a function — at runtime it gets a `dispatch_task_t`, the dispatch layer reads its inputs, calls the language spec (or routes if iterator/comparator), and writes an output. A `data` box is a literal value embedded in the map at compile time — no function, no language runtime involvement, no task in the pool. Its job is to provide a stored value to whatever it's wired to as input. The slot for a data box is filled at startup by the loader and stays filled for the run; consumers read it like any other slot. Conceptually: `call` is a verb, `data` is a noun.\n\n**(2) Per-thread pre-allocation:** Yes, that's the right multiplier. Pre-allocate `n_workers × n_boxes_at_size_S` slots per size class. The reasoning: the worst case is every worker concurrently running a box that allocates an output slot of that size. Anything less risks contention or growth on the hot path. Anything more is waste. Updating 305 (and the recommendation flows to 302).\n\n**(3) No singular entry point:** Glad it lands. The user lays out the initial state via data boxes and entry call boxes, the runner submits them all at once, the graph fires from there.\n\n**(4) Built-in language-agnostic primitives:** Good distinction to draw — there are two separate categories:\n\n- **Dispatch-layer primitives** (graph topology): iterator and comparator. These don't invoke a spec. They live in the dispatch layer because their behavior *is* graph routing. Splitters/fan-out are already free via wire fan-out. I don't see a third primitive that fits this category — what other \"pure topology\" operations are there? Maybe a \"gate\" (only forward when a control input is truthy) and a \"merge\" (forward whichever input arrives first), but those are speculative.\n- **Shipped libraries** (data transformation): JSON parse/serialize, file read/write, string concat/split, regex. These are not language-agnostic at the implementation level — string semantics differ between Lua and C and Bash. They belong in `libs/` per language: `libs/json.lua`, `libs/json.c`, `libs/files.lua`, etc. The user picks the language they're working in, then uses the shipped lib for that language. Already partly done (`libs/ollama.lua`, the existing data lib).\n\nUpdating 305:"

          "new_string":"### 3. Schema validation\nBox kinds and what they mean at runtime:\n\n- **`call`** is a verb — a box that runs a function (or, for iterator\n  and comparator variants, a dispatch-layer routing primitive). Each\n  call box becomes a `dispatch_task_t` in the pool when its inputs\n  are ready.\n- **`data`** is a noun — a literal value embedded in the map. It has\n  no function and produces no task in the pool. Its output slot is\n  allocated and filled at startup by the loader and remains filled\n  for the duration of the run; downstream consumers read it like any\n  other slot.\n\nRequired fields per kind:\n- `id`, `kind` always required.\n- For `kind == \"call\"`: either (a) `lang`, `ref`, `fn` (plain call\n  box), or (b) `iterator_outputs` (iterator box, no `ref`/`fn`), or\n  (c) `comparator` field set (comparator box, no `ref`/`fn`).\n- For `kind == \"data\"`: a `value` field; no `inputs` or `connections`\n  (other than outgoing wires from this box's output slot).\n\nBox ids must be unique across the map. Connection endpoints must\nreference valid box ids and valid input names.",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/305-c-graph-loader.md",

        "input":{
          "new_string":"Iterator and comparator boxes have no `lang` and contribute nothing\nhere.\n\n### Note on built-in primitives vs shipped libraries\n\nThere are two distinct categories of \"things the user gets out of the\nbox,\" and they live in different places:\n\n- **Dispatch-layer primitives** are graph-topology operations whose\n  semantics are routing, not data transformation. Iterator and\n  comparator are the two so far. They have no `lang` / `ref` / `fn` —\n  the dispatch layer implements their behavior directly. Splitter\n  / fan-out is already free via wire fan-out and does not need its\n  own box kind. Possible future primitives: a \"gate\" (forward only\n  when a control input is truthy), a \"merge\" (forward whichever\n  input arrives first). These are not on the roadmap; flagged here\n  so the door stays open.\n- **Shipped libraries** are data-transformation utilities — JSON\n  parse/serialize, file read/write, string concat/split, regex,\n  shell-out. These are language-specific (string semantics differ\n  between Lua, C, and Bash) and ship as `libs/<name>.<ext>` per\n  language. They are not built into the dispatch layer; they are\n  ordinary call-box source files that users wire into their maps.\n  `libs/ollama.lua` is an existing example.\n\nThe distinction matters: dispatch-layer primitives change the graph\nmodel; shipped libraries don't. A dispatch primitive can do things a\nfunction call cannot (like routing on a counter); a library is just\ncode that happens to be vendored.",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/305-c-graph-loader.md",
          "replace_all":false,
          "old_string":"Iterator and comparator boxes have no `lang` and contribute nothing\nhere.\n\n-- also, there should be splitters and concatenators that are built into the\n   system. Also maybe data parsers that either parse json or read in text files?\n   maybe read and write for those. Any other ideas for potential functions we\n   could bundle, that are language agnostic?"
        },
        "id":"toolu_01L8GyCzoj3oFUMaw71Jknqt"
      }]

A dispatch primitive can do things a\nfunction call cannot (like routing on a counter); a library is just\ncode that happens to be vendored.",

        "input":{
          "content":"# 306 — Lua language spec implementation (reference spec)\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nLua boxes today run via `drivers/lua.sh`, which spawns a fresh `luajit`\nprocess per box invocation, feeds it stdin, and reads stdout. Process\nspawn cost dominates; each call is its own fresh interpreter. There is\nno persistent Lua state between calls.\n\n## Concept\nThe Lua language spec implements `lang_spec_t` (issue 303) for Lua. It\nis the first reference implementation of the spec interface and the\nproof that the in-process FFI model works. It is also the simplest\ncase — no compile step, no out-of-process server.\n\nEach worker thread gets its own `lua_State`. States are not shared.\nPer-thread states need no locking on the call path; the state's\ninternals are only ever touched by the worker that owns it.\n\n`langs/lua/spec.c` is built into `langs/lua/spec.so` and loaded by\nthe pool runner via `dlopen` at startup, like any other spec.\n\n## Per-worker state\n\nInit creates a fresh `lua_State` and configures it:\n\n```c\nvoid *lua_init(int worker_idx) {\n    lua_State *L = luaL_newstate();\n    luaL_openlibs(L);\n    set_package_path(L);   // libs/, map src/, meta.json src_dirs\n    return L;\n}\n\nvoid lua_teardown(void *handle) {\n    lua_close((lua_State *)handle);\n}\n```\n\n`set_package_path` writes `package.path` and `package.cpath` to\ninclude:\n- The SoraMech `libs/` directory\n- The map's `src/` directory\n- Every directory listed in `meta.json src_dirs`\n\nThis is the same set the phase 2 runner builds. The path is set once\nat init; it does not change at runtime.\n\n## File-and-function caching\n\nA naive `invoke` would `luaL_loadfile` and look up the function on\nevery call. Both are unnecessary work — the file's chunk does not\nchange during a run, and the function reference is stable.\n\nThe Lua spec keeps a per-handle cache: for each box source file\nloaded, store the table returned by the file's chunk as a Lua\nregistry key (`LUA_REGISTRYINDEX`). On first invocation:\n1. `luaL_loadfile(L, file_path)` — loads the chunk.\n2. `lua_pcall(L, 0, 1, 0)` — runs the chunk, expecting a returned\n   table.\n3. Store the table in the registry under a key derived from `file_path`.\n\nOn subsequent invocations:\n1. Look up the registry entry by `file_path`.\n2. Index it by `fn_name` to get the function reference.\n3. Skip `luaL_loadfile` entirely.\n\nThe cache is per-`lua_State` and therefore per-worker; no\nsynchronization is needed.\n\n## Box file convention\n\nA Lua box file returns a table whose keys are the box's exported\nfunction names:\n\n```lua\n-- maps/<name>/src/classify.lua\nlocal M = {}\n\nfunction M.classify(text)\n    if text:match(\"^%d+$\") then return \"numeric\"\n    elseif text:match(\"[a-z]\") then return \"alpha\"\n    else return \"other\"\n    end\nend\n\nreturn M\n```\n\nThe box JSON references it by `ref = \"classify.lua\"`, `fn = \"classify\"`.\nThe spec loads `classify.lua`, stores its returned table, and indexes\ninto it with `\"classify\"` to get the function.\n\nThis is the existing phase 2 convention — kept as-is.\n\n## Input marshalling\n\nInputs arrive at `invoke` as `(void *bytes, int size)` pairs. The\nspec needs to push them onto the Lua stack as Lua values.\n\nThe simplest, most general encoding: every input is a Lua string\n(`lua_pushlstring(L, bytes, size)`). The Lua function is responsible\nfor parsing strings into numbers, JSON, or whatever it expects. This\nis also what the phase 2 driver does — every argument arrives as a\nstring from argv.\n\nThis means a Lua function that wants a number does:\n```lua\nfunction M.add(a_str, b_str)\n    return tonumber(a_str) + tonumber(b_str)\nend\n```\n\nThe user pays a `tonumber` for numeric inputs. Acceptable for a first\npass. A future optimization could add per-input type hints to the\ngraph and let the spec push numbers directly.\n\n## Return marshalling\n\nThe Lua function returns a single value. The spec converts it to\nbytes:\n- String: `lua_tolstring` → copy into `out_buf`, set `*out_size`.\n- Number: `lua_tonumber` → format with `snprintf(\"%.17g\", ...)` into\n  `out_buf`, set `*out_size` to the string length.\n- Table: serialize to JSON via a vendored Lua JSON library (or a\n  small inline serializer for flat tables).\n- nil: `out_buf[0] = 0`, `*out_size = 0`. (Whether nil is a valid\n  return is an open question — see below.)\n- Other: error, abort.\n\nOutput buffer is sized to the box's declared `output_capacity`\n(issue 305's `box_t`). If the serialized value exceeds that, abort\n(per the hard-crash policy in issue 303).\n\nFor variable-size outputs (the box uses the large-value heap, issue\n302), the spec writes into the large-value heap and stores the\nhandle in `out_buf`. The dispatch layer routes the handle to the\nslot.\n\n## Error handling\n\nEvery `lua_pcall` is wrapped:\n```c\nint rc = lua_pcall(L, n_args, 1, 0);\nif (rc != LUA_OK) {\n    fprintf(stderr, \"[lua spec] %s:%s — %s\\n\",\n            file_path, fn_name, lua_tostring(L, -1));\n    lua_pop(L, 1);\n    return 1;  // dispatch layer aborts the program\n}\n```\n\nLua errors (`error(...)`, runtime errors, syntax errors during file\nload) all surface here as nonzero `pcall` returns. The spec prints\nthe box context and the Lua error message to stderr, then returns\nnonzero. The dispatch layer aborts.\n\nThere is no try-and-recover. Per issue 303, errors crash the program.\n\n## Build\n\n```\nlangs/lua/\n    spec.c          ← lang_spec_t implementation\n    Makefile        ← builds spec.so\n    spec.so         ← built artifact (gitignored)\n```\n\nThe Makefile target:\n```make\nspec.so: spec.c\n\t$(CC) -shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall \\\n\t    -I$(LUA_INCLUDE) \\\n\t    -o $@ $< \\\n\t    -L$(LUA_LIB) -lluajit-5.1\n```\n\nLuaJIT is the assumed runtime — it matches the phase 2 driver and the\nproject preference (LuaJIT-compatible Lua, no 5.4 syntax). The build\nlinks against the system LuaJIT shared library.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Lua `nil` return: should this be an error (every box must return\n  something), or a valid \"empty\" output? The phase 2 driver treats\n  any return as a success. Probably keep that — `nil` serializes to\n  zero bytes in the slot, downstream consumers can interpret as they\n  like.\n- Multiple return values: Lua functions can return multiple values.\n  Phase 2 ignored everything past the first. Keep that — boxes have\n  one output slot, period.\n- Table output serialization: vendor a Lua JSON library (dkjson is\n  already vendored), or write a small inline serializer for the\n  common case. dkjson is already there; reuse it via `require`.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Set up `langs/lua/` directory with a Makefile that builds an empty\n   `spec.so` exporting a stub `soramech_lang_spec`.\n2. Implement `init` and `teardown`. Verify the pool runner can\n   `dlopen` the spec and call `init` per worker without errors.\n3. Implement file-and-function caching — load a file, store its\n   returned table in the registry, look it up later.\n4. Implement input marshalling: push bytes as strings, count args.\n5. Implement `lua_pcall` invocation with error wrapping.\n6. Implement string return marshalling. Smoke test: `maps/hello`\n   end-to-end through the pool.\n7. Implement number return marshalling.\n8. Implement table-via-JSON return marshalling.\n9. Add `package.path` resolution for libs/, src/, and `meta.src_dirs`.\n10. Test against `maps/classify-demo` and `maps/driver-test` (Lua\n    portions).\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `drivers/lua.sh` — phase 2 Lua driver, retired by this spec\n- `langs/lang-spec.h` — interface header (issue 303)\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — spec contract this implements\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — dispatch layer that calls\n  `invoke`\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — large-value heap for\n  variable-size returns\n- `libs/dkjson` (vendored) — table-to-JSON serialization\n- `maps/hello`, `maps/classify-demo` — Lua-only smoke test maps\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/306-lua-language-spec.md"
        },
        "id":"toolu_01BvjTqxCb6XAGWN7k5NfJQs"
      }]

It is also the simplest\ncase — no compile step, no out-of-process server.\n\nEach worker thread gets its own `lua_State`. States are not shared.\nPer-thread states need no locking on the call path; the state's\ninternals are only ever touched by the worker that owns it.\n\n`langs/lua/spec.c` is built into `langs/lua/spec.so` and loaded by\nthe pool runner via `dlopen` at startup, like any other spec.\n\n## Per-worker state\n\nInit creates a fresh `lua_State` and configures it:\n\n```c\nvoid *lua_init(int worker_idx) {\n    lua_State *L = luaL_newstate();\n    luaL_openlibs(L);\n    set_package_path(L);   // libs/, map src/, meta.json src_dirs\n    return L;\n}\n\nvoid lua_teardown(void *handle) {\n    lua_close((lua_State *)handle);\n}\n```\n\n`set_package_path` writes `package.path` and `package.cpath` to\ninclude:\n- The SoraMech `libs/` directory\n- The map's `src/` directory\n- Every directory listed in `meta.json src_dirs`\n\nThis is the same set the phase 2 runner builds. The path is set once\nat init; it does not change at runtime.\n\n## File-and-function caching\n\nA naive `invoke` would `luaL_loadfile` and look up the function on\nevery call. Both are unnecessary work — the file's chunk does not\nchange during a run, and the function reference is stable.\n\nThe Lua spec keeps a per-handle cache: for each box source file\nloaded, store the table returned by the file's chunk as a Lua\nregistry key (`LUA_REGISTRYINDEX`). On first invocation:\n1. `luaL_loadfile(L, file_path)` — loads the chunk.\n2. `lua_pcall(L, 0, 1, 0)` — runs the chunk, expecting a returned\n   table.\n3. Store the table in the registry under a key derived from `file_path`.\n\nOn subsequent invocations:\n1. Look up the registry entry by `file_path`.\n2. Index it by `fn_name` to get the function reference.\n3. Skip `luaL_loadfile` entirely.\n\nThe cache is per-`lua_State` and therefore per-worker; no\nsynchronization is needed.\n\n## Box file convention\n\nA Lua box file returns a table whose keys are the box's exported\nfunction names:\n\n```lua\n-- maps/<name>/src/classify.lua\nlocal M = {}\n\nfunction M.classify(text)\n    if text:match(\"^%d+$\") then return \"numeric\"\n    elseif text:match(\"[a-z]\") then return \"alpha\"\n    else return \"other\"\n    end\nend\n\nreturn M\n```\n\nThe box JSON references it by `ref = \"classify.lua\"`, `fn = \"classify\"`.\nThe spec loads `classify.lua`, stores its returned table, and indexes\ninto it with `\"classify\"` to get the function.\n\nThis is the existing phase 2 convention — kept as-is.\n\n## Input marshalling\n\nInputs arrive at `invoke` as `(void *bytes, int size)` pairs. The\nspec needs to push them onto the Lua stack as Lua values.\n\nThe simplest, most general encoding: every input is a Lua string\n(`lua_pushlstring(L, bytes, size)`). The Lua function is responsible\nfor parsing strings into numbers, JSON, or whatever it expects. This\nis also what the phase 2 driver does — every argument arrives as a\nstring from argv.\n\nThis means a Lua function that wants a number does:\n```lua\nfunction M.add(a_str, b_str)\n    return tonumber(a_str) + tonumber(b_str)\nend\n```\n\nThe user pays a `tonumber` for numeric inputs. Acceptable for a first\npass. A future optimization could add per-input type hints to the\ngraph and let the spec push numbers directly.\n\n## Return marshalling\n\nThe Lua function returns a single value. The spec converts it to\nbytes:\n- String: `lua_tolstring` → copy into `out_buf`, set `*out_size`.\n- Number: `lua_tonumber` → format with `snprintf(\"%.17g\", ...)` into\n  `out_buf`, set `*out_size` to the string length.\n- Table: serialize to JSON via a vendored Lua JSON library (or a\n  small inline serializer for flat tables).\n- nil: `out_buf[0] = 0`, `*out_size = 0`. (Whether nil is a valid\n  return is an open question — see below.)\n- Other: error, abort.\n\nOutput buffer is sized to the box's declared `output_capacity`\n(issue 305's `box_t`). If the serialized value exceeds that, abort\n(per the hard-crash policy in issue 303).\n\nFor variable-size outputs (the box uses the large-value heap, issue\n302), the spec writes into the large-value heap and stores the\nhandle in `out_buf`. The dispatch layer routes the handle to the\nslot.\n\n## Error handling\n\nEvery `lua_pcall` is wrapped:\n```c\nint rc = lua_pcall(L, n_args, 1, 0);\nif (rc != LUA_OK) {\n    fprintf(stderr, \"[lua spec] %s:%s — %s\\n\",\n            file_path, fn_name, lua_tostring(L, -1));\n    lua_pop(L, 1);\n    return 1;  // dispatch layer aborts the program\n}\n```\n\nLua errors (`error(...)`, runtime errors, syntax errors during file\nload) all surface here as nonzero `pcall` returns. The spec prints\nthe box context and the Lua error message to stderr, then returns\nnonzero. The dispatch layer aborts.\n\nThere is no try-and-recover. Per issue 303, errors crash the program.\n\n## Build\n\n```\nlangs/lua/\n    spec.c          ← lang_spec_t implementation\n    Makefile        ← builds spec.so\n    spec.so         ← built artifact (gitignored)\n```\n\nThe Makefile target:\n```make\nspec.so: spec.c\n\t$(CC) -shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall \\\n\t    -I$(LUA_INCLUDE) \\\n\t    -o $@ $< \\\n\t    -L$(LUA_LIB) -lluajit-5.1\n```\n\nLuaJIT is the assumed runtime — it matches the phase 2 driver and the\nproject preference (LuaJIT-compatible Lua, no 5.4 syntax). The build\nlinks against the system LuaJIT shared library.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Lua `nil` return: should this be an error (every box must return\n  something), or a valid \"empty\" output? The phase 2 driver treats\n  any return as a success. Probably keep that — `nil` serializes to\n  zero bytes in the slot, downstream consumers can interpret as they\n  like.\n- Multiple return values: Lua functions can return multiple values.\n  Phase 2 ignored everything past the first. Keep that — boxes have\n  one output slot, period.\n- Table output serialization: vendor a Lua JSON library (dkjson is\n  already vendored), or write a small inline serializer for the\n  common case. dkjson is already there; reuse it via `require`.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Set up `langs/lua/` directory with a Makefile that builds an empty\n   `spec.so` exporting a stub `soramech_lang_spec`.\n2. Implement `init` and `teardown`. Verify the pool runner can\n   `dlopen` the spec and call `init` per worker without errors.\n3. Implement file-and-function caching — load a file, store its\n   returned table in the registry, look it up later.\n4. Implement input marshalling: push bytes as strings, count args.\n5. Implement `lua_pcall` invocation with error wrapping.\n6. Implement string return marshalling. Smoke test: `maps/hello`\n   end-to-end through the pool.\n7. Implement number return marshalling.\n8. Implement table-via-JSON return marshalling.\n9. Add `package.path` resolution for libs/, src/, and `meta.src_dirs`.\n10. Test against `maps/classify-demo` and `maps/driver-test` (Lua\n    portions).\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `drivers/lua.sh` — phase 2 Lua driver, retired by this spec\n- `langs/lang-spec.h` — interface header (issue 303)\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — spec contract this implements\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — dispatch layer that calls\n  `invoke`\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — large-value heap for\n  variable-size returns\n- `libs/dkjson` (vendored) — table-to-JSON serialization\n- `maps/hello`, `maps/classify-demo` — Lua-only smoke test maps\n"
  },

{
