  "attachment":{
    "type":"edited_text_file",
    "snippet":"1\t# 306 — Lua language spec implementation (reference spec)\n2\t\n3\t## Status\n4\topen\n5\t\n6\t## Current behavior\n7\tLua boxes today run via `drivers/lua.sh`, which spawns a fresh `luajit`\n8\tprocess per box invocation, feeds it stdin, and reads stdout. Process\n9\tspawn cost dominates; each call is its own fresh interpreter. There is\n10\tno persistent Lua state between calls.\n11\t\n12\t## Concept\n13\tThe Lua language spec implements `lang_spec_t` (issue 303) for Lua. It\n14\tis the first reference implementation of the spec interface and the\n15\tproof that the in-process FFI model works. It is also the simplest\n16\tcase — no compile step, no out-of-process server.\n17\t\n18\tEach worker thread gets its own `lua_State`. States are not shared.\n19\tPer-thread states need no locking on the call path; the state's\n20\tinternals are only ever touched by the worker that owns it.\n21\t\n22\t`langs/lua/spec.c` is built into `langs/lua/spec.so` and loaded by\n23\tthe pool runner via `dlopen` at startup, like any other spec.\n24\t\n25\t## Per-worker state\n26\t\n27\tInit creates a fresh `lua_State` and configures it:\n28\t\n29\t```c\n30\tvoid *lua_init(int worker_idx) {\n31\t    lua_State *L = luaL_newstate();\n32\t    luaL_openlibs(L);\n33\t    set_package_path(L);   // libs/, map src/, meta.json src_dirs\n34\t    return L;\n35\t}\n36\t\n37\tvoid lua_teardown(void *handle) {\n38\t    lua_close((lua_State *)handle);\n39\t}\n40\t```\n41\t\n42\t`set_package_path` writes `package.path` and `package.cpath` to\n43\tinclude:\n44\t- The SoraMech `libs/` directory\n45\t- The map's `src/` directory\n46\t- Every directory listed in `meta.json src_dirs`\n47\t\n48\t-- I think we should only include the map's src/ directory. The compile button\n49\t   in the editor should copy all the required files into the map's src/ directory\n50\t   so that there's only one place to look for functions and such. That way, we\n51\t   can make these programs portable by just sharing the directory with others.\n52\t\n53\tThis is the same set the phase 2 runner builds. The path is set once\n54\tat init; it does not change at runtime.\n55\t\n56\t## File-and-function caching\n57\t\n58\tA naive `invoke` would `luaL_loadfile` and look up the function on\n59\tevery call. Both are unnecessary work — the file's chunk does not\n60\tchange during a run, and the function reference is stable.\n61\t\n62\tThe Lua spec keeps a per-handle cache: for each box source file\n63\tloaded, store the table returned by the file's chunk as a Lua\n64\tregistry key (`LUA_REGISTRYINDEX`). On first invocation:\n65\t1. `luaL_loadfile(L, file_path)` — loads the chunk.\n66\t2. `lua_pcall(L, 0, 1, 0)` — runs the chunk, expecting a returned\n67\t   table.\n68\t3. Store the table in the registry under a key derived from `file_path`.\n69\t\n70\tOn subsequent invocations:\n71\t1. Look up the registry entry by `file_path`.\n72\t2. Index it by `fn_name` to get the function reference.\n73\t3. Skip `luaL_loadfile` entirely.\n74\t\n75\tThe cache is per-`lua_State` and therefore per-worker; no\n76\tsynchronization is needed.\n77\t\n78\t## Box file convention\n79\t\n80\tA Lua box file returns a table whose keys are the box's exported\n81\tfunction names:\n82\t\n83\t```lua\n84\t-- maps/<name>/src/classify.lua\n85\tlocal M = {}\n86\t\n87\tfunction M.classify(text)\n88\t    if text:match(\"^%d+$\") then return \"numeric\"\n89\t    elseif text:match(\"[a-z]\") then return \"alpha\"\n90\t    else return \"other\"\n91\t    end\n92\tend\n93\t\n94\treturn M\n95\t```\n96\t\n97\tThe box JSON references it by `ref = \"classify.lua\"`, `fn = \"classify\"`.\n98\tThe spec loads `classify.lua`, stores its returned table, and indexes\n99\tinto it with `\"classify\"` to get the function.\n100\t\n101\tThis is the existing phase 2 convention — kept as-is.\n102\t\n103\t## Input marshalling\n104\t\n105\tInputs arrive at `invoke` as `(void *bytes, int size)` pairs. The\n106\tspec needs to push them onto the Lua stack as Lua values.\n107\t\n108\tThe simplest, most general encoding: every input is a Lua string\n109\t(`lua_pushlstring(L, bytes, size)`). The Lua function is responsible\n110\tfor parsing strings into numbers, JSON, or whatever it expects. This\n111\tis also what the phase 2 driver does — every argument arrives as a\n112\tstring from argv.\n113\t\n114\t-- we can't expect the lua functions to do anything different. They should only\n115\t   see the input variables coming in as arguments to the function that's being\n116\t   called. If we need to expand the functionality of the lua_spec runner to\n117\t   handle the parsing step, and populating the argument fields, then so be it.\n118\t\n119\tThis means a Lua function that wants a number does:\n120\t```lua\n121\tfunction M.add(a_str, b_str)\n122\t    return tonumber(a_str) + tonumber(b_str)\n123\tend\n124\t```\n125\t\n126\tThe user pays a `tonumber` for numeric inputs. Acceptable for a first\n127\tpass. A future optimization could add per-input type hints to the\n128\tgraph and let the spec push numbers directly.\n129\t\n130\t## Return marshalling\n131\t\n132\tThe Lua function returns a single value. The spec converts it to\n133\tbytes:\n134\t- String: `lua_tolstring` → copy into `out_buf`, set `*out_size`.\n135\t- Number: `lua_tonumber` → format with `snprintf(\"%.17g\", ...)` into\n136\t  `out_buf`, set `*out_size` to the string length.\n137\t- Table: serialize to JSON via a vendored Lua JSON library (or a\n138\t  small inline serializer for flat tables).\n139\t- nil: `out_buf[0] = 0`, `*out_size = 0`. (Whether nil is a valid\n140\t  return is an open question — see below.)\n141\t\n142\t-- we can't demand anything from the user-defined functions. If they return nil,\n143\t   we have to handle that. unfortunately...\n144\t\n145\t- Other: error, abort.\n146\t\n147\tOutput buffer is sized to the box's declared `output_capacity`\n148\t(issue 305's `box_t`). If the serialized value exceeds that, abort\n149\t(per the hard-crash policy in issue 303).\n150\t\n151\tFor variable-size outputs (the box uses the large-value heap, issue\n152\t302), the spec writes into the large-value heap and stores the\n153\thandle in `out_buf`. The dispatch layer routes the handle to the\n154\tslot.\n155\t\n156\t## Error handling\n157\t\n158\tEvery `lua_pcall` is wrapped:\n159\t```c\n160\tint rc = lua_pcall(L, n_args, 1, 0);\n161\tif (rc != LUA_OK) {\n162\t    fprintf(stderr, \"[lua spec] %s:%s — %s\\n\",\n163\t            file_path, fn_name, lua_tostring(L, -1));\n164\t    lua_pop(L, 1);\n165\t    return 1;  // dispatch layer aborts the program\n166\t}\n167\t```\n168\t\n169\tLua errors (`error(...)`, runtime errors, syntax errors during file\n170\tload) all surface here as nonzero `pcall` returns. The spec prints\n171\tthe box context and the Lua error message to stderr, then returns\n172\tnonzero. The dispatch layer aborts.\n173\t\n174\tThere is no try-and-recover. Per issue 303, errors crash the program.\n175\t\n176\t## Build\n177\t\n178\t```\n179\tlangs/lua/\n180\t    spec.c          ← lang_spec_t implementation\n181\t    Makefile        ← builds spec.so\n182\t    spec.so         ← built artifact (gitignored)\n183\t```\n184\t\n185\tThe Makefile target:\n186\t```make\n187\tspec.so: spec.c\n188\t\t$(CC) -shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall \\\n189\t\t    -I$(LUA_INCLUDE) \\\n190\t\t    -o $@ $< \\\n191\t\t    -L$(LUA_LIB) -lluajit-5.1\n192\t```\n193\t\n194\tLuaJIT is the assumed runtime — it matches the phase 2 driver and the\n195\tproject preference (LuaJIT-compatible Lua, no 5.4 syntax). The build\n196\tlinks against the system LuaJIT shared library.\n197\t\n198\t## Open questions\n199\t\n200\t- Lua `nil` return: should this be an error (every box must return\n201\t  something), or a valid \"empty\" output? The phase 2 driver treats\n202\t  any return as a success. Probably keep that — `nil` serializes to\n203\t  zero bytes in the slot, downstream consumers can interpret as they\n204\t  like.\n205\t\n206\t-- unfortunately, it has to be valid. >.<\n207\t\n208\t- Multiple return values: Lua functions can return multiple values.\n209\t  Phase 2 ignored everything past the first. Keep that — boxes have\n210\t  one output slot, period.\n211\t\n212\t-- if they return multiple values, wrap them into a table and process into json.\n213\t   or skip the table step and write to json, as if it were a table.\n214\t\n215\t- Table output serialization: vendor a Lua JSON library (dkjson is\n216\t  already vendored), or write a small inline serializer for the\n217\t  common case. dkjson is already there; reuse it via `require`.\n218\t\n219\t-- use dkjson.\n220\t\n\n... [30 lines truncated] ...",

    "originalFile":"# 221 — Iterator box: round-robin output routing with per-instance counter\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nNo mechanism exists for a box to distribute output across multiple\ndownstream paths in sequence. The comparator routes based on a value\nthreshold; the iterator routes based on a counter that advances each call.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\n### What it does\nAn iterator box receives one input value and routes it to one of N named\noutput wires. Which wire fires is determined by an internal counter that\nincrements each call and wraps back to 0 after the last output. There is\nno function — the dispatch layer copies input directly to output, no\nlanguage spec is invoked. The iterator is a pure routing primitive.\n\nUseful for distributing work across parallel paths, cycling through a\nlist of consumers, or producing round-robin load balancing in the graph.\n\n### Counter model\nThe counter is per-box-instance, stored in the executor's in-memory\nstate (keyed by box ID). It resets to 0 at the start of each run.\nPersistence across runs is not in scope; that is a separate issue.\n\nIn the compiler output (issue 219), the counter becomes a local variable\nin a generated closure — same reset-per-program-start behavior.\n\nWrap-around: `counter = (counter + 1) % #iterator_outputs`\n\n### No function — pure dispatch primitive\nThere is no iterator function in any language. There are no\n`libs/iterator.lua` / `iterator.sh` / `iterator.c` files. The dispatch\nlayer (issue 304) recognizes iterator boxes by the presence of\n`iterator_outputs` in the box JSON and handles routing itself:\n\n1. Read the input value from the input slot.\n2. Copy it directly into the output slot.\n3. Fire the connection whose `from_branch` matches\n   `iterator_outputs[counter]`.\n4. Increment counter mod `n_iter_outputs`.\n5. Re-spawn a successor dispatch task with the new counter value.\n\nThis replaces the earlier \"passthrough function\" design. The function\nwas always identity, so there was nothing to invoke — the dispatch\nlayer does the copy directly and skips the language spec entirely.\n\n### Data model\nBox JSON has an `iterator_outputs` field — an ordered array of\nuser-defined output path names. Iterator boxes do not carry `ref` or\n`fn`; those fields are absent (or, if present, ignored):\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"router\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"inputs\": [{\"name\": \"data\", \"type\": \"any\"}],\n  \"iterator_outputs\": [\"path_a\", \"path_b\", \"path_c\"],\n  \"connections\": [\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"router\", \"from_branch\": \"path_a\",\n      \"to_box\": \"worker-a\", \"to_input\": \"data\"\n    },\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"router\", \"from_branch\": \"path_b\",\n      \"to_box\": \"worker-b\", \"to_input\": \"data\"\n    },\n    {\n      \"from_box\": \"router\", \"from_branch\": \"path_c\",\n      \"to_box\": \"worker-c\", \"to_input\": \"data\"\n    }\n  ]\n}\n```\n\n`from_branch` is reused for iterator output names — the same field\nthat holds \"lt\" / \"eq\" / \"gt\" for comparators. The dispatch layer\nchecks whether the box has `iterator_outputs`; if so, it routes by\ncounter as described above.\n\n### Auto-grow output slots\nConnecting a wire to the last slot of the iterator's output side appends\na new empty named slot — identical to the auto-grow behavior for variadic\ninputs (issue 217). The user names each slot in the inspector. Connecting\nto the last slot prompts for a name and grows the list. Disconnecting\nremoves the slot and compacts (same rename-and-compact logic as variadic\ninputs).\n\n-- we shouldn't prompt for a name, that just slows the user down. Let's generate\n   a name (like, output_n) and let them modify it if they want. They don't need\n   to.\n\n### Dispatch layer integration\nThe dispatch layer (issue 304) is where iterator semantics live. The\ncounter is stored on the `dispatch_task_t` for each iterator\ninvocation; successor tasks carry the next counter value. There is no\nlanguage driver, no function call, no executor-state table — just the\ncounter on the task struct.\n\nSee issue 304 for the full dispatch flow. The iterator-specific path\nis short: read input slot, copy to output slot, fire the routing\nconnection, increment counter, re-spawn.\n\n### Inspector changes\nThe inspector shows:\n- An \"iterator\" toggle per box (like the variadic toggle on inputs)\n- When toggled on: the output side of the box renders named slots instead\n  of a single dot; a \"+\" row at the bottom adds a new slot\n- Each slot name is editable inline\n- The current counter value is shown as a read-only display (useful for\n  debugging live runs)\n\n### Compiler output (issue 219 integration)\nFor an iterator box, the compiler emits a counter variable and a\nrouting function — no inner function call, since the iterator does\nnot invoke anything:\n\n```lua\nlocal router_counter = 0\nlocal function router(data)\n  local idx = router_counter\n  router_counter = (router_counter + 1) % 3\n  if     idx == 0 then worker_a(data)\n  elseif idx == 1 then worker_b(data)\n  else                 worker_c(data)\n  end\nend\n```\n\nNo iterator lib file is bundled — there is none.\n\n### Threading model\nIterator routing in the thread pool runner is fully described in issue\n304.         "text":"**Answers:**\n\n**(1) Data boxes — what's their content?** Literal values, typed inline in the editor and stored verbatim in the box's `value` field of its JSON. At load time the loader allocates a slot for the data box and fills it with the bytes; consumers read it like any other slot. The editor offers a text input for inline typing and (eventually) a \"load from file\" button — but that button just reads the file and pastes the bytes into `value`, so what's in the map is always literal. No file I/O at runtime, no parsing inside the data box. JSON content goes in as a JSON string and is parsed downstream by a call box using `libs/json.lua`. Database queries, runtime file reads, anything dynamic — those are call boxes. Keeps `data` honest as a noun.\n\n**(2) Fan-out and fan-in:** Both are already supported by the slot model.\n\n- **Fan-out** (one output → many inputs): multiple wires reading from the same output slot. The slot's refcount equals the number of wires. Each downstream consumer `peek`s the slot (non-destructive read) and then `unref`s. The slot is freed when the last consumer unrefs. All consumers see the same single value.\n- **Fan-in** (many outputs → one input): the destination input is a queued slot (multi-cell ring buffer, issue 213). Each producer task pushes its output value into the queue when it completes; the consumer pops in arrival order. Iterators are the typical fan-in consumer — they process one value per invocation across the queue.\n\n**(3) Pool runner's main loop:** Mostly idle. After setup (load graph → start pool → init specs → submit entry boxes), the main thread blocks on a condvar tied to the active-task counter (issue 301). All actual work — box invocations, deferred allocator coalescing (issue 302), comparator/iterator routing — happens inside the worker threads as pool tasks. The deferred cleanup we discussed for 302 is submitted as just another task; a worker runs it, the counter increments and decrements like any task. When the counter hits zero, the main thread wakes and finalizes (writes `last-run.json`, destroys the pool, frees the graph). There is no separate \"admin thread\"; the runner is task-driven. Things you could add to the task stream over time: stats collection, periodic compaction, file-watch handlers — but for now, just box dispatch and allocator cleanup.\n\nCleaning up 221, 305, and applying the 306 corrections:"
      }]

The\ninput slot is a queued (multi-cell) ring buffer that persists across\nre-spawns. See issues 302 (slot store) and 304 (dispatch layer) for\nthe full picture.\n\n## Open questions\n- Should the counter be exposed as a readable data port (wirable to\n  another box as an input) in addition to being shown in the inspector?\n\n-- nah, that's more complexity for the user that most won't need.\n\n- Should auto-grow prompt for the output name immediately on connect, or\n  generate a placeholder (`out_N`) that the user renames afterward?\n\n-- placeholder.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. `src/001-schema.lua` — add `iterator_outputs` to the box validator;\n   when present, `ref` and `fn` are not required.\n2. `src/004-executor.lua` (phase 2 path) — add per-box counter state;\n   extend `fire_connections` to route by `iterator_outputs[counter]`\n   and copy input → output without invoking a driver.\n3. `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — iterator toggle; editable output slots.\n4. `assets/js/006-wires.js` — auto-grow output slots on connect;\n   auto-shrink + rename on disconnect (mirrors variadic input logic).\n5. `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — render N named output dots when\n   `iterator_outputs` is set (replacing the single-wire dot).\n6. (Phase 3) Implement iterator dispatch in `src/008-pool-runner.c` per\n   issue 304 — counter on `dispatch_task_t`, successor re-spawn.\n\n## Relevant files\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — phase 2 fire_connections / route-by-counter\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — box validator (`iterator_outputs` field)\n- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — iterator toggle, slot editor\n- `assets/js/006-wires.js` — auto-grow/shrink for output slots\n- `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — box rendering\n- `issues/217-concat-box-and-dynamic-inputs.md` — variadic input model\n  (auto-grow/shrink logic mirrors this)\n- `issues/completed/108-branch-box-and-predicate-routing.md` — comparator\n  model that `from_branch` and the routing pattern extend from\n- `issues/219-map-compiler.md` — compiler integration\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — phase 3 iterator dispatch (no\n  function invocation; routing only)\n",

    "originalFile":"# 306 — Lua language spec implementation (reference spec)\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nLua boxes today run via `drivers/lua.sh`, which spawns a fresh `luajit`\nprocess per box invocation, feeds it stdin, and reads stdout. Process\nspawn cost dominates; each call is its own fresh interpreter. There is\nno persistent Lua state between calls.\n\n## Concept\nThe Lua language spec implements `lang_spec_t` (issue 303) for Lua. It\nis the first reference implementation of the spec interface and the\nproof that the in-process FFI model works. It is also the simplest\ncase — no compile step, no out-of-process server.\n\nEach worker thread gets its own `lua_State`. States are not shared.\nPer-thread states need no locking on the call path; the state's\ninternals are only ever touched by the worker that owns it.\n\n`langs/lua/spec.c` is built into `langs/lua/spec.so` and loaded by\nthe pool runner via `dlopen` at startup, like any other spec.\n\n## Per-worker state\n\nInit creates a fresh `lua_State` and configures it:\n\n```c\nvoid *lua_init(int worker_idx) {\n    lua_State *L = luaL_newstate();\n    luaL_openlibs(L);\n    set_package_path(L);   // libs/, map src/, meta.json src_dirs\n    return L;\n}\n\nvoid lua_teardown(void *handle) {\n    lua_close((lua_State *)handle);\n}\n```\n\n`set_package_path` writes `package.path` and `package.cpath` to\ninclude:\n- The SoraMech `libs/` directory\n- The map's `src/` directory\n- Every directory listed in `meta.json src_dirs`\n\n-- I think we should only include the map's src/ directory. The compile button\n   in the editor should copy all the required files into the map's src/ directory\n   so that there's only one place to look for functions and such. That way, we\n   can make these programs portable by just sharing the directory with others.\n\nThis is the same set the phase 2 runner builds. The path is set once\nat init; it does not change at runtime.\n\n## File-and-function caching\n\nA naive `invoke` would `luaL_loadfile` and look up the function on\nevery call. Both are unnecessary work — the file's chunk does not\nchange during a run, and the function reference is stable.\n\nThe Lua spec keeps a per-handle cache: for each box source file\nloaded, store the table returned by the file's chunk as a Lua\nregistry key (`LUA_REGISTRYINDEX`). On first invocation:\n1. `luaL_loadfile(L, file_path)` — loads the chunk.\n2. `lua_pcall(L, 0, 1, 0)` — runs the chunk, expecting a returned\n   table.\n3. Store the table in the registry under a key derived from `file_path`.\n\nOn subsequent invocations:\n1. Look up the registry entry by `file_path`.\n2. Index it by `fn_name` to get the function reference.\n3. Skip `luaL_loadfile` entirely.\n\nThe cache is per-`lua_State` and therefore per-worker; no\nsynchronization is needed.\n\n## Box file convention\n\nA Lua box file returns a table whose keys are the box's exported\nfunction names:\n\n```lua\n-- maps/<name>/src/classify.lua\nlocal M = {}\n\nfunction M.classify(text)\n    if text:match(\"^%d+$\") then return \"numeric\"\n    elseif text:match(\"[a-z]\") then return \"alpha\"\n    else return \"other\"\n    end\nend\n\nreturn M\n```\n\nThe box JSON references it by `ref = \"classify.lua\"`, `fn = \"classify\"`.\nThe spec loads `classify.lua`, stores its returned table, and indexes\ninto it with `\"classify\"` to get the function.\n\nThis is the existing phase 2 convention — kept as-is.\n\n## Input marshalling\n\nInputs arrive at `invoke` as `(void *bytes, int size)` pairs. The\nspec needs to push them onto the Lua stack as Lua values.\n\nThe simplest, most general encoding: every input is a Lua string\n(`lua_pushlstring(L, bytes, size)`). The Lua function is responsible\nfor parsing strings into numbers, JSON, or whatever it expects. This\nis also what the phase 2 driver does — every argument arrives as a\nstring from argv.\n\n-- we can't expect the lua functions to do anything different. They should only\n   see the input variables coming in as arguments to the function that's being\n   called. If we need to expand the functionality of the lua_spec runner to\n   handle the parsing step, and populating the argument fields, then so be it.\n\nThis means a Lua function that wants a number does:\n```lua\nfunction M.add(a_str, b_str)\n    return tonumber(a_str) + tonumber(b_str)\nend\n```\n\nThe user pays a `tonumber` for numeric inputs. Acceptable for a first\npass. A future optimization could add per-input type hints to the\ngraph and let the spec push numbers directly.\n\n## Return marshalling\n\nThe Lua function returns a single value. The spec converts it to\nbytes:\n- String: `lua_tolstring` → copy into `out_buf`, set `*out_size`.\n- Number: `lua_tonumber` → format with `snprintf(\"%.17g\", ...)` into\n  `out_buf`, set `*out_size` to the string length.\n- Table: serialize to JSON via a vendored Lua JSON library (or a\n  small inline serializer for flat tables).\n- nil: `out_buf[0] = 0`, `*out_size = 0`. (Whether nil is a valid\n  return is an open question — see below.)\n\n-- we can't demand anything from the user-defined functions. If they return nil,\n   we have to handle that. unfortunately...\n\n- Other: error, abort.\n\nOutput buffer is sized to the box's declared `output_capacity`\n(issue 305's `box_t`). If the serialized value exceeds that, abort\n(per the hard-crash policy in issue 303).\n\nFor variable-size outputs (the box uses the large-value heap, issue\n302), the spec writes into the large-value heap and stores the\nhandle in `out_buf`. The dispatch layer routes the handle to the\nslot.\n\n## Error handling\n\nEvery `lua_pcall` is wrapped:\n```c\nint rc = lua_pcall(L, n_args, 1, 0);\nif (rc != LUA_OK) {\n    fprintf(stderr, \"[lua spec] %s:%s — %s\\n\",\n            file_path, fn_name, lua_tostring(L, -1));\n    lua_pop(L, 1);\n    return 1;  // dispatch layer aborts the program\n}\n```\n\nLua errors (`error(...)`, runtime errors, syntax errors during file\nload) all surface here as nonzero `pcall` returns. The spec prints\nthe box context and the Lua error message to stderr, then returns\nnonzero. The dispatch layer aborts.\n\nThere is no try-and-recover. Per issue 303, errors crash the program.\n\n## Build\n\n```\nlangs/lua/\n    spec.c          ← lang_spec_t implementation\n    Makefile        ← builds spec.so\n    spec.so         ← built artifact (gitignored)\n```\n\nThe Makefile target:\n```make\nspec.so: spec.c\n\t$(CC) -shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall \\\n\t    -I$(LUA_INCLUDE) \\\n\t    -o $@ $< \\\n\t    -L$(LUA_LIB) -lluajit-5.1\n```\n\nLuaJIT is the assumed runtime — it matches the phase 2 driver and the\nproject preference (LuaJIT-compatible Lua, no 5.4 syntax). The build\nlinks against the system LuaJIT shared library.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Lua `nil` return: should this be an error (every box must return\n  something), or a valid \"empty\" output? The phase 2 driver treats\n  any return as a success. Probably keep that — `nil` serializes to\n  zero bytes in the slot, downstream consumers can interpret as they\n  like.\n\n-- unfortunately, it has to be valid. >.<\n\n- Multiple return values: Lua functions can return multiple values.\n  Phase 2 ignored everything past the first. Keep that — boxes have\n  one output slot, period.\n\n-- if they return multiple values, wrap them into a table and process into json.\n   or skip the table step and write to json, as if it were a table.\n\n- Table output serialization: vendor a Lua JSON library (dkjson is\n  already vendored), or write a small inline serializer for the\n  common case. dkjson is already there; reuse it via `require`.\n\n-- use dkjson.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Set up `langs/lua/` directory with a Makefile that builds an empty\n   `spec.so` exporting a stub `soramech_lang_spec`.\n2. Implement `init` and `teardown`. Verify the pool runner can\n   `dlopen` the spec and call `init` per worker without errors.\n3.           "new_string":"## Input marshalling\n\nInputs arrive at `invoke` as `(void *bytes, int size)` pairs. The\nspec is responsible for converting each input's bytes into the Lua\nvalue type the user's function expects. The user's function sees\narguments as native Lua values — never a raw byte buffer that the\nfunction has to parse itself.\n\nEach input has a declared type in the box JSON\n(`{\"name\": \"count\", \"type\": \"number\"}`). The graph loader (issue 305)\nrecords this type on the `input_decl_t` and passes the type alongside\nthe bytes when calling `invoke`. The Lua spec dispatches on type:\n\n| Declared type | Lua spec action                                             |\n|---------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|\n| `string`      | `lua_pushlstring(L, bytes, size)`                           |\n| `number`      | parse with `strtod`, `lua_pushnumber`                       |\n| `integer`     | parse with `strtoll`, `lua_pushinteger`                     |\n| `boolean`     | strcmp against `\"true\"` / `\"false\"`, `lua_pushboolean`      |\n| `json`        | call `dkjson.decode` on the bytes, push the resulting table |\n| `bytes`       | `lua_pushlstring` (raw, may contain nulls)                  |\n| `any`         | treat as `string` for now                                   |\n\nThe Lua function then takes typed arguments:\n\n```lua\nfunction M.add(a, b)            -- both already numbers\n    return a + b\nend\n\nfunction M.classify(payload)    -- payload is already a table\n    return payload.kind\nend\n```\n\nThe user does not write `tonumber` or `dkjson.decode` calls inside\ntheir box function. The spec did that work before the function was\ncalled.\n\nIf a parse fails (`json` input that isn't valid JSON, `number` input\nthat isn't a number), the spec returns nonzero and the dispatch layer\naborts (per issue 303).",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/306-lua-language-spec.md",

          "old_string":"## Input marshalling\n\nInputs arrive at `invoke` as `(void *bytes, int size)` pairs. The\nspec needs to push them onto the Lua stack as Lua values.\n\nThe simplest, most general encoding: every input is a Lua string\n(`lua_pushlstring(L, bytes, size)`). The Lua function is responsible\nfor parsing strings into numbers, JSON, or whatever it expects. This\nis also what the phase 2 driver does — every argument arrives as a\nstring from argv.\n\n-- we can't expect the lua functions to do anything different. They should only\n   see the input variables coming in as arguments to the function that's being\n   called. If we need to expand the functionality of the lua_spec runner to\n   handle the parsing step, and populating the argument fields, then so be it.\n\nThis means a Lua function that wants a number does:\n```lua\nfunction M.add(a_str, b_str)\n    return tonumber(a_str) + tonumber(b_str)\nend\n```\n\nThe user pays a `tonumber` for numeric inputs. Acceptable for a first\npass. A future optimization could add per-input type hints to the\ngraph and let the spec push numbers directly."

    "originalFile":"# 306 — Lua language spec implementation (reference spec)\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nLua boxes today run via `drivers/lua.sh`, which spawns a fresh `luajit`\nprocess per box invocation, feeds it stdin, and reads stdout. Process\nspawn cost dominates; each call is its own fresh interpreter. There is\nno persistent Lua state between calls.\n\n## Concept\nThe Lua language spec implements `lang_spec_t` (issue 303) for Lua. It\nis the first reference implementation of the spec interface and the\nproof that the in-process FFI model works. It is also the simplest\ncase — no compile step, no out-of-process server.\n\nEach worker thread gets its own `lua_State`. States are not shared.\nPer-thread states need no locking on the call path; the state's\ninternals are only ever touched by the worker that owns it.\n\n`langs/lua/spec.c` is built into `langs/lua/spec.so` and loaded by\nthe pool runner via `dlopen` at startup, like any other spec.\n\n## Per-worker state\n\nInit creates a fresh `lua_State` and configures it:\n\n```c\nvoid *lua_init(int worker_idx) {\n    lua_State *L = luaL_newstate();\n    luaL_openlibs(L);\n    set_package_path(L);   // libs/, map src/, meta.json src_dirs\n    return L;\n}\n\nvoid lua_teardown(void *handle) {\n    lua_close((lua_State *)handle);\n}\n```\n\n`set_package_path` writes `package.path` and `package.cpath` to\ninclude exactly one directory: the map's own `src/`. Everything the\nmap needs — vendored libs, helper modules, anything — is copied into\n`src/` by the compile step (issue 222). The compiled map is then a\nself-contained directory: ship the directory to someone else and it\nruns without further setup.\n\nThis is a tightening of the phase 2 path, which also included\nSoraMech's central `libs/` and any `meta.json src_dirs`. The new rule\nis: one place to look for functions, the map's own `src/`, full stop.\nCompile is the step that resolves dependencies into that location.\n\n## File-and-function caching\n\nA naive `invoke` would `luaL_loadfile` and look up the function on\nevery call. Both are unnecessary work — the file's chunk does not\nchange during a run, and the function reference is stable.\n\nThe Lua spec keeps a per-handle cache: for each box source file\nloaded, store the table returned by the file's chunk as a Lua\nregistry key (`LUA_REGISTRYINDEX`). On first invocation:\n1. `luaL_loadfile(L, file_path)` — loads the chunk.\n2. `lua_pcall(L, 0, 1, 0)` — runs the chunk, expecting a returned\n   table.\n3. Store the table in the registry under a key derived from `file_path`.\n\nOn subsequent invocations:\n1. Look up the registry entry by `file_path`.\n2. Index it by `fn_name` to get the function reference.\n3. Skip `luaL_loadfile` entirely.\n\nThe cache is per-`lua_State` and therefore per-worker; no\nsynchronization is needed.\n\n## Box file convention\n\nA Lua box file returns a table whose keys are the box's exported\nfunction names:\n\n```lua\n-- maps/<name>/src/classify.lua\nlocal M = {}\n\nfunction M.classify(text)\n    if text:match(\"^%d+$\") then return \"numeric\"\n    elseif text:match(\"[a-z]\") then return \"alpha\"\n    else return \"other\"\n    end\nend\n\nreturn M\n```\n\nThe box JSON references it by `ref = \"classify.lua\"`, `fn = \"classify\"`.\nThe spec loads `classify.lua`, stores its returned table, and indexes\ninto it with `\"classify\"` to get the function.\n\nThis is the existing phase 2 convention — kept as-is.\n\n## Input marshalling\n\nInputs arrive at `invoke` as `(void *bytes, int size)` pairs. The\nspec needs to push them onto the Lua stack as Lua values.\n\nThe simplest, most general encoding: every input is a Lua string\n(`lua_pushlstring(L, bytes, size)`). The Lua function is responsible\nfor parsing strings into numbers, JSON, or whatever it expects. This\nis also what the phase 2 driver does — every argument arrives as a\nstring from argv.\n\n-- we can't expect the lua functions to do anything different. They should only\n   see the input variables coming in as arguments to the function that's being\n   called. If we need to expand the functionality of the lua_spec runner to\n   handle the parsing step, and populating the argument fields, then so be it.\n\nThis means a Lua function that wants a number does:\n```lua\nfunction M.add(a_str, b_str)\n    return tonumber(a_str) + tonumber(b_str)\nend\n```\n\nThe user pays a `tonumber` for numeric inputs. Acceptable for a first\npass. A future optimization could add per-input type hints to the\ngraph and let the spec push numbers directly.\n\n## Return marshalling\n\nThe Lua function returns a single value. The spec converts it to\nbytes:\n- String: `lua_tolstring` → copy into `out_buf`, set `*out_size`.\n- Number: `lua_tonumber` → format with `snprintf(\"%.17g\", ...)` into\n  `out_buf`, set `*out_size` to the string length.\n- Table: serialize to JSON via a vendored Lua JSON library (or a\n  small inline serializer for flat tables).\n- nil: `out_buf[0] = 0`, `*out_size = 0`. (Whether nil is a valid\n  return is an open question — see below.)\n\n-- we can't demand anything from the user-defined functions. If they return nil,\n   we have to handle that. unfortunately...\n\n- Other: error, abort.\n\nOutput buffer is sized to the box's declared `output_capacity`\n(issue 305's `box_t`). If the serialized value exceeds that, abort\n(per the hard-crash policy in issue 303).\n\nFor variable-size outputs (the box uses the large-value heap, issue\n302), the spec writes into the large-value heap and stores the\nhandle in `out_buf`. The dispatch layer routes the handle to the\nslot.\n\n## Error handling\n\nEvery `lua_pcall` is wrapped:\n```c\nint rc = lua_pcall(L, n_args, 1, 0);\nif (rc != LUA_OK) {\n    fprintf(stderr, \"[lua spec] %s:%s — %s\\n\",\n            file_path, fn_name, lua_tostring(L, -1));\n    lua_pop(L, 1);\n    return 1;  // dispatch layer aborts the program\n}\n```\n\nLua errors (`error(...)`, runtime errors, syntax errors during file\nload) all surface here as nonzero `pcall` returns. The spec prints\nthe box context and the Lua error message to stderr, then returns\nnonzero. The dispatch layer aborts.\n\nThere is no try-and-recover. Per issue 303, errors crash the program.\n\n## Build\n\n```\nlangs/lua/\n    spec.c          ← lang_spec_t implementation\n    Makefile        ← builds spec.so\n    spec.so         ← built artifact (gitignored)\n```\n\nThe Makefile target:\n```make\nspec.so: spec.c\n\t$(CC) -shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall \\\n\t    -I$(LUA_INCLUDE) \\\n\t    -o $@ $< \\\n\t    -L$(LUA_LIB) -lluajit-5.1\n```\n\nLuaJIT is the assumed runtime — it matches the phase 2 driver and the\nproject preference (LuaJIT-compatible Lua, no 5.4 syntax). The build\nlinks against the system LuaJIT shared library.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Lua `nil` return: should this be an error (every box must return\n  something), or a valid \"empty\" output? The phase 2 driver treats\n  any return as a success. Probably keep that — `nil` serializes to\n  zero bytes in the slot, downstream consumers can interpret as they\n  like.\n\n-- unfortunately, it has to be valid. >.<\n\n- Multiple return values: Lua functions can return multiple values.\n  Phase 2 ignored everything past the first. Keep that — boxes have\n  one output slot, period.\n\n-- if they return multiple values, wrap them into a table and process into json.\n   or skip the table step and write to json, as if it were a table.\n\n- Table output serialization: vendor a Lua JSON library (dkjson is\n  already vendored), or write a small inline serializer for the\n  common case. dkjson is already there; reuse it via `require`.\n\n-- use dkjson.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Set up `langs/lua/` directory with a Makefile that builds an empty\n   `spec.so` exporting a stub `soramech_lang_spec`.\n2. Implement `init` and `teardown`. Verify the pool runner can\n   `dlopen` the spec and call `init` per worker without errors.\n3. Implement file-and-function caching — load a file, store its\n   returned table in the registry, look it up later.\n4. Implement input marshalling: push bytes as strings, count args.\n5. Implement `lua_pcall` invocation with error wrapping.\n6. Implement string return marshalling. Smoke test: `maps/hello`\n   end-to-end through the pool.\n7. Implement number return marshalling.\n8. Implement table-via-JSON return marshalling.\n9. Add `package.path` resolution for libs/, src/, and `meta.src_dirs`.\n10. Test against `maps/classify-demo` and `maps/driver-test` (Lua\n    portions).\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `drivers/lua.sh` — phase 2 Lua driver, retired by this spec\n- `langs/lang-spec.h` — interface header (issue 303)\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — spec contract this implements\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — dispatch layer that calls\n  `invoke`\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — large-value heap for\n  variable-size returns\n- `libs/dkjson` (vendored) — table-to-JSON serialization\n- `maps/hello`, `maps/classify-demo` — Lua-only smoke test maps\n",
    "oldString":"## Input marshalling\n\nInputs arrive at `invoke` as `(void *bytes, int size)` pairs. The\nspec needs to push them onto the Lua stack as Lua values.\n\nThe simplest, most general encoding: every input is a Lua string\n(`lua_pushlstring(L, bytes, size)`). The Lua function is responsible\nfor parsing strings into numbers, JSON, or whatever it expects. This\nis also what the phase 2 driver does — every argument arrives as a\nstring from argv.\n\n-- we can't expect the lua functions to do anything different. They should only\n   see the input variables coming in as arguments to the function that's being\n   called. If we need to expand the functionality of the lua_spec runner to\n   handle the parsing step, and populating the argument fields, then so be it.\n\nThis means a Lua function that wants a number does:\n```lua\nfunction M.add(a_str, b_str)\n    return tonumber(a_str) + tonumber(b_str)\nend\n```\n\nThe user pays a `tonumber` for numeric inputs. Acceptable for a first\npass. A future optimization could add per-input type hints to the\ngraph and let the spec push numbers directly.",
    "newString":"## Input marshalling\n\nInputs arrive at `invoke` as `(void *bytes, int size)` pairs. The\nspec is responsible for converting each input's bytes into the Lua\nvalue type the user's function expects. The user's function sees\narguments as native Lua values — never a raw byte buffer that the\nfunction has to parse itself.\n\nEach input has a declared type in the box JSON\n(`{\"name\": \"count\", \"type\": \"number\"}`). The graph loader (issue 305)\nrecords this type on the `input_decl_t` and passes the type alongside\nthe bytes when calling `invoke`. The Lua spec dispatches on type:\n\n| Declared type | Lua spec action                                             |\n|---------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|\n| `string`      | `lua_pushlstring(L, bytes, size)`                           |\n| `number`      | parse with `strtod`, `lua_pushnumber`                       |\n| `integer`     | parse with `strtoll`, `lua_pushinteger`                     |\n| `boolean`     | strcmp against `\"true\"` / `\"false\"`, `lua_pushboolean`      |\n| `json`        | call `dkjson.decode` on the bytes, push the resulting table |\n| `bytes`       | `lua_pushlstring` (raw, may contain nulls)                  |\n| `any`         | treat as `string` for now                                   |\n\nThe Lua function then takes typed arguments:\n\n```lua\nfunction M.add(a, b)            -- both already numbers\n    return a + b\nend\n\nfunction M.classify(payload)    -- payload is already a table\n    return payload.kind\nend\n```\n\nThe user does not write `tonumber` or `dkjson.decode` calls inside\ntheir box function. The spec did that work before the function was\ncalled.\n\nIf a parse fails (`json` input that isn't valid JSON, `number` input\nthat isn't a number), the spec returns nonzero and the dispatch layer\naborts (per issue 303).",

    "originalFile":"# 306 — Lua language spec implementation (reference spec)\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nLua boxes today run via `drivers/lua.sh`, which spawns a fresh `luajit`\nprocess per box invocation, feeds it stdin, and reads stdout. Process\nspawn cost dominates; each call is its own fresh interpreter. There is\nno persistent Lua state between calls.\n\n## Concept\nThe Lua language spec implements `lang_spec_t` (issue 303) for Lua. It\nis the first reference implementation of the spec interface and the\nproof that the in-process FFI model works. It is also the simplest\ncase — no compile step, no out-of-process server.\n\nEach worker thread gets its own `lua_State`. States are not shared.\nPer-thread states need no locking on the call path; the state's\ninternals are only ever touched by the worker that owns it.\n\n`langs/lua/spec.c` is built into `langs/lua/spec.so` and loaded by\nthe pool runner via `dlopen` at startup, like any other spec.\n\n## Per-worker state\n\nInit creates a fresh `lua_State` and configures it:\n\n```c\nvoid *lua_init(int worker_idx) {\n    lua_State *L = luaL_newstate();\n    luaL_openlibs(L);\n    set_package_path(L);   // libs/, map src/, meta.json src_dirs\n    return L;\n}\n\nvoid lua_teardown(void *handle) {\n    lua_close((lua_State *)handle);\n}\n```\n\n`set_package_path` writes `package.path` and `package.cpath` to\ninclude exactly one directory: the map's own `src/`. Everything the\nmap needs — vendored libs, helper modules, anything — is copied into\n`src/` by the compile step (issue 222). The compiled map is then a\nself-contained directory: ship the directory to someone else and it\nruns without further setup.\n\nThis is a tightening of the phase 2 path, which also included\nSoraMech's central `libs/` and any `meta.json src_dirs`. The new rule\nis: one place to look for functions, the map's own `src/`, full stop.\nCompile is the step that resolves dependencies into that location.\n\n## File-and-function caching\n\nA naive `invoke` would `luaL_loadfile` and look up the function on\nevery call. Both are unnecessary work — the file's chunk does not\nchange during a run, and the function reference is stable.\n\nThe Lua spec keeps a per-handle cache: for each box source file\nloaded, store the table returned by the file's chunk as a Lua\nregistry key (`LUA_REGISTRYINDEX`). On first invocation:\n1. `luaL_loadfile(L, file_path)` — loads the chunk.\n2. `lua_pcall(L, 0, 1, 0)` — runs the chunk, expecting a returned\n   table.\n3. Store the table in the registry under a key derived from `file_path`.\n\nOn subsequent invocations:\n1. Look up the registry entry by `file_path`.\n2. Index it by `fn_name` to get the function reference.\n3. Skip `luaL_loadfile` entirely.\n\nThe cache is per-`lua_State` and therefore per-worker; no\nsynchronization is needed.\n\n## Box file convention\n\nA Lua box file returns a table whose keys are the box's exported\nfunction names:\n\n```lua\n-- maps/<name>/src/classify.lua\nlocal M = {}\n\nfunction M.classify(text)\n    if text:match(\"^%d+$\") then return \"numeric\"\n    elseif text:match(\"[a-z]\") then return \"alpha\"\n    else return \"other\"\n    end\nend\n\nreturn M\n```\n\nThe box JSON references it by `ref = \"classify.lua\"`, `fn = \"classify\"`.\nThe spec loads `classify.lua`, stores its returned table, and indexes\ninto it with `\"classify\"` to get the function.\n\nThis is the existing phase 2 convention — kept as-is.\n\n## Input marshalling\n\nInputs arrive at `invoke` as `(void *bytes, int size)` pairs. The\nspec is responsible for converting each input's bytes into the Lua\nvalue type the user's function expects. The user's function sees\narguments as native Lua values — never a raw byte buffer that the\nfunction has to parse itself.\n\nEach input has a declared type in the box JSON\n(`{\"name\": \"count\", \"type\": \"number\"}`). The graph loader (issue 305)\nrecords this type on the `input_decl_t` and passes the type alongside\nthe bytes when calling `invoke`. The Lua spec dispatches on type:\n\n| Declared type | Lua spec action                                             |\n|---------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|\n| `string`      | `lua_pushlstring(L, bytes, size)`                           |\n| `number`      | parse with `strtod`, `lua_pushnumber`                       |\n| `integer`     | parse with `strtoll`, `lua_pushinteger`                     |\n| `boolean`     | strcmp against `\"true\"` / `\"false\"`, `lua_pushboolean`      |\n| `json`        | call `dkjson.decode` on the bytes, push the resulting table |\n| `bytes`       | `lua_pushlstring` (raw, may contain nulls)                  |\n| `any`         | treat as `string` for now                                   |\n\nThe Lua function then takes typed arguments:\n\n```lua\nfunction M.add(a, b)            -- both already numbers\n    return a + b\nend\n\nfunction M.classify(payload)    -- payload is already a table\n    return payload.kind\nend\n```\n\nThe user does not write `tonumber` or `dkjson.decode` calls inside\ntheir box function. The spec did that work before the function was\ncalled.\n\nIf a parse fails (`json` input that isn't valid JSON, `number` input\nthat isn't a number), the spec returns nonzero and the dispatch layer\naborts (per issue 303).\n\n## Return marshalling\n\nThe Lua function returns a single value. The spec converts it to\nbytes:\n- String: `lua_tolstring` → copy into `out_buf`, set `*out_size`.\n- Number: `lua_tonumber` → format with `snprintf(\"%.17g\", ...)` into\n  `out_buf`, set `*out_size` to the string length.\n- Table: serialize to JSON via a vendored Lua JSON library (or a\n  small inline serializer for flat tables).\n- nil: `out_buf[0] = 0`, `*out_size = 0`. (Whether nil is a valid\n  return is an open question — see below.)\n\n-- we can't demand anything from the user-defined functions. If they return nil,\n   we have to handle that. unfortunately...\n\n- Other: error, abort.\n\nOutput buffer is sized to the box's declared `output_capacity`\n(issue 305's `box_t`). If the serialized value exceeds that, abort\n(per the hard-crash policy in issue 303).\n\nFor variable-size outputs (the box uses the large-value heap, issue\n302), the spec writes into the large-value heap and stores the\nhandle in `out_buf`. The dispatch layer routes the handle to the\nslot.\n\n## Error handling\n\nEvery `lua_pcall` is wrapped:\n```c\nint rc = lua_pcall(L, n_args, 1, 0);\nif (rc != LUA_OK) {\n    fprintf(stderr, \"[lua spec] %s:%s — %s\\n\",\n            file_path, fn_name, lua_tostring(L, -1));\n    lua_pop(L, 1);\n    return 1;  // dispatch layer aborts the program\n}\n```\n\nLua errors (`error(...)`, runtime errors, syntax errors during file\nload) all surface here as nonzero `pcall` returns. The spec prints\nthe box context and the Lua error message to stderr, then returns\nnonzero. The dispatch layer aborts.\n\nThere is no try-and-recover. Per issue 303, errors crash the program.\n\n## Build\n\n```\nlangs/lua/\n    spec.c          ← lang_spec_t implementation\n    Makefile        ← builds spec.so\n    spec.so         ← built artifact (gitignored)\n```\n\nThe Makefile target:\n```make\nspec.so: spec.c\n\t$(CC) -shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall \\\n\t    -I$(LUA_INCLUDE) \\\n\t    -o $@ $< \\\n\t    -L$(LUA_LIB) -lluajit-5.1\n```\n\nLuaJIT is the assumed runtime — it matches the phase 2 driver and the\nproject preference (LuaJIT-compatible Lua, no 5.4 syntax). The build\nlinks against the system LuaJIT shared library.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Lua `nil` return: should this be an error (every box must return\n  something), or a valid \"empty\" output? The phase 2 driver treats\n  any return as a success. Probably keep that — `nil` serializes to\n  zero bytes in the slot, downstream consumers can interpret as they\n  like.\n\n-- unfortunately, it has to be valid. >.<\n\n- Multiple return values: Lua functions can return multiple values.\n  Phase 2 ignored everything past the first. Keep that — boxes have\n  one output slot, period.\n\n-- if they return multiple values, wrap them into a table and process into json.\n   or skip the table step and write to json, as if it were a table.\n\n- Table output serialization: vendor a Lua JSON library (dkjson is\n  already vendored), or write a small inline serializer for the\n  common case. dkjson is already there; reuse it via `require`.\n\n-- use dkjson.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Set up `langs/lua/` directory with a Makefile that builds an empty\n   `spec.so` exporting a stub `soramech_lang_spec`.\n2. Implement `init` and `teardown`. Verify the pool runner can\n   `dlopen` the spec and call `init` per worker without errors.\n3. Implement file-and-function caching — load a file, store its\n   returned table in the registry, look it up later.\n4. Implement input marshalling: push bytes as strings, count args.\n5. Implement `lua_pcall` invocation with error wrapping.\n6. Implement string return marshalling. Smoke test: `maps/hello`\n   end-to-end through the pool.\n7. Implement number return marshalling.\n8. Implement table-via-JSON return marshalling.\n9. Add `package.path` resolution for libs/, src/, and `meta.src_dirs`.\n10. Test against `maps/classify-demo` and `maps/driver-test` (Lua\n    portions).\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `drivers/lua.sh` — phase 2 Lua driver, retired by this spec\n- `langs/lang-spec.h` — interface header (issue 303)\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — spec contract this implements\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — dispatch layer that calls\n  `invoke`\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — large-value heap for\n  variable-size returns\n- `libs/dkjson` (vendored) — table-to-JSON serialization\n- `maps/hello`, `maps/classify-demo` — Lua-only smoke test maps\n",

        "input":{
          "content":"# 307 — C language spec implementation\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nC boxes today run via `drivers/c.sh`, which compiles the source on\ndemand (mtime-based recompile to a binary), then spawns the binary as\na subprocess and reads stdout. Process spawn cost dominates; each call\nis its own freshly-launched executable. The phase 2 driver compiles\nto a standalone binary, not a `.so`.\n\n## Concept\nThe C language spec implements `lang_spec_t` (issue 303) for C. It is\nthe second reference implementation, and the first one that exercises\nthe `compile` callback. After compile, invocation is in-process via\n`dlopen` / `dlsym` — the user's compiled function is called directly\nthrough a function pointer, with no subprocess and no IPC.\n\nThis is the \"Option 1 — LuaJIT FFI\" model from\n`docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`, applied to C: same-process call,\nnanosecond-overhead invocation, native-typed access. The only thing\nthe C spec adds over the Lua spec is the compile step.\n\n## Per-worker state\n\n`init` returns a small struct holding the dlopen-handle cache:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    void  *so_handles[MAX_BOXES];   // per-file .so handle, indexed by file id\n    void  *fn_ptrs   [MAX_BOXES];   // per-(file, fn) cached function pointer\n    int    n_cached;\n    // (a hash table could replace these arrays if MAX_BOXES grows large)\n} c_handle_t;\n\nvoid *c_init(int worker_idx);\nvoid  c_teardown(void *handle);    // dlclose every cached handle\n```\n\nEach worker thread has its own cache. The same `.so` will end up\nloaded once per worker, since `dlopen` with the same path on the same\nprocess returns a refcounted handle (the underlying code segment is\nshared across all callers — the per-worker `dlopen` is just a\nrefcount bump after the first).\n\n## Compile callback\n\n```c\nint c_compile(const char *src_path, const char *out_path) {\n    pid_t pid = fork();\n    if (pid == 0) {\n        execlp(\"cc\", \"cc\",\n               \"-shared\", \"-fPIC\", \"-O2\", \"-Wall\",\n               \"-o\", out_path, src_path,\n               (char *)NULL);\n        _exit(127);\n    }\n    int status;\n    waitpid(pid, &status, 0);\n    return WIFEXITED(status) && WEXITSTATUS(status) == 0 ? 0 : 1;\n}\n```\n\nCompile runs once per box source file, at map load (or at editor\ncompile-button time, issue 222). The `.so` lands in the map's\n`compiled/bin/` directory. `invoke` later finds it there.\n\nIf the source is already compiled and the `.so` is newer than the\nsource, compile is skipped. mtime check, like the phase 2 driver did.\n\nThe compiler is invoked as `cc` (the system default — `gcc` on most\nLinux, `clang` on macOS). No SoraMech-specific flags beyond\n`-shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall`. The user can add flags via a `cflags`\nfield in the box JSON if they need them; otherwise defaults apply.\n\n## Box file convention\n\nA C box file defines one or more functions with a fixed signature:\n\n```c\n// maps/<name>/src/classify.c\n#include \"soramech-c.h\"     // shipped helper header\n\nint classify(SM_BOX_ARGS) {\n    const char *text = sm_in_str(0);\n    if (text[0] >= '0' && text[0] <= '9') {\n        sm_out_str(\"numeric\");\n    } else {\n        sm_out_str(\"alpha\");\n    }\n    return 0;\n}\n```\n\n`SM_BOX_ARGS` is a macro that expands to the standardized signature:\n\n```c\n#define SM_BOX_ARGS \\\n    const void **sm_inputs, const int *sm_sizes, int sm_n_inputs, \\\n    void *sm_out_buf, int sm_out_capacity, int *sm_out_size\n```\n\nHelpers (`sm_in_str`, `sm_in_int`, `sm_in_double`, `sm_out_str`,\n`sm_out_int`, etc.) live in `soramech-c.h` (shipped alongside the C\nspec) and provide typed access to the bytes-in / bytes-out interface.\nThe function still returns `int` (0 = ok, nonzero = error), matching\nthe spec contract.\n\nThis keeps the user's surface looking like ordinary C while the\nunderlying ABI is the same fixed signature for every C box. No\nlibffi, no compile-time codegen, no per-box wrapper. Just a header\nand a macro.\n\n## Input handling\n\nC is its own native type for everything; there is no\n\"convert bytes to a Lua value\" step. Inputs arrive as `(void *bytes,\nint size)` pairs, identical to what `invoke` receives. The helpers\nin `soramech-c.h` provide typed extraction:\n\n| Helper                  | Action                                              |\n|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------|\n| `sm_in_str(i)`          | return `(const char *)sm_inputs[i]`                 |\n| `sm_in_int(i)`          | `atoi` on `sm_inputs[i]`                            |\n| `sm_in_double(i)`       | `strtod`                                            |\n| `sm_in_bool(i)`         | `strcmp(\"true\")`                                    |\n| `sm_in_bytes(i, &n)`    | return pointer + size for raw bytes (binary inputs) |\n\nFor JSON inputs, the user includes a JSON library themselves\n(`libs/json.c` or a vendored cJSON) and parses. There is no built-in\nJSON helper because C has no native JSON type — the parsed result has\nto land in a user-defined struct, which the helpers can't generate.\n\n## Output handling\n\nThe user writes bytes into `sm_out_buf` and sets `*sm_out_size`. The\nhelpers wrap common cases:\n\n| Helper                      | Action                                          |\n|-----------------------------|-------------------------------------------------|\n| `sm_out_str(s)`             | `strcpy` + `*sm_out_size = strlen(s)`           |\n| `sm_out_int(n)`             | `snprintf(\"%d\", n)`                             |\n| `sm_out_double(d)`          | `snprintf(\"%.17g\", d)`                          |\n| `sm_out_bool(b)`            | write `\"true\"` or `\"false\"`                     |\n| `sm_out_bytes(buf, n)`      | `memcpy` + `*sm_out_size = n`                   |\n\nIf the write would exceed `sm_out_capacity`, helpers abort the\nprogram (per issue 303 hard-crash policy). Buffer overflow inside a\nbox function is a bug to fix, not a recoverable error.\n\n## Variable-size outputs\n\nFor boxes whose output capacity is not known at compile time (issue\n302's large-value heap), the helpers expose:\n\n```c\nvoid *sm_out_alloc(int n);   // grab n bytes from the large-value heap\nsm_out_handle(ptr, n);       // store the handle in sm_out_buf\n```\n\nThe user writes into the heap-allocated region directly, then calls\n`sm_out_handle` to record the (pointer, size) pair into `sm_out_buf`\nwhere the dispatch layer expects the handle.\n\nThis is identical in shape to what the Lua spec does for variable-\nsize outputs (issue 306) — the helper hides the detail.\n\n## Thread safety of user code\n\nThe same `.so` is loaded by every worker thread that may call into\nit. Static variables and globals declared in the user's C source are\nshared across all workers. Box functions must be reentrant — no\nshared mutable state without explicit locking.\n\nThe C spec does not enforce this; it is a documentation item in\n`docs/005-language-specs.md` (to be written). Authors of C boxes are\nexpected to know the rules of multithreaded C code.\n\n(Future option: load each box's `.so` into its own dlmopen namespace,\ngiving each worker an isolated copy of statics. Defer until someone\nactually hits a static-variable race.)\n\n## Build\n\n```\nlangs/c/\n    spec.c              ← lang_spec_t implementation\n    soramech-c.h        ← user-facing header (shipped to maps via compile step)\n    Makefile            ← builds spec.so\n    spec.so             ← built artifact (gitignored)\n```\n\nSpec Makefile target:\n```make\nspec.so: spec.c\n\t$(CC) -shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall -o $@ $< -ldl\n```\n\nLinking against `libdl` for `dlopen` / `dlsym` is the only\ndependency. No interpreter, no helper library beyond libc.\n\nThe user's C box files are compiled by the `compile` callback at map\nload time, not by this Makefile. The Makefile here builds only the\nspec itself.\n\n## Error handling\n\n- `dlopen` failure (missing `.so`, link errors): print path + `dlerror()`\n  to stderr, return 1, dispatch layer aborts.\n- `dlsym` failure (missing function): print file/fn + `dlerror()`,\n  return 1, abort.\n- Compile failure: `cc` exit nonzero, print compiler stderr (already\n  routed there by `cc`), return 1, abort.\n- User function returns nonzero: propagate that as the spec's return,\n  abort.\n\nNo retry, no fallback. Per issue 303.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Per-box `cflags` in the box JSON: useful for `-O0 -g` debug builds\n  or `-mavx2` SIMD. Or hard-code defaults and tell users to write a\n  separate Makefile if they want custom flags. The hard-coded path\n  is simpler; defer the JSON field until someone needs it.\n- libffi-style typed signatures: skipped for now in favor of the\n  standardized signature + helpers. If users complain about the\n  fixed signature, revisit.\n- dlmopen namespaces for static-variable isolation: skipped until a\n  real race is observed.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Set up `langs/c/` directory with a Makefile that builds an empty\n   `spec.so` exporting a stub `soramech_lang_spec`.\n2. Implement `init` and `teardown` with the dlopen-handle cache.\n3. Implement `compile` — fork/exec `cc` with the standard flags.\n   Smoke test: compile a single hello-world `.c` file.\n4. Implement `invoke` — dlsym, direct call, propagate return.\n5. Write `soramech-c.h` with the `SM_BOX_ARGS` macro and the basic\n   input/output helpers.\n6. Smoke test: a C box that takes one string input, writes a string\n   output, runs end-to-end through the pool.\n7. Add the typed input helpers (`sm_in_int`, `sm_in_double`, etc.).\n8. Add the typed output helpers.\n9. Test against `maps/driver-test` (C portions).\n10. Add variable-size output support (`sm_out_alloc`, `sm_out_handle`).\n11. Document in `docs/005-language-specs.md` once it exists, with a\n    note on thread safety.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `drivers/c.sh` — phase 2 C driver, retired by this spec\n- `langs/lang-spec.h` — interface header (issue 303)\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — spec contract this implements\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — dispatch layer that calls\n  `invoke`\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — large-value heap\n- `issues/222-compile-button-and-assets-directory.md` — where compiled\n  `.so`s live (`compiled/bin/`)\n- `issues/306-lua-language-spec.md` — sister spec; same shape, no\n  compile step\n- `maps/driver-test` — multi-language test map including C boxes\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/307-c-language-spec.md"

After compile, invocation is in-process via\n`dlopen` / `dlsym` — the user's compiled function is called directly\nthrough a function pointer, with no subprocess and no IPC.\n\nThis is the \"Option 1 — LuaJIT FFI\" model from\n`docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`, applied to C: same-process call,\nnanosecond-overhead invocation, native-typed access. The only thing\nthe C spec adds over the Lua spec is the compile step.\n\n## Per-worker state\n\n`init` returns a small struct holding the dlopen-handle cache:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    void  *so_handles[MAX_BOXES];   // per-file .so handle, indexed by file id\n    void  *fn_ptrs   [MAX_BOXES];   // per-(file, fn) cached function pointer\n    int    n_cached;\n    // (a hash table could replace these arrays if MAX_BOXES grows large)\n} c_handle_t;\n\nvoid *c_init(int worker_idx);\nvoid  c_teardown(void *handle);    // dlclose every cached handle\n```\n\nEach worker thread has its own cache. The same `.so` will end up\nloaded once per worker, since `dlopen` with the same path on the same\nprocess returns a refcounted handle (the underlying code segment is\nshared across all callers — the per-worker `dlopen` is just a\nrefcount bump after the first).\n\n## Compile callback\n\n```c\nint c_compile(const char *src_path, const char *out_path) {\n    pid_t pid = fork();\n    if (pid == 0) {\n        execlp(\"cc\", \"cc\",\n               \"-shared\", \"-fPIC\", \"-O2\", \"-Wall\",\n               \"-o\", out_path, src_path,\n               (char *)NULL);\n        _exit(127);\n    }\n    int status;\n    waitpid(pid, &status, 0);\n    return WIFEXITED(status) && WEXITSTATUS(status) == 0 ? 0 : 1;\n}\n```\n\nCompile runs once per box source file, at map load (or at editor\ncompile-button time, issue 222). The `.so` lands in the map's\n`compiled/bin/` directory. `invoke` later finds it there.\n\nIf the source is already compiled and the `.so` is newer than the\nsource, compile is skipped. mtime check, like the phase 2 driver did.\n\nThe compiler is invoked as `cc` (the system default — `gcc` on most\nLinux, `clang` on macOS). No SoraMech-specific flags beyond\n`-shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall`. The user can add flags via a `cflags`\nfield in the box JSON if they need them; otherwise defaults apply.\n\n## Box file convention\n\nA C box file defines one or more functions with a fixed signature:\n\n```c\n// maps/<name>/src/classify.c\n#include \"soramech-c.h\"     // shipped helper header\n\nint classify(SM_BOX_ARGS) {\n    const char *text = sm_in_str(0);\n    if (text[0] >= '0' && text[0] <= '9') {\n        sm_out_str(\"numeric\");\n    } else {\n        sm_out_str(\"alpha\");\n    }\n    return 0;\n}\n```\n\n`SM_BOX_ARGS` is a macro that expands to the standardized signature:\n\n```c\n#define SM_BOX_ARGS \\\n    const void **sm_inputs, const int *sm_sizes, int sm_n_inputs, \\\n    void *sm_out_buf, int sm_out_capacity, int *sm_out_size\n```\n\nHelpers (`sm_in_str`, `sm_in_int`, `sm_in_double`, `sm_out_str`,\n`sm_out_int`, etc.) live in `soramech-c.h` (shipped alongside the C\nspec) and provide typed access to the bytes-in / bytes-out interface.\nThe function still returns `int` (0 = ok, nonzero = error), matching\nthe spec contract.\n\nThis keeps the user's surface looking like ordinary C while the\nunderlying ABI is the same fixed signature for every C box. No\nlibffi, no compile-time codegen, no per-box wrapper. Just a header\nand a macro.\n\n## Input handling\n\nC is its own native type for everything; there is no\n\"convert bytes to a Lua value\" step. Inputs arrive as `(void *bytes,\nint size)` pairs, identical to what `invoke` receives. The helpers\nin `soramech-c.h` provide typed extraction:\n\n| Helper                  | Action                                              |\n|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------|\n| `sm_in_str(i)`          | return `(const char *)sm_inputs[i]`                 |\n| `sm_in_int(i)`          | `atoi` on `sm_inputs[i]`                            |\n| `sm_in_double(i)`       | `strtod`                                            |\n| `sm_in_bool(i)`         | `strcmp(\"true\")`                                    |\n| `sm_in_bytes(i, &n)`    | return pointer + size for raw bytes (binary inputs) |\n\nFor JSON inputs, the user includes a JSON library themselves\n(`libs/json.c` or a vendored cJSON) and parses. There is no built-in\nJSON helper because C has no native JSON type — the parsed result has\nto land in a user-defined struct, which the helpers can't generate.\n\n## Output handling\n\nThe user writes bytes into `sm_out_buf` and sets `*sm_out_size`. The\nhelpers wrap common cases:\n\n| Helper                      | Action                                          |\n|-----------------------------|-------------------------------------------------|\n| `sm_out_str(s)`             | `strcpy` + `*sm_out_size = strlen(s)`           |\n| `sm_out_int(n)`             | `snprintf(\"%d\", n)`                             |\n| `sm_out_double(d)`          | `snprintf(\"%.17g\", d)`                          |\n| `sm_out_bool(b)`            | write `\"true\"` or `\"false\"`                     |\n| `sm_out_bytes(buf, n)`      | `memcpy` + `*sm_out_size = n`                   |\n\nIf the write would exceed `sm_out_capacity`, helpers abort the\nprogram (per issue 303 hard-crash policy). Buffer overflow inside a\nbox function is a bug to fix, not a recoverable error.\n\n## Variable-size outputs\n\nFor boxes whose output capacity is not known at compile time (issue\n302's large-value heap), the helpers expose:\n\n```c\nvoid *sm_out_alloc(int n);   // grab n bytes from the large-value heap\nsm_out_handle(ptr, n);       // store the handle in sm_out_buf\n```\n\nThe user writes into the heap-allocated region directly, then calls\n`sm_out_handle` to record the (pointer, size) pair into `sm_out_buf`\nwhere the dispatch layer expects the handle.\n\nThis is identical in shape to what the Lua spec does for variable-\nsize outputs (issue 306) — the helper hides the detail.\n\n## Thread safety of user code\n\nThe same `.so` is loaded by every worker thread that may call into\nit. Static variables and globals declared in the user's C source are\nshared across all workers. Box functions must be reentrant — no\nshared mutable state without explicit locking.\n\nThe C spec does not enforce this; it is a documentation item in\n`docs/005-language-specs.md` (to be written). Authors of C boxes are\nexpected to know the rules of multithreaded C code.\n\n(Future option: load each box's `.so` into its own dlmopen namespace,\ngiving each worker an isolated copy of statics. Defer until someone\nactually hits a static-variable race.)\n\n## Build\n\n```\nlangs/c/\n    spec.c              ← lang_spec_t implementation\n    soramech-c.h        ← user-facing header (shipped to maps via compile step)\n    Makefile            ← builds spec.so\n    spec.so             ← built artifact (gitignored)\n```\n\nSpec Makefile target:\n```make\nspec.so: spec.c\n\t$(CC) -shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall -o $@ $< -ldl\n```\n\nLinking against `libdl` for `dlopen` / `dlsym` is the only\ndependency. No interpreter, no helper library beyond libc.\n\nThe user's C box files are compiled by the `compile` callback at map\nload time, not by this Makefile. The Makefile here builds only the\nspec itself.\n\n## Error handling\n\n- `dlopen` failure (missing `.so`, link errors): print path + `dlerror()`\n  to stderr, return 1, dispatch layer aborts.\n- `dlsym` failure (missing function): print file/fn + `dlerror()`,\n  return 1, abort.\n- Compile failure: `cc` exit nonzero, print compiler stderr (already\n  routed there by `cc`), return 1, abort.\n- User function returns nonzero: propagate that as the spec's return,\n  abort.\n\nNo retry, no fallback. Per issue 303.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Per-box `cflags` in the box JSON: useful for `-O0 -g` debug builds\n  or `-mavx2` SIMD. Or hard-code defaults and tell users to write a\n  separate Makefile if they want custom flags. The hard-coded path\n  is simpler; defer the JSON field until someone needs it.\n- libffi-style typed signatures: skipped for now in favor of the\n  standardized signature + helpers. If users complain about the\n  fixed signature, revisit.\n- dlmopen namespaces for static-variable isolation: skipped until a\n  real race is observed.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Set up `langs/c/` directory with a Makefile that builds an empty\n   `spec.so` exporting a stub `soramech_lang_spec`.\n2. Implement `init` and `teardown` with the dlopen-handle cache.\n3. Implement `compile` — fork/exec `cc` with the standard flags.\n   Smoke test: compile a single hello-world `.c` file.\n4. Implement `invoke` — dlsym, direct call, propagate return.\n5. Write `soramech-c.h` with the `SM_BOX_ARGS` macro and the basic\n   input/output helpers.\n6. Smoke test: a C box that takes one string input, writes a string\n   output, runs end-to-end through the pool.\n7. Add the typed input helpers (`sm_in_int`, `sm_in_double`, etc.).\n8. Add the typed output helpers.\n9. Test against `maps/driver-test` (C portions).\n10. Add variable-size output support (`sm_out_alloc`, `sm_out_handle`).\n11. Document in `docs/005-language-specs.md` once it exists, with a\n    note on thread safety.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `drivers/c.sh` — phase 2 C driver, retired by this spec\n- `langs/lang-spec.h` — interface header (issue 303)\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — spec contract this implements\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — dispatch layer that calls\n  `invoke`\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — large-value heap\n- `issues/222-compile-button-and-assets-directory.md` — where compiled\n  `.so`s live (`compiled/bin/`)\n- `issues/306-lua-language-spec.md` — sister spec; same shape, no\n  compile step\n- `maps/driver-test` — multi-language test map including C boxes\n"
  },

Process spawn cost dominates; each call\n10\tis its own freshly-launched executable. The phase 2 driver compiles\n11\tto a standalone binary, not a `.so`.\n12\t\n13\t## Concept\n14\tThe C language spec implements `lang_spec_t` (issue 303) for C. It is\n15\tthe second reference implementation, and the first one that exercises\n16\tthe `compile` callback. After compile, invocation is in-process via\n17\t`dlopen` / `dlsym` — the user's compiled function is called directly\n18\tthrough a function pointer, with no subprocess and no IPC.\n19\t\n20\tThis is the \"Option 1 — LuaJIT FFI\" model from\n21\t`docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`, applied to C: same-process call,\n22\tnanosecond-overhead invocation, native-typed access. The only thing\n23\tthe C spec adds over the Lua spec is the compile step.\n24\t\n25\t## Per-worker state\n26\t\n27\t`init` returns a small struct holding the dlopen-handle cache:\n28\t\n29\t```c\n30\ttypedef struct {\n31\t    void  *so_handles[MAX_BOXES];   // per-file .so handle, indexed by file id\n32\t    void  *fn_ptrs   [MAX_BOXES];   // per-(file, fn) cached function pointer\n33\t    int    n_cached;\n34\t    // (a hash table could replace these arrays if MAX_BOXES grows large)\n35\t} c_handle_t;\n36\t\n37\tvoid *c_init(int worker_idx);\n38\tvoid  c_teardown(void *handle);    // dlclose every cached handle\n39\t```\n40\t\n41\tEach worker thread has its own cache. The same `.so` will end up\n42\tloaded once per worker, since `dlopen` with the same path on the same\n43\tprocess returns a refcounted handle (the underlying code segment is\n44\tshared across all callers — the per-worker `dlopen` is just a\n45\trefcount bump after the first).\n46\t\n47\t## Compile callback\n48\t\n49\t```c\n50\tint c_compile(const char *src_path, const char *out_path) {\n51\t    pid_t pid = fork();\n52\t    if (pid == 0) {\n53\t        execlp(\"cc\", \"cc\",\n54\t               \"-shared\", \"-fPIC\", \"-O2\", \"-Wall\",\n55\t               \"-o\", out_path, src_path,\n56\t               (char *)NULL);\n57\t        _exit(127);\n58\t    }\n59\t    int status;\n60\t    waitpid(pid, &status, 0);\n61\t    return WIFEXITED(status) && WEXITSTATUS(status) == 0 ? 0 : 1;\n62\t}\n63\t```\n64\t\n65\tCompile runs once per box source file, at map load (or at editor\n66\tcompile-button time, issue 222). The `.so` lands in the map's\n67\t`compiled/bin/` directory. `invoke` later finds it there.\n68\t\n69\tIf the source is already compiled and the `.so` is newer than the\n70\tsource, compile is skipped. mtime check, like the phase 2 driver did.\n71\t\n72\tThe compiler is invoked as `cc` (the system default — `gcc` on most\n73\tLinux, `clang` on macOS). No SoraMech-specific flags beyond\n74\t`-shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall`. The user can add flags via a `cflags`\n75\tfield in the box JSON if they need them; otherwise defaults apply.\n76\t\n77\t-- how does this persist? wouldn't the editor overwrite any flags the user added?\n78\t\n79\t## Box file convention\n80\t\n81\tA C box file defines one or more functions with a fixed signature:\n82\t\n83\t```c\n84\t// maps/<name>/src/classify.c\n85\t#include \"soramech-c.h\"     // shipped helper header\n86\t\n87\tint classify(SM_BOX_ARGS) {\n88\t    const char *text = sm_in_str(0);\n89\t    if (text[0] >= '0' && text[0] <= '9') {\n90\t        sm_out_str(\"numeric\");\n91\t    } else {\n92\t        sm_out_str(\"alpha\");\n93\t    }\n94\t    return 0;\n95\t}\n96\t```\n97\t\n98\t`SM_BOX_ARGS` is a macro that expands to the standardized signature:\n99\t\n100\t```c\n101\t#define SM_BOX_ARGS \\\n102\t    const void **sm_inputs, const int *sm_sizes, int sm_n_inputs, \\\n103\t    void *sm_out_buf, int sm_out_capacity, int *sm_out_size\n104\t```\n105\t\n106\tHelpers (`sm_in_str`, `sm_in_int`, `sm_in_double`, `sm_out_str`,\n107\t`sm_out_int`, etc.) live in `soramech-c.h` (shipped alongside the C\n108\tspec) and provide typed access to the bytes-in / bytes-out interface.\n109\tThe function still returns `int` (0 = ok, nonzero = error), matching\n110\tthe spec contract.\n111\t\n112\tThis keeps the user's surface looking like ordinary C while the\n113\tunderlying ABI is the same fixed signature for every C box. No\n114\tlibffi, no compile-time codegen, no per-box wrapper. Just a header\n115\tand a macro.\n116\t\n117\t## Input handling\n118\t\n119\tC is its own native type for everything; there is no\n120\t\"convert bytes to a Lua value\" step. Inputs arrive as `(void *bytes,\n121\tint size)` pairs, identical to what `invoke` receives. The helpers\n122\tin `soramech-c.h` provide typed extraction:\n123\t\n124\t| Helper                  | Action                                              |\n125\t|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------|\n126\t| `sm_in_str(i)`          | return `(const char *)sm_inputs[i]`                 |\n127\t| `sm_in_int(i)`          | `atoi` on `sm_inputs[i]`                            |\n128\t| `sm_in_double(i)`       | `strtod`                                            |\n129\t| `sm_in_bool(i)`         | `strcmp(\"true\")`                                    |\n130\t| `sm_in_bytes(i, &n)`    | return pointer + size for raw bytes (binary inputs) |\n131\t\n132\tFor JSON inputs, the user includes a JSON library themselves\n133\t(`libs/json.c` or a vendored cJSON) and parses.
