      "content":"\nThe C spec does not enforce this; it is a documentation item in\n`docs/005-language-specs.md` (to be written). Authors of C boxes are\nexpected to know the rules of multithreaded C code.\n\n(Future option: load each box's `.so` into its own dlmopen namespace,\ngiving each worker an isolated copy of statics. Defer until someone\nactually hits a static-variable race.)\n\n-- if it's static, wouldn't they just be reading it? how can that create a race?\n   globals I understand since they're editable, but static is immutable right?\n\n## Build\n\n```\nlangs/c/\n    spec.c              ← lang_spec_t implementation\n    soramech-c.h        ← user-facing header (shipped to maps via compile step)\n    Makefile            ← builds spec.so\n    spec.so             ← built artifact (gitignored)\n```\n\nSpec Makefile target:\n```make\nspec.so: spec.c\n\t$(CC) -shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall -o $@ $< -ldl\n```\n\nLinking against `libdl` for `dlopen` / `dlsym` is the only\ndependency. No interpreter, no helper library beyond libc.\n\n-- what does dlopen and dlsym do?\n\nThe user's C box files are compiled by the `compile` callback at map\nload time, not by this Makefile. The Makefile here builds only the\nspec itself.\n\n## Error handling\n\n- `dlopen` failure (missing `.so`, link errors): print path + `dlerror()`\n  to stderr, return 1, dispatch layer aborts.\n- `dlsym` failure (missing function): print file/fn + `dlerror()`,\n  return 1, abort.\n- Compile failure: `cc` exit nonzero, print compiler stderr (already\n  routed there by `cc`), return 1, abort.\n- User function returns nonzero: propagate that as the spec's return,\n  abort.\n\nNo retry, no fallback. Per issue 303.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Per-box `cflags` in the box JSON: useful for `-O0 -g` debug builds\n  or `-mavx2` SIMD. Or hard-code defaults and tell users to write a\n  separate Makefile if they want custom flags. The hard-coded path\n  is simpler; defer the JSON field until someone needs it.\n\n-- let's add the json field. where would they edit it, in the editor?\n\n- libffi-style typed signatures: skipped for now in favor of the\n  standardized signature + helpers. If users complain about the\n  fixed signature, revisit.\n\n-- I don't know what this means\n\n- dlmopen namespaces for static-variable isolation: skipped until a\n  real race is observed.\n\n-- I don't know what this means\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Set up `langs/c/` directory with a Makefile that builds an empty\n   `spec.so` exporting a stub `soramech_lang_spec`.\n2. Implement `init` and `teardown` with the dlopen-handle cache.\n3. Add the typed output helpers.\n9. Test against `maps/driver-test` (C portions).\n10. Add variable-size output support (`sm_out_alloc`, `sm_out_handle`).\n11. Document in `docs/005-language-specs.md` once it exists, with a\n    note on thread safety.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `drivers/c.sh` — phase 2 C driver, retired by this spec\n- `langs/lang-spec.h` — interface header (issue 303)\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — spec contract this implements\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — dispatch layer that calls\n  `invoke`\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — large-value heap\n- `issues/222-compile-button-and-assets-directory.md` — where compiled\n  `.so`s live (`compiled/bin/`)\n- `issues/306-lua-language-spec.md` — sister spec; same shape, no\n  compile step\n- `maps/driver-test` — multi-language test map including C boxes\n"

        "type":"text",
        "text":"Let me address each comment, then update 307.\n\n**Answers:**\n\n**(1) cflags persistence** (line 77): The `cflags` field would live in the box JSON, just like `lang` / `ref` / `fn` / `inputs`. The editor saves whatever the user puts in the box's data, including this field — it doesn't overwrite it on save. Editor reads → user edits → editor writes back, with all fields preserved. The compile step reads the field at compile time.\n\n**(2) JSON inputs vs the loader's JSON parser** (line 137): Two different JSON parsers, two different jobs.\n- The graph loader (issue 305) uses a JSON parser to read the **map's structure** — the box files, data files, connection lists. That parser is internal to the runner; user code never sees it.\n- A C box that wants to **parse a JSON string flowing through a slot** needs its own parsing step. We can wire that up: ship a `sm_in_json(i)` helper that parses the bytes into a `cJSON *` (using the same vendored cJSON the loader uses). The user navigates the resulting tree in their function. Updating the C spec to add this.\n\n**(3) Users shouldn't have to edit box functions / accept any library function** (line 159): Significant change to the design. Updating to a wrapper-generation model: the user declares the function's signature in box JSON, the compile step generates a thin C wrapper that marshals SoraMech's bytes-in/bytes-out into the function's natural C arguments. The user can drop in any function — their own, or one from zlib / OpenCV / wherever — by declaring its signature, headers, and libraries to link. No `SM_BOX_ARGS` macro for the user. They write or reference natural C.\n\n**(4) `static` and races** (line 194): `static` in C does not mean immutable — that is `const`. `static` at file scope means \"this symbol has internal linkage\" (only visible within the file); the variable itself is still mutable. `static` inside a function means \"this variable persists across calls\" (function-local static), still mutable. So `static int counter = 0;` in a C box is mutable shared state across worker threads, and races. Clarifying in the issue.\n\n**(5) What `dlopen` / `dlsym` do** (line 216): `dlopen(\"path/to/file.so\", flags)` loads a shared library at runtime — the OS loader maps the library's code into memory and returns a handle. `dlsym(handle, \"name\")` looks up a symbol (function or variable) in that loaded library by name and returns a pointer to it. Together: load a `.so` file, find a function in it by name, get a pointer you can call directly. Same shape as Windows' `LoadLibrary` + `GetProcAddress`. Plugin systems use this. Adding a brief explainer.\n\n**(6) cflags field — where edited?** (line 242): An additional field in the box inspector. When a C-language box is selected, the inspector shows a \"Compile flags\" text input alongside `lang` / `ref` / `fn`. Phase 2 inspector work — flagging it for issue 222 / inspector enhancement.\n\n**(7) libffi** (line 248): A library that lets you call a C function whose signature you don't know at compile time. You describe the signature at runtime (\"two int args, returns int\"), give it the argument values, and libffi handles the calling-convention details (which register goes where, stack alignment, etc.). Used by Python's `ctypes`, Ruby's `FFI`, etc. Skipping it in favor of compile-time wrapper generation: same effect, no runtime dependency.\n\n**(8) dlmopen** (line 253): A Linux variant of `dlopen` that loads a library into an isolated \"namespace\" — each namespace gets its own copy of the library's symbols (including statics). Two threads calling functions in two different namespaces wouldn't share static-variable state. Less portable than `dlopen` (Linux-only). Mentioned only as a future fallback if static-variable races become a real problem.\n\nNow updating 307:"
      }]

Generates a wrapper `.c` file (see \"Wrapper generation\" below) in\n   the map's `compiled/bin/` directory next to where the `.so` will\n   land.\n3. Forks and execs the system `cc` with:\n   - `-shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall` (defaults)\n   - The user's `cflags`, if any\n   - The wrapper `.c` and the user's `src_path` (if `ref` is set)\n   - `-o out_path`\n   - `-l<lib>` for each entry in `box->link_libs`\n4. Waits for the compiler, returns 0 on success, 1 on failure.\n\nIf the resulting `.so` is newer than the user's source and the\nwrapper, compile is skipped (mtime check, same as phase 2).\n\nThe compiler is `cc` — the system default. `gcc` on most Linux,\n`clang` on macOS. No SoraMech-specific compiler dependency.\n\n### cflags in box JSON\nThe `cflags` field on the box JSON is a string of additional compiler\nflags (`-O0 -g`, `-mavx2`, etc.). It is set by the user in the\ninspector — a \"Compile flags\" text input shown when a C-language box\nis selected. The editor saves it as part of the box's JSON; reads\npreserve the field; saves write it back. Nothing overwrites it.",
    "userModified":false
  },

        "input":{
          "new_string":"## Box file convention: any C function, no boilerplate\n\nUsers do not write a SoraMech-specific C signature. They reference\nany C function — whether one they wrote themselves, or one from a\nlibrary (zlib, OpenCV, libcurl, anything they have headers for) —\nand the C spec generates a thin wrapper that bridges SoraMech's\nbytes-in / bytes-out ABI to the function's natural typed C\nsignature.\n\n### What the user provides\nEither:\n- A `.c` file containing the function, referenced by `ref` in the\n  box JSON; or\n- A library function from a header, no `.c` file of their own — the\n  `ref` field is omitted, the function name and headers are\n  declared in the box JSON, and the library is named in\n  `link_libs`.\n\n### Box JSON for a user-written function\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"classify\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"lang\": \"c\",\n  \"ref\": \"classify.c\",\n  \"fn\": \"classify\",\n  \"inputs\": [\n    {\"name\": \"text\",   \"type\": \"string\"},\n    {\"name\": \"weight\", \"type\": \"int\"}\n  ],\n  \"returns\": \"int\"\n}\n```\n\nThe user's `.c` file is naturally written:\n\n```c\n// maps/<name>/src/classify.c\nint classify(const char *text, int weight) {\n    if (text[0] >= '0' && text[0] <= '9') return weight * 1;\n    return weight * 2;\n}\n```\n\nNo header to include, no macro, no `int classify(SM_BOX_ARGS)`.\nJust a function with a typed signature.\n\n### Box JSON for a library function (no user source)\n\n```json\n{\n  \"id\": \"compress\",\n  \"kind\": \"call\",\n  \"lang\": \"c\",\n  \"fn\": \"compress2\",\n  \"headers\": [\"<zlib.h>\"],\n  \"link_libs\": [\"z\"],\n  \"inputs\": [\n    {\"name\": \"src\",   \"type\": \"bytes\"},\n    {\"name\": \"level\", \"type\": \"int\"}\n  ],\n  \"returns\": \"bytes\"\n}\n```\n\nThe wrapper includes `<zlib.h>`, calls `compress2`, and the linker\npulls in `libz` via `-lz`. No user-written `.c` file.\n\n### Wrapper generation\n\nThe compile callback emits a wrapper `.c` for each C box. The\nwrapper has a fixed entry-point name (`sm_box_entry`) that the spec\nalways `dlsym`s. It declares the user's function (extern), unpacks\nSoraMech's input bytes into typed C arguments per the box's `inputs`\ndeclaration, calls the user's function, and writes the return value\ninto `sm_out_buf` per the box's `returns` declaration.\n\nFor `classify` above, the generated wrapper is roughly:\n\n```c\n// generated: classify_wrap.c\nextern int classify(const char *, int);\n\nint sm_box_entry(const void **inputs, const int *sizes, int n,\n                 void *out_buf, int out_cap, int *out_size) {\n    const char *text   = (const char *)inputs[0];\n    int         weight = atoi((const char *)inputs[1]);\n    int         result = classify(text, weight);\n    *out_size = snprintf(out_buf, out_cap, \"%d\", result);\n    return 0;\n}\n```\n\nThe wrapper is mechanical — same template for every box, varying\nonly in the input-marshalling lines and the return-encoding line.\nThe compile step writes it to `compiled/bin/<box-id>_wrap.c` and\ncompiles `<box-id>_wrap.c` plus the user's source (if any) into a\nsingle `.so`.\n\nThis means the C spec implements typed function calls without\nlibffi (which would do the marshalling at runtime via the C ABI\nmetadata). The same effect is achieved at compile time with\nstraightforward generated code, no runtime dependency.",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/307-c-language-spec.md",
          "replace_all":false,
          "old_string":"## Box file convention\n\nA C box file defines one or more functions with a fixed signature:\n\n```c\n// maps/<name>/src/classify.c\n#include \"soramech-c.h\"     // shipped helper header\n\nint classify(SM_BOX_ARGS) {\n    const char *text = sm_in_str(0);\n    if (text[0] >= '0' && text[0] <= '9') {\n        sm_out_str(\"numeric\");\n    } else {\n        sm_out_str(\"alpha\");\n    }\n    return 0;\n}\n```\n\n`SM_BOX_ARGS` is a macro that expands to the standardized signature:\n\n```c\n#define SM_BOX_ARGS \\\n    const void **sm_inputs, const int *sm_sizes, int sm_n_inputs, \\\n    void *sm_out_buf, int sm_out_capacity, int *sm_out_size\n```\n\nHelpers (`sm_in_str`, `sm_in_int`, `sm_in_double`, `sm_out_str`,\n`sm_out_int`, etc.) live in `soramech-c.h` (shipped alongside the C\nspec) and provide typed access to the bytes-in / bytes-out interface.\nThe function still returns `int` (0 = ok, nonzero = error), matching\nthe spec contract.\n\nThis keeps the user's surface looking like ordinary C while the\nunderlying ABI is the same fixed signature for every C box. No\nlibffi, no compile-time codegen, no per-box wrapper. Just a header\nand a macro."
        },

          "type":"direct"
        },
        "input":{
          "new_string":"## Input marshalling (in the generated wrapper)\n\nThe wrapper converts SoraMech's `(bytes, size)` input pairs into the\ntyped C arguments the user's function expects, based on the\ndeclared input types in the box JSON:\n\n| Declared type | Wrapper action                                                  |\n|---------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------|\n| `string`      | `(const char *)inputs[i]`                                       |\n| `int`         | `atoi((const char *)inputs[i])`                                 |\n| `long`        | `strtoll(...)`                                                  |\n| `double`      | `strtod(...)`                                                   |\n| `bool`        | `strcmp(\"true\", inputs[i]) == 0`                                |\n| `bytes`       | `(const void *)inputs[i]`, paired with `sizes[i]` for the size  |\n| `json`        | `cJSON_ParseWithLength(inputs[i], sizes[i])` → `cJSON *`        |\n\nThe `json` case uses the same vendored cJSON the graph loader uses\n(issue 305) — one JSON library shared across the runner. When a box\ninput is declared `\"type\": \"json\"`, the wrapper passes a `cJSON *`\nto the user's function. The user navigates the tree with cJSON's\nAPI (`cJSON_GetObjectItem`, `cJSON_GetArrayItem`, etc.) and the\nwrapper frees the parsed tree after the function returns.\n\nIf a parse fails (a `json` input that is not valid JSON, an `int`\ninput that does not parse as an integer), the wrapper aborts the\nprogram with the box id and the input position (per issue 303).\n\n## Output encoding (in the generated wrapper)\n\nThe wrapper takes the user function's return value and serializes\nit into `sm_out_buf`, based on the declared `returns` type:\n\n| Declared `returns` | Wrapper action                                              |\n|--------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|\n| `string`           | the user returns `const char *`; `strcpy` + set `out_size` |\n| `int`              | `snprintf(\"%d\", ret)`                                       |\n| `long`             | `snprintf(\"%lld\", ret)`                                     |\n| `double`           | `snprintf(\"%.17g\", ret)`                                    |\n| `bool`             | write `\"true\"` or `\"false\"`                                 |\n| `bytes`            | the user returns `(void *, int)` via an out-parameter pair (see below) |\n| `json`             | the user returns `cJSON *`; `cJSON_PrintUnformatted` → bytes |\n| `void`             | `*out_size = 0` (zero-byte output)                          |\n\nFor `bytes` returns, the user function's signature has the form\n`int my_fn(... const char *out_buf, int out_cap, int *out_size)` —\nextra parameters that the wrapper passes through from\n`sm_out_buf` / `sm_out_capacity` / `sm_out_size`. This handles\nlibrary functions like `compress` that write their output via an\nout-pointer rather than a return value. The box JSON declares\n`\"returns\": \"bytes\"` and the wrapper threads the buffer through.\n\nIf the encoded value exceeds `sm_out_capacity`, the wrapper aborts\n(per issue 303). For boxes whose output capacity is not known at\ncompile time, see \"Variable-size outputs\" below — the wrapper\nroutes through the large-value heap.",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/307-c-language-spec.md",
          "replace_all":false,
          "old_string":"## Input handling\n\nC is its own native type for everything; there is no\n\"convert bytes to a Lua value\" step. Inputs arrive as `(void *bytes,\nint size)` pairs, identical to what `invoke` receives. The helpers\nin `soramech-c.h` provide typed extraction:\n\n| Helper                  | Action                                              |\n|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------|\n| `sm_in_str(i)`          | return `(const char *)sm_inputs[i]`                 |\n| `sm_in_int(i)`          | `atoi` on `sm_inputs[i]`                            |\n| `sm_in_double(i)`       | `strtod`                                            |\n| `sm_in_bool(i)`         | `strcmp(\"true\")`                                    |\n| `sm_in_bytes(i, &n)`    | return pointer + size for raw bytes (binary inputs) |\n\nFor JSON inputs, the user includes a JSON library themselves\n(`libs/json.c` or a vendored cJSON) and parses. There is no built-in\nJSON helper because C has no native JSON type — the parsed result has\nto land in a user-defined struct, which the helpers can't generate.\n\n-- aren't we including a json library in the parsing of the tree map graph step?\n   what do you mean by \"JSON inputs\" - is that the data type boxes? if so,\n   aren't we reading them with built-in primitives and outputting them as\n   structs or... something like that?\n\n## Output handling\n\nThe user writes bytes into `sm_out_buf` and sets `*sm_out_size`. The\nhelpers wrap common cases:\n\n| Helper                      | Action                                          |\n|-----------------------------|-------------------------------------------------|\n| `sm_out_str(s)`             | `strcpy` + `*sm_out_size = strlen(s)`           |\n| `sm_out_int(n)`             | `snprintf(\"%d\", n)`                             |\n| `sm_out_double(d)`          | `snprintf(\"%.17g\", d)`                          |\n| `sm_out_bool(b)`            | write `\"true\"` or `\"false\"`                     |\n| `sm_out_bytes(buf, n)`      | `memcpy` + `*sm_out_size = n`                   |\n\nIf the write would exceed `sm_out_capacity`, helpers abort the\nprogram (per issue 303 hard-crash policy). Buffer overflow inside a\nbox function is a bug to fix, not a recoverable error.\n\n-- okay but remember we can't expect users to edit the box functions. We want to\n   accept any library functions, no matter where they found them."

The handle (pointer + size into the\nlarge-value heap) is what ends up in `sm_out_buf`.\n\nFor string returns, similarly: if the returned string exceeds the\ndeclared fixed `output_capacity`, the wrapper falls back to the\nlarge-value heap.           "old_string":"## Variable-size outputs\n\nFor boxes whose output capacity is not known at compile time (issue\n302's large-value heap), the helpers expose:\n\n```c\nvoid *sm_out_alloc(int n);   // grab n bytes from the large-value heap\nsm_out_handle(ptr, n);       // store the handle in sm_out_buf\n```\n\nThe user writes into the heap-allocated region directly, then calls\n`sm_out_handle` to record the (pointer, size) pair into `sm_out_buf`\nwhere the dispatch layer expects the handle.\n\nThis is identical in shape to what the Lua spec does for variable-\nsize outputs (issue 306) — the helper hides the detail."

          "new_string":"## Thread safety of user code\n\nThe same `.so` is loaded by every worker thread that may call into\nit. **Static variables and globals declared in the user's C source\nare shared mutable state across all workers** unless explicitly\nmade `const`.\n\nA note on `static` in C: it does not mean immutable. `static` at\nfile scope means \"this symbol has internal linkage, only visible\ninside this `.c` file.\" `static` inside a function means \"this\nvariable persists across calls.\" Either way, the variable itself is\nmutable — `static int counter = 0; counter++;` is perfectly legal\nand does what it says, just with internal linkage. Immutable in C\nis `const`.\n\nSo:\n- `static int counter = 0;` at file scope — racy, shared across workers.\n- `static int x = 0;` inside a function body — racy, shared across workers calling that function.\n- `const int max = 100;` — safe, immutable.\n- `static const int max = 100;` — safe, immutable.\n\nBox functions must be reentrant — no mutable shared state without\nexplicit locking. The C spec does not enforce this; the rule lives\nin `docs/005-language-specs.md` (to be written) for box authors to\nread.\n\nA future fallback exists: `dlmopen`, a Linux variant of `dlopen`\nthat loads each library into its own isolated \"namespace,\" giving\neach worker its own copy of the library's symbols (statics\nincluded). Two threads using two different namespaces would not\nshare static state. Less portable than `dlopen` (Linux-only), so\nnot the default — flagged here as the escape hatch if static-\nvariable races become a real problem.",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/307-c-language-spec.md",
          "replace_all":false,
          "old_string":"## Thread safety of user code\n\nThe same `.so` is loaded by every worker thread that may call into\nit. Box functions must be reentrant — no\nshared mutable state without explicit locking.\n\nThe C spec does not enforce this; it is a documentation item in\n`docs/005-language-specs.md` (to be written). Authors of C boxes are\nexpected to know the rules of multithreaded C code.\n\n(Future option: load each box's `.so` into its own dlmopen namespace,\ngiving each worker an isolated copy of statics. Defer until someone\nactually hits a static-variable race.)\n\n-- if it's static, wouldn't they just be reading it? how can that create a race?\n   globals I understand since they're editable, but static is immutable right?"

          "new_string":"Linking against `libdl` for `dlopen` / `dlsym` is the only\ndependency. No interpreter, no helper library beyond libc.\n\n### What `dlopen` and `dlsym` do\n- `dlopen(\"path/to/file.so\", flags)` loads a shared library at\n  runtime. The OS loader maps the library's code into the process's\n  memory and returns a handle. Same idea as Windows'\n  `LoadLibrary`.\n- `dlsym(handle, \"name\")` looks up a symbol — a function or a\n  variable — by name inside an already-loaded library, and returns\n  a pointer to it. Same idea as Windows' `GetProcAddress`.\n\nTogether they are how a program loads and calls code that wasn't\nlinked at compile time. Plugin systems are the classic use case.\nHere, every C box compiles to its own `.so`; the spec `dlopen`s the\n`.so` once per worker, `dlsym`s `sm_box_entry` once per file, and\ncalls the resulting function pointer per invocation.",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/307-c-language-spec.md",
          "replace_all":false,
          "old_string":"Linking against `libdl` for `dlopen` / `dlsym` is the only\ndependency. No interpreter, no helper library beyond libc.\n\n-- what does dlopen and dlsym do?"

{

  "toolUseResult":{

    "structuredPatch":[],
    "userModified":false,
    "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/308-bash-language-spec.md",
    "content":"# 308 — Bash language spec implementation\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nBash boxes today run via `drivers/bash.sh`, which `source`s the box\nfile and invokes the function in a fresh subshell per call. Like the\nphase 2 Lua and C drivers, every invocation is a new process; spawn\ncost dominates. There is no persistent Bash interpreter between\ncalls.\n\n## Concept\n\nThe Bash language spec implements `lang_spec_t` (issue 303) for Bash.\nUnlike the Lua and C specs, Bash cannot be embedded in the runner\nprocess — there is no \"libbash.so\" to link against, and no in-process\nAPI for executing Bash code. The Bash spec uses **Option 3 — Unix\ndomain socket servers** from `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`: each\nworker thread starts and talks to its own persistent Bash subprocess\nover a Unix domain socket. The subprocess stays alive for the whole\nrun, accepting one box invocation at a time.\n\nThis makes Bash the proof case that the spec interface accommodates\nlanguages that cannot be embedded. The spec contract from the\ndispatch layer's perspective is the same: byte buffers in, byte\nbuffers out, abort on nonzero return. Where those bytes go (a\n`lua_State`, a function pointer, or a socket) is the spec's\nbusiness.\n\n## Architecture\n\n```\nWorker thread N                  Bash subprocess N\n─────────────────                 ─────────────────\nspec.invoke(...)                  /tmp/soramech-<run-id>-bash-N.sock\n   |                                       |\n   send framed request    ──────────►      receive\n   recv framed response   ◄──────────      execute box function\n                                           send framed response\n```\n\nOne Bash subprocess per worker thread, addressed by a per-worker\nsocket path. The subprocess runs `bash-server.sh` (shipped alongside\n`spec.c`), which `source`s box files on demand, calls the named\nfunction, and writes back the result.\n\nThe subprocess is single-threaded by Bash's nature, but that is\nfine: one worker thread sends one request at a time. A 16-worker\npool means 16 Bash subprocesses, each handling its own thread's\nrequests serially. The pool's parallelism comes from running 16\nworker threads (and 16 subprocesses) concurrently — not from any\none Bash subprocess.\n\n## Per-worker state\n\n`init` for the Bash spec:\n1. Picks a socket path: `/tmp/soramech-<run-id>-bash-<worker_idx>.sock`.\n2. Forks a child process.\n3. Child execs `bash-server.sh <socket-path>`.\n4. Parent waits briefly for the socket to exist, then connects via\n   `connect(AF_UNIX, ...)`.\n5. Returns a handle holding the connected socket fd.\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    int   sock_fd;\n    pid_t server_pid;\n    char  socket_path[256];\n} bash_handle_t;\n```\n\n`teardown`:\n1. Sends a `{ \"op\": \"shutdown\" }` framed message.\n2. `close(sock_fd)`.\n3. `waitpid(server_pid)` to reap the subprocess.\n4. `unlink(socket_path)`.\n\n## Wire protocol\n\nLength-prefix framing, identical in both directions:\n- 4 bytes: big-endian message length, in bytes.\n- N bytes: message body, JSON-encoded.\n\nThis handles bytes containing newlines, nulls, or any other character\nwithout ambiguity.\n\n### Request\n\n```json\n{\n  \"op\": \"invoke\",\n  \"file\": \"/abs/path/to/box.sh\",\n  \"fn\": \"process\",\n  \"args\": [\"arg0_bytes\", \"arg1_bytes\", ...]\n}\n```\n\n### Response (success)\n\n```json\n{\n  \"ok\": true,\n  \"out\": \"result_bytes\"\n}\n```\n\n### Response (error)\n\n```json\n{\n  \"ok\": false,\n  \"err\": \"bash error message\",\n  \"stderr\": \"any captured stderr\"\n}\n```\n\nA nonzero exit from the box function, a syntax error during `source`,\nor a Bash signal all surface as `\"ok\": false`. The spec returns\nnonzero from `invoke`, the dispatch layer aborts (issue 303).\n\n## bash-server.sh\n\nThe subprocess script is small. Roughly:\n\n```bash\n#!/usr/bin/env bash\n# bash-server.sh <socket-path>\nSOCKET=\"$1\"\n\n# Set up a listening socket using socat (or python -c 'socket...' fallback).\n# Read length-prefix framed messages, dispatch.\nwhile read_request; do\n    case \"${OP}\" in\n        invoke)\n            if ! declare -F \"${FN}\" > /dev/null; then\n                source \"${FILE}\"\n            fi\n            OUTPUT=\"$( \"${FN}\" \"${ARGS[@]}\" 2>/tmp/bash-stderr )\"\n            RC=$?\n            if [ \"${RC}\" -eq 0 ]; then\n                send_response_ok \"${OUTPUT}\"\n            else\n                send_response_err \"$(< /tmp/bash-stderr)\"\n            fi\n            ;;\n        shutdown)\n            exit 0\n            ;;\n    esac\ndone\n```\n\nThe actual implementation has more error checking and uses `socat`\nor a small inline tool to handle framed socket I/O (Bash has no\nnative length-prefix socket reader). `socat` is broadly available;\nfor systems without it, a 30-line C tool can ship alongside.\n\nThe `source`-once-per-file caching is automatic from Bash's\nperspective: once a file is sourced, its functions are defined in\nthe shell's environment. Subsequent calls reuse them.\n\n## Box file convention\n\nA Bash box file defines functions by name:\n\n```bash\n# maps/<name>/src/process.sh\nprocess() {\n    local input=\"$1\"\n    local count=\"$2\"\n    echo \"${input}-${count}\"\n}\n```\n\nThe box JSON references it as `ref = \"process.sh\"`, `fn = \"process\"`.\nInputs become positional args (`$1`, `$2`, …). The function's stdout\nis captured and returned as the output value.\n\nThis is the existing phase 2 convention — kept as-is.\n\n## Input marshalling\n\nInputs are passed as positional arguments to the Bash function. Each\ninput is bytes; Bash treats them as strings (with the usual caveat\nthat null bytes are not survivable in Bash variables). Type-aware\nmarshalling like the Lua and C specs do is not applicable — Bash has\none type, \"string.\" Numeric and boolean inputs arrive as their\ntext form (`\"42\"`, `\"true\"`); the function uses arithmetic expansion\nor `[[ ]]` tests as needed.\n\n## Output marshalling\n\nThe function's stdout is captured by `$(...)` and sent back as the\noutput bytes. A `nil` / empty equivalent is just an empty string.\nThe output type declared in the box JSON is advisory for downstream\nconsumers — the bytes themselves are whatever the function `echo`ed.\n\n## Variable-size outputs\n\nFor variable-size outputs (issue 302's large-value heap), the\nspec.c side allocates from the large-value heap on receiving the\nresponse, copies the response bytes there, stores the handle in\n`out_buf`. The Bash subprocess does not interact with the heap —\nit just sends back its full output, and the spec.c places it.\n\n## Idle cost\n\nEach Bash subprocess at rest is blocked on `read` from its socket.\nZero CPU. Roughly 3–5 MB RSS per process. For a 16-worker pool that\nis 50–80 MB total. Acceptable.\n\nThe subprocesses start at pool init and stay alive until pool\nshutdown. There is no per-call subprocess churn.\n\n## Build\n\n```\nlangs/bash/\n    spec.c            ← lang_spec_t implementation (socket client)\n    bash-server.sh    ← persistent subprocess\n    Makefile          ← builds spec.so\n    spec.so           ← built artifact\n```\n\nSpec Makefile target:\n```make\nspec.so: spec.c\n\t$(CC) -shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall -o $@ $<\n```\n\nNo external dependencies beyond libc. The spec uses the standard\nPOSIX socket API. `bash-server.sh` requires `bash` and `socat`\n(or the bundled framing helper) at runtime.\n\n## Error handling\n\n- Subprocess fails to start (missing `bash` or `bash-server.sh`):\n  `init` returns NULL. Pool runner aborts.\n- Subprocess dies mid-run (segfault, killed): `read` returns 0 or\n  short; `invoke` returns nonzero, dispatch layer aborts.\n- Box function nonzero exit: `\"ok\": false` in response, spec\n  returns nonzero, abort.\n- Wire protocol corruption (bad length prefix, malformed JSON):\n  `invoke` returns nonzero, abort.\n\nNo retry, no respawn. Per issue 303, errors crash the program.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- `socat` vs a bundled C framing helper: `socat` is broadly\n  available but is not always installed by default (Alpine, minimal\n  containers). A small bundled tool removes the external dependency.\n  Decide based on what's convenient when implementing.\n- Per-worker stderr capture: the example uses a shared\n  `/tmp/bash-stderr` which would race between workers. Real\n  implementation needs per-worker stderr (e.g., a pipe back to the\n  subprocess that reads in a separate Bash background job, or just\n  per-worker stderr files).\n- Bundled framing helper: if we ship one, it lives in\n  `langs/bash/bash-frame` and is built by the Makefile. Decision\n  deferred.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Set up `langs/bash/` directory with a Makefile that builds an\n   empty `spec.so` exporting a stub `soramech_lang_spec`.\n2. Write `bash-server.sh` standalone — accepts framed requests on\n   a socket, sources files, calls functions, writes framed\n   responses. Test by hand with `socat` from the command line.\n3. Implement `init` in `spec.c`: fork, exec `bash-server.sh`, wait\n   for socket, connect, return handle.\n4. Implement `teardown`: send shutdown, close socket, reap, unlink.\n5. Implement `invoke`: build request JSON, send framed, read framed\n   response, parse, copy output bytes, return.\n6. Smoke test: a Bash box with one input, one output, runs end-to-end\n   through the pool.\n7. Add error-path handling: bad responses, dead subprocess, nonzero\n   exit codes.\n8. Test against `maps/driver-test` (Bash portions).\n9. Add variable-size output support: route large responses through\n   the large-value heap.\n10. Decide socat-vs-bundled-framer based on implementation experience.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `drivers/bash.sh` — phase 2 Bash driver, retired by this spec\n- `langs/lang-spec.h` — interface header (issue 303)\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — spec contract this implements\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — dispatch layer that calls\n  `invoke`\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — large-value heap for\n  variable-size returns\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — Option 3 (Unix domain sockets),\n  the model this spec uses\n- `issues/306-lua-language-spec.md` — sister spec, in-process Lua\n- `issues/307-c-language-spec.md` — sister spec, in-process C with\n  compile step\n- `maps/driver-test` — multi-language test map including Bash boxes\n"
  },

The Bash spec uses **Option 3 — Unix\ndomain socket servers** from `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`: each\nworker thread starts and talks to its own persistent Bash subprocess\nover a Unix domain socket. The subprocess stays alive for the whole\nrun, accepting one box invocation at a time.\n\nThis makes Bash the proof case that the spec interface accommodates\nlanguages that cannot be embedded. The spec contract from the\ndispatch layer's perspective is the same: byte buffers in, byte\nbuffers out, abort on nonzero return. Where those bytes go (a\n`lua_State`, a function pointer, or a socket) is the spec's\nbusiness.\n\n## Architecture\n\n```\nWorker thread N                  Bash subprocess N\n─────────────────                 ─────────────────\nspec.invoke(...)                  /tmp/soramech-<run-id>-bash-N.sock\n   |                                       |\n   send framed request    ──────────►      receive\n   recv framed response   ◄──────────      execute box function\n                                           send framed response\n```\n\nOne Bash subprocess per worker thread, addressed by a per-worker\nsocket path. The subprocess runs `bash-server.sh` (shipped alongside\n`spec.c`), which `source`s box files on demand, calls the named\nfunction, and writes back the result.\n\nThe subprocess is single-threaded by Bash's nature, but that is\nfine: one worker thread sends one request at a time. A 16-worker\npool means 16 Bash subprocesses, each handling its own thread's\nrequests serially. The pool's parallelism comes from running 16\nworker threads (and 16 subprocesses) concurrently — not from any\none Bash subprocess.\n\n## Per-worker state\n\n`init` for the Bash spec:\n1. Picks a socket path: `/tmp/soramech-<run-id>-bash-<worker_idx>.sock`.\n2. Forks a child process.\n3. Child execs `bash-server.sh <socket-path>`.\n4. Parent waits briefly for the socket to exist, then connects via\n   `connect(AF_UNIX, ...)`.\n5. Returns a handle holding the connected socket fd.\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    int   sock_fd;\n    pid_t server_pid;\n    char  socket_path[256];\n} bash_handle_t;\n```\n\n`teardown`:\n1. Sends a `{ \"op\": \"shutdown\" }` framed message.\n2. `close(sock_fd)`.\n3. `waitpid(server_pid)` to reap the subprocess.\n4. `unlink(socket_path)`.\n\n## Wire protocol\n\nLength-prefix framing, identical in both directions:\n- 4 bytes: big-endian message length, in bytes.\n- N bytes: message body, JSON-encoded.\n\nThis handles bytes containing newlines, nulls, or any other character\nwithout ambiguity.\n\n### Request\n\n```json\n{\n  \"op\": \"invoke\",\n  \"file\": \"/abs/path/to/box.sh\",\n  \"fn\": \"process\",\n  \"args\": [\"arg0_bytes\", \"arg1_bytes\", ...]\n}\n```\n\n### Response (success)\n\n```json\n{\n  \"ok\": true,\n  \"out\": \"result_bytes\"\n}\n```\n\n### Response (error)\n\n```json\n{\n  \"ok\": false,\n  \"err\": \"bash error message\",\n  \"stderr\": \"any captured stderr\"\n}\n```\n\nA nonzero exit from the box function, a syntax error during `source`,\nor a Bash signal all surface as `\"ok\": false`. The spec returns\nnonzero from `invoke`, the dispatch layer aborts (issue 303).\n\n## bash-server.sh\n\nThe subprocess script is small. Roughly:\n\n```bash\n#!/usr/bin/env bash\n# bash-server.sh <socket-path>\nSOCKET=\"$1\"\n\n# Set up a listening socket using socat (or python -c 'socket...' fallback).\n# Read length-prefix framed messages, dispatch.\nwhile read_request; do\n    case \"${OP}\" in\n        invoke)\n            if ! declare -F \"${FN}\" > /dev/null; then\n                source \"${FILE}\"\n            fi\n            OUTPUT=\"$( \"${FN}\" \"${ARGS[@]}\" 2>/tmp/bash-stderr )\"\n            RC=$?\n            if [ \"${RC}\" -eq 0 ]; then\n                send_response_ok \"${OUTPUT}\"\n            else\n                send_response_err \"$(< /tmp/bash-stderr)\"\n            fi\n            ;;\n        shutdown)\n            exit 0\n            ;;\n    esac\ndone\n```\n\nThe actual implementation has more error checking and uses `socat`\nor a small inline tool to handle framed socket I/O (Bash has no\nnative length-prefix socket reader). `socat` is broadly available;\nfor systems without it, a 30-line C tool can ship alongside.\n\nThe `source`-once-per-file caching is automatic from Bash's\nperspective: once a file is sourced, its functions are defined in\nthe shell's environment. Subsequent calls reuse them.\n\n## Box file convention\n\nA Bash box file defines functions by name:\n\n```bash\n# maps/<name>/src/process.sh\nprocess() {\n    local input=\"$1\"\n    local count=\"$2\"\n    echo \"${input}-${count}\"\n}\n```\n\nThe box JSON references it as `ref = \"process.sh\"`, `fn = \"process\"`.\nInputs become positional args (`$1`, `$2`, …). The function's stdout\nis captured and returned as the output value.\n\nThis is the existing phase 2 convention — kept as-is.\n\n## Input marshalling\n\nInputs are passed as positional arguments to the Bash function. Each\ninput is bytes; Bash treats them as strings (with the usual caveat\nthat null bytes are not survivable in Bash variables). Type-aware\nmarshalling like the Lua and C specs do is not applicable — Bash has\none type, \"string.\" Numeric and boolean inputs arrive as their\ntext form (`\"42\"`, `\"true\"`); the function uses arithmetic expansion\nor `[[ ]]` tests as needed.\n\n## Output marshalling\n\nThe function's stdout is captured by `$(...)` and sent back as the\noutput bytes. A `nil` / empty equivalent is just an empty string.\nThe output type declared in the box JSON is advisory for downstream\nconsumers — the bytes themselves are whatever the function `echo`ed.\n\n## Variable-size outputs\n\nFor variable-size outputs (issue 302's large-value heap), the\nspec.c side allocates from the large-value heap on receiving the\nresponse, copies the response bytes there, stores the handle in\n`out_buf`. The Bash subprocess does not interact with the heap —\nit just sends back its full output, and the spec.c places it.\n\n## Idle cost\n\nEach Bash subprocess at rest is blocked on `read` from its socket.\nZero CPU. Roughly 3–5 MB RSS per process. For a 16-worker pool that\nis 50–80 MB total. Acceptable.\n\nThe subprocesses start at pool init and stay alive until pool\nshutdown. There is no per-call subprocess churn.\n\n## Build\n\n```\nlangs/bash/\n    spec.c            ← lang_spec_t implementation (socket client)\n    bash-server.sh    ← persistent subprocess\n    Makefile          ← builds spec.so\n    spec.so           ← built artifact\n```\n\nSpec Makefile target:\n```make\nspec.so: spec.c\n\t$(CC) -shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall -o $@ $<\n```\n\nNo external dependencies beyond libc. The spec uses the standard\nPOSIX socket API. `bash-server.sh` requires `bash` and `socat`\n(or the bundled framing helper) at runtime.\n\n## Error handling\n\n- Subprocess fails to start (missing `bash` or `bash-server.sh`):\n  `init` returns NULL. Pool runner aborts.\n- Subprocess dies mid-run (segfault, killed): `read` returns 0 or\n  short; `invoke` returns nonzero, dispatch layer aborts.\n- Box function nonzero exit: `\"ok\": false` in response, spec\n  returns nonzero, abort.\n- Wire protocol corruption (bad length prefix, malformed JSON):\n  `invoke` returns nonzero, abort.\n\nNo retry, no respawn. Per issue 303, errors crash the program.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- `socat` vs a bundled C framing helper: `socat` is broadly\n  available but is not always installed by default (Alpine, minimal\n  containers). A small bundled tool removes the external dependency.\n  Decide based on what's convenient when implementing.\n- Per-worker stderr capture: the example uses a shared\n  `/tmp/bash-stderr` which would race between workers. Real\n  implementation needs per-worker stderr (e.g., a pipe back to the\n  subprocess that reads in a separate Bash background job, or just\n  per-worker stderr files).\n- Bundled framing helper: if we ship one, it lives in\n  `langs/bash/bash-frame` and is built by the Makefile. Decision\n  deferred.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Set up `langs/bash/` directory with a Makefile that builds an\n   empty `spec.so` exporting a stub `soramech_lang_spec`.\n2. Write `bash-server.sh` standalone — accepts framed requests on\n   a socket, sources files, calls functions, writes framed\n   responses. Test by hand with `socat` from the command line.\n3. Implement `init` in `spec.c`: fork, exec `bash-server.sh`, wait\n   for socket, connect, return handle.\n4. Implement `teardown`: send shutdown, close socket, reap, unlink.\n5. Implement `invoke`: build request JSON, send framed, read framed\n   response, parse, copy output bytes, return.\n6. Smoke test: a Bash box with one input, one output, runs end-to-end\n   through the pool.\n7. Add error-path handling: bad responses, dead subprocess, nonzero\n   exit codes.\n8. Test against `maps/driver-test` (Bash portions).\n9. Add variable-size output support: route large responses through\n   the large-value heap.\n10. Decide socat-vs-bundled-framer based on implementation experience.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `drivers/bash.sh` — phase 2 Bash driver, retired by this spec\n- `langs/lang-spec.h` — interface header (issue 303)\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — spec contract this implements\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — dispatch layer that calls\n  `invoke`\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — large-value heap for\n  variable-size returns\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — Option 3 (Unix domain sockets),\n  the model this spec uses\n- `issues/306-lua-language-spec.md` — sister spec, in-process Lua\n- `issues/307-c-language-spec.md` — sister spec, in-process C with\n  compile step\n- `maps/driver-test` — multi-language test map including Bash boxes\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/308-bash-language-spec.md"
        },
        "id":"toolu_01YDfAzFh4JiL3Q2xMu3P65Y"
      }]
  },

        "text":"**307 corrections applied**:\n- Compile callback signature extended to take `box_t *` (small extension to 303). Wrapper generation lives in the C spec's compile.\n- Box file convention rewritten: users do NOT use `SM_BOX_ARGS`. They write natural-signature C functions, or reference library functions with `headers` / `link_libs` declarations and no user `.c` file. The compile step generates a thin wrapper named `sm_box_entry` that marshals SoraMech's bytes to the function's typed args.\n- Input marshalling table updated: `string` / `int` / `long` / `double` / `bool` / `bytes` / `json` (the `json` case now uses cJSON and the user gets a `cJSON *`).\n- Output encoding updated: the wrapper reads the user's return value and serializes per the declared `returns` type. `bytes` returns get out-pointer pass-through for library functions like `compress`. `void` returns produce zero-byte output.\n- Variable-size outputs handled at compile time based on `output_capacity = 0` — the wrapper picks the large-value heap path when the box declares variable-size.\n- Thread-safety section now correctly explains `static` (internal linkage, still mutable) vs `const` (immutable). `dlmopen` explained as the fallback escape hatch.\n- New \"What dlopen and dlsym do\" subsection in Build with plain-language explanation.\n- Open questions resolved: `cflags` field added, libffi noted as the runtime alternative we're skipping in favor of compile-time wrappers, dlmopen kept as a deferred fallback.\n\n**308 written — Bash language spec**:\n- The \"Option 3\" socket-server model — proves the spec interface accommodates languages that can't be embedded.\n- One persistent Bash subprocess per worker thread, addressed by `/tmp/soramech-<run-id>-bash-<N>.sock`. Subprocess stays alive for the whole run.\n- Wire protocol: 4-byte big-endian length prefix + JSON body. Same format both directions. Op-code is `invoke` or `shutdown`.\n- `bash-server.sh` is small: read framed request → `source` file (cached after first time, since Bash keeps function definitions across calls in the same shell) → call function → capture stdout → write framed response.\n- Inputs are positional args (`$1`, `$2`, …). Output is the function's stdout. No type marshalling — Bash has one type, string.\n- Idle cost ~3–5 MB per subprocess; 16 workers ≈ 50–80 MB total.\n- Variable-size outputs handled at the spec.c side, not in Bash — large response bytes get copied into the large-value heap; the subprocess just sends the bytes.\n- Error handling: any failure (subprocess dies, nonzero exit, bad protocol) crashes the program per 303.\n- Open questions: `socat` vs bundled framing helper for the Bash side (Bash has no native length-prefix socket I/O); per-worker stderr capture without races."

Phase 3 changes the shape of the problem — multiple boxes invoking concurrently across worker threads, iterators producing many invocations, possibly a single box running thousands of times. The naive \"append a line per invocation\" gets messy when threads are racing. We need a deliberate design: what gets logged, where it's buffered, how it's flushed, what the editor can render. Concrete, observable, currently undefined.\n\n**Alternatives:**\n\n- **Build system / Makefile orchestration** — top-level Makefile that builds the pool runner, the language spec `.so`s, vendored libs, runs unit tests. There's a real question (should iterator-queue draining outrank new entry submission? should allocator cleanup run only when idle?) but it might be premature to design before we have a workload that hurts under uniform priority. Risk: solving a problem we don't have yet. I'd defer until a concrete pain point shows up.\n- **Compile orchestration** — when does compile run, how does the graph walk drive each spec's `compile` callback. Test maps, parity, the phase demo. Could be its own issue but feels like a phase wrap-up doc rather than an architectural piece.\n\nWant me to write 309 = run output? {
  "timestamp":"2026-05-09T05:51:07.261Z",
  "message":{
    "content":"well, the editor should be entirely disconnected from the run-time elements. It's an editor, not an IDE. I think last-run.json is mostly for LLM parsing and such. Maybe we should consider creating some viewer utility or something for the last-run.json file instead of passing it through the editor?\n\nwe do need the build system to be solid.\n\nfor the priority queue, how about we just build it as defined, then give every task a priority of 1, and set the max priority to 1? that way the functionality is there, but the operation of the system doesn't meaningfully change. That way we can use it if we ever need to.\n\nwe don't want to have task scheduling. Now we just block, and use the priority queue for low priority things, instead of having them run some set time later. If the user wants to make a task that sleeps for however long and then creates a new task, they can do that. Actually, how would they do that? would the runners be blocked, essentially wasting thread computation time? what does that look like?\n\ncompile orchestration doesn't need an issue file.\n\nwe can write the integration tests as an issue file. That way we can have two rounds of planning, so we can better think of all the edge-cases for tests.\n\nhow many issue files does that leave us with?",

        "type":"text",
        "text":"**On the sleep question:** A sleep inside a box function ties up one worker thread for the full duration of the sleep. The thread is sitting inside `lua_pcall` (Lua), or in a `dlsym`'d function (C), or in `read()` waiting on the Bash subprocess that's running `sleep`. It's suspended, doing nothing.\n\nConcretely:\n- 16-worker pool, 1 box sleeping 10s → 15 workers keep running. Fine.\n- 16-worker pool, 16 boxes all sleeping → all workers parked, nothing else runs until a sleep finishes.\n- The pool's CPU budget is also the budget for \"blocking activities.\" Heavy sleep usage means the user bumps `SORAMECH_WORKERS`.\n\nThe cooperative alternative — without a scheduler — is graph-level: the user splits \"kick off the thing\" and \"check if the thing is done\" into two boxes wired through an iterator with a queued input, polling at the graph level. Each individual box returns quickly; the iteration handles the wait. Pattern, not infrastructure.\n\nThis is just documented behavior. Goes in `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` (already mentions blocking semantics) — not its own issue.\n\n**Issue count from your decisions:**\n\nThree confirmed:\n- **309** — Build system & Makefile orchestration\n- **310** — Priority queue (built per spec, every task priority 1, max priority 1; no-op behaviorally, but the mechanism is wired in for later)\n- **311** — Phase 3 integration tests\n\nPossible fourth, if you want it as its own issue rather than folded into 311 or 309:\n- **312** — Run output / `last-run.json` format and writer (decoupled from editor; the viewer utility you mentioned would be a separate phase 4-or-later thing). The questions are real — what gets logged, how do concurrent worker threads write without races, what's the file format for LLM/CLI consumption — but they're not huge. Could fit inside 311's test plan since tests need to read the output.\n\nSo: **3 minimum, 4 if you want run output as its own design issue.** Your call.\n\nWant me to start with 309?"
      }]
  },

    "content":"# 309 — Build system & Makefile orchestration\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nPhase 2 has no compiled binary. The runner is a Lua script\n(`src/007-runner-main.lua`) invoked via `luajit`. Drivers are shell\nscripts that compile per-box C source on demand. There is no\ntop-level Makefile, no vendoring of C dependencies, no link step\nbeyond per-driver compile.\n\nPhase 3 introduces a real C binary (the pool runner) plus a set of\nlanguage spec `.so` files. They need to compile in the right order\nwith the right flags, and the build needs to be reproducible from a\nclean checkout.\n\n## Concept\n\nA top-level `Makefile` at the project root orchestrates the entire\nphase 3 build. It builds:\n\n1. The pool runner binary: `soramech-pool` (statically links the\n   3d-rts task pool, the vendored JSON parser, the slot store, the\n   graph loader, the dispatch layer, the spec registry).\n2. Each language spec: `langs/<name>/spec.so`, built by a small\n   per-spec Makefile.\n3. (Optional) Unit test binaries.\n\nEach component has its own Makefile if it has non-trivial build\nrules. The top-level Makefile delegates to them via `$(MAKE) -C\n<dir>`. A clean checkout becomes a working build with `make`.\n\n## Directory layout\n\n```\nsoramech/\n├── Makefile                       ← top-level orchestration\n├── soramech-pool                  ← built binary (gitignored)\n├── src/\n│   ├── 008-pool-runner.c          ← main entry, pool lifecycle (issue 301)\n│   ├── slot-store.c / .h          ← per-task slot allocator (issue 302)\n│   ├── graph-loader.c / .h        ← C loader, replaces 003-loader.lua (issue 305)\n│   ├── dispatch.c / .h            ← dispatch action (issue 304)\n│   └── spec-registry.c / .h       ← spec dlopen/registry (issue 303)\n├── libs/\n│   ├── task-pool/                 ← vendored 3d-rts pool\n│   │   ├── 900-task-pool.h\n│   │   └── 900-task-pool.c\n│   └── json/                      ← vendored JSON parser (cJSON, jsmn, etc.)\n│       ├── cjson.h\n│       └── cjson.c\n├── langs/\n│   ├── lua/\n│   │   ├── Makefile               ← builds spec.so\n│   │   ├── spec.c\n│   │   └── spec.so                ← built (gitignored)\n│   ├── c/\n│   │   ├── Makefile\n│   │   ├── spec.c\n│   │   ├── soramech-c.h           ← user-facing helper header\n│   │   └── spec.so\n│   └── bash/\n│       ├── Makefile\n│       ├── spec.c\n│       ├── bash-server.sh\n│       └── spec.so\n└── build/                         ← intermediate object files (gitignored)\n```\n\n`build/` holds intermediate `.o` files; binaries land alongside their\nsources or at the project root. `.so` and `.o` files are gitignored;\n`make clean` removes them.\n\n## Top-level targets\n\n```make\n.PHONY: all runner specs clean test\n\nall: runner specs\n\nrunner: soramech-pool\n\nsoramech-pool: $(POOL_OBJECTS)\n\t$(CC) -O2 -Wall -pthread -o $@ $^ -ldl\n\nspecs:\n\t$(MAKE) -C langs/lua\n\t$(MAKE) -C langs/c\n\t$(MAKE) -C langs/bash\n\nclean:\n\trm -f soramech-pool\n\trm -rf build/\n\t$(MAKE) -C langs/lua clean\n\t$(MAKE) -C langs/c clean\n\t$(MAKE) -C langs/bash clean\n\ntest: all\n\t./scripts/run-tests.sh\n```\n\n`POOL_OBJECTS` resolves to the `.o` files for every `src/*.c`,\n`libs/task-pool/*.c`, and `libs/json/*.c`. A pattern rule compiles\neach source into `build/`.\n\n## Per-language spec Makefiles\n\nEach `langs/<name>/Makefile` follows the same shape. Lua's:\n\n```make\nLUA_INCLUDE ?= /usr/include/luajit-2.1\nLUA_LIB    ?= /usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu\n\nCFLAGS  = -shared -fPIC -O2 -Wall -I$(LUA_INCLUDE)\nLDFLAGS = -L$(LUA_LIB) -lluajit-5.1\n\nspec.so: spec.c\n\t$(CC) $(CFLAGS) -o $@ $< $(LDFLAGS)\n\nclean:\n\trm -f spec.so\n```\n\nC's spec links `-ldl`. Bash's links nothing beyond libc. The pattern\nis uniform.\n\nLuaJIT's include and lib paths are set via environment variables so\nthe build works on systems where they live elsewhere (macOS via\nhomebrew, Alpine, etc.). Defaults match Debian/Ubuntu.\n\n## Build modes\n\n```\nmake                  ← release: -O2 -Wall\nmake DEBUG=1          ← debug:   -O0 -g -DDEBUG -Wall -Wextra\nmake STRICT=1         ← strict:  release + -Werror -Wextra -Wpedantic\n```\n\n`DEBUG=1` adds `-g` for symbols and `-DDEBUG` for opt-in debug\nprints in the C sources. `STRICT=1` fails the build on any warning;\nuseful in CI.\n\n## Vendoring\n\nVendored libraries live under `libs/` and are checked into the repo\nas plain source — no submodules, no fetches at build time. To\nupdate a vendored library, copy the new sources in and commit. The\nvendored directory carries a small `VENDOR.md` noting the upstream\nsource and the version that was copied.\n\nInitial vendored libraries:\n- `libs/task-pool/` — 3d-rts task pool (issue 301)\n- `libs/json/` — JSON parser (issue 305 picks cJSON or similar)\n\nFuture additions land alongside these.\n\n## Spec discovery at runtime\n\nThe pool runner finds language specs by scanning the `langs/`\ndirectory at startup, opening each `langs/<name>/spec.so` via\n`dlopen`, and reading the `soramech_lang_spec` symbol via `dlsym`\n(per issue 303). The path to `langs/` is resolved relative to the\nrunner binary's location: the runner reads `/proc/self/exe`\n(Linux), follows the symlink, and looks for `langs/` next to it.\n\nThis means the binary is location-flexible: the user can drop the\nproject tree anywhere, and `./soramech-pool` finds its specs\nwithout a config file.\n\nIf the user wants to override (custom spec dirs for development),\n`SORAMECH_LANGS_DIR=/path/to/langs ./soramech-pool` overrides the\nauto-detected location.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- macOS: `.so` becomes `.dylib`, and there's no `/proc/self/exe`.\n  Use `_NSGetExecutablePath`. Cross-platform spec discovery is a\n  small platform-#ifdef. Fold into the spec registry implementation.\n- Out-of-tree build (a separate `build/` directory holding all\n  artifacts): nice-to-have, not blocking. Current layout uses\n  in-tree `.o` files in `build/` already — full out-of-tree means\n  the `.so`s live in `build/langs/lua/spec.so` instead of next to\n  the source. Defer.\n- Static vs dynamic linking of vendored libs: vendored sources\n  compile straight into the runner binary. No separate `.so` for\n  the task pool or JSON parser. Right call given how small they are.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Write the top-level Makefile with empty `runner`, `specs`,\n   `clean` targets. Verify `make` succeeds against an empty source\n   tree.\n2. Vendor the 3d-rts task pool into `libs/task-pool/`. Add a\n   `VENDOR.md`.\n3. Vendor cJSON (or chosen JSON parser) into `libs/json/`. Add a\n   `VENDOR.md`.\n4. Add the pool-runner build rule. Compiles `src/*.c` plus vendored\n   libs into `soramech-pool`. Initially the runner is just `int\n   main() { return 0; }` to verify the link.\n5. Add `langs/lua/Makefile`. Build `spec.so` from a stub `spec.c`.\n6. Add `langs/c/Makefile`. Same shape.\n7. Add `langs/bash/Makefile`. Same shape.\n8. Add `make DEBUG=1` and `make STRICT=1` modes.\n9. Wire `make test` into a placeholder script (real tests come from\n   issue 311).\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `Makefile` — top-level (to be created)\n- `langs/lua/Makefile`, `langs/c/Makefile`, `langs/bash/Makefile`\n  — per-spec (to be created)\n- `libs/task-pool/`, `libs/json/` — vendored sources (to be added)\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool runner this\n  builds\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — spec discovery uses\n  `dlopen`/`dlsym`\n- `issues/306-lua-language-spec.md`, `307-c-language-spec.md`,\n  `308-bash-language-spec.md` — per-spec build details\n- `issues/311-integration-tests-and-run-output.md` — `make test`\n  consumers\n"
  },

        "input":{
          "content":"# 310 — Priority queue: wired in, no-op behaviorally\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nThe 3d-rts task pool's `pool_spawn` takes a priority parameter:\n\n```c\ntask_id_t pool_spawn(task_pool_t *pool,\n                     action_fn_t  *actions,\n                     void        **action_args,\n                     int           n_actions,\n                     int           priority);\n```\n\nHigher priority tasks are dispatched ahead of lower priority tasks\nwhen multiple are ready. The pool's queue handles the ordering.\n\nPhase 3 needs to specify what SoraMech does with this knob. The\nsimplest answer is the right one for now: do nothing.\n\n## Decision\n\nEvery dispatch task is submitted at priority `1`. The compile-time\nconstant `MAX_PRIORITY` is set to `1`. There is no graph-level or\nbox-level concept of priority. The runner does not expose any user-\nfacing knob for it.\n\nThe mechanism is wired through the codebase — every `pool_spawn`\ncall passes a priority, the constant is referenced rather than\nhard-coded inline — but the behavior is identical to a single-\npriority pool. Tasks run in submission order (modulo whatever\nordering the pool guarantees within a single priority level).\n\n## Why wire it in if it does nothing\n\nTwo reasons:\n\n1. **Future hooks land as config changes, not refactors.** When a\n   real priority use case appears (allocator cleanup at lowest\n   priority; user-marked urgent boxes; iterator queue draining\n   prioritized over new entry submission), raising `MAX_PRIORITY`\n   and emitting different priorities at the right call sites is a\n   line edit, not a structural change. If the priority parameter\n   were stripped out, adding it later means going back through every\n   `pool_spawn` callsite and threading a new argument.\n\n2. **The pool's API requires it.** `pool_spawn` takes a priority.\n   Callers must pass something. Passing `1` consistently is the\n   straightforward expression of \"no priority concept yet.\"\n\n## Specific call sites\n\n```c\n// src/dispatch.c — every dispatch task\npool_spawn(pool, &dispatch_action, &task_arg, 1, SM_PRIORITY_DEFAULT);\n\n// src/008-pool-runner.c — entry-box submission at startup\npool_spawn(pool, &dispatch_action, &task_arg, 1, SM_PRIORITY_DEFAULT);\n\n// src/slot-store.c — deferred allocator cleanup task (issue 302)\npool_spawn(pool, &cleanup_action, &cleanup_arg, 1, SM_PRIORITY_DEFAULT);\n\n// langs/bash/spec.c — ... none, the spec doesn't spawn pool tasks\n```\n\n`SM_PRIORITY_DEFAULT` is `1`. Defined in `src/008-pool-runner.h` (or\na sibling header) so all callers use the same name.\n\n## Future hooks (not in scope, but called out)\n\nWhen `MAX_PRIORITY` is raised, the natural assignments are:\n\n| Future use case                                     | Priority |\n|-----------------------------------------------------|----------|\n| User-marked \"urgent\" boxes (UI / interactive)       | 3        |\n| Iterator continuation when its queue is non-empty   | 2        |\n| Default dispatch task                               | 1        |\n| Allocator cleanup task (deferred coalescing, 302)   | 0        |\n\nThese are speculative. The actual priority schema is decided when\nthere is a workload that demonstrates the need.\n\nA box-level priority field could go in the box JSON (`\"priority\":\n2`) and be plumbed through `dispatch_task_t`. The dispatch action\nreads it, passes it to `pool_spawn` for any successor tasks. This\nis a future change.\n\n## Open questions\n\n(none currently — this is intentionally a small change to the call\nsites. The design conversation about what priorities should mean is\ndeferred until concrete need.)\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Define `SM_PRIORITY_DEFAULT` (= 1) and `SM_MAX_PRIORITY` (= 1)\n   in a runner-wide header.\n2. Make every `pool_spawn` call site pass `SM_PRIORITY_DEFAULT`.\n3. Set the pool's max priority at `pool_create` time using\n   `SM_MAX_PRIORITY` (if the pool API takes a max-priority hint).\n4. That's it. No tests required beyond verifying the constants\n   compile and the pool runs.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — calls `pool_spawn` for entry boxes\n- `src/dispatch.c` — calls `pool_spawn` for successor tasks\n- `src/slot-store.c` — calls `pool_spawn` for deferred cleanup\n- `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.h` — `pool_spawn` priority parameter\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — dispatch task submission\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — deferred cleanup tasks\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/310-priority-queue.md"
        },
        "id":"toolu_01RXsf6p5gNDQd7XY9HQbzSg"

        "input":{
          "content":"# 311 — Integration tests & run output (`last-run.json`)\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nPhase 2 writes a `last-run.json` after every map run, recording per-\nbox invocations, inputs, outputs, and any errors. The editor reads\nit to display a run summary. Phase 2 testing is ad-hoc: a few maps\nin `maps/` (`hello`, `branch-test`, `classify-demo`, `driver-test`)\nthat the developer runs by hand to verify the synchronous executor\nstill works.\n\nPhase 3 changes the shape of the problem: many concurrent\ninvocations, possibly thousands per run when iterators are in play,\nwritten from multiple worker threads. The phase 2 \"build a single\ntable at end of run\" approach does not survive that. And the\nexisting maps cover only a small slice of the new surface (no\nqueued inputs, no large iterator counts, no fan-in).\n\nThis issue covers two things that go together: the format and\nwriter for the run output, and the integration test plan that\nexercises the phase 3 runtime end-to-end.\n\n## Part A — Run output\n\n### Decoupling from the editor\n\nThe editor (phase 2) is being scoped down to a pure map editor — it\ndoes not know how to run maps and does not display run results.\n`last-run.json` is therefore not a UI feed. It exists for:\n\n- LLM consumption — agents reading the file to understand what a\n  run did\n- CLI-driven inspection — a future viewer utility (out of scope\n  here) that pretty-prints the file\n- Test harness consumption — the integration tests below diff the\n  written file against expected output\n\nDecoupling means the writer's design is driven by these consumers,\nnot by editor rendering needs.\n\n### File format: JSON Lines\n\nThe phase 2 single-document format does not work when the runner is\nstreaming events from many threads. Use JSON Lines instead — one\nJSON object per line, each line is one event, the file grows\nmonotonically as the run proceeds.\n\nEvent types:\n\n```jsonl\n{\"event\":\"run_start\", \"ts\":1234567890.123, \"map\":\"maps/classify-demo\", \"n_workers\":16}\n{\"event\":\"task_submit\", \"ts\":..., \"task_id\":42, \"box_id\":\"classify\", \"worker_idx\":-1}\n{\"event\":\"task_start\", \"ts\":..., \"task_id\":42, \"worker_idx\":3}\n{\"event\":\"task_end\", \"ts\":..., \"task_id\":42, \"worker_idx\":3, \"duration_us\":127, \"output_size\":12}\n{\"event\":\"slot_alloc\", \"ts\":..., \"slot_id\":5, \"size\":256, \"n_cells\":1}\n{\"event\":\"slot_free\", \"ts\":..., \"slot_id\":5}\n{\"event\":\"run_end\", \"ts\":..., \"duration_us\":1850, \"n_tasks\":7}\n```\n\nJSONL is append-only, which makes thread-safe writing tractable: a\nsingle mutex around the write call serializes the lines, and each\nline is self-contained so a partial line on crash is recoverable\n(reader skips the broken trailing line).\n\nThe reader (LLM, viewer, test harness) parses one line at a time;\ntotal file size doesn't have to fit in memory.\n\n### What gets logged\n\nPer-task: submission, start, end, duration, output size. Inputs\nand outputs are NOT logged by default — for iterator boxes\nproducing thousands of invocations, logging every value bloats\nthe file unbounded. There is a verbosity switch:\n\n- `SORAMECH_LOG_VALUES=1` — log inputs and outputs (truncated past\n  some byte limit, e.g. 4 KB) per task. For debugging.\n- Default: log task lifecycle but not values.\n\nSlot allocator events (alloc, free, coalesce, grow) at a separate\nverbosity level. Off by default; on under `SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1`.\nFor diagnosing memory issues.\n\n### Writer mechanism\n\nA single dedicated writer thread inside the runner consumes events\nfrom a multi-producer single-consumer ring buffer. Worker threads\npush event records (small fixed-size structs) into the ring; the\nwriter pulls them, serializes to JSON, and writes lines to the\nfile. This avoids per-event mutex contention — the ring buffer is\nthe only shared state, and a well-written MPSC ring is lock-free\non the producer side.\n\nAlternative considered: each worker writes its own log file, merge\nat end. Simpler concurrency, but readers would have to merge by\ntimestamp — and any cross-event reasoning (was task A still\nrunning when task B ended?) requires the merge anyway.\n\nThe writer thread is started after the pool is created and joined\nbefore `pool_destroy`. It also handles `run_end` as the very last\nevent, including the final summary.\n\n### File location\n\n`<map-dir>/last-run.jsonl` (note: `.jsonl` not `.json` — the\nextension reflects the format change). Overwritten on every run.\n\nA rotated archive (`last-run.jsonl.1`, `.2`, …) is out of scope.\nUsers who want history copy the file before re-running.\n\n## Part B — Integration tests\n\n### Scope\n\nEnd-to-end tests of the pool runner against real map directories.\nEach test is:\n\n1. A map directory under `tests/maps/<name>/`\n2. An expected `last-run.jsonl` (or a comparison spec) under\n   `tests/expected/<name>.jsonl`\n3. A test driver script that runs the map and diffs\n\nThe test driver is `scripts/run-tests.sh`. It iterates\n`tests/maps/`, runs each, diffs against expected (with a normalizer\nthat drops timestamps, durations, worker indices — anything non-\ndeterministic), and reports pass/fail.\n\n### Test maps\n\nCoverage targets:\n\n| Test map                  | What it exercises                                    |\n|---------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|\n| `hello`                   | Single Lua box, one input, one output                |\n| `data-only`               | Data box → call box. No inputs, just stored values   |\n| `fan-out-3`               | One output → three consumer boxes (peek, refcount)   |\n| `fan-in-iterator`         | Three producers → iterator with queued input         |\n| `comparator-routing`      | Comparator with all three branches (lt/eq/gt)        |\n| `iterator-100`            | Iterator with 100 input values, round-robin to 3 paths |\n| `multilang`               | One Lua box, one C box, one Bash box, all wired      |\n| `large-output`            | Box producing a 1 MB string (variable-size heap)     |\n| `cycle-detector-fail`     | Non-iterator cycle — load must abort                 |\n| `missing-input-fail`      | Connection references a nonexistent box — load aborts|\n| `box-error-fail`          | Box function returns nonzero — runner aborts         |\n\nThe `*-fail` tests verify error behavior — the runner is expected\nto exit nonzero with a precise error message. The driver matches\nexit code and stderr against expected.\n\n### Test driver\n\n```bash\n# scripts/run-tests.sh\nfor test_dir in tests/maps/*/; do\n    name=$(basename \"${test_dir}\")\n    expected=\"tests/expected/${name}.jsonl\"\n\n    actual=$( \"${SOURCE_DIR}/soramech-pool\" \"${test_dir}\" )\n    rc=$?\n\n    if [ -f \"${expected}.exit\" ]; then\n        # *-fail tests: assert exit code and stderr substring\n        check_failure \"${name}\" \"${rc}\" \"${test_dir}/last-run.jsonl\"\n    else\n        # success tests: diff normalized last-run.jsonl\n        check_success \"${name}\" \"${test_dir}/last-run.jsonl\" \"${expected}\"\n    fi\ndone\n```\n\n`normalize_jsonl` strips timestamps, durations, worker indices,\nslot ids, and task ids (all non-deterministic) and sorts events by\nevent type. The result should be deterministic across runs.\n\n### Phase 3 demo map\n\nA single map under `issues/completed/demos/phase-3/` that\ndemonstrates everything working together:\n\n- Multiple entry-point data boxes\n- Lua, C, and Bash boxes all wired together\n- An iterator with a queued input\n- A comparator routing into different downstream paths\n- A large-output box (variable-size heap)\n- Non-trivial graph topology (≥ 10 boxes)\n\nRun with `./run.sh` from the demo directory. Prints a short summary\nof what happened (parsing the `last-run.jsonl`) so the demo is\nvisible without a viewer utility.\n\nThis satisfies the standing project rule (CLAUDE.md) that each\nphase produces a runnable demo in `issues/completed/demos/`.\n\n### Test infrastructure constraints\n\n- Tests must not depend on the editor or any HTTP server\n- Tests must not depend on internet access\n- Tests must run in under 60 seconds total on a developer machine\n- Tests must be deterministic when normalized (any\n  non-determinism is normalized out, not papered over with retries)\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Whether to log inputs/outputs by default. Useful for development,\n  noisy for production. Current decision: opt-in via env var,\n  default off.\n- Slot-event logging: also opt-in. Useful for diagnosing memory\n  issues. Off by default.\n- File format: JSON Lines is the choice. An alternative was a\n  protobuf or msgpack binary log, which is faster to write but\n  harder to inspect by hand. JSONL wins on inspectability.\n- Whether to keep timestamps as Unix epoch floats or ISO 8601\n  strings. Epoch floats are smaller and easier to diff. Stick with\n  floats.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n### Run output (Part A)\n1. Define the event struct and JSONL line format. Start with\n   `run_start`, `task_start`, `task_end`, `run_end`.\n2. Implement the MPSC ring buffer for events.\n3. Implement the writer thread: pulls from ring, serializes,\n   appends a line to the output file.\n4. Wire event emission into the pool runner: `run_start` at\n   startup, `task_start` and `task_end` in the dispatch action,\n   `run_end` after quiescence.\n5. Add the verbosity env vars and the optional event types.\n\n### Tests (Part B)\n6. Create `tests/maps/` and `tests/expected/` directory structure.\n7. Write the `hello` test as the first end-to-end smoke check.\n8. Write the test driver `scripts/run-tests.sh` and the JSONL\n   normalizer.\n9. Add tests one at a time as each runtime feature lands. The\n   `*-fail` tests can land before their corresponding successful\n   tests if the failure path is implemented first.\n10. Build the phase 3 demo map under `issues/completed/demos/phase-3/`\n    once the rest of phase 3 is implemented.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `scripts/run-tests.sh` — test driver (to be written)\n- `tests/maps/`, `tests/expected/` — test fixtures (to be created)\n- `issues/completed/demos/phase-3/` — phase 3 demo (to be built)\n- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — emits run_start / run_end\n- `src/dispatch.c` — emits task_start / task_end\n- `src/slot-store.c` — emits slot_alloc / slot_free (verbose mode)\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — slot events\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — task lifecycle events\n- `issues/305-c-graph-loader.md` — load-time errors\n- `issues/309-build-system.md` — `make test` invokes this\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — blocking semantics relevant to\n  test design\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/311-integration-tests-and-run-output.md"
        },
        "id":"toolu_01Bf28BaR5YTiuvzdngrnCXC"
      }]
  },
