    "originalFile":"# SoraMech — Language Driver System\n\n## What a driver is\n\nA driver is a shell script. It knows how to invoke a function in one\nlanguage. The runner knows nothing about any language — it looks up the\nfile extension in drivers.json, finds the driver script, and calls it.\n\nLua and C ship with pre-written driver scripts. They are not special\ncases in the runner. They use exactly the same interface a user-written\ndriver uses. If you want to call a Haskell function or a Rust function,\nwrite a driver script and add the extension to drivers.json.\n\n## Driver contract\n\nThe runner invokes a driver as:\n\n  <driver-script> <file-path> <fn-name> <arg-count> [<arg> ...]\n\nArguments are always strings. Structured values (tables, arrays) are\npassed as JSON strings and must be decoded by the driver before use.\n\nThe driver must:\n  - Exit 0 on success, non-zero on failure\n  - Print a single JSON value to stdout on success (string, number,\n    boolean, object, or null) — one output wire per box\n  - Print an error message to stderr on failure (runner captures and logs\n    it)\n\nNothing else. No side channels. The runner reads stdout, decodes the JSON\nvalue, and passes it to all wired downstream inputs.\n\nNote: multi-output tuple returns are not supported. Each box has exactly\none output wire. If multiple values need to travel together, encode them\nas a JSON object or array and decode downstream.\n\n## Shell script vs. binary caller\n\nTwo kinds of refs exist in a box file:\n\n  \"ref\": \"src/strings.lua\",  \"fn\": \"trim\"\n      → source caller. runner looks up \".lua\" in drivers.json and\n        invokes the driver with file + fn + args.\n\n  \"ref\": \"src/trim.sh\"       (no \"fn\")\n      → binary caller. runner invokes the script directly with just\n        the args. The script is its own driver. Stdout is parsed as\n        JSON as with a normal driver.\n\nBinary callers include compiled binaries too: if the ref ends in a\nbinary extension or has no extension, the runner execs it directly.\n\n## Built-in driver scripts\n\nShipped in a global drivers/ directory alongside soramech-runner.lua.\nMaps can override any driver by defining the same extension in their\nlocal drivers.json pointing at a map-local script.\n\n### drivers/lua.sh\n\nInvokes a single function from a Lua file using luajit. The function\nmust be a module-level export (returned from the file or set in a\npackage). Args are decoded from JSON; return values are encoded to JSON.\n\n### drivers/c.sh\n\nCompiles the .c file if its mtime is newer than the cached binary in\ntmp/cache/. The cache key is the source file's absolute path hashed.\nInvokes the compiled binary with the args. The binary must follow the\ndriver output contract (JSON to stdout).\n\nThe binary is expected to expose a `main`-style entry that reads args\nfrom argv and writes JSON to stdout. A small C header (shipped with\nsoramech) provides helpers for this.\n\n### drivers/bash.sh\n\nInvokes a bash function defined in the .sh file by sourcing the file\nand calling the function with the args as positional parameters.\nThe function must echo a JSON value (or array) to stdout.\n\n## User-defined drivers\n\nAdd the file extension and path to the map's drivers.json:\n\n  { \".rs\": \"drivers/rust.sh\" }\n\nWrite drivers/rust.sh. It receives the same arguments as any built-in\ndriver. Compile, interpret, or delegate however the language requires.\nThe runner doesn't care.\n\n## Driver lookup order\n\n  1. Map-local drivers.json (maps/<name>/drivers.json)\n  2. Global drivers.json (alongside soramech-runner.lua)\n  3. Hard error if extension not found — no fallback, no silent skip\n\n## Passing structured values between boxes\n\nAll inter-box values are JSON at the transport layer. Inside a Lua box,\ndkjson decodes input strings to Lua tables. The driver re-encodes return\nvalues to JSON. Inside a C box, the shipped helper header decodes argv\nJSON strings to C structs and encodes results back.\n\nThis means structured values cross language boundaries cleanly: a Lua\ntable produced by one box can be consumed by a C function in the next\nbox, because both sides see JSON at the wire level.\n",

    "content":"# SoraMech — Language Driver System\n\n## Two systems, one filename\n\nPhase 2 used **driver scripts** — shell wrappers under `drivers/`\nthat the synchronous runner invoked one process per box call.\n\nPhase 3 uses **language specs** — `.so` libraries under `langs/`\nloaded by the C pool runner via `dlopen`, with persistent per-worker\nruntimes.\n\nSame idea, different mechanism. Phase 3 replaces phase 2 wholesale\nwhen it lands. This document covers both, since the project lives in\nphase 2 today and the phase 3 design is fully specified.\n\n## Phase 2 — Driver scripts (current)\n\nA driver is a shell script. It knows how to invoke a function in one\nlanguage. The synchronous runner looks up the file extension, finds\nthe driver script, and calls it.\n\n### Driver contract\n\nThe runner invokes a driver as:\n\n```\n<driver-script> <file-path> <fn-name> <arg-count> [<arg> ...]\n```\n\nArguments are always strings. Structured values (tables, arrays) are\npassed as JSON strings and decoded by the driver.\n\nThe driver must:\n- Exit 0 on success, nonzero on failure\n- Print one JSON value to stdout — string, number, boolean, object,\n  or null. One output wire per box.\n- Print error messages to stderr on failure\n\nMulti-output tuple returns are not supported. Each box has exactly\none output wire (issue 218).\n\n### Built-in driver scripts\n\nShipped in the project's `drivers/` directory:\n\n- `drivers/lua.sh` — invokes a Lua function via `luajit`\n- `drivers/c.sh` — compiles `.c` (mtime cache) and runs the binary\n- `drivers/bash.sh` — sources the `.sh` and calls the function\n\nUser-added drivers go in the same directory and are picked up by\nextension.\n\n### What's wrong with this model\n\nProcess spawn cost dominates each call (1–10 ms per language).\nStdout is a fragile channel — debug prints inside box code corrupt\nthe wire value. Each invocation is its own fresh interpreter; there\nis no persistent runtime between calls. These are the limitations\nphase 3 fixes.\n\n## Phase 3 — Language specs (planned)\n\nEach language is a small C library implementing the spec interface\ndefined in issue 303. The pool runner loads every\n`langs/<name>/spec.so` at startup; the spec interface is uniform\nacross languages, with no privileged language.\n\n### Spec interface\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    const char *name;\n    const char *file_ext;\n\n    void *(*init)(int worker_idx);\n    void  (*teardown)(void *handle);\n    int   (*compile)(const char *src_path, const char *out_path,\n                     const box_t *box);\n    int   (*invoke)(void *handle,\n                    const char *file_path, const char *fn_name,\n                    const void **input_data, const int *input_sizes,\n                    int n_inputs,\n                    void *out_buf, int out_buf_capacity,\n                    int *out_size);\n} lang_spec_t;\n```\n\n`init` runs once per worker thread at pool startup. `teardown` runs\nat shutdown. `compile` runs at map load time for languages that need\nit (C). `invoke` runs once per box invocation.\n\nThe spec receives input bytes and writes output bytes — never\ninteracts with slot IDs. The dispatch layer (issue 304) reads\ninputs from slots into byte buffers, hands them to `invoke`, takes\nback bytes, writes them to the output slot.\n\n### Reference specs\n\n- **Lua** (issue 306) — handle is a `lua_State` per worker. `invoke`\n  loads the box file (cached in the registry), pushes typed\n  arguments, calls via `lua_pcall`, serializes the return value.\n- **C** (issue 307) — handle is a `dlopen`-cache per worker.\n  `compile` generates a wrapper from the box's declared inputs and\n  return type, then runs `cc` to produce the `.so`. `invoke` does\n  `dlsym` and a direct function-pointer call.\n- **Bash** (issue 308) — handle is a Unix domain socket connected\n  to a persistent `bash-server.sh` subprocess. `invoke` sends a\n  framed request, reads a framed response.\n\nThe Lua and C specs are in-process (Option 1 in\n`docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`). The Bash spec is out-of-process\n(Option 3) — proof that the spec interface accommodates languages\nthat cannot be embedded.\n\n### Adding a new language\n\nA user adds Python, Rust, or anything else by writing a new spec:\n\n1. Create `langs/<name>/spec.c` implementing the four callbacks.\n2. Create `langs/<name>/Makefile` that builds `spec.so`.\n3. Add the language to `meta.json src_dirs` if necessary so the\n   editor's file browser can see source files.\n\nThe pool runner picks up the new spec at the next startup. No\nSoraMech code change required.\n\nFor full implementation guidance, see the future\n`docs/005-language-specs.md` (referenced from issue 303). For the\nspec contract itself, issue 303.\n\n## Migration: phase 2 → phase 3\n\nWhen phase 3 lands:\n\n| Phase 2                              | Phase 3                              |\n|--------------------------------------|--------------------------------------|\n| `drivers/lua.sh`                     | `langs/lua/spec.so`                  |\n| `drivers/c.sh`                       | `langs/c/spec.so`                    |\n| `drivers/bash.sh`                    | `langs/bash/spec.so`                 |\n| `drivers.json` (per-map)             | (none — spec registry is global)     |\n| stdout as channel                    | direct function call / Unix socket   |\n| One process per call                 | Persistent runtimes                  |\n| Single output wire (JSON-encoded)    | Single output slot (typed bytes)     |\n\nBox JSON does not change shape — `lang`, `ref`, `fn`, `inputs`\nremain. Phase 3 reads the same files phase 2 reads. The runtime\nmechanism beneath the box is what changes.\n\n## Relevant issues\n\n- 102 (completed) — phase 2 driver interface\n- 218 (completed) — single-output driver contract\n- 303 — phase 3 language spec contract\n- 306 — Lua language spec\n- 307 — C language spec\n- 308 — Bash language spec\n"
  },

          "content":"# SoraMech — Language Driver System\n\n## Two systems, one filename\n\nPhase 2 used **driver scripts** — shell wrappers under `drivers/`\nthat the synchronous runner invoked one process per box call.\n\nPhase 3 uses **language specs** — `.so` libraries under `langs/`\nloaded by the C pool runner via `dlopen`, with persistent per-worker\nruntimes.\n\nSame idea, different mechanism. Phase 3 replaces phase 2 wholesale\nwhen it lands. This document covers both, since the project lives in\nphase 2 today and the phase 3 design is fully specified.\n\n## Phase 2 — Driver scripts (current)\n\nA driver is a shell script. It knows how to invoke a function in one\nlanguage. The synchronous runner looks up the file extension, finds\nthe driver script, and calls it.\n\n### Driver contract\n\nThe runner invokes a driver as:\n\n```\n<driver-script> <file-path> <fn-name> <arg-count> [<arg> ...]\n```\n\nArguments are always strings. Structured values (tables, arrays) are\npassed as JSON strings and decoded by the driver.\n\nThe driver must:\n- Exit 0 on success, nonzero on failure\n- Print one JSON value to stdout — string, number, boolean, object,\n  or null. One output wire per box.\n- Print error messages to stderr on failure\n\nMulti-output tuple returns are not supported. Each box has exactly\none output wire (issue 218).\n\n### Built-in driver scripts\n\nShipped in the project's `drivers/` directory:\n\n- `drivers/lua.sh` — invokes a Lua function via `luajit`\n- `drivers/c.sh` — compiles `.c` (mtime cache) and runs the binary\n- `drivers/bash.sh` — sources the `.sh` and calls the function\n\nUser-added drivers go in the same directory and are picked up by\nextension.\n\n### What's wrong with this model\n\nProcess spawn cost dominates each call (1–10 ms per language).\nStdout is a fragile channel — debug prints inside box code corrupt\nthe wire value. Each invocation is its own fresh interpreter; there\nis no persistent runtime between calls. These are the limitations\nphase 3 fixes.\n\n## Phase 3 — Language specs (planned)\n\nEach language is a small C library implementing the spec interface\ndefined in issue 303. The pool runner loads every\n`langs/<name>/spec.so` at startup; the spec interface is uniform\nacross languages, with no privileged language.\n\n### Spec interface\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    const char *name;\n    const char *file_ext;\n\n    void *(*init)(int worker_idx);\n    void  (*teardown)(void *handle);\n    int   (*compile)(const char *src_path, const char *out_path,\n                     const box_t *box);\n    int   (*invoke)(void *handle,\n                    const char *file_path, const char *fn_name,\n                    const void **input_data, const int *input_sizes,\n                    int n_inputs,\n                    void *out_buf, int out_buf_capacity,\n                    int *out_size);\n} lang_spec_t;\n```\n\n`init` runs once per worker thread at pool startup. `teardown` runs\nat shutdown. `compile` runs at map load time for languages that need\nit (C). `invoke` runs once per box invocation.\n\nThe spec receives input bytes and writes output bytes — never\ninteracts with slot IDs. The dispatch layer (issue 304) reads\ninputs from slots into byte buffers, hands them to `invoke`, takes\nback bytes, writes them to the output slot.\n\n### Reference specs\n\n- **Lua** (issue 306) — handle is a `lua_State` per worker. `invoke`\n  loads the box file (cached in the registry), pushes typed\n  arguments, calls via `lua_pcall`, serializes the return value.\n- **C** (issue 307) — handle is a `dlopen`-cache per worker.\n  `compile` generates a wrapper from the box's declared inputs and\n  return type, then runs `cc` to produce the `.so`. `invoke` does\n  `dlsym` and a direct function-pointer call.\n- **Bash** (issue 308) — handle is a Unix domain socket connected\n  to a persistent `bash-server.sh` subprocess. `invoke` sends a\n  framed request, reads a framed response.\n\nThe Lua and C specs are in-process (Option 1 in\n`docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`). The Bash spec is out-of-process\n(Option 3) — proof that the spec interface accommodates languages\nthat cannot be embedded.\n\n### Adding a new language\n\nA user adds Python, Rust, or anything else by writing a new spec:\n\n1. Create `langs/<name>/spec.c` implementing the four callbacks.\n2. Create `langs/<name>/Makefile` that builds `spec.so`.\n3. Add the language to `meta.json src_dirs` if necessary so the\n   editor's file browser can see source files.\n\nThe pool runner picks up the new spec at the next startup. No\nSoraMech code change required.\n\nFor full implementation guidance, see the future\n`docs/005-language-specs.md` (referenced from issue 303). For the\nspec contract itself, issue 303.\n\n## Migration: phase 2 → phase 3\n\nWhen phase 3 lands:\n\n| Phase 2                              | Phase 3                              |\n|--------------------------------------|--------------------------------------|\n| `drivers/lua.sh`                     | `langs/lua/spec.so`                  |\n| `drivers/c.sh`                       | `langs/c/spec.so`                    |\n| `drivers/bash.sh`                    | `langs/bash/spec.so`                 |\n| `drivers.json` (per-map)             | (none — spec registry is global)     |\n| stdout as channel                    | direct function call / Unix socket   |\n| One process per call                 | Persistent runtimes                  |\n| Single output wire (JSON-encoded)    | Single output slot (typed bytes)     |\n\nBox JSON does not change shape — `lang`, `ref`, `fn`, `inputs`\nremain. Phase 3 reads the same files phase 2 reads.         "input":{
          "content":"# SoraMech — Roadmap\n\n## Phase 1 — Foundation (complete)\n\nGoal: a map you can edit in the browser and execute from the\nterminal.\n\nAt the end of phase 1, the user can:\n- Open the editor at `http://localhost:7700/`, see a canvas, create\n  boxes, set their `ref` / `fn` / `inputs`, wire them together\n- Save edits as box files on disk via the HTTP file CRUD server\n- Run `luajit src/007-runner-main.lua <map-dir>` to execute the map\n- Add a custom language driver and have the runner use it\n\nIssues 101–110, all complete and moved to `issues/completed/`.\n\nDemo: `issues/completed/demos/phase-1/`.\n\n## Phase 2 — Editor & graph model (current)\n\nGoal: an editor you can actually use to build maps, and the graph\nmodel the phase 3 runtime will consume.\n\nThis phase is editor-focused with some graph-model cleanup:\n- Map picker, fit-to-view, interaction hints, entry-box marking\n- Source file browser with auto-populated input ports\n- File browser library directories\n- Single-output driver contract (issue 218)\n- Comparator-based branching replaces the old `branch` box kind with\n  named ports (issue 210)\n- Comparator + iterator are the two routing primitives (issues 210,\n  221)\n- Variadic / queued inputs (issues 213, 217)\n- Map compiler (issue 219) and compile button (issue 222) — ties\n  the editor into the phase 3 build path\n- Ollama / LLM library (issue 209)\n\nPhase 2 runs on the synchronous Lua interpreter\n(`src/007-runner-main.lua`). No threading. Drivers per phase 1.\n\nSee `issues/phase-2-progress.md` for the live status.\n\n## Phase 3 — Thread pool runtime (planned, fully designed)\n\nGoal: replace the Lua synchronous runner with a C thread pool runner\nthat executes box graphs in parallel, with persistent per-worker\nlanguage runtimes and proper inter-task value plumbing.\n\nDesigned across issues 301–311:\n\n- 301 — pool lifecycle and per-worker init\n- 302 — wire value slot store (per-task ring buffers, refcount,\n  large-value heap)\n- 303 — language runtime spec (`lang_spec_t` interface)\n- 304 — task dispatch layer\n- 305 — C graph loader (replaces `src/003-loader.lua`)\n- 306 — Lua language spec (in-process via `lua_State`)\n- 307 — C language spec (in-process via `dlopen`, with compile)\n- 308 — Bash language spec (out-of-process via Unix domain socket)\n- 309 — build system & Makefile orchestration\n- 310 — priority queue (wired in, no-op behaviorally)\n- 311 — integration tests & run output (`last-run.jsonl`)\n\nWhen phase 3 lands, the synchronous Lua runner retires. The editor\nand the map directory format do not change — the runtime mechanism\nbeneath the box is what changes. See `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`\nfor the design discussion.\n\n## Phase 4 — SoraMind integration\n\nGoal: boxes that call SoraMind inference endpoints on the Alpine\ncluster.\n\n- LLM call box type — sends a prompt, receives a completion string\n- Prompt assembly: text values wired from upstream boxes, data file\n  sections explicitly loaded into prompt context\n- Comparator-routed classifiers (\"rogue / wizard / else\" via lt/eq/gt\n  on a hashed-class score)\n- Streaming output from SoraMind inference back to the runner\n\nBuilt on the phase 3 runtime — the LLM call is a regular box function,\njust one whose backing service is a network endpoint.\n\n## Phase 5 — Map-to-map calls\n\nGoal: a box that invokes another map as a subroutine.\n\n- Map call box type: specifies another map directory, passes inputs,\n  receives outputs\n- Maps run concurrently with each other (sub-pool per map)\n- Entry/exit contracts defined in `meta.json`\n\n## Phase 6 — Remote runner\n\nGoal: run a map on the Alpine cluster, edit it from a laptop.\n\n- Pool runner on a remote machine\n- File-CRUD server on the same machine exposes map files over HTTP\n- Browser editor on the laptop connects to the remote server\n- Results written to remote `last-run.jsonl`, accessible via server\n\nPhases 4, 5, and 6 are scoped only briefly here — concrete planning\nhappens once phase 3 is done.\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/docs/002-roadmap.md"
        },
        "id":"toolu_01H87w7eXqjRRLf69YMHABs4"

    "originalFile":"# SoraMech — Roadmap\n\n## Phase 1 — Foundation\n\nGoal: a map you can edit in the browser and execute from the terminal.\n\nAt the end of phase 1, the user can:\n- Open index.html, connect it to a running server, and see a canvas\n- Create boxes, set their ref/fn/inputs/outputs, wire them together\n- Edit branch boxes with named ports and predicates\n- Save all edits as box files on disk\n- Run `luajit soramech-runner.lua <map-dir>` and have it execute the map\n- Write a custom language driver and have the runner use it\n\nIssues:\n  101 — project scaffold and map directory format\n  102 — language driver interface\n  103 — runner: graph loader and validator\n  104 — runner: synchronous executor (task boundary)\n  105 — HTTP server: file CRUD API\n  106 — web editor: canvas and box rendering\n  107 — web editor: wiring and connection UI\n  108 — branch box and predicate routing\n  109 — data files: persistent and ephemeral storage\n  110 — phase 1 demo\n\nDemo: a small lua FSM (3-4 boxes) runs via the CLI, exercises a branch\nbox, reads a data file, writes an output. The browser shows the same map\nvisually with correct wiring drawn.\n\n## Phase 2 — Concurrent execution\n\nGoal: boxes whose inputs are all satisfied fire concurrently.\n\n- Coroutine-based non-blocking executor: the ready-queue becomes a\n  coroutine scheduler; boxes yield while waiting on upstream results\n- Cross-language calls use Unix domain socket servers (one per language\n  runtime per worker), non-blocking on the Lua side via LuaSocket\n- Multiple maps running concurrently share nothing (separate processes)\n- Integration path toward the 3d-rts custom thread pool: the coroutine\n  scheduler and task boundary are designed to swap in the thread pool\n  without changing the box execution model\n\n## Phase 3 — SoraMind integration\n\nGoal: boxes that call SoraMind inference endpoints on the Alpine cluster.\n\n- LLM call box type: sends a prompt, receives a completion string\n- Prompt assembly: text values wired from upstream boxes, data file\n  sections explicitly loaded into prompt context\n- Branch box connected to an LLM classifier: \"rogue, wizard, or else\"\n- Else port retry with pseudo-randomized temperature parameter\n- Streaming output from SoraMind inference back to the runner\n\n## Phase 4 — Map-to-map calls\n\nGoal: a box that invokes another map as a subroutine.\n\n- Map call box type: specifies another map directory, passes inputs,\n  receives outputs\n- Maps can run concurrently with each other\n- Entry/exit contracts defined in meta.json\n\n## Phase 5 — Remote runner\n\nGoal: run a map on the Alpine cluster, edit it from a laptop.\n\n- Runner process on a remote machine (Alpine node)\n- Server on the same machine exposes map files over HTTP\n- Browser editor on the laptop connects to the remote server\n- Results written to remote data files, accessible via server\n",

    "content":"# SoraMech — Writing a Language Spec\n\n## Status\nStub. Filled out as the phase 3 specs are implemented (issues\n306–308). For the formal contract, see issue 303. For the existing\noverview, see `docs/003-driver-system.md`.\n\n## What this doc will cover (when complete)\n\nA walk-through of writing a new language spec, intended for a user\nadding Python, Rust, Haskell, or any language not shipped by default.\nSections to fill in once the reference specs are written:\n\n- **The contract.** What `lang_spec_t` requires you to provide\n  (`init`, `teardown`, `compile`, `invoke`). Pointer to issue 303.\n- **In-process vs out-of-process.** Lua and C run in the worker\n  thread directly; Bash talks to a persistent subprocess over a\n  socket. Which model fits your language depends on whether it has\n  an embeddable runtime. Pointer to `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`.\n- **Walkthrough: the Lua spec.** The simplest reference. Covers\n  per-worker `lua_State`, registry-based file caching, typed input\n  marshalling, return-value serialization. Pointer to issue 306.\n- **Walkthrough: the C spec.** Adds compile-time wrapper generation\n  for arbitrary user functions. Pointer to issue 307.\n- **Walkthrough: the Bash spec.** The out-of-process model. Wire\n  protocol, framed length-prefix messages, persistent subprocess\n  lifecycle. Pointer to issue 308.\n- **Adding a new language.** Directory layout, Makefile, the bare\n  minimum to link against the spec interface, dropping the result\n  into `langs/<name>/`.\n- **Thread safety.** Per-worker state isolation. The C spec's\n  `static` and `globals` race story (issue 307); cooperative\n  patterns for languages with mutable global state.\n- **Error handling.** Hard-crash policy (issue 303). What\n  language-level errors look like at the spec boundary. How to\n  catch them without losing context.\n\n## Why a stub now\n\nIssues 303, 306, 307, and 308 reference this document. Creating a\nplaceholder establishes the file path and the table of contents\nabove so cross-references resolve. The full content is written\nincrementally as the reference specs are implemented and there is\nreal code to walk through.\n\n## Relevant issues\n\n- 303 — language runtime spec (the contract)\n- 306 — Lua language spec\n- 307 — C language spec\n- 308 — Bash language spec\n- `docs/003-driver-system.md` — phase 2 driver overview, phase 3\n  spec overview\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — IPC options and threading\n  roadmap\n"
  },
  "uuid":"c5e11a30-144b-4323-b5f9-2775f257d9c9",

    "originalFile":"# 219 — Map compiler: generate standalone source code from a box graph\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nThe soramech-runner interprets the box graph at runtime. To execute a map, the\nuser must have SoraMech installed. The runner shells out to a language driver for\neach box, captures stdout, and routes values to the next box. The runtime\ndependency on SoraMech and the stdout-as-IPC design are both fragile.\n\n## Intended behavior\nThe editor compiles a map into a standalone source file (or script) that runs\nwithout SoraMech. The box graph is an authoring artifact — the output of the\neditor is a real program.\n\n### What the compiler produces\n\n**Pure Lua map** → a single `.lua` file that requires each box's source file\nand chains calls directly:\n```lua\nlocal greet = require(\"src/greet\")\nlocal write = require(\"src/write_result\")\nwrite.write_result(greet.hello())\n```\nRunnable with `luajit generated.lua`. No SoraMech, no drivers, no IPC.\n\n**Mixed-language map** → a shell script that invokes each box's binary or\ninterpreter in sequence, passing values through named temp files rather than\nstdout. Each step reads its input from a file and writes its output to a file.\nThe script is self-contained and inspectable.\n\n**Comparator (branch) nodes** → if/elseif chains in the generated code.\n\n### What stays in the box JSON\nCanvas positions, labels, wire layout — everything the editor needs to display\nand edit the graph. The JSON is the editor's internal representation. The\ncompiled output is the deliverable.\n\n### Why stdout-as-IPC is the wrong model\nThe current runtime pipes each box's return value through stdout. Problems:\n- A box that prints debug output corrupts the wire value\n- Shell process overhead per box\n- Can't pass binary or large values reliably\n- Values are transient — can't inspect mid-run\n\nThe compiler eliminates IPC for same-language maps (direct function calls).\nFor mixed-language maps, file-based IPC is used instead of stdout:\neach wire becomes a named temp file. The generated script writes/reads\nexplicitly. Files persist after the run and can be inspected.\n\n### Language runner libraries (alternative to the current driver model)\nFor multi-language support without a runtime, each language needs a small\nshim that:\n- reads its input value from a file path passed as argv\n- calls the box function\n- writes the output value to a file path passed as argv\n\nThe compiler generates calls to these shims. The shims are minimal (~30 lines)\nand are the only per-language artifact needed. No driver contract, no stdout,\nno JSON array wrapping. A new language requires only a new shim, not a new\ndriver script with a parsing contract.\n\n### The canvas/connection relationship\nThe box JSON currently stores connections in both endpoint files. The compiler\nreads these to determine call order (topological sort). Once compiled, the\nconnections are embedded in the generated code — the JSON is not needed at\nruntime. If someone reads the generated code, they can see exactly which\nfunctions call which, without needing the JSON.\n\n## Design constraints\n- The editor has no conception of running maps. It creates and edits box graphs.\n  The compiler is a separate CLI tool invoked outside the editor.\n- The compiler writes its output into `maps/:name/output/run.lua` (pure Lua) or\n  `maps/:name/output/run.sh` (mixed). The user invokes this directly.\n- No \"compile\" button in the editor. No \"run\" button in the editor.\n\n## Open questions\n- Primary target language: Lua first, shell script fallback for mixed maps?\n- For Lua↔C wires: emit LuaJIT FFI calls (C compiled to `.so`) or persistent\n  subprocess? FFI is faster; subprocess is simpler to generate.\n- For Lua↔Bash wires: persistent subprocess + anonymous pipe (one spawn per\n  bash runtime at program start, reused across all calls).\n- Are runner shims checked into the map's `src/` or shipped globally?\n- Should the compiler use `shm_open` shared memory for cross-language wire\n  values, or persistent subprocess + pipe? Shared memory is language-agnostic\n  and faster; pipe is simpler and works without FFI.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. Write the topological sort: given a box graph, produce a linear execution\n   order respecting dependency edges. (Executor queue logic is the reference.)\n2. Write a Lua code emitter: for a pure-Lua map, emit `require` calls and\n   chained function calls in topo order, handling comparator branches as\n   if/elseif in the generated file.\n3. Write a CLI entry point: `soramech-compile.lua <map-dir>` that loads the\n   graph, runs the emitter, and writes `output/run.lua`.\n4. For mixed maps: choose IPC mechanism (FFI, shm, or persistent subprocess)\n   and emit the appropriate glue in the generated script.\n\n## Relevant files\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — topological sort and execution model to adapt\n- `src/003-loader.lua` — box graph loading, connection traversal\n- `docs/001-architecture.md` — needs update once compiler exists\n- `issues/completed/102-language-driver-interface.md` — driver model reference\n",
    "userModified":false,
    "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/219-map-compiler.md",
    "content":"# 219 — Map compiler: package a map for standalone execution\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nPhase 2's synchronous runner interprets the box graph at runtime,\nshelling out to a language driver per box. The runner is a Lua\nscript (`src/007-runner-main.lua`); to run a map, the user must have\nSoraMech installed.\n\nPhase 3 introduces the C pool runner (`soramech-pool`, issues\n301–311) plus per-language specs under `langs/`. The runner is a\nreal binary, but it still reads the map directory at startup. The\n\"compile\" step bridges from \"an editable map directory\" to \"a\nself-contained deployable directory\" that includes the binary, all\nsource files, all compiled `.so`s, and a manifest.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nThe compile step (triggered by the editor's Compile button, issue\n222, or by the CLI) walks a map and produces a `compiled/`\nsubdirectory:\n\n```\nmaps/<name>/compiled/\n    pool-runner          ← the soramech-pool binary, copied here\n    src/                 ← copy of every source file the map uses\n    bin/                 ← per-box compiled .so files (C boxes)\n    langs/               ← copy of language spec .so files needed\n    manifest.json        ← every box, its language, its compiled artifact path\n```\n\nThe `compiled/` directory is the deployment artifact. Running\n`./compiled/pool-runner` executes the map without any reference to\nthe editor, the live `src/` outside `compiled/`, or any external\nSoraMech installation. Ship the directory to someone else and it\nruns.\n\n### What the compile step does\n\n1. **Walk the graph.** Use the same loader logic the runtime uses\n   (issue 305) to enumerate boxes, languages, and source files.\n2. **Copy source.** Every file referenced by `box.ref` is copied\n   into `compiled/src/`. The map's local `src/` is the only place\n   `package.path` searches at runtime (per issue 306), so all\n   dependencies must land here. This includes vendored libraries\n   the user wired in (`libs/json.lua`, `libs/ollama.lua`, etc.).\n3. **Compile per-box artifacts.** For each language present in the\n   map, invoke that spec's `compile` callback (issue 303). The C\n   spec generates a wrapper from the box's declared signature and\n   produces a `.so` in `compiled/bin/` (issue 307). Lua and Bash\n   specs have no compile step; their files are copied verbatim.\n4. **Copy spec libraries.** The `langs/<name>/spec.so` files for\n   every language used in the map are copied to\n   `compiled/langs/<name>/spec.so`. The pool runner discovers\n   specs relative to its binary location, so this co-location is\n   what makes the deployment self-contained.\n5. **Copy the runner binary.** `soramech-pool` is copied to\n   `compiled/pool-runner`. (A symlink works too, for development.)\n6. **Write the manifest.** `compiled/manifest.json` lists every\n   box, its language, the path of its compiled artifact (or source\n   file for interpreted languages), and the SoraMech build version\n   the deployment was compiled against.\n\n### What stays in the box JSON\nCanvas positions, labels, wire layout — everything the editor needs\nto display and edit the graph. The JSON is the editor's\nrepresentation of the graph. The compiled directory is the\ndeliverable. The two never need to be in sync after compile —\nthe compiled output is frozen at compile time.\n\n### Editor invocation (issue 222)\nThe Compile button in the editor triggers the same compile step via\na new server endpoint `POST /maps/<name>/compile`. The server\nshells out to a `soramech-compile` CLI (or invokes the same code\nin-process — implementation detail). Output / errors stream back to\nthe editor for display. The editor itself does not run the\ncompiled output; the user invokes `./compiled/pool-runner` from a\nterminal.\n\nThis supersedes the earlier \"no compile button in the editor\" stance\nin the original issue text — issue 222 is the formal addition of\nthe button.\n\n### CLI invocation\nA standalone CLI tool `soramech-compile <map-dir>` runs the same\npipeline without the server. Useful for CI and headless deployment.\n\n## Design constraints\n\n- The editor still has no conception of *running* maps — only\n  compiling them. Run is a separate concern (the user invokes the\n  pool-runner binary themselves).\n- Compile is incremental: mtime comparison on each artifact. If a\n  source file is newer than its compiled output, re-compile that\n  one. Otherwise skip. (Per the C spec, issue 307.)\n- Errors at any stage abort the compile and surface a precise\n  message (which box, which file, what failed).\n\n## Open questions\n\n- Whether the compiled directory bundles a copy of `soramech-pool`\n  or a symlink. Bundling makes the directory portable across\n  machines; symlinking saves disk on the dev machine. Configurable\n  via a `--portable` flag.\n- Multi-architecture: a compiled directory built on x86_64 won't\n  run on arm64. Out of scope — users compile on the target\n  architecture. Could later add a cross-compile mode if the SoraMind\n  cluster is mixed-arch.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Walk the map graph using the C loader (issue 305) — the same\n   code the runtime uses. Emit a list of (box, language, files).\n2. Implement the source-copy step. Every `box.ref` file plus any\n   `require`/`source`/`#include` dependencies (resolvable via\n   static analysis or just-copy-the-whole-libs/-directory).\n3. For C boxes: invoke the C spec's `compile` callback (issue 307)\n   per box. Outputs land in `compiled/bin/`.\n4. Copy `langs/<name>/spec.so` for every language present.\n5. Copy or symlink `soramech-pool`.\n6. Write `manifest.json`.\n7. Wire `POST /maps/<name>/compile` in the server (issue 222\n   button calls this).\n8. Smoke test: compile `maps/hello`, run\n   `./maps/hello/compiled/pool-runner`, verify result matches\n   the phase 2 run.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — the runner binary that gets copied in\n- `langs/<name>/spec.so` — language specs that get copied in\n- `langs/<name>/spec.c::compile` — per-language compile callback\n- `issues/222-compile-button-and-assets-directory.md` — UI button\n  that triggers this\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — `compile` interface\n- `issues/305-c-graph-loader.md` — graph-walk logic shared with\n  the runtime\n- `issues/307-c-language-spec.md` — C wrapper generation\n- `docs/001-architecture.md` — describes the `compiled/` directory\n  layout\n- `issues/completed/102-language-driver-interface.md` — phase 2\n  driver model (historical reference)\n"
  },

        "oldStart":73,

    "originalFile":"# 217 — Concat box with per-input variadic ports and auto-grow/shrink\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nNo standard concat box exists. No mechanism exists for a box to have a variable\nnumber of input wires on a single logical port.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\n### Part A — text library box\n`libs/text.lua` exposes two functions:\n\n`M.concat(sep, ...)` — join N strings:\n- `sep` — separator string (e.g. `\"\\n\\n\"`)\n- `...` — any number of text values to join (variadic)\n- returns a single `result` port\n\nThe function is variadic so its `text` input can expand to any count without\nmodifying the source file.\n\n`M.split(text, sep)` — split one string into parts:\n- `text` — the input string\n- `sep` — the separator to split on (plain string, not a pattern)\n- returns a single `result` port containing a JSON-encoded array of the parts\n\nOutput ports are named at wire-design time, so a variable number of runtime\nparts cannot map to separate wires. A JSON array on one port is the only\nconsistent design — the downstream box decodes it.\n\nNote: one output wire per box is a deliberate design constraint, not a missing\nfeature. Positional multi-output was explicitly rejected as fragile (multiple\nreturn statements with the same tuple width are indistinguishable). The\ncomparator (lt/eq/gt branching) is the only multi-path mechanism. Whatever the\nfunction returns goes down the single output wire as one value — arrays or JSON\nobjects if multiple values need to travel together.\n\n### Part B — per-input variadic flag\n\nVariadic is a property of a specific input port, not the box as a whole. A box\ncould have `sep` (fixed) and `text` (variadic). The inspector shows a toggle on\neach input to mark it variadic.\n\n#### Data model\n\nThe box JSON gains a `variadic_inputs` set (array of base names):\n```json\n{\n  \"inputs\": [\"sep\", \"text_0\", \"text_1\", \"text_2\"],\n  \"variadic_inputs\": [\"text\"]\n}\n```\n\nSlots of a variadic input are stored as `<base>_<index>` in the `inputs` array.\nThe executor already passes all inputs positionally — no executor changes needed.\nConnections reference slots by their indexed name (`\"text_0\"`, `\"text_1\"`, etc.).\n\nThe parser (Lua: detects `...`, bash: detects `$@` after shift) can auto-populate\n`variadic_inputs` when a file is selected via the file browser. For other languages\n(C, etc.) the user sets the toggle manually in the inspector — the executor contract\nalready supports N positional args via `arg_count`, so C functions reading `argv[]`\nin a loop work without any changes.\n\n#### Auto-grow\nWhen a wire is connected to the LAST slot of a variadic input, the editor appends\na new empty slot (`text_N+1`) to `box.inputs` and saves the box. The new slot\nappears immediately as an open port.\n\n#### Auto-shrink\nWhen a wire is disconnected from any slot of a variadic input:\n1. Remove that slot from `box.inputs`.\n2. Rename all subsequent slots down by one (`text_2` → `text_1`, etc.).\n3. Update every connection that referenced a renamed slot:\n   - `to_input` in the connection record on this box\n   - The corresponding `from_output` side on the source box (connections are stored\n     in both endpoint files; both must be updated atomically).\n4. Keep at least one slot for the variadic input (never shrink below `text_0`).\n\nMiddle-port removal is handled by the same rename-and-compact step: remove the cut\nslot, shift all higher-indexed slots down, update their wires. The user always sees\na dense, gap-free list of ports.\n\n## Open questions before implementing Part B\n- Rename atomicity: the server's `PUT /maps/:name/boxes/:id` writes one box at a\n  time. Updating the connection in the source box requires a second PUT. These are\n  two separate writes — consider whether a partial failure leaves the map in an\n  inconsistent state, and whether a `PUT /maps/:name/connections` batch endpoint\n  is worth adding first.\n- Should the file browser parser set `variadic_inputs` automatically when it\n  detects `...` in a Lua signature, and if so, which argument specifically?\n\n  -- nah let's just make the user set the variadic property manually. Unless we can put it in the language driver\n     somehow? but I don't think that's really possible in the design. Thoughts?\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. Part A: implement `libs/text.lua` with `M.concat(sep, ...)`.\n2. Part B schema: add `variadic_inputs` to box schema and validator.\n3. Part B editor: auto-grow on wire connect; auto-shrink + rename on wire disconnect.\n4. Part B inspector: variadic toggle per input port.\n5. Part B parser: auto-detect `...` in Lua and set `variadic_inputs`.\n\n## Relevant files\n- `libs/ollama.lua` — reference pattern for a library box\n- `assets/js/006-wires.js` — wire connect/disconnect events\n- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — input port list, toggle rendering\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — box validator (`variadic_inputs` field)\n- `src/005-http-server.lua` — PUT box endpoint (rename propagation)\n- `issues/208-port-literal-values.md` — `sep` will likely use literal port values\n",
    "oldString":"3. Update every connection that referenced a renamed slot:\n   - `to_input` in the connection record on this box\n   - The corresponding `from_output` side on the source box (connections are stored\n     in both endpoint files; both must be updated atomically).",
    "newString":"3. Update every connection that referenced a renamed slot:\n   - `to_input` in the connection record on this box\n   - The corresponding side on the source box (connections are stored in both\n     endpoint files; both must be updated atomically).",

        "input":{
          "content":"---\nname: SoraMech project context\ndescription: Core architecture decisions, file layout, and execution model for SoraMech, across phase 2 (current) and phase 3 (designed)\ntype: project\n---\nSoraMech is a visual FSM/dataflow editor and execution engine at /mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/.\n\n**Why:** Primary use case is LLM orchestration on the SoraMind Alpine cluster. Strings flow between boxes like variables. History is explicit, loaded from disk only when a box needs it.\n\n**Three independent programs sharing a map directory:**\n- `src/006-server-main.lua` — thin HTTP file CRUD proxy. No runner management.\n- Runner — phase 2: `src/007-runner-main.lua` (synchronous Lua). Phase 3: `soramech-pool` (C binary, designed in issues 301–311, not yet built).\n- `assets/index.html` — vanilla JS canvas editor. Editor only — no run button. Compile button (issue 222) is a phase 2 placeholder; it triggers the phase 3 build pipeline (issue 219).\n\n**Key architecture decisions (current truth):**\n- Each box is its own JSON file in `boxes/<id>.json`. Connections written to BOTH endpoint files; loader validates both ends agree — hard error if not.\n- **Single output wire per box** (issue 218 complete). No `outputs` array. The function returns one value; routing is by `from_branch` on the connection.\n- **Comparator-based branching** (issue 210) — replaces the earlier `branch` box kind with named ports. A box may carry a `comparand`; the dispatch layer fires `lt`/`eq`/`gt` connections. No spec is invoked for comparators.\n- **Iterator boxes** (issue 221) — pure routing primitives, no `ref`/`fn`. Dispatch layer cycles through `iterator_outputs` based on a per-task counter.\n- **Phase 2 drivers** are shell scripts under `drivers/` (one process per call, stdout as channel). **Phase 3 language specs** are `.so` libraries under `langs/<name>/spec.so` loaded via `dlopen` (issue 303). Lua and C are in-process; Bash is out-of-process via Unix domain socket.\n- Data files: per-map JSON in `data/`. Section-level `constant` flag. Accessed via `libs/soramech-data.lua`.\n- State/ephemeral: `tmp/` is a symlink to `/tmp/<map-name>/`. Phase 2 writes `last-run.json` (single doc). Phase 3 writes `last-run.jsonl` (JSON Lines, issue 311) — decoupled from the editor, consumed by LLMs / CLI viewers / test harness.\n- **Phase 3 runtime model**: C pool runner owns a 3d-rts task pool; per-task slots in process heap (issue 302) with refcounting and a separate large-value heap; dispatch layer (304) is the worker action; graph loader is C (305), no embedded Lua at the runner level. Phase 2's synchronous executor retires when phase 3 lands.\n\n**How to apply:** When working on any component, respect the three-way separation. Server never knows about runner. Runner never knows about server. Map directory format is the only shared contract. The phase 2 driver model and the phase 3 spec model coexist conceptually (phase 2 is current, phase 3 is fully designed) but the runtime mechanism differs entirely; box JSON and the editor are unchanged across the cutover.\n",
          "file_path":"/home/ritz/.claude/projects/-mnt-mtwo-programs-sora-soramech/memory/project_soramech.md"
        },
        "id":"toolu_01HCHPawo2BvVuRx25nWCrYu"

    "originalFile":"---\nname: SoraMech project context\ndescription: Core architecture decisions, file layout, and north star use case for SoraMech\ntype: project\noriginSessionId: 2029ad16-5678-4b15-931f-3f52d826597a\n---\nSoraMech is a visual FSM/dataflow editor and execution engine at /mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/.\n\n**Why:** Primary use case is LLM orchestration on the SoraMind Alpine cluster. Strings flow between boxes like variables. History is explicit, loaded from disk only when a box needs it.\n\n**Three independent programs sharing a map directory:**\n- `soramech-server.lua` — thin HTTP file CRUD proxy only. No runner management. Started for remote editing.\n- `soramech-runner.lua` — FSM execution engine, invoked from CLI independently. Reads map dir, walks graph, invokes drivers.\n- `index.html` — vanilla JS canvas editor. Editor only, no \"run\" button. Talks to server for file ops.\n\n**Key architecture decisions:**\n- Each box is its own JSON file in `boxes/<id>.json`. Connections written to BOTH endpoint files; runner validates both ends agree — hard error if not.\n- Language drivers are shell scripts. No special cases for any language in the runner. Lua/C/bash ship as pre-written driver scripts, same interface as user-defined ones.\n- Driver invocation: `<driver-script> <file-path> <fn-name> <arg-count> [args...]`. Outputs JSON to stdout.\n- Branch box: dedicated node kind with named output ports + always an \"else\" port. LLM-based \"else\" can be unwired (triggers retry of upstream box with pseudo-randomized retry_vary fields). Numeric/string \"else\" must be wired or map won't start.\n- Data files: per-map JSON in `data/`. Section-level `constant` flag. Accessed via `libs/soramech-data.lua` library (not a built-in runner API).\n- State/ephemeral: `tmp/` is a symlink to `/tmp/<map-name>/`. Logs, last-run snapshot, C binary cache go here.\n- v1 executor: synchronous, each box call wrapped in `task_fn(inputs)->outputs` boundary matching 3d-rts thread pool action chain signature for future swap.\n\n**How to apply:** When working on any component, respect the three-way separation. Server never knows about runner. Runner never knows about server. Map directory format is the only shared contract.\n",
    "userModified":false,
    "filePath":"/home/ritz/.claude/projects/-mnt-mtwo-programs-sora-soramech/memory/project_soramech.md",
    "content":"---\nname: SoraMech project context\ndescription: Core architecture decisions, file layout, and execution model for SoraMech, across phase 2 (current) and phase 3 (designed)\ntype: project\noriginSessionId: 579d58b3-7452-44f3-983a-80ff5821082a\n---\nSoraMech is a visual FSM/dataflow editor and execution engine at /mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/.\n\n**Why:** Primary use case is LLM orchestration on the SoraMind Alpine cluster. Strings flow between boxes like variables. History is explicit, loaded from disk only when a box needs it.\n\n**Three independent programs sharing a map directory:**\n- `src/006-server-main.lua` — thin HTTP file CRUD proxy. No runner management.\n- Runner — phase 2: `src/007-runner-main.lua` (synchronous Lua). Phase 3: `soramech-pool` (C binary, designed in issues 301–311, not yet built).\n- `assets/index.html` — vanilla JS canvas editor. Editor only — no run button. Compile button (issue 222) is a phase 2 placeholder; it triggers the phase 3 build pipeline (issue 219).\n\n**Key architecture decisions (current truth):**\n- Each box is its own JSON file in `boxes/<id>.json`. Connections written to BOTH endpoint files; loader validates both ends agree — hard error if not.\n- **Single output wire per box** (issue 218 complete). No `outputs` array. The function returns one value; routing is by `from_branch` on the connection.\n- **Comparator-based branching** (issue 210) — replaces the earlier `branch` box kind with named ports. A box may carry a `comparand`; the dispatch layer fires `lt`/`eq`/`gt` connections. No spec is invoked for comparators.\n- **Iterator boxes** (issue 221) — pure routing primitives, no `ref`/`fn`. Dispatch layer cycles through `iterator_outputs` based on a per-task counter.\n- **Phase 2 drivers** are shell scripts under `drivers/` (one process per call, stdout as channel). **Phase 3 language specs** are `.so` libraries under `langs/<name>/spec.so` loaded via `dlopen` (issue 303). Lua and C are in-process; Bash is out-of-process via Unix domain socket.\n- Data files: per-map JSON in `data/`. Section-level `constant` flag. Accessed via `libs/soramech-data.lua`.\n- State/ephemeral: `tmp/` is a symlink to `/tmp/<map-name>/`. Phase 2 writes `last-run.json` (single doc). Phase 3 writes `last-run.jsonl` (JSON Lines, issue 311) — decoupled from the editor, consumed by LLMs / CLI viewers / test harness.\n- **Phase 3 runtime model**: C pool runner owns a 3d-rts task pool; per-task slots in process heap (issue 302) with refcounting and a separate large-value heap; dispatch layer (304) is the worker action; graph loader is C (305), no embedded Lua at the runner level. Phase 2's synchronous executor retires when phase 3 lands.\n\n**How to apply:** When working on any component, respect the three-way separation. Server never knows about runner. Runner never knows about server. Map directory format is the only shared contract. The phase 2 driver model and the phase 3 spec model coexist conceptually (phase 2 is current, phase 3 is fully designed) but the runtime mechanism differs entirely; box JSON and the editor are unchanged across the cutover.\n"

          "content":"---\nname: threading_model\ndescription: SoraMech's threading model — phase 2 synchronous, phase 3 thread pool with slots and language specs\ntype: project\n---\n**Phase 2 (current)**: synchronous executor in `src/004-executor.lua`. Single-threaded, sequential box execution. One driver shell-out per box call. The phase 2 path goes away when phase 3 lands — no fallback, no coroutine intermediate. (The earlier \"synchronous → coroutines → thread pool\" roadmap was simplified: coroutines are skipped, we go straight to the pool.)\n\n**Phase 3 (designed, not yet built)**: C pool runner owning a 3d-rts task pool, vendored from `/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h` into `libs/task-pool/`. The architecture is fully specified across issues 301–311.\n\nKey phase 3 concepts:\n- **Per-task slots** in process heap memory (not shared memory across processes — plain `malloc`-class). Each slot is a ring buffer; `n_cells = 1` for single-output, `n_cells > 1` for queued inputs. Reference counted; producers and consumers all hold refs while alive. Variable-size payloads use a separate large-value heap with handles in the slot.\n- **Language specs** under `langs/<name>/spec.so`, loaded by the runner via `dlopen` at startup. Uniform `lang_spec_t` interface (init / teardown / compile / invoke). No language is privileged — Lua, C, and Bash are reference implementations on equal footing.\n- **In-process specs** (Lua, C) call functions directly through `lua_pcall` or `dlsym`. **Out-of-process specs** (Bash) use Unix domain sockets to a persistent subprocess per worker.\n- **Dispatch layer** (issue 304) is the worker-side action: read inputs from slots → invoke the language spec (or route, for comparators / iterators) → write output → unref consumed inputs → fire connections.\n- **Iterator and comparator routing** lives entirely in the dispatch layer. No spec is invoked for those box kinds.\n- **Hard-crash error policy**: nonzero return from any spec aborts the program. No retry, no fallback, no failure propagation.\n- **Blocking semantics**: long-running operations (sleep, blocking I/O) tie up a worker thread for the duration. Pool size is the budget for concurrent blocking activities. Cooperative pattern at graph level (split kick-off + check-done through an iterator with queued input) avoids holding a worker. Documented in `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`.\n\n**Effil is explicitly NOT used** and is removed from all docs and issues. The 3d-rts pool is the chosen mechanism. Coroutines were considered as an intermediate stage but dropped in favor of going straight from sync to pool.\n\n**How to apply:** When discussing threading, parallelism, or cross-language IPC: phase 2 is synchronous shell-out drivers; phase 3 is the C pool runner with `lang_spec_t` and the slot store. Never suggest effil. Reference issues 301–311 for the design and `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` for the threading discussion.\n",

    "content":"---\nname: threading_model\ndescription: SoraMech's threading model — phase 2 synchronous, phase 3 thread pool with slots and language specs\ntype: project\noriginSessionId: 579d58b3-7452-44f3-983a-80ff5821082a\n---\n**Phase 2 (current)**: synchronous executor in `src/004-executor.lua`. Single-threaded, sequential box execution. One driver shell-out per box call. The phase 2 path goes away when phase 3 lands — no fallback, no coroutine intermediate. (The earlier \"synchronous → coroutines → thread pool\" roadmap was simplified: coroutines are skipped, we go straight to the pool.)\n\n**Phase 3 (designed, not yet built)**: C pool runner owning a 3d-rts task pool, vendored from `/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h` into `libs/task-pool/`. The architecture is fully specified across issues 301–311.\n\nKey phase 3 concepts:\n- **Per-task slots** in process heap memory (not shared memory across processes — plain `malloc`-class). Each slot is a ring buffer; `n_cells = 1` for single-output, `n_cells > 1` for queued inputs. Reference counted; producers and consumers all hold refs while alive. Variable-size payloads use a separate large-value heap with handles in the slot.\n- **Language specs** under `langs/<name>/spec.so`, loaded by the runner via `dlopen` at startup. Uniform `lang_spec_t` interface (init / teardown / compile / invoke). No spec is invoked for those box kinds.\n- **Hard-crash error policy**: nonzero return from any spec aborts the program. No retry, no fallback, no failure propagation.\n- **Blocking semantics**: long-running operations (sleep, blocking I/O) tie up a worker thread for the duration. Pool size is the budget for concurrent blocking activities. Cooperative pattern at graph level (split kick-off + check-done through an iterator with queued input) avoids holding a worker. Documented in `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`.\n\n**Effil is explicitly NOT used** and is removed from all docs and issues. The 3d-rts pool is the chosen mechanism. Coroutines were considered as an intermediate stage but dropped in favor of going straight from sync to pool.\n\n**How to apply:** When discussing threading, parallelism, or cross-language IPC: phase 2 is synchronous shell-out drivers; phase 3 is the C pool runner with `lang_spec_t` and the slot store. Never suggest effil. Reference issues 301–311 for the design and `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` for the threading discussion.\n"

        "content":"280\t- `static int x = 0;` inside a function body — racy, shared across workers calling that function.\n281\t- `const int max = 100;` — safe, immutable.\n282\t- `static const int max = 100;` — safe, immutable.\n283\t\n284\tBox functions must be reentrant — no mutable shared state without\n285\texplicit locking. The C spec does not enforce this; the rule lives\n286\tin `docs/005-language-specs.md` (to be written) for box authors to\n287\tread.\n288\t\n289\t-- question... say a library function, let's say it's written in C, requires a\n290\t   certain like... global? variable? to exist? or has some other mutation of a\n291\t   shared state that we can't currently predict. Is there a way for the user, in\n292\t   the editor, to maybe mark that it needs something like that, just a variable\n293\t   or whatever, and for us to reserve a spot for it (at the start of runtime)\n294\t   so that the function functions correctly, without needing to actually be\n295\t   part of whatever ecosystem the function expects?\n296\t\n297\tA future fallback exists: `dlmopen`, a Linux variant of `dlopen`\n298\tthat loads each library into its own isolated \"namespace,\" giving\n299\teach worker its own copy of the library's symbols (statics\n300\tincluded). Two threads using two different namespaces would not\n301\tshare static state. Less portable than `dlopen` (Linux-only), so\n302\tnot the default — flagged here as the escape hatch if static-\n303\tvariable races become a real problem.\n304\t\n305\t## Build\n306\t\n307\t```\n308\tlangs/c/\n309\t    spec.c              ← lang_spec_t implementation",
        "type":"tool_result"
      }],

      "content":"- `static int x = 0;` inside a function body — racy, shared across workers calling that function.\n- `const int max = 100;` — safe, immutable.\n- `static const int max = 100;` — safe, immutable.\n\nBox functions must be reentrant — no mutable shared state without\nexplicit locking. The C spec does not enforce this; the rule lives\nin `docs/005-language-specs.md` (to be written) for box authors to\nread.\n\n-- question... say a library function, let's say it's written in C, requires a\n   certain like... global? variable? to exist? or has some other mutation of a\n   shared state that we can't currently predict. Is there a way for the user, in\n   the editor, to maybe mark that it needs something like that, just a variable\n   or whatever, and for us to reserve a spot for it (at the start of runtime)\n   so that the function functions correctly, without needing to actually be\n   part of whatever ecosystem the function expects?\n\nA future fallback exists: `dlmopen`, a Linux variant of `dlopen`\nthat loads each library into its own isolated \"namespace,\" giving\neach worker its own copy of the library's symbols (statics\nincluded). Two threads using two different namespaces would not\nshare static state. Less portable than `dlopen` (Linux-only), so\nnot the default — flagged here as the escape hatch if static-\nvariable races become a real problem.\n\n## Build\n\n```\nlangs/c/\n    spec.c              ← lang_spec_t implementation"

    "oldString":"Box functions must be reentrant — no mutable shared state without\nexplicit locking. The C spec does not enforce this; the rule lives\nin `docs/005-language-specs.md` (to be written) for box authors to\nread.\n\n-- question... say a library function, let's say it's written in C, requires a\n   certain like... global? variable? to exist? or has some other mutation of a\n   shared state that we can't currently predict. Is there a way for the user, in\n   the editor, to maybe mark that it needs something like that, just a variable\n   or whatever, and for us to reserve a spot for it (at the start of runtime)\n   so that the function functions correctly, without needing to actually be\n   part of whatever ecosystem the function expects?\n\nA future fallback exists: `dlmopen`, a Linux variant of `dlopen`",
    "newString":"Box functions must be reentrant — no mutable shared state without\nexplicit locking. The C spec does not enforce this; the rule lives\nin `docs/005-language-specs.md` (to be written) for box authors to\nread.\n\n### Library functions that need global init\n\nMany real C libraries require a one-time setup call before any of\ntheir functions work — `curl_global_init` for libcurl,\n`OPENSSL_init_crypto` for OpenSSL, etc. A SoraMech box that calls\ninto such a library cannot just be wired in cold; the library's\nstate has to exist before the call.\n\nTwo patterns handle this without changing the spec interface:\n\n1. **Init box wired as an entry point.** The user creates a small C\n   box whose function is the library's init call (e.g.\n   `curl_global_init`). They mark it as an entry box and wire it\n   such that any box using libcurl is downstream of it. The init\n   runs once at startup before any consumer fires. Process-global\n   library state — which is what most C libraries actually use — is\n   set up by the time anyone needs it. Pairs with a teardown box\n   wired as a terminal node if needed.\n\n2. **Per-worker init via spec extension** (future). For libraries\n   that need per-worker setup (each thread gets its own handle),\n   the C spec gains an optional per-box `worker_init_fn` field in\n   the box JSON. The spec calls that function once per worker\n   thread during pool startup, before any box invoke. Not in scope\n   yet — pattern (1) covers the common case.\n\nThe init-box approach is the recommended starting point. The\nspec-extension path is the escape hatch when (1) does not fit.\n\nA future fallback exists: `dlmopen`, a Linux variant of `dlopen`",

Automated behaviors (\"from now on when X\", \"each time X\", \"whenever X\", \"before/after X\") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions (\"allow X\", \"add permission\", \"move permission to\"), env vars (\"set X=Y\"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: \"allow npm commands\", \"add bq permission to global settings\", \"move permission to user settings\", \"set DEBUG=true\", \"when claude stops show X\". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.\n- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: \"rebind ctrl+s\", \"add a chord shortcut\", \"change the submit key\", \"customize keybindings\".\n- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.\n- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.\n- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. \"check the deploy every 5 minutes\", \"keep running /babysit-prs\"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.\n- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run (\"run this once at 3pm\", \"remind me to check X tomorrow\").\n- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).\nTRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.\nSKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.\n- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation\n- review: Review a pull request\n- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch"
