Structured values (tables, arrays) are\n31\tpassed as JSON strings and decoded by the driver.\n32\t\n33\tThe driver must:\n34\t- Exit 0 on success, nonzero on failure\n35\t- Print one JSON value to stdout — string, number, boolean, object,\n36\t  or null. One output wire per box.\n37\t- Print error messages to stderr on failure\n38\t\n39\tMulti-output tuple returns are not supported. Each box has exactly\n40\tone output wire (issue 218).\n41\t\n42\t### Built-in driver scripts\n43\t\n44\tShipped in the project's `drivers/` directory:\n45\t\n46\t- `drivers/lua.sh` — invokes a Lua function via `luajit`\n47\t- `drivers/c.sh` — compiles `.c` (mtime cache) and runs the binary\n48\t- `drivers/bash.sh` — sources the `.sh` and calls the function\n49\t\n50\tUser-added drivers go in the same directory and are picked up by\n51\textension.\n52\t\n53\t### What's wrong with this model\n54\t\n55\tProcess spawn cost dominates each call (1–10 ms per language).\n56\tStdout is a fragile channel — debug prints inside box code corrupt\n57\tthe wire value. Each invocation is its own fresh interpreter; there\n58\tis no persistent runtime between calls. These are the limitations\n59\tphase 3 fixes.\n60\t\n61\t## Phase 3 — Language specs (planned)\n62\t\n63\tEach language is a small C library implementing the spec interface\n64\tdefined in issue 303. The pool runner loads every\n65\t`langs/<name>/spec.so` at startup; the spec interface is uniform\n66\tacross languages, with no privileged language.\n67\t\n68\t### Spec interface\n69\t\n70\t```c\n71\ttypedef struct {\n72\t    const char *name;\n73\t    const char *file_ext;\n74\t\n75\t    void *(*init)(int worker_idx);\n76\t    void  (*teardown)(void *handle);\n77\t    int   (*compile)(const char *src_path, const char *out_path,\n78\t                     const box_t *box);\n79\t    int   (*invoke)(void *handle,\n80\t                    const char *file_path, const char *fn_name,\n81\t                    const void **input_data, const int *input_sizes,\n82\t                    int n_inputs,\n83\t                    void *out_buf, int out_buf_capacity,\n84\t                    int *out_size);\n85\t} lang_spec_t;\n86\t```\n87\t\n88\t`init` runs once per worker thread at pool startup. `teardown` runs\n89\tat shutdown. `compile` runs at map load time for languages that need\n90\tit (C). `invoke` runs once per box invocation.\n91\t\n92\tThe spec receives input bytes and writes output bytes — never\n93\tinteracts with slot IDs. The dispatch layer (issue 304) reads\n94\tinputs from slots into byte buffers, hands them to `invoke`, takes\n95\tback bytes, writes them to the output slot.\n96\t\n97\t### Reference specs\n98\t\n99\t- **Lua** (issue 306) — handle is a `lua_State` per worker. `invoke`",

Structured values (tables, arrays) are\npassed as JSON strings and decoded by the driver.\n\nThe driver must:\n- Exit 0 on success, nonzero on failure\n- Print one JSON value to stdout — string, number, boolean, object,\n  or null. One output wire per box.\n- Print error messages to stderr on failure\n\nMulti-output tuple returns are not supported. Each box has exactly\none output wire (issue 218).\n\n### Built-in driver scripts\n\nShipped in the project's `drivers/` directory:\n\n- `drivers/lua.sh` — invokes a Lua function via `luajit`\n- `drivers/c.sh` — compiles `.c` (mtime cache) and runs the binary\n- `drivers/bash.sh` — sources the `.sh` and calls the function\n\nUser-added drivers go in the same directory and are picked up by\nextension.\n\n### What's wrong with this model\n\nProcess spawn cost dominates each call (1–10 ms per language).\nStdout is a fragile channel — debug prints inside box code corrupt\nthe wire value. Each invocation is its own fresh interpreter; there\nis no persistent runtime between calls. These are the limitations\nphase 3 fixes.\n\n## Phase 3 — Language specs (planned)\n\nEach language is a small C library implementing the spec interface\ndefined in issue 303. The pool runner loads every\n`langs/<name>/spec.so` at startup; the spec interface is uniform\nacross languages, with no privileged language.\n\n### Spec interface\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    const char *name;\n    const char *file_ext;\n\n    void *(*init)(int worker_idx);\n    void  (*teardown)(void *handle);\n    int   (*compile)(const char *src_path, const char *out_path,\n                     const box_t *box);\n    int   (*invoke)(void *handle,\n                    const char *file_path, const char *fn_name,\n                    const void **input_data, const int *input_sizes,\n                    int n_inputs,\n                    void *out_buf, int out_buf_capacity,\n                    int *out_size);\n} lang_spec_t;\n```\n\n`init` runs once per worker thread at pool startup. `teardown` runs\nat shutdown. `compile` runs at map load time for languages that need\nit (C). `invoke` runs once per box invocation.\n\nThe spec receives input bytes and writes output bytes — never\ninteracts with slot IDs. The dispatch layer (issue 304) reads\ninputs from slots into byte buffers, hands them to `invoke`, takes\nback bytes, writes them to the output slot.\n\n### Reference specs\n\n- **Lua** (issue 306) — handle is a `lua_State` per worker. `invoke`"
    }
  },

        "type":"text",
        "text":"Here's the actual lay of the land.\n\n## Where the language-specific code lives\n\n**Wrong place** (in the editor, JS, not in `langs/`):\n- `assets/js/007-filebrowser.js::parse_lua` — extracts `function M.name(args)` and scans for `return` statements.\n- `assets/js/007-filebrowser.js::parse_bash` — extracts function definitions and `$N` references.\n- Driver scripts in `drivers/lua.sh` / `drivers/c.sh` / `drivers/bash.sh` — shell-out to launch each language. These move out at phase 3 (specs replace drivers).\n\n**Right place** (`langs/<name>/`):\n- `langs/lua/lexer.js`, `langs/bash/lexer.js`, `langs/c/lexer.js` — just shipped (issue 223).\n- Phase 3's `langs/<name>/spec.so` — runtime invocation contract.\n\nThe file-browser parsers are the violation. They should move to `langs/<name>/parser.js`, mirroring the lexer pattern. Worth opening an issue.\n\n## Var toggle as user truth, language spec as interpreter\n\nRight — leave the toggle as the user's intent. The translation from \"this group is variadic, here are slots `args_0, args_1, args_2`\" to a language-native variadic call lives in the **dispatch layer** (issue 304), not the spec. Dispatch:\n\n1. Reads variadic_inputs from the box JSON.\n2. Walks `box.inputs` collecting slot values in order: `[\"args_0_value\", \"args_1_value\", \"args_2_value\"]`.\n3. Hands the spec a flat array of values in declared-input order. The spec doesn't know \"variadic\" exists — it just calls the function with N positional args.\n\nHow each language receives N positional args is its own problem:\n- **Lua**: function declared with `function f(a, b, ...)` — Lua's `...` collects them.\n- **Bash**: positional args `$1 $2 $3 ...` — naturally variadic.\n- **C**: needs either a generated wrapper (`compile` callback in issue 307) that takes a count + array, or `va_list`. The wrapper is per-box, generated at compile time.\n\nSo the spec interface stays simple: \"here's a list of byte buffers, invoke.\" Variadic-ness is dispatch-layer accounting.\n\n## Cross-language values and missing args\n\n**Phase 2 wire format**: JSON strings on the command line. Structured values JSON-encoded; the driver decodes per its language. Output is one JSON value on stdout.\n\n**Phase 3 wire format**: byte buffers via `invoke(input_data[], input_sizes[], n_inputs, out_buf, ...)` per `lang_spec_t`. The bytes are still naturally JSON — that's what's already in flight from phase 2 — but the spec API doesn't mandate it; it just says \"byte buffers.\" The convention is JSON.\n\n**Missing values**: a slot with no wire and no literal has no JSON to encode. Two reasonable answers:\n1. **Don't fire the task** until all required inputs are present. This is what the per-task slot store (issue 302) is built for — the dispatch task waits for all wires to deliver.\n2. **Fire with `null`** for missing slots, let the language map JSON null to whatever (Lua nil, Bash empty string, C `NULL`).\n\nThe right one depends on whether the missing-ness is intentional (\"optional input, use default\") or accidental (\"forgot to wire\"). The current phase 2 executor effectively does (2) — the box runs whether or not all slots are connected, missing slots become nil in Lua. Phase 3 should make this explicit per port: a port carries an `optional: true` flag; without it, missing wires stall the task.\n\n**Cross-language translation**: each spec's `invoke` receives bytes the dispatch layer produced from upstream. Lua emits JSON of a number, Bash receives the same JSON string, parses it, treats it however Bash treats numbers (it doesn't — they're all strings, which is fine). The wire format (JSON) is the lingua franca; each language is responsible for converting JSON ↔ native at its boundary. **Null** specifically: JSON null on the wire, each language maps to its own bottom value.\n\nThe Bash subtle case: Bash has no concept of null — it has empty string and unset variable. Convention: JSON null → unset, JSON empty string → empty. The Bash spec (issue 308) needs to settle that.\n\n## Suggested next issues\n\nThree small ones, all phase 2:\n\n1. **Move `parse_lua` and `parse_bash` from `007-filebrowser.js` into `langs/<name>/parser.js`**. Same lazy-import pattern as the lexers. The file browser asks the per-language parser for `{ inputs, outputs, variadic_base? }`. Auto-flips the var toggle when the parser reports a variadic tail.\n2. **Optional-input flag on ports**. Schema accepts `port.optional: true`; dispatch layer (phase 3) treats unset optional as JSON null, unset non-optional as a stall.\n3. **Document the wire format and cross-language null/missing handling** in `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — currently the implicit convention isn't written down.\n\nWant me to open these?"
      }]

    "content":"Can you tell me how the dispatch layer interacts with the threading model?\n\n  Missing values: a slot with no wire and no literal has no JSON to encode. Two reasonable answers:\n  1. Don't fire the task until all required inputs are present. This is what the per-task slot store (issue 302) is built for — the dispatch\n  task waits for all wires to deliver.\n  2. Fire with null for missing slots, let the language map JSON null to whatever (Lua nil, Bash empty string, C NULL).\n\n\nI think we should try to avoid using null whenever we can. It produces silent errors. Instead, what if we require the user to either enter a value, connect a wire, or mark it as optional in the editor? before it'll compile for them.\n\n  The Bash subtle case: Bash has no concept of null — it has empty string and unset variable. Convention: JSON null → unset, JSON empty\n  string → empty. The Bash spec (issue 308) needs to settle that.\n\nsee? here's an example. Null should not be supported and I'm okay being dogmatic about that.\n\nI'm still not understanding the variadic inputs system, can you describe it in more detail for me?     "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"## Dispatch layer × threading\n\nThe pool (issue 301) holds N worker threads. Each worker has a small per-language state cache — one `lua_State`, one set of `dlopen`'d C symbol tables, one persistent Bash subprocess — initialized at pool startup so language launches don't repeat per call.\n\nA **task** is one box invocation. Tasks live in the pool's queue. When a worker is free, it pulls the front task and runs the dispatch action against it.\n\nThe dispatch action is one C function, ~200 lines. Its phases:\n\n1. **Check inputs ready.** Walk the input slots. If any slot has no value yet, the action returns `ACT_BLOCK` and the pool parks the task on that slot's wait list. The slot owns the wait list, not the wire — when an upstream task pushes a value into the slot, it walks the wait list and wakes everyone parked there.\n2. **Read inputs into byte buffers.** The slot store hands back the bytes; the language spec doesn't see slot IDs.\n3. **Branch on box mode.** Plain call → invoke the spec. Comparator → compare input to threshold, produce a branch tag, no spec call. Iterator → copy input straight to output, no spec call.\n4. **Invoke** (plain call only). The spec turns bytes into native types, calls the user function, serializes back to bytes.\n5. **Write output** to the box's output slot. Slot store walks the slot's wait list and wakes parked tasks.\n6. **Unref consumed inputs.** Single-value slots are reference-counted per fan-out wire; queued slots persist (iterators re-pop across invocations).\n7. **Route.** Plain call fires all outgoing connections; comparator fires only the matching branch; iterator fires the counter-th branch and respawns a successor task with `counter+1`.\n8. **Return ACT_DONE.** Pool decrements the active-task count.\n\nSo the threading is: many tasks queued, M < N tasks running in parallel on the pool's workers, each task is one dispatch-action invocation. Blocking-on-input is cooperative — the action returns ACT_BLOCK and the worker is freed for other work; when the slot fills, the parked task is requeued. No thread sleeps on a slot, no spinlocks, no per-box thread.\n\nBoxes don't map to threads. Workers are uniform; any worker can run any box.\n\n---\n\n## No null\n\nAgreed — and the compile button is the natural enforcement point. Three rules:\n\n1. Every input port must have a wire OR a literal value OR `optional: true` on the port.\n2. `optional: true` ports without a wire and without a literal don't fire — the dispatch action treats them as \"not present\" and the receiving function never sees a null. Languages get a way to ask \"is this arg present?\" at the spec boundary; absent means absent.\n3. Compile fails loudly when an input violates rule (1), pointing at the box and the port.\n\nThe Bash null-vs-empty quagmire goes away because absent never reaches Bash — it just doesn't get the variable set, and the spec sees zero positional args for that slot. Lua: missing `optional` arg is `nil` only because Lua's calling convention has no other choice; but that's a language-internal artifact, not a wire-protocol value. Nothing crosses the wire as null.\n\nWorth opening as an issue — it has a real schema change (the `optional` flag), a compile-button hookup, and per-spec \"absent argument\" semantics. Want me to?\n\n---\n\n## Variadic, illustrated\n\nPicture a box on the canvas as a small machine with input plugs on its left side. A normal port is a single plug — one wire goes in. The function on the other end of that plug has a parameter named, say, `text`, and the wire's value lands there.\n\nA variadic port is **a strip of plugs that grows as you use it**. You start with one plug, just like a normal port. You wire something to it. The moment you make that connection, a fresh empty plug appears below, ready for the next wire. Wire that one too, and another empty plug appears. The box keeps the plugs you've wired and always has one empty one waiting at the bottom.\n\nThe function on the other end isn't seeing N separate parameters — it's seeing **one parameter that's a bundle of values**. In Lua, that's `function f(...)` and inside the function you've got a list. In Bash, that's `\"$@\"` — all the positional arguments, however many were passed. The variadic strip on the canvas is the visual representation of \"stuff goes into this collection.\"\n\nWhy bother? Because the alternative — declaring up front \"this function takes exactly 5 strings\" — locks you into 5. A concat box should join however many strings you've got. A logging box should accept however many fields you want to log. A list-builder should take however many items you've got items. Variadic is the editor saying \"I don't know how many you'll wire, and I won't make you guess.\"\n\nThe \"var\" toggle in the inspector is the user telling the editor \"this port is the strip kind, not the single-plug kind.\" The slots `args_0`, `args_1`, `args_2` are how the box JSON tracks the individual plugs (each one a normal connection point with a unique name, so wires can find the right one). The dispatch layer reads the strip in order, hands the values to the function as a flat list, and the language's native variadic syntax does the rest.\n\nWhen you remove a slot, the strip just gets a hole where that plug used to be — the others keep their names. Auto-grow uses \"highest existing slot + 1,\" so holes are harmless. The toggle off collapses the strip back to one plug; the slots and any wires attached to them go away, because the shape changed and the wires no longer mean what they used to.\n\nThree sources of truth, in order:\n1. **The user**, via the var toggle. They mark a port as the strip kind.\n2. **The dispatch layer**, which knows how to walk a strip and produce a flat ordered argument list.\n3. **The language spec**, which knows how to push a flat ordered argument list into its native variadic call convention.\n\nEach layer does one thing. None of them needs to know what the others know."
      }]

## [3568]

```json
{
  "timestamp":"2026-05-09T23:40:53.866Z",
  "message":{
    "content":"  The pool (issue 301) holds N worker threads. Each worker has a small per-language state cache — one lua_State, one set of dlopen'd C symbol\n   tables, one persistent Bash subprocess — initialized at pool startup so language launches don't repeat per call.\n\nhow does the user define these things for the language specs?\n\n  A task is one box invocation. Tasks live in the pool's queue. When a worker is free, it pulls the front task and runs the dispatch action\n  against it.\n\nare the workers themselves pulling the task from the queue, or is there an orchestrator thread? I'd like to eliminate any orchestration threads and have everything done through the task queue. It's okay if there's an orchestrator for initialization but not during general operation.\n\n  1. Check inputs ready. Walk the input slots. If any slot has no value yet, the action returns ACT_BLOCK and the pool parks the task on that\n   slot's wait list. The slot owns the wait list, not the wire — when an upstream task pushes a value into the slot, it walks the wait list\n  and wakes everyone parked there.\n\n\n\"Waking\" in this case means re-adding the pointer to the task to the ready task queue right?\n\n  3. Branch on box mode. Plain call → invoke the spec. Comparator → compare input to threshold, produce a branch tag, no spec call. Iterator\n  → copy input straight to output, no spec call.\n\nConcerned about this. The comparator should be comparing the OUTPUT, not the input. The input should always be accepted, the output is what causes the branch. \"if this function returns a 5, that's greater than the eq value so run the gt function\"\n\n  5. Write output to the box's output slot. Slot store walks the slot's wait list and wakes parked tasks.\n\nwhich thread is doing this slot store walk?\n\n  6. Unref consumed inputs. Single-value slots are reference-counted per fan-out wire; queued slots persist (iterators re-pop across\n  invocations).\n\ncan you explain this part a bit more?\n\n  2. optional: true ports without a wire and without a literal don't fire — the dispatch action treats them as \"not present\" and the\n  receiving function never sees a null. Languages get a way to ask \"is this arg present?\" at the spec boundary; absent means absent.\n\nI'm curious about how we'd implement this... Also, I think it's okay if the user literally types \"NULL\" or \"NIL\" or something, because, idk, maybe some library they're using REQUIRES it somewhere. That's a bad library, but who are we to judge?\n\n... Okay I definitely do judge. I judge them reckless. But we still must support it because... Ugh, because we have to.\n\nSo, maybe we have to have like, a switch statement in the language spec that checks the type and translates the value accordingly. Does that make sense? Do you have a better idea?\n\n  Worth opening as an issue — it has a real schema change (the optional flag), a compile-button hookup, and per-spec \"absent argument\"\n  semantics. Want me to?\n\nYeah we need to be sure that we make issue files for the required changes when we resolve to a solution that needs implementation.\n\nThanks for the description about variadic arguments. Can you explain how we're implementing it in the language spec specifically?",
    "role":"user"
  },

        "type":"text",
        "text":"Lots to answer. Let me work through them:\n\n## How users define language specs\n\nA spec is a small C file that implements `lang_spec_t` (issue 303):\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    const char *name;        // \"lua\"\n    const char *file_ext;    // \"lua\"\n    void *(*init)(int worker_idx);\n    void  (*teardown)(void *handle);\n    int   (*compile)(...);   // optional — only languages that need it\n    int   (*invoke)(void *handle, const char *file_path, const char *fn_name,\n                    const void **input_data, const int *input_sizes, int n_inputs,\n                    void *out_buf, int out_buf_capacity, int *out_size);\n} lang_spec_t;\n```\n\nThe user writes `langs/<name>/spec.c`, `langs/<name>/Makefile` (which builds to `spec.so`), and exports a global `soramech_lang_spec` of type `lang_spec_t`. The pool runner `dlopen`s every `langs/<dir>/spec.so` at startup and indexes by `name` and `file_ext`. Adding a language is: create the directory, write `spec.c`, write `Makefile`, drop in.\n\nThe init/teardown pair is where per-worker state lives — the `lua_State`, the `dlopen`'d C symbol table, the persistent Bash subprocess. Each worker thread calls `init` once at pool startup; the returned `handle` is stored in worker-thread-local state and passed back to `invoke` on every call.\n\n## Workers pull, no orchestrator\n\nAlready the design — main thread loads the graph, creates the pool, submits the entry tasks, then sleeps on a condition variable until the active-task counter hits zero. After that point, **everything is worker-driven**: each worker pulls one task off the pool's queue, runs the dispatch action, and either:\n- Submits successor tasks (regular completion).\n- Parks the task on a slot's wait list (input not ready).\n- Re-submits itself to advance the iterator counter.\n\nSlot-fill from a completing task wakes parked tasks by re-adding them to the queue — done by the same worker that pushed the value, no orchestrator involved. The main thread only re-enters operation at quiescence (counter == 0) to tear down the pool.\n\n## \"Waking\" = re-add to ready queue\n\nYes. Each parked task is just a `dispatch_task_t*` sitting on a slot's wait list. The slot-push code walks the list, takes each pointer off, and `pool_spawn`s it (or whatever the equivalent re-enqueue is in the 3d-rts pool API). The task lands at the back of the ready queue and gets picked up by whichever worker is free next.\n\n## Comparator compares OUTPUT, not input — you're right\n\nIssue 304's text is wrong here. The editor's actual model (and what makes sense): a comparator is a **modifier on a call box**, not a separate routing primitive. The function still runs. Its output is compared to the box's `comparand`. The matching `lt` / `eq` / `gt` branch fires.\n\nSo phase 4 (invoke) runs for comparator boxes too. Phase 5 writes the function's output to the slot. Phase 7 (routing) then compares the output to the threshold and fires the matching branch — and only that branch.\n\nI'll update 304's text to match. The editor is the source of truth here; the issue file drifted.\n\n## Slot-store walk happens on the producing thread\n\nThe thread that just completed phase 5 (write output). After `slot_push`, the same worker walks the wait list, removes the parked tasks, re-submits them. Then it falls through to phase 6 (unref) and 7 (routing), then returns ACT_DONE and pulls the next task from the queue. No handoff to a coordinator.\n\n## Refcount explanation\n\nA slot is a small struct with the value bytes and a refcount. The refcount represents **\"how many consumers haven't read this yet\"** — it's a liveness count, not a producer count.\n\n- When a task is submitted with this slot as one of its inputs, the slot's refcount goes up by 1 (one wire's worth of \"I'm going to need this\").\n- When that task reaches phase 6 (unref consumed inputs), it decrements the count by 1.\n- When the count reaches 0, no consumer has any further interest, and the slot is freed.\n\nFan-out works naturally: if three tasks are wired to the same upstream slot, the refcount starts at 3 (one per wire). Each task reads the value and unrefs; when the third task unrefs, the slot is freed. The order doesn't matter.\n\nQueued slots (iterator inputs) are different — they're ring buffers. Each `slot_pop` drains one cell, but the slot itself stays alive because the iterator hasn't ended yet. The refcount on a queued slot tracks **producer liveness**: each upstream wire holds 1 ref while its producing box hasn't ended. When all producers have ended AND the iterator's own ref drops, the queue is freed.\n\n## Optional inputs and \"NULL\" as a literal\n\nYou're right about both halves. Two cases:\n\n1. **Required input is missing** → compile-time rejection. The user has to wire it, give it a literal, or mark it optional. No runtime null.\n2. **User explicitly wants the value `null`** (because some library demands it). Allowed — they type the literal string `null` (or whatever convention we settle on). That's a string on the wire, just like `42` or `hello`. The receiving language gets the string `null` and decides what to do with it.\n\nYour switch-on-type idea is the right shape. The wire format is JSON, which has a type tag built in (`\"foo\"` is a string, `42` is a number, `null` is null). The spec's `invoke` decodes the JSON byte buffer and translates per language:\n\n```\nJSON value      Lua             Bash             C\n-----------     -----           ----             ----\n\"foo\"           \"foo\"           \"foo\"            \"foo\"\n42              42              \"42\"             42\ntrue            true            \"true\"           1\nnull            nil             \"\"               NULL\n```\n\n(Bash gets every value as a string regardless — that's how Bash works.)\n\nSo: the wire carries typed JSON, the spec translates to the language's natural form. We don't ban null from the wire — we just ban null from being **the result of a missing input**. If the user explicitly wires a literal `null`, that's a real value, fine. If the user forgot to wire, that's a compile error, not a silent null injection.\n\nThe \"is this arg present?\" API at the spec boundary becomes: it isn't. Optional + absent = the spec gets a shorter arg list, period. The function's parameter falls into its language's \"this parameter wasn't passed\" handling (Lua: nil; C: must be the trailing variadic; Bash: not set). That is a separate semantics from \"the value passed was null.\"\n\nSo the rule:\n- **Absent** = arg position not in the call.\n- **null** = arg position is in the call, value is the language's null.\n\nThese are different at the language level, and the spec respects the difference.\n\n## Issues to open\n\nI'll write up two issues:\n\n1. **No-null-from-missing rule** + `optional: true` per-port flag + compile-button check.\n2. **Comparator compares OUTPUT, not input** — fix 304's text to match the editor.\n\nPlus the earlier-promised:\n3. **Move `parse_lua` / `parse_bash` to `langs/<name>/parser.js`** so the editor stops being un-agnostic.\n\nLet me open these now."
      }]

          "content":"# 230 — Required inputs, the optional flag, and no-null-from-missing\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nA box's input port can be left without a wire and without a literal\nvalue. The phase 2 executor runs the box anyway; the function on\nthe other end gets `nil` (Lua), unset (Bash), or whatever default\nthe language hands a missing positional arg. Errors only surface if\nthe function happens to reference the missing arg in a way the\nlanguage can't tolerate (e.g. `string.upper(nil)` in Lua).\n\nThis is a class of silent-error bug. The user had a wiring intent,\nforgot to plug something in, and the runtime quietly papered over\nthe mistake.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nEvery input port is in one of three states by **compile time**:\n\n1. A wire is connected to it.\n2. A literal value is set on it.\n3. It carries `optional: true` on the port record.\n\n**Compile fails** when any port is in none of those states. The\nerror is precise: which box, which port. The Compile button (issue\n222) is the natural enforcement point, with the same check\nduplicating in the phase 3 graph loader (issue 305).\n\n### \"Optional\" is not \"null\"\n\n`optional: true` says \"this argument doesn't have to be passed.\" It\ndoes not mean \"pass null.\" At the spec boundary, an optional\nunwired un-littered port produces a shorter arg list — the language\nsees fewer arguments, not a null argument. Each language handles\nthat natively:\n\n- **Lua**: omitted args are `nil`. That's a language convention,\n  not a wire-level value. Inside the Lua function, `arg or default`\n  works.\n- **Bash**: a positional arg that wasn't passed is unset.\n  `${arg:-default}` provides a default.\n- **C**: the spec's compile callback (issue 307) generates a wrapper\n  that reads `n_inputs` and only forwards the args that are present.\n\n### Null as an explicit value (allowed)\n\nIf the user needs to pass null because some downstream library\nexpects it, they can — by typing the literal `null` into the value\nfield. That's a string on the wire encoded as JSON null. Each spec\nmaps it to its language's native null on the way in:\n\n| JSON value  | Lua    | Bash       | C       |\n|-------------|--------|------------|---------|\n| `null`      | nil    | empty `\"\"` | `NULL`  |\n| `42`        | 42     | `\"42\"`     | 42      |\n| `\"foo\"`     | `foo`  | `foo`      | `\"foo\"` |\n| `true`      | true   | `\"true\"`   | `1`     |\n\nThe crucial distinction: **explicit null arrives through the\nfunction call as a real argument**; **optional-and-absent does not\narrive at all**. Bash empty-string-vs-unset disappears in the\noptional path because the arg position simply isn't passed.\n\n### Schema\n\nAdd `optional` as an optional boolean on input port records:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"name\": \"config_path\",\n  \"type\": \"string\",\n  \"optional\": true\n}\n```\n\nAbsence means `false`. No migration; existing maps work unchanged.\n\n## Compile-time check\n\nThe check walks every box, every input. For each:\n- If the port has `value` set (literal): pass.\n- If any connection has `to_box === box.id && to_input === port.name`:\n  pass.\n- If `port.optional === true`: pass.\n- Otherwise: error, with a precise message:\n  `\"box <id>: input '<port>' has no wire, no literal, and is not optional\"`\n\nThe check runs:\n- **Editor** — on Compile button click (issue 222 → 309). Errors\n  surface in the editor without writing the compiled output.\n- **Loader** — at run time (phase 3 issue 305). Errors abort the\n  run. Belt and suspenders: the editor catches it but a hand-edited\n  map JSON can still trip the loader check.\n\n## Spec API for \"is this arg present?\"\n\nThe spec doesn't need to ask. The dispatch layer assembles\n`input_data[]` and `input_sizes[]` from the slots that actually\nhave values. An optional port that's absent isn't in those arrays;\n`n_inputs` is shorter by one. The spec invokes the language with\nthe args it received. The language's native call convention does\nthe rest.\n\nFor C specifically, the compile-callback-generated wrapper takes\n`int n_inputs` and a count-prefixed array. The wrapper picks the\nfirst M args that match its declared parameters and forwards them;\ntrailing optionals get omitted from the call (or filled with C's\nzero-valued types, depending on the wrapper convention). This is\nissue 307's territory.\n\n## Inspector UI\n\nA small per-port flag in the inspector's port block:\n\n```\n[name] [var] [opt]\n[ value ........... ]\n```\n\n`opt` toggles `port.optional` on the port record. Visual: same\nsmall button as `var` but distinct color.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Whether to allow optional + literal**: yes. A literal is an\n  explicit value; the optional flag is irrelevant when the value\n  is set. The compile check just needs all three signals\n  available; literal wins over optional.\n- **What syntax means \"explicit null literal\"**: lean toward\n  literally typing `null` (case-insensitive) in the value field.\n  An ambiguity arises when the user actually wants the string\n  `\"null\"` — escape it as `\"null\"` (with quotes) which the value\n  parser interprets as a string literal. Worth nailing down before\n  shipping.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — accept `optional` field\n- `src/003-loader.lua` (phase 2) — compile-time check\n- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — `opt` toggle in port block\n- `assets/js/005-app.js` — Compile button hooks check before\n  compile\n- `issues/309-build-system.md` — compile/package step calls the\n  check\n- `issues/305-c-graph-loader.md` — phase 3 check at load time\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — `invoke`'s n_inputs\n  reflects what was actually passed\n- `issues/307-c-language-spec.md` — wrapper handles short-arg case\n- `issues/308-bash-language-spec.md` — null vs unset distinction\n  evaporates in the optional path\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/230-required-inputs-and-optional-flag.md"
        },
        "id":"toolu_019UF8AMnz6HR1VcfwPS9GJP"
      }]

The Compile button (issue\n222) is the natural enforcement point, with the same check\nduplicating in the phase 3 graph loader (issue 305).\n\n### \"Optional\" is not \"null\"\n\n`optional: true` says \"this argument doesn't have to be passed.\" It\ndoes not mean \"pass null.\" At the spec boundary, an optional\nunwired un-littered port produces a shorter arg list — the language\nsees fewer arguments, not a null argument. Each language handles\nthat natively:\n\n- **Lua**: omitted args are `nil`. That's a language convention,\n  not a wire-level value. Inside the Lua function, `arg or default`\n  works.\n- **Bash**: a positional arg that wasn't passed is unset.\n  `${arg:-default}` provides a default.\n- **C**: the spec's compile callback (issue 307) generates a wrapper\n  that reads `n_inputs` and only forwards the args that are present.\n\n### Null as an explicit value (allowed)\n\nIf the user needs to pass null because some downstream library\nexpects it, they can — by typing the literal `null` into the value\nfield. That's a string on the wire encoded as JSON null. Each spec\nmaps it to its language's native null on the way in:\n\n| JSON value  | Lua    | Bash       | C       |\n|-------------|--------|------------|---------|\n| `null`      | nil    | empty `\"\"` | `NULL`  |\n| `42`        | 42     | `\"42\"`     | 42      |\n| `\"foo\"`     | `foo`  | `foo`      | `\"foo\"` |\n| `true`      | true   | `\"true\"`   | `1`     |\n\nThe crucial distinction: **explicit null arrives through the\nfunction call as a real argument**; **optional-and-absent does not\narrive at all**. Bash empty-string-vs-unset disappears in the\noptional path because the arg position simply isn't passed.\n\n### Schema\n\nAdd `optional` as an optional boolean on input port records:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"name\": \"config_path\",\n  \"type\": \"string\",\n  \"optional\": true\n}\n```\n\nAbsence means `false`. No migration; existing maps work unchanged.\n\n## Compile-time check\n\nThe check walks every box, every input. For each:\n- If the port has `value` set (literal): pass.\n- If any connection has `to_box === box.id && to_input === port.name`:\n  pass.\n- If `port.optional === true`: pass.\n- Otherwise: error, with a precise message:\n  `\"box <id>: input '<port>' has no wire, no literal, and is not optional\"`\n\nThe check runs:\n- **Editor** — on Compile button click (issue 222 → 309). Errors\n  surface in the editor without writing the compiled output.\n- **Loader** — at run time (phase 3 issue 305). Errors abort the\n  run. Belt and suspenders: the editor catches it but a hand-edited\n  map JSON can still trip the loader check.\n\n## Spec API for \"is this arg present?\"\n\nThe spec doesn't need to ask. The dispatch layer assembles\n`input_data[]` and `input_sizes[]` from the slots that actually\nhave values. An optional port that's absent isn't in those arrays;\n`n_inputs` is shorter by one. The spec invokes the language with\nthe args it received. The language's native call convention does\nthe rest.\n\nFor C specifically, the compile-callback-generated wrapper takes\n`int n_inputs` and a count-prefixed array. The wrapper picks the\nfirst M args that match its declared parameters and forwards them;\ntrailing optionals get omitted from the call (or filled with C's\nzero-valued types, depending on the wrapper convention). This is\nissue 307's territory.\n\n## Inspector UI\n\nA small per-port flag in the inspector's port block:\n\n```\n[name] [var] [opt]\n[ value ........... ]\n```\n\n`opt` toggles `port.optional` on the port record. Visual: same\nsmall button as `var` but distinct color.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Whether to allow optional + literal**: yes. A literal is an\n  explicit value; the optional flag is irrelevant when the value\n  is set. The compile check just needs all three signals\n  available; literal wins over optional.\n- **What syntax means \"explicit null literal\"**: lean toward\n  literally typing `null` (case-insensitive) in the value field.\n  An ambiguity arises when the user actually wants the string\n  `\"null\"` — escape it as `\"null\"` (with quotes) which the value\n  parser interprets as a string literal. Worth nailing down before\n  shipping.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/001-schema.lua` — accept `optional` field\n- `src/003-loader.lua` (phase 2) — compile-time check\n- `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — `opt` toggle in port block\n- `assets/js/005-app.js` — Compile button hooks check before\n  compile\n- `issues/309-build-system.md` — compile/package step calls the\n  check\n- `issues/305-c-graph-loader.md` — phase 3 check at load time\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — `invoke`'s n_inputs\n  reflects what was actually passed\n- `issues/307-c-language-spec.md` — wrapper handles short-arg case\n- `issues/308-bash-language-spec.md` — null vs unset distinction\n  evaporates in the optional path\n"
  },

        "input":{
          "content":"# 231 — Move per-language signature parsers out of the file browser into `langs/<name>/parser.js`\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\n`assets/js/007-filebrowser.js` carries language-specific code:\n- `parse_lua(content)` — extracts `function M.<name>(<params>)`\n  declarations and scans for `return` statements to enumerate\n  outputs.\n- `parse_bash(content)` — extracts `<name>() {` declarations and\n  uses `parse_bash_inputs` to count `$N` references.\n- `parse_functions(content, filename)` — dispatches on file\n  extension to one of the above.\n\nC has no parser yet. Languages a user might add (Python, Rust, …)\nhave no path to a parser.\n\nThe lexer infrastructure (issue 223, complete) already establishes\nthe right pattern: per-language files under `langs/<name>/`,\nloaded on demand by the editor through dynamic `import()`. The\nsignature parsers belong there, not in the editor.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nEach language directory carries a `parser.js` ES module exporting\na single function:\n\n```js\n// langs/<name>/parser.js\nexport function parse_functions(content) {\n  return [\n    {\n      name: 'write_result',\n      inputs: ['text'],\n      outputs: [],            // empty array → sink box (issue 226)\n      variadic_base: null,    // or 'args' for f(a, ...)\n    },\n    // ...\n  ];\n}\n```\n\nThe editor's file browser drops its `parse_lua` / `parse_bash` /\n`parse_functions` and asks the per-language parser instead. Same\nlazy-load pattern as the lexers: a registry keyed by file\nextension, dynamic `import()` on first need, cached per session.\nFiles with an unknown extension fall back to \"no parser available\"\n— the file browser displays the file name but offers no\nfunction-list step.\n\n### Extended return shape\n\nThe parser returns a richer record than the current shape:\n- `name` — function name (existing).\n- `inputs` — array of parameter names in declaration order\n  (existing).\n- `outputs` — array of return-value names; empty for sinks\n  (existing).\n- `variadic_base` — string or null. Set when the function\n  declaration has a variadic tail (Lua `...`, Bash `\"$@\"`, C\n  `va_list`). Editor uses it to auto-flip the var toggle for that\n  port. Existing parsers don't compute this; new field, optional\n  for parsers that don't bother.\n\n### Why this matters\n\nThe file browser is the editor's single entry point for \"import\nfunction from source.\" Any language-specific logic in it is the\nwrong level of abstraction. Moving it puts the editor on equal\nfooting with the runtime: both treat languages as pluggable, both\ndiscover capabilities through `langs/<name>/`, neither has a\nhardcoded list.\n\nIt also makes adding a new language a self-contained job: drop\n`langs/<name>/parser.js`, `langs/<name>/lexer.js`, and (phase 3)\n`langs/<name>/spec.so` into `langs/`, and the editor and the\nrunner both pick it up.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Create `langs/lua/parser.js` with the existing `parse_lua` /\n   `parse_lua_returns` logic, exporting `parse_functions`.\n2. Create `langs/bash/parser.js` with the existing `parse_bash` /\n   `parse_bash_inputs` logic.\n3. Optionally create `langs/c/parser.js` — a minimal one that\n   extracts `int name(int a, char *b)` style declarations from\n   header files. Defer if not needed yet.\n4. Add a parser registry to `assets/js/007-filebrowser.js` mirroring\n   the lexer registry in `008-source-view.js`:\n   ```js\n   const EXT_TO_LANG = { lua: 'lua', sh: 'bash', bash: 'bash' };\n   const parser_cache = {};\n   async function load_parser(lang) { /* dynamic import */ }\n   ```\n5. Replace `parse_functions(content, filename)` body with a lookup\n   into the registry. The function becomes async; existing callers\n   already `await` async file fetches, so this slots in.\n6. Delete `parse_lua`, `parse_bash`, `parse_lua_returns`,\n   `parse_bash_inputs`, `lua_fn_end` from `007-filebrowser.js`.\n7. (Optional, separate change) Wire `variadic_base` into the\n   on-select handler so the editor auto-flips the var toggle.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Test coverage**: parsers are easy to break with a regex tweak.\n  A small set of fixture sources (`maps/_test/parser-fixtures/*.lua`,\n  `*.sh`) and a JS test harness would catch regressions. Out of\n  scope for this issue, worth a follow-up.\n- **Parsing failure shape**: a parser that throws should be\n  reported as \"parser error\" not \"no parser.\" Add a try/catch in\n  the registry layer with a clear message.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `assets/js/007-filebrowser.js` — current parsers move out\n- `langs/lua/parser.js` — new\n- `langs/bash/parser.js` — new\n- `langs/lua/lexer.js`, `langs/bash/lexer.js` — peer modules; same\n  loading pattern\n- `assets/js/008-source-view.js` — reference implementation for\n  the lazy lexer registry\n- `issues/completed/223-syntax-highlighting-via-user-lexers.md` —\n  established the `langs/<name>/<file>` server-serve route and the\n  dynamic-import loading model\n- `docs/005-language-specs.md` — add a \"parser interface\" section\n  alongside the existing \"lexer interface\"\n",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/231-move-signature-parsers-into-langs.md"
        },

    "content":"# 231 — Move per-language signature parsers out of the file browser into `langs/<name>/parser.js`\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\n`assets/js/007-filebrowser.js` carries language-specific code:\n- `parse_lua(content)` — extracts `function M.<name>(<params>)`\n  declarations and scans for `return` statements to enumerate\n  outputs.\n- `parse_bash(content)` — extracts `<name>() {` declarations and\n  uses `parse_bash_inputs` to count `$N` references.\n- `parse_functions(content, filename)` — dispatches on file\n  extension to one of the above.\n\nC has no parser yet. Languages a user might add (Python, Rust, …)\nhave no path to a parser.\n\nThe lexer infrastructure (issue 223, complete) already establishes\nthe right pattern: per-language files under `langs/<name>/`,\nloaded on demand by the editor through dynamic `import()`. The\nsignature parsers belong there, not in the editor.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nEach language directory carries a `parser.js` ES module exporting\na single function:\n\n```js\n// langs/<name>/parser.js\nexport function parse_functions(content) {\n  return [\n    {\n      name: 'write_result',\n      inputs: ['text'],\n      outputs: [],            // empty array → sink box (issue 226)\n      variadic_base: null,    // or 'args' for f(a, ...)\n    },\n    // ...\n  ];\n}\n```\n\nThe editor's file browser drops its `parse_lua` / `parse_bash` /\n`parse_functions` and asks the per-language parser instead. Same\nlazy-load pattern as the lexers: a registry keyed by file\nextension, dynamic `import()` on first need, cached per session.\nFiles with an unknown extension fall back to \"no parser available\"\n— the file browser displays the file name but offers no\nfunction-list step.\n\n### Extended return shape\n\nThe parser returns a richer record than the current shape:\n- `name` — function name (existing).\n- `inputs` — array of parameter names in declaration order\n  (existing).\n- `outputs` — array of return-value names; empty for sinks\n  (existing).\n- `variadic_base` — string or null. Set when the function\n  declaration has a variadic tail (Lua `...`, Bash `\"$@\"`, C\n  `va_list`). Editor uses it to auto-flip the var toggle for that\n  port. Existing parsers don't compute this; new field, optional\n  for parsers that don't bother.\n\n### Why this matters\n\nThe file browser is the editor's single entry point for \"import\nfunction from source.\" Any language-specific logic in it is the\nwrong level of abstraction. Moving it puts the editor on equal\nfooting with the runtime: both treat languages as pluggable, both\ndiscover capabilities through `langs/<name>/`, neither has a\nhardcoded list.\n\nIt also makes adding a new language a self-contained job: drop\n`langs/<name>/parser.js`, `langs/<name>/lexer.js`, and (phase 3)\n`langs/<name>/spec.so` into `langs/`, and the editor and the\nrunner both pick it up.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Create `langs/lua/parser.js` with the existing `parse_lua` /\n   `parse_lua_returns` logic, exporting `parse_functions`.\n2. Create `langs/bash/parser.js` with the existing `parse_bash` /\n   `parse_bash_inputs` logic.\n3. Optionally create `langs/c/parser.js` — a minimal one that\n   extracts `int name(int a, char *b)` style declarations from\n   header files. Defer if not needed yet.\n4. Add a parser registry to `assets/js/007-filebrowser.js` mirroring\n   the lexer registry in `008-source-view.js`:\n   ```js\n   const EXT_TO_LANG = { lua: 'lua', sh: 'bash', bash: 'bash' };\n   const parser_cache = {};\n   async function load_parser(lang) { /* dynamic import */ }\n   ```\n5. Replace `parse_functions(content, filename)` body with a lookup\n   into the registry. The function becomes async; existing callers\n   already `await` async file fetches, so this slots in.\n6. Delete `parse_lua`, `parse_bash`, `parse_lua_returns`,\n   `parse_bash_inputs`, `lua_fn_end` from `007-filebrowser.js`.\n7. (Optional, separate change) Wire `variadic_base` into the\n   on-select handler so the editor auto-flips the var toggle.\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Test coverage**: parsers are easy to break with a regex tweak.\n  A small set of fixture sources (`maps/_test/parser-fixtures/*.lua`,\n  `*.sh`) and a JS test harness would catch regressions. Out of\n  scope for this issue, worth a follow-up.\n- **Parsing failure shape**: a parser that throws should be\n  reported as \"parser error\" not \"no parser.\" Add a try/catch in\n  the registry layer with a clear message.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `assets/js/007-filebrowser.js` — current parsers move out\n- `langs/lua/parser.js` — new\n- `langs/bash/parser.js` — new\n- `langs/lua/lexer.js`, `langs/bash/lexer.js` — peer modules; same\n  loading pattern\n- `assets/js/008-source-view.js` — reference implementation for\n  the lazy lexer registry\n- `issues/completed/223-syntax-highlighting-via-user-lexers.md` —\n  established the `langs/<name>/<file>` server-serve route and the\n  dynamic-import loading model\n- `docs/005-language-specs.md` — add a \"parser interface\" section\n  alongside the existing \"lexer interface\"\n"
  },

{
  "timestamp":"2026-05-09T23:54:43.482Z",
  "message":{
    "content":"  How users define language specs\n\n  A spec is a small C file that implements lang_spec_t (issue 303):\n\n\nOkay that makes sense to me, but how does it like... know how to interpret values? How does it handle json, I heard we're passing json back and forth?\n\n● Bash(git -C /mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech add issues/230-required-inputs-and-optional-flag.md\n      issues/231-move-signature-parsers-into-langs.md issues/304-task-disp…)\n  ⎿  Interrupted · What should Claude do instead?\n\n\nOoops I didn't mean to stop you. Can you try again? My bad...\n\n  Fan-out works naturally: if three tasks are wired to the same upstream slot, the refcount starts at 3 (one per wire). Each task reads the\n  value and unrefs; when the third task unrefs, the slot is freed. The order doesn't matter.\n\n  Queued slots (iterator inputs) are different — they're ring buffers. Each slot_pop drains one cell, but the slot itself stays alive because\n   the iterator hasn't ended yet. The refcount on a queued slot tracks producer liveness: each upstream wire holds 1 ref while its producing\n  box hasn't ended. When all producers have ended AND the iterator's own ref drops, the queue is freed.\n\n\nOkay I got a question. Let's say there's an upstream box that runs very rapidly 10 times. It puts it's output into a single input slot on another, normal, non-iterator, box. The consumer box runs very slowly, at about 1/10th the speed of the producer box. What happens to the extra values? Are they lost? We should probably have a ring buffer for them too, don't you think?\n\nSo, I have a question. You said that \"the wire format is json\" - what does that look like? Is each ring buffer slot going to be like... a json string, that we're editing every time a value passes through that ring buffer slot? I don't think it makes sense to re-create all the json structural architecture every-time we pass a value from one box to another, but is that what we're planning? Do you have any thoughts about this? Not only is it a re-allocation of memory and values and such, but it's also a lot to pass back and forth. How are we handling that, with pointers? what's the plan here?\n\n  I'll write up two issues:\n\n  1. No-null-from-missing rule + optional: true per-port flag + compile-button check.\n  2. Comparator compares OUTPUT, not input — fix 304's text to match the editor.\n\n  Plus the earlier-promised:\n  3. Move parse_lua / parse_bash to langs/<name>/parser.js so the editor stops being un-agnostic.\n\n\nThanks for opening those issues. We're getting there, bit by bit...",
    "role":"user"
  },

Values\n8\thave no addressable location, no reference count, and no cross-language\n9\taccessibility. Each value vanishes once the pipe is drained.\n10\t\n11\t## Concept\n12\t\n13\t### Slots belong to tasks, not wires\n14\tA **slot** is the memory region that holds a task's output. Slots are\n15\tcreated when tasks are created. A box that runs once produces one slot;\n16\ta box that runs ten times (an iterator) produces ten slots, one per\n17\tinvocation. Slots live in process heap memory, accessible to every\n18\tworker thread in the process. Cross-process visibility is not required:\n19\tlanguage specs (issue 303) only ever receive byte pointers — never\n20\traw slot addresses — so out-of-process specs (Bash) work via sockets,\n21\tnot shared memory.\n22\t\n23\tA **wire** is the relationship between two tasks: it says \"task B's input\n24\tN reads from task A's output M.\" Wires hold references to slots. They\n25\tare the timing mechanism — a task does not become ready until every\n26\tinput wire reports its source slot is filled. They are also the lifetime\n27\tmechanism — a slot is freed only after every wire that referenced it has\n28\treleased it.\n29\t\n30\tThe wire is the arbiter. The slot is just memory.\n31\t\n32\t### All slots are ring buffers\n33\tThere is one slot type. It is a ring buffer of `n_cells` cells, each\n34\tof `cell_capacity` bytes. The `n_cells = 1` case is the trivial ring\n35\tholding a single value; the `n_cells = N` case is a queue.\n36\t\n37\tA single-output box allocates a 1-cell ring. The producer pushes once,\n38\tconsumers read the head. An iterator that produces 10 outputs over its\n39\tlifetime allocates 10 separate 1-cell rings (one per invocation, per\n40\tthe box-not-wire-is-the-slot model below).\n41\t\n42\tA box with a queued input allocates a multi-cell ring as the input's\n43\tholding pen — many upstream wires push into it, the consumer drains it\n44\tin arrival order.\n45\t\n46\tSame data structure, same API, same per-slot lock. The dispatch layer\n47\tparameterizes `n_cells` based on whether the slot is being used for\n48\tfan-out or fan-in.\n49\t\n50\t### Asynchrony\n51\tThe store is fully asynchronous. Slots are allocated, filled, read, and\n52\tfreed at any time, on any thread, with no global lock. Synchronization\n53\tis per-slot. There is no central allocator-wide mutex.\n54\t\n55\t## Slot layout\n56\t\n57\tEach slot is a header followed by `n_cells` cells, each `cell_capacity`\n58\tbytes. The header tracks ring-buffer state and lifetime:\n59\t\n60\t```\n61\tSlot header\n62\tOffset  Size  Field\n63\t------  ----  -----\n64\t0       4     refcount        (atomic int32; lifetime counter)\n65\t4       4     cell_capacity   (bytes per cell, set at allocation)\n66\t8       4     n_cells         (ring size, set at allocation; 1 for single-value)\n67\t12      4     head            (read index, mod n_cells)\n68\t16      4     tail            (write index, mod n_cells; cells_filled = tail - head)\n69\t20      1     touched         (per-slot lock: 0=free, 1=another thread mutating)\n70\t21      3     _pad\n71\t24      …     cells           (n_cells * (4-byte size + cell_capacity bytes))\n72\t```\n73\t\n74\tEach cell stores a 4-byte filled-size followed by `cell_capacity`\n75\tbytes of value data. Cells have wildly different capacities across\n76\tslots — capacity is per-slot, not global. The C convention of passing\n77\tsizes alongside arrays applies: the task that allocates a slot knows\n78\thow big it needs the cells.\n79\t\n80\t`touched` is a single-byte flag toggled around any header mutation\n81\t(push, pop, refcount changes). A reader that finds `touched == 1`\n82\tspins until it clears. This is the simplest possible per-slot lock —\n83\tif contention proves to matter, replace with a proper mutex without\n84\tchanging the API.\n85\t\n86\tWrites to a cell complete with a memory barrier before `tail` is\n87\tadvanced, so a reader that observes `head < tail` is guaranteed to\n88\tsee the complete value at the head cell.\n89\t\n90\t## Reference counting protocol\n91\t\n92\tEvery party that may still touch a slot holds a reference. The slot is\n93\tfreed when the count reaches zero. The references themselves are how\n94\twe track liveness — there is no separate \"is this producer / consumer\n95\tstill alive\" mechanism.\n96\t\n97\t### Single-output (1-cell) slot\n98\t1. Task allocates its output slot with `refcount = 0`.\n99\t2. For each fan-out wire reading from the slot, `slot_ref` is called.\n100\t   The wire holds that reference until its consumer is done reading.\n101\t3. After the consumer reads (peek), it calls `slot_unref`.\n102\t4. When refcount reaches zero, the unrefing task frees the slot.\n103\t\n104\t### Queued (N-cell) slot\n105\tThe consumer's input queue. Producers and the consumer all hold refs:\n106\t1. The consumer task allocates the queue slot with one ref for itself.\n107\t2. Each producer that may push into the queue increments the refcount\n108\t   when it is constructed; the ref is dropped when that producer's\n109\t   box function ends.\n110\t3. The consumer drops its ref when its own box function ends (i.e.\n111\t   when the iterator stops re-spawning because no more inputs are\n112\t   coming).\n113\t4. When the last ref drops, the queue is freed.\n114\t\n115\tThe producer-side ref is what makes \"no more inputs are coming\"\n116\tdetectable: when the queue's refcount equals 1 (only the consumer\n117\tholds it) and the queue is empty, no upstream task can push again,\n118\tso the iterator's natural end-of-stream condition fires.\n119\t\n120\t### Wait list\n121\tEach slot also owns a wait list — pointers to tasks parked on the\n122\tslot waiting for a value. When a producer pushes, the slot walks the\n123\twait list and tells the pool to re-run those tasks. The wait list is\n124\tattached to the slot, not to the producer or the consumer.\n125\t\n126\t## Backing store\n127\t\n128\tSlots are allocated from process heap memory. The slot store owns a\n129\tper-run allocator (described under \"Allocation strategy\" below) that\n130\thands out memory chunks to slots. Plain `malloc`-class memory is\n131\tsufficient — every worker thread in the process can read and write\n132\tit, and no spec ever needs to access it from a child process.\n133\t\n134\tSynchronization within a slot uses the per-slot `touched` flag for\n135\theader mutations and a per-slot wait list (above) for blocked tasks.\n136\tThere is no allocator-wide mutex on the read/write path; only the\n137\tper-size-class free lists in the allocator have their own locks.\n138\t\n139\t## Slot creation\n140\t\n141\tSlot creation happens inside the dispatch layer at task submission. The\n142\tcaller specifies the cell capacity (bytes per value) and the ring size\n143\t(number of cells, 1 for single-value):\n144\t\n145\t```c\n146\tslot_id_t slot_alloc(slot_store_t *store, int cell_capacity, int n_cells);\n147\t```\n148\t\n149\tThe slot is created with `refcount = 0`, `head = tail = 0`. The\n150\tdispatch layer then increments the refcount once per consumer (one ref\n151\tper fan-out wire for a 1-cell slot; one ref for the consumer task on a\n152\tqueued-input slot) before the task is exposed.\n153\t\n154\t## C API surface\n155\t\n156\t```c\n157\tslot_id_t slot_alloc (slot_store_t *s, int cell_capacity, int n_cells);\n158\tvoid      slot_push  (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, const void *data, int size);\n159\tint       slot_peek  (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size); // non-destructive: read head, leave it\n160\tint       slot_pop   (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size); // destructive: read head, advance head\n161\tvoid      slot_wait  (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id); // blocks until tail > head\n162\tvoid      slot_ref   (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id);\n163\tvoid      slot_unref (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id); // frees backing memory when refcount → 0\n164\t```\n165\t\n166\tSingle-value (1-cell) slot use: producer `push` once, each consumer\n167\t`peek` once, then `unref`. Cells are not popped — fan-out consumers\n168\tall read the same value, and the slot is freed when the last consumer\n169\tunrefs.\n170\t\n171\tQueued-input (N-cell) slot use: producers `push` repeatedly, the\n172\tconsumer `pop`s in arrival order. The consumer holds the only ref.\n173\tWhen the consumer task is done with its queue, it `unref`s and the\n174\tslot is freed.\n175\t\n176\t## Submission timing\n177\t\n178\tThe dispatch layer builds the task struct as soon as the graph asks\n179\tfor it — output slots allocated, all known data filled in, input wire\n180\treferences attached. It is then submitted directly to the pool. The\n181\tpool's existing block-and-wake machinery handles the rest:\n182\t\n183\t- If any input slots are unfilled at the moment of submission, the\n184\t  dispatch action immediately `ACT_BLOCK`s on the first unfilled\n185\t  input. The pool parks the task on that slot's wait list.\n186\t- When the upstream producer pushes, it walks the wait list and wakes\n187\t  the parked tasks. The action re-runs from the top, checks the next\n188\t  input, blocks again if needed.\n189\t- When all inputs are present, the action proceeds to invoke the box.\n190\t\n191\tThere is no separate \"blocked tasks\" set held by the dispatch layer.\n192\tThe pool is the only thing that tracks blocked tasks. This avoids\n193\tduplicating the wait-list machinery the pool already has.\n194\t\n195\t## Allocation strategy: size-class free lists with coalescing fallback\n196\t\n197\tThe slot store uses a segregated free-list allocator. The map is\n198\tanalyzed at compile time to enumerate every distinct slot size the\n199\tgraph will need (each call box declares its output slot size; each\n200\tqueued-input ring declares its total size from cell capacity × queue\n201\tdepth). The allocator builds one free list per distinct size class.\n202\t\n203\tVariable-size and unknown-size payloads (a long LLM response, an\n204\tarray whose length is not known until runtime) are handled by a\n205\tseparate **large-value heap** described below — not by allocating\n206\thuge slots up front.\n207\t\n208\t### The lists\n209\tEach size class is an array (or linked list) of free slots of exactly\n210\tthat size. At startup, each list is pre-populated with enough slots\n211\tto cover the static box count for that size. Lists grow during the\n212\trun if demand exceeds the pre-allocation.\n213\t\n214\tEach list has its own mutex — allocation and deallocation in different\n215\tsize classes never contend with each other.\n216\t\n217\t### Allocation\n218\tGiven a request for size N bytes:\n219\t1. Find the smallest size class with `class_size ≥ N`.\n220\t2. If that class has a free slot, pop it. Done.\n221\t3. Otherwise, try the next larger size class. Repeat.\n222\t4. If a larger class hits, the slot is oversized for the request.\n223\t   Try to slice the unused tail into a residual slot. If the residual\n224\t   is at least as large as the smallest size class, push it onto that\n225\t   class's list. Otherwise skip the slice — oversize the allocation\n226\t   and live with the waste until the slot is freed.\n227\t5. If no size class has a free slot, attempt to coalesce: walk the\n228\t   address-ordered chunk list looking for adjacent free chunks that\n229\t   together meet the requested size. If found, merge them and return\n230\t   the combined chunk.\n231\t6. If coalescing fails, grow the region (see \"Growth\" below) and\n232\t   append the new slots to the appropriate lists. Then try again.\n233\t7. After steps 5 or 6 complete, queue a deferred cleanup task on the\n234\t   pool. Cleanup runs on a worker thread later and walks the\n235\t   chunk list to opportunistically coalesce contiguous free chunks\n236\t   into the largest possible chunks. Cleanup is best-effort — it\n237\t   does not block any other thread. If memory fragments faster than\n238\t   cleanup can keep up, the next allocation grows the heap; that's\n239\t   fine.\n240\t\n241\t### Deallocation\n242\tWhen refcount drops to zero, the slot is pushed onto its size class's\n243\tfree list. The deallocator also performs a cheap eager-coalesce step:\n244\tcheck the slot's two physical neighbors; if either is free, merge\n245\tthem and push the combined chunk onto the appropriate size class.\n246\tThis is O(1) given the doubly-linked chunk list (see below) and keeps\n247\tsmall-scale fragmentation in check without needing the deferred\n248\tcleanup task to run.\n249\t\n250\t### Physical-order chunk list (for coalescing)\n251\tCoalescing needs to know which chunks are physically adjacent in\n252\tmemory. The size-class free lists don't carry that information.\n253\t\n254\tTwo viable representations:\n255\t\n256\t- **Doubly-linked list** of all chunks (free and allocated) in\n257\t  address order. Splits and merges are O(1) given the chunk pointer.\n258\t  Neighbor lookup is O(1). Pointer chasing is the cost.\n259\t- **Two parallel arrays** (`start[i]`, `end[i]`) sorted by start\n260\t  address. Lookup by binary search is O(log N), but inserts and\n261\t  deletes are O(N) without an additional index. Cache-friendly to\n262\t  scan.\n263\t\n264\tThe linked list is simpler and has the right asymptotic behavior for\n265\tsplits/merges, which dominate. Start there. If profiling later shows\n266\tlist traversal is hot, switch to the array form with an auxiliary\n267\tindex — the API doesn't change.\n268\t\n269\t### Large-value heap (variable-size payloads)\n270\t\n271\tFor values whose size is not known at compile time — long LLM\n272\tresponses, dynamically-sized arrays, anything where the upper bound\n273\tis not a useful number to allocate — the slot does not hold the value\n274\tdirectly. Instead, the slot holds a small fixed-size handle:\n275\t\n276\t```\n277\t{ uint32_t size; uint32_t lvh_offset; }\n278\t```\n279\t\n280\t`lvh_offset` points into a separate **large-value heap**, a\n281\tplain `malloc`-backed region used only for variable-size payloads.\n282\tWhen a box produces a 4 MB LLM response, the dispatch layer:\n283\t1. Allocates 4 MB in the large-value heap.\n284\t2. Writes the bytes there.\n285\t3. Stores the handle (size = 4 MB, offset = …) in the slot.\n286\t\n287\tThe consumer reads the handle from the slot, follows the offset,\n288\tcopies the bytes (or works with them in place). When the slot's\n289\trefcount hits zero, the slot's deallocator also frees the\n290\tlarge-value-heap region.\n291\t\n292\tThe slot allocator is unchanged — it always sees fixed-size slots.\n293\tThe two-tier approach keeps the hot path simple while still\n294\tsupporting unbounded outputs.\n295\t\n296\tA box opts into large-value output by declaring its output as\n297\t\"variable-size\" in the graph. Compile-time-known outputs use the\n298\tfixed-size path with no indirection.\n299\t\n300\t### Growth\n301\tWhen all size-class lists are exhausted and coalescing cannot satisfy\n302\ta request, the allocator grows by calling `malloc` for a new region,\n303\tdividing it into slots, and appending them to the relevant size-class\n304\tlists. Plain heap memory is fine — no spec needs cross-process access\n305\tto slot memory.\n306\t\n307\t### Why this design\n308\t- Compile-time enumeration makes every common allocation a single\n309\t  pop from a list. No size-comparison loops, no walks of free space.\n310\t- Slicing residuals cannot fragment beyond the granularity of the\n311\t  smallest declared size class, since smaller residuals are simply\n312\t  not split.\n313\t- Coalescing is the safety valve for unusual allocation patterns,\n314\t  and it costs nothing on the common path.\n315\t- Growth is rare — if pre-allocation matches static demand, it never\n316\t  fires.\n317\t\n318\t## No type tags\n319\t\n320\tSlots store opaque bytes. The producer wrote N bytes; the consumer\n321\treads N bytes. What those bytes mean is the language spec's business\n322\ton each side, and the wire's metadata in the graph (issue 219's\n323\tcompiler can check producer-output type vs consumer-input type at\n324\tbuild time). The slot store does not interpret values — it does not\n325\tneed to know if they are strings, numbers, JSON, images, or anything\n326\telse. Removed the type-tag field from the header for that reason.\n327\t\n328\t## Suggested implementation sequence\n329\t1. Write `src/slot-store.h` and `src/slot-store.c` — the C API above.\n330\t2. Unit test single-value slots: thread A writes, thread B reads,\n331\t   refcount decrements, slot freed when last ref dropped.\n332\t3. Unit test ring-buffer slots: multiple producers push, single consumer\n333\t   drains in order, no values lost or duplicated.\n334\t4. Integrate into `src/008-pool-runner.c`: shared memory created at\n335\t   startup, store handle passed to the dispatch layer.\n336\t\n337\t## Relevant files\n338\t- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — pool entry point, owns the shared memory region\n339\t- `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.h` — pool API (refcounting is complementary)\n340\t- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle\n341\t- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — task dispatch reads/writes slots\n342\t- `issues/213-queued-inputs-and-task-model.md` — queued input model that\n343\t  ring-buffer slots implement\n344\t- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — IPC options; shm_open + mmap is Option 2\n345\t",
