Slots are allocated, filled, read, and\nfreed at any time, on any thread, with no global lock. Synchronization\nis per-slot. There is no central allocator-wide mutex.\n\n## Slot layout\n\nEach slot is a header followed by `n_cells` cells, each `cell_capacity`\nbytes. The header tracks ring-buffer state and lifetime:\n\n```\nSlot header\nOffset  Size  Field\n------  ----  -----\n0       4     refcount        (atomic int32; lifetime counter)\n4       4     cell_capacity   (bytes per cell, set at allocation)\n8       4     n_cells         (ring size, set at allocation; 1 for single-value)\n12      4     head            (read index, mod n_cells)\n16      4     tail            (write index, mod n_cells; cells_filled = tail - head)\n20      1     touched         (per-slot lock: 0=free, 1=another thread mutating)\n21      3     _pad\n24      …     cells           (n_cells * (4-byte size + cell_capacity bytes))\n```\n\nEach cell stores a 4-byte filled-size followed by `cell_capacity`\nbytes of value data. Cells have wildly different capacities across\nslots — capacity is per-slot, not global. The C convention of passing\nsizes alongside arrays applies: the task that allocates a slot knows\nhow big it needs the cells.\n\n`touched` is a single-byte flag toggled around any header mutation\n(push, pop, refcount changes). A reader that finds `touched == 1`\nspins until it clears. This is the simplest possible per-slot lock —\nif contention proves to matter, replace with a proper mutex without\nchanging the API.\n\nWrites to a cell complete with a memory barrier before `tail` is\nadvanced, so a reader that observes `head < tail` is guaranteed to\nsee the complete value at the head cell.\n\n## Reference counting protocol\n\nEvery party that may still touch a slot holds a reference. The slot is\nfreed when the count reaches zero. The references themselves are how\nwe track liveness — there is no separate \"is this producer / consumer\nstill alive\" mechanism.\n\n### Single-output (1-cell) slot\n1. Task allocates its output slot with `refcount = 0`.\n2. For each fan-out wire reading from the slot, `slot_ref` is called.\n   The wire holds that reference until its consumer is done reading.\n3. After the consumer reads (peek), it calls `slot_unref`.\n4. When refcount reaches zero, the unrefing task frees the slot.\n\n### Queued (N-cell) slot\nThe consumer's input queue. Producers and the consumer all hold refs:\n1. The consumer task allocates the queue slot with one ref for itself.\n2. Each producer that may push into the queue increments the refcount\n   when it is constructed; the ref is dropped when that producer's\n   box function ends.\n3. The consumer drops its ref when its own box function ends (i.e.\n   when the iterator stops re-spawning because no more inputs are\n   coming).\n4. When the last ref drops, the queue is freed.\n\nThe producer-side ref is what makes \"no more inputs are coming\"\ndetectable: when the queue's refcount equals 1 (only the consumer\nholds it) and the queue is empty, no upstream task can push again,\nso the iterator's natural end-of-stream condition fires.\n\n### Wait list\nEach slot also owns a wait list — pointers to tasks parked on the\nslot waiting for a value. When a producer pushes, the slot walks the\nwait list and tells the pool to re-run those tasks. The wait list is\nattached to the slot, not to the producer or the consumer.\n\n## Backing store\n\nSlots are allocated from process heap memory. The slot store owns a\nper-run allocator (described under \"Allocation strategy\" below) that\nhands out memory chunks to slots. Plain `malloc`-class memory is\nsufficient — every worker thread in the process can read and write\nit, and no spec ever needs to access it from a child process.\n\nSynchronization within a slot uses the per-slot `touched` flag for\nheader mutations and a per-slot wait list (above) for blocked tasks.\nThere is no allocator-wide mutex on the read/write path; only the\nper-size-class free lists in the allocator have their own locks.\n\n## Slot creation\n\nSlot creation happens inside the dispatch layer at task submission. The\ncaller specifies the cell capacity (bytes per value) and the ring size\n(number of cells, 1 for single-value):\n\n```c\nslot_id_t slot_alloc(slot_store_t *store, int cell_capacity, int n_cells);\n```\n\nThe slot is created with `refcount = 0`, `head = tail = 0`. The\ndispatch layer then increments the refcount once per consumer (one ref\nper fan-out wire for a 1-cell slot; one ref for the consumer task on a\nqueued-input slot) before the task is exposed.\n\n## C API surface\n\n```c\nslot_id_t slot_alloc (slot_store_t *s, int cell_capacity, int n_cells);\nvoid      slot_push  (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, const void *data, int size);\nint       slot_peek  (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size); // non-destructive: read head, leave it\nint       slot_pop   (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, void *buf, int buf_size); // destructive: read head, advance head\nvoid      slot_wait  (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id); // blocks until tail > head\nvoid      slot_ref   (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id);\nvoid      slot_unref (slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id); // frees backing memory when refcount → 0\n```\n\nSingle-value (1-cell) slot use: producer `push` once, each consumer\n`peek` once, then `unref`. Cells are not popped — fan-out consumers\nall read the same value, and the slot is freed when the last consumer\nunrefs.\n\nQueued-input (N-cell) slot use: producers `push` repeatedly, the\nconsumer `pop`s in arrival order. The consumer holds the only ref.\nWhen the consumer task is done with its queue, it `unref`s and the\nslot is freed.\n\n## Submission timing\n\nThe dispatch layer builds the task struct as soon as the graph asks\nfor it — output slots allocated, all known data filled in, input wire\nreferences attached. It is then submitted directly to the pool. The\npool's existing block-and-wake machinery handles the rest:\n\n- If any input slots are unfilled at the moment of submission, the\n  dispatch action immediately `ACT_BLOCK`s on the first unfilled\n  input. The pool parks the task on that slot's wait list.\n- When the upstream producer pushes, it walks the wait list and wakes\n  the parked tasks. The action re-runs from the top, checks the next\n  input, blocks again if needed.\n- When all inputs are present, the action proceeds to invoke the box.\n\nThere is no separate \"blocked tasks\" set held by the dispatch layer.\nThe pool is the only thing that tracks blocked tasks. This avoids\nduplicating the wait-list machinery the pool already has.\n\n## Allocation strategy: size-class free lists with coalescing fallback\n\nThe slot store uses a segregated free-list allocator. The map is\nanalyzed at compile time to enumerate every distinct slot size the\ngraph will need (each call box declares its output slot size; each\nqueued-input ring declares its total size from cell capacity × queue\ndepth). The allocator builds one free list per distinct size class.\n\nVariable-size and unknown-size payloads (a long LLM response, an\narray whose length is not known until runtime) are handled by a\nseparate **large-value heap** described below — not by allocating\nhuge slots up front.\n\n### The lists\nEach size class is an array (or linked list) of free slots of exactly\nthat size. At startup, each list is pre-populated with enough slots\nto cover the static box count for that size. Lists grow during the\nrun if demand exceeds the pre-allocation.\n\nEach list has its own mutex — allocation and deallocation in different\nsize classes never contend with each other.\n\n### Allocation\nGiven a request for size N bytes:\n1. Find the smallest size class with `class_size ≥ N`.\n2. If that class has a free slot, pop it. Done.\n3. Otherwise, try the next larger size class. Repeat.\n4. If a larger class hits, the slot is oversized for the request.\n   Try to slice the unused tail into a residual slot. If the residual\n   is at least as large as the smallest size class, push it onto that\n   class's list. Otherwise skip the slice — oversize the allocation\n   and live with the waste until the slot is freed.\n5. If no size class has a free slot, attempt to coalesce: walk the\n   address-ordered chunk list looking for adjacent free chunks that\n   together meet the requested size. If found, merge them and return\n   the combined chunk.\n6. If coalescing fails, grow the region (see \"Growth\" below) and\n   append the new slots to the appropriate lists. Then try again.\n7. After steps 5 or 6 complete, queue a deferred cleanup task on the\n   pool. Cleanup runs on a worker thread later and walks the\n   chunk list to opportunistically coalesce contiguous free chunks\n   into the largest possible chunks. Cleanup is best-effort — it\n   does not block any other thread. If memory fragments faster than\n   cleanup can keep up, the next allocation grows the heap; that's\n   fine.\n\n### Deallocation\nWhen refcount drops to zero, the slot is pushed onto its size class's\nfree list. The deallocator also performs a cheap eager-coalesce step:\ncheck the slot's two physical neighbors; if either is free, merge\nthem and push the combined chunk onto the appropriate size class.\nThis is O(1) given the doubly-linked chunk list (see below) and keeps\nsmall-scale fragmentation in check without needing the deferred\ncleanup task to run.\n\n### Physical-order chunk list (for coalescing)\nCoalescing needs to know which chunks are physically adjacent in\nmemory. The size-class free lists don't carry that information.\n\nTwo viable representations:\n\n- **Doubly-linked list** of all chunks (free and allocated) in\n  address order. Splits and merges are O(1) given the chunk pointer.\n  Neighbor lookup is O(1). Pointer chasing is the cost.\n- **Two parallel arrays** (`start[i]`, `end[i]`) sorted by start\n  address. Lookup by binary search is O(log N), but inserts and\n  deletes are O(N) without an additional index. Cache-friendly to\n  scan.\n\nThe linked list is simpler and has the right asymptotic behavior for\nsplits/merges, which dominate. Start there. If profiling later shows\nlist traversal is hot, switch to the array form with an auxiliary\nindex — the API doesn't change.\n\n### Large-value heap (variable-size payloads)\n\nFor values whose size is not known at compile time — long LLM\nresponses, dynamically-sized arrays, anything where the upper bound\nis not a useful number to allocate — the slot does not hold the value\ndirectly. Instead, the slot holds a small fixed-size handle:\n\n```\n{ uint32_t size; uint32_t lvh_offset; }\n```\n\n`lvh_offset` points into a separate **large-value heap**, a\nplain `malloc`-backed region used only for variable-size payloads.\nWhen a box produces a 4 MB LLM response, the dispatch layer:\n1. Allocates 4 MB in the large-value heap.\n2. Writes the bytes there.\n3. Stores the handle (size = 4 MB, offset = …) in the slot.\n\nThe consumer reads the handle from the slot, follows the offset,\ncopies the bytes (or works with them in place). When the slot's\nrefcount hits zero, the slot's deallocator also frees the\nlarge-value-heap region.\n\nThe slot allocator is unchanged — it always sees fixed-size slots.\nThe two-tier approach keeps the hot path simple while still\nsupporting unbounded outputs.\n\nA box opts into large-value output by declaring its output as\n\"variable-size\" in the graph. Compile-time-known outputs use the\nfixed-size path with no indirection.\n\n### Growth\nWhen all size-class lists are exhausted and coalescing cannot satisfy\na request, the allocator grows by calling `malloc` for a new region,\ndividing it into slots, and appending them to the relevant size-class\nlists. Plain heap memory is fine — no spec needs cross-process access\nto slot memory.\n\n### Why this design\n- Compile-time enumeration makes every common allocation a single\n  pop from a list. No size-comparison loops, no walks of free space.\n- Slicing residuals cannot fragment beyond the granularity of the\n  smallest declared size class, since smaller residuals are simply\n  not split.\n- Coalescing is the safety valve for unusual allocation patterns,\n  and it costs nothing on the common path.\n- Growth is rare — if pre-allocation matches static demand, it never\n  fires.\n\n## No type tags\n\nSlots store opaque bytes. The producer wrote N bytes; the consumer\nreads N bytes. What those bytes mean is the language spec's business\non each side, and the wire's metadata in the graph (issue 219's\ncompiler can check producer-output type vs consumer-input type at\nbuild time). The slot store does not interpret values — it does not\nneed to know if they are strings, numbers, JSON, images, or anything\nelse. Removed the type-tag field from the header for that reason.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. Write `src/slot-store.h` and `src/slot-store.c` — the C API above.\n2. Unit test single-value slots: thread A writes, thread B reads,\n   refcount decrements, slot freed when last ref dropped.\n3. Unit test ring-buffer slots: multiple producers push, single consumer\n   drains in order, no values lost or duplicated.\n4. Integrate into `src/008-pool-runner.c`: shared memory created at\n   startup, store handle passed to the dispatch layer.\n\n## Relevant files\n- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — pool entry point, owns the shared memory region\n- `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.h` — pool API (refcounting is complementary)\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — task dispatch reads/writes slots\n- `issues/213-queued-inputs-and-task-model.md` — queued input model that\n  ring-buffer slots implement\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — IPC options; shm_open + mmap is Option 2\n"
    }
  },

        "type":"text",
        "text":"Three good questions. Let me work through them.\n\n## How the spec interprets bytes (and JSON)\n\nThe spec is **the language ↔ bytes boundary**. The dispatch layer hands `invoke` a list of `(byte_pointer, byte_size)` pairs and a buffer to write the output bytes into. What's IN those bytes is the spec's choice and the spec's convention.\n\n**Convention is JSON** because it's interoperable: every shipped language has a JSON parser, and JSON's type tags (string/number/bool/null/object/array) survive the trip across language boundaries.\n\nIn practice, each spec implements `invoke` like:\n\n```c\n// Lua spec, sketch\nint lua_invoke(handle, file_path, fn_name,\n               input_data[], input_sizes[], n_inputs,\n               out_buf, out_buf_capacity, out_size) {\n    lua_State *L = handle;\n    luaL_loadfile(L, file_path);\n    lua_getfield(L, -1, fn_name);\n\n    for (int i = 0; i < n_inputs; i++) {\n        // each input is a JSON value as bytes; parse into a Lua value\n        cjson_decode_to_lua(L, input_data[i], input_sizes[i]);\n    }\n\n    lua_pcall(L, n_inputs, 1, 0);\n\n    // serialize return value back to JSON bytes\n    *out_size = cjson_encode_from_lua(L, -1, out_buf, out_buf_capacity);\n    return 0;\n}\n```\n\nThe Bash spec is simpler — it passes the bytes as positional args (`\"$1\"`, `\"$2\"`, …) and reads stdout as the return JSON. The C spec compiles a per-box wrapper at `compile` time that knows the function's declared types and emits the right marshalling code.\n\nThe dispatch layer never inspects the bytes. The slot store explicitly says \"no type tags\" — it stores opaque bytes only. The wire format is a **pact between specs**, not a runtime invariant. Two specs that want to skip JSON and pass native bytes can do so — it's just that defaulting to JSON means any pair of specs can talk.\n\n## Fast producer, slow consumer — what happens to the values?\n\nNothing is lost. The buffering happens **in the task queue**, not in any one slot.\n\nThe model is \"one slot per invocation, not one slot per wire.\" If your upstream fires 10 times, that's 10 dispatch tasks, each one allocating its own output slot, each one pushing its value, each one firing its outgoing connections. Firing a connection means **spawning a downstream task** with that specific upstream slot as input. So if upstream A produces 10 outputs, downstream B has 10 tasks queued — each one paired with one of A's slots as its input.\n\nThe pool's ready queue holds those 10 B-tasks. If B is 10× slower than A, all 10 will sit in the queue (or be in flight on different workers, if there's parallelism), and B's worker pulls them one at a time. Each B-task reads its own slot, runs, produces its own output slot. No values overwrite each other — each producer-consumer pair has its own pair of slots.\n\nSo no, you don't need a ring buffer for the plain 1-cell case. The task queue **is** the rate buffer. Values become tasks, tasks queue, consumers drain tasks at their pace.\n\nThe ring-buffer slots are reserved for **iterator inputs** specifically: many upstream producers fanning into one consumer, where the consumer reuses the same slot across its own re-spawns. That's a different topology — fan-in to a long-lived consumer — and it needs the queue to survive across the consumer's invocations.\n\nIf a non-iterator B has multiple upstream wires and one upstream is fast while another is slow, things get more interesting: B can't fire until both inputs are ready. So a B-task spawned for upstream A's invocation N has to wait for the slow upstream's matching invocation N. The pairing is by task, not by slot — the dispatch layer's connection-firing logic figures out which task gets which inputs. (This is where the design gets harder; for current scope it's \"fast producer + slow consumer with a single wire\" which works cleanly.)\n\n## Wire format — JSON, allocation, pointers\n\nThe slot is just bytes. Per 302's slot layout, each cell is a `cell_capacity`-byte region preceded by a 4-byte filled-size. The producer writes raw bytes there. The consumer reads raw bytes from there. **No JSON parsing happens at the slot level** — that's all in the spec.\n\nSo in concrete terms, when an upstream Lua box outputs `42`:\n1. Lua's `invoke` runs, computes the Lua number `42`.\n2. The spec's serializer turns `42` into the JSON byte string `\"42\"` (4 bytes including quotes if it's a string, 2 bytes `42` if it's a number — depends on the spec's chosen encoding).\n3. Those bytes go into `out_buf`.\n4. The dispatch action calls `slot_push(slot, out_buf, *out_size)` — the slot store memcpys into the cell.\n5. Downstream Lua box's `invoke` runs. The dispatch action `slot_peek`s into a stack buffer.\n6. The spec's deserializer parses the bytes back into a Lua number.\n\nSo yes — **encode + decode per hop**. That's the cost of language-agnosticism.\n\n**Re-creating the JSON each time** — that part's true and worth being clear-eyed about. The per-hop cost is \"one serialize + one deserialize per consumer.\" For LLM-call boxes (millisecond-to-second range) it's lost in the noise. For tight numeric loops it would matter, but we don't have that use case.\n\n**Memory:** each slot is its own allocation. The slot store has a size-class allocator — boxes that consistently produce 64-byte outputs all draw from the 64-byte free list, so allocation is a list pop, not a malloc. For variable-size payloads (LLM responses, dynamic arrays), the slot holds a small `{size, offset}` handle into a separate **large-value heap**, and the bytes live there. So small values are inline in the slot (no pointer chase); large values are pointer-chased once.\n\n**No re-editing.** Each `slot_push` is a single memcpy into a fresh cell. No accumulation, no rewriting. The slot lives until its refcount drops to zero, then its memory goes back to the free list.\n\n**Pointers vs values:** the **spec API** never sees slot IDs — it only sees `const void *input_data[i]` and `void *out_buf`. The dispatch layer translates between slot IDs (which are how wires reference the data) and byte pointers (which is what specs work with). So at the spec boundary it's always pointers + sizes. At the wire/graph level it's slot IDs. The slot store is the indirection layer.\n\n**Bypass for hot paths (future):** if it ever matters, two same-language adjacent boxes can negotiate a non-JSON encoding via the spec — e.g., the Lua spec could detect \"upstream is also Lua\" and skip JSON in favor of `lua_dump`/`lua_load` for table values. That's an optimization, not part of the contract; the slot store and dispatch layer wouldn't change.\n\nIf high-throughput numeric pipelines become a real workload, the right move is probably:\n- **Type-annotated wires** at compile time (the box graph already records port types).\n- **Per-type wire encodings** the specs can dispatch on — primitive numbers go raw, strings as length-prefixed bytes, complex types as JSON.\n\nWorth its own issue if it becomes a concern. For now, JSON-as-default is the simplest correct thing."
      }]
  },

If so, then what if we don't know how many inputs those C boxes would need?\n\n  The pairing is by task, not by slot — the dispatch layer's connection-firing logic figures out which task gets which inputs. (This is where\n   the design gets harder; for current scope it's \"fast producer + slow consumer with a single wire\" which works cleanly.)\n\nOkay... Is the dispatch layer an orchestrator thread? What thread is it running on? When does it run? In the phase 3 design of course. I think I know generally what it does, but I don't know *how* it does it.\n\n  So yes — encode + decode per hop. That's the cost of language-agnosticism.\n\nHmmmmm, I see... Maybe we should require language specs to include two things - one, a path for translating to json if the languages are different across the wire barrier, and 2. a path for passing values explicitely, with as little run-time cost as possible, between two invocations of the same language. What do you think? Would that improve performance? How would that be implemented? Where would we be checking the boundaries, at compile time? Would we compile the multiple different files / functions (of the same language) into the same file (binary or script)?\n\n  Re-creating the JSON each time — that part's true and worth being clear-eyed about. The per-hop cost is \"one serialize + one deserialize\n  per consumer.\" For LLM-call boxes (millisecond-to-second range) it's lost in the noise. For tight numeric loops it would matter, but we\n  don't have that use case.\n\n\nUnfortunately, we don't know what the user's workload will look like. We have to plan as if it's high performance requirements, while simultaneously quick and easy to learn with little friction. Because users won't use anything less. The technology industry is high competition now for products like this, sadly... So, unfortunately for us, our standards have to be sky high if we want to make something useful.\n\n  Bypass for hot paths (future): if it ever matters, two same-language adjacent boxes can negotiate a non-JSON encoding via the spec — e.g.,\n  the Lua spec could detect \"upstream is also Lua\" and skip JSON in favor of lua_dump/lua_load for table values. That's an optimization, not\n  part of the contract; the slot store and dispatch layer wouldn't change.\n\n\nOh! You said it exactly as I want it! Let's require that from the users writing language specs. I know I said I want little friction, but the users writing these sorts of things are power-users anyway so they'll love doing that kind of stuff. However, the users using the editor aren't necessarily going to be power users, so we have to make that part at least as low friction as we can.",
    "role":"user"
  },

    "content":"# 232 — Same-language wire fast path: skip JSON for adjacent same-language boxes\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nThe wire format between boxes is JSON (`docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`,\nissue 302's \"no type tags\" — slot store stores opaque bytes; the\nlanguage spec encodes/decodes). Every wire pays the JSON encode +\ndecode cost on every value pass, even when the producer and the\nconsumer are the same language and could use a faster\nlanguage-native serialization.\n\nFor a Lua → Lua wire passing a 10-element table:\n1. Producer's spec: `cjson.encode(table)` → string of N bytes\n2. `slot_push(slot, string, N)`\n3. `slot_peek(slot, buf, N)`\n4. Consumer's spec: `cjson.decode(buf)` → Lua table\n\nSteps 1 and 4 are the cost. They're language-agnostic and unnecessary\nwhen both endpoints share a language.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nEach language spec exposes **two invoke paths**:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    const char *name;\n    const char *file_ext;\n\n    void *(*init)(int worker_idx);\n    void  (*teardown)(void *handle);\n    int   (*compile)(...);\n\n    // Universal path — JSON bytes in, JSON bytes out\n    int   (*invoke_json)  (void *handle, /* common args */);\n\n    // Fast path — language-native bytes in, language-native bytes out\n    int   (*invoke_native)(void *handle, /* common args */);\n\n    // Bridges used when a value crosses a language boundary\n    int   (*native_to_json)(const void *src, int src_size,\n                            void *dst, int dst_capacity, int *dst_size);\n    int   (*json_to_native)(const void *src, int src_size,\n                            void *dst, int dst_capacity, int *dst_size);\n} lang_spec_t;\n```\n\n`invoke_native` is required (every spec implements one). Per-language\n\"native\" format:\n- **Lua**: `lua_dump` for closures, `cjson` or msgpack for tables, raw\n  bytes for strings/numbers. Spec's choice as long as it's\n  symmetric with its own decoder.\n- **C**: raw struct memcpy. The compile-time wrapper (issue 307)\n  knows the types; serialization is `memcpy(slot_buf, &val, sizeof\n  val)`.\n- **Bash**: strings only — Bash has no other native form, so the\n  fast path is identical to the JSON path. Implement as a thin\n  alias.\n\n`invoke_json` is the universal interop format. Required for any\nlanguage that participates in cross-language wires. A spec that\nonly ever talks to itself can skip `invoke_json` (compile error if\na wire crosses to it from another language).\n\n## Compile-time wire classification\n\nEvery wire gets a `fast_path: true | false` flag set at build time\n(issue 309 build step):\n\n```python\nfor wire in graph.wires:\n    src_lang = box_at(wire.from).lang\n    dst_lang = box_at(wire.to).lang\n    wire.fast_path = (src_lang == dst_lang)\n```\n\nThe flag becomes part of the compiled manifest. Runtime never\nre-evaluates language pairing.\n\n## Producer-side decision\n\nA producer's output goes into one slot, but multiple consumers may\nread from it. If they're all the same language, the producer can\nwrite native bytes. If any consumer is in a different language, the\nproducer must write JSON (and same-language consumers convert via\n`json_to_native` to recover native form).\n\nTwo ways to decide:\n1. **Per-output decision** — analyze all consumers of the output\n   slot at compile time. All same lang → native; mixed → JSON.\n2. **Always JSON producer / convert at consumer** — simpler, but\n   pays the encode cost even when no cross-language consumer is\n   present.\n\nOption 1 is the right call. The compile step records the producer's\noutput format on the box record (`output_format: \"native\" | \"json\"`),\nand same-language consumers know to read native bytes directly,\ncross-language consumers call `json_to_native` first.\n\n## Runtime dispatch\n\nThe dispatch action's input-read path branches on the wire flag:\n\n```c\nfor (int i = 0; i < n_inputs; i++) {\n    slot_peek(input_slots[i], buf, buf_capacity);\n    if (input_wires[i].fast_path && producer_format == NATIVE) {\n        // bytes are already this language's native form\n        ...\n    } else if (producer_format == JSON) {\n        // bytes are JSON, decode into native form\n        json_to_native(buf, buf_size, native_buf, native_capacity, &native_size);\n        ...\n    }\n}\n```\n\nThen `invoke_native` is called with native-form bytes regardless of\nhow they were obtained. Same on the output side: if the box's output\nformat is `native`, write native bytes; if `json`, encode then\nwrite.\n\n## Edge cases\n\n- **All-same-language graph**: every wire is fast-path; `invoke_json`\n  never runs. Spec writers can stub it out.\n- **All-different-language graph**: every wire is JSON;\n  `invoke_native` handles bytes that came back from `json_to_native`.\n- **One same-language wire, several cross-language wires from the same\n  producer**: the producer writes JSON. Same-language consumer\n  decodes via `json_to_native` (still cheaper than full encode +\n  decode round-trip — only one direction of conversion is paid,\n  not two).\n- **Type changes mid-development**: a wire that was Lua→Lua becomes\n  Lua→C as the user changes a downstream box's language. Compile\n  flips the flag; the producer now writes JSON. No runtime\n  surprises, no migration.\n\n## Implementation cost\n\nThe two-invoke spec interface adds maybe 30 lines per language\nspec. The compile-time wire classification is one pass over the\ngraph. The dispatch action's input-read branch is one `if` on the\nwire flag. None of this is hot-path complex; the gain is one less\nJSON encode/decode per same-language hop, which is the whole point.\n\n## Future: whole-program same-language compilation\n\nA bigger optimization beyond this issue: at compile time, merge\nall same-language boxes into one translation unit. The C spec\nbecomes whole-program; the Lua spec produces one bytecode chunk\ncovering every Lua function. Box-boundary crossings become regular\nfunction calls — no slot store, no dispatch layer, no spec\ninvocation. Lua's fast path picks a native\n   encoding (cjson for tables; raw bytes for primitives).\n5. **Tests**: smoke tests confirming a 100k-iteration Lua→Lua\n   pipeline with the fast path runs measurably faster than the\n   same pipeline with the JSON path, and that mixed-language\n   pipelines still work.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — adds the new callbacks\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — branch on fast_path\n- `issues/309-build-system.md` — wire-flag enrichment\n- `issues/306-lua-language-spec.md`, `307-c-language-spec.md`,\n  `308-bash-language-spec.md` — per-spec native implementations\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — slot still stores opaque\n  bytes; the format negotiation is at the spec layer, not the\n  store\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Whether a spec must implement `invoke_json`**: leaning yes, so\n  any spec can talk to any other spec. Two conversions for one cross-language\n  hop in this case. Probably fine; it's a corner case.\n"

        "text":"Three big questions. Let me dig in.\n\n## Slot lifecycle and the late-firing producer\n\nThe model is **slots are pre-allocated at graph load time, not at runtime**. The pool runner walks the static graph at startup and:\n\n1. For every non-iterator box, allocates **one** task struct AND its output slot. Both exist before any task runs.\n2. The task's `input_slots[]` array points at the upstream producer boxes' pre-allocated slots — slot identity is fixed at compile time for the static portion of the graph.\n3. Every task (entry-point or not) is **submitted** to the pool at startup. Tasks whose inputs aren't ready immediately ACT_BLOCK on whichever input slot isn't filled yet, and the pool parks them on that slot's wait list.\n\nSo in your A/B/C scenario with B firing 30 tasks later: at program start, the loader allocates A_prod's slot, B_prod's slot, and C_task's slot. C_task re-runs from the top, finds A's slot ready now but B's empty, blocks on B's wait list. Tens of tasks of unrelated work happen. Eventually B_prod runs, pushes to B's slot, walks B's wait list, wakes C_task. C_task re-runs, all inputs ready, invokes the function, writes output, fires its connections. \n\nThe key answer to your \"where does the slot live before B has fired\" question: **the slot exists from the moment the graph loads**. It's just empty (head == tail). The wait list on it is what holds C_task. B_prod's output_slot pointer is also fixed at load time — it's pointing at the same pre-allocated memory C_task is waiting on.\n\nThis works because the graph is static for non-iterator parts. The compile-time enumeration is what makes the size-class allocator efficient in 302 — every distinct slot size is known at startup, and slots get drawn from the right free list with no allocation-on-the-hot-path.\n\n**Iterators are the dynamic part.** An iterator that runs 10 times produces 10 invocation-slots. Each iterator invocation spawns a fresh successor task and a fresh output slot. Downstream of an iterator, the per-invocation tasks are spawned dynamically as well, paired with their corresponding iterator invocation.\n\nYour \"what if A produces between 1 and 50 values\" is the iterator case. Yes — N iterator invocations produce N slots, fire N branches, spawn N downstream tasks. If those downstream tasks have other inputs from a *different* iterator, the pairing problem is real and unresolved in the current design — it's the open question I waved at last time. Probably needs a \"synchronized iterator pair\" concept or per-invocation indices that the dispatch layer can match. Worth an issue when we hit it.\n\n**Why iterators get queued ring buffers and non-iterators don't**: an iterator has one input slot that survives across all its invocations. Multiple upstream producers may push values into that one slot before the iterator gets around to processing them — that's the rate-buffer case where the queue helps. A non-iterator box has one task, one output slot, runs once, done — no queue needed because there's only one push per slot ever.\n\n## Where the dispatch layer runs\n\nThe dispatch layer is **not a thread**. It's a single C function (`dispatch_action`) that **runs on whichever worker pulled the task**. Every task in the pool is \"dispatch this box\" — when a worker pulls a task off the queue, it calls `dispatch_action(task)` on its own thread, runs through the phases (read inputs, invoke spec, write output, fire connections), and returns. Two boxes can be invoked simultaneously on different workers; they only contend on shared slot memory (per-slot lock).\n- The \"main\" thread is asleep on a condition variable waiting for active task count to reach zero. The worker calls `pool_spawn(downstream_task)` — that just enqueues the task onto the pool's ready queue, and the next free worker picks it up. No coordinator.\n\nThe dispatch layer is **code that lives on the worker, not a separate role**. The worker IS the dispatcher when it's running a task.\n\n## Same-language fast path\n\nYes — let's bake this in as a spec contract. Each spec exposes two invoke paths:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    const char *name;\n    const char *file_ext;\n\n    void *(*init)(int worker_idx);\n    void  (*teardown)(void *handle);\n    int   (*compile)(...);\n\n    // Universal path — language-agnostic JSON bytes in/out\n    int   (*invoke_json)(void *handle, ..., const void **input_data,\n                         const int *input_sizes, int n_inputs,\n                         void *out_buf, int out_buf_capacity, int *out_size);\n\n    // Fast path — bytes are this language's own serialization\n    int   (*invoke_native)(void *handle, ..., /* same shape, different bytes */);\n\n    // Optional callbacks the spec uses to convert between native and JSON\n    // forms when a wire crosses language boundaries\n    int   (*native_to_json)(const void *src, int src_size,\n                            void *dst, int dst_capacity, int *dst_size);\n    int   (*json_to_native)(const void *src, int src_size,\n                            void *dst, int dst_capacity, int *dst_size);\n} lang_spec_t;\n```\n\n**Compile-time check:** the build step (issue 309) walks every wire. For each, look up producer's spec and consumer's spec. If they're the same language, mark the wire as `fast_path: true`. If different, `fast_path: false`. The wire flag is part of the compiled manifest.\n\n**Runtime:** the dispatch action checks the wire's flag when reading an input:\n- `fast_path: true` → bytes in the slot are already in the consumer's native serialization. Lua's fast path picks a native\n   encoding (cjson for tables; raw bytes for primitives).\n5. **Tests**: smoke tests confirming a 100k-iteration Lua→Lua\n   pipeline with the fast path runs measurably faster than the\n   same pipeline with the JSON path, and that mixed-language\n   pipelines still work.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — adds the new callbacks\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — branch on fast_path\n- `issues/309-build-system.md` — wire-flag enrichment\n- `issues/306-lua-language-spec.md`, `307-c-language-spec.md`,\n  `308-bash-language-spec.md` — per-spec native implementations\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — slot still stores opaque\n  bytes; the format negotiation is at the spec layer, not the\n  store\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Whether a spec must implement `invoke_json`**: leaning yes, so\n  any spec can talk to any other spec. A spec that wants to\n  shortcut can declare cross-language wires unsupported via\n  compile-time error, but that's an opt-out, not the default.\n- **How to share the bridge functions across consumers**: native_to_json\n  on the producer side runs once per output (not per consumer), and\n  the JSON bytes go in the slot. Each cross-language consumer pays\n  json_to_native independently. Same-language consumers pay nothing.\n  Symmetrically: if the producer chose native and there's one\n  cross-language consumer, that consumer pays native_to_json then\n  json_to_native_their_lang. Two conversions for one cross-language\n  hop in this case. Probably fine; it's a corner case.\n",

    "originalFile":"# 232 — Same-language wire fast path: skip JSON for adjacent same-language boxes\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nThe wire format between boxes is JSON (`docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`,\nissue 302's \"no type tags\" — slot store stores opaque bytes; the\nlanguage spec encodes/decodes). Every wire pays the JSON encode +\ndecode cost on every value pass, even when the producer and the\nconsumer are the same language and could use a faster\nlanguage-native serialization.\n\nFor a Lua → Lua wire passing a 10-element table:\n1. Producer's spec: `cjson.encode(table)` → string of N bytes\n2. `slot_push(slot, string, N)`\n3. `slot_peek(slot, buf, N)`\n4. Consumer's spec: `cjson.decode(buf)` → Lua table\n\nSteps 1 and 4 are the cost. They're language-agnostic and unnecessary\nwhen both endpoints share a language.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nEach language spec exposes **two invoke paths**:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    const char *name;\n    const char *file_ext;\n\n    void *(*init)(int worker_idx);\n    void  (*teardown)(void *handle);\n    int   (*compile)(...);\n\n    // Universal path — JSON bytes in, JSON bytes out\n    int   (*invoke_json)  (void *handle, /* common args */);\n\n    // Fast path — language-native bytes in, language-native bytes out\n    int   (*invoke_native)(void *handle, /* common args */);\n\n    // Bridges used when a value crosses a language boundary\n    int   (*native_to_json)(const void *src, int src_size,\n                            void *dst, int dst_capacity, int *dst_size);\n    int   (*json_to_native)(const void *src, int src_size,\n                            void *dst, int dst_capacity, int *dst_size);\n} lang_spec_t;\n```\n\n`invoke_native` is required (every spec implements one). Per-language\n\"native\" format:\n- **Lua**: `lua_dump` for closures, `cjson` or msgpack for tables, raw\n  bytes for strings/numbers. Spec's choice as long as it's\n  symmetric with its own decoder.\n- **C**: raw struct memcpy. The compile-time wrapper (issue 307)\n  knows the types; serialization is `memcpy(slot_buf, &val, sizeof\n  val)`.\n- **Bash**: strings only — Bash has no other native form, so the\n  fast path is identical to the JSON path. Implement as a thin\n  alias.\n\n`invoke_json` is the universal interop format. Required for any\nlanguage that participates in cross-language wires. A spec that\nonly ever talks to itself can skip `invoke_json` (compile error if\na wire crosses to it from another language).\n\n## Compile-time wire classification\n\nEvery wire gets a `fast_path: true | false` flag set at build time\n(issue 309 build step):\n\n```python\nfor wire in graph.wires:\n    src_lang = box_at(wire.from).lang\n    dst_lang = box_at(wire.to).lang\n    wire.fast_path = (src_lang == dst_lang)\n```\n\nThe flag becomes part of the compiled manifest. Runtime never\nre-evaluates language pairing.\n\n## Producer-side decision\n\nA producer's output goes into one slot, but multiple consumers may\nread from it. If they're all the same language, the producer can\nwrite native bytes. If any consumer is in a different language, the\nproducer must write JSON (and same-language consumers convert via\n`json_to_native` to recover native form).\n\nTwo ways to decide:\n1. **Per-output decision** — analyze all consumers of the output\n   slot at compile time. All same lang → native; mixed → JSON.\n2. **Always JSON producer / convert at consumer** — simpler, but\n   pays the encode cost even when no cross-language consumer is\n   present.\n\nOption 1 is the right call. The compile step records the producer's\noutput format on the box record (`output_format: \"native\" | \"json\"`),\nand same-language consumers know to read native bytes directly,\ncross-language consumers call `json_to_native` first.\n\n## Runtime dispatch\n\nThe dispatch action's input-read path branches on the wire flag:\n\n```c\nfor (int i = 0; i < n_inputs; i++) {\n    slot_peek(input_slots[i], buf, buf_capacity);\n    if (input_wires[i].fast_path && producer_format == NATIVE) {\n        // bytes are already this language's native form\n        ...\n    } else if (producer_format == JSON) {\n        // bytes are JSON, decode into native form\n        json_to_native(buf, buf_size, native_buf, native_capacity, &native_size);\n        ...\n    }\n}\n```\n\nThen `invoke_native` is called with native-form bytes regardless of\nhow they were obtained. Same on the output side: if the box's output\nformat is `native`, write native bytes; if `json`, encode then\nwrite.\n\n## Edge cases\n\n- **All-same-language graph**: every wire is fast-path; `invoke_json`\n  never runs. Spec writers can stub it out.\n- **All-different-language graph**: every wire is JSON;\n  `invoke_native` handles bytes that came back from `json_to_native`.\n- **One same-language wire, several cross-language wires from the same\n  producer**: the producer writes JSON. Same-language consumer\n  decodes via `json_to_native` (still cheaper than full encode +\n  decode round-trip — only one direction of conversion is paid,\n  not two).\n- **Type changes mid-development**: a wire that was Lua→Lua becomes\n  Lua→C as the user changes a downstream box's language. Compile\n  flips the flag; the producer now writes JSON. No runtime\n  surprises, no migration.\n\n## Implementation cost\n\nThe two-invoke spec interface adds maybe 30 lines per language\nspec. The compile-time wire classification is one pass over the\ngraph. The dispatch action's input-read branch is one `if` on the\nwire flag. None of this is hot-path complex; the gain is one less\nJSON encode/decode per same-language hop, which is the whole point.\n\n## Future: whole-program same-language compilation\n\nA bigger optimization beyond this issue: at compile time, merge\nall same-language boxes into one translation unit. The C spec\nbecomes whole-program; the Lua spec produces one bytecode chunk\ncovering every Lua function. Box-boundary crossings become regular\nfunction calls — no slot store, no dispatch layer, no spec\ninvocation. Only cross-language wires retain the slot machinery.\n\nThis is a phase-3.5+ optimization and a much bigger lift —\nrequires the spec's `compile` callback to coordinate across all\nboxes of its language, plus a runtime mode that bypasses the\ndispatch layer for fully-merged regions of the graph. The\nwire-level fast path in this issue is the immediate, smaller win.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. **Spec interface** (issue 303): add `invoke_native`,\n   `invoke_json`, `native_to_json`, `json_to_native` callbacks.\n   Update the contract doc.\n2. **Compile step** (issue 309): walk wires, set `fast_path` flag,\n   set `output_format` per box.\n3. **Dispatch action** (issue 304): branch on `fast_path` /\n   `output_format` when reading inputs and when writing the\n   output.\n4. **Per-language specs** (306, 307, 308): implement both invoke\n   paths. Bash's fast path is a thin alias around the JSON path.\n   C's fast path is `memcpy`. Lua's fast path picks a native\n   encoding (cjson for tables; raw bytes for primitives).\n5. **Tests**: smoke tests confirming a 100k-iteration Lua→Lua\n   pipeline with the fast path runs measurably faster than the\n   same pipeline with the JSON path, and that mixed-language\n   pipelines still work.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — adds the new callbacks\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — branch on fast_path\n- `issues/309-build-system.md` — wire-flag enrichment\n- `issues/306-lua-language-spec.md`, `307-c-language-spec.md`,\n  `308-bash-language-spec.md` — per-spec native implementations\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — slot still stores opaque\n  bytes; the format negotiation is at the spec layer, not the\n  store\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Whether a spec must implement `invoke_json`**: leaning yes, so\n  any spec can talk to any other spec. A spec that wants to\n  shortcut can declare cross-language wires unsupported via\n  compile-time error, but that's an opt-out, not the default.\n- **How to share the bridge functions across consumers**: native_to_json\n  on the producer side runs once per output (not per consumer), and\n  the JSON bytes go in the slot. Each cross-language consumer pays\n  json_to_native independently. Same-language consumers pay nothing.\n  Symmetrically: if the producer chose native and there's one\n  cross-language consumer, that consumer pays native_to_json then\n  json_to_native_their_lang. Two conversions for one cross-language\n  hop in this case. Probably fine; it's a corner case.\n",

    "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"Now your other questions:\n\n## Why iterators have ring buffers and non-iterators don't\n\nThe difference comes from the **task lifecycle**, not from any property of the values being passed.\n\nA non-iterator box's task lives once. It runs, produces one slot full of bytes, fires its outgoing connections, and dies. Each consumer downstream got spawned as its own task with that producer's slot in its inputs. The slot only ever needs to hold **one** value because the producer only ever produces one. Multiple consumers of the same producer all peek into that same one cell.\n\nAn iterator's task lives **across many invocations**. Its input slot has to persist long enough for many upstream pushes — the iterator pops one, processes, re-spawns itself, the new spawn pops the next. Because the upstream may have already produced the next value (or several) before the iterator gets to consume them, the slot needs **N cells** to hold the backlog.\n\nIf you tried to give a non-iterator slot a ring buffer, you'd be modeling something that can't happen: a single-task producer can't produce multiple values because it only runs once. The \"fast producer / slow consumer\" you described isn't fast-multiple-pushes-into-one-slot — it's many-task-instances-with-many-slots, queued through the **pool's task queue**, not through a slot ring buffer. The pool's queue is the rate buffer for plain wires; the slot's ring buffer is the rate buffer for iterators specifically.\n\n## How language specs handle bytes/JSON\n\nThe dispatch action hands `invoke` a list of `(byte_pointer, byte_size)` pairs. The spec's job is the bridge between bytes and language-native types. **Convention is JSON** as the lowest-common-denominator encoding because every shipped language has a JSON parser and JSON's type tags carry the right shape across language boundaries.\n\nFor a Lua box receiving a wire value:\n1. Spec's `invoke` is given `input_data[0] = \"\\\"hello\\\"\"`, `input_sizes[0] = 7`.\n2. Spec parses those bytes (cjson decode) into a Lua value pushed on the Lua stack.\n3. Calls the user function via `lua_pcall`.\n4. Reads the return from the Lua stack.\n5. Encodes back to JSON bytes, writes them to `out_buf`, sets `*out_size`.\n\nThe slot store never sees what's IN the bytes. The bytes are opaque to it — they could be JSON, msgpack, raw struct memcpy, or hieroglyphs. Whatever the producer's spec wrote is what the consumer's spec gets, byte-for-byte.\n\nThe fast-path issue (312) lets two specs of the same language agree to use a non-JSON encoding for their slots, skipping the encode/decode cost on same-language wires. Different-language wires still go through JSON because that's the only thing both endpoints can speak.\n\n## High-performance is the bar, agreed\n\nThen the same-language fast path (312) goes from \"future optimization\" to \"default behavior.\" A user wiring two Lua boxes together pays no JSON cost; a user wiring Lua to C pays one encode + one decode (unavoidable cross-language tax).\n\nThe whole-program same-language merge mentioned at the bottom of 312 — where the C spec compiles every C box into one translation unit and every box-boundary becomes a regular function call with no slot-store involvement at all — is the right end state for tight inner loops. It's a bigger lift but worth tracking. I'll fold it into 312 as the explicit phase-3.5 next step rather than just an offhand mention.\n\nWant me to also open a follow-on for **type-annotated wire encodings** — primitives go raw bytes, strings as length-prefixed UTF-8, complex types as JSON — so the high-throughput numeric case has a path even across language boundaries? That's where the performance ceiling actually lifts; same-language fast-path is necessary but not sufficient."
      }]
  },

Mark it as low priority and block it until the rest of phase 3 is complete.\n\n  A non-iterator box's task lives once. It runs, produces one slot full of bytes, fires its outgoing connections, and dies. Each consumer\n  downstream got spawned as its own task with that producer's slot in its inputs. Because the upstream may have already produced the next value (or several)\n  before the iterator gets to consume them, the slot needs N cells to hold the backlog.\n\n  If you tried to give a non-iterator slot a ring buffer, you'd be modeling something that can't happen: a single-task producer can't produce\n   multiple values because it only runs once. The pool's queue is the\n  rate buffer for plain wires; the slot's ring buffer is the rate buffer for iterators specifically.\n\n\nSo, is there a reason we're not treating iterators as we do regular boxes?     "originalFile":"# 312 — Same-language wire fast path: skip JSON for adjacent same-language boxes\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\n\nThe wire format between boxes is JSON (`docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`,\nissue 302's \"no type tags\" — slot store stores opaque bytes; the\nlanguage spec encodes/decodes). Every wire pays the JSON encode +\ndecode cost on every value pass, even when the producer and the\nconsumer are the same language and could use a faster\nlanguage-native serialization.\n\nFor a Lua → Lua wire passing a 10-element table:\n1. Producer's spec: `cjson.encode(table)` → string of N bytes\n2. `slot_push(slot, string, N)`\n3. `slot_peek(slot, buf, N)`\n4. Consumer's spec: `cjson.decode(buf)` → Lua table\n\nSteps 1 and 4 are the cost. They're language-agnostic and unnecessary\nwhen both endpoints share a language.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\nEach language spec exposes **two invoke paths**:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    const char *name;\n    const char *file_ext;\n\n    void *(*init)(int worker_idx);\n    void  (*teardown)(void *handle);\n    int   (*compile)(...);\n\n    // Universal path — JSON bytes in, JSON bytes out\n    int   (*invoke_json)  (void *handle, /* common args */);\n\n    // Fast path — language-native bytes in, language-native bytes out\n    int   (*invoke_native)(void *handle, /* common args */);\n\n    // Bridges used when a value crosses a language boundary\n    int   (*native_to_json)(const void *src, int src_size,\n                            void *dst, int dst_capacity, int *dst_size);\n    int   (*json_to_native)(const void *src, int src_size,\n                            void *dst, int dst_capacity, int *dst_size);\n} lang_spec_t;\n```\n\n`invoke_native` is required (every spec implements one). Per-language\n\"native\" format:\n- **Lua**: `lua_dump` for closures, `cjson` or msgpack for tables, raw\n  bytes for strings/numbers. Spec's choice as long as it's\n  symmetric with its own decoder.\n- **C**: raw struct memcpy. The compile-time wrapper (issue 307)\n  knows the types; serialization is `memcpy(slot_buf, &val, sizeof\n  val)`.\n- **Bash**: strings only — Bash has no other native form, so the\n  fast path is identical to the JSON path. Implement as a thin\n  alias.\n\n`invoke_json` is the universal interop format. Required for any\nlanguage that participates in cross-language wires. A spec that\nonly ever talks to itself can skip `invoke_json` (compile error if\na wire crosses to it from another language).\n\n## Compile-time wire classification\n\nEvery wire gets a `fast_path: true | false` flag set at build time\n(issue 309 build step):\n\n```python\nfor wire in graph.wires:\n    src_lang = box_at(wire.from).lang\n    dst_lang = box_at(wire.to).lang\n    wire.fast_path = (src_lang == dst_lang)\n```\n\nThe flag becomes part of the compiled manifest. Runtime never\nre-evaluates language pairing.\n\n## Producer-side decision\n\nA producer's output goes into one slot, but multiple consumers may\nread from it. If they're all the same language, the producer can\nwrite native bytes. If any consumer is in a different language, the\nproducer must write JSON (and same-language consumers convert via\n`json_to_native` to recover native form).\n\nTwo ways to decide:\n1. **Per-output decision** — analyze all consumers of the output\n   slot at compile time. All same lang → native; mixed → JSON.\n2. **Always JSON producer / convert at consumer** — simpler, but\n   pays the encode cost even when no cross-language consumer is\n   present.\n\nOption 1 is the right call. The compile step records the producer's\noutput format on the box record (`output_format: \"native\" | \"json\"`),\nand same-language consumers know to read native bytes directly,\ncross-language consumers call `json_to_native` first.\n\n## Runtime dispatch\n\nThe dispatch action's input-read path branches on the wire flag:\n\n```c\nfor (int i = 0; i < n_inputs; i++) {\n    slot_peek(input_slots[i], buf, buf_capacity);\n    if (input_wires[i].fast_path && producer_format == NATIVE) {\n        // bytes are already this language's native form\n        ...\n    } else if (producer_format == JSON) {\n        // bytes are JSON, decode into native form\n        json_to_native(buf, buf_size, native_buf, native_capacity, &native_size);\n        ...\n    }\n}\n```\n\nThen `invoke_native` is called with native-form bytes regardless of\nhow they were obtained. Same on the output side: if the box's output\nformat is `native`, write native bytes; if `json`, encode then\nwrite.\n\n## Edge cases\n\n- **All-same-language graph**: every wire is fast-path; `invoke_json`\n  never runs. Spec writers can stub it out.\n- **All-different-language graph**: every wire is JSON;\n  `invoke_native` handles bytes that came back from `json_to_native`.\n- **One same-language wire, several cross-language wires from the same\n  producer**: the producer writes JSON. Same-language consumer\n  decodes via `json_to_native` (still cheaper than full encode +\n  decode round-trip — only one direction of conversion is paid,\n  not two).\n- **Type changes mid-development**: a wire that was Lua→Lua becomes\n  Lua→C as the user changes a downstream box's language. Compile\n  flips the flag; the producer now writes JSON. No runtime\n  surprises, no migration.\n\n## Implementation cost\n\nThe two-invoke spec interface adds maybe 30 lines per language\nspec. The compile-time wire classification is one pass over the\ngraph. The dispatch action's input-read branch is one `if` on the\nwire flag. None of this is hot-path complex; the gain is one less\nJSON encode/decode per same-language hop, which is the whole point.\n\n## Future: whole-program same-language compilation\n\nA bigger optimization beyond this issue: at compile time, merge\nall same-language boxes into one translation unit. The C spec\nbecomes whole-program; the Lua spec produces one bytecode chunk\ncovering every Lua function. Box-boundary crossings become regular\nfunction calls — no slot store, no dispatch layer, no spec\ninvocation. Only cross-language wires retain the slot machinery.\n\nThis is a phase-3.5+ optimization and a much bigger lift —\nrequires the spec's `compile` callback to coordinate across all\nboxes of its language, plus a runtime mode that bypasses the\ndispatch layer for fully-merged regions of the graph. The\nwire-level fast path in this issue is the immediate, smaller win.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. **Spec interface** (issue 303): add `invoke_native`,\n   `invoke_json`, `native_to_json`, `json_to_native` callbacks.\n   Update the contract doc.\n2. **Compile step** (issue 309): walk wires, set `fast_path` flag,\n   set `output_format` per box.\n3. **Dispatch action** (issue 304): branch on `fast_path` /\n   `output_format` when reading inputs and when writing the\n   output.\n4. **Per-language specs** (306, 307, 308): implement both invoke\n   paths. Bash's fast path is a thin alias around the JSON path.\n   C's fast path is `memcpy`. Lua's fast path picks a native\n   encoding (cjson for tables; raw bytes for primitives).\n5. **Tests**: smoke tests confirming a 100k-iteration Lua→Lua\n   pipeline with the fast path runs measurably faster than the\n   same pipeline with the JSON path, and that mixed-language\n   pipelines still work.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — adds the new callbacks\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — branch on fast_path\n- `issues/309-build-system.md` — wire-flag enrichment\n- `issues/306-lua-language-spec.md`, `307-c-language-spec.md`,\n  `308-bash-language-spec.md` — per-spec native implementations\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — slot still stores opaque\n  bytes; the format negotiation is at the spec layer, not the\n  store\n\n## Open questions\n\n- **Whether a spec must implement `invoke_json`**: leaning yes, so\n  any spec can talk to any other spec. A spec that wants to\n  shortcut can declare cross-language wires unsupported via\n  compile-time error, but that's an opt-out, not the default.\n- **How to share the bridge functions across consumers**: native_to_json\n  on the producer side runs once per output (not per consumer), and\n  the JSON bytes go in the slot. Each cross-language consumer pays\n  json_to_native independently. Same-language consumers pay nothing.\n  Symmetrically: if the producer chose native and there's one\n  cross-language consumer, that consumer pays native_to_json then\n  json_to_native_their_lang. Two conversions for one cross-language\n  hop in this case. Probably fine; it's a corner case.\n",
    "oldString":"## Open questions",
    "newString":"## Implementation note: ask the user about type-annotated cross-language encodings\n\nBefore implementing this issue, the implementer must ask the user\nto decide on **type-annotated wire encodings** for cross-language\nhops — primitives go raw bytes (4-byte int as 4 bytes, not as the\nJSON string `\"42\"`), strings go length-prefixed UTF-8, structured\ntypes go JSON. That decision affects the spec interface (whether\n`json_to_native` is enough or whether we need a `decode_wire(type,\nbytes)` shape) and the wire-format byte layout. Don't proceed with\nthe implementation without explicit user direction on this; the\ntwo designs aren't trivially interchangeable later.\n\n## Open questions",
    "replaceAll":false,
    "userModified":false
  },

  "toolUseResult":{
    "type":"create",

    "userModified":false,
    "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/313-research-whole-program-same-language-merge.md",
    "content":"# 313 — Research: whole-program same-language compilation\n\n## Status\nresearch / low priority / blocked until rest of phase 3 is complete\n\n## Concept\n\nInstead of one box = one function call going through the dispatch\nlayer + slot store + spec invocation, **merge all same-language\nboxes at compile time into a single translation unit** for that\nlanguage. Box-to-box transitions within a language region become\nordinary function calls — the optimizer can inline across them, the\nlanguage runtime stays warm, and the slot store and dispatch layer\ndon't run for those transitions at all. Only cross-language wires\nretain the slot machinery.\n\nFor C: every C box becomes a function in one big `.c` file, with\nthe build emitting one `.so`. Wire endpoints become direct calls;\nthe optimizer inlines based on its usual heuristics.\n\nFor Lua: every Lua function gets pre-compiled into one bytecode\nchunk loaded into one shared `lua_State` per worker. Wire\nendpoints become direct `lua_pcall`s into that chunk — no JSON\nencode/decode, no slot push/pop, no spec re-entry per call.\n\nFor Bash: probably no benefit — Bash is already process-per-call;\nfusing scripts doesn't help much. Skip.\n\n## Why this is research, not a feature\n\nThree open questions that need code-level investigation before\nthe design is concrete:\n\n1. **Loop and iterator boundaries**: a same-language region with an\n   iterator inside it has dynamic re-spawning. Is the iterator\n   merged in (a loop in the generated code) or does it remain a\n   spec-mediated boundary? If the latter, the merge buys less.\n2. **Compile time**: whole-program optimization is slow. Does the\n   incremental-compile model (issue 309's mtime check) still apply,\n   or do edits require a full rebuild of the merged region?\n3. **Debug story**: a stack trace inside the merged region needs to\n   point back to a specific box. Either source-map-style mapping or\n   per-function preserved names — both have costs.\n\nThe right way to answer these is to prototype: take a small all-Lua\ngraph (like the hello map) and see what a merged version looks\nlike, both for runtime cost and for build-system complexity. The\nprototype should be able to fall back to the per-box path if the\nmerge fails for any reason.\n\n## Why blocked until rest of phase 3 completes\n\nThe merge optimization piggybacks on the per-box model — same\nspecs, same compile callback, same dispatch layer for cross-language\nwires. Building it before the per-box model is settled risks\ndesigning against a target that's still moving. After phase 3 ships\nand the per-box path is stable, the merge becomes a clean\n\"everything except spec invocation gets shorter for this region.\"\n\nIt's also genuinely lower priority than getting the runtime working\nat all. The same-language fast path (issue 312) captures the\n~2x JSON-skip win without any of this complexity. The merge wins a\nfurther factor only if profile data shows function-call overhead\nmatters at all after 312 ships.\n\n## Scope of the research output\n\nThe deliverable is a written design (not code) with:\n- Concrete answers to the three questions above.\n- A worked example: the merged C generated from a 5-box C-only\n  graph, showing what the build artifact looks like.\n- Estimated runtime cost of the per-box path vs the merged path\n  on that example.\n- A recommendation: ship as a feature, ship as an opt-in flag, or\n  shelve indefinitely.\n\nAfter the design is reviewed, a separate implementation issue\nopens (or doesn't, depending on the recommendation).\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `issues/312-same-language-wire-fast-path.md` — the immediate JSON-\n  skip win this builds on\n- `issues/307-c-language-spec.md` — `compile` callback that would\n  grow whole-program-aware semantics\n- `issues/306-lua-language-spec.md` — Lua-side bytecode pre-compile\n- `issues/309-build-system.md` — how the merge integrates with the\n  compile/package step\n\n## Open questions (for the research, not for now)\n\n- Cross-language wires inside the merged region: the merged region\n  still has cross-language outputs that exit to other regions. The\n  spec interface still applies at those boundaries, so the merge is\n  region-internal optimization, not a global rearchitecture.\n- C ABI for inlined wrappers: with whole-program optimization the\n  wrapper-per-box generation might collapse to nothing. If the\n  optimizer can prove a wire endpoint is always called from the\n  merged region with known types, it can skip the wrapper.\n- Iterators-with-side-effects: an iterator self-rescheduling its\n  own task is normally dispatch-layer machinery. Inside a merged\n  region, it could become a `while` loop. Whether that's safe\n  depends on whether other tasks are blocked on the iterator's\n  output slots — which they shouldn't be in a same-language region,\n  but the analysis has to confirm.\n"
  },
  "uuid":"c0669524-59b5-4017-99d5-9a8e103af0cb",

    "oldString":"## Concept\n\n### Slots belong to tasks, not wires\nA **slot** is the memory region that holds a task's output. Slots are\ncreated when tasks are created. A box that runs once produces one slot;\na box that runs ten times (an iterator) produces ten slots, one per\ninvocation. Slots live in process heap memory, accessible to every\nworker thread in the process. Cross-process visibility is not required:\nlanguage specs (issue 303) only ever receive byte pointers — never\nraw slot addresses — so out-of-process specs (Bash) work via sockets,\nnot shared memory.\n\nA **wire** is the relationship between two tasks: it says \"task B's input\nN reads from task A's output M.\" Wires hold references to slots.     "newString":"## Concept\n\n### Slots belong to input ports, not tasks\n\nEach box has **one slot per input port**, allocated when the graph\nloads and persisting for the life of the run. A wire is a routing\ndeclaration: \"the producer's output port pushes a copy of its value\ninto this consumer's named input slot.\" The producer never owns a\nslot — its output is a routing event, not a stored value.\n\nWhen a producer fires, the dispatch layer copies the value into\nevery downstream input slot wired to that output. Fan-out is N\npushes (one per consumer); fan-in is N producers all pushing into\nthe same consumer's slot. Both behaviors fall out of the same\npush-into-input-slot mechanic.\n\nSlots live in process heap memory, accessible to every worker\nthread. Cross-process visibility is not required: language specs\n(issue 303) only ever receive byte pointers — never raw slot\naddresses — so out-of-process specs (Bash) work via sockets, not\nshared memory.\n\n### Tasks are ephemeral; box state is durable\n\nA **task** is one invocation: pop one value from each of the box's\ninput slots, run the box's logic, push the output to every\ndownstream input slot. Tasks have no persistent identity — they're\njust stack frames on workers. Tasks are spawned dynamically by the\ndispatch layer when a box's input set is ready (every input slot\nholds at least one value).\n\nThe **box** is the durable thing: it owns its input port slots, any\ncounter state (for iterators), its language spec handle, and so\non. The box exists from graph load until run end. Tasks come and\ngo.\n\nThis is uniform across iterator and non-iterator boxes. Both run N\ntimes where N depends on how many invocations their inputs supply\n(possibly 1, possibly thousands). The difference is just what the\ntask does:\n- **Plain call task**: invoke spec on the popped values, push the\n  return to outputs.\n- **Iterator task**: read box's counter, route the popped value to\n  output port `iterator_outputs[counter]`, increment counter mod N.\n  No spec invocation.\n- **Comparator task**: invoke spec on the popped values, compare\n  the return against `comparand`, route to the matching `lt` /\n  `eq` / `gt` branch.",

          "new_string":"### All slots are ring buffers\n\nThere is one slot type. It is a ring buffer of `n_cells` cells,\neach of `cell_capacity` bytes. Every input port has a ring buffer\nof compile-time-determined size:\n\n- **Default size**: enough cells to absorb the maximum number of\n  pushes that can happen before the box can drain. For a port fed\n  by a single non-iterator producer, that's 1. For a port fed by\n  an iterator, it's the iterator's worst-case backlog (statically\n  inferred or capped at a high default like 64 with growth).\n- **Upper bound**: lists grow if backlog exceeds the pre-allocated\n  size, so n_cells isn't a hard cap on correctness — only on\n  pre-allocation efficiency.\n\nThe producer pushes one cell per fan-out path; the consumer pops\none cell per invocation. Fan-in is multiple producers pushing into\nthe same input slot in arrival order; the consumer pops in FIFO\norder.",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md",
          "replace_all":false,
          "old_string":"### All slots are ring buffers\nThere is one slot type. It is a ring buffer of `n_cells` cells, each\nof `cell_capacity` bytes. The `n_cells = 1` case is the trivial ring\nholding a single value; the `n_cells = N` case is a queue.\n\nA single-output box allocates a 1-cell ring. The producer pushes once,\nconsumers read the head. An iterator that produces 10 outputs over its\nlifetime allocates 10 separate 1-cell rings (one per invocation, per\nthe box-not-wire-is-the-slot model below).\n\nA box with a queued input allocates a multi-cell ring as the input's\nholding pen — many upstream wires push into it, the consumer drains it\nin arrival order.\n\nSame data structure, same API, same per-slot lock. The dispatch layer\nparameterizes `n_cells` based on whether the slot is being used for\nfan-out or fan-in."

        },
        "input":{
          "new_string":"## Lifetime and end-of-stream\n\nSlots are owned by the box that holds the input port. They live\nfrom graph load until run end. There is no per-slot reference\ncounting — the slot is freed when the run ends, alongside its\nowning box.\n\n### End-of-stream detection (replacing producer refcounts)\n\nEach slot tracks the set of upstream producer boxes that may still\npush into it. When a producer's \"no more pushes\" condition fires\n— either it has finished all its invocations, or it transitively\ndepends only on producers that have finished — the dispatch layer\nremoves that producer from the slot's producer set.\n\nWhen the producer set is empty AND the slot's queue is drained,\nthe consumer box has reached end-of-stream on that port. For an\niterator, this is what tells the iterator to stop re-spawning. For\na non-iterator, this means no further invocations are coming;\ncombined with the same condition on its other input ports, the\nbox itself is done.\n\nThis replaces the per-slot refcount machinery. The \"are upstreams\nstill alive\" check is done at the producer-set level, which is\ncheaper and avoids the contention of refcount churn on hot paths.",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md",
          "replace_all":false,
          "old_string":"## Reference counting protocol\n\nEvery party that may still touch a slot holds a reference. The slot is\nfreed when the count reaches zero. The references themselves are how\nwe track liveness — there is no separate \"is this producer / consumer\nstill alive\" mechanism.\n\n### Single-output (1-cell) slot\n1. Task allocates its output slot with `refcount = 0`.\n2. For each fan-out wire reading from the slot, `slot_ref` is called.\n   The wire holds that reference until its consumer is done reading.\n3. After the consumer reads (peek), it calls `slot_unref`.\n4. When refcount reaches zero, the unrefing task frees the slot.\n\n### Queued (N-cell) slot\nThe consumer's input queue. Producers and the consumer all hold refs:\n1. The consumer task allocates the queue slot with one ref for itself.\n2. Each producer that may push into the queue increments the refcount\n   when it is constructed; the ref is dropped when that producer's\n   box function ends.\n3. The consumer drops its ref when its own box function ends (i.e.\n   when the iterator stops re-spawning because no more inputs are\n   coming).\n4. When the last ref drops, the queue is freed.\n\nThe producer-side ref is what makes \"no more inputs are coming\"\ndetectable: when the queue's refcount equals 1 (only the consumer\nholds it) and the queue is empty, no upstream task can push again,\nso the iterator's natural end-of-stream condition fires."

    "replaceAll":false,
    "oldString":"## Reference counting protocol\n\nEvery party that may still touch a slot holds a reference. The slot is\nfreed when the count reaches zero. The references themselves are how\nwe track liveness — there is no separate \"is this producer / consumer\nstill alive\" mechanism.\n\n### Single-output (1-cell) slot\n1. Task allocates its output slot with `refcount = 0`.\n2. For each fan-out wire reading from the slot, `slot_ref` is called.\n   The wire holds that reference until its consumer is done reading.\n3. After the consumer reads (peek), it calls `slot_unref`.\n4. When refcount reaches zero, the unrefing task frees the slot.\n\n### Queued (N-cell) slot\nThe consumer's input queue. Producers and the consumer all hold refs:\n1. The consumer task allocates the queue slot with one ref for itself.\n2. Each producer that may push into the queue increments the refcount\n   when it is constructed; the ref is dropped when that producer's\n   box function ends.\n3. The consumer drops its ref when its own box function ends (i.e.\n   when the iterator stops re-spawning because no more inputs are\n   coming).\n4. When the last ref drops, the queue is freed.\n\nThe producer-side ref is what makes \"no more inputs are coming\"\ndetectable: when the queue's refcount equals 1 (only the consumer\nholds it) and the queue is empty, no upstream task can push again,\nso the iterator's natural end-of-stream condition fires.",
    "newString":"## Lifetime and end-of-stream\n\nSlots are owned by the box that holds the input port. They live\nfrom graph load until run end. There is no per-slot reference\ncounting — the slot is freed when the run ends, alongside its\nowning box.\n\n### End-of-stream detection (replacing producer refcounts)\n\nEach slot tracks the set of upstream producer boxes that may still\npush into it. When a producer's \"no more pushes\" condition fires\n— either it has finished all its invocations, or it transitively\ndepends only on producers that have finished — the dispatch layer\nremoves that producer from the slot's producer set.\n\nWhen the producer set is empty AND the slot's queue is drained,\nthe consumer box has reached end-of-stream on that port. For an\niterator, this is what tells the iterator to stop re-spawning. For\na non-iterator, this means no further invocations are coming;\ncombined with the same condition on its other input ports, the\nbox itself is done.\n\nThis replaces the per-slot refcount machinery. The \"are upstreams\nstill alive\" check is done at the producer-set level, which is\ncheaper and avoids the contention of refcount churn on hot paths.",
    "userModified":false
  },

        "input":{
          "new_string":"## Slot creation\n\nSlot creation happens at **graph load**, not per task. The graph\nloader walks every box, allocates one ring buffer per input port,\nand parks the slot on the box's per-port slot table. The dispatch\nlayer never allocates new slots at runtime in the steady state —\nall slots that will ever exist are created up front.\n\n```c\nslot_id_t slot_alloc(slot_store_t *store, int cell_capacity, int n_cells);\n```\n\n`cell_capacity` and `n_cells` come from compile-time analysis of\nthe graph. Boxes downstream of iterators get larger `n_cells` to\nabsorb the iterator's worst-case backlog.\n\nIf a slot's pre-allocated `n_cells` proves too small at runtime\n(producer outpaces consumer beyond the pre-allocation), the slot's\nring grows — see \"Allocation strategy\" below.",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md",
          "replace_all":false,
          "old_string":"## Slot creation\n\nSlot creation happens inside the dispatch layer at task submission. The\ncaller specifies the cell capacity (bytes per value) and the ring size\n(number of cells, 1 for single-value):\n\n```c\nslot_id_t slot_alloc(slot_store_t *store, int cell_capacity, int n_cells);\n```\n\nThe slot is created with `refcount = 0`, `head = tail = 0`. The\ndispatch layer then increments the refcount once per consumer (one ref\nper fan-out wire for a 1-cell slot; one ref for the consumer task on a\nqueued-input slot) before the task is exposed."
        },
        "id":"toolu_016GiW9ArDfsxptb7xdgV5nW"
      }]
