        "input":{
          "new_string":"## Submission timing\n\nTasks are spawned dynamically in response to slot pushes, not at\ngraph-load time. Each box has a small per-box state used by the\ndispatch layer to decide when to spawn:\n\n```\nbox_runtime_state {\n    slot_id_t  *input_slots;     // one per input port (set at load)\n    int         n_inputs;\n    int         pending_invocations;  // counter; >0 means a task is queued\n    int         counter;         // iterator only; 0 otherwise\n};\n```\n\nThe spawning rule:\n- When a producer pushes to one of a box's input slots, the\n  dispatch layer checks **does every input slot now hold at least\n  one value?** If yes, spawn a task. The task pops one cell from\n  each input slot when it runs.\n- If multiple input slots get pushed concurrently, one task spawns\n  per \"all inputs available\" event — the pending_invocations\n  counter prevents over-spawning.\n\nThis makes the pool's queue the rate buffer: pushes accumulate\n(possibly multiple per slot), and one task per accumulated set\ngets spawned in arrival order.\n\nTasks never block on slots. They're spawned after inputs are\nready, run to completion, and disappear. Blocking-and-waking\nmachinery is unnecessary — the spawn-on-arrival rule is the\nsynchronization primitive.\n\nThe pool's queue is the only queue. There is no separate \"blocked\ntasks\" structure.",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md",
          "replace_all":false,
          "old_string":"## Submission timing\n\nThe dispatch layer builds the task struct as soon as the graph asks\nfor it — output slots allocated, all known data filled in, input wire\nreferences attached. It is then submitted directly to the pool. The\npool's existing block-and-wake machinery handles the rest:\n\n- If any input slots are unfilled at the moment of submission, the\n  dispatch action immediately `ACT_BLOCK`s on the first unfilled\n  input. The pool parks the task on that slot's wait list.\n- When the upstream producer pushes, it walks the wait list and wakes\n  the parked tasks. The action re-runs from the top, checks the next\n  input, blocks again if needed.\n- When all inputs are present, the action proceeds to invoke the box.\n\nThere is no separate \"blocked tasks\" set held by the dispatch layer.\nThe pool is the only thing that tracks blocked tasks. This avoids\nduplicating the wait-list machinery the pool already has."
        },
        "id":"toolu_01KGnfgcSmbM7udnJHABpPxV"
      }]
  },

          "new_string":"## Task struct\n\nA task is one ephemeral invocation of a box. Its struct carries\njust enough to point the action at the box and the snapshot of its\ncounter at spawn time:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    int  box_id;          // index into the graph's box array\n    int  counter;         // iterator only; snapshot at spawn time\n} dispatch_task_t;\n```\n\nThere is no `input_slots` array on the task — the box's input\nslots are durable per-box state (see issue 302). The action looks\nup the input and output slots through `box_runtime_state[box_id]`.\n\nThere is no `output_slot` either — output is a routing event, not\na stored value. When the action finishes, it pushes copies of the\nreturn value into the input slots of every downstream box wired\nto this output (and only the matching branch for comparators and\niterators).\n\nTasks are spawned by the dispatch layer's \"spawn on input ready\"\nrule (issue 302). Each spawn allocates a fresh `dispatch_task_t`\non the pool's task allocator, pre-populated with the box ID and\ncounter value. The action's first read of the input slots is what\ndrains them — pop one cell per input port.",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md",
          "replace_all":false,
          "old_string":"## Task struct\n\nThe dispatch layer's per-task state lives in a `dispatch_task_t`\nallocated when the task is submitted to the pool:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    int           box_id;          // index into the graph's box array\n    int           n_inputs;\n    slot_id_t    *input_slots;     // array of n_inputs slot IDs\n    slot_id_t     output_slot;     // single output slot\n    int           counter;         // iterator only; ignored otherwise\n} dispatch_task_t;\n```\n\nThe pool passes this pointer to the action via `task_ctx_t.args`.\nMultiple successor invocations of an iterator produce multiple\n`dispatch_task_t`s (with new counter values), each with its own output\nslot."
        },

        },
        "input":{
          "new_string":"### 1. Read inputs into byte buffers\n\nTasks are spawned only when every input port has at least one\nvalue (issue 302's spawn-on-input-ready rule), so the action does\nnot need to check or block — input availability is the spawn\nprecondition.\n\nFor each input port: `slot_pop` from the box's input slot into a\nheap-allocated buffer sized to the slot's `cell_capacity`. Pop\ndrains one cell from the front of the ring; subsequent values\nbehind it are still queued and will spawn further tasks.\n\nVariable-size payloads work via the large-value heap (issue 302):\nthe popped cell holds a `{size, offset}` handle that points into\nthe heap; the spec follows the handle if it needs the bytes.\n\nBuffers are freed when the action ends.",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md",
          "replace_all":false,
          "old_string":"### 1. Check inputs\nWalk `input_slots`. For each, ask the slot store whether a value is\navailable (`tail > head`, cell filled).\n\nIf any input is unavailable, the dispatch action returns `ACT_BLOCK`\nwith `ctx->block_on` set to a wait handle for that slot. The pool\nparks the task on **the slot's** wait list — not on a wire's list and\nnot on the upstream box's list. The slot owns the wait list because\nthe slot is the thing that gets filled; whoever pushes into the slot\nwalks its wait list and wakes everyone parked there. When the action\nis re-run, it starts again at phase 1, checks the next input, blocks\nagain if needed.\n\n### 2. Read inputs into byte buffers\nFor each input:\n- Single-value slot (`n_cells = 1`): `slot_peek` into the input\n  buffer. The cell is not drained — fan-out consumers all peek.\n- Queued slot (`n_cells > 1`): `slot_pop` into the input buffer. The\n  head cell is drained.\n\nBuffer ownership: the action allocates the input buffer on the heap,\nsized exactly to the slot's `cell_capacity`. There is no fixed cap —\na slot whose cell holds 4 KB gets a 4 KB buffer, a slot whose cell\npoints into the large-value heap (variable-size payloads, issue 302)\ngets enough buffer to hold the handle, and the spec is given the\nhandle to follow if it needs the bytes. The buffer is freed when the\naction ends."
        },
        "id":"toolu_0129ApAMfWNiivu61Sor41Ng"
      }]
  },
  "slug":"snug-booping-dove",

        },
        "input":{
          "new_string":"### 6. End-of-stream propagation\n\nSlots are durable for the life of the run; there is no per-task\nunref step. Instead, the action checks whether the **producer set**\non each pushed-to slot has changed: if this push was the last\npush from a producer that's now finished, the producer is removed\nfrom each of that consumer's input slots' producer sets. When a\nconsumer's producer set goes empty AND its slot is drained, the\nconsumer is at end-of-stream on that port.\n\nFor an iterator, \"end-of-stream on the input\" is what tells the\ndispatch layer to stop spawning successor tasks. For a non-iterator\nthat's done with all its expected invocations, the same condition\napplies — no further pushes will arrive, no more tasks spawn.",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md",
          "replace_all":false,
          "old_string":"### 6. Unref consumed inputs\nFor each single-value input slot (`n_cells = 1`), the dispatch action\ncalls `slot_unref` after peeking. Each fan-out wire holds one ref; as\neach consumer reads and unrefs, the count decrements. When the last\nconsumer unrefs, the slot is freed.\n\nQueued input slots are different. They are not unref'd at the end of\neach invocation. The same queue persists across multiple invocations\nof the same iterator: an iterator pops one value, runs, re-spawns\nitself with a new dispatch_task_t, and the new task uses the **same**\nqueued-input slot to pop the next value. The slot stays alive\nbecause:\n- Each upstream producer holds a ref while the producer is alive.\n- The consumer (iterator) holds a ref while it is still consuming.\n- The slot is freed when all upstream producers have ended (their\n  refs dropped) and the iterator has ended (its ref dropped).\n\nSo the slot's lifetime ≠ one invocation; it equals the duration of\nthe iterator's whole consumption cycle."
        },
        "id":"toolu_012eTFmG42V8AquZXL6w4qKA"
      }]
  },
  "slug":"snug-booping-dove",

          "new_string":"### 7. Post-action: counter advancement (iterators only)\n\nRouting already happened in phase 5 — pushes targeted the right\ndownstream input slots based on the box's mode. The remaining\npost-action work is iterator-specific:\n\n- **Iterator**: increment `box_runtime_state[box_id].counter`\n  modulo `n_iter_outputs`. The next iterator task spawned for this\n  box (when its input slot has another value) will read the\n  updated counter value from the box state.\n\nThere is no \"successor task\" spawned by the iterator itself. The\nspawn-on-input-ready rule in issue 302 handles iterator\nre-invocation the same way it handles every other box: the\niterator's input slot has further values queued, the spawn rule\nfires again automatically.\n\nPlain call and comparator boxes do nothing in phase 7.",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md",
          "replace_all":false,
          "old_string":"### 7. Post-action: routing\nThree cases, dispatched by box mode:\n\n- **Plain call**: fire all outgoing connections unconditionally.\n- **Comparator**: the dispatch layer compares the *function's\n  output value* (just written to the output slot in phase 5) to\n  the box's `comparand`, producing a branch tag (`lt` / `eq` /\n  `gt`). Fire only the connection whose `from_branch` matches.\n  The output slot carries the function's actual output — downstream\n  boxes on the matching branch see the value the function returned.\n- **Iterator**: fire only the connection whose `from_branch` matches\n  `iterator_outputs[counter]`. Then increment `counter` modulo\n  `n_iter_outputs` and spawn a successor `dispatch_task_t` with the\n  same input slot pointers and the new counter value. The successor\n  immediately blocks on the input queue if empty; otherwise it picks\n  up the next queued value on its first wake.\n\n\"Firing\" a connection means submitting a `dispatch_task_t` for the\ndownstream box, with `input_slots[i]` set to the upstream's\n`output_slot` for the wired input position. Refcount on the upstream\nslot is incremented per fan-out wire at firing time."
        },
        "id":"toolu_01X3EzBgWpBugamoXNf5yrvP"
      }]
  },

    "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"Now your questions answered, with the architectural updates I just made:\n\n## A box called 30 or 50 times\n\nThe fix is in 302/304 just now: I rewrote the slot model to **slots belong to input ports, not tasks**. Each box has one slot per input port, allocated at graph load and persisting for the run. Tasks are ephemeral — each one pops one value from each input slot, runs, and disappears. A box invoked 30 times is 30 task instances over the same 30 inputs flowing through the same set of port slots.\n\nSo my earlier \"non-iterators run once\" was wrong. Non-iterators run **as many times as their inputs supply values**. The iterator-vs-non-iterator distinction collapses at the slot level: both have queued input slots, both spawn dynamically.\n\n## Where slots live before producers fire\n\nOn the consumer's box, in its per-port slot table. Allocated at load time, empty until something gets pushed in. The wait is at the **dispatch layer's spawn-check**, not on a slot's wait list — when no input has been pushed yet, the spawn rule simply doesn't fire. The slot exists, ready to receive.\n\n## How the dispatch layer creates new tasks\n\nIt allocates a `dispatch_task_t` from the pool's task allocator and submits it. The task struct is small (`box_id` + counter snapshot) — slots aren't on it because they're durable per-box state. When phase 5 (push to downstream input slots) of a producer's task completes, each pushed-to slot's owning box checks the spawn rule; if all input slots now hold a value, the dispatch layer allocates a fresh task for that box and queues it.\n\n## Iterators: simpler, no self-respawn\n\nYou called this exactly. With per-port queued slots, an iterator no longer needs to re-spawn itself. The dispatch layer's spawn-on-input-arrival rule handles re-invocation automatically — every push to the iterator's input slot triggers a spawn-check. The iterator's counter is per-box state, not per-task, so each new task just reads the box's current counter, routes its output to that branch, and increments. After 5 inputs there are 5 task instances, after the 6th there's a 6th — counter just keeps incrementing mod N.\n\n## \"Box exists at runtime\" — yes\n\nA `box_runtime_state` struct per box holds the counter, the input slot table, the language spec handle, the producer set (for end-of-stream detection). Tasks are stack frames on workers; boxes are durable structs. Your sketch was right: each box has its input slots, and the dispatch layer pops + spawns when inputs are ready.\n\n## Cross-iterator pairing\n\nTwo iterators A and B feeding a non-iterator C: C has its own per-port queue, A pushes into one queue and B pushes into the other, C spawns tasks FIFO — each task pops one from each queue. If A and B push in deterministic order, pairing is `(A_i, B_i)`. If they push concurrently from different workers, pairing depends on race winners.\n\nFor phase 3 the policy is **FIFO** with an explicit note that workloads needing strict-index pairing get per-invocation index tags on values. Added that note to 304.\n\n## Same-language merge — opened as 313\n\nResearch-only, low priority, blocked until rest of phase 3 ships. The deliverable is a written design — not code — answering: how do iterators interact with merging, what's the compile-time hit, how do stack traces work. Recommendation comes out of the research, not before.\n\n## 312 note\n\nAdded: implementer must ask the user about type-annotated cross-language encodings (primitive numbers as raw bytes vs as JSON strings) before coding the fast path. The decision affects the spec interface shape, so it can't be retrofitted cheaply.\n\n## What changed in the issue files\n\n- **302**: slot model rewritten. Per-port slots replace per-task slots. Refcounting replaced with producer-set tracking. Spawning is \"all inputs available\" trigger, not \"task submitted then blocks.\"\n- **304**: task struct simplified (no input_slots, no output_slot — those are on the box). Phase 1 (check inputs) deleted (input availability is the spawn precondition). Iterator self-respawn removed. Cross-iterator pairing section added.\n- **312**: implementation-time note added.\n- **313**: new, research/blocked.\n\nWant me to walk through the new 302/304 text to check it lands right?"
      }]
  },
  "slug":"snug-booping-dove",

```json
{
  "timestamp":"2026-05-10T00:51:01.980Z",

    "content":[{
        "tool_use_id":"toolu_01QodsFNGaPbjwEHEkFtMNXJ",
        "content":"1\t# 302 — Per-task slot store with wire-held references\n2\t\n3\t## Status\n4\topen\n5\t\n6\t## Current behavior\n7\tWire values are passed through stdout pipes and transient strings. Values\n8\thave no addressable location, no reference count, and no cross-language\n9\taccessibility. Each value vanishes once the pipe is drained.\n10\t\n11\t## Concept\n12\t\n13\t### Slots belong to input ports, not tasks\n14\t\n15\tEach box has **one slot per input port**, allocated when the graph\n16\tloads and persisting for the life of the run. A wire is a routing\n17\tdeclaration: \"the producer's output port pushes a copy of its value\n18\tinto this consumer's named input slot.\" The producer never owns a\n19\tslot — its output is a routing event, not a stored value.\n20\t\n21\tWhen a producer fires, the dispatch layer copies the value into\n22\tevery downstream input slot wired to that output. Fan-out is N\n23\tpushes (one per consumer); fan-in is N producers all pushing into\n24\tthe same consumer's slot. Both behaviors fall out of the same\n25\tpush-into-input-slot mechanic.\n26\t\n27\tSlots live in process heap memory, accessible to every worker\n28\tthread. Cross-process visibility is not required: language specs\n29\t(issue 303) only ever receive byte pointers — never raw slot\n30\taddresses — so out-of-process specs (Bash) work via sockets, not\n31\tshared memory.\n32\t\n33\t### Tasks are ephemeral; box state is durable\n34\t\n35\tA **task** is one invocation: pop one value from each of the box's\n36\tinput slots, run the box's logic, push the output to every\n37\tdownstream input slot. Tasks have no persistent identity — they're\n38\tjust stack frames on workers. Tasks are spawned dynamically by the\n39\tdispatch layer when a box's input set is ready (every input slot\n40\tholds at least one value).\n41\t\n42\tThe **box** is the durable thing: it owns its input port slots, any\n43\tcounter state (for iterators), its language spec handle, and so\n44\ton. The box exists from graph load until run end. Tasks come and\n45\tgo.\n46\t\n47\tThis is uniform across iterator and non-iterator boxes. Both run N\n48\ttimes where N depends on how many invocations their inputs supply\n49\t(possibly 1, possibly thousands).       "content":"# 302 — Per-task slot store with wire-held references\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nWire values are passed through stdout pipes and transient strings. Values\nhave no addressable location, no reference count, and no cross-language\naccessibility. Each value vanishes once the pipe is drained.\n\n## Concept\n\n### Slots belong to input ports, not tasks\n\nEach box has **one slot per input port**, allocated when the graph\nloads and persisting for the life of the run. A wire is a routing\ndeclaration: \"the producer's output port pushes a copy of its value\ninto this consumer's named input slot.\" The producer never owns a\nslot — its output is a routing event, not a stored value.\n\nWhen a producer fires, the dispatch layer copies the value into\nevery downstream input slot wired to that output. Fan-out is N\npushes (one per consumer); fan-in is N producers all pushing into\nthe same consumer's slot. Both behaviors fall out of the same\npush-into-input-slot mechanic.\n\nSlots live in process heap memory, accessible to every worker\nthread. Cross-process visibility is not required: language specs\n(issue 303) only ever receive byte pointers — never raw slot\naddresses — so out-of-process specs (Bash) work via sockets, not\nshared memory.\n\n### Tasks are ephemeral; box state is durable\n\nA **task** is one invocation: pop one value from each of the box's\ninput slots, run the box's logic, push the output to every\ndownstream input slot. Tasks have no persistent identity — they're\njust stack frames on workers. Tasks are spawned dynamically by the\ndispatch layer when a box's input set is ready (every input slot\nholds at least one value).\n\nThe **box** is the durable thing: it owns its input port slots, any\ncounter state (for iterators), its language spec handle, and so\non. The box exists from graph load until run end. Tasks come and\ngo.\n\nThis is uniform across iterator and non-iterator boxes. Both run N\ntimes where N depends on how many invocations their inputs supply\n(possibly 1, possibly thousands). The difference is just what the\ntask does:\n- **Plain call task**: invoke spec on the popped values, push the\n  return to outputs.\n- **Iterator task**: read box's counter, route the popped value to\n  output port `iterator_outputs[counter]`, increment counter mod N.\n  No spec invocation.\n- **Comparator task**: invoke spec on the popped values, compare\n  the return against `comparand`, route to the matching `lt` /\n  `eq` / `gt` branch.\n\n### All slots are ring buffers\n\nThere is one slot type. It is a ring buffer of `n_cells` cells,\neach of `cell_capacity` bytes. Every input port has a ring buffer\nof compile-time-determined size:\n\n- **Default size**: enough cells to absorb the maximum number of\n  pushes that can happen before the box can drain. For a port fed\n  by a single non-iterator producer, that's 1. For a port fed by\n  an iterator, it's the iterator's worst-case backlog (statically\n  inferred or capped at a high default like 64 with growth).\n- **Upper bound**: lists grow if backlog exceeds the pre-allocated\n  size, so n_cells isn't a hard cap on correctness — only on\n  pre-allocation efficiency.\n\nThe producer pushes one cell per fan-out path; the consumer pops\none cell per invocation. Fan-in is multiple producers pushing into\nthe same input slot in arrival order; the consumer pops in FIFO\norder.\n\n### Asynchrony\nThe store is fully asynchronous. Slots are allocated, filled, read, and\nfreed at any time, on any thread, with no global lock. Synchronization\nis per-slot. There is no central allocator-wide mutex.\n\n## Slot layout\n\nEach slot is a header followed by `n_cells` cells, each `cell_capacity`\nbytes. The header tracks ring-buffer state and lifetime:\n\n```\nSlot header\nOffset  Size  Field\n------  ----  -----\n0       4     refcount        (atomic int32; lifetime counter)\n4       4     cell_capacity   (bytes per cell, set at allocation)\n8       4     n_cells         (ring size, set at allocation; 1 for single-value)\n12      4     head            (read index, mod n_cells)\n16      4     tail            (write index, mod n_cells; cells_filled = tail - head)\n20      1     touched         (per-slot lock: 0=free, 1=another thread mutating)\n21      3     _pad\n24      …     cells           (n_cells * (4-byte size + cell_capacity bytes))\n```\n\nEach cell stores a 4-byte filled-size followed by `cell_capacity`\nbytes of value data. Cells have wildly different capacities across\nslots — capacity is per-slot, not global. The C convention of passing\nsizes alongside arrays applies: the task that allocates a slot knows\nhow big it needs the cells.\n\n`touched` is a single-byte flag toggled around any header mutation\n(push, pop, refcount changes). A reader that finds `touched == 1`\nspins until it clears. This is the simplest possible per-slot lock —\nif contention proves to matter, replace with a proper mutex without\nchanging the API.\n\nWrites to a cell complete with a memory barrier before `tail` is\nadvanced, so a reader that observes `head < tail` is guaranteed to\nsee the complete value at the head cell.\n\n## Lifetime and end-of-stream\n\nSlots are owned by the box that holds the input port. They live\nfrom graph load until run end. There is no per-slot reference\ncounting — the slot is freed when the run ends, alongside its\nowning box.\n\n### End-of-stream detection (replacing producer refcounts)\n\nEach slot tracks the set of upstream producer boxes that may still\npush into it. When a producer's \"no more pushes\" condition fires\n— either it has finished all its invocations, or it transitively\ndepends only on producers that have finished — the dispatch layer\nremoves that producer from the slot's producer set.\n\nWhen the producer set is empty AND the slot's queue is drained,\nthe consumer box has reached end-of-stream on that port. For an\niterator, this is what tells the iterator to stop re-spawning. For\na non-iterator, this means no further invocations are coming;\ncombined with the same condition on its other input ports, the\nbox itself is done.\n\nThis replaces the per-slot refcount machinery. The \"are upstreams\nstill alive\" check is done at the producer-set level, which is\ncheaper and avoids the contention of refcount churn on hot paths.\n\n### Wait list\nEach slot also owns a wait list — pointers to tasks parked on the\nslot waiting for a value. When a producer pushes, the slot walks the\nwait list and tells the pool to re-run those tasks. The wait list is\nattached to the slot, not to the producer or the consumer.\n\n## Backing store\n\nSlots are allocated from process heap memory. The slot store owns a\nper-run allocator (described under \"Allocation strategy\" below) that\nhands out memory chunks to slots. Plain `malloc`-class memory is\nsufficient — every worker thread in the process can read and write\nit, and no spec ever needs to access it from a child process.\n\nSynchronization within a slot uses the per-slot `touched` flag for\nheader mutations and a per-slot wait list (above) for blocked tasks.\nThere is no allocator-wide mutex on the read/write path; only the\nper-size-class free lists in the allocator have their own locks.\n\n## Slot creation\n\nSlot creation happens at **graph load**, not per task. The graph\nloader walks every box, allocates one ring buffer per input port,\nand parks the slot on the box's per-port slot table. The dispatch\nlayer never allocates new slots at runtime in the steady state —"

    "stop_reason":"end_turn",
    "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"Walkthrough of the design as it stands. Let me go layer by layer.\n\n## 1. The big picture\n\nSoraMech is split into three programs:\n- **Editor** (web, JS): visual graph editor that writes `maps/<name>/` directory contents.\n- **Runner** (C, phase 3): pool runner that executes a map.\n- **Server** (Lua, phase 2 → eventually disposable): file CRUD between editor and disk.\n\nThe map directory is the contract between editor and runner. Boxes live in `maps/<name>/boxes/*.json`; source files in `maps/<name>/src/`; meta in `maps/<name>/meta.json`. The editor writes and the runner reads.\n\n## 2. The graph\n\nA **box** is a node. Two kinds:\n- `call`: invokes a user-written function in some language.\n- `data`: language-agnostic file source / sink (issue 229, planned — currently behaves like a colored call box).\n\nA **port** is an input or output position on a box. Inputs are named (from the parsed function signature). Outputs are either a single unnamed port, or three named branches `lt`/`eq`/`gt` (comparator), or N user-named slots (iterator).\n\nA **wire** is a routing declaration: producer's named output port → consumer's named input port. Wires don't own data; they're metadata in the graph.\n\nThree **box modes**, all set per-box rather than per-kind:\n- **Plain call**: function runs, returns one value, value goes to all wired downstream consumers unconditionally.\n- **Comparator**: same, plus the value is compared to the box's `comparand` field; only the matching branch fires.\n- **Iterator**: no function. Per invocation, the box copies its input to one of N output ports based on a counter, then increments. Pure routing.\n\n## 3. Startup (issue 301)\n\nThe pool runner's `main`:\n1. Parse map path from argv.\n2. Load + validate the graph (C loader, issue 305 — replaces phase 2's `003-loader.lua`).\n3. For each box: allocate one ring-buffer slot per input port. Sizes from compile-time analysis (1 for non-iterator-fed, larger for iterator-fed, growable on demand).\n4. Build per-box runtime state: `box_runtime_state[box_id]` holding the input slot table, the iterator counter (0), the producer set per slot (boxes that may still push there).\n5. Create the worker pool (3d-rts vendored library, `libs/task-pool/`). Each worker calls each language spec's `init(worker_idx)` to stand up its per-thread state — one `lua_State`, one persistent Bash subprocess, one C dlopen table per worker.\n6. Push every input port's literal value (if set) directly into its slot.\n7. For each box whose input set is now satisfied (every input slot has a value), spawn a `dispatch_task_t` and submit to the pool.\n8. Main thread sleeps on a condition variable waiting for the active-task counter to hit zero.\n9. On wake, write `last-run.jsonl`, tear down workers, exit.\n\nAfter step 8, **no main-thread orchestration**. Workers drive everything.\n\n## 4. Slots (issue 302, revised)\n\nEach box owns one ring-buffer slot per input port. Slot header is 20 bytes:\n\n```\ncell_capacity (4) | n_cells (4) | head (4) | tail (4) | touched (1) | _pad (3)\nfollowed by n_cells * (4-byte size + cell_capacity bytes) of cell data\n```\n\nPushes write a cell + advance `tail`; pops read at `head` + advance `head`. `touched` is a per-slot spinlock byte.\n\n**Allocation strategy**: size-class free lists. Compile time enumerates every distinct slot size; lists pre-populate at startup; allocations are list pops (O(1)). Variable-size payloads (LLM responses, dynamic arrays) live in a separate **large-value heap**; the slot stores a `{size, offset}` handle into it. When a slot's pre-allocated `n_cells` proves too small, the slot grows (lists grow during the run).\n\n**Lifetime**: durable for the run. No per-slot refcounting. End-of-stream is detected via the **producer set** per slot: the dispatch layer tracks which producer boxes may still push, and removes producers as they finish. When the set is empty AND the slot is drained, the consumer has end-of-stream on that port.\n\n## 5. Dispatch (issue 304, revised)\n\nA **task** is `{ box_id, counter }`. That's it. Slots aren't on the task because they're durable on the box.\n\n**Spawning rule** (the synchronization primitive of the whole system):\n> When a push to box B's input slot completes, check: does every input slot on B now hold at least one value? If yes, allocate a task with `box_id=B, counter=B.counter`, submit to the pool.\n\n**The dispatch action** (`dispatch_action(task)`), runs on whichever worker pulled the task:\n\n1. **Read inputs**: `slot_pop` from each of B's input slots into heap buffers. Pop drains; values queued behind move forward.\n2. **Branch on box mode**:\n   - Plain call → invoke spec, write return to outputs.\n   - Comparator → invoke spec, write return to outputs, compare return to `comparand`, fire only matching branch.\n   - Iterator → no spec, route popped value to `iterator_outputs[counter]`, increment counter mod N.\n3. **Push to downstream input slots**: the box's connection list has the wire targets. For each wire that should fire (per mode), `slot_push(downstream_input_slot, bytes, size)`. After each push, run the spawn-rule check for that downstream box — possibly spawn another task.\n4. **End-of-stream propagation**: if this push was the producer's last expected push, remove this producer from each pushed-to slot's producer set. Empty set + drained queue = consumer's end-of-stream on that port.\n5. Return ACT_DONE. Pool decrements active-task counter. If counter hits zero, signal main thread.\n\nNo phase blocks. No wait lists. Tasks are spawn-then-run-to-completion.\n\n**Cross-iterator pairing**: when a non-iterator C has two upstream iterators A and B, each port has its own queue, FIFO pop pairs `(A_i, B_i)` deterministically iff A and B push in deterministic order. Concurrent pushes from different workers risk race. Phase 3 ships FIFO; per-invocation index tags are a follow-on if a workload needs strict pairing.\n\n## 6. Language specs (issue 303 + 312)\n\nEach language ships `langs/<name>/spec.so` and `langs/<name>/lexer.js` and `langs/<name>/parser.js` (issue 231, planned).\n\nSpec interface (with the 312 fast-path additions):\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    const char *name, *file_ext;\n\n    void *(*init)(int worker_idx);\n    void  (*teardown)(void *handle);\n    int   (*compile)(const char *src_path, const char *out_path, const box_t *box);\n\n    int   (*invoke_json)  (handle, file, fn, in_data[], in_sizes[], n, out_buf, out_cap, out_size);\n    int   (*invoke_native)(handle, file, fn, in_data[], in_sizes[], n, out_buf, out_cap, out_size);\n\n    int   (*native_to_json)(src, src_size, dst, dst_cap, dst_size);\n    int   (*json_to_native)(src, src_size, dst, dst_cap, dst_size);\n} lang_spec_t;\n```\n\nThe pool runner `dlopen`s every `langs/<name>/spec.so` at startup and indexes by name and extension.\n\n**Wire format** is JSON by default — every spec implements `invoke_json` for cross-language hops. Same-language wires use `invoke_native` with a per-language native serialization (Lua tables via msgpack or `lua_dump`; C structs via memcpy; Bash strings as-is). The compile step (issue 309) classifies each wire as `fast_path: true | false` based on whether endpoints share a language, and tags the producer's output_format. Dispatch action's input-read branches on this flag — no runtime negotiation.\n\n**Type-annotated cross-language encodings** (primitives as raw bytes, strings length-prefixed, structures as JSON) — open question per 312's implementation note. Decision deferred to implementation start.\n\n**Per-language specs**:\n- Lua (306): `lua_State` per worker, file caching via Lua registry, in-process invocation.\n- C (307): `dlopen`/`dlsym` per worker, compile callback generates a per-box wrapper that takes a count + pointer array and forwards to the user function.\n- Bash (308): persistent subprocess per worker, length-prefixed message protocol over Unix domain socket. Out-of-process because Bash has no embeddable runtime.\n\n## 7. Build / compile (issue 309)\n\nTop-level Makefile orchestrates. Targets:\n- `runner` → `soramech-pool` binary, statically linking the pool, slot store, graph loader, dispatch, spec registry.\n- `specs` → recurses into each `langs/<name>/Makefile` to build `spec.so`.\n- `clean`, `test`, `DEBUG=1`, `STRICT=1` modes.\n\n**Compile-and-package step** (folded in from issue 219, closed): turns an editable map directory into `maps/<name>/compiled/` with the runner binary, source files, per-box `.so`s, language spec `.so`s, and a manifest. Triggered by the editor's Compile button (issue 222) via a `POST /maps/<name>/compile` endpoint and by a CLI `soramech-compile <map-dir>`.\n\n**Compile-time validations** (also during compile):\n- Required-input rule (issue 230): every input port has a wire, a literal, or `optional: true`. Compile fails loudly if not.\n- Wire fast-path classification (issue 312): each wire tagged `fast_path` per same/different language pair.\n- Producer-set determination per input slot for end-of-stream tracking.\n- Output sizes per box for the slot-store size-class allocator.\n\n## 8. Quiescence and run output\n\nEach task spawn increments the active-task counter; each ACT_DONE decrements. When the counter hits zero, no task is running and no further spawns are pending — run is over. Iterators that hit end-of-stream stop spawning successors naturally; the counter drains.\n\n**No deadlock concern** at runtime. The graph loader rejects non-iterator cycles and inputs without producers at load time. Spec errors abort the program (no halfway-complete state). Iterator-parked-on-empty-input is the natural EOS condition, not a deadlock.\n\n`last-run.jsonl` is written at the end (issue 311): one JSON line per box invocation with timing, inputs, outputs, errors. Replay-friendly format.\n\n## 9. Cross-cutting concerns\n\n- **No null from missing inputs** (issue 230): compile fails on unwired non-optional ports; absent ≠ explicit null at the spec boundary.\n- **Variadic** (per-box flag, issue 217 complete; issue 231 planned for per-language parser): user-tagged in editor, dispatch flattens slots into ordered arg list, language's native variadic syntax handles it.\n- **Self-loop wires** (issue 228 complete): allowed; dispatch just pushes from a box's output to its own input slot like any other push.\n- **Optional inputs** (issue 230): port's `optional: true` flag; spawn rule allows the task even with that slot empty; the spec's invocation passes a shorter arg list.\n\n## 10. Editor surface to runtime\n\nThings in the editor that produce runtime state:\n- `kind`, `ref`, `fn` → which box, which language, which function.\n- `inputs[].name`, `inputs[].value`, `inputs[].optional` → input port names, literals, optionality.\n- `comparand` → comparator threshold.\n- `iterator_outputs[]` → iterator branch names + count.\n- `variadic_inputs[]` → which input names are variadic group bases.\n- `connections[]` → wires.\n- `has_output` → sink box flag.\n\nThe runtime never reads anything outside this set from the box JSON. The editor is the source of truth for graph shape; the runner is the source of truth for execution.\n\n---\n\nThat's the design end-to-end. Where do you want to dig deeper, or what doesn't sit right?"
      }]
  },

        "text":"Good catches — several of these point at design holes. Let me work through them, then we update the issues.\n\n## 1. Why iterator-fed ports get larger buffers\n\nIt's backlog absorption. A non-iterator producer pushes its slot **once** for its lifetime; one cell is enough. An iterator produces N values across N invocations; if N is 50 and the consumer can only drain at half the producer's rate, the slot has to hold up to 25 unconsumed values at any moment.\n\nFor non-iterator-fed ports, the producer-rate question doesn't arise — there's only ever one push.\n\n## 2. Owning the thread pool, not vendoring 3d-rts\n\nAgreed. The pool is part of SoraMech's surface area; we want full control over the spawn primitive, the worker-context model, and any extensions (tying iterators to specific workers, see §8 below). We'll write a SoraMech-specific pool and refer to 3d-rts only as the design reference / inspiration. Worth updating issue 301.\n\n## 3. Init synchronization\n\nRight — we need a barrier after every worker has called every spec's `init` and before any task is submitted. Otherwise the main thread could push tasks while a worker is still bringing up its `lua_State`, and a task that lands on the not-yet-initialized worker would read a null handle.\n\nThe shape: pool startup is a join point. Workers come up, each one runs all the spec inits in some defined order, and signals readiness on a counter. Main thread waits until all N workers have signaled, **then** pushes literals and spawns initial tasks. Worth updating 301.\n\n## 4. The literal re-push problem (you found a real hole)\n\nRight. With the pop-draining model I wrote, a literal pushed once at startup gets consumed by the first task and the second task finds an empty slot. Broken for any box that runs more than once.\n\nThe fix is to bring back a distinction I'd flattened: **non-iterator-fed slots are peek-not-pop, iterator-fed slots are pop-and-drain**. Original 302 had this; I lost it in the rewrite.\n\nConcretely:\n- A 1-cell slot's read mode is **peek**: the value stays after a read, every subsequent task on this box reads the same value.\n- An N-cell slot's read mode is **pop**: each read drains one cell, subsequent tasks see the next value.\n\nFor the user's question: a literal pushed at startup stays in the slot. If the box runs 50 times because some other input port (iterator-fed, N-cell, drained) supplies 50 values, each of those 50 task instances peeks the literal. The literal isn't re-pushed — it doesn't need to be.\n\nThe spawn-rule check becomes: \"every input port's slot has at least one value **available**\" — which means \"non-empty cell\" for both kinds, just with different semantics on read.\n\nThis deserves an update to 302, both the slot-read section and the spawn-rule section.\n\n## 5. End-of-stream / producer set — you're right, drop it\n\nYour read is exactly right: the producer-set machinery is overengineering. The active-task counter (issue 301) already handles run termination correctly:\n- Each task spawn increments.\n- Each ACT_DONE decrements.\n- When it hits zero with no pending spawns, the run is over.\n\nThe producer-set was answering \"should this iterator stop expecting more inputs?\" — but iterators don't need to ask that question. They just stop getting tasks when their input slot stops getting pushed. The active-task counter naturally drains, the run ends.\n\nI shouldn't have added the producer-set thing. Let me strip it from 302/304. The end-of-stream condition becomes trivial: there is no end-of-stream condition, just an active-task counter reaching zero.\n\nBox JSON has the producer→consumer relationships; runtime doesn't need to mutate that. You're right that mutating-the-graph-at-runtime felt like garbage collection — it was, and the cost wasn't worth it.\n\n## 6. Large value passed C → Lua\n\nHonest answer: **cross-language large values get copied at the boundary, no way around it**.\n\nLua's string memory is owned by Lua's GC. C-allocated memory has no relationship to Lua's string table. There's no zero-copy path: even Lua's userdata, which can wrap a C pointer, requires Lua code to call back into C to read bytes — defeating the purpose if you're trying to pass it to a Lua function expecting a string.\n\nThe flow:\n1. C spec produces 4MB string. Writes it to the large-value heap. Slot cell holds `{size: 4MB, offset: ...}`.\n2. Lua spec invoked. Receives the 16-byte handle. Follows the offset, finds the bytes in the large-value heap.\n3. **Copies** those bytes into a Lua string via `lua_pushlstring(L, bytes, 4MB)`. Lua's GC now owns a copy.\n4. The user's Lua function gets a normal Lua string.\n\nThe 4MB copy is the price of going across the language boundary. Lua's memory model is incompatible with referencing external memory.\n\nSame-language paths can avoid the copy: C → C can pass the handle directly; the consumer's wrapper reads from the same large-value heap with no copy. Lua → Lua can reuse Lua's own table-passing via `lua_dump`/`lua_load` or msgpack. That's what the same-language fast path (issue 312) buys you.\n\nYou're right that this is \"an impossible optimization\" for cross-language. The right move isn't to optimize the cross-language case — it's to design graphs so large values don't cross language boundaries. The same-language merge research issue (313) eventually lets the build system warn about this kind of crossing.\n\n## 7. Counter as invisible input port\n\nBoth work. The choice is between:\n\n**A: Per-box counter state** (current 304). Box has `counter` field. Each spawn snapshots `counter` into the task; box's counter increments. Pro: simple, one int per iterator box, no extra slot machinery. Con: special-cases iterator boxes in the runtime.\n\n**B: Counter as a hidden input slot.** Box has a 1-cell slot named `__counter__` (invisible to user). At spawn time, the dispatch layer pops the counter value, runs the action, pushes counter+1 back to the slot. Pro: counter goes through the same machinery as everything else; no special box state. Con: more pushes/pops on the hot path; the slot is conceptually special even if structurally uniform.\n\nI'd lean A for performance; B is more elegant. Worth picking explicitly — let me know which way and I'll lock it in 304.\n\n## 8. Cross-iterator pairing under \"phase 3 as designed\"\n\nOK, let's commit to a pairing answer.\n\nThe race you're worried about: iterator A produces 50 invocations. Task 1 produces value `a0`, task 2 produces `a1`, etc. Tasks could run on different workers in parallel; if task 2 finishes before task 1, the pushes to consumer C's slot arrive in the wrong order.\n\nBut — iterator tasks share the **per-box counter** as state. To spawn task 2, the dispatch layer reads the counter, snapshots it, then increments. Two iterator tasks of the same iterator can't really run in parallel anyway: they have a serial dependency through the counter.\n\nThe cleanest answer is **iterators are pinned to a single worker**. Each iterator has its tasks executed sequentially on that worker. Push order = invocation order = FIFO arrival at the consumer's slot, deterministic.\n\nTrade-off: an iterator's invocations don't parallelize across workers. Other tasks (downstream consumers, parallel iterators on different workers) absolutely do. Most graphs aren't bottlenecked on a single iterator's throughput; they're bottlenecked on the consumers' work.\n\nFor cases where one iterator IS the bottleneck and parallel invocations would help — that's the \"indexed pairing\" follow-on. Each push tags its value with the iterator's counter snapshot; consumer's slot becomes a priority-insert structure that pops in tag order. Strict ordering, parallel iterator invocations. Complex enough that we don't ship it without proof we need it.\n\nSo phase 3 as designed: **single-worker iterators + FIFO consumer slots, deterministic pairing as a free consequence**.\n\n---\n\n## Issue updates this implies\n\nLet me consolidate. I'd update:\n\n1. **301** — replace \"vendored 3d-rts\" with \"SoraMech-owned pool, design referenced from 3d-rts.\" Add an explicit init-barrier section before task submission begins.\n2. **302** — restore the peek-vs-pop distinction (1-cell slots peek, N-cell slots pop). Drop the producer-set section. Update the spawn-rule wording.\n3. **304** — drop end-of-stream propagation. Pick between counter-as-box-state vs counter-as-hidden-slot (waiting on your call). Add the iterator-pinned-to-worker rule for deterministic pairing.\n\nShould I make these updates? And which counter model do you want — per-box state, or hidden input slot?"
      }]

  "timestamp":"2026-05-10T02:38:53.832Z",

    "content":"  1. Why iterator-fed ports get larger buffers\n\n  It's backlog absorption. A non-iterator producer pushes its slot once for its lifetime; one cell is enough. An iterator produces N values\n  across N invocations; if N is 50 and the consumer can only drain at half the producer's rate, the slot has to hold up to 25 unconsumed\n  values at any moment.\n\n  For non-iterator-fed ports, the producer-rate question doesn't arise — there's only ever one push.\n\n\nOkay, when you say iterators, producers, and consumers here, do you mean the BOX, or the TASK? Also, keep in mind that an iterator pushes it's values to more target boxes, but it doesn't necessarily do it more than a regular, non iterator task - every time input values come in, a box processes them according to it's rules (a regular box runs a function on them, an iterator simply routes them, but they are \"processed\" none-the-less). It doesn't matter how many times a box runs, it will always do the same thing. Similarly, an iterator doesn't provide more instances of the same data to a particular target - it simply provides it's values to *different* destinations each time.\n\n  2. Owning the thread pool, not vendoring 3d-rts\n\n  Agreed. The pool is part of SoraMech's surface area; we want full control over the spawn primitive, the worker-context model, and any\n  extensions (tying iterators to specific workers, see §8 below). We'll write a SoraMech-specific pool and refer to 3d-rts only as the design\n   reference / inspiration. Worth updating issue 301.\n\n\nWe should update not just the issue file, but all the relevant docs. Also, consider checking your memory files for 3d-rts references.\n\n  The shape: pool startup is a join point. Workers come up, each one runs all the spec inits in some defined order, and signals readiness on\n  a counter. Main thread waits until all N workers have signaled, then pushes literals and spawns initial tasks. Worth updating 301.\n\nYes, please make the required updates. This seems like a good design.\n\n  The fix is to bring back a distinction I'd flattened: non-iterator-fed slots are peek-not-pop, iterator-fed slots are pop-and-drain.\n  Original 302 had this; I lost it in the rewrite.\n\n  Concretely:\n  - A 1-cell slot's read mode is peek: the value stays after a read, every subsequent task on this box reads the same value.\n  - An N-cell slot's read mode is pop: each read drains one cell, subsequent tasks see the next value.\n\n\nwhat does 1-cell and n-cell mean in this context? Are you referring to the memory sizes?\n\n  A: Per-box counter state (current 304). Box has counter field. Each spawn snapshots counter into the task; box's counter increments. Pro:\n  simple, one int per iterator box, no extra slot machinery. Con: special-cases iterator boxes in the runtime.\n\nwe should do this approach, though if you can think of a way to do it that's more \"functional programming\" style, please let me know before we commit.\n\n  But — iterator tasks share the per-box counter as state. To spawn task 2, the dispatch layer reads the counter, snapshots it, then\n  increments. Two iterator tasks of the same iterator can't really run in parallel anyway: they have a serial dependency through the counter.\n\nwe should try and design a way that they can run in parallel. Ideally, they'd be so similar to any other box that the engine would treat them exactly the same. If the dependency on the counter is the only blocker, I bet we can come up with a solution if we iron out the dataflow. The goal eventually is to allow functions to iterate their outputs themselves, similarly to how we're handling the comparator functionality.\n\n  The cleanest answer is iterators are pinned to a single worker. Each iterator has its tasks executed sequentially on that worker. Push\n  order = invocation order = FIFO arrival at the consumer's slot, deterministic.\n\nthe cleanest answer in this case is not the optimal answer. Let's keep trying.\n\n  Should I make these updates? And which counter model do you want — per-box state, or hidden input slot?\n\nmake any updates that aren't contradicted or blocked by the further follow up questions I have here.",

        "text":"Right, you're correcting valid mistakes in my framing. Let me work through the answers, then make the updates.\n\n## 1. Box vs task clarification\n\nYou're right, my terminology was sloppy. To re-state precisely:\n\n**Boxes** are graph nodes — static, defined in JSON, exist for the run. **Tasks** are box invocations — ephemeral, allocated when a spawn fires. A box may have 1 or N tasks during a run.\n\nWhat I meant by \"iterator producer pushes 50 times\": *the iterator box, across its 50 task invocations, performs 50 pushes total.* Each individual iterator task does the same single push that any task does. The box is what fires multiple times; each task does exactly one thing.\n\nYou're also right that \"iterator vs non-iterator\" isn't really the buffer-size axis. **Any box can have many tasks**. A non-iterator downstream of an iterator runs as many times as the iterator fires its branch. Its output gets pushed downstream that many times.\n\nSo buffer-size analysis is really: \"how many task invocations of the producer box, and how many of the consumer box, and what's the worst-case backlog at the slot.\" Iterator-fed is the most common case where N>1, but not the only one. I'll restate 302 to use the \"box invocation count\" framing.\n\n## 2. 1-cell vs N-cell\n\n`n_cells` is the number of cells in the ring buffer — i.e., how many distinct values the slot can hold simultaneously. `cell_capacity` is the size in bytes of a single cell. A 1-cell slot holds one value (single-value); an N-cell slot is a queue with N positions.\n\nThe *read mode* (peek vs pop) was historically tied to capacity in the design — 1-cell peek, N-cell pop. They're orthogonal in principle, but coupling them simplifies the API: if you need to keep a value around, allocate 1-cell + peek; if you need a queue, allocate N-cell + pop.\n\n## 3. Counter approach + functional alternative\n\nFunctional alternative I considered: an iterator is a regular box with two inputs — `value` and `counter` — where `counter` is fed by a separate \"counter generator\" box. The counter generator self-loops: takes its previous output as input, emits previous+1. The iterator routes `value` to `outputs[counter % N]`. No iterator-internal state, fully data-driven.\n\nWhy I'd still go with per-box counter for our case: the functional version **serializes counter generation** through the counter box's tasks. Each counter task depends on the previous via the self-loop. To parallelize iterator invocations you'd need the counter box to pre-emit faster than consumers drain, which essentially requires a separate scheduling discipline for the counter box.\n\nThe per-box-counter-with-atomic-increment-at-spawn version gets parallelism for free: at task spawn, atomic fetch-and-add on the counter, snapshot into the task. Sibling iterator tasks run on different workers with independent counter values. Counter is a single int + atomic op per spawn.\n\nSo I'd ship per-box counter with atomic spawn-time increment, but I'll note the functional alternative in 304 as a documented trade-off for future reconsideration if it ever bites.\n\n## 4. Parallel iterator execution — yes, achievable\n\nWith atomic spawn-time counter increment, iterator tasks can run in parallel. The race that's left is **push ordering at the consumer**: if iterator A's tasks 5 and 6 run on different workers, task 6 might push to consumer C first.\n\nSolution: **each push carries a tag** equal to the source iterator's counter at task-spawn time. Consumer slots become tag-ordered (priority queue): pop returns the lowest-tag value, not the head value. For non-iterator producers, tag is always 0 (or omitted); FIFO falls out for free.\n\nCost: ~4-8 bytes per cell for the tag field. Slot pop becomes O(log n) instead of O(1) for tag-ordered slots. Compile-time analysis tags only the slots that need ordering (downstream of iterators, in branches that preserve order).\n\nThis restores deterministic pairing and lets iterator tasks parallelize. It's the \"indexed pairing\" follow-on, but for \"phase 3 as designed\" we should pull it forward. Worth specifying now, not later.\n\n## 5. Now updating the issues\n\nLet me start with the search."
      }]

The phase 2 path goes away when phase 3 lands — no fallback, no coroutine intermediate.\n\n**Phase 3 (designed, not yet built)**: C pool runner with a SoraMech-owned thread pool. The 3d-rts pool at `/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h` is the **design reference**, not vendored — SoraMech owns its pool implementation so the spawn primitive, worker context, init barrier, and iterator-pinning extensions are all under our control. No blocking, no wait lists; tasks spawn on input arrival and run to completion.\n- **Iterator and comparator routing** in the dispatch layer. Comparator runs the function and routes by output value. Iterator skips the function and routes by per-box counter (atomic spawn-time increment). Iterator tasks parallelize across workers; ordering preserved via per-push counter tags on consumer slots.\n- **No-null rule** (issue 230): every input port must be wired, given a literal, or marked optional. Compile fails on missing inputs.\n- **Init barrier**: pool startup waits until every worker has run every spec's `init(worker_idx)` before submitting tasks. Avoids tasks landing on uninitialized handles.\n- **Hard-crash error policy**: nonzero return from any spec aborts the program.\n- **Blocking semantics**: long-running operations tie up a worker. Pool size is the budget. Cooperative split (kickoff + check-done iterator) avoids holding a worker. See `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md`.\n\n**Effil is explicitly NOT used.** Coroutines are not used. The C pool is the chosen mechanism. 3d-rts is referenced as design inspiration, not vendored.\n\n**How to apply:** When discussing threading, parallelism, or cross-language IPC: phase 2 is synchronous shell-out drivers; phase 3 is the SoraMech-owned C pool runner with `lang_spec_t`, per-port slot stores, and dispatch-layer routing. Never suggest effil. 3d-rts is a reference, not a dependency. Issues 301–313 carry the design.\n",
          "file_path":"/home/ritz/.claude/projects/-mnt-mtwo-programs-sora-soramech/memory/project_threading.md"
        },

      "content":"## Intended behavior\n\n### Pool source\nThe thread pool is the 3d-rts pool library at\n`/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h`\n(and its `.c` companion). It is vendored into SoraMech — copied, not\nsymlinked — so SoraMech's compilation does not depend on the 3d-rts\nworking tree. Vendored copy lives at `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.h`\nand `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.c`.\n\n### Where the pool lives in the process\nThe pool is owned by the map runner's C entry point. One pool per map\nrun. It is created after the graph is loaded and validated, and\ndestroyed after the run completes.\n\nThe C entry point (`src/008-pool-runner.c`):\n\n```c\nint main(int argc, char **argv) {\n    // 1. parse map path from argv\n    // 2. load and validate graph (C loader, no Lua involved)\n    // 3. determine which language runtimes the map uses\n    // 4. pool = pool_create(n_workers)\n    // 5. init per-worker language runtime handles for each language present\n    // 6. submit tasks for all entry-point boxes\n    // 7. wait for active task count to reach zero\n    // 8. pool_destroy(pool)\n    // 9. write last-run.json\n}\n```\n\n### Graph loading: ported to C\nThe graph loader is ported from `src/003-loader.lua` to C and lives\ninside (or alongside) `008-pool-runner.c`. The pool runner has no\nembedded Lua state for loader purposes. JSON parsing uses a small\nvendored C JSON library (cJSON or similar; decision deferred to\nimplementation).\n\nLua appears in the runner only when a box's language is Lua — and even\nthen, only inside that worker's language runtime handle. The pool\nrunner itself does not link to liblua at the top level.\n\n### Per-worker language runtimes\nNo language is treated as the \"native\" or preferred language at the\nthread level. Every box — regardless of language — goes through the\nsame task dispatch path. The per-box cost is determined by that box's\ninvocation wrapper, not by any map-level language setting.\n\nEach worker thread holds a set of language runtime handles, one per\nlanguage it may be asked to run. These are initialized once at pool\nstartup, before any tasks are submitted, and torn down at shutdown:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    void   *handles[N_LANGS];   // opaque per-language runtime state\n    int     thread_idx;\n} worker_ctx_t;\n```\n\nOnly the language handles actually needed by the map are initialized.\nIf the map contains no Bash boxes, no Bash handle is started for any\nworker. The graph loader determines which languages are present and\npasses that set to the pool runner at startup.\n\nThe per-language initialization protocol is defined by the language\nruntime spec (issue 303). The pool runner calls each spec's `init`\nfunction at startup and its `teardown` function at shutdown.\n\n### Worker context access\nWorker context is stored in thread-local storage (`__thread\nworker_ctx_t *current_worker`), set by each worker immediately after\nthe thread is started. This avoids per-task `pthread_self()` lookups.\n\n### Pool size\nNumber of worker threads defaults to the number of logical CPUs\n(`sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_ONLN)`), capped at a compile-time maximum\n(`MAX_WORKERS`, initially 16). Can be overridden by an environment\nvariable `SORAMECH_WORKERS=N`.\n\n### Slots are owned by tasks (issue 302)\nSlots are allocated when a task is created, not pre-allocated at\nstartup. A task allocates its output slot(s) at submission time, with\nsize specified by the task's language and function. The pool runner\ndoes not own a slot region — slots are per-task allocations that\noutlive the task only as long as wires hold references to them. See\nissue 302 for the slot lifecycle.\n\n### Quiescence\nThe runner tracks an active-task counter, incremented on `pool_spawn`\nand decremented when a task reaches `ACT_DONE`. The main thread waits"

    "originalFile":"# 301 — Thread pool lifecycle and per-worker initialization\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nThe executor (`src/004-executor.lua`) runs boxes synchronously in a\nsingle Lua coroutine. There is no thread pool, no pthreads, and no\nper-thread language runtime state.\n\n## Phase model\n\nPhase 2 is the synchronous interpreter path. It is the development\ntarget while editor work is in progress.\n\nPhase 3 is the thread pool path. It is the only execution path going\nforward. The synchronous interpreter does not stay around as an\nalternative entry point — once phase 3 lands, the pool runner\nreplaces it. There is no \"fallback to synchronous\" mode.\n\n### Phase 2 → 3 refactor surface\n\nThe following components are replaced (not extended) in phase 3:\n\n| Phase 2 file                  | Phase 3 replacement                  |\n|-------------------------------|--------------------------------------|\n| `src/003-loader.lua`          | C loader inside `src/008-pool-runner.c` |\n| `src/004-executor.lua`        | C task dispatch layer (issue 304)    |\n| `src/007-runner-main.lua`     | `src/008-pool-runner.c`              |\n| `drivers/*.sh`                | Language runtime spec (issue 303)    |\n\nAll threading-pool-adjacent functionality is C code that lives next to\nthe pool. There is no embedded Lua runtime for graph loading or\ndispatch — Lua appears only as a language runtime that boxes can use,\non equal footing with C, Bash, and any future language.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\n### Pool source\nThe thread pool is the 3d-rts pool library at\n`/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h`\n(and its `.c` companion). It is vendored into SoraMech — copied, not\nsymlinked — so SoraMech's compilation does not depend on the 3d-rts\nworking tree. Vendored copy lives at `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.h`\nand `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.c`.\n\n### Where the pool lives in the process\nThe pool is owned by the map runner's C entry point. One pool per map\nrun. It is created after the graph is loaded and validated, and\ndestroyed after the run completes.\n\nThe C entry point (`src/008-pool-runner.c`):\n\n```c\nint main(int argc, char **argv) {\n    // 1. parse map path from argv\n    // 2. load and validate graph (C loader, no Lua involved)\n    // 3. determine which language runtimes the map uses\n    // 4. pool = pool_create(n_workers)\n    // 5. init per-worker language runtime handles for each language present\n    // 6. submit tasks for all entry-point boxes\n    // 7. wait for active task count to reach zero\n    // 8. pool_destroy(pool)\n    // 9. write last-run.json\n}\n```\n\n### Graph loading: ported to C\nThe graph loader is ported from `src/003-loader.lua` to C and lives\ninside (or alongside) `008-pool-runner.c`. The pool runner has no\nembedded Lua state for loader purposes. JSON parsing uses a small\nvendored C JSON library (cJSON or similar; decision deferred to\nimplementation).\n\nLua appears in the runner only when a box's language is Lua — and even\nthen, only inside that worker's language runtime handle. The pool\nrunner itself does not link to liblua at the top level.\n\n### Per-worker language runtimes\nNo language is treated as the \"native\" or preferred language at the\nthread level. Every box — regardless of language — goes through the\nsame task dispatch path. The per-box cost is determined by that box's\ninvocation wrapper, not by any map-level language setting.\n\nEach worker thread holds a set of language runtime handles, one per\nlanguage it may be asked to run. These are initialized once at pool\nstartup, before any tasks are submitted, and torn down at shutdown:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    void   *handles[N_LANGS];   // opaque per-language runtime state\n    int     thread_idx;\n} worker_ctx_t;\n```\n\nOnly the language handles actually needed by the map are initialized.\nIf the map contains no Bash boxes, no Bash handle is started for any\nworker. The graph loader determines which languages are present and\npasses that set to the pool runner at startup.\n\nThe per-language initialization protocol is defined by the language\nruntime spec (issue 303). The pool runner calls each spec's `init`\nfunction at startup and its `teardown` function at shutdown.\n\n### Worker context access\nWorker context is stored in thread-local storage (`__thread\nworker_ctx_t *current_worker`), set by each worker immediately after\nthe thread is started. This avoids per-task `pthread_self()` lookups.\n\n### Pool size\nNumber of worker threads defaults to the number of logical CPUs\n(`sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_ONLN)`), capped at a compile-time maximum\n(`MAX_WORKERS`, initially 16). Can be overridden by an environment\nvariable `SORAMECH_WORKERS=N`.\n\n### Slots are owned by tasks (issue 302)\nSlots are allocated when a task is created, not pre-allocated at\nstartup. A task allocates its output slot(s) at submission time, with\nsize specified by the task's language and function. The pool runner\ndoes not own a slot region — slots are per-task allocations that\noutlive the task only as long as wires hold references to them. See\nissue 302 for the slot lifecycle.\n\n### Quiescence\nThe runner tracks an active-task counter, incremented on `pool_spawn`\nand decremented when a task reaches `ACT_DONE`. The main thread waits\non a condition variable that signals when the counter reaches zero.\n\nThis naturally handles iterators that re-queue themselves: each\nre-queue increments the counter, each completion decrements. When the\ncounter reaches zero, the run is over.\n\nDeadlock is not a concern at runtime. The graph validator (running at\nload) rejects non-iterator cycles and inputs without producers. Errors\ninside a task crash the program (issue 303), so there is no\nhalf-completed-producer case to worry about. An iterator parking\nbecause its upstream queue is empty is not deadlock — it is the\nnatural end-of-stream condition; once the active-task counter reaches\nzero with the iterator parked, the run ends cleanly.\n\n## Open questions\n- Vendored JSON library: cJSON, jsmn, or hand-rolled. cJSON is heavier\n  but easiest. Decision deferred.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. Vendor `900-task-pool.h` + `.c` into `libs/task-pool/`.\n2. Vendor a JSON parser into `libs/json/`.\n3. Port `003-loader.lua` to C inside `src/008-pool-runner.c`.\n4. Write the pool lifecycle skeleton: pool_create, worker context TLS,\n   active-task counter, quiescence wait.\n5. Add `Makefile` target `soramech-pool` that compiles the C runner and\n   links against the vendored pool and JSON parser.\n6. Smoke test: single-box Lua map, pool with 2 workers, box runs, result\n   written. No task graph complexity yet.\n\n## Relevant files\n- `/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h` — pool API\n- `src/003-loader.lua` — current Lua loader, to be ported to C\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — current synchronous executor, to be replaced\n- `src/007-runner-main.lua` — current Lua runner, to be replaced\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — per-task slot lifecycle\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — per-language init/call/teardown\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — replaces 004-executor.lua\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — threading roadmap and IPC options\n",

Each worker's startup runs all `lang->init(worker_idx)` calls in\n   a defined order, populating its `worker_ctx_t.handles[]`.\n2. After completing its inits, each worker increments a shared\n   atomic `workers_ready` counter and blocks on a condition\n   variable.\n3. The main thread waits until `workers_ready == n_workers`.\n4. Main thread broadcasts the condition variable; all workers\n   release simultaneously and begin pulling tasks.\n\nThis is a one-shot barrier — it runs once at pool startup. After\nquiescence it doesn't re-engage; teardown takes a different path.\n\nThe barrier also protects against partial init failures: if any\nworker's `init` returns an error, the barrier never completes and\nthe main thread can detect it via a timeout or per-worker status\nflag.",

    "originalFile":"# 301 — Thread pool lifecycle and per-worker initialization\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nThe executor (`src/004-executor.lua`) runs boxes synchronously in a\nsingle Lua coroutine. There is no thread pool, no pthreads, and no\nper-thread language runtime state.\n\n## Phase model\n\nPhase 2 is the synchronous interpreter path. It is the development\ntarget while editor work is in progress.\n\nPhase 3 is the thread pool path. It is the only execution path going\nforward. The synchronous interpreter does not stay around as an\nalternative entry point — once phase 3 lands, the pool runner\nreplaces it. There is no \"fallback to synchronous\" mode.\n\n### Phase 2 → 3 refactor surface\n\nThe following components are replaced (not extended) in phase 3:\n\n| Phase 2 file                  | Phase 3 replacement                  |\n|-------------------------------|--------------------------------------|\n| `src/003-loader.lua`          | C loader inside `src/008-pool-runner.c` |\n| `src/004-executor.lua`        | C task dispatch layer (issue 304)    |\n| `src/007-runner-main.lua`     | `src/008-pool-runner.c`              |\n| `drivers/*.sh`                | Language runtime spec (issue 303)    |\n\nAll threading-pool-adjacent functionality is C code that lives next to\nthe pool. There is no embedded Lua runtime for graph loading or\ndispatch — Lua appears only as a language runtime that boxes can use,\non equal footing with C, Bash, and any future language.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\n### Pool source\nThe thread pool is **SoraMech-owned**, written from scratch under\n`libs/task-pool/`. The 3d-rts pool at\n`/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h`\nis the **design reference**, not a dependency. We need full control\nover the spawn primitive, the worker context, the init barrier\n(below), and iterator-pinning extensions — all reasons not to inherit\nan external implementation.\n\nThe pool exposes (at minimum):\n\n```c\npool_t *pool_create(int n_workers);\nvoid    pool_destroy(pool_t *p);\nvoid    pool_spawn(pool_t *p, action_fn_t fn, void *arg);\nvoid    pool_wait_quiescent(pool_t *p);   // blocks until active count hits zero\nvoid    pool_init_barrier(pool_t *p);     // see \"Init barrier\" below\n```\n\n3d-rts's frame-ring + park-on-slot machinery is referenced for\npatterns; we don't reimplement features we don't need.\n\n### Where the pool lives in the process\nThe pool is owned by the map runner's C entry point. One pool per map\nrun. It is created after the graph is loaded and validated, and\ndestroyed after the run completes.\n\nThe C entry point (`src/008-pool-runner.c`):\n\n```c\nint main(int argc, char **argv) {\n    // 1. parse map path from argv\n    // 2. load and validate graph (C loader, no Lua involved)\n    // 3. determine which language runtimes the map uses\n    // 4. allocate per-input-port slots for every box (issue 302)\n    // 5. pool = pool_create(n_workers)\n    // 6. init per-worker language runtime handles for each language present\n    // 7. pool_init_barrier(pool)  ← block until every worker is fully initialized\n    // 8. push every input port's literal value into its slot\n    // 9. spawn tasks for boxes whose input set is now satisfied\n    // 10. pool_wait_quiescent(pool)\n    // 11. write last-run.jsonl\n    // 12. pool_destroy(pool)\n}\n```\n\n### Init barrier\n\nWorkers are not safe to dispatch tasks to until **every worker has\nfully completed init for every language spec the map uses**. If the\nmain thread spawns a task before a worker's `lua_State` is up, the\ntask lands on a null handle.\n\n`pool_init_barrier` is the join point:\n\n1. Each worker's startup runs all `lang->init(worker_idx)` calls in\n   a defined order, populating its `worker_ctx_t.handles[]`.\n2. After completing its inits, each worker increments a shared\n   atomic `workers_ready` counter and blocks on a condition\n   variable.\n3. The main thread waits until `workers_ready == n_workers`.\n4. Main thread broadcasts the condition variable; all workers\n   release simultaneously and begin pulling tasks.\n\nThis is a one-shot barrier — it runs once at pool startup. After\nquiescence it doesn't re-engage; teardown takes a different path.\n\nThe barrier also protects against partial init failures: if any\nworker's `init` returns an error, the barrier never completes and\nthe main thread can detect it via a timeout or per-worker status\nflag.\n\n### Graph loading: ported to C\nThe graph loader is ported from `src/003-loader.lua` to C and lives\ninside (or alongside) `008-pool-runner.c`. The pool runner has no\nembedded Lua state for loader purposes. JSON parsing uses a small\nvendored C JSON library (cJSON or similar; decision deferred to\nimplementation).\n\nLua appears in the runner only when a box's language is Lua — and even\nthen, only inside that worker's language runtime handle. The pool\nrunner itself does not link to liblua at the top level.\n\n### Per-worker language runtimes\nNo language is treated as the \"native\" or preferred language at the\nthread level. Every box — regardless of language — goes through the\nsame task dispatch path. The per-box cost is determined by that box's\ninvocation wrapper, not by any map-level language setting.\n\nEach worker thread holds a set of language runtime handles, one per\nlanguage it may be asked to run. These are initialized once at pool\nstartup, before any tasks are submitted, and torn down at shutdown:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    void   *handles[N_LANGS];   // opaque per-language runtime state\n    int     thread_idx;\n} worker_ctx_t;\n```\n\nOnly the language handles actually needed by the map are initialized.\nIf the map contains no Bash boxes, no Bash handle is started for any\nworker. The graph loader determines which languages are present and\npasses that set to the pool runner at startup.\n\nThe per-language initialization protocol is defined by the language\nruntime spec (issue 303). The pool runner calls each spec's `init`\nfunction at startup and its `teardown` function at shutdown.\n\n### Worker context access\nWorker context is stored in thread-local storage (`__thread\nworker_ctx_t *current_worker`), set by each worker immediately after\nthe thread is started. This avoids per-task `pthread_self()` lookups.\n\n### Pool size\nNumber of worker threads defaults to the number of logical CPUs\n(`sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_ONLN)`), capped at a compile-time maximum\n(`MAX_WORKERS`, initially 16). Can be overridden by an environment\nvariable `SORAMECH_WORKERS=N`.\n\n### Slots are owned by tasks (issue 302)\nSlots are allocated when a task is created, not pre-allocated at\nstartup. A task allocates its output slot(s) at submission time, with\nsize specified by the task's language and function. The pool runner\ndoes not own a slot region — slots are per-task allocations that\noutlive the task only as long as wires hold references to them. See\nissue 302 for the slot lifecycle.\n\n### Quiescence\nThe runner tracks an active-task counter, incremented on `pool_spawn`\nand decremented when a task reaches `ACT_DONE`. The main thread waits\non a condition variable that signals when the counter reaches zero.\n\nThis naturally handles iterators that re-queue themselves: each\nre-queue increments the counter, each completion decrements. When the\ncounter reaches zero, the run is over.\n\nDeadlock is not a concern at runtime. The graph validator (running at\nload) rejects non-iterator cycles and inputs without producers. Errors\ninside a task crash the program (issue 303), so there is no\nhalf-completed-producer case to worry about. An iterator parking\nbecause its upstream queue is empty is not deadlock — it is the\nnatural end-of-stream condition; once the active-task counter reaches\nzero with the iterator parked, the run ends cleanly.\n\n## Open questions\n- Vendored JSON library: cJSON, jsmn, or hand-rolled. cJSON is heavier\n  but easiest. Decision deferred.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. Vendor `900-task-pool.h` + `.c` into `libs/task-pool/`.\n2. Vendor a JSON parser into `libs/json/`.\n3. Port `003-loader.lua` to C inside `src/008-pool-runner.c`.\n4. Write the pool lifecycle skeleton: pool_create, worker context TLS,\n   active-task counter, quiescence wait.\n5. Add `Makefile` target `soramech-pool` that compiles the C runner and\n   links against the vendored pool and JSON parser.\n6. Smoke test: single-box Lua map, pool with 2 workers, box runs, result\n   written. No task graph complexity yet.\n\n## Relevant files\n- `/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h` — pool API\n- `src/003-loader.lua` — current Lua loader, to be ported to C\n- `src/004-executor.lua` — current synchronous executor, to be replaced\n- `src/007-runner-main.lua` — current Lua runner, to be replaced\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — per-task slot lifecycle\n- `issues/303-language-runtime-spec.md` — per-language init/call/teardown\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — replaces 004-executor.lua\n- `docs/004-ipc-and-threading.md` — threading roadmap and IPC options\n",

{
  "timestamp":"2026-05-10T02:43:47.077Z",

        "tool_use_id":"toolu_012juGtJxyVa4vQLPzFu5ivR",
        "content":"60\t### All slots are ring buffers\n61\t\n62\tThere is one slot type. It is a ring buffer of `n_cells` cells,\n63\teach of `cell_capacity` bytes. Every input port has a ring buffer\n64\tof compile-time-determined size:\n65\t\n66\t- **Default size**: enough cells to absorb the maximum number of\n67\t  pushes that can happen before the box can drain. For a port fed\n68\t  by a single non-iterator producer, that's 1. For a port fed by\n69\t  an iterator, it's the iterator's worst-case backlog (statically\n70\t  inferred or capped at a high default like 64 with growth).\n71\t- **Upper bound**: lists grow if backlog exceeds the pre-allocated\n72\t  size, so n_cells isn't a hard cap on correctness — only on\n73\t  pre-allocation efficiency.\n74\t\n75\tThe producer pushes one cell per fan-out path; the consumer pops\n76\tone cell per invocation. Fan-in is multiple producers pushing into\n77\tthe same input slot in arrival order; the consumer pops in FIFO\n78\torder.\n79\t\n80\t### Asynchrony\n81\tThe store is fully asynchronous. Slots are allocated, filled, read, and\n82\tfreed at any time, on any thread, with no global lock. Synchronization\n83\tis per-slot. There is no central allocator-wide mutex.\n84\t\n85\t## Slot layout\n86\t\n87\tEach slot is a header followed by `n_cells` cells, each `cell_capacity`\n88\tbytes. The header tracks ring-buffer state and lifetime:\n89\t\n90\t```\n91\tSlot header\n92\tOffset  Size  Field\n93\t------  ----  -----\n94\t0       4     cell_capacity   (bytes per cell, set at allocation)\n95\t4       4     n_cells         (ring size, set at allocation)\n96\t8       4     head            (read index, mod n_cells)\n97\t12      4     tail            (write index, mod n_cells; cells_filled = tail - head)\n98\t16      1     touched         (per-slot lock: 0=free, 1=another thread mutating)\n99\t17      3     _pad\n100\t20      …     cells           (n_cells * (4-byte size + cell_capacity bytes))\n101\t```\n102\t\n103\tEach cell stores a 4-byte filled-size followed by `cell_capacity`\n104\tbytes of value data. Cells have wildly different capacities across\n105\tslots — capacity is per-slot, not global. The C convention of passing\n106\tsizes alongside arrays applies: the task that allocates a slot knows\n107\thow big it needs the cells.\n108\t\n109\t`touched` is a single-byte flag toggled around any header mutation\n110\t(push, pop, refcount changes). A reader that finds `touched == 1`\n111\tspins until it clears.
