The \"are upstreams\n142\tstill alive\" check is done at the producer-set level, which is\n143\tcheaper and avoids the contention of refcount churn on hot paths.\n144\t\n145\t### No wait lists\n146\t\n147\tTasks never park on slots.       "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md",
      "numLines":100,
      "startLine":60,
      "totalLines":394,
      "content":"### All slots are ring buffers\n\nThere is one slot type. It is a ring buffer of `n_cells` cells,\neach of `cell_capacity` bytes. Every input port has a ring buffer\nof compile-time-determined size:\n\n- **Default size**: enough cells to absorb the maximum number of\n  pushes that can happen before the box can drain. For a port fed\n  by a single non-iterator producer, that's 1. For a port fed by\n  an iterator, it's the iterator's worst-case backlog (statically\n  inferred or capped at a high default like 64 with growth).\n- **Upper bound**: lists grow if backlog exceeds the pre-allocated\n  size, so n_cells isn't a hard cap on correctness — only on\n  pre-allocation efficiency.\n\nThe producer pushes one cell per fan-out path; the consumer pops\none cell per invocation. Fan-in is multiple producers pushing into\nthe same input slot in arrival order; the consumer pops in FIFO\norder.\n\n### Asynchrony\nThe store is fully asynchronous. Slots are allocated, filled, read, and\nfreed at any time, on any thread, with no global lock. Synchronization\nis per-slot. There is no central allocator-wide mutex.\n\n## Slot layout\n\nEach slot is a header followed by `n_cells` cells, each `cell_capacity`\nbytes. The header tracks ring-buffer state and lifetime:\n\n```\nSlot header\nOffset  Size  Field\n------  ----  -----\n0       4     cell_capacity   (bytes per cell, set at allocation)\n4       4     n_cells         (ring size, set at allocation)\n8       4     head            (read index, mod n_cells)\n12      4     tail            (write index, mod n_cells; cells_filled = tail - head)\n16      1     touched         (per-slot lock: 0=free, 1=another thread mutating)\n17      3     _pad\n20      …     cells           (n_cells * (4-byte size + cell_capacity bytes))\n```\n\nEach cell stores a 4-byte filled-size followed by `cell_capacity`\nbytes of value data. Cells have wildly different capacities across\nslots — capacity is per-slot, not global. The C convention of passing\nsizes alongside arrays applies: the task that allocates a slot knows\nhow big it needs the cells.\n\n`touched` is a single-byte flag toggled around any header mutation\n(push, pop, refcount changes). A reader that finds `touched == 1`\nspins until it clears. This is the simplest possible per-slot lock —\nif contention proves to matter, replace with a proper mutex without\nchanging the API.\n\nWrites to a cell complete with a memory barrier before `tail` is\nadvanced, so a reader that observes `head < tail` is guaranteed to\nsee the complete value at the head cell.\n\n## Lifetime and end-of-stream\n\nSlots are owned by the box that holds the input port. They live\nfrom graph load until run end. There is no per-slot reference\ncounting — the slot is freed when the run ends, alongside its\nowning box.\n\n### End-of-stream detection (replacing producer refcounts)\n\nEach slot tracks the set of upstream producer boxes that may still\npush into it. When a producer's \"no more pushes\" condition fires\n— either it has finished all its invocations, or it transitively\ndepends only on producers that have finished — the dispatch layer\nremoves that producer from the slot's producer set.\n\nWhen the producer set is empty AND the slot's queue is drained,\nthe consumer box has reached end-of-stream on that port. For an\niterator, this is what tells the iterator to stop re-spawning. For\na non-iterator, this means no further invocations are coming;\ncombined with the same condition on its other input ports, the\nbox itself is done.\n\nThis replaces the per-slot refcount machinery. The \"are upstreams\nstill alive\" check is done at the producer-set level, which is\ncheaper and avoids the contention of refcount churn on hot paths.\n\n### No wait lists\n\nTasks never park on slots. Tasks are spawned by the dispatch\nlayer's spawn-on-input-arrival rule and run to completion; they\nnever block. A slot that has no value yet simply means the\nspawn rule hasn't fired for that consumer yet. No wait list,\nno per-slot wake-up traversal — just a check after each push.\n\n## Backing store\n\nSlots are allocated from process heap memory. The slot store owns a\nper-run allocator (described under \"Allocation strategy\" below) that\nhands out memory chunks to slots. Plain `malloc`-class memory is\nsufficient — every worker thread in the process can read and write\nit, and no spec ever needs to access it from a child process."
    }

          "new_string":"### All slots are ring buffers; read mode varies\n\nThere is one slot type. It is a ring buffer of `n_cells` cells,\neach of `cell_capacity` bytes. The number of cells (`n_cells`) and\nthe read mode are both compile-time properties of the input port:\n\n- **1-cell + peek mode**: the value the producer wrote stays in the\n  cell. Tasks read via `slot_peek` — read without draining — and\n  every subsequent task on this consumer reads the same value\n  unless the producer overwrites it. Used for **single-push wires**\n  (a literal, or a wire from a producer box whose invocation count\n  is exactly 1). Multiple consumer tasks read the value as many\n  times as needed; the cell is never empty.\n- **N-cell + pop mode**: a queue. Producers push; consumers\n  `slot_pop` — drain one cell per task. Used for **multi-push wires**:\n  any wire whose producer has more than one task invocation\n  during the run. The producer's pushes accumulate, the consumer\n  drains in pop order.\n\nCompile-time analysis classifies each wire. A producer is\n\"runs-once\" if no transitive ancestor is an iterator; otherwise\nit's \"runs-N-times.\" Wires from runs-once producers get 1-cell\npeek slots; wires from runs-N-times producers get N-cell pop slots.\n\n`n_cells` for pop slots is sized for worst-case backlog (or a\ndefault like 64 with growth on demand). Lists grow if the producer\noutruns the consumer past the pre-allocation.\n\nFan-in: multiple producers pushing into the same N-cell pop slot\nland in arrival order. The consumer pops FIFO unless the cell\ncarries an ordering tag (see \"Cell tagging\" below).\n\n### Cell tagging (for parallel-iterator ordering)\n\nA cell can optionally carry a 4-byte ordering tag alongside its\nsize and data:\n\n```\nCell layout (N-cell pop slot)\nOffset  Size  Field\n------  ----  -----\n0       4     filled_size\n4       4     tag      (0 if untagged; iterator counter snapshot otherwise)\n8       …     data\n```\n\nSlots created for wires from parallel iterators (issue 304) are\ntagged. Pop on a tagged slot returns the cell with the lowest tag,\nnot the head cell — preserving iterator-counter order across pushes\nthat arrived out of order from parallel iterator workers.\n\nUntagged slots default tag to 0 and pop FIFO at no extra cost. The\ntag-aware pop is a per-slot mode flag set at allocation time.",

        "oldStart":150,

    "replaceAll":false,
    "oldString":"## Lifetime and end-of-stream\n\nSlots are owned by the box that holds the input port. They live\nfrom graph load until run end. There is no per-slot reference\ncounting — the slot is freed when the run ends, alongside its\nowning box.\n\n### End-of-stream detection (replacing producer refcounts)\n\nEach slot tracks the set of upstream producer boxes that may still\npush into it. When a producer's \"no more pushes\" condition fires\n— either it has finished all its invocations, or it transitively\ndepends only on producers that have finished — the dispatch layer\nremoves that producer from the slot's producer set.\n\nWhen the producer set is empty AND the slot's queue is drained,\nthe consumer box has reached end-of-stream on that port. For an\niterator, this is what tells the iterator to stop re-spawning. For\na non-iterator, this means no further invocations are coming;\ncombined with the same condition on its other input ports, the\nbox itself is done.\n\nThis replaces the per-slot refcount machinery. The \"are upstreams\nstill alive\" check is done at the producer-set level, which is\ncheaper and avoids the contention of refcount churn on hot paths.\n\n### No wait lists\n\nTasks never park on slots. Tasks are spawned by the dispatch\nlayer's spawn-on-input-arrival rule and run to completion; they\nnever block. A slot that has no value yet simply means the\nspawn rule hasn't fired for that consumer yet. No wait list,\nno per-slot wake-up traversal — just a check after each push.",
    "newString":"## Lifetime\n\nSlots are owned by the box that holds the input port. They live\nfrom graph load until run end. There is no per-slot reference\ncounting and no end-of-stream propagation — the slot is freed\nwhen the run ends, alongside its owning box.\n\nRun termination is governed entirely by the pool's active-task\ncounter (issue 301): when no task is running and no further spawns\nare pending, the run is over. There's nothing the slot store needs\nto track to make this work.\n\n### No wait lists\n\nTasks never park on slots. Tasks are spawned by the dispatch\nlayer's spawn-on-input-arrival rule and run to completion; they\nnever block. A slot that has no value yet simply means the\nspawn rule hasn't fired for that consumer yet. No wait list,\nno per-slot wake-up traversal — just a check after each push.",
    "userModified":false
  },

          "new_string":"## Submission timing\n\nTasks are spawned dynamically in response to slot pushes. Each box\nhas small per-box state used by the dispatch layer:\n\n```\nbox_runtime_state {\n    slot_id_t  *input_slots;     // one per input port (set at load)\n    int        *port_modes;      // PEEK or POP, per input port\n    int         n_inputs;\n    int         counter;         // iterator only; 0 otherwise\n};\n```\n\nThe spawning rule:\n- When a producer pushes to one of a box's input slots, the\n  dispatch layer checks **does every input slot have a value\n  available?** \"Available\" means:\n  - For peek-mode (1-cell) slots: cell has been written at least\n    once. Once a peek slot is filled, it stays available — every\n    subsequent spawn-check on this box passes the peek-port check.\n  - For pop-mode (N-cell) slots: queue is non-empty.\n- If yes, spawn a `dispatch_task_t` and submit to the pool. The\n  task pops (or peeks) one value from each input slot when it\n  runs.\n- Each push that completes the input set triggers exactly one\n  spawn. Multiple pushes accumulate in pop slots; each pop\n  consumes one, and if more remain, the next push (or check)\n  re-fires the spawn rule.\n\nThis makes the pool's queue the rate buffer: pushes accumulate\nin pop slots (possibly multiple per slot), and one task per\naccumulated value gets spawned.\n\nTasks never block on slots. They're spawned after inputs are\nready, run to completion, and disappear. Blocking-and-waking\nmachinery is unnecessary — the spawn-on-arrival rule is the\nsynchronization primitive.\n\nThe pool's queue is the only queue. There is no separate \"blocked\ntasks\" structure.",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md",
          "replace_all":false,
          "old_string":"## Submission timing\n\nTasks are spawned dynamically in response to slot pushes, not at\ngraph-load time. Each box has a small per-box state used by the\ndispatch layer to decide when to spawn:\n\n```\nbox_runtime_state {\n    slot_id_t  *input_slots;     // one per input port (set at load)\n    int         n_inputs;\n    int         pending_invocations;  // counter; >0 means a task is queued\n    int         counter;         // iterator only; 0 otherwise\n};\n```\n\nThe spawning rule:\n- When a producer pushes to one of a box's input slots, the\n  dispatch layer checks **does every input slot now hold at least\n  one value?** If yes, spawn a task. The task pops one cell from\n  each input slot when it runs.\n- If multiple input slots get pushed concurrently, one task spawns\n  per \"all inputs available\" event — the pending_invocations\n  counter prevents over-spawning.\n\nThis makes the pool's queue the rate buffer: pushes accumulate\n(possibly multiple per slot), and one task per accumulated set\ngets spawned in arrival order.\n\nTasks never block on slots. They're spawned after inputs are\nready, run to completion, and disappear. Blocking-and-waking\nmachinery is unnecessary — the spawn-on-arrival rule is the\nsynchronization primitive.\n\nThe pool's queue is the only queue. There is no separate \"blocked\ntasks\" structure."

## [3814]

```json
{
  "timestamp":"2026-05-10T02:45:13.625Z",
  "message":{
    "content":[{
        "tool_use_id":"toolu_019UrEQoYGdtj2uKQovkY4jG",
        "content":"28\t## Task struct\n29\t\n30\tA task is one ephemeral invocation of a box. Its struct carries\n31\tjust enough to point the action at the box and the snapshot of its\n32\tcounter at spawn time:\n33\t\n34\t```c\n35\ttypedef struct {\n36\t    int  box_id;          // index into the graph's box array\n37\t    int  counter;         // iterator only; snapshot at spawn time\n38\t} dispatch_task_t;\n39\t```\n40\t\n41\tThere is no `input_slots` array on the task — the box's input\n42\tslots are durable per-box state (see issue 302). The action looks\n43\tup the input and output slots through `box_runtime_state[box_id]`.\n44\t\n45\tThere is no `output_slot` either — output is a routing event, not\n46\ta stored value. When the action finishes, it pushes copies of the\n47\treturn value into the input slots of every downstream box wired\n48\tto this output (and only the matching branch for comparators and\n49\titerators).\n50\t\n51\tTasks are spawned by the dispatch layer's \"spawn on input ready\"\n52\trule (issue 302). Each spawn allocates a fresh `dispatch_task_t`\n53\ton the pool's task allocator, pre-populated with the box ID and\n54\tcounter value. The action's first read of the input slots is what\n55\tdrains them — pop one cell per input port.\n56\t\n57\t## The dispatch action\n58\t\n59\t```c\n60\taction_result_t dispatch_action(task_ctx_t *ctx, void *arg);\n61\t```\n62\t\n63\tPhases, in order:\n64\t\n65\t### 1. Read inputs into byte buffers\n66\t\n67\tTasks are spawned only when every input port has at least one\n68\tvalue (issue 302's spawn-on-input-ready rule), so the action does\n69\tnot need to check or block — input availability is the spawn\n70\tprecondition.\n71\t\n72\tFor each input port: `slot_pop` from the box's input slot into a\n73\theap-allocated buffer sized to the slot's `cell_capacity`.   "slug":"snug-booping-dove",
  "gitBranch":"master",

  "toolUseResult":{
    "type":"text",
    "file":{
      "filePath":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md",
      "numLines":60,
      "startLine":28,
      "totalLines":280,
      "content":"## Task struct\n\nA task is one ephemeral invocation of a box. Its struct carries\njust enough to point the action at the box and the snapshot of its\ncounter at spawn time:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    int  box_id;          // index into the graph's box array\n    int  counter;         // iterator only; snapshot at spawn time\n} dispatch_task_t;\n```\n\nThere is no `input_slots` array on the task — the box's input\nslots are durable per-box state (see issue 302). The action looks\nup the input and output slots through `box_runtime_state[box_id]`.\n\nThere is no `output_slot` either — output is a routing event, not\na stored value. When the action finishes, it pushes copies of the\nreturn value into the input slots of every downstream box wired\nto this output (and only the matching branch for comparators and\niterators).\n\nTasks are spawned by the dispatch layer's \"spawn on input ready\"\nrule (issue 302). Each spawn allocates a fresh `dispatch_task_t`\non the pool's task allocator, pre-populated with the box ID and\ncounter value. The action's first read of the input slots is what\ndrains them — pop one cell per input port.\n\n## The dispatch action\n\n```c\naction_result_t dispatch_action(task_ctx_t *ctx, void *arg);\n```\n\nPhases, in order:\n\n### 1. Read inputs into byte buffers\n\nTasks are spawned only when every input port has at least one\nvalue (issue 302's spawn-on-input-ready rule), so the action does\nnot need to check or block — input availability is the spawn\nprecondition.\n\nFor each input port: `slot_pop` from the box's input slot into a\nheap-allocated buffer sized to the slot's `cell_capacity`. Pop\ndrains one cell from the front of the ring; subsequent values\nbehind it are still queued and will spawn further tasks.\n\nVariable-size payloads work via the large-value heap (issue 302):\nthe popped cell holds a `{size, offset}` handle that points into\nthe heap; the spec follows the handle if it needs the bytes.\n\nBuffers are freed when the action ends.\n\n### 3. Dispatch by box mode\nThe action now branches on the box's mode:\n\n- **Plain call box**: proceed to phase 4 (invoke) and phase 5 (write\n  output) as below."
    }
  },

          "type":"direct"
        },
        "input":{
          "new_string":"## Iterator counter and parallel iteration\n\nThe iterator's per-box counter is read and incremented **at task\nspawn time**, atomically:\n\n```c\nint counter_for_this_task = atomic_fetch_add(&box->counter, 1) % n_iter_outputs;\nspawn(task{ box_id, counter_for_this_task });\n```\n\nThe counter is snapshotted into the task struct. The atomic\nfetch-add means concurrent spawns get distinct counter values, so\n**iterator tasks can run in parallel** on different workers — each\nhas its own counter, picks its own output branch independently.\nSibling iterator tasks don't share runtime state.\n\nThe serial dependency is reduced to one atomic op per spawn (cheap)\nrather than a serialized task chain.\n\n## Cross-iterator pairing under parallel iteration\n\nWith parallel iterator tasks, push ordering at the consumer is\nnon-deterministic — task 6 of iterator A may push to consumer C\nbefore task 5 if 6 happened to land on a faster worker. FIFO pop\nat C would consume them out of iteration order.\n\nThe fix is **counter-tagged pushes**. Each iterator push (in phase\n5) carries the counter value snapshotted at spawn:\n\n```c\nslot_push(downstream.input_slot, output_buf, output_size,\n          /* tag = */ task->counter);\n```\n\nConsumer slots downstream of iterators are allocated with the\n`SLOT_TAGGED` flag (issue 302). `slot_pop` on a tagged slot\nreturns the cell with the lowest tag — preserving iterator-counter\norder regardless of push race.\n\nCompile-time analysis decides which slots are tagged: any slot\nwhose feeding wire originates (transitively, through a fan-out\nchain) at an iterator branch gets tagged. Slots not downstream of\niterators are untagged and pop FIFO at no extra cost.\n\nPlain-call and comparator pushes carry tag = 0 (or the snapshot of\ntheir own iterator-ancestor's counter, if applicable, propagated\nthrough their phase-5 pushes). Tags compose naturally through\nmulti-hop chains.\n\n### Cross-iterator pairing of multiple iterator inputs\n\nWhen non-iterator consumer C has two input ports wired from two\ndifferent iterators A and B, each input port has its own tagged\nqueue. Both queues pop in tag order independently:\n- C's task K pops the K-th tag from A's queue (which equals A's\n  K-th invocation's value).\n- The same K-th tag from B's queue.\n\nPairing by tag = `(A_K, B_K)` for every K, deterministic\nregardless of which iterator's tasks run faster.",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md",
          "replace_all":false,
          "old_string":"## Cross-iterator pairing\n\nWhen a non-iterator consumer C has two input ports wired from two\ndifferent iterators A and B, each input port has its own queue.\nTasks for C spawn FIFO: task 1 pops the first value from each\nqueue; task 2 pops the second from each; etc.\n\nPairing is deterministic **as long as A and B push in deterministic\norder**. In a single-threaded run that's automatic. In a parallel\nrun where A and B run on different workers and push concurrently,\nthe pairing depends on push ordering — which is non-deterministic\nacross runs.\n\nFor phase 3, FIFO pairing is the policy. If a workload needs\nstrict pairing (a_i with b_i regardless of push race), the right\nfix is per-invocation index tags on the values: each iterator\npush tags its value with its counter, the consumer's queues sort\nby tag before popping. That's a follow-on issue (no number yet),\nopened only if a real workload needs it."
        },
        "id":"toolu_01RWkWopUGAQbpLWXCR3Eiok"
      }]

Each iterator push (in phase","+5) carries the counter value snapshotted at spawn:","+","+```c","+slot_push(downstream.input_slot, output_buf, output_size,","+          /* tag = */ task->counter);","+```","+","+Consumer slots downstream of iterators are allocated with the","+`SLOT_TAGGED` flag (issue 302). `slot_pop` on a tagged slot","+returns the cell with the lowest tag — preserving iterator-counter","+order regardless of push race.","+","+Compile-time analysis decides which slots are tagged: any slot","+whose feeding wire originates (transitively, through a fan-out","+chain) at an iterator branch gets tagged. Slots not downstream of","+iterators are untagged and pop FIFO at no extra cost.","+","+Plain-call and comparator pushes carry tag = 0 (or the snapshot of","+their own iterator-ancestor's counter, if applicable, propagated","+through their phase-5 pushes). Both queues pop in tag order independently:","+- C's task K pops the K-th tag from A's queue (which equals A's","+  K-th invocation's value).","+- The same K-th tag from B's queue.","+","+Pairing by tag = `(A_K, B_K)` for every K, deterministic","+regardless of which iterator's tasks run faster.","+"," ## Comparator vs iterator vs plain call"," "," Three box modes drive routing differently:"],
        "oldStart":184,

      }],
    "replaceAll":false,
    "oldString":"## Cross-iterator pairing\n\nWhen a non-iterator consumer C has two input ports wired from two\ndifferent iterators A and B, each input port has its own queue.\nTasks for C spawn FIFO: task 1 pops the first value from each\nqueue; task 2 pops the second from each; etc.\n\nPairing is deterministic **as long as A and B push in deterministic\norder**. In a single-threaded run that's automatic. In a parallel\nrun where A and B run on different workers and push concurrently,\nthe pairing depends on push ordering — which is non-deterministic\nacross runs.\n\nFor phase 3, FIFO pairing is the policy. If a workload needs\nstrict pairing (a_i with b_i regardless of push race), the right\nfix is per-invocation index tags on the values: each iterator\npush tags its value with its counter, the consumer's queues sort\nby tag before popping. That's a follow-on issue (no number yet),\nopened only if a real workload needs it.",
    "newString":"## Iterator counter and parallel iteration\n\nThe iterator's per-box counter is read and incremented **at task\nspawn time**, atomically:\n\n```c\nint counter_for_this_task = atomic_fetch_add(&box->counter, 1) % n_iter_outputs;\nspawn(task{ box_id, counter_for_this_task });\n```\n\nThe counter is snapshotted into the task struct. The atomic\nfetch-add means concurrent spawns get distinct counter values, so\n**iterator tasks can run in parallel** on different workers — each\nhas its own counter, picks its own output branch independently.\nSibling iterator tasks don't share runtime state.\n\nThe serial dependency is reduced to one atomic op per spawn (cheap)\nrather than a serialized task chain.\n\n## Cross-iterator pairing under parallel iteration\n\nWith parallel iterator tasks, push ordering at the consumer is\nnon-deterministic — task 6 of iterator A may push to consumer C\nbefore task 5 if 6 happened to land on a faster worker. FIFO pop\nat C would consume them out of iteration order.\n\nThe fix is **counter-tagged pushes**. Each iterator push (in phase\n5) carries the counter value snapshotted at spawn:\n\n```c\nslot_push(downstream.input_slot, output_buf, output_size,\n          /* tag = */ task->counter);\n```\n\nConsumer slots downstream of iterators are allocated with the\n`SLOT_TAGGED` flag (issue 302). `slot_pop` on a tagged slot\nreturns the cell with the lowest tag — preserving iterator-counter\norder regardless of push race.\n\nCompile-time analysis decides which slots are tagged: any slot\nwhose feeding wire originates (transitively, through a fan-out\nchain) at an iterator branch gets tagged. Slots not downstream of\niterators are untagged and pop FIFO at no extra cost.\n\nPlain-call and comparator pushes carry tag = 0 (or the snapshot of\ntheir own iterator-ancestor's counter, if applicable, propagated\nthrough their phase-5 pushes). Tags compose naturally through\nmulti-hop chains.\n\n### Cross-iterator pairing of multiple iterator inputs\n\nWhen non-iterator consumer C has two input ports wired from two\ndifferent iterators A and B, each input port has its own tagged\nqueue. Both queues pop in tag order independently:\n- C's task K pops the K-th tag from A's queue (which equals A's\n  K-th invocation's value).\n- The same K-th tag from B's queue.\n\nPairing by tag = `(A_K, B_K)` for every K, deterministic\nregardless of which iterator's tasks run faster.",
    "userModified":false
  },

    "originalFile":"# Phase 3 Progress\n\nGoal: replace the Lua synchronous runner with a C thread pool runner\nthat executes box graphs in parallel.\n\nThe phase is fully designed; implementation has not yet started.\nIssues 301–311 are the architectural specification. |\n|-----|-------------------------------------------------------------|----------|\n| 301 | thread pool lifecycle and per-worker initialization         | designed |\n| 302 | per-task slot store with        | designed |\n| 310 | priority queue: wired in, no-op behaviorally                | designed |\n| 311 | integration tests & run output (`last-run.jsonl`)           | designed |\n| 312 | Vendored 3d-rts task pool builds clean\n- [ ] Slot store unit-tested (single-value + ring buffer + refcounting)\n- [ ] C graph loader passes phase 2's existing maps\n- [ ] Lua spec runs `maps/hello` end-to-end\n- [ ] C spec compiles and runs a typed-signature box\n- [ ] Bash spec runs an out-of-process box via the socket protocol\n- [ ] Pool runner runs a multi-language map with concurrent workers\n- [ ] Iterator box routes via dispatch layer (no spec invoked)\n- [ ] Comparator box routes via dispatch layer (no spec invoked)\n- [ ] Variable-size outputs work via the large-value heap\n- (`src/004-executor.lua`,\n      `src/007-runner-main.lua`, `src/003-loader.lua`, `drivers/*.sh`)\n\n## Implementation order suggestion\n\nDesigned to surface concrete artifacts early so subsequent issues can\nbuild on them.\n\n1. **309 (build system)** — top-level Makefile, vendored deps, empty\n   stubs for runner and specs. Verify everything compiles.\n2. **302 (slot store)** — pure C, unit-testable, no pool dependency.\n3. **305 (graph loader)** — pure C, parses existing phase 2 maps.\n4. **301 (pool lifecycle)** — wire pool startup, per-worker context,\n   active-task counter, quiescence.\n5. **303 (lang spec interface)** — header file + stub spec to validate\n   the loading mechanism.\n6. **306 (Lua spec)** — easiest reference.       "content":"## Execution model — phase 3 (thread pool)\n\nThe C pool runner owns a 3d-rts task pool with N worker threads.\nEach box invocation is a task. The dispatch layer (issue 304) is the\nworker-side action: read inputs from slots → invoke the language\nspec (or route, for comparators / iterators) → write output to a\nslot → unref consumed inputs → fire downstream connections.\n\nSlots are per-task ring buffers with reference-counted lifetime\n(issue 302). Wires hold references; producers push, consumers peek\nor pop. The wait list on each slot is the synchronization primitive\nthat parks blocked tasks until a producer fills the slot.\n\nThe pool runner has no embedded Lua. Format:\n\n```json\n{\n  \"constant\": false,\n  \"fields\": {\n    \"history\": [],\n    \"config\": { \"constant\": true, \"value\": { \"model\": \"soramind-default\" } }\n  }\n}"

Each box\ninvocation is a task. The dispatch layer (issue 304) is the\nworker-side action: read inputs from slots → branch on box mode\n→ invoke the language spec (or route directly, for comparators /\niterators) → push output to downstream input slots.\n\nSlots are **per-input-port** ring buffers (issue 302), allocated\nat graph load and durable for the run. 1-cell slots use peek\n(literals, single-push wires); N-cell slots use pop (multi-push\nwires, queues from iterators). Iterator counter is per-box state,\nincremented atomically at task spawn time so iterator tasks can\nparallelize across workers; pushes carry counter tags so consumer\nslots preserve invocation order.     }

    "originalFile":"# 310 — Priority queue: wired in, no-op behaviorally\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nThe 3d-rts task pool's `pool_spawn` takes a priority parameter:\n\n```c\ntask_id_t pool_spawn(task_pool_t *pool,\n                     action_fn_t  *actions,\n                     void        **action_args,\n                     int           n_actions,\n                     int           priority);\n```\n\nHigher priority tasks are dispatched ahead of lower priority tasks\nwhen multiple are ready. The pool's queue handles the ordering.\n\nPhase 3 needs to specify what SoraMech does with this knob. The\nsimplest answer is the right one for now: do nothing.\n\n## Decision\n\nEvery dispatch task is submitted at priority `1`. The compile-time\nconstant `MAX_PRIORITY` is set to `1`. There is no graph-level or\nbox-level concept of priority. The runner does not expose any user-\nfacing knob for it.\n\nThe mechanism is wired through the codebase — every `pool_spawn`\ncall passes a priority, the constant is referenced rather than\nhard-coded inline — but the behavior is identical to a single-\npriority pool. Tasks run in submission order (modulo whatever\nordering the pool guarantees within a single priority level).\n\n## Why wire it in if it does nothing\n\nTwo reasons:\n\n1. **Future hooks land as config changes, not refactors.** When a\n   real priority use case appears (allocator cleanup at lowest\n   priority; user-marked urgent boxes; iterator queue draining\n   prioritized over new entry submission), raising `MAX_PRIORITY`\n   and emitting different priorities at the right call sites is a\n   line edit, not a structural change. If the priority parameter\n   were stripped out, adding it later means going back through every\n   `pool_spawn` callsite and threading a new argument.\n\n2. **The pool's API requires it.** `pool_spawn` takes a priority.\n   Callers must pass something. Passing `1` consistently is the\n   straightforward expression of \"no priority concept yet.\"\n\n## Specific call sites\n\n```c\n// src/dispatch.c — every dispatch task\npool_spawn(pool, &dispatch_action, &task_arg, 1, SM_PRIORITY_DEFAULT);\n\n// src/008-pool-runner.c — entry-box submission at startup\npool_spawn(pool, &dispatch_action, &task_arg, 1, SM_PRIORITY_DEFAULT);\n\n// src/slot-store.c — deferred allocator cleanup task (issue 302)\npool_spawn(pool, &cleanup_action, &cleanup_arg, 1, SM_PRIORITY_DEFAULT);\n\n// langs/bash/spec.c — ... none, the spec doesn't spawn pool tasks\n```\n\n`SM_PRIORITY_DEFAULT` is `1`. Defined in `src/008-pool-runner.h` (or\na sibling header) so all callers use the same name.\n\n## Future hooks (not in scope, but called out)\n\nWhen `MAX_PRIORITY` is raised, the natural assignments are:\n\n| Future use case                                     | Priority |\n|-----------------------------------------------------|----------|\n| User-marked \"urgent\" boxes (UI / interactive)       | 3        |\n| Iterator continuation when its queue is non-empty   | 2        |\n| Default dispatch task                               | 1        |\n| Allocator cleanup task (deferred coalescing, 302)   | 0        |\n\nThese are speculative. The actual priority schema is decided when\nthere is a workload that demonstrates the need.\n\nA box-level priority field could go in the box JSON (`\"priority\":\n2`) and be plumbed through `dispatch_task_t`. The dispatch action\nreads it, passes it to `pool_spawn` for any successor tasks. This\nis a future change.\n\n## Open questions\n\n(none currently — this is intentionally a small change to the call\nsites. The design conversation about what priorities should mean is\ndeferred until concrete need.)\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n\n1. Define `SM_PRIORITY_DEFAULT` (= 1) and `SM_MAX_PRIORITY` (= 1)\n   in a runner-wide header.\n2. Make every `pool_spawn` call site pass `SM_PRIORITY_DEFAULT`.\n3. Set the pool's max priority at `pool_create` time using\n   `SM_MAX_PRIORITY` (if the pool API takes a max-priority hint).\n4. That's it. No tests required beyond verifying the constants\n   compile and the pool runs.\n\n## Relevant files\n\n- `src/008-pool-runner.c` — calls `pool_spawn` for entry boxes\n- `src/dispatch.c` — calls `pool_spawn` for successor tasks\n- `src/slot-store.c` — calls `pool_spawn` for deferred cleanup\n- `libs/task-pool/900-task-pool.h` — `pool_spawn` priority parameter\n- `issues/301-pool-lifecycle-and-worker-init.md` — pool lifecycle\n- `issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md` — dispatch task submission\n- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — deferred cleanup tasks\n",
    "oldString":"## Current behavior\nThe 3d-rts task pool's `pool_spawn` takes a priority parameter:",
    "newString":"## Current behavior\nThe SoraMech thread pool's `pool_spawn` (modeled on 3d-rts's API)\ntakes a priority parameter:",
    "replaceAll":false,
    "userModified":false

      "content":"\nExecution model (v1)\n--------------------\n\nThe runner is synchronous in v1. Each box invocation is wrapped in a\ntask_fn(inputs) -> outputs boundary — the same signature as the 3d-rts\nthread pool's action chain — so the transition to concurrent execution is\na runtime swap, not a rewrite.\n\neffil-jit is available for threading when the custom thread pool (from\nthe 3d-rts project) is ready to be integrated. The target model is:\nboxes whose inputs are all satisfied fire concurrently; boxes that depend\non a still-running box park until that result arrives.\n\nMultiple maps can run concurrently as separate runner processes. Each map\nis a cohesive program. Maps calling into other maps is a future feature;\nfor now they are separate.\n\nFuture directions\n-----------------\n\n  — Integration with SoraMind: boxes that call inference endpoints on the\n    Alpine cluster, routing results through the map graph.\n\n  — Concurrent execution via the custom thread pool from 3d-rts,\n    replacing the synchronous v1 runner.\n\n  — Map-to-map calls: a box that invokes another map as a subroutine,\n    passing values across the boundary.\n\n  — Remote runner: a runner process on the Alpine cluster, controlled by\n    the web editor from another machine, results written to shared storage.\n\n  — Visual run trace: replay a completed run in the browser, seeing which\n    boxes fired and what values flowed through each wire."
    }

    "originalFile":"SoraMech — Vision\n=================\n\nA visual editor and execution engine for finite state machines built from\ncomposable boxes. Each box is a function call. Boxes are wired together by\nexplicit data connections. The result is a program you can see, edit in a\nbrowser, and run from a terminal — without writing a line of control flow.\n\nThe primary use case is LLM orchestration: wiring inference calls on the\nSoraMind Alpine cluster into coherent multi-step reasoning pipelines.\nStrings are first-class values. Text flows between boxes like water.\nHistory is explicit — loaded from disk only when a box needs it.\n\nWhy this shape?\n---------------\n\nMost orchestration tools hide the wiring. You write code that calls other\ncode, and the shape of the program lives only in your head. SoraMech makes\nthe shape visible and editable. The map file IS the program. If you can\nread JSON, you can read the program. If you can draw boxes, you can change\nit.\n\nThe second reason is language agnosticism. A box can call a Lua function,\na C function, a bash script, or a program written in anything the user\ndefines a driver for. The engine doesn't care. It invokes a driver, gets\noutputs, threads them to the next box. The map author picks the language;\nthe engine picks up the result.\n\nComponents\n----------\n\nThree programs share one data format — the map directory:\n\n  soramech-server.lua   — thin HTTP file proxy. Receives edits from the\n                          browser, reads and writes map files on disk.\n                          Started when remote editing is desired. Ignorant\n                          of the runner.\n\n  soramech-runner.lua   — FSM execution engine. Reads a map directory,\n                          walks the graph, invokes language drivers,\n                          threads outputs through wires. Started by the\n                          user from the CLI, a cronjob, or any external\n                          trigger. Ignorant of the server. Writes output\n                          to map-defined locations (data files, /tmp/).\n\n  index.html            — browser editor. Infinite-canvas box diagram.\n                          Reads and writes map files by talking to the\n                          server (local or remote). Never knows whether\n                          the runner is active.\n\nThe map directory is the stable interface. Server and runner share nothing\nbut the files.\n\nMap file layout\n---------------\n\nEach map lives in its own directory:\n\n  maps/<map-name>/\n    boxes/\n      <id>.json         — one file per box, self-contained, lists both\n                          incoming and outgoing connections\n    data/\n      <name>.json       — persistent data files (lua tables as JSON)\n                          sections are flagged constant: true or false\n    drivers.json        — language driver definitions (how to invoke each\n                          file extension)\n    meta.json           — map name, description, entry box id\n\n  tmp/                  — symlink to /tmp/<map-name>/\n                          holds ephemeral state: run logs, scratch tables,\n                          last-run snapshot\n\nBox file format\n---------------\n\nEach box is a JSON file in boxes/. It contains:\n\n  id          unique string identifier\n  label       human-readable name shown in the UI\n  kind        \"call\" | \"branch\" | \"data\"\n  ref         for \"call\": path like \"src/strings.lua\" or \"src/trim.sh\"\n  fn          for \"call\": function name (omitted for binary/shell refs)\n  inputs      list of {name, type} — what the box expects\n  outputs     list of {name, type} — what the box returns (tuple order)\n  connections list of {from_output, to_box_id, to_input, predicate?}\n              — written to BOTH endpoint files; runner validates at load\n\nBranch boxes have named output ports instead of positional outputs. Each\nport carries an optional predicate (comparator + literal). An \"else\" port\nalways exists. For LLM-based classification, \"else\" retries upstream\n(user wires it); for numeric/string predicates, \"else\" must be explicitly\nhandled or the runner refuses to start the map.\n\nLanguage drivers\n----------------\n\ndrivers.json maps file extensions to shell commands. Example:\n\n  {\n    \".lua\":  \"drivers/lua-driver.sh\",\n    \".c\":    \"drivers/c-driver.sh\",\n    \".sh\":   \"drivers/bash-driver.sh\"\n  }\n\nEach driver script receives: file path, function name, arg count, args...\nIt returns outputs on stdout, one per line (or as JSON for structured\nvalues). Lua and C ship as pre-written driver scripts — no special cases\nin the engine. If the user wants Rust, they write a driver script.\n\nThe C driver checks whether the source has changed since the last compile\n(by comparing mtime of .c against mtime of cached binary). If changed, it\ncompiles before invoking. Cache lives in tmp/.\n\nState and output\n----------------\n\nPersistent data lives in maps/<map-name>/data/ as JSON files. Each file\nis a Lua table serialized with dkjson. A file-level or section-level\n\"constant\" flag marks read-only data.\n\nEphemeral state (run logs, scratch variables, last-run snapshot) lives in\ntmp/ which is a symlink to /tmp/<map-name>/. It is fast, in RAM, and\nintentionally discarded on reboot.\n\nExecution model (v1)\n--------------------\n\nThe runner is synchronous in v1. Each box invocation is wrapped in a\ntask_fn(inputs) -> outputs boundary — the same signature as the 3d-rts\nthread pool's action chain — so the transition to concurrent execution is\na runtime swap, not a rewrite.\n\neffil-jit is available for threading when the custom thread pool (from\nthe 3d-rts project) is ready to be integrated. The target model is:\nboxes whose inputs are all satisfied fire concurrently; boxes that depend\non a still-running box park until that result arrives.\n\nMultiple maps can run concurrently as separate runner processes. Each map\nis a cohesive program. Maps calling into other maps is a future feature;\nfor now they are separate.\n\nFuture directions\n-----------------\n\n  — Integration with SoraMind: boxes that call inference endpoints on the\n    Alpine cluster, routing results through the map graph.\n\n  — Concurrent execution via the custom thread pool from 3d-rts,\n    replacing the synchronous v1 runner.\n\n  — Map-to-map calls: a box that invokes another map as a subroutine,\n    passing values across the boundary.\n\n  — Remote runner: a runner process on the Alpine cluster, controlled by\n    the web editor from another machine, results written to shared storage.\n\n  — Visual run trace: replay a completed run in the browser, seeing which\n    boxes fired and what values flowed through each wire.\n",

        "lines":["   — Integration with SoraMind: boxes that call inference endpoints on the","     Alpine cluster, routing results through the map graph."," ","-  — Concurrent execution via the custom thread pool from 3d-rts,","-    replacing the synchronous v1 runner.","+  — Concurrent execution via SoraMech's own thread pool (3d-rts as","+    design reference), replacing the synchronous v1 runner."," ","   — Map-to-map calls: a box that invokes another map as a subroutine,","     passing values across the boundary."],
        "oldStart":147,

    "originalFile":"SoraMech — Vision\n=================\n\nA visual editor and execution engine for finite state machines built from\ncomposable boxes. Each box is a function call. Boxes are wired together by\nexplicit data connections. The result is a program you can see, edit in a\nbrowser, and run from a terminal — without writing a line of control flow.\n\nThe primary use case is LLM orchestration: wiring inference calls on the\nSoraMind Alpine cluster into coherent multi-step reasoning pipelines.\nStrings are first-class values. Text flows between boxes like water.\nHistory is explicit — loaded from disk only when a box needs it.\n\nWhy this shape?\n---------------\n\nMost orchestration tools hide the wiring. You write code that calls other\ncode, and the shape of the program lives only in your head. SoraMech makes\nthe shape visible and editable. The map file IS the program. If you can\nread JSON, you can read the program. If you can draw boxes, you can change\nit.\n\nThe second reason is language agnosticism. A box can call a Lua function,\na C function, a bash script, or a program written in anything the user\ndefines a driver for. The engine doesn't care. It invokes a driver, gets\noutputs, threads them to the next box. The map author picks the language;\nthe engine picks up the result.\n\nComponents\n----------\n\nThree programs share one data format — the map directory:\n\n  soramech-server.lua   — thin HTTP file proxy. Receives edits from the\n                          browser, reads and writes map files on disk.\n                          Started when remote editing is desired. Ignorant\n                          of the runner.\n\n  soramech-runner.lua   — FSM execution engine. Reads a map directory,\n                          walks the graph, invokes language drivers,\n                          threads outputs through wires. Started by the\n                          user from the CLI, a cronjob, or any external\n                          trigger. Ignorant of the server. Writes output\n                          to map-defined locations (data files, /tmp/).\n\n  index.html            — browser editor. Infinite-canvas box diagram.\n                          Reads and writes map files by talking to the\n                          server (local or remote). Never knows whether\n                          the runner is active.\n\nThe map directory is the stable interface. Server and runner share nothing\nbut the files.\n\nMap file layout\n---------------\n\nEach map lives in its own directory:\n\n  maps/<map-name>/\n    boxes/\n      <id>.json         — one file per box, self-contained, lists both\n                          incoming and outgoing connections\n    data/\n      <name>.json       — persistent data files (lua tables as JSON)\n                          sections are flagged constant: true or false\n    drivers.json        — language driver definitions (how to invoke each\n                          file extension)\n    meta.json           — map name, description, entry box id\n\n  tmp/                  — symlink to /tmp/<map-name>/\n                          holds ephemeral state: run logs, scratch tables,\n                          last-run snapshot\n\nBox file format\n---------------\n\nEach box is a JSON file in boxes/. It contains:\n\n  id          unique string identifier\n  label       human-readable name shown in the UI\n  kind        \"call\" | \"branch\" | \"data\"\n  ref         for \"call\": path like \"src/strings.lua\" or \"src/trim.sh\"\n  fn          for \"call\": function name (omitted for binary/shell refs)\n  inputs      list of {name, type} — what the box expects\n  outputs     list of {name, type} — what the box returns (tuple order)\n  connections list of {from_output, to_box_id, to_input, predicate?}\n              — written to BOTH endpoint files; runner validates at load\n\nBranch boxes have named output ports instead of positional outputs. Each\nport carries an optional predicate (comparator + literal). An \"else\" port\nalways exists. For LLM-based classification, \"else\" retries upstream\n(user wires it); for numeric/string predicates, \"else\" must be explicitly\nhandled or the runner refuses to start the map.\n\nLanguage drivers\n----------------\n\ndrivers.json maps file extensions to shell commands. Example:\n\n  {\n    \".lua\":  \"drivers/lua-driver.sh\",\n    \".c\":    \"drivers/c-driver.sh\",\n    \".sh\":   \"drivers/bash-driver.sh\"\n  }\n\nEach driver script receives: file path, function name, arg count, args...\nIt returns outputs on stdout, one per line (or as JSON for structured\nvalues). Lua and C ship as pre-written driver scripts — no special cases\nin the engine. If the user wants Rust, they write a driver script.\n\nThe C driver checks whether the source has changed since the last compile\n(by comparing mtime of .c against mtime of cached binary). If changed, it\ncompiles before invoking. Cache lives in tmp/.\n\nState and output\n----------------\n\nPersistent data lives in maps/<map-name>/data/ as JSON files. Each file\nis a Lua table serialized with dkjson. A file-level or section-level\n\"constant\" flag marks read-only data.\n\nEphemeral state (run logs, scratch variables, last-run snapshot) lives in\ntmp/ which is a symlink to /tmp/<map-name>/. It is fast, in RAM, and\nintentionally discarded on reboot.\n\nExecution model (v1)\n--------------------\n\nThe runner is synchronous in v1. Each box invocation is wrapped in a\ntask_fn(inputs) -> outputs boundary — matching the action signature of\nSoraMech's own thread pool (whose design references the 3d-rts pool) —\nso the transition to concurrent execution is a runtime swap, not a\nrewrite.\n\nThe phase 3 thread pool is SoraMech-built; 3d-rts serves as the design\nreference. The target model is: boxes whose inputs are all satisfied\nfire concurrently; iterators parallelize across workers via atomic\ncounter snapshots and counter-tagged pushes.\n\nMultiple maps can run concurrently as separate runner processes. Each map\nis a cohesive program. Maps calling into other maps is a future feature;\nfor now they are separate.\n\nFuture directions\n-----------------\n\n  — Integration with SoraMind: boxes that call inference endpoints on the\n    Alpine cluster, routing results through the map graph.\n\n  — Concurrent execution via the custom thread pool from 3d-rts,\n    replacing the synchronous v1 runner.\n\n  — Map-to-map calls: a box that invokes another map as a subroutine,\n    passing values across the boundary.\n\n  — Remote runner: a runner process on the Alpine cluster, controlled by\n    the web editor from another machine, results written to shared storage.\n\n  — Visual run trace: replay a completed run in the browser, seeing which\n    boxes fired and what values flowed through each wire.\n",
    "oldString":"  — Concurrent execution via the custom thread pool from 3d-rts,\n    replacing the synchronous v1 runner.",

        "oldStart":196,

      }],
    "originalFile":"# 301 — Thread pool lifecycle and per-worker initialization\n\n## Status\nopen\n\n## Current behavior\nThe executor (`src/004-executor.lua`) runs boxes synchronously in a\nsingle Lua coroutine. There is no thread pool, no pthreads, and no\nper-thread language runtime state.\n\n## Phase model\n\nPhase 2 is the synchronous interpreter path. It is the development\ntarget while editor work is in progress.\n\nPhase 3 is the thread pool path. It is the only execution path going\nforward. The synchronous interpreter does not stay around as an\nalternative entry point — once phase 3 lands, the pool runner\nreplaces it. There is no \"fallback to synchronous\" mode.\n\n### Phase 2 → 3 refactor surface\n\nThe following components are replaced (not extended) in phase 3:\n\n| Phase 2 file                  | Phase 3 replacement                  |\n|-------------------------------|--------------------------------------|\n| `src/003-loader.lua`          | C loader inside `src/008-pool-runner.c` |\n| `src/004-executor.lua`        | C task dispatch layer (issue 304)    |\n| `src/007-runner-main.lua`     | `src/008-pool-runner.c`              |\n| `drivers/*.sh`                | Language runtime spec (issue 303)    |\n\nAll threading-pool-adjacent functionality is C code that lives next to\nthe pool. There is no embedded Lua runtime for graph loading or\ndispatch — Lua appears only as a language runtime that boxes can use,\non equal footing with C, Bash, and any future language.\n\n## Intended behavior\n\n### Pool source\nThe thread pool is **SoraMech-owned**, written from scratch under\n`libs/task-pool/`. The 3d-rts pool at\n`/home/ritz/programming/ai-stuff/games/3d-rts/libs/900-task-pool.h`\nis the **design reference**, not a dependency. We need full control\nover the spawn primitive, the worker context, the init barrier\n(below), and iterator-pinning extensions — all reasons not to inherit\nan external implementation.\n\nThe pool exposes (at minimum):\n\n```c\npool_t *pool_create(int n_workers);\nvoid    pool_destroy(pool_t *p);\nvoid    pool_spawn(pool_t *p, action_fn_t fn, void *arg);\nvoid    pool_wait_quiescent(pool_t *p);   // blocks until active count hits zero\nvoid    pool_init_barrier(pool_t *p);     // see \"Init barrier\" below\n```\n\n3d-rts's frame-ring + park-on-slot machinery is referenced for\npatterns; we don't reimplement features we don't need.\n\n### Where the pool lives in the process\nThe pool is owned by the map runner's C entry point. One pool per map\nrun. It is created after the graph is loaded and validated, and\ndestroyed after the run completes.\n\nThe C entry point (`src/008-pool-runner.c`):\n\n```c\nint main(int argc, char **argv) {\n    // 1. parse map path from argv\n    // 2. load and validate graph (C loader, no Lua involved)\n    // 3. determine which language runtimes the map uses\n    // 4. allocate per-input-port slots for every box (issue 302)\n    // 5. pool = pool_create(n_workers)\n    // 6. init per-worker language runtime handles for each language present\n    // 7. pool_init_barrier(pool)  ← block until every worker is fully initialized\n    // 8. push every input port's literal value into its slot\n    // 9. spawn tasks for boxes whose input set is now satisfied\n    // 10. pool_wait_quiescent(pool)\n    // 11. write last-run.jsonl\n    // 12. pool_destroy(pool)\n}\n```\n\n### Init barrier\n\nWorkers are not safe to dispatch tasks to until **every worker has\nfully completed init for every language spec the map uses**. If the\nmain thread spawns a task before a worker's `lua_State` is up, the\ntask lands on a null handle.\n\n`pool_init_barrier` is the join point:\n\n1. Each worker's startup runs all `lang->init(worker_idx)` calls in\n   a defined order, populating its `worker_ctx_t.handles[]`.\n2. After completing its inits, each worker increments a shared\n   atomic `workers_ready` counter and blocks on a condition\n   variable.\n3. The main thread waits until `workers_ready == n_workers`.\n4. Main thread broadcasts the condition variable; all workers\n   release simultaneously and begin pulling tasks.\n\nThis is a one-shot barrier — it runs once at pool startup. After\nquiescence it doesn't re-engage; teardown takes a different path.\n\nThe barrier also protects against partial init failures: if any\nworker's `init` returns an error, the barrier never completes and\nthe main thread can detect it via a timeout or per-worker status\nflag.\n\n### Graph loading: ported to C\nThe graph loader is ported from `src/003-loader.lua` to C and lives\ninside (or alongside) `008-pool-runner.c`. The pool runner has no\nembedded Lua state for loader purposes. JSON parsing uses a small\nvendored C JSON library (cJSON or similar; decision deferred to\nimplementation).\n\nLua appears in the runner only when a box's language is Lua — and even\nthen, only inside that worker's language runtime handle. The pool\nrunner itself does not link to liblua at the top level.\n\n### Per-worker language runtimes\nNo language is treated as the \"native\" or preferred language at the\nthread level. Every box — regardless of language — goes through the\nsame task dispatch path. The per-box cost is determined by that box's\ninvocation wrapper, not by any map-level language setting.\n\nEach worker thread holds a set of language runtime handles, one per\nlanguage it may be asked to run. These are initialized once at pool\nstartup, before any tasks are submitted, and torn down at shutdown:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    void   *handles[N_LANGS];   // opaque per-language runtime state\n    int     thread_idx;\n} worker_ctx_t;\n```\n\nOnly the language handles actually needed by the map are initialized.\nIf the map contains no Bash boxes, no Bash handle is started for any\nworker. The graph loader determines which languages are present and\npasses that set to the pool runner at startup.\n\nThe per-language initialization protocol is defined by the language\nruntime spec (issue 303). The pool runner calls each spec's `init`\nfunction at startup and its `teardown` function at shutdown.\n\n### Worker context access\nWorker context is stored in thread-local storage (`__thread\nworker_ctx_t *current_worker`), set by each worker immediately after\nthe thread is started. This avoids per-task `pthread_self()` lookups.\n\n### Pool size\nNumber of worker threads defaults to the number of logical CPUs\n(`sysconf(_SC_NPROCESSORS_ONLN)`), capped at a compile-time maximum\n(`MAX_WORKERS`, initially 16). Can be overridden by an environment\nvariable `SORAMECH_WORKERS=N`.\n\n### Slots are owned by input ports (issue 302)\nEach box has one ring-buffer slot per input port, allocated at\ngraph load time and durable for the run. The pool runner walks\nevery box during the load step and populates a per-box slot table.\nSlots are not allocated per-task; tasks pop and push but never\nallocate. See issue 302 for the slot lifecycle and lifetime model.\n\n### Quiescence\nThe runner tracks an active-task counter, incremented on `pool_spawn`\nand decremented when a task reaches `ACT_DONE`. The main thread waits\non a condition variable that signals when the counter reaches zero.\n\nThis naturally handles iterators that re-queue themselves: each\nre-queue increments the counter, each completion decrements. When the\ncounter reaches zero, the run is over.\n\nDeadlock is not a concern at runtime. The graph validator (running at\nload) rejects non-iterator cycles and inputs without producers. Errors\ninside a task crash the program (issue 303), so there is no\nhalf-completed-producer case to worry about. An iterator parking\nbecause its upstream queue is empty is not deadlock — it is the\nnatural end-of-stream condition; once the active-task counter reaches\nzero with the iterator parked, the run ends cleanly.\n\n## Open questions\n- Vendored JSON library: cJSON, jsmn, or hand-rolled. cJSON is heavier\n  but easiest. Decision deferred.\n\n## Suggested implementation sequence\n1. Vendor `900-task-pool.h` + `.c` into `libs/task-pool/`.\n2. Vendor a JSON parser into `libs/json/`.\n3. Port `003-loader.lua` to C inside `src/008-pool-runner.c`.\n4. Write the pool lifecycle skeleton: pool_create, worker context TLS,\n   active-task counter, quiescence wait.\n5. Add `Makefile` target `soramech-pool` that compiles the C runner and\n   links against the vendored pool and JSON parser.\n6. Smoke test: single-box Lua map, pool with 2 workers, box runs, result\n   written.         "text":"All updates landed. Summary of what changed:\n\n**Memory files**: `project_threading.md` rewritten to reflect the per-port slot model, owned pool, init barrier, and parallel iterator semantics. `project_related.md` reframed 3d-rts as design reference.\n\n**Issue 301**: `pool_create` / `pool_destroy` / `pool_spawn` / `pool_wait_quiescent` / `pool_init_barrier` listed as the SoraMech-built API. Init-barrier section spells out the join: every worker runs all spec inits, increments a shared atomic, blocks on a CV; main thread waits until all workers signal ready, then broadcasts. Slot ownership pointer corrected to per-input-port.\n\n**Issue 302**: 1-cell peek + N-cell pop distinction restored. Compile-time wire classification (runs-once → 1-cell peek, runs-N-times → N-cell pop) drives slot allocation. Cell tagging support added — cells carry a 4-byte ordering tag, tagged slots `slot_pop` returns the lowest-tag cell. Slot lifetime simplified: durable for the run, no refcounting, no producer-set, no wait list. The `slot_alloc` API gains a `flags` argument (e.g., `SLOT_TAGGED`); `slot_push` gains a tag parameter (zero for untagged).\n\n**Issue 304**: Iterator counter is per-box state, atomically `fetch_add`'d at task spawn. Each spawn snapshots its counter into the task; iterator tasks can run in parallel on different workers. Phase-5 pushes from iterators carry the counter as a tag, so consumer slots downstream (allocated `SLOT_TAGGED`) preserve invocation order regardless of push race. End-of-stream propagation phase removed; phase 6 disappears entirely. Cross-iterator pairing section rewritten — pairing is now deterministic by tag, no FIFO race.\n\n**Issue 309 + 310**: pool framing updated. Vendored references replaced with \"SoraMech-built; 3d-rts as reference.\"\n\n**Vision and architecture docs**: same reframing.\n\n---\n\nA few things I didn't change because they need your call:\n\n1. **Counter via hidden slot vs per-box state** — went with per-box atomic snapshot (your recommendation), noted the functional alternative as a possible future revisit but didn't ship it. If you want me to also document the alt path inline in 304 as a \"considered and deferred\" entry, say.\n\n2. **Cross-language large values** — left as documented in 302 (large-value heap, copy at the language boundary). The deeper \"zero-copy across languages\" optimization isn't tractable without language-runtime cooperation that doesn't exist; the same-language fast path (issue 312) is the real lever.\n\n3. **Per-invocation tag propagation through fan-out chains** — phase-5 pushes carry the upstream task's counter. If a non-iterator A is downstream of iterator B, A's pushes inherit B's counter (so two-hop chains preserve ordering). I implied this in 304 but didn't spell out the propagation rule explicitly. Worth nailing down before implementation; let me know if you want a more rigorous pass on that.\n\nWant to walk through the design once more with these revisions in place? Or pick a different thread to pull on?"
      }]

    "content":"  2. 1-cell vs N-cell\n\n  n_cells is the number of cells in the ring buffer — i.e., how many distinct values the slot can hold simultaneously. cell_capacity is the\n  size in bytes of a single cell. A 1-cell slot holds one value (single-value); an N-cell slot is a queue with N positions.\n\n  The read mode (peek vs pop) was historically tied to capacity in the design — 1-cell peek, N-cell pop. They're orthogonal in principle, but\n   coupling them simplifies the API: if you need to keep a value around, allocate 1-cell + peek; if you need a queue, allocate N-cell + pop.\n\n\nI understand now. Thanks.\n\n  3. Counter approach + functional alternative\n\nwhat if, every time an iterative function is called, it pushes it's counter + 1 to the input slot of the iterative box? It's okay if it doesn't exactly resolve to FIFO - we make no guarantees that inputs will route to output ports in a deterministic way. Is there a reason we couldn't merge the iterator and comparator functionality, or at least duplicate it mostly for the iterator functionality? How would that architecture look?",

    "content":[{
        "type":"text",
        "text":"Let me work through both threads.\n\n## Self-push counter\n\nThe design works:\n\n```\nIterator box (call type)\n  Inputs:\n    value    (from upstream, N-cell pop slot)\n    counter  (self-loop, N-cell pop slot, primed with 0 at startup)\n  Outputs (N branches)\n    output_0, output_1, ... output_{N-1}\n    next_counter (self-loop wire back to counter input)\n\nPer invocation:\n  pop value, pop counter\n  route value to outputs[counter % N]\n  push (counter + 1) to next_counter\n```\n\nCounter is data, not box state. Conceptually clean — the iterator becomes a regular call box that happens to self-loop one of its outputs.\n\n**The catch you already identified**: tasks serialize through the counter dependency. Task K can't spawn until task K-1 has pushed counter=K. Even though we accept non-deterministic routing, the dispatch chain is still single-file because no task has its counter input ready until the previous one finishes. So we lose the parallelism the atomic-fetch-add design buys.\n\nYou said \"we make no guarantees that inputs will route to output ports in a deterministic way\" — that's about *which* branch a value goes to, not about whether tasks run in parallel. Even with ordering-relaxed semantics, the counter input being a single-stream queue forces serial execution.\n\nTo get parallelism with the self-push design, the counter input would need to be **pre-populated** with multiple values upfront (so task 0, 1, 2 can all spawn immediately). That requires knowing N at compile time, which we don't.\n\nSo: self-push is the cleaner design conceptually, atomic-fetch-add is the better design for performance. Given high-performance is a stated goal, I'd stick with atomic-fetch-add. Functional purity isn't worth losing core-scaling.\n\n## Merging iterator and comparator\n\nThere are three levels at which they could merge. Worth picking explicitly.\n\n### Level A — Mental-model unification only\n\nBoth are \"branching boxes\" in the editor and docs. Same conceptual category: \"this box has multiple output branches, only one fires per invocation, the box's settings decide which.\" Comparator and iterator are two presets under that umbrella. Editor UI groups them. Runtime keeps them as separate dispatch-action paths.\n\nCost: zero code change.\nWin: clearer narrative for users learning the editor.\n\n### Level B — Unified router schema, separate dispatch paths\n\nA box has a `routing` field:\n\n```json\n{ \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"comparator\", \"comparand\": 4 } }\n{ \"routing\": { \"kind\": \"iterator\",   \"outputs\": [\"a\",\"b\",\"c\"] } }\n```\n\nBoth kinds carry their own params; the dispatch layer reads `routing.kind` and branches into the appropriate code path. The schema is unified; the runtime isn't really.\n\nCost: small refactor (current `comparand` and `iterator_outputs` move under `routing`). Editor UI consolidates.\nWin: one place to add routing kinds (e.g., user-defined router via spec callback), one place for compile validation.\n\n### Level C — One unified dispatch path\n\nA \"router\" abstraction at the dispatch layer:\n\n```\nDispatch action for a router box:\n  1. (optional) Invoke spec on inputs → returns value (and possibly a branch hint)\n  2. Compute branch via routing_rule:\n       - \"comparand\"        → compare(value, params.comparand) → lt/eq/gt\n       - \"counter\"          → params.counter++ % N → output_K\n       - \"function_return\"  → spec returned (value, branch); use branch\n       - \"fan_all\"          → no branch, fire all (= plain call)\n  3. Push value (or popped input, for counter-mode without spec) to selected branch(es)\n```\n\nBox modes become routing-rule values:\n- Plain call → `\"fan_all\"`\n- Comparator → spec runs + `\"comparand\"` rule\n- Iterator → no spec + `\"counter\"` rule\n- (New) Function-decided routing → spec runs + `\"function_return\"` rule\n\nCost: real refactor. Dispatch-action code consolidated. Spec interface grows a way for `invoke` to return a branch tag (already on the table for \"function-defined routing\" anyway).\nWin: future routing kinds slot in cleanly. Iterator-with-function (your \"functions iterating their own outputs\") becomes natural — just a router with both spec and counter rule, or with `function_return` rule.\n\n### Recommendation\n\nI'd ship **Level B now**, queue **Level C** for after phase 3 ships. Level B is a small refactor, makes the schema coherent, and sets up Level C cleanly. Level C is the right end-state but requires settling the spec-returns-branch contract, which is a bigger commit.\n\nLevel A happens for free as part of B (the doc reframes naturally).\n\nWant me to:\n1. Open an issue for Level B (the schema unification)?\n2. Add Level C as a planned-but-deferred follow-on?\n\nOr pick a different path through this?"
      }]
  },

## [3917]

```json
{
  "timestamp":"2026-05-10T03:01:43.235Z",
  "message":{
    "content":"  The catch you already identified: tasks serialize through the counter dependency. Task K can't spawn until task K-1 has pushed counter=K.\n  Even though we accept non-deterministic routing, the dispatch chain is still single-file because no task has its counter input ready until\n  the previous one finishes. So we lose the parallelism the atomic-fetch-add design buys.\n\n\nwhat if we added a special type of peek/pop that increments the value when it's read, atomically? looping back to 0 of course if we need to. that way, if we're ever spawning a task based on an iterative box, it'll always have a new counter value available for the other threads who are spawning additional instances of that iterative task.\n\nSo, my issue with level C is that it puts details about the box into the spec code. I'd prefer if the spec treated them as abstract functions and datastructures, and the only part that knows about boxes is the editor and map file. Hmmmm, okay the C thread pool needs to know too, because that's where we store input slots and (maybe?) the counter variable.\n\nI feel like level B is the most solid approach. Level A lacks meaningful functionality change.",
    "role":"user"
  },

No push is ever","+performed; reads do the work. From the dispatch action's","+perspective it's just another slot; from the slot store's","+perspective the read op is special-cased.","+"," ### Cell tagging (for parallel-iterator ordering)"," "," A cell can optionally carry a 4-byte ordering tag alongside its"],

    "replaceAll":false,
    "oldString":"### Cell tagging (for parallel-iterator ordering)",
    "newString":"### Atomic-counter slot mode\n\nA slot allocated with `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER` carries a single\n4-byte unsigned integer cell, read via a special op:\n\n```c\nuint32_t slot_read_inc(slot_store_t *s, slot_id_t id, uint32_t mod);\n// Returns the current value mod `mod`, then atomically increments\n// the underlying counter. Concurrent readers each get a distinct\n// value. Counter wraps at 2^32; mod handles N-branch routing.\n```\n\nUsed for iterator counters (issue 304): the iterator box has an\nauto-allocated `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER` slot at load time; the\ndispatch action calls `slot_read_inc(counter_slot, n_branches)`\nto pick its output branch. Multiple iterator tasks can read\nconcurrently from the same counter slot in parallel — each gets a\nunique routing index — without any per-box mutable state and\nwithout the serial dependency of a self-push counter.\n\nThe slot's \"cell\" is just an `atomic_uint32_t`. No push is ever\nperformed; reads do the work. From the dispatch action's\nperspective it's just another slot; from the slot store's\nperspective the read op is special-cased.\n\n### Cell tagging (for parallel-iterator ordering)",
    "userModified":false

Let me describe what it solves, then ship the changes.\n\n## Atomic-counter slot — yes, this works\n\nA new slot mode that's just \"an atomic int with a special read op\":\n\n```c\n// Allocated with SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER flag\nslot_alloc(store, /*cell_capacity*/ 4, /*n_cells*/ 1, SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER);\n\n// Read-and-increment, atomic\nint slot_read_inc(store, slot_id, int mod);\n// equivalent to:\n//   uint32_t v = atomic_fetch_add(&slot->cell[0].data, 1);\n//   return v % mod;\n```\n\nFrom the outside: a regular slot. Consumers see a slot value that moves; they don't see the box state. Concurrent readers each get a unique value because of the atomic fetch-add. No push needed; the read is the increment.\n\nThe iterator box's dispatch action becomes:\n```\n1. Pop value from value-input slot.\n2. branch_idx = slot_read_inc(counter_slot, n_outputs);\n3. Push value to outputs[branch_idx], with tag=branch_idx\n4. Done.\n```\n\nCounter lives in a slot, not in `box_runtime_state`. Iterators don't have any per-box mutable state — they're just a routing rule plus a designated atomic-counter slot. Parallel iterator tasks all read from the same atomic slot independently; each gets a unique value. Counter overflow wraps mod N gracefully.\n\nThe slot store knows about this read mode (it owns the atomic primitive); the dispatch layer just calls `slot_read_inc`. The spec never sees any of it.\n\nThis unifies nicely: atomic-counter slots are a building block that any feature needing \"thread-safe sequence\" can use, not just iterators.\n\n## Now updating the issues"
      }]
  },

          "new_string":"## Task struct\n\nA task is one ephemeral invocation of a box. Its struct carries\njust the box ID:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    int  box_id;          // index into the graph's box array\n} dispatch_task_t;\n```\n\nThere is no per-task counter. Iterator counter state lives in a\n`SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER` slot owned by the box (see issue 302); the\naction reads and atomically increments it via `slot_read_inc`\nwhen it needs the routing index.\n\nThere is no `input_slots` or `output_slot` array on the task —\nthe box's input slots are durable per-box state (see issue 302).\nThe action looks them up through `box_runtime_state[box_id]`.\n\nOutput is a routing event, not a stored value. When the action\nfinishes, it pushes copies of the return value into the input\nslots of every downstream box wired to this output (or only the\nmatching branch for comparators and iterators).\n\nTasks are spawned by the dispatch layer's \"spawn on input ready\"\nrule (issue 302). Each spawn allocates a fresh `dispatch_task_t`\non the pool's task allocator, pre-populated with the box ID. The\naction's first read of the input slots is what drains them — pop\nor peek one cell per input port, per the port's mode.",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md",
          "replace_all":false,
          "old_string":"## Task struct\n\nA task is one ephemeral invocation of a box. Its struct carries\njust enough to point the action at the box and the snapshot of its\ncounter at spawn time:\n\n```c\ntypedef struct {\n    int  box_id;          // index into the graph's box array\n    int  counter;         // iterator only; snapshot at spawn time\n} dispatch_task_t;\n```\n\nThere is no `input_slots` array on the task — the box's input\nslots are durable per-box state (see issue 302). The action looks\nup the input and output slots through `box_runtime_state[box_id]`.\n\nThere is no `output_slot` either — output is a routing event, not\na stored value. When the action finishes, it pushes copies of the\nreturn value into the input slots of every downstream box wired\nto this output (and only the matching branch for comparators and\niterators).\n\nTasks are spawned by the dispatch layer's \"spawn on input ready\"\nrule (issue 302). Each spawn allocates a fresh `dispatch_task_t`\non the pool's task allocator, pre-populated with the box ID and\ncounter value. The action's first read of the input slots is what\ndrains them — pop one cell per input port."

          "new_string":"## Iterator counter and parallel iteration\n\nThe iterator's counter lives in a `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER` slot\nallocated for the box at graph load time (issue 302). The\ndispatch action reads and increments it atomically, mid-action:\n\n```c\nuint32_t branch_idx = slot_read_inc(box->counter_slot, n_iter_outputs);\nslot_push(downstream[branch_idx].input_slot, output_buf, output_size,\n          /* tag = */ branch_idx);\n```\n\n`slot_read_inc` returns the current counter value `mod\nn_iter_outputs` and atomically advances the underlying counter.\nConcurrent iterator tasks on different workers each call\n`slot_read_inc` independently and each get a unique value —\n**iterator tasks parallelize across workers**, picking distinct\nbranches without coordination.\n\nNo box-side mutable state, no per-task counter snapshot. The\ncounter is just data in a slot the dispatch layer reads.\n\n## Cross-iterator pairing under parallel iteration\n\nWith parallel iterator tasks, push ordering at the consumer is\nnon-deterministic — task 6 of iterator A may push to consumer C\nbefore task 5 if 6 happened to land on a faster worker. FIFO pop\nat C would consume them out of iteration order.\n\nThe fix is **counter-tagged pushes**. Each iterator push (in phase\n5) carries the counter value the action read for this invocation:\n\n```c\nslot_push(downstream.input_slot, output_buf, output_size,\n          /* tag = */ branch_idx_or_counter_snapshot);\n```",
          "file_path":"/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech/issues/304-task-dispatch-layer.md",
          "replace_all":false,
          "old_string":"## Iterator counter and parallel iteration\n\nThe iterator's per-box counter is read and incremented **at task\nspawn time**, atomically:\n\n```c\nint counter_for_this_task = atomic_fetch_add(&box->counter, 1) % n_iter_outputs;\nspawn(task{ box_id, counter_for_this_task });\n```\n\nThe counter is snapshotted into the task struct. The atomic\nfetch-add means concurrent spawns get distinct counter values, so\n**iterator tasks can run in parallel** on different workers — each\nhas its own counter, picks its own output branch independently.\nSibling iterator tasks don't share runtime state.\n\nThe serial dependency is reduced to one atomic op per spawn (cheap)\nrather than a serialized task chain.\n\n## Cross-iterator pairing under parallel iteration\n\nWith parallel iterator tasks, push ordering at the consumer is\nnon-deterministic — task 6 of iterator A may push to consumer C\nbefore task 5 if 6 happened to land on a faster worker. FIFO pop\nat C would consume them out of iteration order.\n\nThe fix is **counter-tagged pushes**. Each iterator push (in phase\n5) carries the counter value snapshotted at spawn:\n\n```c\nslot_push(downstream.input_slot, output_buf, output_size,\n          /* tag = */ task->counter);\n```"
        },
        "id":"toolu_01VpJq2BBvRiA3bFSB7p6BmG"

{
  "timestamp":"2026-05-10T03:05:07.149Z",
  "message":{
